blocks: At that time Samuel the prophet died too, a righteous and good man, who ruled Israel after Eli for twelve years alone and for eighteen years after Saul became king. David went off to the desert of Maon. He sent men to Nabal of Carmel, a rich man who was shearing his flocks, to greet him and ask him to give to those with him and to himself whatever he chose, since they had kept his flocks and shepherds unharmed. Nabal, who was harsh and reckless, answered David's men churlishly and shamelessly, saying: "Who is David? And who is the son of Jesse?" and calling him a runaway. David was furious at this, swore to destroy all that Nabal had, and set out against him with four hundred armed men. Nabal's wife, who was sensible and beautiful, learned how David had greeted her husband, how he had kept their property unharmed, and what insults Nabal had answered David; without saying anything to her own husband she loaded the asses with many gifts of every kind and went to David. Meeting him, she bowed down and begged him not to bear a grudge against her husband, for his mind was like his name (for Nabal means folly), but to let his anger go and accept what was brought. David praised the woman, pardoned them and went back. When the woman returned to Nabal, she told him of David's approach; and he, seized with fear and grief, lived no more than ten days and his life broke off. Learning this, David sent to Abigail to woo her for himself. She said she was not worthy to live with such a man, but went all the same; and David took her as his wife.

Saul was still plotting against him, and with three thousand picked men he camped by the hill of Hachilah, where David was staying with the six hundred men he had with him. At night David himself and Abishai went to Saul's camp and entered where Saul was sleeping. When Abishai set out to kill him, David did not let him; but taking the king's spear and his jar of water, they went out without anyone noticing, though Abner, the commander of his force, and many others lay round the king. Going up to the top of the mountain, David shouted to Abner: "Why do you not guard the king? See, some men went in to kill him, and you did not know. Look for the spear and the jar of water, and you will know what danger has passed you by." Saul recognized David's voice, and how he had spared him again when he could have killed him; he said that he had sinned and acted foolishly, and begged him to take heart and return to his home. David said: "May the Lord reward each according to his righteousness and his faithfulness."

David went off with the six hundred with him to Achish, the king of Gath, and stayed there four months. When the Philistines wished to march against Israel, Achish said to David: "Will you go out to the war with me, you and those with you?" And he readily promised to fight on his side. When the foreigners had already advanced into the country of the Israelites, Saul was alarmed and asked God whether he should fight. When He did not answer, he sought a woman who had a familiar spirit and went to her in disguise, so that he might not be recognized, and asked for the soul of Samuel to be brought up for him. When it seemed to have been brought up by certain spells, Saul said: "I am in great distress, for the foreigners have gathered against me and the Lord has left me." The apparition of Samuel answered: "The Lord has done to you what He foretold through me; He is taking the kingdom from you and giving it to David, and He is subjecting the people to the enemy; and you and your sons will fall tomorrow." Saul was greatly grieved at hearing this and went away.

The foreigners camped, and David and the six hundred with him at the rear. But it did not please the satraps that David should march with them, and they said: "He may do us some harm by going over to his own countrymen in the battle," and they asked that he be sent back. Achish, yielding to the satraps, told David to go away. He went off with those with him and found Ziklag, which Achish had given him to live in, burned, and both his wives and all who were there taken captive by the Amalekites. David and those with him lamented over this, and he asked God through the high priest Abiathar whether he should pursue them. God allowed it, and he pursued with four hundred, leaving two hundred to guard the baggage. Finding them scattered, eating and drinking, he fell on them suddenly and killed them all except four hundred who fled on swift camels, and recovered all the booty. When they returned, the four hundred who had been with David did not want the two hundred to share with them, but thought they should be content with having their wives saved. David judged this opinion unjust and declared that the spoil must be shared equally among all. This became a law from then on, ordering those who guard the baggage to share the spoils equally with those who fight.

When battle broke out between the Israelites and the Philistines, very many of the Hebrews were killed, and the three sons of Saul fell, and Saul himself was wounded below the ribs. Knowing that he had been struck mortally and would not live, he told his armour-bearer to run him through, so that he might not be taken alive by the enemy. When the man would not do as he was told, he fell on his own sword and died. His armour-bearer, seeing the king fallen, killed himself too. The next day the foreigners, stripping the fallen Israelites, came on the bodies of Saul and his sons on the mountains of Gilboa; they cut off their heads and sent them to their own country, making a show of them everywhere and spreading the good news, dedicated their armour to their own gods, and hung the bodies on the wall of Bethshan, which was afterwards called Scythopolis. When the inhabitants of the city of Jabesh in Gilead learned what had befallen Saul, the strongest of them went out, and pressing on through the whole night they took down the bodies of Saul and Jonathan, brought them to Jabesh, burned them, gathered the bones and buried them. Saul reigned eighteen years while Samuel was still alive, and twenty-two after his death.

blocks: David had just returned from the slaughter of the foreigners when a man came to him reporting the defeat of the Israelites and the death of Saul and Jonathan. Questioned whether his report was true, he said that Saul had been mortally wounded, and, being unable through weakness to kill himself, had begged him, so that he might not be taken alive by the enemy, to drive home the wound as he fell on his own sword; and that he had done as he was ordered and finished the king off. As proof of his words he held out the royal crown from Saul's head and the gold from his arms, and gave them to David. David and those with him lamented Saul and Jonathan, and he punished the man who had killed Saul, because he had laid his hand on the Lord's anointed. After this, at God's command, he went up to Hebron, a city of Judah, with both his wives, Ahinoam and Abigail, and the men with him with all their households; and there he was chosen king by the tribe of Judah. David blessed the men of Jabesh for having buried the bodies of Saul and Jonathan.

Abner, Saul's commander-in-chief, took the surviving son of his lord, Ishbosheth, and proclaimed him king over all Israel except Judah. Ishbosheth was forty years old when he became king, and he held the kingdom for two years. Abner was angry with the tribe of Judah for having made David king, and set out against it. Joab, David's commander-in-chief, met him with a force. First twelve from each army fought in single combat; when all of them had fallen, both armies attacked each other, and Abner's men were defeated. Abishai and Asahel were Joab's brothers. Asahel, proud of his swiftness of foot, pursued Abner from behind. Abner urged him to turn back, and when he could not persuade him, he struck him behind with a mortal blow and killed him. The dead man's brothers, angry at their brother's death, chased Abner. He stood on the top of one of the hills and called out to Joab: "Do not stir up men of the same nation to battle. Asahel too did wrong by not heeding my advice to turn back, and so he was wounded and died." Joab, taking these words as an appeal, ordered the trumpet to sound the recall and stopped the pursuit. From that time civil war began among the Hebrews and lasted very long, David's side growing stronger and Saul's growing weak.

Six sons were born to David by different wives while he was at Hebron, of whom the first-born was Amnon. When Abner lay with a concubine of Saul, Ishbosheth was angry with him because of his father's concubine. This was the reason for Abner's going over to David. David sent to Ishbosheth asking for his own wife Michal. He took her away from the husband to whom Saul had given her after David's flight, and sent her to David. Abner spoke with the elders of the Israelite multitude and the captains, and persuaded them to change over to David, all of them being eager for it. Having done this he came to David to receive sworn pledges. Welcomed gladly, he went off to gather the multitude, so that David might be proclaimed by all. Joab came to Hebron, learned what had happened about Abner, and, afraid that Abner would rise above him, said much against the man to David; failing to persuade him, he secretly sent someone to call Abner back as if from David, and Abner turned back. Joab met him, and leading him away from his men as if to tell him something secret, killed him, striking him with a sword under the flank. When David learned this he was deeply grieved, cursed the man who had killed him, lamented the dead man and buried him with honour.

A little later Ishbosheth was the victim of a plot and was murdered as he slept. His killers, who were two, took his head and brought it to David. He not only did not think the men had done him a favour, but ordered them to be put to death, exacting justice for the murder. Then all Israel went to David and anointed him king of all the tribes. David was thirty years old when he became king over Judah; he ruled at Hebron over the tribe of Judah alone for seven years, and over all Israel for thirty-three.
text: David had just returned from the slaughter of the foreigners when a man came to him reporting the defeat of the Israelites and the death of Saul and Jonathan. Questioned whether his report was true, he said that Saul had been mortally wounded, and, being unable through weakness to kill himself, had begged him, so that he might not be taken alive by the enemy, to drive home the wound as he fell on his own sword; and that he had done as he was ordered and finished the king off. blocks: He left Hebron, he and those with him, and came to Jerusalem. At that time the Jebusites lived in the city and that land, which is why the city was called Jebus; they were akin by race to the Canaanites. In mockery they set the blind, the lame and the otherwise maimed on the battlements, and said that they would not let David enter the city. Angered by this, David took the city by siege, drove the Jebusites out, rebuilt it and named it after himself the City of David; in Abraham's time it was called Solyma. He lived in it, having built a palace. More children were born to him by several wives and concubines.

The foreigners marched against David, and he, with God's consent, went out against them with his army and won. They gathered again in much greater numbers and came on. When David asked God again, God ordered him to camp with the army in the groves of the Weeping, and not to attack the enemy until the groves began to shake. Doing this, he routed the enemy, and pursuing them as far as their borders he killed them.

After this David called the priests and Levites and all the people together to Kiriath-jearim. The priests put the ark of the Lord on a new cart to bring it down to Jerusalem, and the people and the king sang as they went before it. When the ark was in danger of being overturned, Uzzah the son of Abinadab stretched out his hand, held it and steadied it so that it should not fall. He died at once, God being angry because he had touched the ark, since he was not a priest; and from this that place was called the Breach. David was afraid to bring the ark into the city, and placed it in the house of Obed-edom, a Levite; it stayed there three months, and the house of that man enjoyed many blessings. Hearing this, David brought the ark from there to his own city, with seven choirs going before it; and he himself struck the lyre and danced in play. His wife Michal, seeing him dancing and leaping, reproached him for behaving unseemly; but he said that he was not ashamed, since these things were not unseemly when done for God. They brought in the ark and placed it in the tabernacle which David had pitched for it.

Then he wished to build a house for the ark. God commanded the prophet Nathan to tell David: "You shall not build me a house, but your son, who will succeed to your kingdom when you die." When the prophet told this to David, he turned to thanksgiving. After this he struck the foreigners and routed them and their allies, made Syria tributary and set a garrison in Damascus. On his way back he struck Idumaea, and all the Idumaeans became David's slaves.

Remembering his agreement with Jonathan the son of Saul, David inquired whether anyone of the family of Saul was left; and learning that a son of Jonathan survived, lame in his feet, called Mephibosheth, he sent for him, gave the man all his grandfather's property, ordered him to share his table always, and assigned him his father's servants as well; one of them, called Ziba, he entrusted with managing what had been given to his master and bringing him its revenue. Mephibosheth lived in Jerusalem and ate at the king's table.

blocks: About that time the king of the Ammonites, who was a friend of David, died, leaving a son, Hanun, who succeeded to his father's rule. David sent men to Hanun to console him in his grief for his father and to tell him that David would keep the friendship with him too. But Hanun, supposing that those sent were spies, shaved off half their beards, cut off half their cloaks and sent the men away. When David saw them in this state, he gave the flower of the army to Joab his commander-in-chief and sent him against the Ammonites. Joab engaged them and defeated them and their Syrian allies, and they turned to flight. They took on allies again and came to battle. David engaged them with his whole army and killed many, and Shobach, the commander of the enemy's force, was mortally wounded in the battle and died of the wound. The allies of the Ammonites, who were Syrians from Mesopotamia, surrendered to David. Again he sent Joab against the Ammonites; he shut them up in the chief city of their country and besieged it.

David, staying in Jerusalem, saw from the palace a woman bathing in her house, called Bathsheba, and fell in love with her. He sent for the woman and lay with her. She conceived and told the king. He called her husband, named Uriah, from the siege, asked him about the army, gave him food from his own table and bade him go to his house. But he did not go, saying it was not right for his general and his fellow soldiers to suffer hardship in the camp while he lay with his wife. When the king again urged him to go home, and plied him with toasts until he was almost drunk, he slept in front of the doors of the palace. So the king sent Uriah back to the camp, handing him a letter to Joab which ordered him to station Uriah where the enemy were hardest to fight, and for those with him to turn back and leave him there alone, so that he might be killed in this way. It was done as the king had ordered, and Uriah died. His wife mourned for her husband; and when she had finished mourning David took her as his wife, and she bore him a son.

God was angry and sent Nathan to David. He came to the king and said: "There were two men; one had flocks and herds, and the other owned one ewe lamb. When a guest came to the rich man, he did not sacrifice from his own, but took the poor man's one lamb, slaughtered it and feasted his friend." David sentenced the man who had done this to repay the lamb fourfold, and to die. Nathan said: "You have pronounced sentence against yourself, O king; for you are the one who has done this lawless deed." And he listed for him the adultery and the murder, and God's anger because of them, and foretold what he would suffer, and that the son born to him from the adultery would die. David cried out with deep feeling, "I have sinned against the Lord," and Nathan answered that the sin had been passed over by God.

Afterwards the child born of Bathsheba fell ill. David was deeply grieved; for seven days he would not eat, put on black, lay on sackcloth and prayed to God for the child's life. On the seventh day the child died; and learning this he rose, bathed, changed his clothes, gave thanks to God and ordered a table to be prepared for him. When the king's servants wondered at what had happened, he said: "While the child was still alive, I humbled myself and prayed, hoping that God would be moved"; but now that he was dead, grief and prayer for him were in vain. Bathsheba bore David another son, and he called him Solomon.

Joab, besieging the Ammonites, had the capture of the city very close, and told the king. He went there, took the city and gave it to the army to plunder; he took the crown of its king and wore it himself, which weighed a talent of gold and had a precious stone in it; and he destroyed the population of the city. He did the same to the other cities of the Ammonites, and returned to Jerusalem.

blocks: David had a daughter named Tamar, a full sister of Absalom. Amnon, David's first-born son, loved her, and his love was so great that the lover fell ill. When his father came to visit him, he asked that Tamar come to wait on him, and David consented. So Tamar came and prepared cakes for him. He sent everyone out and asked that his sister alone wait on him. When the girl was left alone, he forced her, and having violated her he at once felt a hatred opposite to his former love, told her to leave immediately and ordered his servant to throw her out. She, deeply grieved at the violence and the outrage, tore her tunic, sprinkled dust on her head and went away lamenting. Her brother Absalom advised her to keep quiet, but he nursed his anger against Amnon because of his sister. The king, learning what had happened, was distressed, but did not wish to grieve Amnon, since he was his first-born.

When two years had passed, Absalom was about to shear his own flocks, and he invited his brothers to a drinking party. He ordered his servants, as the drinking went on, to strike Amnon and kill him; and Absalom's servants did so. The other sons of the king, seeing what had happened, fled. When a rumour went ahead that Absalom had killed all the king's sons, David tore his clothes and fell on the ground lamenting. Meanwhile the king's sons arrived and, mourning, reported the murder of Amnon. Absalom fled to his grandfather on his mother's side, the king of Geshur, and stayed there for three years.

When anger had eased with time, Joab contrived to reconcile the king with Absalom. He prepared a woman to come to the king as if in mourning and lament that she had two sons, and one had killed the other, and her kinsmen were seeking to kill the survivor for his brother's murder; and to beg the king to grant her the boy's safety. She came to the king and said this with deep feeling, and the king promised to grant her the boy's life. The woman thanked him: "But so that I may have a pledge of what you have promised," she said, "first be reconciled yourself with your own son, and do not add a second, willing death to the death of the son who died against your will." The king understood that the woman's words were a pretext and had been devised by Joab, and allowed him to bring Absalom back. Joab went and brought him to Jerusalem; but he was not allowed to come into his father's sight.

After this the king was reconciled with Absalom, called him, pardoned him when he asked forgiveness, and promised him an amnesty for his offence. Absalom acquired horses and chariots and many followers, went every day to the palace, and by speaking to the people to win their favour made many well disposed to him. When four years had gone by since his return, he made the pretext of going to Hebron to sacrifice, as he had vowed to do while in exile; and his father let him go. Once there, he sent to many, and very many flocked to him, among others Ahithophel, his father's counsellor. And he was proclaimed king by all.

Learning this, David left Jerusalem with those about him; and the six hundred men who had been with him in Saul's time set out with him again. It was reported to him too that Ahithophel had gone over to Absalom, which made his fear greater and his grief more. He called on God and entrusted the judgement of everything to Him. Hushai, a companion of David, deserted to Absalom in pretence, as David wished. As David went away, Ziba, the servant of Mephibosheth, came to him leading a pair of asses carrying provisions, and accused his master of staying in Jerusalem and expecting that the kingdom would come round to him, as the people would choose him. David was indignant at this, and gave Ziba everything he had given Mephibosheth before. Then on the road Shimei, a man of Saul's family, came at him, threw stones at the king, cursed him and called him a man of blood and a lawbreaker. When those with David set out to kill Shimei, the king did not allow it, saying: "The Lord has told him to do this; leave him alone." Coming to the Jordan, he let those with him, who were worn out, refresh themselves there.

blocks: When Absalom came to Jerusalem, he said to Hushai when he came to him: "Why have you, my father's companion, left him and come to me?" He said: "I will be with the one chosen by God, and follow the one preferred by all the people." Absalom asked Ahithophel what he ought to do. He advised him to lie with his father's concubines, "so that all may know that your enmity towards your father admits no truce." Absalom did as this advice said. When Ahithophel asked for ten thousand men, so that he might pursue King David at once while he and those with him were exhausted with toil, strike him down and bring the others back, Absalom asked Hushai about the advice. He declared it was not good, saying: "You know the courage and experience of your father and those with him. I think you should gather an army from the whole country and so set out yourself against your father and command in the war; and you will surely win, clashing with few when you have many." Absalom and those with him said: "The counsel of Hushai is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." Hushai told the priests Zadok and Abiathar to make all this known to David. They sent men to David to tell him what had happened. Absalom was told about the men and pursued them. Learning this, they took refuge in someone's house, went down into a well and hid there unseen; and coming out of it they reported to David what they had been told. He crossed the Jordan by night with those with him. Ahithophel, outdone in reputation and knowing that evil would befall Absalom, went off to his house and hanged himself.

David counted those with him and found four thousand. He divided the army into three parts and set a general over each; he himself was not allowed by his friends to march out with them, for they said that if they were routed with him there they would lose all hope, but while he was safe some hope was still left them. So he sent his people out to fight, and begged them to spare Absalom if they won. Battle was joined, and David's men prevailed and pursued Absalom as he fled. He was riding a mule, and as he went into a wood his hair caught in a great oak (for he grew his hair very long), and he was left hanging from the oak while the mule went on. Someone, seeing Absalom hanging like this, reported it to Joab. Joab shot him with three darts through the heart and killed him, and sent off a man to report the victory to the king. When the victory was announced to him, he asked whether his son was alive; and hearing that he was dead, he lamented. Joab came to the king and by what he said persuaded him to stop lamenting; and when he had stopped and appeared before the soldiers, he praised them. All submitted to him as before.

He went off to Jerusalem; and as he went Shimei met him, asking pardon for the wrong he had done. David swore to forgive him his offence too, and all who had wronged him. Mephibosheth also met him. The king asked why he had not shared his flight. He said that Ziba was most to blame for this, for not preparing what he needed for the journey, while he himself, being lame in his feet, could not follow; and that Ziba had also slandered him maliciously and lied about him. At this David pardoned him, and ordered half his property to be restored to him.
text: When Absalom came to Jerusalem, he said to Hushai when he came to him: "Why have you, my father's companion, left him and come to me?" He said: "I will be with the one chosen by God, and follow the one preferred by all the people." Absalom asked Ahithophel what he ought to do. He advised him to lie with his father's concubines, "so that all may know that your enmity towards your father admits no truce." Absalom did as this advice said. When Ahithophel asked for ten thousand men, so that he might pursue King David at once while he and those with him were exhausted with toil, strike him down and bring the others back, Absalom asked Hushai about the advice. He declared it was not good, saying: "You know the courage and experience of your father and those with him. I think you should gather an army from the whole country and so set out yourself against your father and command in the war; and you will surely win, clashing with few when you have many." Absalom and those with him said: "The counsel of Hushai is better than the counsel of Ahithophel." Hushai told the priests Zadok and Abiathar to make all this known to David. They sent men to David to tell him what had happened. Absalom was told about the men and pursued them. Learning this, they took refuge in someone's house, went down into a well and hid there unseen; and coming out of it they reported to David what they had been told. He crossed the Jordan by night with those with him. Ahithophel, outdone in reputation and knowing that evil would befall Absalom, went off to his house and hanged himself. David counted those with him and found four thousand. He divided the army into three parts and set a general over each; he himself was not allowed by his friends to march out with them, for they said that if they were routed with him there they would lose all hope, but while he was safe some hope was still left them. So he sent his people out to fight, and begged them to spare Absalom if they won. Battle was joined, and David's men prevailed and pursued Absalom as he fled. He was riding a mule, and as he went into a wood his hair caught in a great oak (for he grew his hair very long), and he was left hanging from the oak while the mule went on. Someone, seeing Absalom hanging like this, reported it to Joab. Joab shot him with three darts through the heart and killed him, and sent off a man to report the victory to the king. When the victory was announced to him, he asked whether his son was alive; and hearing that he was dead, he lamented. Joab came to the king and by what he said persuaded him to stop lamenting; and when he had stopped and appeared before the soldiers, he praised them. All submitted to him as before. He said that Ziba was most to blame for this, for not preparing what he needed for the journey, while he himself, being lame in his feet, could not follow; and that Ziba had also slandered him maliciously and lied about him. At this David pardoned him, and ordered half his property to be restored to him.

blocks: When the king reached Gilgal, all the people of Israel gathered there, complaining that the tribe of Judah had come to him secretly. Those of Judah said they ought not to be blamed for this, being of the king's own kin. This answer seemed harsh to the people. A Benjamite, seditious and wicked, called Sheba, cried out: "We have no portion in David, nor inheritance in the son of Jesse"; and blowing a horn he made all fall away from David, only the tribe of Judah staying with him. The king appointed Amasa general and sent him out to gather an army from the tribe of Judah and come back within three days. When Amasa delayed, he ordered Joab to take the force that was there and set out against Sheba, "so that," he said, "the enemy may not be better prepared through our delay." Joab at once set out to war. As he went with a great force, Amasa met him; and Joab, as Amasa came up to him, let the sword he wore fall out of its scabbard, picked it up from the ground, and coming close to Amasa to embrace him, thrust the sword into his belly and killed him. Taking his men too, he pursued Sheba, who took refuge in a strong city. Joab besieged the city, and a sensible woman cried out to him from the wall: "Why do you wish to destroy a mother city of Israel?" He answered: "Because of Sheba." She went to the citizens and persuaded them to cut off Sheba's head and throw it out. When this had been done, Joab raised the siege and went off to Jerusalem, and was appointed again commander-in-chief of the whole force.

After this there was a famine, and for three years it pressed on the people. When the king inquired about it, God revealed that the famine came because of the Gibeonites, and that they must have vengeance for those of them whom Saul had killed, not keeping the oaths made to them by Joshua and the council of elders. So the king called the Gibeonites and asked what they wished done for them in atonement; they asked for seven men of the house of Saul to be given to them. The king gave them the seven men, as they asked, sparing Mephibosheth; and they took the men and killed them. And God brought down rain on the earth.

When there was war after this with the foreigners, David pursued the enemy with his own army. He became worn out and slackened from exhaustion; and one of the enemy, seeing him so, rushed to strike him down, but Abishai, the brother of Joab, shielded the king and killed the foreigner. Because of this David's men swore that they would never again allow him to go out to war. When the foreigners took the field once more, the king sent an army against them and caused many to be killed and the survivors to flee. After a short interval the foreigners came again against the country of the Israelites. There was among them a man of giant size, with six fingers on each hand and likewise on his feet; Jonathan, David's nephew, grappled with him, threw him down, stripped him of his armour and turned the scale towards victory for his countrymen. The foreigners did not again attempt to fight the Hebrews.

blocks: Having peace from then on, David composed songs to God, and making instruments he taught the Levites to sing the hymns with them. The instruments were these: the lyre had ten strings and was struck with a plectrum; the harp, with twelve notes, was plucked with the fingers; and there were cymbals of bronze, large and broad. About David there was also a company of brave men; the most distinguished of them were thirty-seven, who often won the prize of valour. Once, when the foreigners were camped at Bethlehem, the king longed to drink water from the well at Bethlehem. Three of the brave men about him ran off, went through the middle of the enemy's camp and drew water from that well; and passing back through the enemy, who were struck by their daring and kept still, they brought the water to the king. But he said: "The Lord be merciful to me, I will not drink this, brought at the cost of these men's blood and the danger of their lives." So he did not drink it, but poured it out as an offering to God.

Wishing to number the whole people, he ordered Joab to carry out the count. When Joab did not approve the plan and said the deed was not good, the king would not listen. Joab went and numbered the people, and the number of Israel was eight hundred thousand men of strength who drew the sword, and five hundred thousand fighting men of the tribe of Judah. Then David repented and confessed that he had sinned. The prophet Gad, at God's command, went to David and said: "Choose from these three whichever you will: do you choose that for seven years there be famine in your country, or that for three months you be pursued by your enemies, or that death fall on your people for three days?" He said: "I am hemmed in on every side, but it is better for me to fall into the hands of God." Death came on the people from morning until the hour of the midday meal, and seventy thousand of all the people died. David besought God. The angel destroying the people stretched out his hand over Jerusalem. Then the king said: "I have sinned, Lord, I the shepherd; but the flock, the people, have not sinned. I deserve punishment, and not they." God, moved by the king's contrition, stopped the destruction, and through the prophet Gad ordered him to set up an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite and sacrifice there. David did so, buying the threshing floor from Araunah. As Josephus wrote, it was to that place that Abraham is said to have brought Isaac to offer him as a burnt offering. David wished to build a temple to God there too, but was prevented by God.

When David had grown very old, he could not keep warm because of his age. So they chose a young girl, named Abishag, and the girl lay with the king and warmed him. And he did not know her; for because of his age he could not have intercourse. Adonijah, the fourth of the king's sons, very handsome, seeing his father grown old, laid claim to the kingdom, with the help of Joab the commander-in-chief and Abiathar the high priest. Once he prepared a lavish sacrifice and invited his brothers, the leading men of the tribe of Judah, Abiathar and Joab; but he did not invite Solomon, the prophet Nathan, or Benaiah, the captain of the bodyguard. So Nathan said to Bathsheba: "Have you heard that Adonijah has become king?" She went in to the king and said: "You swore, my lord the king, that Solomon your son would reign after you; and see, Adonijah has become king, and you do not know." While Bathsheba was still speaking, the prophet Nathan too came in and asked the king whether Adonijah had become king with his consent. He swore by God: "Today Solomon shall be king." Calling Zadok the high priest and Benaiah, he ordered them, taking the prophet and the armed men of the royal court, to set Solomon on the king's mule, take him outside the city to the spring called Gihon, anoint him with the holy oil, proclaim him king with the sounding of horns, and escort him through the middle of the city. They did at once as they were ordered, and the proclamation of Solomon was noised everywhere. When it became known to Adonijah and those feasting with him, the rest went off to their homes, but Adonijah, the more afraid, fled to the altar and asked Solomon for pledges of his safety. Solomon pardoned him his offence for the time; "but if he is found doing anything evil again," he said, "he shall be put to death."

David, seeing death drawing near, called Solomon and charged him to keep God's commandments and live by His laws, "so that our seed," he said, "as the Lord promised me, may be on my throne for ever." He added that he should not leave Joab unpunished, who had killed Abner and Amasa, nor Shimei, who had cursed him in his flight. He gave him other charges too, and bade him build a temple to the Lord, gave him the plan for the building of the temple, and roused him, the rulers and the tribe of Levi to the work with words, saying that he was leaving much for the building of the temple: ten thousand talents of gold, a hundred thousand talents of silver, emeralds and other costly stones, bronze and iron beyond number and other material in abundance; and that he was now adding to what had already been gathered three thousand talents of pure gold for the inner sanctuary, and ten thousand staters, and ten thousand talents of silver. And whoever had a precious stone brought it and handed it over to the treasuries. A little later David died, having lived seventy years and reigned seven years at Hebron and thirty-three at Jerusalem, a man who had achieved every virtue fitting for a king. His son Solomon buried him royally in Jerusalem and buried great wealth with him.

blocks: Solomon was very young when he received the kingdom, in the twelfth year of his age. But Adonijah went to Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and said: "You know that the kingdom belonged to me both by seniority and by the people's choice; but it has passed to Solomon my brother, and I must accept what has happened as having happened by God's will. I make one request: that the girl who lay with my father, Abishag, be given me in marriage, since my father did not know her because of his age, but she is still a virgin." Bathsheba promised to put his words to her son and to bring about the marriage for him with all zeal. She went to her son and begged him to give Abishag to his brother Adonijah. He, angered at the request, said he wondered that she did not ask him to give up the kingdom to Adonijah as the elder. At once he ordered Benaiah, the captain of the bodyguard, to kill Adonijah. He ordered Abiathar to go to his native place and live on his estates. "For," he said, "all the toils you shared with my father save you from death." So, as God had foretold to Eli, the honour of the priesthood was taken from the house of Ithamar and passed to Zadok, who was of the line of Phinehas. Joab the general, learning this and terrified, fled to the altar, and when called said he would never come out, but would die there and nowhere else. This was reported to the king and persuaded him to send men to kill Joab there. From then on Benaiah was appointed general of the whole force, and Zadok was granted the high priesthood. Shimei the king confined to Jerusalem, so that he might not leave it; if he did, he fixed death as his penalty. Three years later, when some slaves of his ran away, he went out in search of them; and learning this, Solomon ordered the man to be put to death.

Solomon married a daughter of Pharaoh, and raised the walls of Jerusalem higher and made them stronger. God spoke to him in his sleep and told him to ask what he wished; and he asked to be given understanding and wisdom. God, pleased with his request, promised to give him wisdom and a great mind such as no one before him or after him had, and to add what he had not asked, wealth, victory and glory, if he kept His commandments and ordinances.

After this two women came to him. One said: "O king, we lived together and no one with us. We both gave birth to a boy at the same time. A little later this woman lay on her son, and when she woke she found him dead. While I slept she put the dead child in my arms, took the living one from me and claimed it as her own. When I discovered the deed, I asked for my child, but she will not give him to me." The other insisted that the living child was hers and the dead one her opponent's, and swore she had not gone so far in wickedness. Those standing by were at a loss how the truth might be found, but the king ordered the living child to be cut in two with a sword and half given to each of the women. The true mother of the baby took this hard, begged him to withdraw the sentence and entreated that the child be given alive to her opponent; but the one who falsely called herself the boy's mother praised the judgement and urged on the dividing. And the king ordered the child to be given alive to the woman who begged that he not be divided, saying: "This is his mother, who was grieved beyond bearing when the child was about to be slaughtered." All the people took this as a sure proof of the king's wisdom.

He surpassed all who had gone before in wisdom and understanding. He composed three thousand parables and five thousand songs, and wrote about everything from the cedar to the hyssop; he studied and discoursed on the nature of animals, those that walk, fly and swim, and their properties; and against demons he discovered spells for the good of men and left methods of exorcism by which demons were driven out. Josephus says that this cure was still effective in his own day, and tells a story of this kind to confirm it. He says that Eleazar, one of his countrymen, had a ring with, under its seal, a root of the kind Solomon had shown; he would hold it to the nostrils of the possessed man, and with the smell draw the demon out through the sufferer's nostrils; then, invoking Solomon, he would say spells from those Solomon had composed and adjure the demon never to come back into the man. He says Eleazar did this in the presence of Vespasian and his sons; and to give proof of his power over the demons he would set down a cup full of water and command the demon, as it came out of the sufferer, to overturn it; and the cup would be overturned with no one seeing who overturned it.

blocks: He began building the temple in the fourth year of his reign, four hundred and forty years after the people's departure from Egypt. About the measurements of its height and length and about its construction, the Third Book of Kingdoms and Josephus, writing about the temple in the eighth book of the Antiquities, do not agree, but differ in most things. Whoever wishes to examine the differences closely, and about the two cherubim which he made of gold and set in the inner sanctuary, the ark, the bronze sea and the basins, how large the bronze altar was, what the golden table was like, how many vessels of silver and gold Solomon dedicated to the temple, and the rest, will find the Third Book of Kingdoms and Josephus in the Antiquities enough to set out the exact details of each.

The king finished the temple and everything about it in seven years, and called the people together to Jerusalem. The priests lifted the ark, the tabernacle which Moses had pitched and the vessels used in the sacrifices and carried them to the temple, with the king and all the multitude going before, and the Levites pouring libations and burning incense. The ark was placed in the inner sanctuary between the two cherubim, with the two stone tablets inside it. When the priests came out of the inner sanctuary, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord and a cloud was spread over the whole temple, from which they imagined that God had come to the temple and taken up His dwelling in it. The king, glad at this, gave thanks to God, blessed the people and prayed that the Divine would hear all who prayed in it. Then he brought sacrifices to the altar. And God, showing that He had received them graciously, made fire flash through the air and come down on the altar and consume the whole sacrifice. Seeing this, the people blessed God and the king gave thanks; and after feasting lavishly they broke up the gathering. A dream that came to the king showed that God had heard his prayer, and that the temple would be preserved and he himself raised to the height of good fortune, and that his descendants would rule the country, if he and they and the people did not transgress the divine commands; but if they did, He threatened to cut off his race root and branch, to subject the people to slavery and countless afflictions, to give the temple over to burning and plunder, and the city to destruction and pillage.

So Solomon completed the temple. After this he built himself a palace, costly and splendid, strengthened the walls of Jerusalem further, built other cities as well, and brought under him the Canaanites on Mount Lebanon, who had not been subdued before, and made them tributary. Hiram, the king of the Tyrians, sent him puzzles and riddling sayings, asking him to explain them; and he solved them all and showed their meaning. Josephus records that ancient writers mention this, Dius and besides him Menander.

When the wisdom and understanding of Solomon were noised everywhere, a queen of Egypt and Ethiopia, who loved and sought wisdom, came to Jerusalem. The king received her with honour and easily solved the puzzles she set, so that the queen was astonished and said she saw more than she had heard. She also admired the palace, the lavishness of the dinners, the whole royal service, the sacrifices in the temple and the good order of those who sacrificed. She presented the king with gold, precious stones, spices beyond telling and roots of balsam, so that from her the balsam came to grow in Palestine. Solomon repaid the queen with many good things, and she went back to her own country.
text: He began building the temple in the fourth year of his reign, four hundred and forty years after the people's departure from Egypt. About the measurements of its height and length and about its construction, the Third Book of Kingdoms and Josephus, writing about the temple in the eighth book of the Antiquities, do not agree, but differ in most things. Whoever wishes to examine the differences closely, and about the two cherubim which he made of gold and set in the inner sanctuary, the ark, the bronze sea and the basins, how large the bronze altar was, what the golden table was like, how many vessels of silver and gold Solomon dedicated to the temple, and the rest, will find the Third Book of Kingdoms and Josephus in the Antiquities enough to set out the exact details of each. The king finished the temple and everything about it in seven years, and called the people together to Jerusalem. The priests lifted the ark, the tabernacle which Moses had pitched and the vessels used in the sacrifices and carried them to the temple, with the king and all the multitude going before, and the Levites pouring libations and burning incense. The ark was placed in the inner sanctuary between the two cherubim, with the two stone tablets inside it. When the priests came out of the inner sanctuary, the house was filled with the glory of the Lord and a cloud was spread over the whole temple, from which they imagined that God had come to the temple and taken up His dwelling in it. The king, glad at this, gave thanks to God, blessed the people and prayed that the Divine would hear all who prayed in it. Then he brought sacrifices to the altar. And God, showing that He had received them graciously, made fire flash through the air and come down on the altar and consume the whole sacrifice. Seeing this, the people blessed God and the king gave thanks; and after feasting lavishly they broke up the gathering. A dream that came to the king showed that God had heard his prayer, and that the temple would be preserved and he himself raised to the height of good fortune, and that his descendants would rule the country, if he and they and the people did not transgress the divine commands; but if they did, He threatened to cut off his race root and branch, to subject the people to slavery and countless afflictions, to give the temple over to burning and plunder, and the city to destruction and pillage. Solomon repaid the queen with many good things, and she went back to her own country.

blocks: But the king, who had become the most glorious of all before him and excelled in wisdom and wealth, did not abide by the divine ordinances. He fell sick with incontinence in love and went mad for women; he was not content with women of his own race, but married very many foreigners too, and to please them, for love's sake, he worshipped their gods as well. For he married seven hundred daughters of famous rulers, and had three hundred concubines, and the daughter of the king of the Egyptians. So the Lord said to Solomon: "Because you have not kept what I commanded you, I will tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant. Yet I will not take the rule from you while you live, for your father's sake; but when you have died I will do this to your son. Nor will I take the whole kingdom from him; leaving him two tribes and Jerusalem, for the sake of his grandfather David, I will give the ten to his servant."

Not much time passed before Hadad became an enemy to Israel. Hadad was an Idumaean of royal descent, who as a boy had fled to Egypt when Joab subdued Idumaea in David's time; he was kindly received by Pharaoh, grew dear to him and married the sister of Pharaoh's wife. When he had grown to manhood and learned that David and Joab were dead, he asked to go back to his ancestral realm, but Pharaoh would not allow it. When Solomon's affairs were already going badly, Hadad was allowed to go and returned to Idumaea. Since it was securely guarded, he went to Syria, and gathering a band of robbers about him he took possession of it and plundered the land of the Hebrews.

Jeroboam, the son of Nebat, served the king as a youth. Solomon, seeing that he was noble in spirit, put him in charge of the building when he set a wall round Jerusalem. Once, as Jeroboam was going somewhere, the prophet Ahijah the Shilonite met him, and taking him aside from the road tore his own cloak into twelve pieces and gave him ten, saying: "So will the Lord tear the kingdom of Solomon; to his son He will leave two tribes for his grandfather's sake, but to you He will give the ten and make you king over them. But you, keep to the laws of the Lord and be just." Elated by this, Jeroboam attempted a revolt. The king learned of the matter and sought to kill him. He fled to Egypt and stayed there until Solomon died.

King Solomon died, as the book of Kingdoms records, having lived fifty-two years (for he is recorded to have come to the throne at twelve) and reigned forty years; but as Josephus wrote, he lived ninety-four years and reigned eighty. He lived happily and gloriously, but broke the law in his old age, persuaded by unholy loves for foreign women and following their worship.

blocks: He was succeeded in the kingdom by his son Rehoboam. All the people gathered before him and begged him to lighten for them the yoke of slavery which Solomon had laid on them, and to show himself kinder than his father. He said he would consider it and answer within three days. So he called the older of his father's attendants and asked what he should answer the people; and they advised him to speak to them gently, not haughtily or pompously. After the elders he shared the question with the young men who had been brought up with him, telling them the advice of the older men too. They advised him to address the people more harshly and make his words fit the grandeur of his rule and the royal dignity. He sided with them, and when the multitude had gathered again he said: "If my father made your yoke hard, I will put a heavier one on you; and if he used whips against you, I will punish you with scorpions; and you will find my little finger thicker than my father's loins." When the multitude heard this they cried out, "What portion have we in David?" and went away in anger. When Rehoboam sent one of his household to talk to them and calm them, they stoned the man to death in their rage. Rehoboam, afraid, fled to Jerusalem; the tribe of Judah stayed with him, and with it the tribe of Benjamin. The rest, since Jeroboam had already returned from Egypt after Solomon's death, called him and chose him king. Rehoboam prepared to fight the Israelites and Jeroboam for the kingdom, but was prevented by God through the prophet Shemaiah.

Jeroboam, afraid that the multitude, going to Jerusalem and mixing with the people there, might turn back to their former king and abandon him, made two heifers of gold, and set one at Bethel and the other at Dan. Calling the multitude to an assembly he said: "Men, God is everywhere, and not only in Jerusalem. See, I have made two heifers in the name of God, and you no longer need to go to Jerusalem. Go to them, bow down and sacrifice; and I will appoint priests from among yourselves." Deceived by this, the people transgressed their ancestral customs and provoked God, so that Israel was given over into captivity to the foreigners.

Jeroboam made priests and an altar and held a festival, and went up to the altar himself with the priests about him. As he was about to sacrifice, a prophet sent by God stood before him and said: "Thus says the Lord: Altar, there shall be one of David's line called Josiah, who will sacrifice your priests on you and burn their bones. And so that it may be clear that my words are true, see, the altar will be split, and the fat on it poured out on the ground." At once the altar split and the fat of the victims was poured out. Jeroboam stretched out his hand, ordering the prophet to be seized; but it withered and stayed motionless. When Jeroboam begged the prophet, his hand moved again and worked. He asked him to dine with him. The prophet would not consent, saying that God had forbidden him to eat bread or drink water in that city, or to return by the road by which he had come into the city; and he went off by another way.

There was in that city a false prophet who deceived Jeroboam and spoke to please him. Learning what the prophet of God had said and done and that he was leaving, he pursued him, and overtaking him asked him to turn back and be his guest. When he refused, since God had forbidden it, that wicked man said: "But I too am a prophet, and I have come at God's command to bring you back to share my table." The prophet believed the false prophet's words and returned. While he was a guest there, the word of the Lord came to the prophet that, because he had not kept what he had been commanded, he would be killed on the road by a lion. As he went back a lion killed him, and sat by and guarded the body and the beast of burden. The false prophet, learning what had happened, brought in the dead man's body and buried it, and ordered his own sons to bury his own body with the prophet when he died. What was his scheme in this? That when, according to the prophet's prophecy, the altar was razed and the bones of the priests and false prophets given to the fire, he himself might escape the outrage by being laid with the man of God.

blocks: So these things happened. Jeroboam kept to the same impiety, and even went further in breaking the law every day, and offered the false priesthood of the high places for sale for money to any who wished. This deed was reckoned to him as a sin, and brought about the disappearance and ruin of his house. If selling that unholy priesthood for money was reckoned a sin, what could one say of those who sell and buy the truly divine priesthood, that which performs the awesome and bloodless sacrifice?

Abijah, the son of Jeroboam, fell ill, and the king sent his wife to the prophet Ahijah to ask whether he would live. She put on the dress of a common woman and went. The prophet, seeing through the play, said: "Do not hide yourself, wife of Jeroboam. Go and tell your husband: Since you have abandoned God and made yourself molten gods, expect that the kingdom will be taken from you and you yourself destroyed with all your family; and because the multitude followed you in your impiety, that too will not stay unpunished. But go, woman, and you will find your child dead, and he will be buried with lamentation; for he alone of Jeroboam's line was good." The woman went away, found the child dead, and told her husband what the prophet had said. But he was not made any better by it at all, being without understanding.

While Rehoboam, the son of Solomon, was reigning in Jerusalem, the priests and Levites among the Israelites, and those of the multitude who understood what was good, left their own cities and came to Jerusalem; and from this Rehoboam's kingdom grew. But he too was impious towards God, and the whole house of Judah neglected the worship of God. So Shishak, the king of Egypt, came up against Jerusalem with a heavy force in the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign. Rehoboam, shutting himself and the people up in the city, prayed to God to grant them safety, and they confessed their sins against God. God, entreated, said He would not destroy them, but would make them subject to the Egyptians. So when Rehoboam received the Egyptian into the city on terms, he broke the treaty, plundered the treasures of God, emptied the royal ones, and took away all the golden shields which Solomon had made and the golden spears which David had dedicated. Rehoboam died having lived fifty-seven years, of which he reigned seventeen, leaving his son Abijah as successor.

Against him came Jeroboam, who had always been at war with Rehoboam too. Abijah did not cower at the attack, but set his own men against him and won a famous victory, so that Jeroboam no longer dared to face him. Abijah died having reigned three years in Jerusalem, having done evil in the sight of the Lord; and his son Asa became king, who kept the divine ordinances like David his forefather.

Jeroboam also died, having held the rule for twenty-two years. He was succeeded by his son Nadab, who was as impious as his father. While besieging Gibbethon, a city of the foreigners, he was the victim of a plot by Baasha, the son of Ahijah, and died after ruling two years. Baasha, having gained the kingdom of the ten tribes, destroyed the whole race of Jeroboam. He too broke the law like Jeroboam and made the people sin likewise. God threatened him through the prophet Jehu to destroy his house like the house of Jeroboam. He too died, having reigned over Israel for twenty-four years. Elah his son succeeded to his father's kingdom. Zimri, the commander of his cavalry, killed him while he was drunk, after he had reigned two years, took the kingdom from him and destroyed the whole race of Baasha. The army of the Israelites, which was besieging Gibbethon, learning that Zimri had killed Elah and become king, proclaimed their own general, Omri, in the camp, and, seizing the city of Tirzah with him first, held it. Zimri, the first, went into the innermost part of the palace and set it on fire, destroying himself with it, after holding the rule seven days. Then the people were divided: one part chose Omri, the other Tibni. But Omri's men prevailed, killed Tibni and secured the rule for Omri without dispute. He reigned first at Tirzah, then on the mountain of Shemer, on which he built the city that is called Samaria, for he called the mountain Samareon after Shemer, from whom he had bought it. He was worse than those before him. He ended his life in Samaria, having reigned twelve years; and the kingdom passed to his son Ahab.

So the kings of the Israelites were destroyed one after another within a short time because of their lawlessness. But Asa, the king of Jerusalem, was dear to God. In the tenth year of his reign the king of the Ethiopians marched against him with a heavy force. He called on God as his ally, and engaging the Ethiopians he killed many, pursued the rest as they fled and plundered their camp, and he and the people carried off much spoil. As the king and the army were returning, the prophet Azariah met him and said that God had given the victory to him and to the people because they cared for justice; and he promised them happiness in the future too if they pursued virtue, but much sorrow if they neglected God's commandments. Asa, having spent his life in piety and reached a great age, died after reigning forty-one years, leaving the rule to his son Jehoshaphat.

blocks: Ahab held the palace in Samaria, outrunning those before him in impiety, and drawn further into wickedness by his wife Jezebel, who was the daughter of the king of Tyre and Sidon, a reckless and bold woman. She built a temple to her own god Bel, planted a grove and appointed priests and false prophets for him. Elijah the prophet, from the city of Tishbe, zealous at the impieties of the king and the people, said to Ahab: "As the Lord lives, there shall be no rain except by my word." With these words he went away to the brook Cherith, at God's command; there he was fed by ravens, which brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and the brook gave him drink. When it dried up, obeying God, he went to Zarephath, a city between Sidon and Tyre. Meeting a woman before the city, he begged her to bring him water. As the woman went off, he asked her to bring him bread as well. She swore she had only one handful of flour and very little oil, and that she was gathering sticks to go and make a little food for herself and her children; when it was gone, they too would perish of hunger. The prophet told her to take heart; for neither would flour fail from the jar that held it nor oil from the flask until there was rain. She went, and fed the prophet, who lodged with her, and herself and her children from that very little flour until the famine had passed.

When this woman's son fell ill and died, she railed against the prophet. He asked to be given the dead child. Taking him, he carried him up to the upper room where he lived and laid him on his bed; and praying to God he breathed three times on the dead boy, and he came back to life. He gave the boy alive to his mother, and she gave thanks.

After this God commanded Elijah to go and tell Ahab beforehand that there would be rain. The famine had grown severe in Samaria and the whole country. Ahab took his steward Obadiah, a good man, and went out to see if he could find fodder for the horses. He went one way and Obadiah another, searching where they might find grass by springs or brooks. Elijah met Obadiah and asked him to tell the king about him. Obadiah said that Ahab was searching hard for him, to kill him if he found him, and advised him to hide; he said that he himself was hiding a hundred prophets, feeding them and so saving them, since Jezebel had killed all the others. Elijah swore that he would be seen by Ahab that very day. So Obadiah went and told the king about Elijah. When he saw the prophet, he asked whether he was the man who was perverting Israel. Elijah said: "Rather you and your father's house are perverting the people, abandoning the Lord and honouring false gods. But gather the people at Carmel, and your prophets and your wife's."

When all had gathered, Elijah said: "I alone am left as a prophet of God, but the false prophets are very many. Give me alone one ox, and them all another; let us sacrifice the oxen and put the victims on wood, but not set fire to it; and let each call on his own god; and the one by whom fire blazes out of itself and burns up the wood and the victims, let him be reckoned the true God." The multitude approved his words, and the priests of shame did so: they sacrificed the calf and put it on the wood without fire, and called on Baal from morning until noon. The prophet, mocking them, advised them to shout loudly, in case their god was asleep or had some business. When nothing came of their many prayers, the prophet took twelve stones, one for each tribe, built an altar, dug a trench, stacked the split wood on the altar, put the victims on it, and ordered water to be poured over the altar until the trench was filled. Then he called on God, and fire came down from heaven on the altar as all watched, and consumed the sacrifice, the wood and the stones, the water and the dust. The people, amazed, fell on the ground, confessing one God, true and great. At the prophet's command they seized the false prophets and killed them. He told the king that God would send rain soon, and as he had foretold there was a violent downpour.

When Jezebel threatened to kill Elijah, he was afraid and fled, and in the desert, in despair, he prayed God that he might die. He fell asleep and was woken by someone telling him to get up and eat. He saw there a loaf of spelt and water. He ate and slept again, and again the angel told him to eat, since a long journey lay before him. He ate again, and strengthened by that food he journeyed forty days. Coming to Mount Horeb he went into a cave, and heard a voice: "Why have you come here?" He said: "Because in my zeal I killed Jezebel's prophets, and she is seeking to kill me." The voice answered him again: "Go out tomorrow and stand before the Lord." He did so, and felt a wind and an earthquake, and saw a fire burning. Then, when a gentle breeze came, he heard a voice from it bidding him go back and anoint Hazael king of Syria, Jehu king over Israel, and Elisha prophet in his own place, who would destroy the impious. Elijah went back as he was told and found Elisha ploughing, and threw his mantle on him. He left everything and followed him, having been judged worthy to prophesy.
text: Ahab held the palace in Samaria, outrunning those before him in impiety, and drawn further into wickedness by his wife Jezebel, who was the daughter of the king of Tyre and Sidon, a reckless and bold woman. She built a temple to her own god Bel, planted a grove and appointed priests and false prophets for him. Elijah the prophet, from the city of Tishbe, zealous at the impieties of the king and the people, said to Ahab: "As the Lord lives, there shall be no rain except by my word." With these words he went away to the brook Cherith, at God's command; there he was fed by ravens, which brought him bread in the morning and meat in the evening, and the brook gave him drink. When it dried up, obeying God, he went to Zarephath, a city between Sidon and Tyre. Meeting a woman before the city, he begged her to bring him water. As the woman went off, he asked her to bring him bread as well. She swore she had only one handful of flour and very little oil, and that she was gathering sticks to go and make a little food for herself and her children; when it was gone, they too would perish of hunger. The prophet told her to take heart; for neither would flour fail from the jar that held it nor oil from the flask until there was rain. She went, and fed the prophet, who lodged with her, and herself and her children from that very little flour until the famine had passed. When this woman's son fell ill and died, she railed against the prophet. He asked to be given the dead child. Taking him, he carried him up to the upper room where he lived and laid him on his bed; and praying to God he breathed three times on the dead boy, and he came back to life. He gave the boy alive to his mother, and she gave thanks. After this God commanded Elijah to go and tell Ahab beforehand that there would be rain. The famine had grown severe in Samaria and the whole country. Ahab took his steward Obadiah, a good man, and went out to see if he could find fodder for the horses. He went one way and Obadiah another, searching where they might find grass by springs or brooks. Elijah met Obadiah and asked him to tell the king about him. Obadiah said that Ahab was searching hard for him, to kill him if he found him, and advised him to hide; he said that he himself was hiding a hundred prophets, feeding them and so saving them, since Jezebel had killed all the others. Elijah swore that he would be seen by Ahab that very day. So Obadiah went and told the king about Elijah. When he saw the prophet, he asked whether he was the man who was perverting Israel. Elijah said: "Rather you and your father's house are perverting the people, abandoning the Lord and honouring false gods. But gather the people at Carmel, and your prophets and your wife's." When all had gathered, Elijah said: "I alone am left as a prophet of God, but the false prophets are very many. Give me alone one ox, and them all another; let us sacrifice the oxen and put the victims on wood, but not set fire to it; and let each call on his own god; and the one by whom fire blazes out of itself and burns up the wood and the victims, let him be reckoned the true God." The multitude approved his words, and the priests of shame did so: they sacrificed the calf and put it on the wood without fire, and called on Baal from morning until noon. The prophet, mocking them, advised them to shout loudly, in case their god was asleep or had some business. When nothing came of their many prayers, the prophet took twelve stones, one for each tribe, built an altar, dug a trench, stacked the split wood on the altar, put the victims on it, and ordered water to be poured over the altar until the trench was filled. blocks: Naboth, who owned a vineyard near the fields of King Ahab, was asked to sell it to the king or exchange it, but he would not agree; and the king was grieved at this. Jezebel, learning the cause of his grief, wrote a letter as from Ahab to the leading men of the district where Naboth lived, ordering them to accuse the man of having blasphemed against God and the king, to prepare some men to bear witness against him, and to stone him. She sealed this letter with the king's seal and sent it to the men. They did as they were ordered: Naboth was stoned and died, and Jezebel told Ahab to inherit Naboth's vineyard now that he was dead. He was grieved at the murder, but took the vineyard for himself. Elijah, at God's command, went to Ahab and said: "Because you have murdered Naboth to get his vineyard, therefore thus says the Lord: Where the dogs licked his blood, there they will lick your blood and your wife's, and the harlots will bathe in your blood, and your whole race will be destroyed." At this Ahab was pierced to the heart; he wept, put on sackcloth and fasted, repenting of what had been done. God, because of his repentance, revealed to the prophet that He would not bring on him what He had threatened, but would fulfil it in the days of his son.

The son of Hadad, king of Syria, marched against Samaria with a heavy force and many allies. Besieging it, he sent to Ahab, saying: "Your wealth, your wives and your children are mine; for I will take them in war. But if you let me take whatever I wish, I will raise the siege and go away." Ahab said: "I and all mine are yours." He gathered the elders of the land and told them what the enemy had sent to him. The multitude advised him not to give in to him. He told the enemy's envoys that he could not do what was demanded. This, reported to the king of Syria, roused him to anger, and he ordered a palisade to be thrown round the city and mounds raised. A prophet told Ahab that God was giving the enemy into his hands if he attacked them with the young men of the princes; he counted the young men and found two hundred and thirty-two. While the enemy were feasting and drunk at midday, Ahab went out taking the young men. The king of Syria, seeing them, ordered some of his men to bring those who were coming to him bound. The young men engaged their attackers and killed many. The whole force of Israel, following behind the young men, suddenly charged the Syrians and put them to flight, so that their king barely escaped and was saved. Returning from the pursuit, Ahab plundered the enemy's camp and went back to Samaria.

The prophet foretold to him another attack by the Syrian. When spring had come, the Syrian marched again against Israel and camped in a plain; for those about him told him that the God of the Hebrews had power on mountains, but not in valleys. The prophet promised Ahab victory, "so that," he said, "God may show His strength in valleys too." For some days the armies kept quiet, but on the seventh battle was joined and the Syrians fled; and Ahab pursued and killed them. Many who escaped to the city of Aphek perished there when the wall fell on them. The son of Hadad fled with a few and hid. Those about him put on sackcloth, tied ropes round their heads, came to Ahab and begged him to spare their lord; and he consented. They brought their leader to Ahab as he rode in his chariot. He took him up into the chariot, embraced him and told him to take heart. Then he let him go on terms, after giving him many gifts.

The prophet Micaiah asked one of his countrymen to strike him on the head. When he would not, he foretold that he would be struck down by a lion; and the prediction came true. Then he made the same request of another; when he had struck him, he bound up his head, came to Ahab and said that he had received a prisoner from his captain to guard, and when he escaped the captain was going to kill him. When Ahab said this was just, he unbound his head and was recognized as the prophet Micaiah. He said to Ahab: "Since you have let the king of Syria, a deadly man, go unpunished, you yourself will die in his place, and your people in place of his people." Ahab was grieved at hearing this.

After three years of peace, wishing to take from the Syrians the city of Ramoth, as belonging to him, he asked Jehoshaphat, the king of Jerusalem, to march out with him. Jehoshaphat consented, and advised him to ask God through a prophet whether He approved. Ahab called his own prophets together and asked whether he should go to war. When they promised victory, King Jehoshaphat asked for a prophet of the Lord. Ahab said there was one, but that he loathed him because he foretold evil. Jehoshaphat asked for him to be called. When Micaiah was called, Ahab asked him whether he should fight or not. He said: "I have seen Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock without a shepherd. The Lord told me that they would be saved and return, but that you alone would fall at Ramoth." When Micaiah had said this, Ahab said to Jehoshaphat: "Did I not tell you that he always prophesies evil for me?" Zedekiah, one of the false prophets, struck Micaiah on the cheek. He said to him: "Soon you will go from one inner room to another, hiding." King Ahab ordered him to be shut up until he himself returned. Micaiah said: "If you return in peace, the Lord has not spoken through me."

When the kings had set out, the king of the Syrians drew up against them, ordering his soldiers to fight no one else but Ahab alone. Ahab changed his royal robe and put on that of a common man. The commanders of the Syrians, seeing Jehoshaphat in royal dress, thought he was Ahab and surrounded him; but when they saw he was not the king of Israel, they withdrew. But one man drew his bow and shot Ahab. Knowing he was mortally wounded, he ordered his charioteer to drive the chariot out of the battle, and about sunset he died. The Syrians, learning that Ahab was dead, went home, and the king's body was brought to Samaria and buried. The chariot, stained with the king's blood, they washed in the spring of Samaria, and the dogs licked the blood and the harlots bathed at the spring, as Elijah had foretold. Ahab died where Micaiah had foretold, not escaping destruction though it had been foretold to him, after reigning twenty-two years. His son Ahaziah received the kingdom after him.
