blocks: When Jehoshaphat, the king of Jerusalem, returned from his alliance with Ahab, the prophet Jehu reproached him for having fought on the side of an impious man; but he said that he had been rescued by God, though God was displeased at his deed. The king gave thanks. Then, going round the country under him, he commanded them to keep the laws, and appointing judges everywhere he ordered them to judge justly. When the Moabites and Ammonites, taking the Arabs with them, attacked him, he called on God for help. A prophet said that God would fight for him, and bade him lead out the army, but not engage the enemy, and stand and watch the help from God. At dawn the king went out with the army and ordered it to stand there, and the priests to stand before the army with the trumpets, and the Levites and singers to sing a song of thanksgiving to God. The enemy turned against one another and killed one another, so that none was saved. Jehoshaphat gave the enemy's camp to the army to plunder. From then on the foreigners, fearing him as one who had God for his ally, kept quiet.

Ahaziah, the king of the Israelites, was like his parents in wickedness. About the second year of his reign the Moabites held back the tribute they had paid to his father. Falling ill, he sent to the god of Ekron, called the Fly, to ask whether he would recover. Elijah met those who had been sent and told them to turn back and say to the man who had sent to the god of the foreigners, as if Israel had no God, that he would not rise from his bed. The men went back and said what they had heard. Ahaziah asked who it was who had said this. When they said they did not know, he demanded that they describe the man's appearance. When they said he was hairy and wore a leather belt, he understood that it was Elijah. He sent a captain of fifty with his men and ordered the prophet to be brought. The man who was sent found him on the top of the mountain and told him to come to the king. Elijah prayed, and fire flowing from heaven destroyed the captain of fifty and those with him. The king sent another captain of fifty with the fifty; and fire from heaven consumed them likewise. Again a third captain was sent with his men. He came to the prophet, fell down and bowed before him, and begged to be spared his punishment, saying he had come unwillingly, obeying the king's command, and asked him to come to the king. Elijah, since an angel told him to go and not be afraid, came down from the mountain, went to the king and said: "Since you sent to a foreign god to ask whether you would live, know that you will not rise from your sickness, but will die." So Ahaziah died according to the prophet's prediction, leaving the kingdom to his brother Jehoram. He broke the pillars of Baal which Ahab his father had set up, but in other things he was impious and wicked and like his parents.

When Elijah was about to be taken up, he went with Elisha. Coming to the Jordan, he struck the water with his mantle, and the water was divided, and they both crossed on dry ground. Then he said to Elisha: "Ask what I shall do for you." He asked that a double portion of the grace of the Spirit in him might come on him. Elijah said the request was a heavy one, "but if you see me taken up, it shall be yours." While they were still talking, a chariot of fire with horses of fire appeared and snatched Elijah away. As he was carried up, he threw his mantle down to Elisha. Elisha took it, and seeing Elijah no more, went back. Coming to the Jordan, he made trial whether he had received the grace he had asked for, and struck the water with the mantle; but it was not divided. He said, "Where is the God of Elijah?" and struck it again, and the water parted, and he crossed. Fifty of the sons of the prophets, seeing him, said, "The spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha," and followed him. They asked to go and search, in case the Spirit of the Lord had taken Elijah up and thrown him down on one of the mountains or hills. Elisha would not allow it, but when they pressed him he consented. Fifty men went and searched for three days and did not find him.

Elisha was at Jericho. The men of the city came to him begging him to change the water of that place, which was bad and made women barren. He asked for salt to be brought to him in a new vessel, and when it was brought he threw the salt into the spring of the water, calling on God, and the water changed from bitterness to sweetness, and nothing harmful remained in it for them. Once, as the prophet Elisha was going somewhere, little boys mocked him, shouting, "Go up, baldhead." Pained by this, he cursed them. Bears came out of the mountain and killed forty-two of the children.

Jehoram the son of Ahab, about to march against the Moabites, asked Jehoshaphat, the king of Judaea, to fight on his side. He promised, and to take as an ally too the king of the Idumaeans, who was subject to him. The three kings joined and marched through the desert for seven days, and the water gave out for the armies. So the three kings came to Elisha and begged him to save them and the army. He said to Jehoram: "Go to the prophets of your father and your mother," and swore that he would not have answered him except for Jehoshaphat. Then he ordered a harpist to be called. As he played, the Spirit of the Lord inspired the prophet, and he ordered many pits to be dug by the brook: "For you will see," he said, "the brook full, though no wind has blown and no rain has fallen, and you will drink your fill and master your enemies." So he foretold; and at dawn the next day the brook was filled with water, and the flood covered the whole face of that land. When the sun rose fiery and struck the waters, they looked red in the sun's light. So the Moabites, who were camped in the mountains and watching from above, took the water for blood, and thinking that the kings had fought one another and their soldiers had killed one another, rushed in disorder to plunder the spoil. The enemy surrounded them; some were killed and others fled. The Israelites, pursuing, invaded the land of Moab, pulled down the cities and laid the country waste. The king of Moab, going back into the city, led his first-born son up onto the wall and in despair sacrificed him as a burnt offering to God. The kings, seeing this and pitying him in his despair, raised the siege.

Jehoshaphat returned to Jerusalem and died, having lived sixty years and reigned twenty-five of them, a man who was god-fearing and just. He left many sons, and made the eldest successor to the kingdom, called Jehoram, the same name as the king of the Israelites, who was his mother's brother.

So the Moabites, who were camped in the mountains and watching from above, took the water for blood, and thinking that the kings had fought one another and their soldiers had killed one another, rushed in disorder to plunder the spoil. The enemy surrounded them; some were killed and others fled. The Israelites, pursuing, invaded the land of Moab, pulled down the cities and laid the country waste. The king of Moab, going back into the city, led his first-born son up onto the wall and in despair sacrificed him as a burnt offering to God. The kings, seeing this and pitying him in his despair, raised the siege. Jehoshaphat returned to Jerusalem and died, having lived sixty years and reigned twenty-five of them, a man who was god-fearing and just. He left many sons, and made the eldest successor to the kingdom, called Jehoram, the same name as the king of the Israelites, who was his mother's brother.

blocks: While Elisha was staying in Samaria, a widow came to him lamenting that she owed a debt and, having no means to pay it, her sons were being taken by the lender to be his slaves. The prophet asked her what she had in the house. She said she had nothing but a very little oil. He told her to borrow many vessels and pour from the oil into them all. The woman did as she was told, and all were filled with oil; and she told the prophet what had happened. He advised her to sell the oil, pay the debt and use the rest for her living.

He was a guest of the Shunammite woman and rested in her house; she had no son, and he foretold to her that she would conceive and bear a son. According to the prophet's prediction she bore one. When the child had grown, he died; and the woman went to Elisha at Carmel, fell at his feet and lamented her misfortune. He told his disciple Gehazi to go, giving him his own staff to lay on the dead child. The woman swore that she would not go back unless he himself came with her. So the prophet agreed, went and found the boy laid on his bed; and after praying he went up on the bed, lay down with the boy and breathed into him. When the prophet had done so seven times, the dead boy came back to life, and he gave him alive to his mother.

From there he went to Gilgal. There was a famine, and the sons of the prophets came to him. He ordered his servant to prepare a stew for them. The man gathered herbs from the field, with which wild gourd was mixed (the plant is poisonous), stewed them and set them before the men. As they ate they recognized the gourd and cried out to the prophet that they would die. He ordered meal to be thrown into the pot and let them eat, and no one came to any harm from the food. When someone brought him twenty loaves and cakes of figs, he told his servant to set them before the people. When he said, "What would these be among a hundred men?", Elisha said: "Give them, for they will be satisfied and leave some over." And the word came true.

Naaman, a great man with the king of Syria, was a leper. A young Israelite girl had been taken captive, and Naaman's wife had her as a slave. She said to her mistress: "If my master went to the prophet Elisha, he would be rid of his disease." She told her husband the girl's words, and Naaman reported what had been said to the king of Syria. The king wrote a letter to the king of Israel about the healing of Naaman. Naaman, taking ten talents of silver, six thousand gold pieces and ten changes of clothing, went to Samaria and handed the letter to the king. He read it, tore his clothes and said: "The king of Syria is seeking a pretext against us." Elisha, learning this, sent word to the king of Israel: "Let Naaman come to me." When he came, Elisha sent to tell him to go to the Jordan and bathe seven times, and so he would be rid of the leprosy. Naaman was angry that the prophet did not come out to him, pray and lay his hand on him, and in indignation he went off, saying: "Are there not rivers in our country better than the Jordan? I will go and bathe in them and be cleansed." As he went off, his servants said to him: "Do what the prophet says, since it is easy." Naaman went down and dipped himself seven times in the Jordan and was cleansed; and returning he thanked the prophet, confessed that there was no other god but the one in Israel, and asked him to take something of what he had brought; but he refused. And Naaman went back. Gehazi pursued him and said: "The prophet has sent me to take from you a talent of silver and two robes, to give to some needy men who have just come to him." Naaman gave them to him, and Gehazi returned to Elisha. But the prophet knew what Gehazi had done, and said to him: "Since you took the silver and the clothes from Naaman, his leprosy shall cling to you and your seed." And he went out a leper.

The sons of the prophets who were with Elisha went to the Jordan to cut wood to make themselves huts, and Elisha went with them. As they cut the wood, the iron head of one man's axe fell into the river. The owner of the axe called on the prophet and showed him the place where the iron had sunk. He took a piece of wood and threw it in there. The iron came up, and when it floated the man who had lost it took it.

The king of Syria set an ambush to catch King Jehoram. The prophet sent to Jehoram telling him to be on his guard and not go out hunting. He did not go out, and Hadad, having failed in his plot, suspected that his own men were betraying his plans. When they said that it was not they, but the prophet Elisha who revealed his secrets to Jehoram, he sent an army to Dothan to seize him. The prophet's servant, seeing the troops round the city, came to him in terror reporting it. He said, "Do not be afraid," and prayed God to show his servant how he was guarded by Him. And God gave the prophet's servant the grace to see him surrounded by chariots and horses of fire. The prophet, praying, also darkened the eyes of the enemy, and going out to them said: "Follow me, and I will give you Elisha." They followed, harmed both in sight and in mind. He led them to Samaria and told the king to surround them with his force. And he asked God to take the mist from their eyes. When it was taken away, the Syrians saw themselves caught in the midst of their enemies. Elisha allowed no one to attack them, but advised that they rather be entertained and released unharmed. So Jehoram, according to the prophet's word, feasted them generously and let them go. They went off and told their own king what had happened, and he was astonished.

blocks: After this the king of Syria came against Samaria with his whole army and besieged it. There was a very severe famine in it, so that an ass's head was sold for fifty pieces of silver, and a sextarius of pigeons' dung for five pieces of the same. As King Jehoram was going round the wall, a woman cried out: "Save me, O king." Thinking the woman was asking for food, he cursed her and said: "How shall I save you, when I have neither threshing floor nor winepress?" When she said she was asking for judgement, he allowed her to speak. The woman said: "I made an agreement with another woman, my neighbour, to sacrifice our children and feed each other a day at a time. I sacrificed mine, but she is breaking what was agreed." Hearing this, the king was overcome with grief and tore his clothes, and he was enraged against the prophet for not praying God to end the affliction, and sent a man to kill him. Elisha, talking with his disciples, told them beforehand: "The son of a murderer has sent to kill me; but shut the door and keep the slayer from entering, for the king will follow, having repented." They did as the prophet said, and Jehoram, changing his mind, came in haste to the prophet and blamed him for not praying God to end their sufferings. He said: "Tomorrow two measures of barley will be sold for a shekel, and a measure of fine flour for a shekel." One of those attending the king said: "You say incredible things, prophet." He said: "You will see what has been promised, but you will not enjoy it, because of your unbelief."

That night God put into the ears of the Syrians the clatter of chariots, horses and arms, and the war-cry of a multitude. Thinking that Jehoram had taken on a great allied force and that it was coming against them, they left their camp and ran away in terror. There were four lepers outside the city, since the law ordered lepers to be put out of the cities. These lepers, now perishing of hunger, decided to go to the camp of the Syrians, saying: "Either they will spare us and we shall eat and live, or we shall be killed and be rid of our miseries." So they came at dawn to the Syrian camp, and no one was to be seen; they went into one tent and found it empty of men; from it they went into another and found it deserted; and when they went into more and met no one, they first ate and drank, then took gold, silver and clothing from there and hid them, and so came into the city and proclaimed what had happened. The king, hearing it, said it was an ambush of the enemy and ordered that no one go out, but sent men to scout. They went off and met no one along the road, but found it full of clothing and equipment. Learning this, the king allowed the multitude to plunder the camp. From this there came such abundance of necessities that two measures of barley were sold for a shekel, and a measure of fine flour for a shekel (the measure is an Italian half-medimnus). Only the king's officer did not enjoy that abundance, as the prophet had said, because he had disbelieved his prediction; for when the multitude flocked to the gate of the city he was trampled and died.

After this the king of Damascus fell ill. Elisha went to Damascus then; and the sick man heard about the prophet and sent Hazael, the most honoured of his attendants, to him to ask whether he would live. He also sent him many gifts. When the prophet was asked, he foretold that the sick king would die, but told Hazael not to say anything to him; and he himself wept. Asked by Hazael the cause of his weeping, he said: "I lament, foreseeing what terrible things will befall the Israelites from you; for you will be king of Syria." Hazael returned to his master and reported that the prophet said he would live. The next day he threw a soaked net over him and smothered him, and seized the kingdom himself.

blocks: Jehoram, the king of Judah (for both kings had the same name), was rolled down into impiety by his wife Athaliah, who was the daughter of Ahab. He killed his brothers and his father's attendants, and forced the people to share his impiety. While he was living so, the prophet wrote to him, revealing his coming ruin and the destruction of his wives and children because of his impiety and the affliction of the people. These things came to pass when the Arabs invaded Judaea, and one of his sons, Ahaziah, survived. Afterwards Jehoram fell ill, as the prophet had foretold, and died a violent death, having lived forty years and reigned eight. The rule passed to his son Ahaziah.

The other Jehoram, the king of the Israelites, marching against the Syrians, happened to be shot by an arrow in the battle. He withdrew to have his wound treated, leaving Jehu the son of Nimshi as commander of the army. Elisha sent one of his disciples to anoint Jehu king, since God had chosen him. The disciple came, took Jehu aside from the others as if to tell him something secret, went into the inner room and poured the oil on his head, saying that God chose him as king so that he might wipe out the race of Ahab. As soon as he had said it, he ran quickly out of the inner room. When those with Jehu asked what the man who had called him wanted, likening him to a madman, Jehu said: "You judged rightly, for he told me words full of madness; he said that God appoints me king." Hearing this, the people sounded the trumpet and proclaimed Jehu king.

He at once took the picked men of the cavalry and set out, so as to fall suddenly on Jehoram and his men. When the watchman told Jehoram that horsemen were coming, he sent someone to ask what they wanted. Jehu gave no answer and bade him follow. Then he sent a second; when he too did not come back, Jehoram himself mounted his chariot, with Ahaziah, his sister's son, who had come to visit him, and met Jehu in the field of Naboth, and asked how things stood with the army; but Jehu poured abuse on him. Jehoram turned and fled in fear. Jehu drew his bow and shot him. He fell from the chariot and died, and was thrown into the field of Naboth, according to the prophecy Elijah had made to Ahab. Jehu shot Ahaziah too as he fled, and he died of the wound a little later, having reigned one year.

Jezebel, leaning out from the tower, adorned to make herself more alluring, said: "A good servant, who killed his master!" Jehu ordered the eunuchs to throw her down from above. As she fell, the wall was spattered with her blood, and she died. When Jehu ordered her to be buried because of her royal birth, those who were ordered found nothing of her body but the bones alone; for she had been torn to pieces by dogs, as Elijah had prophesied.

Ahab had seventy sons in Samaria. Jehu wrote to the rulers of Samaria and the guardians of Ahab's sons, bidding them make the best of them king. He wrote this to test the men. They wrote back that they had him as their master. Jehu wrote again that if they acknowledged themselves his slaves, they should bring him the heads of all Ahab's sons. They did what they were ordered. He ordered the heads to be set in two heaps before the gate of the city. When this had been done he came out and said: "I killed the king; but these have perished according to the prophet's prediction." And searching out all Ahab's kinsmen too, Jehu killed them. As he went to Samaria, Jehonadab met him, greeted him and blessed him for having destroyed the race of Ahab.

Then, so that none of the false prophets and priests of Baal might escape, he proclaimed that he was going to offer a lavish sacrifice, and ordered all the priests and prophets of Baal to be present; if anyone was not present, he said, the penalty would be death. When they had gathered, he gave them robes, went with them into the house of Baal and ordered that no one else be mixed in with them. When they said that no one else was present, he set soldiers round outside and ordered them to kill those within. They killed them all and burned the house of Baal and its pillar; but he did not remove the golden heifers. God promised him, for having wiped out the house of Ahab, that the kingdom would last to the fourth generation of his children.

blocks: So the race of Ahab was destroyed. But his daughter Athaliah, who had been the wife of Ahaziah, the king of Jerusalem, took control of the kingdom of Judah when he died, and she too set herself the task of destroying the race of David. She killed them all except one. For Ahaziah's sister, called Jehosheba, when her brother's sons were being killed, was able to hide one who was an infant, named Joash, and she brought him up for six years in secret. In the seventh year Jehoiada the high priest, whose wife Jehosheba was, called some of the captains of hundreds, showed them Joash, and conferring with the men persuaded them to rise against Athaliah and recover the boy's ancestral kingdom for him. They confirmed their agreement with oaths, went away and gathered the priests, Levites and heads of tribes before Jehoiada. He showed them Joash, saying: "This is your king, of the seed of David." He surrounded the temple with the people, and setting Joash in the middle he put the diadem on him, poured the oil of anointing over him and declared him king; and the people acclaimed him.

Athaliah, hearing the shout, rushed out of the palace in alarm, with the soldiers following her. When she came to the temple the priests let her in, but the multitude kept those with her from entering. Seeing the boy crowned, she threatened to kill those who had made an attempt on her rule. Jehoiada told the captains of hundreds to drag Athaliah outside and kill her. They did so, and Jehoiada put the king and the people on oath to honour God and keep the laws. They went at once to the temple of Baal, razed it, broke the images of Baal and killed his priest. They installed the king in the palace, being then seven years old. The high priest Jehoiada took great care that faith in God was kept and the laws observed.

When the king came of age he married two wives. Since the temple had been damaged in some parts by Athaliah, Joash was eager to restore it. He called Jehoiada the priest and ordered him to send men to ask from the whole country, for the repair of the temple, half a shekel of silver for each head. Jehoiada, seeing that the people would think this burdensome, went about collecting the money another way. He made a chest closed on every side, cut a hole in the top of it, put it by the temple and asked people to put in through the hole as much as each wished for the restoration of the temple. Since what was given was left to each one's choice, they gave without resentment and vied with one another in paying in money, so that much gold and a very great deal of silver was gathered; from it the temple was repaired and many vessels were made for the sacrifices, which were offered generously to God as long as Jehoiada lived. When he had lived justly and according to the law for a hundred and thirty years and so ended his life, King Joash grew careless about honouring God, and the heads of the tribes and the other leaders of the multitude were corrupted with him; and though prophets warned them about their impiety towards God, they did not stop. When Zechariah, the son of the high priest Jehoiada, prophesied and urged the king and the people to live by the laws, Joash was angry and ordered him to be stoned. As he was being killed, the prophet prayed that God would judge, since he was being robbed of his life by the man who had been so well served by his father. And God judged quickly: Hazael, the king of the Syrians, came and besieged Jerusalem. Joash took all the treasures, both those of God and the royal ones, and all that was in offerings, and gave them to Hazael; and he, pleased with the quantity of money, gave up the siege.
This Syrian, attacking the Israelites, did them great harm. Jehu, the king of the Israelites, who had broken the divine commandments,
text: So the race of Ahab was destroyed. But his daughter Athaliah, who had been the wife of Ahaziah, the king of Jerusalem, took control of the kingdom of Judah when he died, and she too set herself the task of destroying the race of David. She killed them all except one. For Ahaziah's sister, called Jehosheba, when her brother's sons were being killed, was able to hide one who was an infant, named Joash, and she brought him up for six years in secret. In the seventh year Jehoiada the high priest, whose wife Jehosheba was, called some of the captains of hundreds, showed them Joash, and conferring with the men persuaded them to rise against Athaliah and recover the boy's ancestral kingdom for him. They confirmed their agreement with oaths, went away and gathered the priests, Levites and heads of tribes before Jehoiada. He showed them Joash, saying: "This is your king, of the seed of David." He surrounded the temple with the people, and setting Joash in the middle he put the diadem on him, poured the oil of anointing over him and declared him king; and the people acclaimed him. Athaliah, hearing the shout, rushed out of the palace in alarm, with the soldiers following her. When she came to the temple the priests let her in, but the multitude kept those with her from entering. Seeing the boy crowned, she threatened to kill those who had made an attempt on her rule. Jehoiada told the captains of hundreds to drag Athaliah outside and kill her. They did so, and Jehoiada put the king and the people on oath to honour God and keep the laws. They went at once to the temple of Baal, razed it, broke the images of Baal and killed his priest. They installed the king in the palace, being then seven years old. The high priest Jehoiada took great care that faith in God was kept and the laws observed. When the king came of age he married two wives. Since the temple had been damaged in some parts by Athaliah, Joash was eager to restore it. He called Jehoiada the priest and ordered him to send men to ask from the whole country, for the repair of the temple, half a shekel of silver for each head. Jehoiada, seeing that the people would think this burdensome, went about collecting the money another way. He made a chest closed on every side, cut a hole in the top of it, put it by the temple and asked people to put in through the hole as much as each wished for the restoration of the temple. Since what was given was left to each one's choice, they gave without resentment and vied with one another in paying in money, so that much gold and a very great deal of silver was gathered; from it the temple was repaired and many vessels were made for the sacrifices, which were offered generously to God as long as Jehoiada lived. When he had lived justly and according to the law for a hundred and thirty years and so ended his life, King Joash grew careless about honouring God, and the heads of the tribes and the other leaders of the multitude were corrupted with him; and though prophets warned them about their impiety towards God, they did not stop. When Zechariah, the son of the high priest Jehoiada, prophesied and urged the king and the people to live by the laws, Joash was angry and ordered him to be stoned. As he was being killed, the prophet prayed that God would judge, since he was being robbed of his life by the man who had been so well served by his father. And God judged quickly: Hazael, the king of the Syrians, came and besieged Jerusalem. Joash took all the treasures, both those of God and the royal ones, and all that was in offerings, and gave them to Hazael; and he, pleased with the quantity of money, gave up the siege. This Syrian, attacking the Israelites, did them great harm. Jehu, the king of the Israelites, who had broken the divine commandments,

blocks: died after reigning twenty-seven years, and his son Jehoahaz took the kingdom. In his reign the leader of the Syrians afflicted the country, took many of his cities and put his army to the sword. Meanwhile Jehoahaz prayed to God and found deliverance and a respite from his troubles. He died after reigning seventeen years, having as successor to the kingdom his son Joash, who had the same name as the king of the tribe of Judah. This Joash was not like his father, but good. When Elisha fell ill and was dying, he lamented, calling him father and weapon, since through him he prevailed over his enemies. The prophet comforted him and told him to take a bow and shoot arrows. When the king had shot three times and stopped, Elisha said: "If you had shot more arrows, you would have cut out the rule of the Syrians by the root; but now you will win as many victories over them as the arrows, and recover for your rule the land they took away." Then the prophet died and was given a magnificent burial. Some robbers, having killed a man, threw him into the prophet's tomb; and the man who was thrown in came back to life and stood up.

Hazael, the king of Syria, also died, leaving his son Hadad as successor. Joash, the king of the Israelites, engaged him, defeated him three times and recovered for Israel the country and cities which Hazael, Hadad's father, had taken.

Joash, the king of Judah, who was seven years old when he was proclaimed, died after reigning forty years, killed by his attendants. His son Amaziah took on the kingdom of Jerusalem; he was pious, twenty-five years old when he came to the throne, and he held the kingdom for twenty-nine years. He punished those who had killed his father, but let their children go unharmed, according to the law that says: "Fathers shall not die for sons, nor sons because of fathers." Marching against the Idumaeans and Amalekites, he hired allies from the Israelites. A prophet advised him to leave his allies behind and fight the war with his own men alone. He obeyed and dismissed the Israelites, letting them keep their pay. Engaging the foreigners, he won. But the dismissed allies, in anger, overran the country of the Jews and killed many.

Amaziah, puffed up by his success and impious towards God, sent to Joash, the king of Israel, demanding that he come to him, since he ought to be subject to him as the descendant of David and Solomon. Joash sent back word to him: "The thorn asked the cedar for a marriage alliance for its children. Meanwhile the beasts of the field, passing by, trampled the thorn, and it perished. Let this be example enough for you; and do not be proud because you have had the good fortune to strike down the foreigners, nor drive your people and yourself into danger." Angered at this, Amaziah marched against Joash. Fear fell on his army, and it turned to flight; Amaziah, left alone, was captured by the enemy and brought to Joash. He brought him bound to Jerusalem, pulled down part of the wall, drove through the breach into the city in a chariot, and took the sacred treasures and all that was stored in the palace. Then he released Amaziah and returned to Samaria. He died after reigning sixteen years in all, and his son Jeroboam became king. Amaziah afterwards fell victim to a plot and was killed, having lived fifty-four years and reigned twenty-nine. His son Uzziah was anointed king at the age of sixteen.

blocks: Jeroboam the son of Joash was impious and lawless. Yet, such as he was, since God took pity on the Israelite people in their humiliation, he made war on the Syrians and won, the prophet Jonah having foretold the victory to him.

God sent this prophet to the city of Nineveh to proclaim its overthrow and the destruction of the Ninevites. But he did not go, and ran away by boarding a ship. A storm arose and the ship was in danger. When those on board tried by lot to learn who was to blame, the lot fell on Jonah. Questioned who he was, he told his story, and urged them to throw him into the sea; "for in no other way," he said, "will you escape the danger." So he was thrown in, and the storm abated. A sea monster swallowed the prophet and after three days and as many nights spat him out alive and well. He asked God's pardon for his disobedience, and was sent again to proclaim what he had been ordered. He went and proclaimed that Nineveh would be overthrown after three days. The king of the city and all the people believed the prophet, turned to repentance and besought God to have mercy on them. And He, bent by the repentance of the multitude, turned the destruction away from them.
Jeroboam died after reigning forty-one years, and after him his son Zechariah held the rule.

Uzziah, the king of Jerusalem, was pious towards God and just towards his subjects; so he defeated many of the foreigners and made them tributary. But having prospered and grown conceited, he fell away from what was fitting. Robed as a priest, he set about burning incense to God on the golden altar; and when Azariah the high priest and the priests tried to stop him and urged him not to break the law, he threatened them with death unless they kept quiet. Then a kind of light shone out in the temple and struck the king's face, and made leprosy break out on it. The priests told the king of his misfortune and advised him to leave the city. He lived so for some time, and died of despondency, having reigned fifty-two years and lived sixty-eight in all, handing the rule to his son Jotham.

Zechariah the son of Jeroboam died after six months as king of the Israelites, having lived impiously, murdered by Shallum. Shallum, after reigning thirty days, was killed by Menahem, who reigned over Israel in his place. When Pul, the king of the Assyrians, made war on him, he gave him a thousand talents of silver, which he collected from the people, and ended the war. Menahem, after reigning ten years, impious and harsh, died, passing the kingdom to his son Pekahiah. He too was impious and cruel, and was murdered by Pekah the son of Remaliah, who reigned in place of the murdered man, and he too held the rule impiously and lawlessly. At that time Tiglath-pileser, the king of the Assyrians, invaded the country of the Israelites, overthrew many cities and carried off to his own country a host of captives not easy to count.

Jotham the son of Uzziah, king of Jerusalem, was pious and just; he cared for the city and the temple, and made the Ammonites tributary after defeating them in battle. Nahum, who was prophesying then, foretold the overthrow of Nineveh; and his prediction came true when a hundred and fifteen years had passed. Jotham's life failed him when he had lived forty-one years and reigned sixteen.

blocks: The rule of Jerusalem passed to his son, who was impious towards God and broke His laws; for he bowed down to idols, set up an altar to them in Jerusalem and offered his own son to them as a burnt offering. Against him Rezin, the ruler of the Syrians, and Pekah, the king of the Israelites, made common cause and besieged him for a long time in Jerusalem. Rezin, having taken other cities, killed their inhabitants, settled Syrians in them and returned to Damascus. Ahaz, when Pekah alone was left, engaged him and was defeated, losing a hundred and twenty thousand of his people and many men of note, and his son. Pekah went back to Samaria, he and his army, carrying a great multitude of captives away to their own country. But a prophet met them before the walls of Samaria, rebuked them for taking their kinsmen captive and advised them to set them free; and they were persuaded and released the captives.

Ahaz asked the king of the Assyrians to help him against the Syrians and the Israelites. He came, ravaged the country of the Syrians, took Damascus, killed Rezin, overran the country of the Israelites and carried off very many captives. In return for this Ahaz gave Tiglath-pileser the royal treasures and all that was stored in the temple. He went so far in impiety that he not only worshipped the gods of the foreigners, but also shut up the temple and plundered its offerings. Having lived so, he died at thirty-six, after reigning sixteen years, leaving the kingdom to his son Hezekiah. It happened that the king of the Israelites also died then, through the plot of Hoshea. He too was wicked; so when Shalmaneser, the king of the Assyrians, marched against him, he was made his slave and ordered to pay tribute every year.

Hezekiah, being pious and just, called an assembly of the priests and Levites, ordered them to open the temple and sacrifice as was their law, and bade the people put nothing before the honour of God. He also sent to the whole country, calling everyone to keep the feast of unleavened bread, which had not been celebrated for a long time because of the lawlessness of those in power. He urged the Israelites too to worship the God of their fathers according to the ancient custom. But they would not be persuaded, and even murdered the prophets who urged the same; though some, persuaded, turned to piety and flocked to Jerusalem to worship God. King Hezekiah went with the leaders of the people to the temple, offered lavish sacrifices through the priests, gave the people many animals for feasting, and ordered the priests to go out into the country and purify it. Then he made war on the foreigners and took cities from them.

Hoshea, the king of the Israelites, called on So, the king of Egypt, to ally with him against the Assyrians. Learning this, Shalmaneser was angry; he besieged Samaria for three years, took the city and wiped out the kingdom, and carried the people captive into his own country, with Hoshea, the king of the Israelites, himself. Moving other nations out of his own country, from a place called Cuthah, he settled them in Samaria and its territory. So the ten tribes of the Israelites were carried away nine hundred and forty-seven years after they left Egypt, and two hundred and forty years and seven months after they abandoned Rehoboam and chose Jeroboam as their king.

Those who were moved into Samaria, called Cuthaeans from the place in Persia where they had lived before, being five nations, again worshipped their own gods. As the Fourth Book of Kingdoms says, God roused lions and destroyed many of them; as Josephus records, a plague fell on them. Knowing that the evils came on them through God's anger, they begged their king to send them priests from among the Israelites, to initiate them in the worship of the Hebrews; and when this was done the destruction stopped. They are called Cuthaeans by the Hebrews, and Samaritans by the Greeks.

blocks: In the fourteenth year of the reign of Hezekiah, king of Jerusalem, Sennacherib, the reigning king of the Assyrians, came against Judaea and took all the cities of the two tribes. Hezekiah, afraid for Jerusalem, sent to him promising to pay whatever tribute he imposed. Sennacherib asked for three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold, and gave sworn pledges that he would withdraw if he received them. Having received them, he set off himself against the Egyptians and Ethiopians, and left his commander-in-chief Rabshakeh with two other generals and a heavy force to sack Jerusalem. They threw up a palisade before the walls and asked to speak with Hezekiah. He was afraid to go out, but sent three men of rank under him. Rabshakeh said to them: "If Hezekiah trusts in the Egyptians, he is a fool, like a man leaning on a staff of reed, and a cracked one, which gave no help to the man holding it, but he fell and the reed pierced his hand. Such is Pharaoh the Egyptian." Rabshakeh said this in Hebrew to those who had been sent. They asked him to speak to them in the Syrian language, so that the multitude might not understand what was said. But he raised his voice the more and said again in Hebrew, in the hearing of all: "Do not let Hezekiah deceive you, saying, 'The Lord will rescue us.' Did He rescue Samaria?"

They reported this to Hezekiah. Hearing it, he tore his clothes and put on sackcloth, and falling down he prayed to God, asking for help in a hopeless plight; and he sent to Isaiah the prophet and begged him to pray to God to be merciful to the people. Isaiah foretold that the enemy would be defeated without a battle, and that Sennacherib would come back from Egypt having achieved nothing and be killed. Sennacherib also wrote to Hezekiah: "Do not let your God, in whom you trust, encourage you that Jerusalem will not be delivered into my hands. Consider where are the kings of the nations whom my fathers destroyed." Hezekiah read this letter, laid it in the temple and besought God, saying: "See, Lord, and hear the words of Sennacherib, which he sent to taunt you, the living God, and save us from his hand." Isaiah encouraged the king, saying that God had heard him. That night an angel killed a hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians, and at daybreak their bodies were found dead. What was left of the army departed from Jerusalem.

Sennacherib, besieging Pelusium, raised the siege when in a single night mice ate the bows of the Assyrians and the rest of their arms. This is not recorded in the book of Kingdoms, but Josephus tells it, having found it in Herodotus. He says that Berossus, who wrote the history of Chaldaea, states that when Sennacherib returned from the war with the Egyptians he found the army with Rabshakeh at Jerusalem; and when God struck the Assyrians with a pestilence, in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand perished, with their commanders and captains. Afraid for the rest of the army, he left there with the force that remained and went off to Nineveh. Shortly after, he fell victim to a plot by his elder sons and was killed; his murderers fled, and his son Esarhaddon succeeded to the rule.

Hezekiah, freed from fear, gave thanks to God. Shortly after, when he fell ill, Isaiah came to him at God's command and said: "Set your house in order, for you will not live." The expectation of death, and that, having no children, he would leave the kingdom without a lawful heir, made the misfortune greater for him; and despondent at this he wept, asking God to grant him more life. Isaiah came again and brought him the good news of health after the third day and an addition of fifteen years of life. Considering how extraordinary the wonder was, he asked the prophet to show him a sign as pledge of what had been promised. When the prophet prayed God that a sign be given, the sun, which had already declined ten steps and cast a shadow, turned back ten steps. From then on Hezekiah was rid of the disease.

Baladan, the king of the Babylonians, sent an embassy to Hezekiah with gifts, asking to have him as ally and friend. He showed the envoys his treasures, his arms and all the royal splendour, sent gifts back to the Babylonian and dismissed them. Isaiah said to Hezekiah: "Days will come, and the wealth you have put on show will be carried off to Babylon, and your sons will be eunuchs to the king of Babylon." Hezekiah, since the word of God could not fail, said: "Let there be peace in my days." He lived out the time added to him peacefully and died, having reached his fifty-fourth year and reigned twenty-nine.

His son Manasseh, succeeding to the rule, at first showed every kind of wickedness and impiety, defiling the temple and not even sparing the prophets. God, angered at this, moved the army of the Babylonians against Judaea, which plundered the country and captured Manasseh. He, understanding that he himself was the cause of his misfortune, turned to repentance and begged God to release him from his troubles. And God heard him, freed him from captivity and restored him to the kingdom. When he returned he pursued piety himself and persuaded the people to pursue it. Having lived so, he became admired for his piety, and died after reigning fifty-five years and living sixty-seven in all.

What was left of the army departed from Jerusalem. Sennacherib, besieging Pelusium, raised the siege when in a single night mice ate the bows of the Assyrians and the rest of their arms. This is not recorded in the book of Kingdoms, but Josephus tells it, having found it in Herodotus. He says that Berossus, who wrote the history of Chaldaea, states that when Sennacherib returned from the war with the Egyptians he found the army with Rabshakeh at Jerusalem; and when God struck the Assyrians with a pestilence, in one night a hundred and eighty-five thousand perished, with their commanders and captains. Afraid for the rest of the army, he left there with the force that remained and went off to Nineveh. Shortly after, he fell victim to a plot by his elder sons and was killed; his murderers fled, and his son Esarhaddon succeeded to the rule. Hezekiah, freed from fear, gave thanks to God. Shortly after, when he fell ill, Isaiah came to him at God's command and said: "Set your house in order, for you will not live." The expectation of death, and that, having no children, he would leave the kingdom without a lawful heir, made the misfortune greater for him; and despondent at this he wept, asking God to grant him more life. Isaiah came again and brought him the good news of health after the third day and an addition of fifteen years of life. Considering how extraordinary the wonder was, he asked the prophet to show him a sign as pledge of what had been promised. When the prophet prayed God that a sign be given, the sun, which had already declined ten steps and cast a shadow, turned back ten steps. From then on Hezekiah was rid of the disease. Baladan, the king of the Babylonians, sent an embassy to Hezekiah with gifts, asking to have him as ally and friend. He showed the envoys his treasures, his arms and all the royal splendour, sent gifts back to the Babylonian and dismissed them. Isaiah said to Hezekiah: "Days will come, and the wealth you have put on show will be carried off to Babylon, and your sons will be eunuchs to the king of Babylon." Hezekiah, since the word of God could not fail, said: "Let there be peace in my days." He lived out the time added to him peacefully and died, having reached his fifty-fourth year and reigned twenty-nine. His son Manasseh, succeeding to the rule, at first showed every kind of wickedness and impiety, defiling the temple and not even sparing the prophets. God, angered at this, moved the army of the Babylonians against Judaea, which plundered the country and captured Manasseh. He, understanding that he himself was the cause of his misfortune, turned to repentance and begged God to release him from his troubles. And God heard him, freed him from captivity and restored him to the kingdom. When he returned he pursued piety himself and persuaded the people to pursue it. Having lived so, he became admired for his piety, and died after reigning fifty-five years and living sixty-seven in all.

blocks: The kingdom passed to his son Amon, who imitated his father's youth. He died the victim of a plot, having lived twenty-four years and reigned two. The multitude punished his murderers and declared his son Josiah king, then in his eighth year; he was pious and persuaded the people to be pious. Wishing to repair the temple, he urged his subjects to give for the repair as much as each wished. With the money collected in this way the temple was restored, and he used what was left over for mixing-bowls, libation cups and bowls, under the supervision of the high priest Hilkiah. While bringing the silver out of the temple treasury, Hilkiah came upon the sacred books of Moses, which were stored there, and sent them to the king by the scribe. When they were read to him, he tore his clothes and sent Hilkiah the high priest and others to the prophetess Huldah, the wife of Shallum, asking her to appease God. She said that God had already passed sentence against the country and the people for their impiety, but because the king was just He would not bring the evils now; when he had passed away, what had been decreed would happen. Hearing this, he gathered the people at Jerusalem and had the sacred books read in the hearing of all. Then he required oaths from all to keep the laws and worship God. And the people, sacrificing, appeased the Lord.

He also burned the offerings to the idols, put their priests to death, and burned the bones of the false prophets on the altar which Jeroboam had set up, according to the prediction of the prophet who came to Jeroboam as he sacrificed and foretold that a descendant of David, Josiah, would do these things three hundred and sixty-one years later. Josiah also went to the Israelites who had escaped the captivity and urged them to worship the God of their fathers and live by the laws. Having wiped out the idols from the whole country, he gathered the multitude at Jerusalem and kept the feast of unleavened bread, which they call Pascha. He led a peaceful life, but at the end he was shot by an arrow and died. For Necho, the king of the Egyptians, was going off to make war on the Medes, and Josiah tried to stop him passing through his country. Necho told him that he was not marching against him; but Josiah would not give way. So they were drawn up to fight, and the Egyptian shot Josiah as he was marshalling his own people, and so ended the war. The king went back to Jerusalem and died, having reigned thirty-one years and lived eight before his reign.

In his time Jeremiah was the prophet, who foretold the terrible things that would befall Jerusalem and its capture by the Romans. And not he alone wrote about these things beforehand: Ezekiel too was the first to leave two books about them. Both were of the priestly tribe.

When Josiah died, his son Jehoahaz ruled, at twenty-three years old, an impious man. The king of the Egyptians, returning from the war, put him in chains and gave the kingdom to his elder brother Eliakim, renaming him Jehoiakim, and imposed on the country a tribute of a hundred talents of silver and one of gold. Jehoahaz he took away to Egypt, where he died. The length of his reign was three months and ten days.

Jehoiakim, who was impious and wicked, was already in the fourth year of his reign when Nebuchadnezzar took on the rule of the Babylonians. He defeated Necho the Egyptian and took away a great part of his country. In the eighth year of Jehoiakim's reign he invaded Judaea with a heavy force. Jehoiakim, afraid, made his country tributary to the Babylonian. For three years he brought the tribute; then, hearing that the Egyptians were marching against the Babylonian, he held back the payment of tribute, although the prophet Jeremiah foretold the capture of the city by the Babylonian and the death of King Jehoiakim, and not only said it but also wrote it and read the writing in the hearing of the multitude. The leaders took it and brought it to the king; and he, enraged at what was written, burned the writing in the fire, and sought to punish the prophet and his scribe Baruch. They fled and avoided his anger. Not long after, the Babylonian marched against him, and Jehoiakim received him into the city without resistance. But he killed the better citizens and the king himself, carried off three thousand of the finest as captives, among whom was the prophet Ezekiel, then a boy, and declared the son of the murdered king, also named Jehoiakim, king of Judaea. So Jehoiakim met his end, having lived thirty-six years and reigned eleven.

The Babylonian, suspecting that his son would bear a grudge for the murder of his father and revolt, sent and besieged him. He, not wishing the city to be endangered because of him, gave himself and his kin up to the enemy on terms that they would do no harm to the city or to them. The Babylonian broke these terms, ordering all the youth in the city and the craftsmen to be brought to him, who numbered ten thousand eight hundred and thirty-two. Jehoiakim, his mother and his friends he shut up and kept under guard, after he had reigned three months

blocks: and ten days. He handed over the kingdom of Jerusalem to Zedekiah, Jehoiakim's uncle, who swore that he would not favour the Egyptians, but would keep the country for him. Zedekiah was young, for he was twenty-one when he received the rule, and he despised what was just and fitting; he did not heed Jeremiah when he urged him to give up his impieties and lawlessness, nor believe him when he told of the calamities that would come on him and on the people, which Ezekiel too foretold in Babylon and wrote and sent to Jerusalem. Zedekiah disbelieved both prophets because they seemed to disagree. On other matters they agreed, but about Zedekiah himself they seemed to contradict each other: Ezekiel prophesied that he would not see Babylon, while Jeremiah foretold that he would be led in chains to Babylon. But what was foretold about him agreed with both prophets; for he was blinded in Judaea and led away in chains, and did not see Babylon.

This Zedekiah kept faith with the Babylonian for eight years, and then turned to the Egyptians. So Nebuchadnezzar marched out and besieged Jerusalem. When the Egyptians came to help the Jews, the Babylonian went out to meet them, routed them and pursued them. The false prophets said that the enemy would no longer besiege them; but Jeremiah foretold that they would come back, take the city, raze it, burn the temple, and carry off as captives of war the people who were left by then, to serve for seventy years until the Persians and Medes put an end to the rule of the Babylonians; and then they would be freed from captivity and rebuild the temple and the city. Jeremiah said this; but the king and those about him mocked his words. As the prophet was going to his native place, Anathoth, one of the officials met him, seized him as a deserter and brought him to the rulers; and they mistreated him and kept him for punishment.

In the ninth year of Zedekiah's reign the Babylonian came against Jerusalem the second time, and for a year and a half besieged the city hard. Famine came with the siege, and after it pestilence. Jeremiah, though imprisoned, urged the multitude to receive the Babylonian, for so they would be saved; if not, they would stay and perish by famine or the sword; "but whoever goes over to the enemy," he said, "will escape death." Yet no one thought the prophet trustworthy, and the leaders even stirred up the king against him. He, courting them because of the crisis, let them deal with the prophet as they wished. And they threw him into a muddy pit. Zedekiah, learning this, ordered him to be pulled out of there, called him secretly and asked what he said about the present dangers. He advised him to hand over the city to the Babylonian. Zedekiah said he was afraid he would be killed. The prophet insisted that if he did so he would meet with nothing hard. So the king let him go; but the Babylonian pressed the siege of the city with violent assaults and took it in the eleventh year of Zedekiah's rule.

Zedekiah fled from the city with his wives, children, kin and friends. The enemy pursued him and caught him alone, for his leaders and friends had scattered. They took him alive with his children and wives and brought them to the Babylonian. He reproached him with ingratitude and faithlessness, ordered his sons and his friends to be killed before his eyes, then blinded him and took him in chains to Babylon. Then he understood that both prophets had foretold the truth.

This was the end of those of the seed of David who had reigned. They were twenty-one in all, and five hundred and fourteen years, six months and sixteen days had passed since Saul came to the throne. Nebuzaradan, the chief cook of the Babylonian, was sent and burned the temple and the palace, razed the city and plundered everything in the temple. The temple was burned four hundred and seventy years, six months and ten days from the time it was built; one thousand and sixty-two years, six months and ten days after the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt; one thousand nine hundred and fifty-seven years, six months and ten days after the flood; and from the bringing forth of the first man until then three thousand five hundred and thirteen years, six months and ten days had passed.

blocks: Nebuzaradan, having razed Jerusalem, took the people, the high priest Seraiah and the sacred vessels to Babylon. Nebuchadnezzar dedicated the vessels of God to his own gods and settled the captives in his own country. Nebuzaradan left in Judaea those who had deserted to the Babylonians during the siege, and the poor, and set over them as governor Gedaliah, a man of good family, fair and just; he told them to work the land and ordered them to pay tribute to Nebuchadnezzar. He urged the prophet Jeremiah to go to Babylon; but he wished to live among the ruins of his country. So he left him there, ordering Gedaliah to take every care of him. He also released to him his disciple Baruch, who was exceptionally learned in his native tongue. All who had escaped from Jerusalem because of the siege came to Gedaliah. He advised them to farm the land, to live in whatever city each wished, and to rebuild the ruins. Knowing Gedaliah to be a good man, they loved him dearly.

Among the others there returned a man called Ishmael, of the royal family, who had fled to the Ammonites at the time of the siege. When he came to Gedaliah, some told him that Ishmael was plotting against him, and that if he would let them kill the man he would escape the plot. But he did not believe it, and said he thought it better to die himself than to kill a man who had trusted himself to him. Some time later this Ishmael came to Gedaliah with others, and when he had been entertained he killed Gedaliah and his fellow guests. Then, falling by night on the Babylonians left in the city, he killed them and all the Jews there. The next day, when eighty men came from the country to Gedaliah with gifts, Ishmael killed them too, except a few, who promised to show him furniture, clothing and grain hidden in the fields. Taking many captives as well, he went off to the Ammonites. Some leaders of the Jews, learning this and rousing those with them, pursued him; they recovered the captives, but Ishmael escaped with eight men.

The survivors, afraid of the Babylonians, planned to go to Egypt. Jeremiah advised them to stay, saying that if they stayed God would watch over them so that they suffered no harm, but if they left He would not be with them; but they did not believe him, and disobeying they departed for Egypt, taking Jeremiah and Baruch with them. When the prophet had gone there, God revealed the future to him. He foretold to his countrymen that the Babylonian would march against the Egyptians and master Egypt, and would kill some of them and carry off others as captives. For this he was stoned to death by his fellow tribesmen. But what he foretold happened: in the fifth year after the sack of Jerusalem Nebuchadnezzar set out against Coele Syria, and having taken it he attacked the Ammonites and Moabites, and from there marched on Egypt; he subdued it, killed its king and set up another, and carried the Jews there off to Babylon. Jeremiah was buried in Egypt, and it is said that King Alexander, when he became master of Egypt among other lands, and the Egyptians were singing the prophet's praises, moved his bones to the city he had founded, Alexandria.

So the prophet foretold, as I have said, what would happen; and the race of the Hebrews met this end, carried beyond the Euphrates. For the ten tribes were taken captive by the Assyrians from Samaria in the reign of Hoshea, and the two tribes were taken captive afterwards by Nebuchadnezzar, with all who were left after the capture of Jerusalem. Shalmaneser moved the nation of the Cuthaeans from Persia to Samaria, but Nebuchadnezzar left Judaea empty, and it remained so for seventy years. The time between the captivity of the ten tribes from Samaria and that of the two from Jerusalem was a hundred and thirty years, six months and ten days.

blocks: The Babylonian made eunuchs of the noblest boys among the captives, those related to King Zedekiah and those who surpassed the rest in vigour and beauty, handed them to tutors, and had them taught the letters of the Chaldaeans and the learning of the country, assigning them their food from his own table. Four of the boys were of the royal family, handsome in looks and good in nature. The Babylonian renamed the one called Daniel Belteshazzar, the one named Hananiah Shadrach, the other, called Mishael, Meshach, and the last, Azariah, Abednego. He held them in more honour than the rest, since through their gifts they were advancing in wisdom. These young men begged the eunuch in charge of them not to feed them on what was supplied from the royal table, but on pulses, dates and other such things. He said he was afraid that if they were fed on such things their bodies would grow thin, and that he himself would be punished by the king for it. They begged him to feed them so for ten days; if the condition of their bodies did not change, he should feed them so from then on, but if he saw their bodies growing thin, he should go back to the former diet. The man in charge of the boys agreed, and when he did so and saw that they suffered nothing from such food, but rather became more flourishing than the others, he gave them food without meat. With their minds made keener, they mastered the whole of Chaldaean and Assyrian learning. Daniel also applied himself to the interpretation of dreams.

Then Nebuchadnezzar saw an extraordinary dream, and learning its interpretation in his sleep, he forgot both the dream and its interpretation. So at dawn he sent for the Chaldaeans, the seers and the magi, and demanded that they tell him the dream and its meaning. They wanted him first to tell the dream, and then ask them what it signified. The king was angry at this, and condemned them all to death when they said they could not find the dream. As wise men, Daniel and the three boys were summoned and condemned with them. Daniel went to the commander of the royal bodyguard and asked that the execution of the condemned be put off for one night; "for perhaps," he said, "during it we shall pray to God and come to know the dream." The king granted the request. Daniel, taking with him the three boys, his kinsmen, besought God through the night. Both the dream and what it signified were revealed to him by God. At daybreak he went to the king and told him that the dream and its meaning had been made known to him by God, who had pitied those in danger of dying unjustly for it, "and no less you, who wished to kill so many without cause because you demanded impossible things, which are known to the divine nature alone. What you saw is this. You seemed to see a great statue standing, whose head was of gold, its shoulders and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, and its legs and feet partly of iron and partly of clay. Then a stone broken off from a mountain seemed to fall on the statue and shatter it, and to grind the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron and the clay so fine that they were winnowed and scattered by the wind. The stone seemed to grow and reach such a size that the whole earth was filled by it. That is your dream. And what is revealed to you by it, as you ponder about the kingdom and who will rule after you, is this. The golden head is you and the other kings of the Babylonians, and the gold shows the great wealth of your rule. He imaged it by the legs because it came later in time: for the kingdom of the Romans is later than the other great kingdoms, and the legs and feet are the last parts of the body. text: The Babylonian made eunuchs of the noblest boys among the captives, those related to King Zedekiah and those who surpassed the rest in vigour and beauty, handed them to tutors, and had them taught the letters of the Chaldaeans and the learning of the country, assigning them their food from his own table. Four of the boys were of the royal family, handsome in looks and good in nature. The Babylonian renamed the one called Daniel Belteshazzar, the one named Hananiah Shadrach, the other, called Mishael, Meshach, and the last, Azariah, Abednego. He held them in more honour than the rest, since through their gifts they were advancing in wisdom. These young men begged the eunuch in charge of them not to feed them on what was supplied from the royal table, but on pulses, dates and other such things. He said he was afraid that if they were fed on such things their bodies would grow thin, and that he himself would be punished by the king for it. They begged him to feed them so for ten days; if the condition of their bodies did not change, he should feed them so from then on, but if he saw their bodies growing thin, he should go back to the former diet. The man in charge of the boys agreed, and when he did so and saw that they suffered nothing from such food, but rather became more flourishing than the others, he gave them food without meat. With their minds made keener, they mastered the whole of Chaldaean and Assyrian learning. Daniel also applied himself to the interpretation of dreams. Then Nebuchadnezzar saw an extraordinary dream, and learning its interpretation in his sleep, he forgot both the dream and its interpretation. So at dawn he sent for the Chaldaeans, the seers and the magi, and demanded that they tell him the dream and its meaning. They wanted him first to tell the dream, and then ask them what it signified. The king was angry at this, and condemned them all to death when they said they could not find the dream. As wise men, Daniel and the three boys were summoned and condemned with them. Daniel went to the commander of the royal bodyguard and asked that the execution of the condemned be put off for one night; "for perhaps," he said, "during it we shall pray to God and come to know the dream." The king granted the request. Daniel, taking with him the three boys, his kinsmen, besought God through the night. Both the dream and what it signified were revealed to him by God. At daybreak he went to the king and told him that the dream and its meaning had been made known to him by God, who had pitied those in danger of dying unjustly for it, "and no less you, who wished to kill so many without cause because you demanded impossible things, which are known to the divine nature alone. What you saw is this. You seemed to see a great statue standing, whose head was of gold, its shoulders and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze, and its legs and feet partly of iron and partly of clay. Then a stone broken off from a mountain seemed to fall on the statue and shatter it, and to grind the gold, the silver, the bronze, the iron and the clay so fine that they were winnowed and scattered by the wind. The stone seemed to grow and reach such a size that the whole earth was filled by it. That is your dream. And what is revealed to you by it, as you ponder about the kingdom and who will rule after you, is this. The golden head is you and the other kings of the Babylonians, and the gold shows the great wealth of your rule. The two hands and the shoulders image two kingdoms by which your rule will be brought to an end. The bronze belly and thighs show a king clothed in bronze, who will overthrow those who end your rule. blocks: If one wished to refer the vision to the earlier condition of the Roman government, when the senate, the dictators, the consuls, the tribunes and the people shared in managing public affairs, he will find the people often at odds with the senate and seditions arising, the senate ordering some things and the multitude bringing in others against them, so that from this they fought one another, and their affairs, through the discord, at times tipped towards the worse and weaker. One might image the senate by iron, for the firmness of its judgement; and the multitude, mixed with those in office and with the council, might be likened to clay, both for its rabble-like and lowly nature (for such is the mud from which clay is made) and for its changeability and weakness of mind. For the multitude is apt to be unstable and easily led and to change its mind; and anyone who reads the ancient writings about the Roman state will find this happening to it very often.

If, then, one refers the difference of the materials and their mixing to the earlier condition of the Roman state, he might perhaps reckon so. But if to the later one, when the affairs of the Romans passed from aristocracy to monarchy, and to the condition of the empire that followed, he would find then too that the discord of the Romans with one another did the state very great harm. For Caesar, reaching for sole rule, brought about civil wars against Pompey the Great and the others who laid claim to the old liberty; Caesar Augustus and Antony in turn fought similar battles against those who killed him; and then these two, quarrelling with each other over sole power, stirred up heavy wars, men of the same race perishing on both sides in all the battles, so that the Roman power was diminished. Nor would one see the seditions abate in the times that followed. And if one compares the nature of iron and clay with the later reigns, he will find the rule of the Romans strong in one way and weak in another, having lost the greater part of its ancient dominion, and now confined to a small fraction of that ancient empire.

So much for the four kingdoms. The remaining one, which cannot be destroyed, imaged by the stone which was cut without hands, ground fine the materials of which the image was made and filled the whole earth, which the prophet said would not be destroyed for ever, would be the future appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ. It will appear when the iron kingdom has become weaker through the admixture of clay; then all things will be subjected to Him, and He will grant an endless and incorruptible kingdom to those who have made themselves worthy of it. For Scripture is accustomed to call Christ a stone. David said: "The stone which the builders rejected, this has become the head of the corner"; and Isaiah says in the person of God: "See, I lay in Zion a cornerstone." The great Paul too calls Christ the cornerstone, on which he wrote that the believers are built up; and again he says: "No one can lay another foundation than the one that is laid, which is Jesus Christ"; and again elsewhere: "They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ." He is also called a rock of offence and a stone of stumbling, and in many places the Lord may be found called a stone and a rock. That it was cut without hands foretold His birth beyond nature, without seed and without marital union. For the mountain may be taken as the tribe of Judah, from which David came; the stone is Christ, cut from it in His human nature; and without hands, because He came forth not by the laws of nature but from a holy womb that knew no man. He seemed small at first because of the nature of His humanity, but as He went on He filled the whole inhabited world with His glory, and will fill it yet more at His future appearing.

So the prophet told Nebuchadnezzar the dream and revealed its interpretation. Amazed, he fell on his face, bowed down before Daniel and ordered sacrifice to be made to him, that arrogant and haughty man not giving all the honour to him, but to the God whom he worshipped. For he said: "In truth this God of yours is God of gods and Lord of kings, and a revealer of mysteries." He gave him many gifts, made him ruler of all Babylon, and named him Belteshazzar, giving him the name of his own god.

blocks: Then he set up a golden statue, sixty cubits high and six broad, and called together the leading men from all his realm, ordering that when they heard the trumpet they should fall down and worship the statue, and that those who disobeyed should be thrown into the furnace of fire, which he lit there, great and fierce. While all were worshipping, the three young men whom the history has recorded as Daniel's kinsmen, unwilling to break their ancestral laws, did not worship. They were thrown at once into the furnace; but the fire did not touch them, and standing in the midst of that irresistible flame they sent up a hymn to God. With those three stood a fourth: it was an angel who had come down with them and was turning that fiery air into a dewy breeze. This astonished the beastlike and stubborn soul of that king; putting aside his conceit, he came forward, called the young men by name and blessed their God, held those men worthy of honour and made them leaders of all the Jews in Babylon.

A little later that Assyrian saw another dream. He saw a tree, great and reaching to the ends of the earth, beautiful with leaves and laden with fruit. Under it the wild beasts made their dwelling, and the birds lived in its branches. Then he saw a Watcher come from heaven and call out with strength: "Cut down the tree, strip off its branches, shake off its leaves and scatter its fruit; but leave the stock of its roots. With a band of iron, in the grass of the earth and in the dew of heaven he shall lodge, and his portion shall be with the beasts; his heart shall be changed from that of men, the heart of a beast shall be given him, and seven times shall pass over him." Seeing this vision, he again called together the magi and the wise men of Babylon and sought to learn what was signified by it. They were at a loss and could not tell the meaning of the dream. Then again he had recourse to Daniel, told him the dream and asked him to give its interpretation; "for you can," he said, "since the holy Spirit of God is in you." He said: "My lord the king, may this dream be for those who hate you." Then he explained its meaning to him, saying: "The great tree which you saw is you, O king, for you have become great and strong, and your greatness has reached to heaven and your lordship to the ends of the earth." By greatness he meant the exaltation of his mind and the arrogance of his spirit. "And since you saw a holy Watcher coming down from heaven," that is, a divine angel (for ir, put into Greek, means "the one who is awake", by which the bodiless is hinted at; for one who wears a body is enslaved to sleep, but one not enslaved to it has a bodiless nature), "since, then," he said, "you saw that Watcher call out that the tree be cut down but the stock of its roots be left, and the rest, expect to fall from the kingdom and be driven out of the company of men, to live with the beasts and eat grass; yet not to be wholly deprived of the kingdom, but to have it restored to you again; for this is what the leaving of the stock of the tree's roots signifies."

Such was the interpretation of the vision that Daniel gave Nebuchadnezzar. And everything happened according to the divine oracle: the king fell sick with madness because of his boastfulness and arrogance and spent seven years in the desert; and since no one laid hands on his kingdom, he recovered it after appeasing God. He died after reigning forty-three years. Josephus says that many of the ancient historians mention him, Berossus, Megasthenes, Diocles and Philostratus.

When he died, his elder son Evil-merodach succeeded to the rule. He at once released from his chains King Jehoiakim, also called Jeconiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had kept in prison, held him worthy of honour, gave him gifts, and had him at his table always.
