blocks: When he too had passed away, the kingdom went to his brother, called Belshazzar, against whom Cyrus marched with the Persians and Medes. This man gave a drinking party for his nobles, and as he lay at table with his concubines and was getting drunk, he ordered the sacred vessels to be brought which Nebuchadnezzar had carried off from Jerusalem and dedicated to his own gods. When they were brought, he used them, though his father had not, and as he drank he blasphemed against God. Then he saw the knuckles of a human hand coming out of the wall and writing on the plaster of the wall; he was beside himself and his looks changed. He called the Chaldaeans and the magi and demanded the meaning of the letters, and proclaimed that he would give great rewards to whoever made their sense clear; but what was written was unknown to all. When the king was despondent and troubled, his grandmother said: "If Belteshazzar the Jew is sent for, who explained many things to Nebuchadnezzar that no one else could tell, he will reveal to you the secret of these syllables; for the holy Spirit of God is in him." So Belshazzar the ruler at once called Daniel and asked him to explain the letters to him, and not to hold back even if what they signified was gloomy; and he promised to give him as a reward to wear purple and a gold collar, and the third part of the rule.

Daniel declined the gifts, but said the writing foretold to him the end of his life, because he had not been taught restraint even by what his father had suffered for impiety, but had used the vessels of God for service with his concubines. He read the letters thus: "Mene, tekel, peres"; and interpreting their meaning he said: "God has numbered the time of your life and your rule, and it has come to be very short." For the word, put into Greek, would mean number. So he interpreted mene; and tekel, he said, meant weight: "God, having weighed the limit of your kingdom, shows that it is sinking and broken"; and tekel means a fragment in the Greek language. Peres the prophet interpreted as division, for that is what the word means when put into Greek speech, and he said that his kingdom had been divided by God between the Persians and Medes. So Daniel read what was written on the wall and gave such an interpretation of those syllables, that is, an explanation; and grief seized the king. Soon after, the prophet's prediction came true, when Cyrus, king of the Persians, marched against him; Babylon was taken by him and Belshazzar was killed in the capture. Some say that on that night on which he saw the knuckles writing, the city was taken and he was killed.

After the capture of Babylon the prophet Daniel was taken to Media by Darius the Mede (who was also named Cyaxares and was Cyrus's uncle on his mother's side, being the son of Astyages, who had reigned over the Medes) and was held worthy of every honour. In this position he was envied by the leading men among the Medes, and they contrived a means by which they hoped to destroy him. Seeing him pray to God three times a day, they came to Cyaxares, also called Darius, and asked him to make a law that for thirty days no one should pray to the gods or make requests of the king himself, and that whoever did not keep the law should be thrown into the pit of lions. He, not knowing what they were devising against Daniel, put out an edict ordering what has been said. The others kept quiet according to the decree, but Daniel prayed to God as was his custom. The satraps denounced him to the king and demanded that by the law he be thrown into the pit of lions. When the prophet had been thrown in there, the king sealed the stone over the mouth and withdrew. In anguish and pain he passed the night without sleep; for he hoped that Daniel would not be harmed by the beasts, knowing that the holy Spirit of God was in him, yet he was afraid and anxious that some harm might befall him, being a barbarian and not fully knowing the power of God. As soon as day dawned he stood at the pit and called Daniel, and he answered. The king at once ordered the prophet to be pulled up, and was astonished to see him untouched and safe. When those who had denounced him said that the lions were full of food and so had not touched Daniel, the king, hating them for their wickedness and understanding their scheme and trick against the prophet, ordered abundant food to be set before the beasts, and when they were full ordered the prophet's accusers to be thrown into the beasts' pit, saying: "So that we may know whether the lions will not touch them because they are full." When those wicked men were torn to pieces at once, it became clear to all that a divine power had preserved Daniel by muzzling the beasts. So the king magnified the prophet's God, and held him in still greater honour.

blocks: These things happened later; but in the first year of the reign of Belshazzar the prophet saw a dream. The vision was this. Four beasts seemed to come up out of the sea. The first had the form of a lioness and wings like an eagle's; it was lifted up from the earth and made to stand on the feet of a man, and the heart of a man was given to it. The sea signified human life, with its many waves, undergoing very many and continual changes and reversals; the beast, the lioness, imaged the kingdom of the Assyrians; and its being lifted from the earth showed the ending of that rule and the taking away of its power. Its standing on the feet of a man hinted that it would become equal to its subjects; and the heart of a man being given to it, that it would be taught by experience to think human thoughts and not imagine anything beyond human nature out of arrogance; for the wings which grew on the beast against nature showed the pride of those kings and the way their minds soared above the clouds in haughtiness.

The second beast was like a bear, and it stood on one side, and it had three ribs and wings in its mouth; and it was told: "Arise, eat much flesh." The bear was a figure of the kingdom of the Persians, because of the cruelty and harshness of the nation; for of all the barbarians the Persians are the harshest in punishing, inflicting the most bitter and longest punishments by the boats and by flaying.

Some probably do not know the punishment of the boats; so it is well to make it clear to those who do not know it. They fit two equal boats together, cutting them so that the head of the man being punished is left outside the boats, and his hands, and his feet too; they lay the victim on his back inside, and so nail the boats to each other. Then they mix honey and milk and pour it into the mouth of that wretched man until he is more than sated; and they pour some of the mixture over his face, feet and hands, and setting him in the open they let him bake in the sun, and do this to him every day. Flies, wasps and bees, gathering because of the sweetness of what has been poured on, settle on his face and the other limbs which, as has been said, are left outside the boats, some tormenting the wretch and some even stinging him. His belly, filled with the honey and milk, lets out liquid excrement, and as it rots maggots and worms swarm up; and he, his flesh rotting in the wet and himself consumed by the worms, so dies more pitifully and slowly. Parysatis, the mother of Cyrus and Artaxerxes, is recorded to have used this punishment against the man who boasted of having killed Cyrus as he fought his brother for the kingdom; he lasted under the punishment of the boats until the fourteenth day. Such, then, the punishment of the boats is recorded to be.

"Arise, eat flesh" is not a permission but a prediction of what would be; for there was a great slaughter of the Assyrians and their allies by the Persians and Medes. One might also say that "eat much flesh" signifies the cruelty of the nation. The three ribs, or wings, which it held in its mouth foreshadowed its rule over three parts of the inhabited world. For Cyrus, who destroyed the kingdom of the Assyrians, subdued the whole east as far as the Hellespont; his son Cambyses brought Egypt and Ethiopia under him, and these lands are in the south; and Darius the son of Hystaspes also subdued the nomad Scythians, who live in the northern region. Xerxes the son of Darius set out against Europe too, trying to master it, but was beaten back, defeated by the Athenians in a sea battle, and went home in disgrace. The beast's standing on one side signifies that it would not lose its rule entirely, but be confined to a small part of it. For that kingdom, which had ruled all Asia before and Ethiopia, Egypt, Palestine, Phoenicia and Libya itself, lost the rest, and Media and Persis were left to it. Or the beast's standing on one side may be taken in another way: that the kingdom of the Persians would be idle for a time and do nothing. For when Alexander had destroyed it and then died, his sole rule was divided into four realms; and when his successors turned against one another and were weakened in their battles with each other, the Persians seized their chance, took heart again and recovered much of their rule.

The third beast was like a leopard, and it had four wings of a bird on its back, and four heads grew on this beast, and he says that power was given to it. This beast imaged the Macedonian kingdom. Alexander was likened to a leopard for his swiftness and nimbleness, which the wings also showed. Their being four hinted at the four parts of the inhabited world, which he went through like a bird and mastered almost entirely. The four heads signified the division of the rule after his death. For his dominion was divided into four kingdoms: Ptolemy the son of Lagus ruled Egypt, and his descendants down to Cleopatra; Seleucus became master of Syria and the lands next to it; Antigonus brought Asia under himself; and Antipater ruled Macedonia, or, as some record, Arrhidaeus, Alexander's half-brother on his father's side. For Plutarch of Chaeronea says that Perdiccas, who had the greatest power after Alexander's death, at once dragged Arrhidaeus about as a kind of bodyguard of the kingship, though he was born of an obscure and common woman and was deficient in mind; not that he was born so, but Olympias had ruined his understanding with drugs.
text: These things happened later; but in the first year of the reign of Belshazzar the prophet saw a dream. The vision was this. Four beasts seemed to come up out of the sea. The first had the form of a lioness and wings like an eagle's; it was lifted up from the earth and made to stand on the feet of a man, and the heart of a man was given to it. The sea signified human life, with its many waves, undergoing very many and continual changes and reversals; the beast, the lioness, imaged the kingdom of the Assyrians; and its being lifted from the earth showed the ending of that rule and the taking away of its power. Its standing on the feet of a man hinted that it would become equal to its subjects; and the heart of a man being given to it, that it would be taught by experience to think human thoughts and not imagine anything beyond human nature out of arrogance; for the wings which grew on the beast against nature showed the pride of those kings and the way their minds soared above the clouds in haughtiness. blocks: Of the fourth beast the prophet did not give the form, but said it was fearful and exceedingly terrible, with great teeth of iron, devouring and grinding and trampling the rest, and he said it was very different from the beasts before it. By it the kingdom of the Romans is signified. That is why the prophet gave it neither form nor name. For the rule of the Romans has had many forms: first it was directed by kings, from Romulus to the Tarquins; when their tyranny was ended it was an aristocracy, the senate and the consuls managing affairs, and at times a democracy, when the people often rose against the senate; afterwards it fell again into monarchy, and from this it came back to the name of kingship. He called the beast fearful and terrible because this kingdom became more powerful than the others, and brought under itself all that the Macedonian kingdom had not subdued: the whole of Greece, Carthage with Libya, Sicily, Sardinia and other islands, and various other western nations, which Alexander did not rule. Whoever wishes to know these things, let him read the books of the Roman Dio and the writings of Polybius.

He said the beast was fearful and terrible and had teeth of iron, since the rule of the Romans became more dreadful than all the other kingdoms; for in the image seen by Nebuchadnezzar in the dream he set iron as the figure of the fourth kingdom. So he said that the beast devoured and ground with its iron teeth, and trampled the rest with its feet. Devouring and grinding are taken to mean the levying of taxes, since heavier tributes were laid on the subjects, which feed and fatten the rulers but make those from whom they are exacted thin with poverty. Those who would not endure paying tribute, claiming their freedom, the beast trampled with its feet and destroyed; and by the feet the soldiery is hinted at, since the kingdom rests and stands on it and moves by it from one place to another. He says the beast had ten horns, suggesting that at the last the kingdom will be divided into many realms. In the midst of the ten a little horn came up, and three of the horns were uprooted by it; that horn had eyes and a mouth speaking great things, and made war on the saints. Some have taken this horn to mean the Antichrist. It was called little as being destined to spring from a small tribe of the Hebrews. He will destroy three of the ten kings. By the eyes he hinted at his wickedness and cunning, since through these he will deceive many; by the mouth speaking great things he revealed his boastfulness and the pride of his spirit. Making war with the saints shows that he will display all zeal to make everyone share his own wickedness and blasphemy. And "he will speak words against the Most High" shows his blasphemy against God.

After this the prophet went on: "I watched until thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat down; his garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was a flame of fire, its wheels burning fire; a river of fire flowed out before him; a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him. The court sat, and books were opened." What the horn has been said to do was shown to Daniel as not lasting long, until the Eternal One set the court, that is, fixed the time of judgement, and unrolled the record of what each had done. For he called the records books, and the Eternal One the Ancient of Days. The whiteness of the hair and of the garment shows His purity and blamelessness in every way. And to show that what the Antichrist will do will happen by God's permission, and not as if the divine nature were unable to stop it or to refuse to let it happen at all, he brought in the thousand thousands of ministers and the ten thousand times ten thousand standing by, the throne of fire, the wheels like it and the flaming river. And he watched until the beast was killed and its body given to be burned with fire. For because of the madness of the Antichrist the whole kingdom will be taken away. And it is not the beast itself that will be given to the burning, but its body. For since the beast hints at the kingdom, it is likely that in the kingdom there are many who worship God and pursue virtue. It is not these, he says, who are given to the burning, but the workers of wickedness, those always devoted to the desires of the body and who have had no spiritual thought.

After the destruction of the beast the prophet says he saw one like a son of man coming on the clouds and reaching the Ancient of Days; to him, he says, were given rule and honour and the kingdom, and all peoples, tongues and tribes served him; his power would be eternal and would not pass away, and his kingdom would not be destroyed. This clearly foretells the second appearing of our Saviour Jesus Christ. He is called son of man because of our nature, which He took on, and coming on the clouds according to His own promise, when He said: "You will see the Son of Man coming on the clouds of heaven."

blocks: These things Daniel was taught in the first year of the reign of Belshazzar; and in the third he saw another vision. "For being in Susa," he says, "I raised my eyes, and see, a ram standing at the Ubal, and it had high horns, and one was higher than the other, and the higher came up last. It was butting towards the sea, the north and the south, and no beasts could stand before it; and it did as it pleased and grew great." Here again the prophet is taught about the kingdoms. The rule of the Persians was likened to a ram because of the wealth that surrounded it; and the ram stood at the Ubal, that is, at the gate of Susa, for this city was the capital of the Persians, the kings had their palace there, and the prophet saw the vision while living in this city. The two horns, which directed this kingdom, figured two families. The lesser horn imaged Cyrus and his son Cambyses, for the rule of the kingdom stopped with him, and the line of Cyrus went no further; the greater horn hinted at the line of Darius, which went on until the last Darius, whom Alexander defeated. For when Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, died, the magi seized the kingdom by trickery; and when they had ruled a short time and it was discovered who they were, the seven houses of the Persians overthrew them. Of these Darius the son of Hystaspes became king, and his line lasted to the end of the kingdom. This is what the prophet shows when he adds that the higher came up last: that one of the horns lasted long, until the end of the Persian kingdom.

The ram butted towards the south, the north and the sea: for it subdued the southern region and the northern, and enslaved most of the islands, which he hinted at by the sea; and the islanders fought on the side of Xerxes when he marched against Greece; that is why the prophet saw the ram butting towards the sea. And none of the beasts could stand before it. He called the lesser kingdoms beasts, as fearsome to their subjects; these would be that of the Syrians, the Cilicians, the Arabs, the Egyptians, the Jews and others. None of them could hold out in the end against the rule of the Persians, but it subdued all it attacked. "And it grew great": either because the rule became great, mastering many nations and lands, or because, swollen with good fortune, it imagined things great and beyond human nature.

While the prophet was at a loss about what he saw, he saw a he-goat coming from the south-west over the whole earth, and it had one conspicuous horn between its eyes. Reaching the ram, it was enraged against it, struck it, broke its horns, threw it to the ground and trampled it, and there was no one to rescue the ram from its hand. The he-goat prefigured the Macedonian kingdom, for it is swifter than the ram and more nimble. It came from the south-west, because Alexander first brought Egypt under him and then set out against Darius the second time, routed him and ended the kingdom of the Persians. For he had engaged him earlier at Issus in Cilicia and defeated him, and captured his wife, his daughters, his chariot and his bow and plundered the Persian camp; Darius fled from there, gathered forces again and fought Alexander when he set out against him from Egypt, and was defeated again at Arbela and perished in flight. He calls the horn conspicuous, meaning notable and admired; by this too he hints at the kingship of Alexander. He says the horn grew between its eyes because of Alexander's quickness of mind, his understanding and the nobility of his spirit. "And the he-goat came," he says, "to the ram that had the horns, and I saw it reach the ram, and it was enraged against it, struck the ram and broke both its horns, and the ram had no strength to stand before it, and it threw it to the ground and trampled it." Both the ram's horns were broken, he says, when the he-goat dashed against it: that is, both the forces in which it trusted, the Persian and the Median. For the kings of the Persians ruled Persians and Medes, since Cyrus, as has been said, was sprung from both and held the kingdom of both under him, and both these races ended the kingdom of the Assyrians. "And the he-goat grew very great." For he not only brought under himself the subjects of the Assyrian rule, but subdued many others too: he attacked India, defeated Porus, won over Taxiles and took other parts of India. Then the prophet, showing that he too, after prospering, would pass away soon, went on: "And when it was strong, the great horn was broken, and four horns grew up beneath it." For when Alexander died soon after that success, his rule was divided into four, as has already been said about the third beast, which seemed to Daniel in his sleep to come out of the sea, having four heads.

"And from one of the horns came out a fearful horn, and it grew exceedingly great towards the south and the east and the south-west and towards the host. And it grew great up to the host of heaven, and some of the host and of the stars fell to the earth, and it trampled them." By this Daniel is taught beforehand about Antiochus Epiphanes, who was the son of Antiochus the Great, but grew stronger than the kings before him, those descended from Seleucus; he mastered Egypt and other lands, marched against the Jews, became master of the city of Jerusalem and indeed of the whole nation, plundered the temple and defiled it by sacrificing swine in it, set up an altar to Zeus and forced the whole nation to adopt Greek ways, forbidding them to circumcise their males. "It grew great up to the host of heaven" hints at his madness against God. And "some of the host and of the stars fell to the earth, and it trampled them" signifies those of the Jewish people who turned impious under the compulsion brought on them by him, and fell from the lawful and divine way of life, yielding to the tyrant and being trampled by him. They were called stars because of the purity and brightness of piety, or because God promised Abraham to multiply his seed like the stars of heaven.

"And it set itself up even against the prince of the host": for he raged even against God Himself, the ruler of the powers above. "And the sacrifice was disturbed by a fall, and it came to pass and prospered, and sin was laid on the sacrifice, and righteousness was thrown to the ground." For by offering forbidden victims he disturbed the sacrifice, that is, confounded and defiled it. He calls the swine falls, and the sin laid on the sacrifice the lawlessness done at it. By "righteousness was thrown to the ground" the setting aside of the laws is shown, and the unjust murders of those who would not accept impiety. Yet even while doing these things and being so impious, he says, Antiochus prospered.

After this Daniel adds: "And one holy one said to Phelmouni, How long will the vision stand, and the sacrifice taken away, and the sin of desolation that has been given? And he said to him, Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days, and the sanctuary will be cleansed." Angels are sent to the prophet in his anguish at what he saw, to show him that the troubles will have an end and to teach him the time of their passing. One asked the other; for phelmouni, put into Greek, means "a certain one". He asked not as not knowing, but so that Daniel might learn. The one asked answered: "Two thousand days, until evening and morning, and the sanctuary will be cleansed." He called evening the beginning of the troubles, or their whole duration, for sorrows are like night and darkness; and morning the peaceful state after the calamities. This then is what he signifies by saying that from the beginning of the evils to their end so much time will pass. The days, counted as years, make six years and as many months by the Hebrew reckoning; for so long did the calamity brought on the Jews under Antiochus prevail. These things were taught to the prophet by the archangel Gabriel when he sought understanding.

"And the sacrifice was disturbed by a fall, and it came to pass and prospered, and sin was laid on the sacrifice, and righteousness was thrown to the ground." For by offering forbidden victims he disturbed the sacrifice, that is, confounded and defiled it. He calls the swine falls, and the sin laid on the sacrifice the lawlessness done at it. By "righteousness was thrown to the ground" the setting aside of the laws is shown, and the unjust murders of those who would not accept impiety. Yet even while doing these things and being so impious, he says, Antiochus prospered. After this Daniel adds: "And one holy one said to Phelmouni, How long will the vision stand, and the sacrifice taken away, and the sin of desolation that has been given? And he said to him, Until evening and morning, two thousand three hundred days, and the sanctuary will be cleansed." Angels are sent to the prophet in his anguish at what he saw, to show him that the troubles will have an end and to teach him the time of their passing. One asked the other; for phelmouni, put into Greek, means "a certain one". He asked not as not knowing, but so that Daniel might learn. The one asked answered: "Two thousand days, until evening and morning, and the sanctuary will be cleansed." He called evening the beginning of the troubles, or their whole duration, for sorrows are like night and darkness; and morning the peaceful state after the calamities. This then is what he signifies by saying that from the beginning of the evils to their end so much time will pass. The days, counted as years, make six years and as many months by the Hebrew reckoning; for so long did the calamity brought on the Jews under Antiochus prevail. These things were taught to the prophet by the archangel Gabriel when he sought understanding.

blocks: Then, under Darius again, the ruler of the Medes, who was also named Cyaxares and Ahasuerus, the son of Astyages, as the prophet was lamenting the captivity of his countrymen and praying to God, a man whose name was Gabriel touched him. He touched him about the hour of the evening sacrifice, either at the time of the evening service, or for as long a time as the evening service was being performed. And he said to Daniel: "Now I have come out to give you understanding and tell you that you are a man of desires. Consider the word and understand the vision"; that is, pay close attention to what is said, since it is in riddles and needs more effort. Sometimes divine things are revealed through riddles, so that they may not be plain to all and so be easily despised. Daniel was called a man of desires either as one who played the man against fleshly desires and nobly resisted them, or as one who desired to learn what would befall the people and his fellow tribesmen, or because he was desirable and lovable for the virtue he pursued.

Then the angel goes on: "Seventy weeks have been cut off for your people and for your holy city, until the transgression grows old and the sin is completed, and to seal sin and atone for iniquity, and to bring in everlasting righteousness, and to seal vision and prophet, and to anoint the holy of holies." The prophet in his prayer said to God, "your people and your city"; but the angel says to Daniel, "your people and your city", as though the people were not worthy to be called God's. The same is found in the time of Moses, when the Israelites made the calf and offered sacrifice to it; for then too, when the prophet prayed, God spoke in the same way. So the angel says that Jerusalem will be built and your people will return and remain for four hundred and ninety years; for the seventy weeks add up to this number, each day being counted as a year. "Have been cut off" stands for "have been decided and fixed". "Until the transgression grows old and the sin is completed": that is, until it lasts and grows; for this is what the sin growing old and becoming complete means. By this he shows the daring and the frenzy of the Jews against the Lord. For they had sinned much before this and paid the penalty, but were called back again; but when they raged against the Saviour and reached the extreme of wickedness and committed sin in full, they were no longer called back.

"To seal sin and atone for iniquity" signifies the forgiveness of failings given by the Lord to those who believe in Him; for He is the one who takes away the sin of the world; and sealing signifies stopping. "To bring in everlasting righteousness" means that He came into the world, who is righteousness and redemption and sanctification. "To seal vision and prophet" signifies that the prophecies have reached their end, either because what the prophets said about Christ has already come to pass, or because the gift of prophecy has failed among the Jews, or both. For Christ, when He came, sealed the prophecies, that is, fulfilled and confirmed them, and also ended them; for there is no longer among them ruler or prophet or leader. "And to bring in everlasting righteousness", which is our Lord and Saviour Himself. For the apostle says: "He was made for us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption"; and elsewhere, writing about the gospel, he says: "In it righteousness is revealed." And the Lord teaches: "Seek the kingdom of God and His righteousness", which He Himself brought in, making it manifest to us by His teaching. "To anoint the holy of holies" signifies the coming of the Master Christ Himself. For who else could be called the holy of holies except our Lord and Saviour? He, being the fountain of holiness, is anointed with the Holy Spirit in His humanity, as Isaiah proclaimed beforehand, saying: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He has anointed me"; and as David sang, saying: "God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your fellows"; and as Peter, the chief and crown of the apostles, taught, writing of the Saviour that "God anointed Him with the Holy Spirit and with power". He seals and confirms the old Scriptures, doing and suffering everything that had been foretold in them, and atones for iniquity, reconciling sinners to God the Father and making Him gracious to those who have failed.

Then the divine archangel goes on: "And you will know and understand: from the going out of the word to answer and to build Jerusalem until Christ the leader, seven weeks and sixty-two weeks." The temple began to be built under Cyrus; for Cyrus first allowed the nation of the Jews to return; but it was stopped by Cambyses, the son of Cyrus, through the envy of the nations bordering on them, and the raising of it was permitted to the Jews again when Darius the son of Hystaspes came to the throne of the Persians. Counted from neither of these is the time found to fit the archangel's words, but it is exceeded; but if the time is counted from the years of the reign of Artaxerxes, it would be found neither too long nor too short. And it must be counted from then, because it was then that the city was surrounded with a wall, what was lacking was added to the temple and the city was filled with inhabitants, when Nehemiah, Artaxerxes' cupbearer, begged him to let him return to his country, and went and walled the city, settled it and completed the temple, which was unfinished. If, then, one counts back the time from the appearing of the Saviour, through whom alone forgiveness of sins was given, righteousness brought in and the predictions of the prophets fulfilled, he will find it completed back to the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, when Nehemiah was permitted to go back to Jerusalem; which the history will tell more fully as it proceeds in order. Him whom he called above the holy of holies, he now called Christ the leader, naming Him in His humanity. For as He is called the first-born of the new creation and the first-born from the dead, so He is also called leader. And the divine apostle Peter named the Saviour the author of life when speaking to the Jews, as the divine Luke wrote in the Acts. And as He is called, according to the great Paul, our first-born and the first among us in His humanity, so too He is called leader by the archangel Gabriel.

blocks: One might ask why the weeks are counted separately and not together, divided into seven and sixty-two and one more. The archangel did not do this at random, but to teach by it certain new things that would happen at the divisions of time. For if the years are counted from the building of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, as has been said, to the high priest Hyrcanus, in whose time the line of the Hasmonaeans ceased to be priests, the number of sixty-two weeks is completed. From the twentieth year of the reign of Artaxerxes, who granted Nehemiah the return to Jerusalem to wall it, to Darius the son of Arsames, whom Alexander overthrew, there are a hundred and fourteen years; from the overthrow of the kingdom of the Persians, which happened in the sixth year of Alexander's campaign into Asia, to Gaius Julius Caesar, who was the first to attempt monarchy over the Romans, two hundred and eighty-two years passed; and from Caesar's sole rule to the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, when Christ was baptized by John and began His signs, seventy-three years; so that these add up to four hundred and sixty-nine years. These years make four hundred and eighty-three years by the Hebrew reckoning of years. For the Hebrews do not reckon the year as we do, but counting it by the course of the moon they reckon it at three hundred and fifty-four days, so that eleven days are left over from each year; and when these extra days are added up into years, the four hundred and eighty-three Hebrew years result. And the angel, speaking to Daniel, a Hebrew, surely spoke of years familiar to him.

So the sixty-two weeks were measured out up to the death of the high priest Hyrcanus, whom King Herod killed (the story of this will be told more fully). From then on, since the high priesthood was no longer fixed for life on those thought worthy of it, as the law required, but was given unlawfully for a year or limited to a shorter time, and those who wished bought it with money, as Josephus records, the seven weeks passed. Showing this, the divine archangel said: "And after the sixty-two weeks the anointing will be destroyed, and there is no judgement in it"; that is, the anointing of the high priesthood will be ruined. For since those promoted to it were anointed unlawfully, the anointing did not have its proper force, but, being corrupted, lacked the divine grace. That is why he added, "and there is no judgement in it": that is, they will not be appointed by judgement and examination, but without judgement, for favour or for money. While this was happening the seven weeks too slipped away, lasting, that is, until the appearing of the Lord.

The division of the sixty-two weeks and the seven was made for these reasons. Since one more remains of the seventy weeks spoken of at first, the archangel said this about it too: "And one week will strengthen the covenant for many, and in the half of the week sacrifice and libation will be taken away, and on the temple the abomination of desolation, and until the end of the time an end will be put to the desolation." The remaining week, he says, after the sixty-nine, will bring in the new covenant so strong that through it the sacrifices and libations will be taken away, that is, removed, in the half of the week. For after His baptism Christ taught for three years and more and showed signs, and so came to His passion; and when He, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, was sacrificed for the whole world, the sacrifice and libation according to the law ceased. From then on the Jews sacrificed (as they still do) unlawfully, but their sacrifice and libation were not acceptable to God. "Will strengthen the covenant for many" may also be taken in another way: that that week will make the holy apostles strong for the preaching. For the archangel appears to divide the week into two, the time before the passion and the time after it. For the Lord, having preached for about three and a half years, according to the gospel of the son of thunder, and having established His divine apostles in faith in Him by the truth of His words and the display of wonderful works, so went to His passion, accepted the cross and endured death. Then, for the rest of the week, after the resurrection from the dead, the ascent to the Father's bosom, from which He had never been parted, and the coming of the Comforter and His divine inspiration, His holy disciples in Jerusalem, confirming the gospel and the preaching with wonders and drawing multitudes of men to the knowledge of the true God, scattered among the nations and enlightened them. Foretelling this to the prophet Daniel, the archangel said, "One week will strengthen the covenant for many," that is, will gird many with power, namely the disciples. Having joined the time before the Lord's passion and the time after it, during which the apostles first stayed and preached in Jerusalem and then went round to the ends of the world and taught, he divides this week again, saying: "And in the half of the week sacrifice and libation will be taken away," foretelling by this the ending of the shadow of the law.

Then he goes on: "And on the temple the abomination of desolation." For when these things happen, he says, the temple, formerly holy and revered, will be reckoned an abomination; or after this last week some abomination will be brought into the temple, a sign of the desolation of it and of the city. This happened under Pilate, when he brought in by night standards bearing the emperor's images, which the Jews thought an abomination; for they were forbidden to possess or revere an image of a man or of any animal. And the Lord said: "When you see the abomination of desolation standing in the holy place, know that its desolation has drawn near," that is, Jerusalem's. And elsewhere the Lord said: "See, your house is left to you desolate." Teaching Daniel these things beforehand, the archangel, after foretelling that the worship of the law would be removed, adds: "And on the temple the abomination of desolation." And so that the Jews might not think the desolation temporary, as if the city would be rebuilt for them again and the temple raised, as had happened often before to the temple and the city, he went on: "And until the end of the time an end will be put to the desolation"; that is, the desolation will remain until the age is ended, and it too will end then, when there is no longer time for either the city or the temple to rise.

These things Daniel saw and was taught about his countrymen. But he saw other visions and dreams too, through which the change to come in the affairs of the world was revealed to him beforehand by God. He was taught not only the foreknowledge of the change, but also the times at which each of them would be fulfilled. Whoever wishes will surely learn these by going through the book of the prophet's visions more fully, and will gain from it a firm grasp that nothing is without providence or carried along at random and by chance, but everything is governed and directed by divine providence. So these things stand, and for the pious

blocks: are glorified. But we must not pass over the story of the manly-minded woman Judith, who destroyed Holofernes and saved her city and the whole nation. Her story is this. In the twelfth year of his reign the leader of the Assyrians, Nebuchadnezzar, made war on Arphaxad, the king of the Medes, and called the surrounding nations to his alliance. When many others, and the Jews among them, did not accept the summons and refused to fight on his side, Nebuchadnezzar was enraged, and swore that when he had finished the war against the Medes he would come against Cilicia, Damascus, Syria, Judaea and Egypt, ravage and sack them and make them a desert. So he drew up against Arphaxad the Mede and prevailed over him by force, mastered his other cities and Ecbatana itself, where Arphaxad had his palace, and captured and killed him. Then he called Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of his own force, and ordered him to fulfil the oath he had sworn: to march with a heavy force against those who would not fight on his side when he went against the Medes; to preserve those who submitted to him and leave their cities unsacked, but not to spare the disobedient, but to put the men to the sword and give their cities over to plunder and destruction.

Nebuchadnezzar gave these orders to his chief satrap. Holofernes marched out and, attacking the nations against which he had been sent, dealt with the others as he had been ordered; but when he was about to march against the Israelites and take up arms against them (for they did not come to him or submit), he asked who these people were and in what they trusted to resist. Achior, the leader of the sons of Ammon, told him their genealogy, how they had first settled in those cities, and the strength of their God. Then he went on: "Now we must consider: if they are sinning against their God, we will go up and defeat them in war; but if not, let my lord pass them by, lest their God shield them and we be defeated." When Achior said this, Holofernes, seized with anger, ordered those standing by him to bind Achior, lead him away and hand him over to the sons of Israel, so that he might be taken with them and punished. They seized the man and led him off to Bethulia, and the people of the city shot at them with slings and arrows as they came near. They threw Achior down, bound, at the foot of the hill and went back. The men of the city came down, untied Achior, brought him into their city and asked what had happened; and he told them everything. They called on God for help.

The next day Holofernes led his army against Bethulia, a hundred and seventy thousand foot and twelve thousand horse, apart from the baggage train, and camped by it. Then he decided not to fight, but to seize first the waters from which they drew, so that they would perish when they ran out through thirst or surrender their city. He set part of the army round the waters as guards. When the enemy had sat round them for thirty-four days, their water failed them, and the people gathered before the rulers and asked them to surrender the city and themselves to the enemy, so that they might either serve them and live, or be slaughtered and be rid of their sufferings. Ozias, the foremost man of the city, said: "Brothers, let us wait five more days; if help comes to us from God, well; if not, I will do as you advise."

When Achior said this, Holofernes, seized with anger, ordered those standing by him to bind Achior, lead him away and hand him over to the sons of Israel, so that he might be taken with them and punished. They seized the man and led him off to Bethulia, and the people of the city shot at them with slings and arrows as they came near. They threw Achior down, bound, at the foot of the hill and went back. The men of the city came down, untied Achior, brought him into their city and asked what had happened; and he told them everything. They called on God for help. The next day Holofernes led his army against Bethulia, a hundred and seventy thousand foot and twelve thousand horse, apart from the baggage train, and camped by it. Then he decided not to fight, but to seize first the waters from which they drew, so that they would perish when they ran out through thirst or surrender their city. He set part of the army round the waters as guards. When the enemy had sat round them for thirty-four days, their water failed them, and the people gathered before the rulers and asked them to surrender the city and themselves to the enemy, so that they might either serve them and live, or be slaughtered and be rid of their sufferings. Ozias, the foremost man of the city, said: "Brothers, let us wait five more days; if help comes to us from God, well; if not, I will do as you advise."

blocks: There was in that city a woman named Judith, a widow, chaste, sensible and beautiful to look at. Hearing what the people and the rulers had decided, she sent for Ozias and the other rulers of the city and rebuked them for testing God by saying they would surrender the city to the enemy after five days unless some help came to them from God in that time. They agreed that she spoke well, but pleaded the people's thirst and the pressure from them. She told them to stand at the gate of the city that night; she herself, she said, would go out with her maid, but she would not tell them what she was planning until it had been carried through to action. They said to her: "Go." They went away, and she turned to entreating God. Then she put off the mourning garments of her widowhood, bathed her body in water, anointed it with perfume, changed into a festive robe and put on ornaments. Adorned to make herself more alluring, she gave her maidservant wine and oil in vessels to carry and a bag full of parched grain, fig cakes and loaves, and she and her maid went out of the city towards the enemy's camp.

Meeting the outpost of the Assyrians, she was held and brought to Holofernes. He admired her beauty and said to her: "Do not be afraid; you have come to safety." The woman said to him: "Receive my words, lord, and let the word that Achior spoke be in your heart; for it is true that unless the sons of Israel sin, no sword will prevail against them. But now, since their food and water have failed them, they have resolved to touch even what is forbidden by the law, and they have decided to consume the first-fruits of the grain and the tithes of the wine kept for the priests, which no one else may lawfully even touch. Since those who live in Jerusalem have resolved this too, they have sent to the council of elders there, asking for permission. And if they break the law in this way, there will be no help for them from God, and they will be given over to destruction. Knowing this, I am running away from the city to escape the destruction. Now I will stay with you, master, and go out at night into the ravine and pray to God, and He will tell me when they have sinned, and I will report it to you, and lead you through Judaea to Jerusalem and set your throne in the midst of it." Holofernes was pleased with her words, and ordered her to be brought into the tent where his treasures were and given food. She said: "I will not eat of your food, lest it become a stumbling block to me, but I will feed on what I have brought." Holofernes said to her: "And if this runs out, where will such things be supplied to you?" She answered: "As your soul lives, my lord, my food will not run out before God has done by my hand what He has planned." At midnight she asked to go out to the ravine to pray, and Holofernes allowed it; and she did so for three days.

On the fourth day Holofernes prepared a drinking party and said to the eunuch Bagoas, who was in charge of all he had: "Persuade the Hebrew woman to come to us; for it would be shameful for us to let such a woman go without having had her company." Bagoas said to Judith: "Come to my lord, to be honoured in his presence, drink wine with us, and become like one of the women who attend in the house of Nebuchadnezzar." Judith adorned herself and went, and coming in to Holofernes she reclined, and ate and drank what her maid had prepared for her. Holofernes' heart was beside itself and burned with love for the woman. The drinking went on long, and he drank a great deal of wine and was drunk. He lay on his bed heavy-headed from drink, and all went away, and Bagoas closed the tent, leaving Judith alone inside. She had told her maidservant to watch for her coming out, for she would go out to pray. Holofernes lay sunk in drunkenness, sleeping the sleep that is death's brother; and she, calling on God, drew his short sword, cut off his head, went out and gave it to her maidservant, and went off as if to pray according to her custom.

Coming near her city, she called to those at the gates to open to her. Going in, she told the wonders God had done through her, brought out the head of Holofernes, and advised them to hang it from the battlements, and to put on their armour and go out at dawn: "For when the Assyrians see you," she said, "they will run to the tent of their commander-in-chief, and finding him killed they will be beside themselves, fear will fall on them and they will turn to flight; and you will follow them and cut them down, and the plains will be filled with the dead." Having given this advice to her fellow citizens, she said: "Call Achior to me"; and when he came she showed him the head of Holofernes. The man was astonished and said: "Tell me all you have done." She told before them all what God had done through her, and how He had kept her chastity and widowhood undefiled. Achior believed in God and was circumcised. The rulers of the city and its multitude hung the head of Holofernes from the wall and did the rest according to Judith's advice. They cut the Assyrians down like grass, plundered their camp and were filled with much spoil. The tent of Holofernes and everything in it were set apart for Judith, and she went to Jerusalem and dedicated them as an offering to God. Crowned with a shoot of olive, she sang a song to Him, with all Israel; and she returned to her house, grew old in chastity and died at the age of a hundred and five.

blocks: So much for the story of Judith. Next, the story of Tobit must be told in brief. Tobit was descended from the tribe of Naphtali, and had been taken captive in the days of Enemessar, king of the Assyrians. He was pious towards God and just towards men; when his fellow tribesmen sacrificed to Baal, he went to Jerusalem and sacrificed to God, ordered his life according to the commands of the law, and when taken captive did not defile himself with gentile food. He became honoured by Enemessar and acquired much property, and shared it with the needy of his own race. Travelling to Media, he deposited ten talents of silver with Gamael, one of his countrymen living there. He married Anna, a woman of his own people, and had a son by her, Tobias.

When Enemessar died, his son Sennacherib succeeded to the rule of the Assyrians; he marched against Judaea, fled shamefully from there and came back home, and in anger at his defeat killed very many of the Israelites; and Tobit buried them by night. He was found out doing this, and when he was sought he fled, and everything in his house was plundered. Before fifty days had passed, Sennacherib was killed by his sons; the parricides fled in fear, and another son of his, Esarhaddon, succeeded to his father's kingdom. He made a kinsman of Tobit, called Achiacharus, the manager of his affairs. This man interceded with the king for Tobit, and he returned to Nineveh.

When Pentecost came, which the Jews kept after seven weeks, a lavish meal was prepared for Tobit. He said to his son Tobias: "Go, child, and bring whatever needy man of our brothers you find who is mindful of the Lord, to share our table." He went and came back saying: "One of our race has been strangled and thrown out in the market-place." At once Tobit went, took up the body and brought it into the house, and when the sun had set he buried him. Returning, he did not go into the house, since by the law he was unclean, having touched the dead, but slept by the wall in the courtyard. Sparrows spending the night on the wall dropped their dung into his eyes, from which white films formed in them, and from these Tobit was blinded. Being in want, he was fed by his wife, who spun for pay. Once, receiving her pay and a kid besides, she came to Tobit. Hearing the kid's bleating, he asked whether it was stolen. She said: "It was given me as a gift besides my pay." He pressed her, saying: "If it is stolen, let it be given back to its owners." The woman, deeply hurt and as if mocking her husband for his strictness about justice, said: "Where are your almsgivings and your righteous deeds?" Tobit, distressed, wept and asked God to be released from life.

On that same day, at Ecbatana in Media, it happened that Sarah, the daughter of Raguel, was reproached by her father's maidservants for strangling her husbands, since she had been married to seven and had belonged to none of them. For a demon called Asmodaeus killed them when they went in to her. Unable to bear the reproach, she decided to hang herself. But so as not to give her father grief and reproach, she did not do it, but stood in prayer and called on God, asking to die and be freed from the reproaches, or to be pitied and so escape the reproach.

So the prayer of both was heard, and the archangel Raphael was sent by God to heal Tobit's blindness, to betroth Sarah to Tobias, and to bind Asmodaeus, the evil demon, so that he might do Tobias no harm if he married Sarah. Tobit called his son Tobias and, after giving him much advice, said to him at last: "I deposited ten talents of silver with Gamael, the son of Gabrias, at Rages in Media; go and get them." And he gave him the bond for them and told him to look for a man who would go with him for pay. Looking for a travelling companion, he met the archangel Raphael, who appeared to him in the form of a man and declared that he knew the road and the house of Gamael and would go with him. Taking him, as a man called Azarias, he set off. In the evening they came to the river Tigris and camped there. Tobias went into the river to wash, and a fish leapt out of it to swallow the youth. The angel told him to catch the fish, and when it was pulled to land he told him to cut it open, and advised Tobias to take its heart, liver and gall and keep them safe.

blocks: As they travelled and drew near Ecbatana, Tobias said: "Brother Azarias, what use will the heart, liver and gall of the fish be to us?" He answered: "The heart and liver, burned as incense, drive away demons if they trouble anyone; and the gall, smeared on eyes that have white films, clears them and gives sight." When they were already near Ecbatana, the angel said to Tobias: "Today we shall lodge with Raguel, who is your kinsman, who has a daughter Sarah, sensible and beautiful, and I will speak to have her given to you as wife." He said: "I have heard that the girl has been given to seven husbands and that all died in the bridal chamber, because a demon loves her and destroys those who woo her; and I am afraid that I too will be killed by it." The angel said: "Listen to me, and take no account of the demon. When you go into the bridal chamber, put some of the heart and liver of the fish on coals, and the demon will smell their odour and flee, and will not come back."

They went into Raguel's house. Learning that Tobias was the son of Tobit, he kissed him, and hearing that Tobit was blind, he wept and received them gladly. The angel told Raguel to give Sarah to him in marriage; he consented, called his daughter, took her by the hand, gave her to Tobias, and taking a document wrote a contract. After dinner they brought Tobias to her in the inner room. As he went he took coals, put some of the heart and liver of the fish on them and made smoke, and the smell drove the demon away. At daybreak Raguel sent one of the maidservants to see whether Tobias was alive. When she came back and said he was alive, Raguel blessed God. He said to Tobias: "Let us celebrate the wedding for fourteen days, and you shall not leave here before they have passed. Then take half of what I have and go; the rest you shall take when I and my companion in life are dead." So Tobias said to Raphael: "Brother Azarias, take the bond for me, go to Gamael at Rages and bring the silver; for if we delay, my father will be greatly distressed." The angel went, handed the bond to Gamael, received the silver and came back.

When the days of the wedding had passed, Tobias said to Raguel, "Send me away," and taking his wife and half of Raguel's property he set off. When they were near Nineveh, the angel said to him: "Let us run on ahead and prepare the house. Take the gall of the fish in your hands; your father will open his eyes, and you smear them with the gall; feeling the sting, he will rub them and shed the white films." His mother sat watching the road; and when she saw her son coming, she hurried and said to Tobit, "Your son is coming," and running to him she kissed him and said: "I have seen you, child, and now if I die, I do not care." Tobit came out to the door, stumbling. Tobias took hold of him and smeared the gall on his eyes, and they stung, and he rubbed them, and the white films peeled off them. Seeing his son, he blessed God. When Tobit was told what had happened to Tobias in Media, he went out to meet his daughter-in-law, and seeing her he blessed her. The people of Nineveh, seeing him able to see and hearing of the great things God had done, were amazed.

Tobit said to his son: "Give the man who went with you his pay, child, and indeed we must add something to it." He said: "Father, it is right that he take half of what I have brought." And he said to Raphael: "Brother Azarias, take half of all we have brought, and go in health." Then the angel called the two of them aside and told them all the great things God had done with them, and said that he was Raphael, and had come not of himself but sent by God. He urged them to bless God and give thanks for all He had done with them. "For it is good," he said, "to hide a king's secret, but to proclaim the works of God gloriously." Hearing this, they fell at his feet; and when they rose they saw him no more, and they gave thanks to God for the wonders He had done with them.

Tobit was fifty-eight years old when he lost his sight, and after eight years he was restored to sight; and from then on he feared God the more and did what was good. Having grown very old, he said to his son: "Child, see, I have grown old and am near death; take your sons and go to Media. For I am persuaded that what Jonah foretold about Nineveh, that it would be overthrown, will come to pass, and that Jerusalem will be desolate and the temple burned, and God will again have mercy on the city, and the people will return and build it. But you, keep the law and be merciful and just." Having given his son such charges he died, at the age of a hundred and fifty-eight. Tobias buried him with honour, and his mother, and went off with his wife to Ecbatana, to his father-in-law Raguel; and he buried him too in his old age and inherited from him. Tobias died too, at a hundred and twenty-seven, at Ecbatana in Media, and before he died he heard of the destruction of Nineveh, taken by Nebuchadnezzar and Ahasuerus.

blocks: The whole nation of the Hebrews, as has been told, was taken captive by the Assyrians and carried away, and Jerusalem was left desolate; and it was not freed from captivity until the rule of the Assyrians was ended by the Medes and Persians, according to the prophetic prediction, and the seventy years had passed which the prophet Jeremiah had proclaimed beforehand. It would not be out of place to go through the overthrow of the kingdom of the Assyrians in brief too, and to show that the prophetic prediction was true, which foretold that it would be ended by the Medes and Persians. It went as follows.

The Medes and the Persians were kingdoms each by itself. Astyages ruled the one, and Cambyses that of the Persians. Cambyses was married to the daughter of Astyages, called Mandane, who bore Cambyses a son, Cyrus. Brought up under the laws of the Persians, he became most brave and most self-controlled, sensible and most just. The customs of the Persians were these, as Xenophon wrote. They had a square called the Free Square, on which their palace and the other public buildings were built; from it goods for sale, traders, their bustle and their cries were driven away, so as not to mix with the good order of the educated. The Free Square was divided into four quarters: one was set aside for boys, another for youths, another for grown men, and the last assigned to those past the years of military service; and each attended at his own place. It was the custom for the youths to sleep about the public buildings with their light arms, except those who were married; these were not sought unless notice had been given, and were not often allowed to be absent. Each group had twelve officers, for the Persians were divided into twelve tribes.

The boys, going to the schools, learned justice, their officers spending most of the day judging cases for them. For among boys too there were charges against one another, as among men, of theft, violence, robbery, deceit, insult and other things. Those they found guilty of these, they punished; and those they found accusing unjustly, they chastised. They taught the boys self-control, by watching their elders living with self-control; and they taught them restraint in food and drink. When the boys were to eat, they ate with their teacher, bringing bread from home and cress as relish; and for drink they took a cup of river water. Before eating they learned to shoot the bow and throw the javelin. The boys did this until they were sixteen or seventeen; from then they were enrolled among the youths, and for ten years they slept about the public buildings, and during the day they put themselves at the disposal of the officers for whatever they needed them for on public business. When the king went out hunting, he took out half their number. They hunted together, because this exercise seemed to them akin to training for war: it accustomed them to rise early and endure cold and heat, exercised them in marches and running, taught them to shoot and throw at a beast, and prepared them to face one of the fierce beasts. On the hunt they carried a meal larger than the boys', but otherwise similar. And they did not eat it while hunting, unless they had to stay for a beast or wished otherwise to spend time on the hunt. Making their dinner of this meal, they hunted the next day until dinner, and counted these two days as one. They did this so that they might be able to do it if needed in war. For relish they had whatever they caught, and if not, the cress. The tribes that stayed at home spent their time practising, among other things, shooting and throwing the javelin and competing with each other in these. The officers used the youths who stayed for public works needing strength or speed.

When the youths had spent ten years in these things, they passed into the grown men, and from then they lived so for twenty-five years. If they had to go to war, they no longer took bows or javelins, but the arms called close-fighting: a breastplate on the chest, a wicker shield on the left arm, and in the right hand a sword or cleaver. All the officials too were appointed from these. When they had completed the twenty-five years, being over fifty years from birth, they then went out into the elders. The elders no longer served on campaign outside their own country, but stayed at home and judged all cases public and private; they also judged capital cases and chose all the officials. If anyone among the youths or the men broke any of the customs, the elders expelled him; and the one expelled lived in disgrace for the rest of his life. Among the Persians it was thought shameful to spit, to blow one's nose, to be seen full of wind, or to be seen urinating or relieving one's bowels. They could not do these things unless they kept a moderate diet and used up the moisture by exertion. These were the ways and customs of the Persians.

blocks: Cyrus, brought up and educated in these, passed beyond the age of youth and was enrolled among the men, and won distinction in everything. When his mother's father Astyages, king of the Medes, had died, his son Cyaxares, who was also named Darius, succeeded to his father's rule, being Cyrus's uncle.

The ruler of the Assyrians, since his kingdom had grown great, ruled the numerous Assyrian race, had brought the Arabs under him, made the Hyrcanians subjects and the Syrians tributary, was besieging the Bactrians, had already subdued the race of the Hebrews and had made very many other nations subject, thought that if he weakened the Medes he would more easily master all those round about. With this in mind he made his subjects ready, and sent to Croesus, the king of the Lydians, to both the Phrygians, to the Paphlagonians and Indians, and to the Carians and Cilicians, asking them to ally with him as he set out against the Medes, since the war was to their advantage too; for he said the nation was powerful, had made marriage ties with the Persians and gained their help besides, and each was strengthened by the other, so that unless someone weakened them first they would attack each of the nations and master them. He sent such words to each of the nations; and some, moved by these words, some won over by money and gifts, and some overcome by fear of the Assyrian, agreed to ally with him.

Cyaxares, learning this, made his own preparations, and sent to the Persians, both to the commonwealth and to their king Cambyses, asking for an alliance and asking that his nephew Cyrus come as commander of the allies; for he had already been counted among the grown men. When the Persians agreed to the alliance, the elders chose Cyrus as commander of the army for the Medes, and gave him thirty thousand targeteers, archers and slingers. Chosen, he took leave of his father and set off for the Medes with the army. When he arrived, since the Assyrian had not yet come, he ordered his men to practise the arts of war.

Meanwhile a messenger came from Cyaxares saying that an embassy of Indians had come, and "you must be present too. I bring you a very fine robe; for he wishes to present you dressed most splendidly, so that you may be seen so by the Indians." When he came to Cyaxares' door with the army, and went in to him dressed in the Persian way, Cyaxares was annoyed at the plainness of his dress. The Indians were called in and said they had been sent by their king to ask the reason for the war between the Medes and the Assyrian, that they would learn the same from him too, and tell both that the king of the Indians, having considered the right, would side with the wronged. To this Cyaxares said: "We have done the Assyrian no wrong; ask him what he says." Cyrus said: "If the Assyrian says he is wronged by us, Indians, we choose your king himself as judge."

When they had heard this they went away. Cyrus, not wishing his army to sit idle, said to Cyaxares: "I remember hearing you say recently that the Armenian neither sends you an army nor pays the tribute, having broken the agreement. If you wish, send me, giving me a moderate number of horsemen, and I think, with the gods' help, he will both send the army and pay the tribute." When Cyaxares let him go, promising to send him the horsemen when he came near the borders of Armenia, Cyrus set off as if going out to hunt; for he was accustomed to hunt on the borders of both, I mean of the Medes and the Armenians. He went off and hunted, and climbed the mountains of Armenia, moving forward quietly. When Cyaxares learned this, he sent him the horsemen. When they came, Cyrus called together the captains and revealed the secret, saying he had come because of the Armenian, who had behaved unfairly towards Cyaxares. He ordered Chrysantas to take half the Persians and get into the mountains of the Armenians, taking care that it should not be known that there was an army there, but sending ahead some men looking like robbers in number and dress, so that if anyone met them, they would think them thieves. Chrysantas went to the mountains with the Persians, and Cyrus sent to the Armenian ordering him to bring the tribute and the army as quickly as possible, and himself advanced in battle order.

When the Armenian heard this he was terrified, and sent to gather his army, and sent his wives, his younger son and his wealth to the mountains; for no wall surrounded their dwelling place. When those sent to the mountains fell in with those lying in wait there, and the Armenian's wives, son and daughters were captured, he was at a loss and gave himself up to Cyrus.

blocks: Meanwhile the Armenian's elder son Tigranes, who had been abroad and had once been Cyrus's hunting companion, came back, and learning what had happened went straight to Cyrus as he was; and seeing his father, mother, sisters and his own wife captive, he wept. Cyrus said: "You have come at the right time." After talking at length with the Armenian and convicting him of wrongdoing, he said at last: "Tell me how great a force you have, and how much money." When he said there were eight thousand horsemen and forty thousand foot, and money reckoned in silver more than three thousand talents, Cyrus said: "Send half the army with me; of the money, pay Cyaxares twice the fifty talents of the yearly tribute instead of the fifty; and lend me," he said, "another hundred." With these words he gave the Armenian his wife and children as a gift, and Tigranes his own wife, whom he had just married, and let them all go. The Armenians and their neighbours the Chaldaeans always had quarrels and battles; Cyrus reconciled them with each other, and so went away. The army he had received from the Armenian he sent to Cyaxares; and when he came to the Medes he shared the money among his captains.

Then he invaded the enemy country with Cyaxares, and they camped and gathered much booty from there. When they learned that the Assyrians too were approaching, they advanced in battle order, and they camped a parasang apart. The next day Cyrus led out his army and drew it up, Cyaxares with the Medes on one wing, and opposite them the Assyrians and their allies. Urging one another on, the Persians charged at a run to close quarters, and Cyrus himself. The enemy no longer stood, but fled into their fortification. The Persians, following on as they pushed in, cut down many, and leaping in on those who fell into the ditches killed them. The Median horsemen too charged the enemy horsemen, and they gave way; and there was a pursuit of horses and men and slaughter on both sides. When the women of the Assyrians and their allies saw this, they cried out and ran about in terror, tearing their robes and lacerating their cheeks, begging all to defend them, their children and themselves. Then the kings themselves, with their most trusted men, took their stand at the entrances and fought and urged on the others. Cyrus, afraid that his men, being few, would be overcome by many if they forced their way into the entrenchment, ordered them to draw back step by step out of range; and they quickly did as they were told. Then he led his men back as far as seemed good and camped.

The Assyrians, their ruler having been killed and almost all the best men with him, were despondent. Croesus and all their other allies, seeing this, were distressed. So they left the camp and went away by night. When at daybreak the enemy's entrenchment was seen to be deserted, Cyrus took the Persians across first, and then Cyaxares' men crossed too. Cyrus thought they should pursue the enemy, but Cyaxares preferred the very opposite. Cyrus said: "Then give me some of the Medes to march with me, those who are eager to follow me as volunteers." Cyaxares allowed it, and sent with Cyrus a man to announce this to the Medes.

Meanwhile messengers came from the Hyrcanians. The Hyrcanians are neighbours of the Assyrians, a nation not numerous, and so they were subjects of the Assyrians, who used them without sparing them in labours or dangers. Then too, being about a thousand horsemen, they had been posted to bring up the rear, so that if any danger came from behind it might fall on them before the Assyrians. They, considering how they were treated, sent messengers to Cyrus to say that the Assyrians were justly hated by them, and that if he wished to go against them they would be his allies and guides. He asked whether they would overtake them; and the Hyrcanians said that even if they set out lightly equipped at dawn tomorrow they would overtake them. Cyrus asked for pledges that they spoke the truth; they agreed to give hostages, if he too would give his right hand and pledges by the gods. Cyrus gave them pledges that if they made good what they said, he would treat them as friends and faithful men, and they would have no less from him than the Persians or the Medes.

After this, while it was still light, Cyrus led out the army, Tigranes being with him with the Armenians, and he told the Hyrcanians to wait, so that they might go together. Almost all the Medes went out with Cyrus. He ordered the Hyrcanians to lead; and after covering a long way he came near the army of the Hyrcanians. The messengers told Cyrus this, and he ordered that, if they were friends, they should come to meet him as quickly as possible holding up their right hands. The Hyrcanians, hearing this, came at once, holding up their right hands as had been said. Greeting them, he said: "Tell me, how far is it from here to where the enemy's commanders and their main body are?" They said a little more than a parasang. So he ordered the Hyrcanians to lead. They led, and he went on with the Persians holding the centre, and he posted the horsemen on either side. When it was light and the enemy saw what was happening, no one fought, but some fled and others perished without a battle.

blocks: Croesus, the king of the Lydians, had sent the women ahead by night in their covered carriages, so that they might travel more easily in the cool, for it was summer, and he followed himself with the horsemen. They say the ruler of Phrygia by the Hellespont did the same. When the fugitives overtook them and they learned what was happening, they too fled. The king of the Cappadocians, who was still near, the Hyrcanians killed. The others pursued, but Cyrus ordered those with him to ride round the camp, to kill those who came out with arms, and he proclaimed to those who stayed that they should bring out their arms bound together and leave their horses at the tents, and that whoever did not do so would lose his head. Those who had arms brought them out and threw them in one place, and those assigned to it burned them.

Cyrus, considering that they had come with neither food nor drink, proclaimed that all the stewards of the tents should come, and when they came he said: "Come, men, prepare in each tent twice as much food as you used to make each day for your masters and their servants." They did as they were ordered. Some of the Medes caught wagons that had set out ahead, turned them back full of what an army needs and drove them in; others brought covered carriages of the noblest women, and showing Cyrus what they were bringing, drove them off again. Cyrus was stung at this and blamed himself, and calling the captains together he advised that the Persians too should acquire cavalry, so that with it they might pursue horsemen and overtake fugitives; and the others agreed.

When it was already past midday, the Median and Hyrcanian horsemen rode in, bringing captive horses and men. To the captive men he said: "Go away, working your land, living in your houses, living with your wives and enjoying your children, and tell this to the others; for one thing will be new for you, that the same man will not rule you as before, but everything else will be the same for you." They bowed down and went away. Cyrus said: "Now it is time, Medes and Armenians, to dine; dinners have been prepared for you, good friends, as best we could. And you, Hyrcanians," he said, "take them to the tents, the officers to the largest and the others as seems best, and dine yourselves; for your tents are safe and untouched." They did as they were told; and Cyrus sent many of the Persians round to guard the camp, so that if anyone approached from outside he would not go unnoticed, and if anyone inside ran away he would be caught. So the Persians passed the night.

The next day he ordered the spoils to be distributed to the soldiers, and the horses given to the Persians, so that they too might be horsemen. "And for Cyaxares," he said, "choose whatever you know will please him; for the Persians with me whatever is left over will be enough. For we have not been brought up in luxury, so you would perhaps laugh at us if you put anything grand on us; just as I know we shall give you much laughter sitting on the horses, and also, I think, falling on the ground." Calling the captains, he ordered them to take the horses, and to cast lots and each take an equal number.
