blocks: At that time there was in Rome a woman named Paulina, honoured for her distinguished family and her good character, and exceedingly rich. She was graceful in looks and of the age in which women take pride, and she was adorned with modesty. She was married to Saturninus, a man in no way behind her in any good quality. Decius Mundus, a man of great standing among the knights of the time, was taken with love for her and tried her with gifts; for he offered two hundred thousand Attic drachmas for one night. She would not bear it. He was inflamed still more with love, so that he courted death for himself by refusing food. He had a freedwoman of his father's named Ida, skilled in every kind of evil. Seeing the young man in this state, she encouraged him with words and revived him with promises, saying she would need only fifty thousand to bring the deed about for him. Taking the money she asked for, since she saw that Paulina could not be caught by money, but knew that she was most warmly devoted to the worship of Isis (she was then held a goddess by the Romans), she went to some of the priests of that false goddess, and with money persuaded them to deceive Paulina by whatever tricks they could and bring her to bed with Mundus. Charmed by the money, they set about the deed. The eldest of them went to Paulina, met her in private, and said he had come sent by Anubis, since the god, being in love with her, ordered her to come to him. The message seemed to her most welcome, if she was loved by a god; and she shared the news with her husband, and he agreed, knowing his wife's modesty. So she went to the precinct; and when it was time for sleep, a place had been prepared for the woman to sleep inside the temple, and the lamps were put out. Mundus, who had been hidden there, had his fill of her all night, coming to her as Anubis. Then he went away, and she went to her husband and told him of the appearance of Anubis, and boasted to the women she knew of having been thought worthy of a god's company. On the third day after the deed Mundus met her and said: "Paulina, I have kept the two hundred thousand, and you have served me without them. Your insults to Mundus did not touch me at all, once I had taken the name of Anubis." At this the woman understood the outrage, tore her dress, and showed her husband the plot; and he went to Tiberius. The emperor examined what had happened, crucified the priests and Ida, pulled down the temple, sank the statue of Isis in the river Tiber, and punished Mundus with exile, granting him pardon so that he was not punished more heavily because of the violence of his love.

These things were done in Rome; and in Samaria there was a disturbance. A man ordered the Samaritans to gather with him on Mount Gerizim, which they hold the holiest of mountains; and he promised to show them, when they came, the sacred vessels buried there by Moses. They gathered and were in arms. Pilate sent soldiers and killed some, put others to flight, and put to death the leaders among those taken alive. The Samaritans went to Vitellius, governor of Syria, accusing Pilate over the slaughter of their countrymen. Vitellius sent Marcellus to take care of the Jews, and ordered Pilate to go away to Rome to answer before the emperor for what he was charged with. He went away, having governed Judaea for ten years; but before he came near Rome, Tiberius had already died.

Vitellius came to Jerusalem while the feast of the Passover was being held, and was received magnificently. He remitted to the people of Jerusalem the taxes on the fruits of the land, and allowed the high priest's robe to be kept in the temple and to be in the priests' charge as before. At that time it was kept in the tower; for one of the high priests, namely the first Hyrcanus, built a tower close to the temple and lived in it, and kept there the high priest's robe that belonged to him as high priest. The same was done by him and by those after him. Herod, rebuilding that tower more richly, renamed it after Antony, being his friend; and finding the robe in it, he kept it there. Archelaus did this too, and after him the Romans did the same with the robe, which was kept there under the seals of the priests and the treasurers. When a feast came, it was given back to the high priests by the commander of the fort, and one day after the feast it was put back there again. Vitellius gave the robe up to the nation. He removed the high priest Joseph, also called Caiaphas, from the priesthood, and gave it to Jonathan, the son of Ananus the high priest. On Tiberius's orders Vitellius made a treaty with Artabanus, king of the Parthians, who sent his son Darius with many gifts as a hostage. Herod the tetrarch, who was present at the treaty, at once wrote and sent an account of what had happened to Caesar. Then, when Vitellius wrote about these things to Tiberius, he wrote back that he had learned everything from Herod. This moved Vitellius to anger against Herod; he nursed his anger in secret, and took revenge on him when Gaius came to power.

blocks: At that time Philip, this Herod's brother, died too, in the twentieth year of Tiberius's rule, having ruled for thirty-seven years. He was quiet in character and moderate to his subjects, making his progresses with a few chosen men; and if anyone came up to him as he went, asking for help, at once his throne was set down on the spot (for the men carrying it followed him), and he sat and heard him, punished the wrongdoers and released those unjustly accused. Since Philip had no children, Tiberius added his realm to the province of Syria.

Herod the tetrarch, setting out for Rome, stayed with his brother Herod, whom the daughter of Simon the high priest had borne to King Herod. Falling in love with Herodias, his brother's wife, the daughter of their brother Aristobulus and the sister of Agrippa the Great, he spoke to her of marriage. She accepted and agreed to move to him if he would cast out the daughter of Aretas. He sailed to Rome on these terms; and when he came back, his wife, the daughter of Aretas, learning of the agreement with Herodias, asked to be sent to the fortress of Machaerus, which was on the border of Aretas's realm and Herod's. Herod sent her, not knowing what she intended; and from there she set off to her father in Arabia, and told him of Herod's purpose towards her. He took this as a ground for enmity; a battle was fought between them through their generals, and Herod's men were beaten and his whole army fell. Herod reported this by letter to Tiberius; and he wrote to Vitellius to make war on Aretas, and either send him to Rome a prisoner if taken alive, or send his head if he was killed.

Some thought that Herod's army had been destroyed by God, since he was paying the penalty for the murder of John, the prophet and baptist. For Josephus wrote this about him too, word for word: "For Herod killed him, a good man, who bade the Jews practise virtue, use justice towards one another and piety towards God, and so come together for baptism; for so the baptism would appear acceptable to him. Herod, fearing that his great power of persuasion over men might lead to some sedition (for they seemed ready to do anything on his advice), thought it far better to forestall him and kill him before any revolt came from him, rather than fall into trouble when a change came and then repent. So because of Herod's suspicion he was sent in chains to Machaerus and killed there; and the Jews thought that the destruction of the army came as punishment for him, God wishing to harm Herod."

Vitellius hurried to make war on Aretas. When he set out to march through the country of the Jews, their leading men begged him not to go through their land; for it was not their ancestral custom for images to be carried through their country, and many images were on the standards. Persuaded, he took the army across through the great plain, and himself went up with Herod to Jerusalem to sacrifice to God. Staying there three days, he removed Jonathan from the high priesthood and put in his brother Theophilus. On the fourth day, when letters were brought to him about the death of Tiberius, he made the multitude swear loyalty to Gaius, and called back the army. They say that Aretas too, having taken the auspices, said that it was impossible for the army to fight; for one of the leaders would die, either the one who ordered the war, or the one ordered, or the one against whom the order had been made.

blocks: Vitellius went back to Antioch; and Agrippa, the son of Aristobulus, happened to be in Rome when Tiberius died. A little before the death of his grandfather Herod the Great he had been brought up in Rome, and became a companion of Drusus, the son of Tiberius, and known to Antonia, the wife of the elder Drusus, since his mother Berenice was honoured by her. Agrippa was magnificent and lavish in giving, and when his mother died he spent some of the money on himself, living expensively, some on gifts, and most on Caesar's freedmen. Quickly he was in want. When Tiberius's son died, Tiberius forbade his son's companions to come into his sight, so that he might not be reminded of him through them and stirred to grief. For this reason, then, and because he had run out of money, he went back to Judaea in a bad way. Pressed to pay his creditors his debts, which were many, and having nothing, he thought of killing himself. His wife Cypros understood his intention. She was the daughter of Phasael, the nephew of King Herod, born to him by Salampsio, Herod's daughter, whom he had by Mariamme, the one he killed, as has been told. This Cypros, then, the wife of Agrippa, perceiving his plan, held him back from it, and sent to Herodias, the wife of Herod the tetrarch, who was Agrippa's sister, telling her of her brother's intention, and asking her to help and to call on her own husband to help too. They sent for him and gave him Tiberias to live in, and assigned him some money for his expenses. But after a time a quarrel arose between Herod and Agrippa, and Agrippa moved to Flaccus, governor of Syria, who had been friendly to him since Rome, and lived there, Flaccus receiving him. Agrippa's brother Aristobulus was there too; quarrelling with his brother, he made Flaccus his enemy by slanders; and Agrippa was driven out from there.

Brought to the last extremity of want, he wished to sail to Italy, and asked Marsyas, his freedman, to get him money from somewhere by borrowing. Marsyas went to Peter, a freedman of Berenice, Agrippa's mother; and Peter said that if he made a bond for twenty thousand Attic drachmas, he could take the sum less two thousand five hundred. Agrippa agreed, and taking the loan was about to sail away. But Herennius Capito, the procurator of Jamnia, demanded from him three hundred thousand pieces of silver owed to Caesar, and ordered him to stay on that account. Agrippa pretended to obey, but went off by night. Sailing to Alexandria, he asked Alexander the alabarch to lend him two hundred thousand. He said he would not lend it to him, but lent it to his wife Cypros, because of her love for her husband and her other virtues. When she had received the loan, Agrippa sailed off to Italy, and Cypros went back to Judaea with the children.

Coming to Caesar Tiberius, Agrippa was received kindly. But when a letter from Herennius Capito was brought to Caesar, saying that Agrippa had run away while being pressed for a debt of three hundred thousand, he was angry, and ordered that he should not be allowed to come to him until he paid the debt. Agrippa borrowed and paid the debt, and went in to Tiberius again. Caesar told him to keep company with his grandson and look after him. But Agrippa leaned rather to Gaius, who was the grandson of Antonia, the mother of Germanicus and of Claudius, who became sole ruler after Gaius. By courting him he won his friendship. Once, as the two were driving together, talk arose about Tiberius. Agrippa, calling on the gods, prayed that Tiberius might quickly step down from the rule in favour of Gaius. Eutychus, a freedman of Agrippa, who heard the words, went to Caesar as if to tell him something for his safety. But Tiberius had become slow in everything, and paid no attention even to those who reported something for his own sake. He did not deal quickly with envoys, saying that otherwise, if they went back quickly, others would come, and he would have a crowd about him; nor did he replace the governors and procurators he had sent out with successors, unless they died first. He said he did this out of care for his subjects, so that, having had enough gain in the time, they might be duller towards wrongdoing. Well then. He gave as an example a wounded man whose wounds were covered with flies; someone, pitying him, tried to drive them off, and when he stopped him, the one who was trying to drive off the flies asked the reason; and the wounded man answered: "These, being full of blood, do not trouble me much; but if they were chased away, fresh, hungry ones would come and hurt me more." A further proof of Tiberius's slowness in this is that in twenty-two years of his sole rule he sent the Jews only two men to govern their nation, Gratus and Pilate. Being like this in everything, he did not think Eutychus worth a hearing either.

Pressed to pay his creditors his debts, which were many, and having nothing, he thought of killing himself. His wife Cypros understood his intention. She was the daughter of Phasael, the nephew of King Herod, born to him by Salampsio, Herod's daughter, whom he had by Mariamme, the one he killed, as has been told. This Cypros, then, the wife of Agrippa, perceiving his plan, held him back from it, and sent to Herodias, the wife of Herod the tetrarch, who was Agrippa's sister, telling her of her brother's intention, and asking her to help and to call on her own husband to help too. They sent for him and gave him Tiberias to live in, and assigned him some money for his expenses. But after a time a quarrel arose between Herod and Agrippa, and Agrippa moved to Flaccus, governor of Syria, who had been friendly to him since Rome, and lived there, Flaccus receiving him. Agrippa's brother Aristobulus was there too; quarrelling with his brother, he made Flaccus his enemy by slanders; and Agrippa was driven out from there. Brought to the last extremity of want, he wished to sail to Italy, and asked Marsyas, his freedman, to get him money from somewhere by borrowing. Marsyas went to Peter, a freedman of Berenice, Agrippa's mother; and Peter said that if he made a bond for twenty thousand Attic drachmas, he could take the sum less two thousand five hundred. Agrippa agreed, and taking the loan was about to sail away. But Herennius Capito, the procurator of Jamnia, demanded from him three hundred thousand pieces of silver owed to Caesar, and ordered him to stay on that account. Agrippa pretended to obey, but went off by night. Sailing to Alexandria, he asked Alexander the alabarch to lend him two hundred thousand. He said he would not lend it to him, but lent it to his wife Cypros, because of her love for her husband and her other virtues. When she had received the loan, Agrippa sailed off to Italy, and Cypros went back to Judaea with the children. Coming to Caesar Tiberius, Agrippa was received kindly. But when a letter from Herennius Capito was brought to Caesar, saying that Agrippa had run away while being pressed for a debt of three hundred thousand, he was angry, and ordered that he should not be allowed to come to him until he paid the debt. Agrippa borrowed and paid the debt, and went in to Tiberius again. Caesar told him to keep company with his grandson and look after him. But Agrippa leaned rather to Gaius, who was the grandson of Antonia, the mother of Germanicus and of Claudius, who became sole ruler after Gaius. By courting him he won his friendship. Once, as the two were driving together, talk arose about Tiberius. Agrippa, calling on the gods, prayed that Tiberius might quickly step down from the rule in favour of Gaius. Eutychus, a freedman of Agrippa, who heard the words, went to Caesar as if to tell him something for his safety. But Tiberius had become slow in everything, and paid no attention even to those who reported something for his own sake. He did not deal quickly with envoys, saying that otherwise, if they went back quickly, others would come, and he would have a crowd about him; nor did he replace the governors and procurators he had sent out with successors, unless they died first. He said he did this out of care for his subjects, so that, having had enough gain in the time, they might be duller towards wrongdoing. Well then. He gave as an example a wounded man whose wounds were covered with flies; someone, pitying him, tried to drive them off, and when he stopped him, the one who was trying to drive off the flies asked the reason; and the wounded man answered: "These, being full of blood, do not trouble me much; but if they were chased away, fresh, hungry ones would come and hurt me more." A further proof of Tiberius's slowness in this is that in twenty-two years of his sole rule he sent the Jews only two men to govern their nation, Gratus and Pilate. Being like this in everything, he did not think Eutychus worth a hearing either.

blocks: Agrippa begged Antonia to get Caesar to hear Eutychus. Antonia was held in the highest honour by Tiberius, both as having been the wife of his brother Drusus and for her chastity. For being widowed young she remained a widow and refused a second marriage, though the emperor urged it on her, and she lived her life so as to be above reproach. For this she was honoured by Tiberius, and also because she had been his benefactor, having revealed a plot formed by many powerful men. So, when she asked him to examine Eutychus, he said: "Let the gods know, Antonia, that what will be done will be not by my will, but at your urging." And he ordered Eutychus to be brought. Standing before him, he said: "Gaius and Agrippa, master, were talking together, and Agrippa said: 'If only the day would come when this old man departs and appoints you ruler of the world! For Tiberius his grandson will be no hindrance to us, dying at your hand. And the world would be blessed, and I before it.'" Tiberius thought the words true; and at the same time, keeping a grudge against Agrippa because he had not chosen to look after his grandson but had gone over entirely to Gaius, he ordered one of those standing by to bind him. He was led away in chains still in purple, and stood before the palace leaning on a tree in despair. Others in chains were there too. When a bird flew down onto that tree (the Romans call the bird bubo), one of the prisoners, seeing it, asked the soldier guarding him who the man in purple was; and when he learned, he asked the soldier chained to him to go near. On getting his wish, he said: "Young man, I bring you good news of a very quick release from your chains, and of advancement to the greatest rank and power; you will be envied by those who now pity you, and will die in happiness, leaving your wealth to your children. But when you see this bird again, know that your death will then come after five days. When you have prospered according to our prediction, remember us too, so that we may escape the misfortune in which we now are." When he said this he was laughed at then, but later he was seen to deserve wonder.

Agrippa was in chains for six months. Tiberius, failing as his illness grew stronger, ordered Euodus, who was the most honoured of his freedmen, to bring the children to him, so that he could talk to them before his death. He had no children; for his son Drusus had died; but he had by him a grandson, Tiberius Gemellus, and a nephew Gaius, the son of his brother Germanicus, already a young man, schooled in learning and loved and honoured by the people for his father's virtue. So Tiberius ordered the children to be brought in early the next day. His wish was above all to leave the rule to his grandson; but he took it as an omen that the divine wished the rule to come round to whichever reached him first, and he sent ordering his grandson's tutor to bring the boy early. When day had come, he sent Euodus to call in whichever of the children was there; he found Gaius before the room and brought him in to Tiberius. Tiberius, reflecting on the power of the divine, lamented for his grandson as if he were lost. Though troubled by this, he said to Gaius: "My boy, though Tiberius is closer kin to me than you, I myself, both by my own will and by the vote of the gods, put the rule of the Romans into your hands. I ask you not to forget your kinship with Tiberius, but to care for him as a kinsman; for whatever is done against justice does not go unpunished by divine providence." So Tiberius, having declared Gaius successor to the rule, lived on a few days and died, having ruled twenty-two years, seven months and as many days; and Gaius was left as emperor.

blocks: The death of Tiberius was announced to the Romans; but they did not believe the report, because they wished so much for the thing. For he had done the Roman nobles very many terrible things, being harsh in anger and punishing even the slightest slips with death. Marsyas, Agrippa's freedman, learning of Tiberius's death, ran to him and said in Hebrew: "The lion is dead." He promised him thanks, if he had brought true news. The centurion, seeing Agrippa joyful, suspected that something new had happened, and asked what the news might be; and Agrippa, having already become familiar with the man, revealed the secret. He shared his pleasure and set out a dinner. While they were feasting, someone came saying that Tiberius was alive. The centurion, afraid because he had been living with a prisoner of the emperor, ordered him to be bound, though he had already loosed him. The next day the report of Tiberius's death was widespread, and letters were sent by Gaius, one to the senate, announcing Tiberius's death and his own succession to the rule, the other to Piso, the prefect of the city, instructing him to move Agrippa from the camp to the house in which he had been before he was bound.

Gaius brought Tiberius's body to Rome and buried it lavishly, and wished to free Agrippa at once; but Antonia prevented it, not out of hatred for the one to be freed, but out of concern for the one who would free him, so that he might not seem to rejoice at the emperor's death by freeing his prisoner so quickly. When a few days had passed he sent for Agrippa, had his overgrown hair cut and changed his clothes, then put the diadem on him and made him king of Philip's tetrarchy, adding the tetrarchy of Lysanias too as an increase; and he exchanged gold for bronze, giving him in place of the iron chain with which he had been bound a golden one of equal weight.

In the second year of Gaius's sole rule Agrippa asked to be allowed to go home, and promised to come back again once he had arranged the affairs of his realm as they should be; and when Gaius allowed it, he sailed. Herodias, his sister, envied her brother his good fortune, especially when she saw him doing business with the crowds with the insignia of kingship; and she stirred her husband to sail to Rome and seek an equal rule for himself. He wished to keep quiet. But his wife pestered her husband more fiercely, urging him to do everything for the kingship, and did not let up until she had brought Herod to her view even against his will. So he set sail for Rome with his wife. Agrippa too prepared to go to Rome, and sent ahead one of his freedmen bringing gifts to the emperor and letters against Herod. They found Gaius at Baiae, a small town in Campania. As soon as Herod came into his sight, Gaius read Agrippa's letters, which accused Herod of an agreement with Sejanus against the rule of Tiberius, and again with Artabanus the Parthian, at that time, against Gaius's own. As proof of the charge he gave a store of arms in Herod's armouries, enough for seventy thousand heavy infantry. Gaius was moved by what had been written, and asked Herod if the story about the arms was true. When he admitted it, Gaius, believing in his revolt, took away his tetrarchy and added it to Agrippa's kingdom, and likewise gave his money to Agrippa, and condemned Herod to exile for life. To Herodias, as Agrippa's sister, he gave all the money that belonged to her, and told her she need not share her husband's exile, for Agrippa's sake. She thanked Gaius, but said it was not right, having shared her husband's prosperity, to desert him in his misfortunes.

Gaius handled affairs fairly moderately for the first year and the next, but as he went on he made himself divine and tried to make himself a god. When a quarrel had arisen between the Jews and the Greeks in Alexandria, three from each side came

blocks: to Gaius as envoys. Apion, one of the envoys of the Alexandrians, accused the Jews of many things, and in particular that, while all who were under the Romans set up altars and temples to Gaius and honoured him as a god, these alone thought it shameful to honour him with statues and to swear by his name. At this Philo, the head of the Jews' embassy, a man of note and not unskilled in philosophy, was ready to make a defence for his countrymen. But Gaius would not bear it, ordered them to go away out of his sight, and plainly meant to harm them. Philo went out, having been insulted, and said to the Jews with him that they must take heart; for Gaius had raged not against them but against the divine itself.

The emperor, thinking it terrible not to be worshipped as a god by the Jews, sent out Petronius as successor to Vitellius's command, ordering him to invade Judaea with a large force and set up his statue in the temple of God; and if they did not give way willingly, to do it after defeating them in war. Petronius, having taken over the command of Syria, hurried to carry out Caesar's orders. When he reached Ptolemais, many tens of thousands of Jews came to him, begging him not to force them to break their ancestral customs. "If you cannot be moved," they said, "kill us first and so set up the statue." Petronius answered: "If I were doing this of my own accord, your plea to me would be just; but since Caesar has ordered it, I am under every necessity to carry out what he has decided." Saying this he went to Tiberias, to see what the Jews had in mind. Many tens of thousands met him there, begging him not to put them under compulsion or defile the city with a statue. Petronius said: "Will you go to war, then?" They said: "We will not go to war, but we will die before we break our ancestral customs," and offered themselves to be slaughtered. This went on for forty days. Aristobulus, the brother of Agrippa, and others of the chief men begged Petronius not to drive the multitude to desperation, but to write to Gaius of their unbending refusal to receive the statue; for perhaps he would soften and give up his decision; and if he held to his vote again, then he could take the matter in hand himself. Petronius was persuaded and wrote to Gaius about the matter.

King Agrippa, living in Rome, was advancing in his intimacy with Gaius. When he was admired for the lavishness and magnificence with which he entertained the emperor at dinner, he was urged to ask for whatever he wished. He said: "I will ask you for nothing that brings wealth, but for something that will bring you a reputation for piety and me renown. I ask you to give up, for my sake, the setting up of the statue that you order Petronius to place in the temple of the Jews." Gaius, ashamed to seem false before so many witnesses, agreed, and wrote to Petronius that if he had already set up the statue he should not take it down, but if he had not yet set it up, he should not try to do it any more: "for I no longer wish it to be set up, because of Agrippa, a man honoured by me." Gaius wrote this to Petronius before he read Petronius's letters showing that the Jews were being driven to revolt because of the statue. Deeply pained at this, he wrote to Petronius: "Since the gifts of the Jews have counted for more with you than my orders, consider for yourself what you must do about yourself. For I shall make you an example to men now and hereafter, not to set aside an emperor's orders." Petronius did not receive this letter while Gaius was still alive; he received first the letters about his death, and only then Gaius's letter to him.

So Gaius, having been most wicked, perished, killed by a plot. The manner of the plot against him, and by whom he was killed, the narrative will tell when it goes through the affairs of the emperors. When he had been killed, Claudius, who was hiding out of fear, was brought out by the soldiers and proclaimed emperor, Agrippa too having worked hard for his proclamation. As soon as his sole rule was confirmed, he confirmed Agrippa's realm, praised him, and added to it all that King Herod, his grandfather, had ruled. Agrippa also asked Claudius for the kingdom of Chalcis for his brother Herod; and it was given him by Caesar.

blocks: At this time the Jews there rose against the Alexandrians. For since Gaius had been ill disposed towards them, in the way that has been told, they had been mistreated by the Greeks in the city while he was sole ruler; but when Gaius died they took heart and were in arms. Claudius wrote to the prefect in Egypt to put down the strife, and at the request of the two kings, Agrippa and Herod, he also sent an edict to Syria, to Alexandria and to all the rest of the world that was subject to the Romans, saying: "Though the Jews from of old were granted equal citizenship with the Alexandrians and the citizens of the other cities, Gaius out of madness humbled them, because the nation of the Jews would not bear to call him a god. But I ordain that the nation shall lose none of its ancient rights because of his folly, and that their former rights shall be kept for them while they abide by the customs of the Jews; the kings Agrippa and Herod, most dear to me, having asked me for this."

He also sent Agrippa off to his kingdom, which had become more splendid. Coming to Jerusalem he offered sacrifices of thanksgiving, and hung up over the treasury the golden chain given him by Gaius, as a proof of the power of God and of the change of fortune, and that great things sometimes fall and the lowly are raised up. Having sacrificed lavishly, he removed Theophilus son of Ananus from the high priesthood, and gave the honour to Simon son of Boethus, whose surname was Cantheras. Simon had two brothers, and his father was Boethus, whose daughter King Herod married, as has been told. He repaid the people of Jerusalem for their goodwill towards him by remitting to them the tax on each house. He appointed Silas commander of the cavalry of his whole army, a man who had shared many of his labours.

Some young men of Dora, reckless and bold, brought a statue of Caesar into the synagogue of the Jews and set it up. This disturbed Agrippa; at once he went to Publius Petronius, governor of Syria, and accused the people of Dora. Petronius sent a centurion and ordered those who had done the bold deed to be brought to him, and wrote to the magistrates of Dora to show the centurion the guilty men, if they did not wish to seem accomplices in the deed. Agrippa took the priesthood from Simon Cantheras and brought Jonathan son of Ananus to it again. But he declined, saying he was content to have held the high priesthood once, and asked that his brother Matthias be advanced to it as worthy of the honour. The king was persuaded and gave the high priesthood to Matthias.

Silas, Agrippa's cavalry commander, trusting in the dangers he had run for him, claimed an untimely freedom of speech, and was tiresome, reminding him of the gloomy times of his fortune and boasting of his own zeal and loyalty then. Agrippa was displeased at his unrestrained frankness; and when Silas did not give way, the king was provoked to anger, and not only removed him from the cavalry command but even put him in chains. In time his anger was blunted, and reckoning how many labours Silas had endured for him, on the day he was celebrating his birthday he invited Silas to feast with him. But he would not obey, saying: "To what honour is the king calling me back, one that will soon be lost? Or does he think I have stopped speaking freely? Now I shall cry out all the more about the dangers I saved him from, the labours I bore winning him safety and honour; for which my reward is chains and a dark prison, which I shall never forget." The king, learning this, and seeing that he was incurably disposed, left him in custody again.

This king was beneficent in his gifts no less than his grandfather Herod; but while Herod showed his generosity to foreigners and not to the Jews, Agrippa was beneficent to all alike and gentle in character. He liked to live constantly in Jerusalem, and kept the ancestral customs purely. There was one Simon in Jerusalem, reputed to be exact in the law; he gathered a crowd and dared to denounce the king while he was away at Caesarea. This did not escape Agrippa. So he sent for Simon and said: "Tell me, what of the things being done is against the law?" He, having nothing to say, begged to be pardoned. And the king, beyond expectation, was reconciled with him and sent him away with gifts. He took the high priesthood from Matthias and gave it to Elionaeus, the son of Cithaerus.

When he had reigned three years over all Judaea, he held games in the city of Caesarea, which was formerly called Strato's Tower. On the second day of the games he put on a robe made of silver and came into the theatre at the start of the day. Lit by the first rays of the rising sun, the silver shone wonderfully, glittering in a way that struck awe in those who gazed at it. At once the flatterers cried out, one from here and another from there, calling him a god and adding: "Be gracious to us; for if until now we feared you as a man, from now on we acknowledge you as greater than mortal nature." The king did not rebuke them, nor reject the impious flattery. Looking up a little later, he saw the bird, the owl, above his head, and understood it then as a messenger of evil, as it had once been the herald of good. He felt a pain to the heart, and a sudden pain of the belly came on him. He said to his friends: "I, your god, am now ending my life; and I who was called immortal by you am hastening to die." As he said this he was overcome by the growing pain, and was quickly carried to the palace. When word went round that he was dying, the multitude at once, with women and children, sat in sackcloth according to the ancestral law and begged God for the king, and all lamented. Agrippa, lying in a high room and looking down on them falling on their faces, was not without tears himself. For five days he was worn down by the pain of the belly and ended his life, having lived fifty-four years and reigned seven, four under Gaius
text: At this time the Jews there rose against the Alexandrians. For since Gaius had been ill disposed towards them, in the way that has been told, they had been mistreated by the Greeks in the city while he was sole ruler; but when Gaius died they took heart and were in arms. Claudius wrote to the prefect in Egypt to put down the strife, and at the request of the two kings, Agrippa and Herod, he also sent an edict to Syria, to Alexandria and to all the rest of the world that was subject to the Romans, saying: "Though the Jews from of old were granted equal citizenship with the Alexandrians and the citizens of the other cities, Gaius out of madness humbled them, because the nation of the Jews would not bear to call him a god. But I ordain that the nation shall lose none of its ancient rights because of his folly, and that their former rights shall be kept for them while they abide by the customs of the Jews; the kings Agrippa and Herod, most dear to me, having asked me for this." He also sent Agrippa off to his kingdom, which had become more splendid. Coming to Jerusalem he offered sacrifices of thanksgiving, and hung up over the treasury the golden chain given him by Gaius, as a proof of the power of God and of the change of fortune, and that great things sometimes fall and the lowly are raised up. Having sacrificed lavishly, he removed Theophilus son of Ananus from the high priesthood, and gave the honour to Simon son of Boethus, whose surname was Cantheras. Simon had two brothers, and his father was Boethus, whose daughter King Herod married, as has been told. He repaid the people of Jerusalem for their goodwill towards him by remitting to them the tax on each house. He appointed Silas commander of the cavalry of his whole army, a man who had shared many of his labours. Some young men of Dora, reckless and bold, brought a statue of Caesar into the synagogue of the Jews and set it up. This disturbed Agrippa; at once he went to Publius Petronius, governor of Syria, and accused the people of Dora. Petronius sent a centurion and ordered those who had done the bold deed to be brought to him, and wrote to the magistrates of Dora to show the centurion the guilty men, if they did not wish to seem accomplices in the deed. Agrippa took the priesthood from Simon Cantheras and brought Jonathan son of Ananus to it again. But he declined, saying he was content to have held the high priesthood once, and asked that his brother Matthias be advanced to it as worthy of the honour. The king was persuaded and gave the high priesthood to Matthias. Silas, Agrippa's cavalry commander, trusting in the dangers he had run for him, claimed an untimely freedom of speech, and was tiresome, reminding him of the gloomy times of his fortune and boasting of his own zeal and loyalty then. Agrippa was displeased at his unrestrained frankness; and when Silas did not give way, the king was provoked to anger, and not only removed him from the cavalry command but even put him in chains. In time his anger was blunted, and reckoning how many labours Silas had endured for him, on the day he was celebrating his birthday he invited Silas to feast with him. But he would not obey, saying: "To what honour is the king calling me back, one that will soon be lost? Or does he think I have stopped speaking freely? Now I shall cry out all the more about the dangers I saved him from, the labours I bore winning him safety and honour; for which my reward is chains and a dark prison, which I shall never forget." The king, learning this, and seeing that he was incurably disposed, left him in custody again. This king was beneficent in his gifts no less than his grandfather Herod; but while Herod showed his generosity to foreigners and not to the Jews, Agrippa was beneficent to all alike and gentle in character. blocks: and three under Claudius. While his death was still unknown to the multitude, Herod his brother, the ruler of Chalcis, and Helcias the cavalry commander agreed together, sent men to Silas, who was their enemy, and murdered him, as if the king had ordered it.

So Agrippa died, leaving a son Agrippa of seventeen years and three daughters: one was married to Herod, her father's brother, and was called Berenice, while the two, Mariamme and Drusilla, were unmarried. When the king's death became known, the people of Caesarea and Sebaste, forgetting his benefits, reviled him, seized the statues of the king's daughters, carried them to the brothels and abused them, and held public feasts, wearing garlands and perfume and pouring libations to Charon.

The dead man's son Agrippa was then living in Rome, being brought up at the court of Claudius Caesar. Claudius was eager to send him at once to succeed to the kingdom; but those about him turned him from his purpose, saying it was risky to entrust so great a kingdom to one so young. So he sent Cuspius Fadus as procurator of Judaea and the whole kingdom, ordering him to rebuke the people of Caesarea and Sebaste for their insult to the dead man. Fadus, on reaching Judaea, put down a sedition that had arisen, cleared the country of bandits, and ordered the high priest's robe to be stored in the fortress Antonia, as before. The priests and the leading men of Jerusalem did not dare to oppose him, but still asked him to allow them to send envoys to Caesar to ask that the sacred robe be kept by them; and they were allowed. When the envoys reached Rome, Agrippa's son, the younger Agrippa, who was living there, as has been said, asked Caesar to grant the Jews to keep the sacred robe. Claudius granted it, and wrote to Fadus about it. Herod too, Agrippa's brother and ruler of Chalcis, asked Caesar for authority over the temple and the sacred money and for the appointment of the high priests. He got his request, and from him the authority remained with all his descendants until the capture of Jerusalem. He removed Cantheras from the high priesthood, bringing in instead Joseph son of Camei.

blocks: At this time Helena, the queen of the Adiabenians, and her son Izates changed their way of life to the customs of the Jews. For Monobazus, king of the Adiabenians, whose surname was also Bazaeus, was taken with love for his sister Helena and married her. Once, lying with her when she was pregnant, he put his hand on her belly, and falling asleep he seemed to hear a voice telling him to take his hand from the womb and not to press the babe in it, who by God's providence would have a happy beginning and a happy end. Troubled by the voice, he told this to his wife. And when the son was born he named him Izates. He had another son older than him, born of Helena, and other children by other wives, but he loved Izates as if he were an only child. So his brothers envied him. His father, fearing for him, sent him to Abennerigus, king of Spasinou Charax. He received Izates gladly, made him his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter, and gave him land. Monobazus, grown old, wished to see Izates before he died. So he sent for him, greeted him affectionately, and assigned him a district, in which he lived until his father's death.

When Monobazus died, Queen Helena sent for the grandees and the satraps; and when they came she said: "It has not escaped you that my husband wished Izates to succeed to the kingdom. But knowing that he is fortunate who receives the kingdom not from one but from the many, and those willing, I have put the matter to your judgement." They said they confirmed the king's judgement, and would gladly yield to Izates, who had rightly been preferred to his brothers in accordance with everyone's prayers; and that his brothers and kin must first be killed, so that he might rule safely. The queen advised them to hold back their opinion about killing Izates's relatives until he came and approved it with them. They urged that the men be kept in chains meanwhile until his arrival. The queen set her eldest son over affairs until his brother came back, and gave him his father's signet ring too. So Izates came, and his brother received him and stood aside from the rule for him.

While he had been abroad, a Jew called Ananias had come to know him and taught him about God and the customs of the Jews. It happened too that Helena, instructed by another Jew, had been converted to the Jewish ways. So Izates, coming and finding his kin in chains, was displeased; he freed them, but sent them away, so that they might not be under suspicion by being present, some to Rome as hostages and others to the Parthians. Learning that his mother had embraced the Jewish ways, he was eager to be converted to them himself, and was ready to be circumcised. But his mother prevented him, saying that his subjects would turn to ill will because of it, and would not bear to be ruled by a king who followed Jewish ways. He referred her words to Ananias, who was present. When he advised the same, the king was persuaded for the time; but another Jew, Eleazar, came from Galilee, and finding him reading the law of Moses, said: "You ought not only to read the words, king, but also to do what they ordain. How long will you stay uncircumcised?" He did not put off the deed, but was circumcised; and he told his mother and Ananias that the thing had been done. They fell into fear that both the king and they themselves would be in danger. But God did not allow their fear to come to pass.

Helena had a desire to go to Jerusalem and worship at the temple of God. Her son allowed it and gave her a great deal of money, and she went away to Jerusalem. Finding many there dying of famine, she brought grain from Alexandria and a cargo of dried figs from Cyprus, bought at great cost, and shared them out among the needy. Her son too sent much money to the leading men of Jerusalem, so that the starving might be helped by it as far as possible.

So much for that. Artabanus, the king of the Parthians, learning of a plot that the satraps had formed against him, came to Izates, bringing about a thousand kinsmen and servants. He met Izates on the road and said: "Do not overlook me, king, brought low by a change of fortune and become a private man instead of a king, but help me." He said this with tears. Izates, hearing the name, leapt down from his horse and said: "Take heart, king; for either I shall restore you to the kingdom of the Parthians, or I shall give up my own to you." He said this and set him on the horse, and himself followed on foot. Artabanus swore that unless he too mounted his horse and led the way, he would get down himself. Izates was persuaded and leapt onto his horse, and paid the Parthian every honour, bringing him to the palace. He wrote to the Parthians to receive Artabanus. The Parthians agreed to receive him, but said they could not give up the rule, which had already been entrusted to another; but Cinnamus, as the man who had taken over the kingdom was named, wrote to Artabanus (for he had been brought up by him and was a good man), urging him to come in trust and take back the rule. Artabanus trusted him and went. Cinnamus met him, made obeisance, hailed him as king, took the diadem from his own head and put it on his. So Artabanus, restored to his rule after six years, did not forget Izates's kindness, but repaid him.

Some time later, when Artabanus died, his son Vardanes girded on the kingdom. He came to Izates and asked him to be his ally against the Romans; but he would not be persuaded, and even advised him to give up his campaign against them and not to attempt the impossible. Vardanes declared war on Izates for not obeying. But the Parthians, learning that he meant to march against the Romans, killed him and gave the kingdom to his brother Gotarzes; when he died by a plot, his brother Vologeses succeeded him.

Izates's brother Monobazus and his kin also wished to follow Jewish ways, and carried their wish into action. What they had done became known to their subjects. They wrote to Abias, king of the Arabs, promising to give him much money if he would march against their king, and promising that they would desert Izates at the first encounter. The Arab was persuaded by this, and came against Izates bringing a large force. When battle was joined, Izates's men deserted him by agreement and turned their backs and fled. Izates, learning that the betrayal had come from the grandees, withdrew to his camp, found those responsible and punished them. The next day he engaged and won, put the Arabs to flight, and drove their king, pursued, into a fortress. He killed himself as he was being captured, and the fortress was taken and its contents plundered. Izates returned home.

The grandees of the Adiabenians wrote to Vologeses, king of the Parthians, asking him to kill Izates and set up a ruler over them from among the Parthians; for they hated their own king for having become a convert to a foreign religion. The Parthian at once set out with a very large force, and Izates encamped against him. A man sent by the Parthian told Izates how great the force of the Parthians was, and that Vologeses threatened to exact punishment from him for having been ungrateful to his masters; for not even the God he worshipped could save him from his hands. To this Izates answered that he knew the power of the Parthians, but knew that God was more powerful than men. He said this and prayed to God. That very night Vologeses received letters that enemies had invaded Parthia and were ravaging it, and at once hurried off without achieving anything. So by the providence of God Izates escaped the Parthian's threats. Some time later he died, having lived fifty-five years and spent twenty-four in his rule; he died leaving twenty-four sons and as many daughters. He left the rule to his brother Monobazus.

blocks: who was a sorcerer, named Theudas, persuaded most of the crowd to take up their possessions and follow him to the Jordan; for he said he was a prophet and could divide the river by his command; and he deceived very many. Fadus sent a squadron of horse against them and killed many, and took no fewer alive, among them Theudas himself, whose head they cut off and brought to Jerusalem. Fadus was succeeded by Tiberius Alexander, the son of Alexander who had been alabarch in Alexandria. The sons of Judas the Galilean, James and Simon, were also put to death; it was Judas who had made the people revolt when Quirinius was assessing; Alexander crucified them. Herod, who reigned over Chalcis, removed Joseph son of Cemedes from the high priesthood and gave it to Ananias son of Nedebaeus.

Cumanus came as successor to Tiberius Alexander. In the eighth year of Claudius's sole rule Herod, the brother of Agrippa the Great, died, leaving three sons; and Claudius gave his realm to the younger Agrippa. While Cumanus was procurator of Judaea, a multitude gathered in Jerusalem for the feast of the Passover. So, to prevent any revolt by the multitude, which was large, Cumanus stationed armed soldiers on the porticoes of the temple to put down any uproar that arose; those before him had done this too. On the fourth day of the feast a soldier on the porticoes uncovered his private parts and showed them to the crowds. They were enraged, since the soldier had committed impiety against God, and the bolder among them abused Cumanus. He was provoked by the abuse, and ordered the whole army to come to the fortress Antonia, which overlooks the temple. The multitude, seeing the soldiers, rushed to flee; and since the exits were narrow, many were pressed together in the flight, crushed and trampled by one another, and died, so that those who died then were counted at twenty thousand; and there was mourning instead of a festival.

This grief had not yet been laid to rest when another evil was added. Some of those who delighted in revolution robbed Stephen, a slave of Caesar, on the road and seized all his property. So Cumanus sent soldiers, ordering them to plunder the neighbouring districts and bring the most notable people to him in chains. While those places were being ravaged, a young soldier, bold and reckless, came upon the laws of Moses kept reverently in a village, and before the eyes of many tore them up, blaspheming and mocking. So the Jews went to Cumanus, begging him to avenge not them but God, whose laws had been insulted. Cumanus, afraid that the multitude would revolt again, beheaded the man who had insulted the laws and put an end to the strife.

So Cumanus sent soldiers, ordering them to plunder the neighbouring districts and bring the most notable people to him in chains. While those places were being ravaged, a young soldier, bold and reckless, came upon the laws of Moses kept reverently in a village, and before the eyes of many tore them up, blaspheming and mocking. So the Jews went to Cumanus, begging him to avenge not them but God, whose laws had been insulted. Cumanus, afraid that the multitude would revolt again, beheaded the man who had insulted the laws and put an end to the strife.

blocks: The Samaritans too came into enmity with the Jews; and the cause was this. Galileans going to Jerusalem were travelling through a village of the Samaritans, and some men attacked them and killed many. So the leading men of the Galileans went to Cumanus, asking for the dead to be avenged. But he was bribed and took no thought for vengeance. The Galileans, enraged, took to arms, and set fire to some villages of the Samaritans and plundered them. Cumanus came against the Galileans with a force, killed many of them and took more alive. The leading men of Jerusalem put on sackcloth, sprinkled their heads with ashes, and urged the rebels to change their minds, throw down their arms and keep quiet; and they persuaded them. So they dispersed, but from that time the country was full of banditry.

The Samaritans went to Quadratus, governor of Syria, accusing the Jews of having burned their villages. The Jews blamed the Samaritans as the cause of the strife, and before them Cumanus, who had been corrupted by gifts and had not avenged the dead. Quadratus put off the judgement, saying he would come to Judaea and declare his decision there when he had learned the truth. So he came to Samaria, examined what had been done, and judged the Samaritans to be responsible for the disturbance; but the Jews whom Cumanus held in chains he crucified as rebels. Ananias the high priest and those with him, and Ananus the captain, he put in chains and sent to Rome to give account to Claudius of what had been done. He also ordered the leading men of the Samaritans and of the Jews, Cumanus the procurator and Celer the tribune to go to the emperor themselves, to be judged on their disputes with one another. When they had gone, Claudius sat as judge, and finding the Samaritans the authors of the evils, ordered those who had come up to him to be put to death, and condemned Cumanus to exile; but Celer the tribune he ordered to be taken to Jerusalem, dragged through the city in sight of all, and so put to death.

Caesar sent Felix to be procurator of the Jews; and he gave Agrippa the tetrarchy of Philip, and Batanaea and Trachonitis with Abila (these had been the tetrarchies of Lysanias), and took Chalcis from him, after he had ruled it four years. Agrippa gave his sister Drusilla in marriage to Azizus, king of Emesa, who was willing to be circumcised, after Antiochus Epiphanes had declined the marriage because he would not follow Jewish ways; and he betrothed Mariamme to Archelaus, the son of Helcias, to whom Agrippa their father had formerly promised her. Felix, while procurator of Judaea, saw Drusilla, who was exceedingly beautiful, was taken with love for her, and persuaded her to leave her husband and marry him. She bore him a son and named him Agrippa. It is said that in the time of Titus the woman, with her son, who had become a young man, perished at Mount Vesuvius, which is fire-bearing and then burst into fire more than ever. Berenice, another sister of Agrippa, who had been married to Herod her uncle, was joined after his death to Polemo, who was willing to be circumcised, because of the rumour that said she was living with her brother as his lover, so that she might show the slander to be false. The marriage did not last long, since Berenice left Polemo.

Claudius Caesar died, having reigned thirteen years, eight months and twenty days. The story was that he had been killed by poison by his wife Agrippina. Her father was Germanicus, Caesar's brother, and her husband Domitius Ahenobarbus, one of the notable men in Rome; when he died, Claudius married her as a widow, and she had a son Domitius, named after his father. For Claudius had earlier put to death his wife Messalina out of jealousy, by whom he had children, Britannicus and Octavius. He also had Octavia, the eldest of the siblings, by an earlier wife, and he married her to Nero; for Caesar later renamed Agrippina's son Domitius so, when he adopted him. So, to win the sole rule for him, his mother Agrippina killed Claudius with poison. But these things will be told in their proper times and places; let the narrative keep to its sequence.

blocks: So Nero held the rule of the Romans after Claudius; and affairs in Judaea went continually from bad to worse. The country was full of bandits and of sorcerers who deceived the crowd, many of whom Felix arrested and put to death. Felix was hostile to Jonathan the high priest, who often admonished him to govern the affairs of Judaea better, and he looked for a pretext by which to get rid of the man who was constantly troubling him; and he killed him through the bandits. They came into the temple as if to worship, carrying daggers under their clothes, mingled with the multitude and killed Jonathan. Since the bold deed went unpunished, the bandits went up without fear and killed some who were their own enemies and others for pay on behalf of others. Sorcerers and deceivers persuaded the crowd to follow them into the desert, where they would show them clear signs and wonders done by God; and Felix punished many of them. The bandits stirred the people to war with the Romans, wishing not to obey them, and they burned and destroyed the villages of those who would not be persuaded.

Syrians and Jews lived in Caesarea, and the Jews claimed the first place, since Herod their king had built the city; the Syrians admitted what concerned Herod, but said that formerly it had been a city called Strato's Tower, and that at that time no Jew lived in the city. When the people of Caesarea quarrelled over this, those in charge of the country punished the guilty with blows and lulled the uproar for a little. The Jews, who surpassed the Syrians in wealth and despised them for that reason, abused them. They, though beaten in money, took confidence because most of those serving under the Romans were from Caesarea, and for a time they too answered the Jews' insults with words; then they threw stones at each other, until many on both sides were wounded and fell; and the Jews won. Felix ordered the Jews to stop, and when they did not obey he let loose the soldiers on them; he killed many, held more alive, and allowed the soldiers to plunder houses. The more reasonable and leading men among the Jews begged Felix to call off the soldiers, to spare them, and to give them a chance to repent of what they had done. And Felix was persuaded.

King Agrippa gave the high priesthood to Ishmael, the son of Phabi. The high priests and the priests, together with the leading men of Jerusalem, were in strife with one another; they abused one another and threw stones, and there was no one to rebuke them or stop the strife. The high priests went so far in shamelessness as even to send to the threshing floors and take by force the tithes owed to the priests, so that the poor among the priests died of want.

When Porcius Festus was sent by Nero as successor to Felix, the Jews of Caesarea accused Felix before Nero; and he would perhaps have paid the penalty for his wrongs to them, had not Pallas, his brother, who had great power with Nero, begged off his anger. The Syrians in Caesarea, winning over Beryllus, Nero's tutor, with money, obtained through him a letter of Caesar declaring void the Jews' equal citizenship with the Syrians in Caesarea. From this the later evils grew for the nation; for because of this letter the Jews clung all the more to their strife with the Syrians, until the war was kindled.

blocks: Festus, coming to Judaea, found it harmed by bandits. For those called sicarii, who were also bandits, then gathered in greater numbers. They used curved daggers like those called sicae by the Romans, from which they were named sicarii. At the feasts they mingled with the multitude and easily slaughtered whom they wished, and they plundered and burned the villages. Festus sent a force against those deceived by a sorcerer who promised salvation to those willing to follow him into the desert; and those sent destroyed both that deceiver and his followers.

King Agrippa built a large room in the palace, and from it watched what was done in the temple. The people of the city were angry at this. So they raised a wall which cut off the view not only from the royal house but also from the western portico, where the Romans kept guard at the feasts because of the temple. Agrippa was indignant at this, and Festus more so, and he wished to pull down the wall. But they asked to be allowed to petition Caesar. When Festus allowed it, they sent to Nero ten of the leading men, with Ishmael the high priest and Helcias the treasurer. Nero, as a favour to his wife Poppaea, who pleaded for the Jews, ordered the building to be left. Poppaea let the others go back, but kept Ishmael and Helcias with her as hostages. King Agrippa, learning this, gave the high priesthood to Joseph called Decabi, the son of Simon, who had been high priest; then he took it from Joseph and assigned it to Ananus, the son of Ananus.

This young Ananus, having received the high priesthood, was reckless and bold. So, when Festus had died and Albinus, who had been sent by Nero as procurator of Judaea in place of Festus, had not yet reached Judaea, he assembled a council, to use Josephus's own words, and brought before it the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, whose name was James, and some others, accusing them of having broken the law, and handed them over to be stoned. Those in the city who were thought most reasonable and exact about the laws took this hard, and denounced him both to Albinus and to Agrippa. So the king took the high priesthood from him, after he had held it three months, and appointed Jesus son of Mnaseas.

Albinus, coming to Jerusalem, made efforts to bring peace to the country, and destroyed many of the sicarii. Agrippa gave the high priesthood to Jesus son of Gamaliel, removing Jesus son of Mnaseas. So strife arose among the high priests, who took the boldest as their partners, and the strife went on from insults to one another as far as stones. So from that time above all the city of Jerusalem came to be in a bad way, and everything went from bad to worse. Albinus, learning that Gessius Florus was coming as his successor, brought out the prisoners, ordered those who plainly deserved to die to be put to death, and took money and released those imprisoned on small charges. So the prison was emptied of prisoners, and the country was filled with bandits. Agrippa removed Jesus son of Gamaliel from the high priesthood and gave it to Matthias son of Theophilus, in whose time the war against the Romans began.

The high priesthood began from Aaron; after him his sons received it, and from them the honour remained with their descendants. So it was an ancestral custom among the Jews that no one should take the high priesthood, even if a king aimed at it, except those of the blood of Aaron; though the custom was not kept for all time. From Aaron down to Phinehas, who was declared high priest by the rebels during the war, there were eighty-three in all.

Gessius Florus, arriving in Judaea as successor to Albinus, filled the Jews with many evils, and became so very wicked that by the excess of his wickedness Albinus was praised as a benefactor. For Albinus hid his wickedness and was careful not to be caught in his wrongdoing, but Florus committed his crimes against the nation openly and shamelessly, as if making a display of them. And why should I count up his evils one by one? I shall show the whole by saying this much: it was Florus who forced the Jews to take up war against the Romans. The war began in the second year of Florus's procuratorship and the twelfth of Nero's sole rule.

blocks: From this the revolt of the Jews broke out into the open, and the war began. To tell each part of it would be a greater task than the present undertaking. I have decided to leave the rest aside, and only to give an abridgement of the capture of Jerusalem itself.

Vespasian, entrusted by Nero with the conduct of the war when Nero learned of the revolt of the Jews, did not attack Jerusalem first, but hurried to take first the cities under the mother city, and so to subdue the mother city itself. So he took Ptolemais, and there joined his son Titus, who came from Alexandria bringing the fifteenth legion. Titus had been sent by him from Achaea, where he had been appointed commander of the war by Nero; for Vespasian happened to be in Achaea when the revolt of the Jews was reported to him. He set out first against Galilee, and attacking first the city of Jotapata, and besieging it for forty days, he sacked it, and captured Josephus, who was general of Galilee and defending that city. From there he went against other forts and towns, and brought some under the Romans by agreement and others by siege. Having done this, he was preparing to engage the mother city itself, which was in a bad way, since those in it were at strife with one another and had rolled into civil fighting and mutual slaughter, and its fighting strength was being destroyed by this.

But the news that Nero had fallen from his sole rule, fled Rome in secret and killed himself checked Vespasian's impulse. Then, learning that Galba had become emperor, he sent Titus to him, to greet him and to learn what he ordered about the Jews. While Titus was still on his way, Galba too was killed. Hearing this, Titus went back to his father. And because of the uncertainty about the rule of the Romans they did not undertake the attack on Jerusalem, but stayed quiet in Caesarea. When Galba had been killed, Otho succeeded to the rule. The legions in Germany proclaimed Vitellius emperor. So Otho sent forces and made war on Vitellius. When those he had sent were defeated, Otho killed himself. Vitellius went off to Rome with the armies; for by now Otho's men too had gone over to him. Vespasian, if any small towns of the Jews were left not yet taken, sent forces and sacked these too, so that only the city of Jerusalem was now left as the Romans' target.

The city's affairs were terribly sick, as has been said. For outside, Simon and his men were more fearsome to the Jews than the Romans, and inside, those called Zealots and John their leader were harsher than both the Romans and Simon. Since the Zealots oppressed those in the city most violently, the people were forced to invite Simon and the crowd with him and bring him into the city, thinking he would perhaps free them from the Zealots' tyranny; but without knowing it they had received a worse tyrant against themselves. While this was happening in Jerusalem, Vitellius reached Rome, proclaimed emperor. When Vespasian learned this he was not pleased, and disdained to have Vitellius as master. The commanders of the legions with him, and the soldiers too, came together and proclaimed Vespasian emperor.

blocks: As he was about to sail, Vespasian entrusted the siege of Jerusalem to his son Titus. He gathered the forces and went off to Jerusalem, and having encamped thirty stades away, he took six hundred picked horsemen from there and went to view the city and the temper of those inside. Countless men ran out from the city against them. Most of those with Titus, seeing the frenzied onrush of the Jews, were checked from going forward, and Titus, cut off with a few of the others, was caught in the midst of the enemy. Seeing himself in danger, he turned his horse, shouted to those about him to follow, charged the Jews, and driving back his attackers with his sword, got safely to the camp; two of those following him fell.

After a day he came to Scopus (a place so called, seven stades from the city, from which the city and the temple can be seen), and ordered a camp to be built. Those in the city were always clashing with one another, but then the great war coming from outside put a stop to their quarrel. So the Jews ran out of the city and fought those building the camp, and did harm to their opponents, but suffered more harm themselves. When the war from outside eased a little, the strife inside rose again. John with the Zealots seized the temple by a trick, and many were killed; and he took heart against Simon.

Titus ordered the space from Scopus to the wall to be levelled. While this was being done, the Jews contrived an ambush against the Romans. The boldest of the rebels came out of the city, as if they had been thrown out by those who wanted peace, and huddled about the wall; others stood on the wall, as though they were of the people, shouted for peace and asked for terms, calling the Romans as if to open the gates to them. The soldiers suspected nothing and went to the task, but Titus suspected the strangeness of the invitation. For a day before, when he had invited them through Josephus to come to terms, he found them thinking nothing reasonable. So he ordered the soldiers to stay where they were. But some had already run to the gates; at first those who seemed to have been thrown out fell back, but when the Romans were between the city's towers, they ran out and surrounded them. Those on the wall shot missiles at them and hurled stones, killing many and wounding more. The Jews leapt about brandishing their shields, while Titus and the officers threatened the soldiers.

When the ground before the walls had been levelled, wishing to move the camp there, Titus drew up the strongest part of his force facing the wall; and with the Jews' sallies blocked in this way, the Romans encamped there. The city was surrounded by three walls; where the nature of the ground fortified it, it was girded with one circuit. With the city like this, an attack seemed impracticable to Titus. For the moment, then, he decided to attack at the tomb of John the high priest. He ordered his men to lay waste the area before the city and gather timber, so as to raise earthworks. They carried out the order, and when the earthworks had been raised Titus ordered the rams brought up to strike the wall.

When the rams had begun at three points, and a tremendous crash echoed round the city, a cry went up from those inside, and the rebels in fear came to agreement, settling to make common defence against the enemy. But though the rams struck, the wall did not give way under the blows; only a corner of one of the towers was shaken, and the wall was intact. The Jews, watching the Romans scattered about the camp, all ran out, bringing fire against the engines. A fierce battle took place round the siege engines, some forcing their way to set them alight, the others to stop them; and the Jews prevailed out of desperation. The fire was catching the engines, and they would have been burned up had Titus not come to help with the horsemen. As it was, about twelve of the Jews' front fighters fell, and the rest gave way and were driven into the city. One of the Jews taken alive was crucified before the wall, in case the rest might be terrified at the sight and give in. When Titus had built towers of timber, each fifty cubits high, and set them on the earthworks, the Jews no longer stopped the blows of the rams, being shot at and harmed from the towers. When the wall was already giving way to Nico (for the Jews themselves called the Romans' largest engine so), most of them lost heart and withdrew. And when the Romans climbed onto it, all fled to the second wall.

So the Romans took the first wall in fifteen days. After this they attacked the second wall. The siege engine was brought up; and when the tower against which it was striking shook, the others had fled,
text: As he was about to sail, Vespasian entrusted the siege of Jerusalem to his son Titus. He gathered the forces and went off to Jerusalem, and having encamped thirty stades away, he took six hundred picked horsemen from there and went to view the city and the temper of those inside. Countless men ran out from the city against them. Most of those with Titus, seeing the frenzied onrush of the Jews, were checked from going forward, and Titus, cut off with a few of the others, was caught in the midst of the enemy. Seeing himself in danger, he turned his horse, shouted to those about him to follow, charged the Jews, and driving back his attackers with his sword, got safely to the camp; two of those following him fell. After a day he came to Scopus (a place so called, seven stades from the city, from which the city and the temple can be seen), and ordered a camp to be built. Those in the city were always clashing with one another, but then the great war coming from outside put a stop to their quarrel. So the Jews ran out of the city and fought those building the camp, and did harm to their opponents, but suffered more harm themselves. When the war from outside eased a little, the strife inside rose again. John with the Zealots seized the temple by a trick, and many were killed; and he took heart against Simon. Titus ordered the space from Scopus to the wall to be levelled. While this was being done, the Jews contrived an ambush against the Romans. The boldest of the rebels came out of the city, as if they had been thrown out by those who wanted peace, and huddled about the wall; others stood on the wall, as though they were of the people, shouted for peace and asked for terms, calling the Romans as if to open the gates to them. The soldiers suspected nothing and went to the task, but Titus suspected the strangeness of the invitation. For a day before, when he had invited them through Josephus to come to terms, he found them thinking nothing reasonable. So he ordered the soldiers to stay where they were. But some had already run to the gates; at first those who seemed to have been thrown out fell back, but when the Romans were between the city's towers, they ran out and surrounded them. blocks: but a sorcerer named Castor, with ten others, stretched out his hands as if in supplication and called on Titus. Titus believed him and checked the blows of the ram. Castor said he wished to come down on terms, and of the ten with him, some joined in pretending to supplicate, while others shouted that they would never be slaves to the Romans. While the time was being wasted on this, Castor let Simon know that he should take counsel about urgent matters, since he was fooling the Romans and holding back their attack. At last he was found to be dragging out the time by deceit, and he provoked the Romans to make the blows of the ram more powerful. So the second wall too was taken on the fifth day after the first.

Titus went inside and stopped his men from killing those caught, and ordered the soldiers not to set fire to the houses either; nor did he wish much of the wall to be pulled down; for he set more store on saving the city for himself and the temple for the city. So the rebels attacked the Romans who had entered the city; some shot at them in the narrow streets, some from the houses, some from the wall. The Roman guards leapt down from the towers and withdrew to the camp. The Jews, knowing the narrow streets, wounded many, fell on them and drove them out. So the Romans, having taken the second wall too, were driven out again, and the rebels' spirits were raised.

By now famine was creeping over the city and destroying many good men through want of necessities. This pleased the rebels, who thought that only those who did not want peace deserved to be saved, and that the destruction of the others was a relief to themselves. The Romans tried again to take the second wall, and the Jews prevented them; for three days they held out, but on the fourth, unable to bear the attack, they withdrew further in.

Again Titus took the wall, and at once pulled down its northern part; he put a garrison in the rest and prepared to attack the third. He divided the legions in two and began to raise earthworks. Of those inside, the rebels were unbending and unyielding, but the people were moved to desertion, and many deserted in secret. Those whom the rebels found wishing to do so, or about whom they had even a shadow of suspicion, they at once slaughtered; and fastening a false charge of desertion on the well-off, they killed them at once and plundered their property. The famine at its height increased the cruelty of the rebels. For through want of food they burst into the houses and searched them, and if they found food when the occupants had denied having any, they tortured them, and if they did not find it, they examined them more carefully, as having hidden it. They took the bodies of the wretched people as evidence of whether they had food or not. For those who still had some strength were thought to have it, while those whose bodies had wasted away were passed by. If anyone had a supply of wheat or barley, he locked his house and ate; some, under the force of the famine, even swallowed the grain unprepared. Mothers snatched the food from the very mouths of their babes, children from their fathers, wives from their husbands. Yet even eating so, they did not escape the rebels. Wherever they saw a house locked or smoke rising, they took it as a sign that those inside were eating, and breaking down the doors they brought the food up out of their throats; and there was no pity for grey hairs or for youth. On those who had managed to eat what they had first, they inflicted terrible and merciless punishments as if they were wrongdoers, blocking the passages of their private parts with vetch and cruelly driving sharp stakes into their seats. Someone would suffer things dreadful even to hear of, to make him confess to one loaf, or betray a single handful of barley meal to the bandits. To go through each of the things that happened then would be difficult or even impossible; but to put it briefly, no other city ever suffered such things, nor did any other race from the beginning of time prove more fertile in wickedness.
