blocks: Such were the sufferings of the Jews; and Titus's earthworks went forward, though the soldiers were harmed from the wall. Those who went out to gather food were ambushed (they were not only common people, but also some of the fighters, no longer content with plunder), and when caught by the Romans, after every torture, they were crucified before the wall. To Titus the suffering seemed pitiable, since five hundred or even more were caught each day. But he judged it unsafe either to guard them or to let them go; and at the same time he hoped that the rest would give in at the sight. The rebels dragged the relatives of the deserters onto the wall, and those of the people who were eager to learn, and showed them what those who fled to the Romans suffered, lying about both the enemy and their own people.

When the earthworks had been finished, the siege engines were brought up. But the Jews from inside had dug under the space from the Antonia to the earthworks, propped up the tunnels with timber and left the earthworks hanging. Then they filled the trench with fuel and set fire to it; and when the supporting timbers burned, the mine suddenly gave way and the earthworks collapsed; and the Romans were struck with dismay and despondency at the device. Elsewhere the Romans brought up the siege engines and shook the wall; but some men rushed out recklessly, set fire to them and burned them all. With the earthworks destroyed, the Romans were despondent, and Titus took counsel with his commanders. Some urged raising others again, others to sit down before the city without earthworks and guard their exits and the bringing in of supplies, and so, they said, the city would be taken by famine; others thought it best to bring up the whole force and make an attempt on the wall, since the Jews would not bear the assault. But none of these pleased Titus; he decided to surround the city with a wall, so as to block every way out for those inside. He divided the work among the army. A rivalry fell on them for the work, and a kind of superhuman zeal, and the work was quickly built. Having shut in the city with the wall, he went round and inspected the first watch of the night himself, and entrusted the rest to others; and the guards took turns to sleep.

With the exits, every hope of safety was shut off from the Jews, and the famine fed on the people by houses and families. The roofs were full of women and babes who had collapsed, and the narrow streets of dead old men; children and young men, swollen, went round the market places like ghosts, and fell wherever each happened to give out. Those still alive had no strength to bury their kin; and many who set out to bury them died on top of those they were burying. The rebels became harsher even than the evils of the famine, robbing tombs and plundering houses. At first they ordered the dead to be buried from the public treasury, not bearing the stench; then they threw them from the walls into the ravines. Titus, going round and seeing these filled with the dead, and a thick discharge running from the rotting bodies, groaned, and raising his hands called God to witness that the work was not of his choosing. And he set about earthworks again, though the timber was hard to get; for it was brought from ninety stades away.

Many of the people deserted, some throwing themselves down from the walls, others going out as if to battle with stones and taking refuge with the Romans. Even so, most of them perished; for they were starving, and meeting plenty of food and gorging themselves greedily, they burst. Something else also happened that destroyed the deserters. Some of them who had gold coins swallowed them when they were about to desert to the Romans, so that they would not be robbed of them if caught. When they were with the Romans, they passed the coins out with the excrement of the belly, and picked them out and took them. One of the deserters was caught doing this; and when a rumour went round the camp that the deserters were coming full of gold, the wretches had their bellies cut open, so that from this a great destruction of the Jews came about; for in one night more than three thousand were ripped open. Titus, learning this, threatened the army; but Titus's anger helped the deserters little or not at all. Money was found in few of them, and the rest perished for nothing but hopes. It is said that the dead carried out through the gates of the city and thrown out, of the poor alone, amounted to six hundred thousand, and the number of the others could not be found out, while a medimnus of grain was sold for a talent.

blocks: With the city walled round by the Romans, as I have said above, it was not even possible to gather grass; so they searched out the old dung of animals and made it their food. The Romans had now raised their earthworks, and the wall of the Antonia was being struck by the siege engines, but it did not fall under the blows. Some of the soldiers made a roof of their shields over their bodies, dug under the foundations with crowbars, and shook out four of the stones. Night came on and stopped the fighting on both sides; and during it the wall, shaken by the rams, suddenly collapsed. But another wall was seen built up inside, which turned the Romans' joy at the fall into despondency. Titus spoke to the soldiers and roused their spirits. A man from Syria named Sabinus, holding his shield over his head with his left hand and drawing his sword with his right, went at the wall; and eleven others followed him, eager to match his courage. Those on the wall hurled javelins at them, shot missiles, and rolled down huge stones, by which some of the eleven were swept away. But Sabinus did not check his rush until he had climbed onto the wall and routed the enemy. Just when he had succeeded in the attempt, he tripped on a rock and fell headlong on it with a clash of arms. The Jews turned at the noise, and seeing him alone and lying down, shot at him from every side. He rose to his knee and defended himself, but under the number of his wounds his right arm gave out, and he was buried under the missiles. Of the rest, they killed three with stones when they had already reached the top, and the eight were carried wounded to the camp.

Two days later, at night, some men quietly climbed up through the ruins into the Antonia, slaughtered the guards there as they slept, and sounded the trumpet. The other guards fled, and Titus went up with his picked men, and the legions followed. The Jews fled into the temple, and Titus's men burst in through the tunnel that the Jews had dug under the Romans' earthworks. A fierce battle broke out about the entrances; they drew their swords and grappled, and there was great slaughter on both sides. When the Roman line was already giving way, one Julian, a centurion, an excellent man, leapt forward and alone routed the victorious Jews. The crowd fled and scattered. As that brave man pursued the scattered men, he slipped on the paving, since he had many nails in his boots, as the other soldiers did too. The Jews surrounded him and wounded him from all sides. Even lying down he defended himself, until, covered with wounds, he gave in, admired even by the enemy themselves.

So the Jews drove back the Romans and shut them up in the Antonia. Titus, after many appeals to the rebels both through Josephus and himself, when he saw them implacable, went again, though unwillingly, to war. He chose the best men and ordered them to attack the guards about the ninth hour of the night. They did not find the guards asleep, but they knew of the attack and closed with them, and at the shout the others came together too. The fighting went on from the ninth hour of the night to the fifth of the day, and the battle was evenly matched, victory weighing down on neither side. So the fighters then parted. The rest of the Roman force in seven days overthrew the foundations of the Antonia and made a broad way up to the temple. The legions, approaching the first enclosure, began earthworks. These were raised with great toil; and the Jews set fire to the part of the northern and western portico joined to the Antonia and broke off about twenty cubits, beginning to burn the holy places with their own hands. The Romans too set fire to the neighbouring portico; and when the fire had gone as far as fifteen cubits, the Jews cut away the roof. The rebels in the temple attacked the soldiers on the earthworks openly, and defended themselves with tricks.

Those who died of famine were a countless multitude. Things happened to those still alive dreadful to tell and hard for hearers to believe; of which I shall tell one. A woman from beyond the Jordan, not undistinguished in family and wealth, had fled to Jerusalem and was besieged there with the others. When she often got food for herself, the bandits in the city plundered it. Indignant at this, and driven by anger and famine, she killed the child she had at the breast, roasted it, and ate part, keeping the rest for a second meal. The rebels, when the smell reached them, were there at once, and threatened to slaughter her unless she gave up what she had prepared. She uncovered the remains of the child; and they were struck out of their wits at the sight and shuddered, and withdrew trembling, barely leaving this food to the mother.

When the earthworks were finished, the rams were brought up; but they achieved nothing because of the hardness of the wall. Others dug under the foundations, and not even so was the wall shaken down. So, despairing of other means, they brought ladders to the porticoes. The Jews were not quick enough to stop them, but fell on those who climbed up and fought them; and there was no small slaughter of them.

blocks: Titus, when he saw that sparing the temple was turning to the harm of his soldiers, ordered the gates to be set on fire. When the fire was brought to them, the silver with which they were plated melted and let the flame take hold of the wood, and from there it caught the porticoes. As the Jews saw the fire all round, their spirits gave way along with their bodies. That day and the following night the fire prevailed; for they had been able to set the porticoes alight part by part, not all together from every side. The next day Titus ordered part of the force to put out the fire and make a road by the gates for an easier way up for the legions, and himself summoned the six chief commanders and took counsel about the temple. Some thought it best to use the law of war and spare nothing; others advised that if the Jews mounted it and fought from it, it should be burned, since then a fortress would be burned and no longer a temple, but if not, it should be saved. But Titus said that even if the Jews mounted it and fought from it, he would not take vengeance on lifeless things instead of men, nor burn so great a work; for its destruction would be a loss to the Romans, just as it would be an ornament of their empire if it were saved.

So Titus's aim was to attack with his whole force the next day and take possession of the temple; but God, it seems, had long since decreed its destruction. For the rebels attacked the guards of the outer temple, and they, overcome by the numbers and fury of those running out, gave way. Titus, seeing this from above in the Antonia, came to help with the picked horsemen. The Jews did not stand the charge, but were shut up in the inner temple. When Titus withdrew, the rebels rested a little and attacked the Romans again. The Romans routed them and came as far as the temple. One of the soldiers snatched a piece of the burning wood, and being lifted up by another soldier, threw the fire into a golden window. As the flame rose, a cry went up from the Jews, and they ran together to defend it; and Titus, learning of it, ran to the temple to stop the fire, and with voice and right hand signalled to the fighters to put out the fire. But they neither heard him shouting nor heeded the signs of his hand. The legions, coming in and nearing the temple, pretended not even to hear Titus's orders, and urged those in front of them to throw in fire. The rebels were helpless, having given up defence, and there was slaughter and rout everywhere.

Titus, since he could not check the impulses of the frenzied soldiers and the fire was prevailing, went in with his commanders and beheld the holy place of God and what was in it. Since the flame had not yet got inside, but was spreading over the buildings round the temple, he thought the work could still be saved, and himself tried to urge the soldiers to put out the fire, and ordered one of those with him to hold back the disobedient by beating them with clubs. But they, overcome by fury and hatred of the Jews, were checked neither by respect for Titus nor by fear of the one restraining them. Hope of plunder also spurred on most of them, since they believed that what was inside was full of riches. Someone managed to throw fire into the hinges of the gate; and when a flame suddenly appeared from inside, the commanders withdrew and Titus himself, and no one any longer stopped those setting fire.

So the temple received the fire, a purging of the things impiously done in it, or a punishment of those who did them. One might wonder that the burning of the temple fell on the same month and day on which the earlier temple too had been burned by the Babylonians. From the first building, which Solomon made, to the destruction now being told, which took place in the second year of Vespasian's sole rule, there are one thousand one hundred and thirty years, seven months and fifteen days; and from the later one, which began to be built in the second year of the reign of Cyrus, to the last capture, six hundred and thirty-nine years and forty-five days.

blocks: While the temple burned there was plunder of whatever came to hand and slaughter of those caught. Nowhere could the ground be seen for the dead, but the soldiers ran after the fugitives climbing over heaps of bodies. The crowd of bandits pushed back the Romans and broke out into the city, and what was left of the common people fled to the outer portico. Some of the priests withdrew onto the wall, which was eight cubits thick, and stayed there. Two of the notable men threw themselves into the fire and were burned with the temple. The Romans, judging it useless to spare the buildings round the temple now that it was burning, set fire to them all; and the fire caught the treasuries too, in which a countless amount of money had been stored, and countless costly garments and other valuables. For all the wealth of the Jews had been heaped up there from every side, since those who owned it laid it up there as in a safe storehouse.

A countless crowd of the common people perished, and the cause of their destruction was a false prophet, who proclaimed to those in the city that God ordered them to go up to the temple to receive the signs of their deliverance. Many such men were put up by the tyrants to say this, so that people would desert less; and by them the wretched crowd was led astray and, as if thunderstruck, did not believe the clear signs.

There were many signs. A star like a sword stood over the city, and a comet appeared and lasted a year; and once before the war a light shone round the temple and the altar, so that it seemed bright day, and lasted half an hour. A cow brought to be sacrificed gave birth to a lamb. The eastern gate of the inner temple, which was of bronze and massive, so that it was opened and shut with difficulty by twenty men, and had very deep bars and bolts, was seen at night opened of its own accord. This showed that the security of the temple was being undone, and that the entry would be easy for the enemy. At another time a supernatural apparition was seen before sunset, chariots passing through the air over the whole country, and armed troops darting through the clouds. At the feast of Pentecost the priests who went into the inner temple felt a movement and a crash, and then heard a voice saying: "Let us depart from here."

Four years before the war, at the feast of Tabernacles, one Jesus, a countryman, came to the feast and began to cry out: "A voice from the east, a voice from the west, a voice from the four winds, a voice against Jerusalem and the temple, a voice against bridegrooms and brides, a voice against all the people." And he went round the city crying this day and night. He was beaten for his ill-omened words, but he cried nothing else than the same words. He was brought before the Roman who was then procurator of the country, and though flayed with whips he neither begged nor wept, but turning his voice to a lament, at each blow he cried: "Woe to Jerusalem," until Albinus (for he was procurator then) judged him mad and let him go. From then until the war he lamented: "Woe to Jerusalem." At the feasts above all he cried out the gloomy omen. He did this for seven years and five months, until during the siege, going round on the wall, he again cried piercingly: "Woe to the city, and to the temple, and to the people." When at last he added: "Woe to me too," a stone from the stone-thrower struck him and killed him.

blocks: The rebels had fled into the city, and with the temple and everything round it burning, the Romans brought their standards into the sacred precinct and with the loudest acclamations declared Titus emperor. All the soldiers made so much money from plunder that in Syria a weight of gold was sold for half its former value. The priests who had climbed onto the wall of the temple, as has been said, held out for five days and, starving, came down begging to be spared. But Titus said that the time for pardon too had passed, and saying that since the temple was gone the priests must perish with it, he ordered the men to be punished.

The tyrants' party, unable to escape, invited Titus to a parley. He came, reproached them for their madness, and promised to grant them their lives if they threw down their arms and surrendered themselves. The bandits said they could not accept terms from him, since they had sworn never to do so, but asked to go out with their wives and children, and they would leave the city to him. Titus was indignant at this, and told them that none of them should desert any more or hope for terms, for he would spare no one, but they should fight and save themselves as best they could. He ordered the soldiers to burn and plunder the city; and they set fire everywhere. The rebels rushed to the royal palace, in which many had stored their possessions because of its strength, drove the Romans from it, slaughtered all of the people gathered there, numbering eight thousand four hundred, and plundered the money. The next day the Romans drove the bandits out of the lower city and burned everything as far as Siloam. The rebels, seeing the city burning, said with cheerful faces that they awaited their end in good spirits. They would neither bear to surrender nor were able to fight the Romans, but scattering over the outer parts of the city they slaughtered any they found wishing to desert. No place in the city was bare, but every one held a corpse either of famine or of strife. The tyrants and the bandits with them were warmed by a last hope, in the tunnels: if they fled into them, they did not expect to be searched out, and when the Romans marched away they were confident they could come out and escape. But this was only a dream; for they were not going to escape either God or the Romans. They were also at war with one another over the plunder.
Caesar, since it was impossible to take the upper city without earthworks, being surrounded by cliffs, assigned his force to the works.

blocks: In these days the leaders of the Idumaeans sent five men to Titus and begged him to give them terms. He, hoping that the tyrants too would give in once the Idumaeans were drawn away, granted them their safety. But Simon, learning their intention, at once killed the five who had met Titus, and seized the leaders and imprisoned them. He kept the Idumaeans under guard, and watched the wall with closer guards because of the deserters. Many were slaughtered, but more escaped. The Romans received them all, out of weariness of killing and hope of gain. For letting only the common people go, they sold the others with their wives and children, each at the lowest price, because of the number of those sold and the fewness of the buyers. Those sold off were a countless multitude, and of the common people more than forty thousand were saved. One of the priests, named Jesus, receiving an oath for his safety on condition of handing over some of the treasures, came out and handed over two lampstands, a table, mixing bowls and libation bowls, all of solid gold, and the curtains, the vestments of the high priests and many other vessels. Phinehas, the treasurer of the temple, was arrested and showed them the tunics and girdles of the high priests and many of the other treasures.

When the earthworks were finished the Romans brought their engines up to the wall. Of the rebels some withdrew to the citadel, some slipped down into the tunnels, and many defended themselves. When part of the wall had been broken away, fear fell on the tyrants too, and they were in suspense to flee. Since they no longer had those who had long been loyal (for they had scattered), and the enemy were reported to be near, they fell on their faces and lamented their own folly, and came down of their own accord from the towers, from which they could never have been taken by force, but only by famine, and fled to the ravine of Siloam, and then slipped down into the tunnels. The Romans, having taken the walls without bloodshed, slaughtered those they caught and set fire to the houses. They stopped towards evening. The next day Titus went inside and wondered at the strength of the city and of the towers, and said: "We have fought with God's help, and it was God who brought the Jews down from these strongholds." While destroying the rest of the city and razing the walls, he left these towers as a memorial of his own fortune, with which as his fellow soldier he had overcome what could not be taken.

The number of all the prisoners taken in the whole war came to ninety-seven thousand, and of those who perished during the whole siege, one million one hundred thousand. Most of these were of the same race, but not natives; for they had gathered from the whole country for the feast of Unleavened Bread, were suddenly caught by the war, and the war surrounded the city when it was full of men.

When the Romans had killed some of those in the open and taken others prisoner, they searched those in the tunnels, and breaking up the ground they killed all they came upon. More than two thousand dead were found there too. A terrible stench met those who stooped over the bodies, so that many at once withdrew. Others out of greed went in, treading on heaps of dead; for they found many of the treasures in the tunnels. Many prisoners held by the tyrants were also brought up and released.

Of these avengers, John, starving in the tunnels with his brothers, begged to receive terms from the Romans; Simon was caught later, while Titus was staying at the Caesarea called Philip's. For during the siege of Jerusalem he was in the upper city, and when the Romans got inside the city, Simon took the most loyal of his friends, and with them stonecutters and the iron tools needed for the work, and let himself down with them into one of the tunnels; and going through the old excavation he mined the earth, so that they might go further and come up in safety. But when the miners had gone a little way, their food ran out. Then he put on white tunics, pinned a purple cloak about him, and came up out of the earth at the place where the temple had formerly been. At first amazement fell on those who saw him; then they came nearer and asked who he was. Simon told them to call their commander. Terentius Rufus came when called, who had been left in command of the army. When Simon had made known to him who he was, he was seized, bound and kept under guard. His capture was reported to Titus. He was kept for the triumph, in which he was put to death, dragged with a noose in the forum at Rome, where it is the Romans' custom to kill those put to death for crimes.

This was the end of Simon son of Gioras; and John, the other fury of the Jews, was condemned to chains for life. Of the multitude of prisoners, some were sent to the works in Egypt, and others perished in the shows held in the cities, either given to fight wild beasts or killing one another. Simon's coming up out of the earth caused a great number of the other rebels too to be found in the tunnels, so that from this even the foundations of the temple were dug up.

blocks: Danger was brought not only on the Jews in Jerusalem, but also on those in the other cities. To tell it all would be hard work; but what happened at Antioch to the Jews living there must be told. The nation of the Jews is widely scattered over the whole world, having often been taken captive, as has already been told, and dispersed everywhere; but it is mingled most of all with Syria because it is its neighbour, and more than the other cities of Syria Antioch had Jewish inhabitants, both because of the size of the city and because the kings after Antiochus granted them safe residence in it. For Antiochus Epiphanes sacked Jerusalem and plundered the temple, but the kings after him allowed them to share in the city equally with the Greeks. So they grew in number, bringing a great number of Greeks over to their religion.

At the time when the war of Jerusalem broke out and Vespasian sailed to Syria, and hatred of the nation was at its height everywhere, a Jew named Antiochus, the son of the chief of the Jews at Antioch, came before the assembly of the Antiochenes and accused his father, and accused the rest of the Jews too, of having planned to burn the whole city; and he handed over some foreign Jews as sharers in the plan. The common people of Antioch at once burned those handed over, and rushed against the native Jews to punish them too. Antiochus, the accuser of his countrymen, saying he had given up his ancestral religion, sacrificed as is the custom of the Greeks, and urged that the others be forced to do likewise; for the plotters would be revealed by not forswearing their religion. When the Antiochenes made the test, a few gave way, and those who would not bear to become Greek were destroyed. This Antiochus also got soldiers from the Roman governor and was harsh to his countrymen, not allowing them to rest on the seventh day; and he made the compulsion so strong that not only at Antioch was the rest of the sabbath abolished, but in the other cities too this prevailed for some time.

Not only this befell the Jews in Antioch; a second disaster was added. It happened that the city's square market place was burned, with the magistrates' offices and the record offices. Antiochus blamed the Jews for the fire, and stirred up the Antiochenes, who already suspected them, against them; and all rushed as if frenzied at those accused. Some barely restrained them, advising them to refer the matter to Titus. Meanwhile some, making a careful inquiry into the matter, found the race of the Jews not guilty, but that wicked men had dared the deed through the pressure of debts, thinking that if they burned the market place and the public records they would be rid of the demands.

Meanwhile Titus arrived at Antioch. The people of the Antiochenes went out to meet him and acclaimed him, and joined to their acclamations a petition asking him to expel the Jews from the city. He then heard what was said quietly and passed on; but later, when the Antiochenes pressed very insistently for the Jews to be driven out of the city, he said: "But their own country, to which they ought to go back, has been destroyed, and no place would receive them any longer." So, failing in this request, they turned to a second, and asked for the bronze tablets on which the rights of the Jews had been written to be taken away. But Titus did not assent to this either, and left everything to the Jews at Antioch as they had it before. He himself, going away to Alexandria and seeing Jerusalem on his way, pitied the destruction of the city, cursing those responsible for the revolt as responsible for the desolation of the city, a city ancient and prosperous. Parts of its very deep wealth were still being found even in the ruins themselves. For the Romans dug up much, and the prisoners showed them more, which the owners had stored underground against the uncertain turns of the war.

For Antiochus Epiphanes sacked Jerusalem and plundered the temple, but the kings after him allowed them to share in the city equally with the Greeks. So they grew in number, bringing a great number of Greeks over to their religion. At the time when the war of Jerusalem broke out and Vespasian sailed to Syria, and hatred of the nation was at its height everywhere, a Jew named Antiochus, the son of the chief of the Jews at Antioch, came before the assembly of the Antiochenes and accused his father, and accused the rest of the Jews too, of having planned to burn the whole city; and he handed over some foreign Jews as sharers in the plan. The common people of Antioch at once burned those handed over, and rushed against the native Jews to punish them too. Antiochus, the accuser of his countrymen, saying he had given up his ancestral religion, sacrificed as is the custom of the Greeks, and urged that the others be forced to do likewise; for the plotters would be revealed by not forswearing their religion. When the Antiochenes made the test, a few gave way, and those who would not bear to become Greek were destroyed. This Antiochus also got soldiers from the Roman governor and was harsh to his countrymen, not allowing them to rest on the seventh day; and he made the compulsion so strong that not only at Antioch was the rest of the sabbath abolished, but in the other cities too this prevailed for some time. Not only this befell the Jews in Antioch; a second disaster was added. It happened that the city's square market place was burned, with the magistrates' offices and the record offices. Antiochus blamed the Jews for the fire, and stirred up the Antiochenes, who already suspected them, against them; and all rushed as if frenzied at those accused. Some barely restrained them, advising them to refer the matter to Titus. Meanwhile some, making a careful inquiry into the matter, found the race of the Jews not guilty, but that wicked men had dared the deed through the pressure of debts, thinking that if they burned the market place and the public records they would be rid of the demands. Meanwhile Titus arrived at Antioch. The people of the Antiochenes went out to meet him and acclaimed him, and joined to their acclamations a petition asking him to expel the Jews from the city. He then heard what was said quietly and passed on; but later, when the Antiochenes pressed very insistently for the Jews to be driven out of the city, he said: "But their own country, to which they ought to go back, has been destroyed, and no place would receive them any longer." So, failing in this request, they turned to a second, and asked for the bronze tablets on which the rights of the Jews had been written to be taken away. But Titus did not assent to this either, and left everything to the Jews at Antioch as they had it before. He himself, going away to Alexandria and seeing Jerusalem on his way, pitied the destruction of the city, cursing those responsible for the revolt as responsible for the desolation of the city, a city ancient and prosperous. Parts of its very deep wealth were still being found even in the ruins themselves. For the Romans dug up much, and the prisoners showed them more, which the owners had stored underground against the uncertain turns of the war.

blocks: Titus went to Egypt and reached Alexandria, and being about to sail from there to Italy, he ordered the leaders of the prisoners, John and Simon, and seven hundred other men outstanding in size and beauty of body, to be taken to Italy at once, so that they might fill out the procession in the triumph.

After Titus's arrival in Rome, Lucilius Bassus was sent as commander to Judaea. He won over the fortress at Herodium with those holding it; then, gathering all the soldiers there were there, he marched on Machaerus. This fortress was very hard to take, being a rocky hill fortified with a wall; and it had been so made by nature that it could not even be approached, for it was moated on every side by deep ravines. Strong as it was, it also had inside a palace wonderful for the size and beauty of its buildings, and many cisterns for collecting water in the most suitable places. Besides the rest, there was in the palace a rue plant worth wonder for its size; for it fell short of no fig tree in height and thickness. The story was that it had lasted from the times of Herod, and it would perhaps have lasted a very long time, had it not been cut down by the Jews who took over the place.

In the ravine on the north of the fortress there is a place called Baaras, and it grows a root called by the same name. It is like flame in colour, and about evening it flashes out a light. It is not easy to take for those who wish to, but shrinks away and does not stand still until someone pours a woman's urine or her menstrual blood on it. Even then, death is certain for those who touch it, unless someone happens to carry off the root itself hanging from his hand. It is also taken safely in another way. They dig round it, so that the part of the root hidden in the earth is very small, then tie a dog to it, and when the dog rushes to follow the man who tied it, the root is easily pulled up, but the dog dies at once; and there is no fear for those who take it after that. It is much sought after for one power. For the so-called demons, which enter into some people, it quickly drives out, even if it is only brought near the sick.

Wishing to bring this fortress over, Bassus tried to fill in the ravine on its east. The Jews shut in there separated themselves from the foreigners, forced them to stay in the lower town, and held the upper fortress themselves. They made sallies eagerly every day, and grappling with whoever they met, many of them died, and they killed many of the Romans labouring at the earthworks.

But by chance the fortress was surrendered even without the earthworks. There was among the besieged a young man, bold in daring and vigorous with his hands, called Eleazar, who, urging the many to go out and hinder the filling-in, became most conspicuous in the battles, doing the Romans much harm. Once, when the fighting had broken off, he stayed outside the gates himself and talked with those on the wall. One Rufus of the Roman camp, an Egyptian by race, suddenly ran up, lifted Eleazar with his armour and all, and got him across to the Roman camp before anyone could stop him. When the commander ordered him to be stripped and whipped in sight of those in the town, the whole town wailed together. Bassus made this a stratagem against the enemy, and ordered a cross to be fixed in the ground, as if to hang Eleazar at once. Those in the fortress, seeing it, were pained the more and wailed piercingly. Eleazar begged them not to stand by and see him die so, and to provide for their own safety by yielding to the strength and fortune of the Romans. They, broken by his words, and with many inside pleading for him (for he was of a large and very numerous family), gave way to pity, and sent to offer the surrender of the fortress, on condition that they might go away unharmed, taking Eleazar.

When the commander accepted this, those in the lower town, learning of the agreement made privately with the Jews, planned to escape by night themselves. When they opened their gates, word came to Bassus from those who had made the agreement. The strongest of those going out managed to break through, but of those caught inside, one thousand seven hundred men were killed, and the women and children were enslaved. Bassus, keeping his agreement with those who surrendered the fortress, let them go and gave back Eleazar.

Having done this, he hurried to the forest called Jardes; for many who had earlier escaped from the sieges had gathered there. Coming to the place, he surrounded it all with the horsemen, and ordered the foot soldiers to cut down the trees. The Jews who had fled there rushed out together with a shout and fell on those surrounding them. Since the Romans received them stoutly, no short time was spent in the battle, but its end did not turn out alike for the opposing sides. For of the Romans twelve fell and a few were wounded, but of the Jews none escaped from this battle; all, not fewer than three thousand, were taken and died.

Bassus and Laberius Maximus, who was procurator, were ordered by Caesar to sell off all the land of the Jews. To eight hundred men alone, discharged from the army, he gave a place to live in, which is called Emmaus and is thirty stades from Jerusalem. He imposed a tax on the Jews wherever they were, each to pay two drachmas yearly to the Capitol, just as they had formerly contributed to the temple in Jerusalem.

blocks: When Bassus died, Flavius Silva succeeded to the command. He marched against the fortress of Masada, the only one of the rebels' places still left. Sicarii held it, led by a powerful man, Eleazar, a descendant of Judas, who had persuaded many of the Jews not to submit to the registration under Quirinius. Silva at once took control of the country, and surrounded the fortress with a wall, blocking those inside from escaping. Then he turned to the siege, and having raised an earthwork where it was possible (for the fortress had been built on a high rock ringed by ravines of boundless depth), he brought up the siege engine and broke down part of the wall. But another was seen built up inside by the sicarii in its place, such as would not yield even to the blows of the engines. For it was made of timbers in two parallel rows, between which they packed earth. So the blows of the engines not only did not break it, but made it firmer, settling together with the shaking; and so Silva ordered the soldiers to hurl burning torches at it all together. The structure, being of wood, caught fire and sent up a great flame. At first a north wind blowing from above drove the flame onto the Romans, and it nearly caught the engines; then a strong south wind blew against it and drove it onto the wall, and the whole was soon burned down.

At this the Romans intended to attack the enemy the next day; but Eleazar spoke to those in the fortress and persuaded them all to kill their own wives and children and then go after them, each one. When this had been decided, they embraced their wives and hugged their children, clinging to them with kisses and weeping, and they killed their dearest with their own hands, as though it were no concern of theirs. Then they gathered all their property and set fire to it. Choosing by lot ten to be the slayers of all, each was slain by them beside his dearest. Then again the one chosen by lot killed the nine, and looking round in case anyone was left alive anywhere, when he knew all had been killed, set fire to the palace, drove his sword right through himself and fell beside his own family. They died believing that no one had been left alive; but an old woman and another, with five children, hidden in the tunnels, escaped notice. The number of the slain, with women and children, was two hundred and sixty.

The Romans attacked at dawn; but seeing none of the enemy, and great quiet inside and fire burning, they were at a loss. At last they raised a war cry, in case they might call out any of those inside. The women heard the shout, came up out of the tunnels and told the Romans what had been done; but they did not believe it. But when they went into the palace and came upon the slain, they wondered at the nobility of the men and their contempt for death.

Such was the capture of Masada. At Alexandria in Egypt too it happened that many Jews died. For those who had fled there from the faction of the sicarii persuaded many of those who received them to lay claim to freedom. If any of the Jews of standing opposed them, they killed some and called on the others to revolt. The leading members of the council gathered the Jews into an assembly, exposed the madness of the sicarii, and urged the multitude to guard against the destruction that would come from them and to hand them over to the Romans. The multitude was persuaded by what was said, and rushing at the sicarii they seized them. About six hundred were caught, and those who escaped then were captured not long after and brought back. Every torture was applied to them to make them acknowledge Caesar as master, but none gave in; all kept their resolve stronger than compulsion. Most of all the age of the children amazed those who watched; for not one of them was overcome into naming Caesar master.

The madness of the sicarii touched the cities about Cyrene too. Jonathan, a most wicked man and a weaver by trade, escaped there and persuaded some of the poor to follow him, and led them into the desert, promising to show signs and wonders. The leading men of the Jews at Cyrene reported this to Catullus, the governor of Cyrene. He sent soldiers and seized those with Jonathan. Jonathan himself escaped at the time, but was searched for carefully and caught, and brought before the governor he contrived an escape from punishment for himself, and provided Catullus with openings for unjust gain. For he said, lying about them, that the richest of the Jews had been his teachers in what had been done; and the governor eagerly accepted the slanders. Besides believing readily, he also taught the sicarii the false accusation; and prompted by him they denounced many.

Here, then, the sufferings of the Jews came to an end for that time, when Jerusalem underwent its last capture by the Romans. Again, when Aelius Hadrian ruled the Romans, the Jews revolted and took up arms against the Romans. But then too they were defeated and crushed, many tens of thousands perishing, so that very few were left; this will be told in its own place.

Since the history has mentioned the Romans and assigned them an invincible power, it is altogether necessary to tell, and to teach or remind the minds of those who read this work, who the Romans were, and from where their nation arose at the beginning, and from where it got its name, what forms of government it used, what fortunes it met, and how it advanced to the height of prosperity, so as to become master of nearly the whole world and to wreathe its power over almost all; and how, being ruled by kings at the beginning, it changed to an aristocracy, that is to dictatorships and consulships, and was transferred again to a democracy, and then came back to monarchy. So I must speak of these things too and tell them, cutting down the breadth of the narrative as far as I can and keeping it from running long, so that the affairs of the history may be easy to survey and may not escape the memory of those who read them.

blocks: As they grew up both were spirited and manly; but Romulus seemed superior in intelligence, and by nature more fit to command than to obey. Once, when a quarrel arose between Numitor's herdsmen and those of Amulius, the brothers beat Numitor's men and cut off a large part of the herd. Numitor's herdsmen lay in wait for Remus, when he was walking alone with a few others, seized him and took him to Numitor; and Numitor went to Amulius and asked for justice, since he was his brother and had been outraged by his men. Amulius handed Remus over to Numitor to treat as he wished. Numitor went home, and seeing the young man outstanding in size and strength, and wondering at the boldness and unbroken spirit of his soul, asked him gently who he was and where he came from. He answered boldly: "We are twin brothers, and our birth is said to be a secret, and our nurture and nursing more wonderful still, since we were fed by beasts and birds as we lay in a trough by the great river; the trough is still kept, with faint letters engraved on its bronze bands."

Numitor was led by Remus's words and his looks to think of the exposure of his daughter's children; and Faustulus, learning of Remus's capture, urged Romulus to help, then telling him plainly about his birth (for before he had only hinted at it, so that they might not think small of themselves), and himself, carrying the trough, went to Numitor full of haste and fear. He was suspicious of the guards at Amulius's gates and confused in his answers, and did not escape notice as he covered the trough with his cloak. Thinking he was carrying something stolen, they brought the trough out into the open. There happened to be present one of those who had exposed the babes; recognising the trough, he ran and told Amulius. Faustulus, questioned by the king, admitted that the children were alive, but said they were tending herds far from Alba; and that he was bringing the trough to Ilia, the children's mother, who longed to see it. Amulius, troubled by this, sent a man to Numitor to ask if he had learned anything about the children as being alive. The man sent was one of Numitor's friends. So, going off and finding Numitor embracing Remus, he encouraged him and advised them not to delay, and himself helped them. Just then Romulus too was near, bringing a large band of countrymen; and not a few of the citizens came over to him out of hatred of Amulius. With things having come together so, Amulius, having done or planned nothing for his safety, was killed.

blocks: Romulus and Remus assigned the rule of Alba to their mother's father, and fitting honour to their mother, and decided to be on their own; for they would not bear to be ruled, and they wished to found a city where they had been brought up. When they had set out to build the city, a quarrel arose between the brothers about the rule and about the city, and they came to a fight, in which Remus died. Another story has it that when Romulus was already digging a trench that was to be the outwork of the city's wall, Remus sometimes hindered the work and sometimes mocked it; and at last, as he leapt across it as being easy to attack, some say he fell struck by Romulus, others by someone else. From this it came to be the custom that whoever dared to cross the trench of a camp other than by the usual ways should be put to death.

Romulus buried his brother and founded the city. Yoking a bull with a cow, and putting a bronze share in the plough, he himself drew a deep furrow in a circle, and those following turned all the clods that the plough threw up inside the furrow. Where the wall was to rise, the furrow was cut, as has been said; but where they meant to set gates, they left a break in the furrow, lifting the plough over it. For they hold every wall sacred; but if they thought the gates sacred, it would not be possible to bring in some necessary things through them and send out others that are unclean.

The founding of this city was completed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, which would rather be the twentieth of April; and the Romans keep this day as a feast, calling it the birthday of their country. Romulus is recorded to have been eighteen years old when he founded Rome. He founded it around the dwelling of Faustulus; and the place was named the Palatium.

When the city had been founded, he divided the multitude of military age into army units; each unit was of three thousand foot and three hundred horse, and was called a legion, because the fighting men were picked from all; the rest he treated as the people. He named the people populus; from which in the law books too an action brought by the people is called popularis. Of the men more distinguished for birth, intelligence and choice of life he appointed a hundred councillors, naming them patricians; and the whole body he called the senate, which is the council of elders. The councillors were called patricians either because they were fathers of legitimate children, or rather because they could each show who their fathers were, being of known family, or from patronia; for so they called protection; for they called those who took care of others and helped them patroni. One would best guess Romulus's intention if one thought that by this name he meant to show that the first and most powerful men of the city ought to care for the humbler with a father's care, and at the same time to lead the people, by the name of patricians, not to resent the honours of their betters, but to be well disposed to them, thinking of them as fathers and calling them so.

When many had settled in the city, few of whom were joined to wives, Romulus took thought that they too should get wives for themselves. For being a mixed rabble, from poor and obscure families, they were scorned for marriage by the neighbouring peoples. So he planned for his citizens to take wives by seizing them, and proclaimed that he was going to hold a sacrifice, a contest and a festival show, since an altar of a new god had been found. Many came together. He himself sat in front with the best men, dressed in purple; and he gave the people as a signal for the attempt the unfolding of the purple robe and the wrapping of it round him again. When this was done, they drew their swords with a shout, rushed in and seized the daughters of the Sabines, virgins, not anyone's wives.

When the seizure had been dared, the Sabines, who were many and warlike and lived in unwalled villages because they were proud of being colonists of the Lacedaemonians, sent an embassy to Romulus, asking him to undo the work of violence and to bring about friendship and kinship between the peoples by persuasion and law. Romulus would not give up the girls, but asked the Sabines to accept the partnership; and while the others spent their time in deliberation, Acron, king of the Caeninenses, a spirited and most warlike man, rose up first and went against Romulus with a large force. When they had met, they challenged each other to fight, the armies keeping still. In the single combat between the two Romulus struck down Acron, and when battle was joined he routed his army too; and he took the city, but did no harm to those in it, only ordering them to pull down their houses and follow him to Rome, to become citizens and be granted equal rights.

Then other Sabines too fought the Romans and were defeated. After this the rest of the Sabines appointed Tatius general, marched on Rome, and took the Capitol, which was betrayed by Tarpeia, the daughter of the commander of the garrison. For she went down for water, was seized and brought to Tatius, and was persuaded to betray the stronghold, having fallen in love with the golden armlets that the Sabines wore on their left arms, and having asked to receive them as pay for the betrayal. When Tatius agreed, she opened one gate by night and let the Sabines in. When all did the same, she was struck by the gold and buried under the shields, and died from their number and weight. So in deed he did what Caesar and Antigonus later said in words: for the one said he loved treason but hated the traitor; and Antigonus said that he gladly received those who were betraying, but hated those who had betrayed.
text: Romulus and Remus assigned the rule of Alba to their mother's father, and fitting honour to their mother, and decided to be on their own; for they would not bear to be ruled, and they wished to found a city where they had been brought up. When they had set out to build the city, a quarrel arose between the brothers about the rule and about the city, and they came to a fight, in which Remus died. Another story has it that when Romulus was already digging a trench that was to be the outwork of the city's wall, Remus sometimes hindered the work and sometimes mocked it; and at last, as he leapt across it as being easy to attack, some say he fell struck by Romulus, others by someone else. From this it came to be the custom that whoever dared to cross the trench of a camp other than by the usual ways should be put to death. Romulus buried his brother and founded the city. Yoking a bull with a cow, and putting a bronze share in the plough, he himself drew a deep furrow in a circle, and those following turned all the clods that the plough threw up inside the furrow. Where the wall was to rise, the furrow was cut, as has been said; but where they meant to set gates, they left a break in the furrow, lifting the plough over it. For they hold every wall sacred; but if they thought the gates sacred, it would not be possible to bring in some necessary things through them and send out others that are unclean. The founding of this city was completed on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, which would rather be the twentieth of April; and the Romans keep this day as a feast, calling it the birthday of their country. Romulus is recorded to have been eighteen years old when he founded Rome. He founded it around the dwelling of Faustulus; and the place was named the Palatium. When the city had been founded, he divided the multitude of military age into army units; each unit was of three thousand foot and three hundred horse, and was called a legion, because the fighting men were picked from all; the rest he treated as the people. He named the people populus; from which in the law books too an action brought by the people is called popularis. Of the men more distinguished for birth, intelligence and choice of life he appointed a hundred councillors, naming them patricians; and the whole body he called the senate, which is the council of elders. The councillors were called patricians either because they were fathers of legitimate children, or rather because they could each show who their fathers were, being of known family, or from patronia; for so they called protection; for they called those who took care of others and helped them patroni. One would best guess Romulus's intention if one thought that by this name he meant to show that the first and most powerful men of the city ought to care for the humbler with a father's care, and at the same time to lead the people, by the name of patricians, not to resent the honours of their betters, but to be well disposed to them, thinking of them as fathers and calling them so. blocks: When the citadel had been taken by the Sabines, a hard battle broke out between them and the Romans, in which many fell, and Romulus was struck on the head by a stone. As the Sabines were preparing to fight still, their daughters who had been seized held them back, appearing to them from all sides with shouting and wailing, some carrying babes in their arms, others holding out their loosened hair, and all calling on now the Sabines, now the Romans, by the dearest names. So the opponents were moved, and parted to let them stand in the middle between the lines, and weeping spread through them all. When the women had spoken, the leaders came to a parley and agreed that those of the women who wished should live with the men who had them, freed from every work and service except spinning wool; that the Romans and Sabines should live in the city in common, and that it should be called Rome after Romulus, and the Romans Quirites after Cures, Tatius's country; and that both should reign and command in common. The place in which they made the agreement is called the Comitium, that is, a place of coming together; for the Romans say comire for coming together. A further hundred from the Sabines were enrolled among the patricians. The kings did not take counsel together in common at once, but each first in private with his hundred; then they all gathered in one place.

In the fifth year of Tatius's joint reign with Romulus, some of his kinsmen met envoys on the road from Laurentum going to Rome, tried to take by force the money they were carrying, and when they would not give it up but defended themselves, killed them. Romulus voted that the wrongdoers be punished, but Tatius put it off and turned it aside; and this alone became a cause of open quarrel between them. The relatives of the dead, failing to get justice, fell on Tatius as he was sacrificing with Romulus at the Alban mount and killed him; but they escorted Romulus away with praises as a just man. The murder of their ruler did not disturb the Sabines, but some out of goodwill towards Romulus, others out of fear of his power, went on yielding to him. Then a plague fell on the city, bringing sudden deaths on men without illness, and failure of crops and barrenness of flocks; and the city was rained on with drops of blood. The same things befell the people of Laurentum too. So it seemed that divine wrath was pursuing the cities for the murder of Tatius and of the envoys killed by the Sabines. When the murderers had been handed over and punished, the troubles abated.

As the Romans' affairs grew strong, the weaker of their neighbours submitted, but the powerful thought they ought not to overlook it, but to cut short their growth. The first of the Etruscans to begin war were the Veientes. They engaged, lost many, and made an agreement and friendship for a hundred years, and gave fifty of their best men as hostages.

Romulus, having conquered them, held a triumph. Then, lifted up by his unexpected good fortune and taking on a heavier pride, he departed from his popular ways and changed into a monarchy oppressive and offensive in its outward show. For he wore a purple tunic, put on a toga bordered with purple, wore red shoes, and did business sitting on a throne with a back; and there were always many of the young men about him, whom he called Celeres, which in the Romans' language means "the swift"; and others walked in front keeping off the crowd with staves, girded with straps to bind those they were ordered to.

When his grandfather Numitor died at Alba, and the kingdom came to Romulus, he himself put the government into the hands of the people to court them, and appointed a ruler for the Sabines each year; and so he provoked the powerful men in Rome to seek a constitution without a king and with self-government. For not even those called patricians had a share in affairs; they had a name and an outward show, gathering in the council house more out of custom than for their opinion; then, while Romulus acted, they listened in silence, and went away having only this advantage over the rest, that they learned his decision before others. So he seemed to treat the senate with contempt; and for this reason the senate was suspected when, a little later, Romulus disappeared.

For it is said that as he was holding an assembly at the place called the Goat's Marsh, the light of the sun failed, night came on, and there were terrible thunders and blasts of wind driving a storm. Meanwhile the crowd fled, and the powerful gathered together. When the disturbance in the air had abated and many had come together again, the king was looked for; but the powerful did not allow inquiry about him, and urged all to honour and worship Romulus as having been caught up to the gods, and as one who would be a god for them instead of a good king.

The many went away persuaded by these words, buoyed up by good hopes; but some held the patricians under suspicion and stirred things up, saying that they were persuading the people of foolish things, having themselves been the king's murderers. And they would have caused trouble for the powerful, had not one of the knights, Julius Proculus, most esteemed in family, good in character and loyal to Romulus, come into the forum and said on oath that Romulus had appeared to him, fair and tall as never before, adorned with bright, blazing armour; and that he had asked: "What has befallen you, king, that you have left us under wicked charges and the whole city in mourning?" And that he had answered: "It pleased the gods, Proculus, that we should be with men so long, and then dwell in heaven again, having come from there. But farewell, and tell the Romans that by practising self-control and courage they will reach the greatest height of human power. And I shall be gracious to you as Quirinus." Because of the speaker's oath and his character, this seemed so credible to the Romans that no one spoke against it, but laying aside all suspicion and slander they prayed to Quirinus and invoked him as a god. They say that Romulus got this surname either because they named the citizens Quirites, or because the ancients called the spear-point or spear quiris; so that Romulus was named Quirinus as a warlike or spear-bearing god. He is said to have lived fifty-four years, and to have vanished from among men in the thirty-eighth year of his reign.

blocks: When this had befallen Romulus, all thought they should be ruled by a king, but a dispute and strife grew among those in Rome, not only about the man who would lead, but also about which of the two peoples would provide the ruler. For to those who had first founded the city with Romulus it seemed unbearable that the Sabines, whom they had admitted into citizenship, should force their way to rule over those who had received them; while the Sabines on the other side, since on Tatius's death they had let Romulus rule alone, claimed that the ruler should be chosen from themselves.

So both sides disputed in this way, and while the state was in suspense over this, the patricians, being a hundred and fifty, arranged that each in turn, adorned with the royal insignia, should sacrifice to the gods and do business, for six hours of the night and six of the day. For the sharing out of the times equally to each seemed well both for the rulers and for the ruled themselves; for the very quick laying down of power took away envy, since the ruled saw the same man become a private person from a king in the same day and night. I know that other things too are said about this kind of rule, but I have followed the more credible. This form of rule was named by the Romans an interregnum.

But even so disturbances arose out of suspicion, the patricians being suspected of turning the state into an oligarchy and not wishing to be ruled by a king; and from this they quarrelled. When all agreed that the future king should be chosen, the Sabines gave the Romans the first choice; and they chose from the Sabines Numa Pompilius, a man known to all for his virtue. So envoys were sent to him from Rome; for he had not moved to Rome, but was among the Sabines and lived in the city of Cures. He was the son of Pomponius, a man of good repute, and he had trained himself in every virtue by nature and education. From this he had a great name and reputation, so that even Tatius, who reigned with Romulus, made him his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter Tatia, the only child he had; she lived with Numa for thirteen years and then departed this life. Numa, leaving the pursuits of the town, wished to live mostly in the country and spend his time in meadows and groves.

So the envoys came from Rome, calling him to the kingship when he was already in his fortieth year; but he refused. The envoys pressed him, contriving every way to persuade him, and begging him not to throw the city again into strife and civil war, since there was no one else to whom both sides would incline. In private his father too urged Numa to accept the rule as a divine gift and a service to God, which would be for a wise and good man a cause of noble and great deeds, and a bond of goodwill and friendship for his own country and the whole Sabine nation with a powerful and flourishing city.

Numa gave way to this, sacrificed to the gods and went on to Rome; and the senate and people met him with acclamations and rejoicing. When they reached the forum and the royal insignia were brought to him, he told them to wait, and said he needed God too to confirm the kingship for him. So he went up to the Capitol, sacrificed, and only then put on the royal dress and came down.

Having received the rule, first he disbanded the body of three hundred whom Romulus always had about his person; for he said he ought not to distrust those who trusted him, nor did he think it right to reign over those who distrusted him. Then he tried to make the city, from hard and warlike, softer and more peaceful. He forbade the Romans to set up an image of God in the form of a man or a beast; so they had no painted or moulded form of God, and in a hundred and seventy years, while temples were being raised for them, they made no statue with a form, since it was not holy to liken the better to the worse, nor was it possible to lay hold of God otherwise than by thought. He ordained that sacrifices be made without blood, with barley meal and libations; for the gods, being guardians of peace and justice, should be pure of slaughter; and that they should neither hear nor see anything of divine matters in passing and carelessly, but at leisure from other things and with their minds attentive, as to the greatest of actions, that concerning piety. By these and many other things, which we have passed over for their number, Numa created in the men of that time, by habit, a disposition towards the divine. They say that he himself hung his hopes so on the divine that once, when it was reported to him as he was sacrificing that enemies were coming, he smiled and said: "But I am sacrificing." The land that Romulus had won by the spear he shared out among the poor citizens, taking poverty away from them as a necessity that makes men do wrong, and turning them to farming, since this tames the people and can create a keen love of peace.

It is said that January and February too were added to the months by him, since he laid down that the year should be reckoned as twelve months by the course of the moon, while before it had been ten months, as among some of the barbarians it is three months, and among the Greeks for the Arcadians four months and for the Acarnanians six. For the Egyptians the year was a month, and then four months; so they seem very ancient though they are not, bringing in a vast number of years in their genealogies, because they set the months down as a number of years. Numa also assigned January to the beginning of the year.

When he had accustomed his subjects to justice and piety, war was removed altogether. For not only was the Roman people tamed by the king's good order and mildness, but the cities round about too began to change, and a longing flowed into all for peace and justice, to plant the land, bring up children in quiet and worship the gods. For neither war nor strife nor revolution in the state is recorded while Numa reigned, nor is any enmity or envy against him, or any gathering of men and plot from love of kingship, recorded to have arisen anywhere. Having a daughter, Pompilia, he married her to Marcius; and of her a grandson, Ancus Marcius, was born to him, who reigned after Tullus Hostilius. Numa left him five years old and died, wasting away little by little from old age and a gentle illness, having lived three years beyond eighty, and reigned forty-three years.

So that the sole rule might not seem a kingship, they also voted him a colleague, Tarquinius Collatinus, the husband of that Lucretia, since he was believed to be hostile to the tyrants because of the violence done to his wife. Envoys came to Rome from Tarquinius to discuss his return; and when they achieved nothing, others came again, saying that Tarquinius would give up the kingship and stop the war, if the money were given to him and his friends and kin, on which they could live in exile. When many were moved, even Collatinus, Brutus's colleague, Brutus ran out of the council house into the forum, calling Collatinus a traitor who was granting the means for war and tyranny.

The envoys, staying on in Rome on the pretext of the money, managed to corrupt some of the notable men, and with them they persuaded two sons of Brutus to join in the betrayal. When the youths had been won over, it was decided that an oath should be taken too, and for this they met in a house. The house was deserted and dark. So a slave named Vindicius was inside without their knowing, not by design but by chance, and hidden there he was a witness of what was done and heard what was planned, which was to kill the consuls and betray the city; and they sent this to Tarquinius by the envoys. When the conspirators had left the room, the slave came out and revealed everything. Those who had planned the betrayal were seized and the letters were brought; and when they were brought into the forum, they set Vindicius before them. The letters were read; and the others were downcast and silent, but Brutus, calling each of his sons by name, said: "Do you not answer the charge?" When they kept silent, he turned to the attendants and said: "The rest of the work is now yours." They seized the young men and scourged them with rods. While the others were moved by their suffering, the father neither turned his eyes elsewhere nor showed any pity, until they had cut off his sons' heads with the axe. This is not easy either to praise or to blame; for either the height of virtue set his soul beyond feeling, or the greatness of his feeling set it beyond pain; neither is small or human, but either godlike or beastlike.

When these had died in this way, Brutus was asked to give his vote about the other conspirators too. He said: "For my sons I am judge enough myself; about the others I yield the vote to the citizens, who are free." So when the vote was given, all were beheaded. Some of them were related to Collatinus, and he was angry on their account. So Brutus so provoked the people against him that they nearly killed him with their own hands. They did not do this, but they forced him to give up his office. In his place they chose as colleague Publius Valerius, who was surnamed Publicola; the name rendered into Greek means one who cares for the people, or most popular.

Tarquinius, despairing of recovering the kingship by betrayal, went to the Etruscans. They tried to bring him back with a heavy force. The consuls led out the Romans against them. As the battle began, Arruns, the son of Tarquinius, and Brutus, the consul of the Romans, fell upon each other and fought, and not sparing themselves in their fury, died together. The battle was great and many fell on both sides, and the victory was undecided. When night came on, the grove beside which they were encamped is said to have shaken, and a great voice came out of it saying that one more of the Etruscans had died than of the Romans. At the voice the Romans raised a loud and confident war cry, while panic fell on the Etruscans; and in their alarm they abandoned their camp; and the Romans took it and plundered it. When the dead of those who fell in the battle were counted, those of the Etruscans were found to be eleven thousand three hundred, and the Romans as many less one. Valerius Publicola held a triumph, the first to do so as consul.

Tarquinius, after the great battle in which he lost his son too, fighting with Brutus, fled to Clusium and begged the help of Lars Porsena, the man with the greatest power among the Italian kings; and he promised to help him. First he sent to Rome ordering them to receive Tarquinius, and when they did not obey, he came with a heavy force. Valerius Publicola, chosen to office for the second time, joined battle, was wounded, and was carried out of the battle on a litter. As Porsena pressed the city, famine took hold of the Romans. But through some chance, or rather by providence, Porsena ended the war against the Romans.

For a man named Mucius Cordus, good in every virtue and best in war, surnamed Scaevola, which means one-handed or not sound of hand, planned to kill Porsena and went into his camp wearing Etruscan dress and using a like speech. Not knowing Porsena clearly, and afraid to ask, he drew his sword and killed his secretary, who was sitting with him and was dressed much the same. He was seized and questioned; and since a brazier had been made ready for Porsena, who was then about to sacrifice, he held his hand over it, and while the flesh burned he stood looking at Porsena with an unmoved face (from this, when his hand was destroyed, he got his surname), until Porsena in wonder let him go. Scaevola outwitted the enemy in another way, and said: "Having overcome your fear, Porsena, I have been conquered by your virtue, and out of gratitude I reveal what I would not have told under compulsion. Three hundred Romans with the same purpose as mine are staying in your camp; of whom I, chosen by lot, made the first attempt, and I do not grieve at my fortune, having missed a good man, who ought rather to be a friend than an enemy to the Romans." From this Porsena became more eager for terms.

Publicola, consul for the third time, then kept challenging Tarquinius to a trial, to prove him most wicked and most justly put out of his rule, with Porsena as judge. When Tarquinius answered that he would not choose Porsena as arbiter, if he was changing sides though an ally, Porsena condemned him and ended the war. After this the Tarquins often tried to recover the kingship, fighting alongside the peoples neighbouring the Romans, but all were destroyed in the battles except the old man, who was also called Superbus, which a Greek would render as "arrogant." He too later went to Cumae in Opicia and died there.

blocks: This had just happened, and Marcus Furius Camillus was chosen dictator. He attacked the city, and when he achieved nothing, he dug an underground passage, beginning far off, leading into the citadel. When the tunnel was ready, since many had come over to him from Rome too as volunteers, he took them as well, attacked the city and surrounded the wall on every side; and while those inside were scattered round the whole circuit, others got inside through the tunnels without being noticed. When the city had been taken and the Romans were plundering what was in it, Camillus, watching what was being done from the citadel, groaned and wept and said: "O gods, if some retribution is owed to balance this good fortune, I pray that it may end on myself." He took out the tenth of the booty, against the soldiers' will, and dedicated it to Apollo, having made this vow before. He also dedicated a golden mixing bowl made from the women's ornaments; and in return an honour was at once voted to them, which was that they should go to the festivals in carriages, having before gone to them on foot. But the people were vexed with Camillus and resented him, partly because he had taken out the god's share of the spoils not while they were being plundered but after the time had passed, and partly because he held his triumph haughtily in other ways, and was the first of the Romans to drive in the victory procession with a team of four white horses.

The victory procession, which they also called a triumph, went like this. When some great success worth a triumph had been won, the general was at once named imperator by the soldiers, and he bound sprigs of laurel round the rods and gave them to the couriers announcing the victory to the city to carry. Coming home he assembled the senate and asked them to vote him the triumph. If he got the vote of the senate and the people, the title of imperator was confirmed for him too. If he was still in the office in which he had won, he held the procession in it. But if the time of his office had passed, he received some other name suited to it; for a private man was forbidden to hold a triumph. Dressed in the triumphal dress, taking armlets, binding on a crown of laurel and holding a branch in his right hand, he called the people together; and having praised those who had served with him, both in common and some individually, he gave them money and honoured them with decorations, giving some armlets and spears without iron, and giving crowns, some of gold, some of silver, bearing the name of each and the image of his deed of valour. For if someone had been first to mount a wall, the crown bore the form of a wall; or if he had taken a place by siege, this too was pictured. If someone had won at sea, the crown was adorned with ships; if someone had won with cavalry, something to do with horses was stamped on it. But the one who had saved a citizen from a battle or another danger or from a siege had the greatest praise and received a crown made of oak, which was held far more honourable than all, both the silver and the gold. These were given not only to individual men who had done valiantly, but also to companies and whole armies. Much of the spoils was shared among those who had served; and sometimes some even gave it out to the whole people, spent it on the festival and made it public, and if anything was left, spent it on temples, porticoes or some other public work.

Having done this, the man holding the procession mounted the chariot. The chariot was like neither a racing nor a war chariot, but was made in the shape of a round tower. He was not alone in the chariot, but if he had children or some relatives, he set the girls and the infant boys in it, and put the older ones on the horses, both the yoke horses and the trace horses; and if there were more, they rode beside the man in procession on riding horses and joined the procession. None of the others rode, but all walked crowned with laurel. A public slave rode with him in the chariot itself, holding over him the crown of gold-set stones, and said to him: "Look behind," that is, look to what is behind and what follows in life, and do not be lifted up by the present and grow arrogant. A bell and a whip hung from the chariot, showing that he too could meet misfortune, so as to be flogged or even condemned to die. For it was the custom for those condemned to die for some crime to wear a bell, so that no one coming near them as they walked might be filled with pollution.

Arrayed so, they entered the city, with the spoils and trophies going before them, and in pictures the captured forts, cities, mountains, rivers, lakes and seas, and everything that had been taken. If one day was enough for the procession of these, well; if not, it was held on a second and third day too. When these had gone ahead, the man holding the procession, carried into the Roman forum, ordered some of the prisoners to be taken to the prison and put to death, and drove up to the Capitol; there he performed some rites, brought offerings, dined in the porticoes there, and towards evening went home with pipes and flutes. Such were the triumphs of old; but factions and the power of great men brought very many innovations into them.
