blocks: Though the people hated Camillus, as has already been told, the war against the Faliscans forced them to vote him military tribune. They defeated them in battle, but besieging a strong city of theirs called Falerii, they achieved nothing. For those in the city so despised the siege that even their children went about beside the walls with their teacher to take exercise. And the Romans would have given up the siege, had not something happened. For this teacher, plotting against the citizens, either from some anger or in hope of gain, led the children out to the wall every day, near at first, and brought them back in at once when they had exercised; but at last he took them all into the Roman outposts and told them to take him to Camillus, and standing before him said that he was handing over the whole city through the children. But Camillus, thinking the deed terrible, and saying that the great general should make war trusting in his own virtue and not in another's wickedness, ordered the teacher to be stripped and his hands bound behind him, and rods and whips given to the children, so that they might beat the traitor with them and drive him into the city. The citizens had just learned of the betrayal, and there was a rush to the walls and lamenting of men and women. While they were in this state, the children brought up their teacher naked. The Faliscans, seeing this and learning how it had happened, came of their own accord and surrendered themselves to Camillus, saying that because of his justice they welcomed defeat before freedom.

So he took money, made a treaty and withdrew. But the soldiers, who had expected to plunder Falerii, accused him of hating the people. Envied still more, he was accused of having given the public treasury no benefit from the Etruscan money, but of having appropriated it himself. They were so angry with him that they felt no pity for him in the misfortune that had befallen him; for one of his sons had fallen ill and died. When he begged his friends not to stand by while he was unjustly condemned, and they refused to help him with the vote but promised to help pay the fine if he were condemned, he would not bear it and decided to leave the city. As he went out he prayed that, if he was being driven out not justly but by the insolence and envy of the people, those same citizens might soon need him and seek him.
He moved to the Rutulians, and was condemned in his absence, and a verdict was passed against him with a fine of fifteen thousand asses, which in silver comes to one thousand five hundred drachmas.

blocks: The European Gauls, of whom the Asiatic Gauls are thought to be colonists, being of Celtic race, left their own land as not enough to feed them; some set out for the Rhipaean mountains, and others settled near the Alps and lived there a long time. Then, when wine was brought from Italy, they tasted it and wondered at it greatly, took up arms, brought their parents with them, and went looking for the land that yields such fruit. They marched against an Etruscan city called Clusium and besieged it. The people of Clusium fled to the Romans for help. Envoys were sent to the Gauls from Rome; the Gauls received them with honour because of the name of the Romans, stopped assaulting the wall and came to a parley. Meanwhile the people of Clusium laid an ambush and, with the envoys from Rome, attacked the Gauls. Brennus, the king of the Gauls, angry at this, left the people of Clusium alone and at once moved his army against Rome as it was, since the envoys were not handed over to him for punishment; and he moved so fast that they came upon the city before the Romans learned of their approach.

The divine, however, is said to have announced the approach to them. For Marcus Caedicius, walking somewhere at night, heard a voice saying: "The Gauls are coming." When Marcus told this to the people and the senate, they made a joke of the story and laughed, until the Gauls themselves brought the news by being near them. Then they went out in haste, fought in disorder and were most shamefully defeated. Many fell in the battle, many died caught as they fled, and very many were pushed into the river Tiber and perished; of the rest, scattered, some were able to reach Rome and others went elsewhere.

Those in Rome, learning what had happened, were helpless, and in despair they neither set a guard on the walls nor shut the city's gates; some left it and fled, others ran up to the Capitol with their wives and children. Only eighty men, whom some say were priests and others the first of the Romans in age, wealth and birth, put on sacred or most costly robes and sat in the forum on ivory chairs, awaiting the fortune to come. The Gauls came to Rome the next day, but seeing the gates open and the wall unguarded, they held back and did not go in, suspecting an ambush. On the third day they took courage, rushed in and took the city. The king of the barbarians set a guard on the Capitol, and himself, going through the forum, wondered at those men sitting in front, seeing them in their finery, unmoving and silent. Amazement at the strangeness held the Gauls, and they hesitated to go up to them. At length one dared to stand beside one of them, took hold of the man's beard, which was long, and pulled it down; and he struck him on the head with his staff. The barbarian drew his sword and killed the man. So the barbarians fell on the rest too and killed them, and sacked and burned the houses. Then they attacked the Capitol as well; and since they achieved nothing after trying for many days, some guarded the Capitol and others overran the country getting food, scattering and going about here and there, not together, since they were proud of their success; and they were tripped up by drunkenness; for coming upon much wine they drank it too unmixed, never having tasted such a drink before.

Camillus, seeing the Gauls in this state, since they were also plundering the land of the Ardeates, and the Ardeates themselves were enough in number but lacked daring through inexperience and want of training for battle, put it to the younger men that they should ascribe the barbarians' success not to their courage but to the Romans' misfortune, and he insisted that if they were eager and took heart, they would beat the enemy without danger. Having persuaded the young men in this way, and then the rest, he armed those of age, and in the dead of night he himself with the Ardeates fell on the barbarians while they were drunk. He cut most of them down there, and if some were able to escape in the darkness, horsemen caught them after daybreak and destroyed them.

When rumour quickly proclaimed the success everywhere, those of the Romans who had escaped from the first battle with the Gauls and were safe took their arms and went to Camillus, begging him to take command of them. He said he would not consent unless those safe on the Capitol first voted him the command. There was difficulty in finding someone to take the message to those on the Capitol. But one of the young men, Pontius Cominius, a lover of glory, undertook the task, slipped through the midst of the enemy unnoticed, came near the hill of the Capitol, crept up with difficulty and barely clambered to the top, and was brought by the guards to the Romans in office; he announced Camillus's victory, told what the soldiers had decided, and urged them to confirm Camillus's command. They voted Camillus dictator. He gathered the Romans outside, about twenty thousand, and many from the allies, and prepared for an attack.

The barbarians, going about after daybreak, found out where Pontius had climbed to the Capitol (they guessed it from the broken fragments of rock and the grass, of which there was much there, some pulled up and some trampled down), and planned to go up that way themselves by night. They set about the task, and with difficulty, but still they climbed, and they would have reached the outwork and attacked the guards without being noticed, had there not been geese kept about the temple of Juno, which, being by nature sharp of sense and frightened by noise, quickly perceived the Gauls' approach, and rushing at the guards with a noisy cackling, roused them all. So the Romans fell on those climbing up, killed some, pushed others down the rock, and escaped the danger.

From this the Celts were more despondent, having been worn down by the siege for seven months. So Brennus, the king of the barbarians, and Sulpicius, the military tribune of the Romans, talked about terms. It was agreed that the Romans should pay the Gauls a thousand pounds of gold, and that those who received the gold should at once withdraw from the city and the country. When the gold was brought, and the barbarians were secretly cheating over the weights, Brennus took off his sword together with his belt and put it on the weights. When the tribune asked what was happening, he said: "What else but woe to the vanquished?" At this moment Camillus with his army stood at the gates of the city; and learning what was happening, he hurried on to the Romans. Coming up, he lifted the gold from the scale and gave it to his attendants, and told the Celts to take the scale and the weights and go away, saying that it was the Romans' ancestral custom to save their country with iron and not with gold. When Brennus said he was being wronged, since the agreement was being broken, Camillus answered that the treaty was not valid, since it had been made without him when he had already been chosen dictator. Brennus, disturbed, went as far as drawing swords, but still led the Celts back to their camp; then he left the city, went sixty stades and encamped. At daybreak Camillus was upon him, leading the Romans, who had now taken heart, routed the barbarians with great slaughter and took their camp.

So Rome was taken unexpectedly and saved more unexpectedly still; and Camillus held a triumph. Since the city had been utterly destroyed, the multitude did not wish to rebuild it, being strong neither in money nor in body, and they would nearly have left it. For they were not persuaded either by those in office or by the senate, who urged and advised them not to leave the town, which had now been saved from the enemy; until, while all were deliberating about this in the forum, a centurion leading a guard and happening to pass by the assembly itself, shouted to those following him: "Halt here; for here you must stay." They thought this had been said by divine providence, and gave up moving away, and turned eagerly to the renewal of Rome, and renewed both the walls and the private houses within a year.
text: The European Gauls, of whom the Asiatic Gauls are thought to be colonists, being of Celtic race, left their own land as not enough to feed them; some set out for the Rhipaean mountains, and others settled near the Alps and lived there a long time. Then, when wine was brought from Italy, they tasted it and wondered at it greatly, took up arms, brought their parents with them, and went looking for the land that yields such fruit. They marched against an Etruscan city called Clusium and besieged it. The people of Clusium fled to the Romans for help. Envoys were sent to the Gauls from Rome; the Gauls received them with honour because of the name of the Romans, stopped assaulting the wall and came to a parley. Meanwhile the people of Clusium laid an ambush and, with the envoys from Rome, attacked the Gauls. Brennus, the king of the Gauls, angry at this, left the people of Clusium alone and at once moved his army against Rome as it was, since the envoys were not handed over to him for punishment; and he moved so fast that they came upon the city before the Romans learned of their approach. The divine, however, is said to have announced the approach to them. For Marcus Caedicius, walking somewhere at night, heard a voice saying: "The Gauls are coming." When Marcus told this to the people and the senate, they made a joke of the story and laughed, until the Gauls themselves brought the news by being near them. Then they went out in haste, fought in disorder and were most shamefully defeated. Many fell in the battle, many died caught as they fled, and very many were pushed into the river Tiber and perished; of the rest, scattered, some were able to reach Rome and others went elsewhere. Those in Rome, learning what had happened, were helpless, and in despair they neither set a guard on the walls nor shut the city's gates; some left it and fled, others ran up to the Capitol with their wives and children. Only eighty men, whom some say were priests and others the first of the Romans in age, wealth and birth, put on sacred or most costly robes and sat in the forum on ivory chairs, awaiting the fortune to come. On the third day they took courage, rushed in and took the city. The king of the barbarians set a guard on the Capitol, and himself, going through the forum, wondered at those men sitting in front, seeing them in their finery, unmoving and silent. Amazement at the strangeness held the Gauls, and they hesitated to go up to them. At length one dared to stand beside one of them, took hold of the man's beard, which was long, and pulled it down; and he struck him on the head with his staff. The barbarian drew his sword and killed the man. So the barbarians fell on the rest too and killed them, and sacked and burned the houses. Then they attacked the Capitol as well; and since they achieved nothing after trying for many days, some guarded the Capitol and others overran the country getting food, scattering and going about here and there, not together, since they were proud of their success; and they were tripped up by drunkenness; for coming upon much wine they drank it too unmixed, never having tasted such a drink before. Having persuaded the young men in this way, and then the rest, he armed those of age, and in the dead of night he himself with the Ardeates fell on the barbarians while they were drunk. blocks: Epitome of Histories, collected and written by John the monk Zonaras. The former book contains the affairs of the Hebrews, of Rome and of the consulships; this one contains the histories of the emperors.

From the beginning, then, as I have told in the former book, the rule of the Romans was given over to kings until the tyranny and overthrow of the Tarquins; from then on the management of public affairs was entrusted to praetors and dictators, consuls and military tribunes, and also tribunes of the people; and Roman affairs were steered by such forms of government until Pompey the Great and Gaius Julius Caesar.

Pompey was the son of Strabo, one of the notable Romans, who had been granted a generalship and was opposed to Cinna, who was using his office too tyrannically. For by now the affairs of the Romans were sick, and their rulers inclined to tyranny and did not wish to rule lawfully. His father Strabo was hated by the Romans for his love of money, but Pompey was loved for the trustworthiness of his character, his affability, his moderation in his way of life and his training in arms. So great was the affection for him that when, fearing Cinna because of a slander, he slipped secretly out of the camp, and was not to be seen, and a report spread that he had been killed by Cinna, those who hated Cinna anyway rushed against him; and Cinna was killed as he fled, caught by one of the centurions.

When Cinna had perished in this way, Carbo took over affairs, a more reckless tyrant than he. When Sulla set himself up against Carbo, Pompey too joined him; but he did not come to him until he had begun some service to him. He was then twenty-three years old, and having raised a force he went round the cities, driving out of them those who sided with Carbo, and making his way to Sulla. As he went, three generals of Carbo's party surrounded him. He routed them and received the cities that came over to him. Then again, when Scipio the consul came against him, Scipio's soldiers greeted Pompey's men and streamed over to him, and Scipio fled. When Carbo sent many squadrons of horse against him, he routed these too, so that in despair of safety they gave themselves up to him. Sulla received him in such a way that he leapt down from his horse, and when hailed as imperator by Pompey, hailed Pompey as imperator in return. The rest matched these first kindnesses; for he rose when Pompey came in, and did other things in his honour that he was not seen doing readily for others.

When Sulla had become master of Italy and been proclaimed dictator, he rewarded the other commanders and generals by enriching them and appointing them to offices, but he was eager to bind Pompey to himself; and he persuaded him to send away the wife he had and marry his own stepdaughter Aemilia, whom Metella, Sulla's wife, had borne to Scaurus, her former husband. The marriage was a tyrant's act; for Aemilia had already been given to a husband and was pregnant.

Having bound Pompey to himself in this way, Sulla sent him to Sicily with a heavy force; for the island was a base for Carbo's party. When Pompey went there, the enemy left the island, and he took over the cities, which had been worn down, and treated them kindly. He caught Carbo too and killed him. Hearing that the soldiers were disorderly on the march, he put seals on their swords, and whoever did not keep his seal was punished.

blocks: While doing this in Sicily he received letters from the senate and Sulla ordering him to sail to Libya and make war on Domitius. He sailed, and seven thousand of Domitius's men came over to him. When Domitius drew up against him the armies clashed, and Pompey's men won, and Domitius was killed. Of the cities some came over at once and others were taken by storm. He invaded Numidia, and having overcome all he met in forty days in all, he received letters from Sulla to dismiss the rest of the army and himself with one legion to wait at Utica for the general who would succeed him. At this he was vexed in private, while the army was openly indignant. When Pompey wished to go forward, they spoke ill of Sulla and would not let him trust himself to the tyrant. He tried to calm them, but they told him to stay and command, until, as they kept pressing and shouting, he swore he would kill himself if they used force; and so with difficulty they stopped.

At first it was reported to Sulla that Pompey had revolted; then, learning the truth, he went to meet him as he came and, greeting him, called him Magnus in a loud voice; Magnus means great. When Pompey asked for a triumph, Sulla objected that it was the custom for a consul or praetor to hold a triumph, and no one else; and if Pompey, who had hardly a beard yet, held a triumph, when because of his age he had no share in the senate, the honour would bring envy on him. When Sulla said this, Pompey did not cower, but said that he should reflect that more people worship the rising sun than the setting, showing by this that his own power was growing while Sulla's was shrinking and fading. At this Sulla was struck with amazement and cried out twice in a row: "Let him triumph." When the soldiers wished to make trouble and an uproar, since they had not got as much as they expected, Pompey said he would rather give up the triumph than flatter the soldiers. At which Servilius, a notable man who had spoken against the triumph before, said: "Now Pompey is truly Magnus and worthy to triumph." Sulla was pained to see how far Pompey was advancing in glory and power, but ashamed to hinder him he kept quiet.

Lepidus, having got the consulship through Pompey's efforts, tried to take over Sulla's power when Sulla died, and was at once in arms, stirring up the remnants of the factions. Pompey was appointed to command an army against Lepidus, who had already roused much of Italy and held Cisalpine Gaul through Brutus. Pompey easily overcame the others, but spent time sitting down against Brutus. Then Brutus gave himself up to him, either changing sides or betrayed. He was killed (his son was the Brutus who later did away with Caesar), and Lepidus, driven out of Italy, died of disease.

Sertorius, who held Iberia, was fearsome. So Pompey was sent against him too, to fight alongside Metellus Pius, who was fighting Sertorius. Arriving in Iberia, he first faced two of Sertorius's generals, and winning, killed more than ten thousand; then he engaged Sertorius himself and had a doubtful contest. When a big man on foot came at Pompey, who was on horseback, Pompey was struck on the hand by him, but Pompey cut off the man's hand. Joining Metellus, he honoured him and was honoured. When Sertorius was treacherously murdered by his friends, Perperna, the chief of his commanders, tried to do as he had done, taking over his forces. But Pompey drew up against him and overcame them all; most of the commanders perished in the battle, and Perperna himself, taken alive, he put to death. He stayed there, settled affairs and quenched the disturbances, and then led the army back to Italy.

There was suspicion and fear that he would not let the army go, but would march in arms to begin a monarchy. But he removed this suspicion too, saying he would dismiss the army after the triumph. One thing more those who envied him blamed him for, that he gave himself to the people rather than to the senate; which was true. For there was no one with whom the people of the Romans fell more madly in love. So a consulship and a second triumph were voted him; and Crassus too was voted to be consul with him, through his efforts. But when they had been declared consuls they quarrelled, and in the senate Crassus was stronger, while Pompey prevailed with the people.

He also declined a command abroad. It was the custom for Roman knights, when they had served their lawful time, to lead their horse into the forum before the censors, to name each of the generals and commanders under whom they had served, to give account of their service and so be discharged, with honour or disgrace assigned as fitted each one's life. On that occasion the censors sat in front and the knights were passing by to be examined, when Pompey too was seen coming into the forum, with the other insignia of his office, but leading his horse by hand himself. The people looked on in wonder and silence. Then one of the censors said: "I ask you, Pompey Magnus, whether you have served all the campaigns required by law." He answered in a loud voice: "I have served them, and all under myself as commander." At this the people cried out, and the censors, to please the citizens, rose and escorted him home.

blocks: When his term of office was finished, Pompey laid it down. After this the war against the pirates was entrusted to him. The pirate power had started from Cilicia, having put itself at the service of the king in the Mithridatic War; then, while the Romans were clashing with one another in the civil wars, the sea, being unguarded, drew them on little by little; and having gained power, they attacked not only those sailing but also tore away islands and coastal cities. The pirate ships came to more than a thousand, and the cities taken by them to more than four hundred. They also plundered many inviolable temples, and insulted the Romans too. For whenever a captive cried out that he was a Roman, they pretended to be astonished and afraid, struck their thighs and fell at his feet; some put shoes on him and others threw a toga round him, and having mocked him in this way, at last in the middle of the sea they let down a ladder and told him to step off and go away and farewell; and if he did not wish to, they pushed him and drowned him.

Since the whole sea could not be sailed by merchants, there was a shortage of necessities in the market. When it was decided to send Pompey against the pirates, Gabinius, one of Pompey's intimates, drafted a law giving him not a naval command but plainly a monarchy. For the law gave him command of the sea within the Pillars of Heracles, and of all the mainland for four hundred stades from the sea, and the right to choose fifteen legates from the senate for the separate commands, to take as much money as he wished from the treasuries and the tax farmers, and two hundred ships. The people eagerly accepted this; but the more prudent of the senate thought the unlimited and undefined power a thing to fear, and spoke against it, except Caesar; he spoke for the law, not for Pompey's sake, but courting the people and winning them to himself. For the time, however, the decree was ratified. Pompey came into the assembly and managed to get double what had been voted.

So he divided the seas and stretches of water into thirteen parts, assigned a number of ships and a commander to each, and in forty days cleared the Tyrrhenian Sea, the Libyan Sea, and the waters round Sardinia, Corsica and Sicily of pirates. Then, sailing past the cities in haste, he did not pass by Athens. Going up, sacrificing and addressing the people, he found inscriptions made for him, of which the one inside the gate said: "As far as you know yourself to be a man, so far are you a god"; and the one outside: "We awaited, we worshipped, we saw, we escort you on your way."

blocks: So the pirate war was ended and the bands of pirates everywhere on the sea were removed in no more than three months. When this was reported in Rome, Manilius, one of the tribunes, drafted a law that Pompey should take over all the country that Lucullus governed, and Bithynia besides, and make war on the kings Mithridates and Tigranes, keeping the naval force and command of the sea too, as he had already received it; and this was to put the empire of the Romans in one man's hands altogether. The decree was ratified, since the aristocrats feared the people and kept silent, and Pompey, on receiving the letters, is said to have drawn his brows together and struck his thigh, as if annoyed and weighed down by the command. Not even his closest friends easily bore this pretence.

For the time he distributed the fleet to guard the sea between Phoenicia and the Bosporus, and himself marched against Mithridates. When Mithridates left a mountain where he was encamped, hard to attack but waterless, Pompey occupied it, and judging from the nature of the plants growing there and the slopes of the ground that the place had springs, he ordered wells to be dug. And quickly the camp was full of water. Then he encamped round Mithridates and walled him in. After being besieged for forty-five days, Mithridates escaped unnoticed with the strongest part of his force, having killed the useless and the sick. Pompey caught up with him near the Euphrates, and so that he might not cross the river first, he led the army against him from midnight. So they were forced to fight for their stockade. The moon was setting, and this tripped up the king's men; for the Romans had the moon at their backs, and since it was near setting the shadows of their bodies, going far ahead of them, gave the enemy the impression that the Romans were close to them, and they threw their javelins and reached no one. The Romans, seeing this, charged with a shout and killed them as they fled, so that far more than ten thousand died. Mithridates himself escaped with a larger number.

Pompey invaded Armenia, since the younger Tigranes called him in; for he had already revolted from his father. King Tigranes, who had been crushed by Lucullus, learning that Pompey was gentle, gave himself up and received a garrison in the palace. Coming to Pompey, he took the tiara from his head and set out to lay it at his feet and throw himself down. But Pompey took him by the right hand, drew him to him and seated him beside him, with his son on the other side, and said that he must blame Lucullus for the rest, since Syria, Phoenicia, Cilicia, Galatia and Sophene had been taken from him by Lucullus, but what had been kept down to Pompey's time he should have, and his son should reign over Sophene. Tigranes was content with this, but his son was displeased, and when invited to dinner said he did not need Pompey to honour him so; for he would find another Roman himself. For this he was put in chains and kept for the triumph.

Leaving Afranius to guard Armenia, Pompey himself marched against Mithridates through the peoples living round the Caucasus. The greatest of these peoples are the Albanians and the Iberians, the Iberians reaching to the Moschian mountains and the Pontus, the Albanians to the east and the Caspian Sea. These at first gave Pompey passage when he asked, then, gathering not fewer than forty thousand, attacked him, were routed and perished in great numbers. When their king sent envoys, he made a treaty and went off against the Iberians, who were more warlike than the Albanians and had not yielded to the Medes or Persians, and had escaped the rule of the Macedonians too, since Alexander left Hyrcania quickly. But these too he routed in a great battle, killing many and taking more alive. From there he invaded the land of the Colchians. When the Albanians revolted again, he marched against them by a waterless and painful road, carrying water in many skins. He engaged them, led by the brother of their king, and won; and when the brother came at him and struck him, Pompey drove his spear through him at close quarters and killed him. At this time Amazons too are said to have fought alongside the Albanians. For after the battle, when the dead were stripped, the Romans came upon Amazonian shields and boots, but no woman's body was found. They live in the parts of the Caucasus reaching down to the Hyrcanian Sea. Between them and the Albanians live the Gelae and the Legae. Each year the women meet them by the river Thermodon and keep company with them for two months; then they go off and live by themselves; and when they give birth they carry the male children to the land of the fathers and expose them, but bring up the girls.

blocks: to him, Pompey knew none of them. Stratonice, who had the highest rank with Mithridates and guarded the richest in gold of his forts, brought Pompey many gifts and handed over the fort. Of what was brought, he took only what gave adornment to temples and splendour to the triumph, and told Stratonice to keep the rest. When the king of the Iberians sent him a couch, a table and a throne, all of gold, he handed these too over to the quaestors for the public treasury. When he saw that Mithridates was harder to deal with fleeing than fighting, he said he would leave him an enemy stronger than himself, famine, and himself went forward with the army. Having subdued through Afranius the Arabs round Amanus, he went down into Syria and declared it a province and possession of the Romans; and he subjected Judaea and seized its king Aristobulus, as has already been told in the Jewish history. Great was the name of his power, and greater that of his virtue and mildness. The king of the Arabs round Petra, afraid, wrote to Pompey that he would obey him in everything. And news came to him that Mithridates too was dead, his son Pharnaces having made away with him. So when Pompey reached Amisus, many gifts from Pharnaces were brought to him, and many bodies, and the corpse of Mithridates himself.

On his way back his return was made painful by his wife Mucia, who had behaved outrageously while he was away; and when he came near Italy he sent her a divorce. In Rome there was talk about him and an uproar, as though he would bring the army against the city and make himself sole ruler. But as soon as he set foot in Italy he assembled the soldiers and told each to go home and gather again for the triumph. When the army had been dispersed in this way, the cities, seeing Pompey unarmed and travelling with few men, poured out in delight and escorted him, bringing him down to Rome with a larger force than before. Since the law did not allow him to enter the city before the triumph, he sent asking the senate to put off the consular elections. Since Cato opposed it he did not get it; and so he wished to bind the man to himself. Cato had two nieces, and Pompey sought to take one himself and marry the other to his son. When Cato refused the connection as likely to corrupt his character, his sister and his wife were annoyed. But when Afranius was seeking the consulship through Pompey, and for this was spending money on the tribes, and was ill spoken of for it, as making the office a thing for sale to those unworthy of it, Cato said to the women: "We would have had to share these reproaches if we had become kin to Pompey."

Because of the size of the triumph, though it was divided over two days, the time was not enough, and many of the things prepared were left out of the show. Placards carried in front showed the peoples over whom he was triumphing. They were these: Pontus, Armenia, Paphlagonia, Cappadocia, Media, the Colchians, the Iberians, the Albanians, Syria, Cilicia, Mesopotamia, the parts round Phoenicia and Palestine, Judaea, Arabia, and the whole pirate power, defeated by land and sea; and among these, forts taken not fewer than a thousand, cities not far short of nine hundred, eight hundred pirate ships, and thirty-nine settlements of cities founded. Besides this the placards declared that five thousand myriads came from the taxes before, and from what he himself had added the Romans receive eight thousand five hundred myriads, and that twenty thousand talents in coin and in vessels of silver and gold were being brought into the public treasury, apart from what had been given to the soldiers. Besides the pirate chiefs, there were led in the procession as prisoners the son of Tigranes the Armenian with his wife and daughters, Zosime, the wife of King Tigranes himself, Aristobulus king of the Jews, kinsmen of Mithridates, and many others. The greatest thing for his glory was that, having triumphed three times, bringing the first from Libya, the second from Europe and the last from Asia, he seemed in a way to have led the world in his three triumphs. He was then forty years old.

After this, when a shortage of grain gripped Rome and its neighbourhood, he sailed to Sicily, Sardinia and Libya and gathered grain. When he was about to put to sea and the helmsmen hesitated because of violent winds, he went on board first himself, ordered them to raise the anchors and cried out: "To sail is necessary; to live is not necessary." Using such daring and good fortune, he filled the markets with grain and the sea with ships. He would have done well to end his life there; for the time after brought him good fortune that roused envy, and misfortunes beyond remedy. For having joined Caesar and raised him up by his own glory and power, he was overturned and cast down by him. So as not to tell the same things twice, the rest of Pompey's story will be told among the affairs of Caesar, since it falls in with his history.

blocks: Caesar, having been fortunate in his commands and having won many wars, courted the people, seeking their favour for himself; and being in love with monarchy, since he saw some opposed to him, and above all Pompey, who was then very powerful, he came back to Rome from Iberia. He had been allotted it before this, and as soon as he set foot in it he marched against the Lusitanians and the Callaicans; and having overcome them, he went as far as the outer sea, subduing the peoples that had not yielded to the Romans before. He left the province with a good reputation, having become rich himself and having benefited the soldiers. Wishing to hold a triumph for the victory, and having come in time for the consular elections themselves, and seeking the consulship for himself, he found himself caught between two laws. For it was the custom that those about to triumph should stay outside the city, while those wishing to seek the consulship had to do so in person, meeting the voters. So he gave up the triumph, went into the city and stood for the consulship.

Among those with great power in the senate was Crassus too, to whom Caesar was close, and who happened to be a political opponent of Pompey. Caesar brought these two from quarrel to friendship, and escorted, as it were, by both, he was raised to the consulship; and at once he brought in laws by which he won over the people. Further, attaching Pompey's strength to himself, Caesar betrothed his own daughter Julia to him. So Pompey married her and at once filled the forum with arms, ratified the laws together with the people, and assigned to Caesar Cisalpine and all Transalpine Gaul and Illyricum with four legions for five years. Since those of the senate who spoke against this were grossly insulted, very few met with Caesar in the senate while he was consul. When one of the very old men said that they did not meet out of fear of the arms and the soldiers, Caesar said: "Why then do you not stay at home too, fearing these things?" He said: "Because my old age makes me unafraid; for the life still left me is very short."

Fighting the Gallic wars, he conquered and subdued the Helvetii and Tigurini; and when about to engage the Germans, seeing his officers losing heart, especially the notable and young ones, he told them to go away and not run risks against their will, being so unmanly and soft; and said that he himself would take the tenth legion and march against the barbarians, since he was not about to fight enemies stronger than the Cimbri, nor was he himself a worse general than Marius. From this all became full of zeal and eagerness and followed, and fighting brilliantly they routed their opponents, so that there were eighty thousand dead. Their king Ariovistus got across the Rhine first with a few men.

Having done this, he went down to Gaul about the Po, where he stayed and courted the people, as many came to him from Rome, winning the citizens over with money from the enemy. From there he went against other peoples, won brilliantly, and returned again to winter in the districts about the Po, making those in Rome well disposed to him with money; he supplied it to those seeking offices for themselves, and made them corrupt the people with it, and vote offices to those who gave the money; and they did everything that was likely to increase his power. Then he conquered other Gallic peoples too, bridged the Rhine and crossed it with his army. Returning from there, he learned of the death of his daughter, who was married to Pompey, that she had died in childbirth, and that soon after the child too followed its mother. Caesar and Pompey mourned the misfortune, and the friends of both took the loss hard, since the bond of their connection had been undone.

blocks: Caesar, having now become great and having raised his own glory by his successes, set himself up as Pompey's rival. When Crassus, who had been left in reserve against both him and Pompey, perished among the Parthians, he planned to bring Pompey down, and Pompey in turn Caesar. Since the state was sick, those seeking offices bought them, the people used not votes but arms for those who had paid them, and the city was drifting badly like a ship without a helmsman, the more sensible thought it welcome if from such a storm the Roman state came round to monarchy and nothing worse, since otherwise their affairs were beyond remedy; and that they must accept the mildest of physicians to treat this sickness, hinting at Pompey. He, though in word he pretended to refuse the office, by his actions was eager to be declared dictator. So, so that he might not force a vote for the dictatorship, the senate put him forward as sole consul, soothing his desire with this monarchy.

After this Caesar too sent and stood for the consulship. When others opposed it Pompey kept silent. But when Caesar had won many over to his side with money, Pompey, fearing the combination, openly worked through himself and his friends to have Caesar removed from his command by vote; Caesar paid no attention to this at all. Caesar demanded that he and Pompey both lay down their arms together and become private men; but if they took the command from him and confirmed it for Pompey, they were making the other a tyrant. It is said that one of the officers sent by Caesar, learning that the senate would not give Caesar more time in his command, said: "But this will give it," striking the hilt of his sword with his hand. Then a motion was brought that if Caesar did not lay down his arms by a fixed day, the man should be considered an enemy. When Antony and those acting for Caesar asked that both Caesar and Pompey give up their commands, all agreed to the motion. When letters came from Caesar giving up the rest, but asking to be given the province within the Alps and Illyricum with two legions, Pompey offered the rest but took away the soldiers. The consuls drove Antony and those with him out of the senate. They, out of fear, changed into slaves' clothes and left Rome in hired carts. This provoked the soldiers, who saw men of standing and magistrates outrageously insulted.

Caesar, after turning over many calculations and being of different minds, at last uttered that common saying, "Let the die be cast," set off, crossed the river Rubicon, and took Ariminum, a large city of Gaul. It is said that on the night before the crossing he saw a lawless dream; for he dreamed that he was having the unspeakable union with his own mother.

When Ariminum had been taken, Rome, as if filled with surge and storm by winds, was nearly overturned by itself. For the consuls and most of the senators fled, and Pompey himself was struck with dismay, and people from every side troubled the man, blaming him for having raised Caesar up against himself and the state, and no one let him use his own judgement. So he left the city, ordering the senate to follow. Most followed, choosing exile as their country because of Pompey, and fleeing Rome as Caesar's camp. At this time Labienus too, a man counted among Caesar's friends who had fought most zealously with him in the wars, left him and came to Pompey. Even though he had deserted him, Caesar sent his money and baggage after him. Domitius, who held Corfinium, when Caesar came against him, despaired of his situation and drank poison to die; then, learning that Caesar was treating the captured with wonderful kindness, he lamented himself. When the doctor said that the drug was a sleeping draught and not deadly, he went off to Caesar, received his pledge, and then slipped away again to Pompey.

For the consuls and most of the senators fled, and Pompey himself was struck with dismay, and people from every side troubled the man, blaming him for having raised Caesar up against himself and the state, and no one let him use his own judgement. So he left the city, ordering the senate to follow. Most followed, choosing exile as their country because of Pompey, and fleeing Rome as Caesar's camp. At this time Labienus too, a man counted among Caesar's friends who had fought most zealously with him in the wars, left him and came to Pompey. Even though he had deserted him, Caesar sent his money and baggage after him. Domitius, who held Corfinium, when Caesar came against him, despaired of his situation and drank poison to die; then, learning that Caesar was treating the captured with wonderful kindness, he lamented himself. When the doctor said that the drug was a sleeping draught and not deadly, he went off to Caesar, received his pledge, and then slipped away again to Pompey.

blocks: This news, reported in Rome, made people more cheerful, and some came back. Caesar, having grown strong, now marched against Pompey himself. Pompey fled to Brundisium and sailed away. Caesar, lacking ships, turned back to Rome, and became master of all Italy without bloodshed in sixty days. Finding the city settled and many of the senate in it, he spoke reasonably to them, asking them to send to Pompey for terms. No one was persuaded. When the tribune Metellus tried to stop him from taking money from the reserve funds, and cited laws, he said that the time for arms and for laws was not the same: "Now get out of the way; for war does not need free speech. When I lay down my arms, then you will make speeches to the people. And I say this," he said, "giving up my own rights; for you are mine, you and all of those who rose against me whom I have taken." When the keys could not be found, he ordered the doors to be broken open. When Metellus again tried to stop him, and some praised him, he threatened to kill him if he did not stop, saying: "Young man, do you not know that it is harder for me to say this than to do it?"

He marched into Iberia, and having brought the forces and the provinces there under himself, he then marched against Pompey. Chosen dictator by the senate, he brought back exiles and dealt with other matters of state. In eleven days he gave up the sole rule, declared himself and Servilius Isauricus consuls, and kept to the campaign. Crossing the Ionian Sea he took Oricum and Apollonia. From Apollonia, unknown to all, he boarded a boat with twelve oars in the dress of a servant, planning to be taken across to Brundisium, since the sea was held by the enemy with great fleets. It was winter, and the voyage seemed impossible to the helmsman, and he told the sailors to put about to turn the boat back. Then Caesar revealed himself. And as the helmsman was struck with amazement at the sight, he said: "Be bold and do not fear; you carry Caesar and Caesar's fortune sailing with him."

Antony too came over by sea bringing the forces. And Caesar took heart and challenged Pompey. Scattered battles were always taking place round Pompey's fortifications, and Caesar won all but one, in which, when a great rout took place, he was in danger of losing his camp, and himself came close to death. For he laid his hand on a big, strong man who was fleeing and told him to stand and turn against the enemy; but the man, full of panic, raised his sword to strike him, and would have struck him, had not Caesar's shield-bearer cut off his shoulder first. Caesar then so despaired of his situation that, when Pompey did not finish off his great work but shut the fugitives into their stockade and withdrew, Caesar said: "Today the victory would have been the enemy's, if they had had a man who knew how to win."

Moving from there, he led the army into Macedonia against Scipio. This elated Pompey's army and the commanders about him, who thought they should follow in pursuit of Caesar as beaten and fleeing. Pompey was cautious about this, and wished to wear down and wither the enemy's strength. Cato alone praised this plan, out of care for the citizens. He, when he saw the fallen of the enemy, about a thousand, went away with his head covered, weeping. All the others reproached Pompey for avoiding battle. From this he went to battle against his will, pursuing Caesar. When both had entered Pharsalia and encamped, Pompey again held to his earlier opinion, since unfavourable signs had come to him and a vision in his sleep (for he seemed to see himself in the theatre being applauded by the Romans), while those about him were bold and had already seized victory in their hopes.

Caesar asked his own soldiers whether they chose to fight by themselves or to wait for others who were already near; and they begged him not to wait. When Caesar sacrificed, the seer indicated that within three days there would be a decision with the enemy. When Caesar asked what he foresaw about the outcome, he said that a great change and reversal to the opposite was signified: "If, then, you are doing well at present, expect the worse fortune; if badly, the better."

blocks: On the night before the battle, as Caesar went round the guards about midnight, a torch of heavenly fire was seen, which seemed to pass over his camp, grow bright and fiery, and fall into Pompey's. When day had already dawned the scouts reported that the enemy were coming down for battle. Overjoyed, he set out for battle, and engaging Pompey's men, routed them. Pompey, seeing his horsemen scattered in flight, was no longer himself, nor did he remember that he was Pompey the Great, but as if struck by a god he went off speechless to his tent, and sat waiting for what would come. When the enemy were mounting the stockade, he put on clothing fit for a fugitive and slipped out.

Caesar took the enemy's stockade too, mixed those taken alive into his own legions, and gave safety to many of the notable men; among them was Brutus, who later killed him. He pursued Pompey. Pompey boarded a merchant ship, sailed along by Amphipolis and put in at Mitylene, wishing to take up his wife Cornelia and his son from there. She was the daughter of Metellus Scipio; she had been married as a virgin to Publius, the son of Crassus, and when he died among the Parthians she married Pompey. The young woman was outstanding in beauty, and also well trained in letters, the lyre and geometry, and was used to listening to philosophical discourses with profit; and besides this she had a character free of meddlesomeness. So, hearing that Pompey had come with one ship, and that not his own, as a fugitive, she fell to the ground and lay speechless. When she had barely come to herself, she ran down to the sea. When Pompey met her and embraced her, she said: "I see you, husband, not by the work of your fortune but of mine, cast upon one boat, you who before your marriage to Cornelia sailed this sea with five hundred ships. How fortunate a wife I would have been if I had died before hearing that Publius, my maiden husband, lay dead among the Parthians, and how virtuous if after him I had given up my own life, as I set out to do. But I was kept alive to become a calamity to you too, Pompey the Great." To this he said: "So, Cornelia, you knew only one fortune, the better, which perhaps deceived you too, because it stayed with me longer than usual. But we must bear this too, being men, and we must still try fortune. For it is not beyond hope that he who has come from that state into this should change from this back to that."

Taking up his wife and his friends, he went on. Coming to Attaleia, a city of Pamphylia, he found triremes from Cilicia and soldiers, and many of the senators gathered round him. After much deliberation, the view prevailed at last that he should flee to Egypt. Learning that Ptolemy was staying at Pelusium, he put in there. Since Ptolemy was very young, Pothinus the eunuch managed affairs. Learning about Pompey, he gathered a council of those most powerful at court. Some advised driving Pompey away, others receiving him; but Theodotus of Chios, the rhetorician, proposed killing him, adding that a dead man does not bite. So some men were sent to invite him over. When those with him saw that the reception was not royal or splendid, but a few men sailing up in one fishing boat, they suspected the slight, and urged Pompey to back his ship out to sea. When the fishing boat came near, they greeted him in Greek and asked him to cross into it, saying there were many shallows, and the sea had no depth and could not be sailed by a trireme, having a sandy bottom. So he embraced Cornelia, who was mourning his end in advance, told two centurions to board with him, and one of his freedmen, Philip, and a servant named Scythes, and turning to his wife and son he quoted these iambic lines of Sophocles: "Whoever goes to traffic with a tyrant is his slave, though he go there free." With these words he went aboard. Since it was a long way to the land, Pompey read over a speech in Greek written by himself in a small book, which he had prepared to use with Ptolemy. As they came near the land, Cornelia with the friends watched from the trireme in great distress for what would come; and at this moment, as Pompey took Philip's hand to rise, Septimius first ran him through from behind with his sword, then Achillas too and others. He drew his toga over his face with his hands, only groaning and saying nothing unworthy of himself, and endured the blows, having lived fifty-nine years.

Those on the ships, when they saw the slaughter, raised a lament heard as far as the land and fled. They cut off Pompey's head, threw the rest of his body naked out of the fishing boat, and left it to those who wanted such a sight. Philip stayed by him until they had had their fill of the sight; then, washing the body in the sea and wrapping it in one of his own tunics, and finding the remains of a small fishing boat, he burned it on these, with the help of a Roman man already old, who had served his first campaigns with Pompey when Pompey was still young. He came up to Philip and said: "Who are you, fellow, that you mean to bury Pompey the Great?" When Philip said he was his freedman, he said: "But this honour shall not be yours alone; take me too as a partner, as in a pious windfall, to touch and lay out with my own hands the greatest commander of the Romans."

blocks: So Pompey was buried. Not long after, Caesar came to Egypt. He turned away from the man who brought him Pompey's head as from a murderer, and when he received the man's signet ring he wept; and he put Achillas and Pothinus to death. King Ptolemy himself, beaten in a battle by the river, disappeared. Theodotus the sophist escaped punishment from Caesar by slipping out of Egypt, living in humble circumstances and hated; but he fell in with Marcus Brutus, who killed Caesar, in Asia, and was put to death after suffering every outrage at his hands. All Pompey's friends who had been seized by the ruler of Egypt Caesar treated well and won over.

There he got himself into a war too. He secretly sent for Cleopatra from the country, who had already been driven out of the kingdom and the city by the eunuch Pothinus. She, with only Apollodorus the Sicilian, boarded a small boat and put in at the palace, and getting into a bedding sack she stretched herself out at full length; and Apollodorus tied the sack with a strap and carried it in through the doors to Caesar. Since she seemed bold by this trick, and he was conquered by the rest of her company and charm, he reconciled her with her brother to reign with him. While they were feasting over the reconciliation, Caesar discovered a plot being hatched by Achillas the general and Pothinus the eunuch; he killed Pothinus, but Achillas fled to the camp and surrounded him with a heavy war. At this time, when Caesar set fire to the fleet, the great library too was burned. When fighting broke out, he leapt down from the mole into a boat, and when the Egyptians sailed at him from many sides, he threw himself into the sea and barely swam away. It is said that at this time he held many small books and did not let go of them as he swam, but held them up above the sea with his other hand, though he was being shot at. At last, when the king went over to the enemy, Caesar came on, joined battle and won; many fell, and the king disappeared.

Leaving Cleopatra reigning over Egypt (and a little later she bore him a son, whom the Alexandrians called Caesarion), he set out for Syria. He made war on Pharnaces, the son of Mithridates, drove him out of Pontus, and utterly destroyed his army. Showing the speed and sharpness of this battle, he wrote three words to Rome: "I came, I saw, I conquered." From there he went to Italy and up to Rome, as the year was ending for which he had been chosen dictator for the second time, though this office had never before lasted a year; and for the following year he was declared consul.

Since Cato's and Scipio's party had fled to Libya after the battle at Pharsalus and gathered considerable forces, Caesar marched against them; in a small part of one day he took three camps, and having killed fifty thousand of the enemy he did not lose even fifty of his own. Of the men of consular and praetorian rank who fled from the battle, some killed themselves as they were being captured, and Caesar put many to death when they were taken. When Cato killed himself, he was plainly stung; but why he was grieved is not clear; at any rate he said: "Cato, I grudge you your death; for you grudged me your safety." Returning to Rome from Libya, he held triumphs and put on shows of sea fights and gladiators. When a census was taken, in place of the former three hundred and twenty thousand only one hundred and fifty thousand in all were found surviving; so great a destruction of the people the civil war had brought about.

Then, chosen consul for the fourth time, he marched into Iberia against the sons of Pompey, who were still young, but showed a daring worthy of command. At that time Caesar came into such danger that he ran through his ranks shouting to ask whether they were not ashamed to take him and hand him over to the boys. After the battle he said to his friends that he had often fought for victory, but now for the first time for his life. When Caesar won, the younger of Pompey's sons escaped, and some days later the head of the elder was brought to him. This was the last war Caesar fought.

blocks: When he returned to Rome he was voted dictator for life, which was plainly a tyranny, since to the irresponsibility of monarchy it added permanence. Having established himself in monarchy in this way, he released many of those who had fought against him, and to some he even gave offices and honours, among them Brutus and Cassius; and he set up again Pompey's statues, which had been thrown down. When his friends asked him to have a bodyguard, he refused, saying: "It is better to die once than always to expect it." Longing for greater things and newer glory, he formed a plan to march against the Parthians and through Hyrcania to invade Scythia.

Other things roused men's hatred against him, but the greatest cause was his love of kingship, because of which those about him even spread a story among the people that it appeared from the Sibylline books that the Parthians' land would not otherwise be taken by the Romans unless a king campaigned with them. And as Caesar was going from Alba to Rome, some dared to hail him as king. When the people were in an uproar, he said that he was called not king but Caesar.

He was called Caesar, as some think, because his mother died in giving birth, and he was brought into the light by cutting. But this is not true; for those who have written about him have recorded that his mother was alive even when he had grown to manhood. Coming into life by cutting did not happen to him but to one of his ancestors, and from him his descendants got the name.

Once, when the consuls and praetors came to him with the whole senate following, because he did not rise from his seat he grieved not only the senate but also the people, as though the city were being insulted in the senate, and most went away at once downcast. To these offences was added the insult to the tribunes. A festival was being held in the city, and Caesar, sitting on a golden chair, was dressed in triumphal dress; and Antony, who was consul, burst into the forum carrying a diadem wound with a laurel wreath and offered it to Caesar. There was applause, not loud, from those prepared for it; but when Caesar pushed it away the whole people applauded; and when this had happened twice the attempt was shown up, and Caesar rose. When his statues too were seen crowned with royal diadems, the tribunes tore these off, and led those who had hailed Caesar as king off to prison. The people applauded at this and called the men Brutuses; for Brutus, as has been told above, was the one who overthrew Tarquinius and brought power from monarchy back to the commonwealth. Caesar, provoked at this, took their office from the tribunes, and in accusing them, insulting the people at the same time, often called the men Brutuses.

From this the many turned to Marcus Brutus, who was thought to draw his descent from the Brutus of old; and those who wanted a change, looking to him alone or first, did not dare to speak with him, but at night threw notes about the platform and the chair on which he did business as praetor, saying: "Are you asleep, Brutus?" and "You are no Brutus." Cassius too spurred him on.

Many signs are said to have come to Caesar showing his death, of which this is one. Sleeping beside his wife, he noticed her uttering indistinct sounds and inarticulate groans; for she dreamed she was weeping over him, holding him murdered in her arms. In the day she begged her husband not to go out to the senate. When the seers too, having sacrificed, said the omens were bad, he decided to send Antony to dismiss the senate. But Brutus Albinus, who was trusted by Caesar but shared in the conspiracy with Marcus Brutus and Cassius, mocked the seers and attacked Caesar for bringing slanders on himself of contempt for the senate. For it had come at his command, and all were ready to vote that he be proclaimed king of the provinces outside Italy, and wear a diadem as he went over the rest of land and sea. Saying this, Brutus took Caesar by the hand and led him. A slave belonging to someone else, eager to meet him as he went, and unable to, gave himself up to Caesar's wife to keep, saying he had great matters to report to Caesar on his return. A sophist, Artemidorus of Cnidus, having written a paper about the conspiracy, came near him and said: "Read this, Caesar, alone and quickly; for it tells you great things that concern you." Caesar took it and set out to read it, but being prevented by those meeting him, held it in his hand and so went into the senate. The senate rose to him. Of Brutus's party some stood round behind his chair, and others met him as if pleading for some exile. Brutus Albinus kept Antony, who was loyal to Caesar and strong, back outside. When Caesar sat down and kept putting off their pleas, he was struck in the neck with a sword by Casca first, a wound not deadly. text: When he returned to Rome he was voted dictator for life, which was plainly a tyranny, since to the irresponsibility of monarchy it added permanence. Having established himself in monarchy in this way, he released many of those who had fought against him, and to some he even gave offices and honours, among them Brutus and Cassius; and he set up again Pompey's statues, which had been thrown down. When his friends asked him to have a bodyguard, he refused, saying: "It is better to die once than always to expect it." Longing for greater things and newer glory, he formed a plan to march against the Parthians and through Hyrcania to invade Scythia. Other things roused men's hatred against him, but the greatest cause was his love of kingship, because of which those about him even spread a story among the people that it appeared from the Sibylline books that the Parthians' land would not otherwise be taken by the Romans unless a king campaigned with them. And as Caesar was going from Alba to Rome, some dared to hail him as king. When the people were in an uproar, he said that he was called not king but Caesar. He was called Caesar, as some think, because his mother died in giving birth, and he was brought into the light by cutting. But this is not true; for those who have written about him have recorded that his mother was alive even when he had grown to manhood. Coming into life by cutting did not happen to him but to one of his ancestors, and from him his descendants got the name. Once, when the consuls and praetors came to him with the whole senate following, because he did not rise from his seat he grieved not only the senate but also the people, as though the city were being insulted in the senate, and most went away at once downcast. To these offences was added the insult to the tribunes. A festival was being held in the city, and Caesar, sitting on a golden chair, was dressed in triumphal dress; and Antony, who was consul, burst into the forum carrying a diadem wound with a laurel wreath and offered it to Caesar. There was applause, not loud, from those prepared for it; but when Caesar pushed it away the whole people applauded; and when this had happened twice the attempt was shown up, and Caesar rose. When his statues too were seen crowned with royal diadems, the tribunes tore these off, and led those who had hailed Caesar as king off to prison. The people applauded at this and called the men Brutuses; for Brutus, as has been told above, was the one who overthrew Tarquinius and brought power from monarchy back to the commonwealth. Caesar, provoked at this, took their office from the tribunes, and in accusing them, insulting the people at the same time, often called the men Brutuses. From this the many turned to Marcus Brutus, who was thought to draw his descent from the Brutus of old; and those who wanted a change, looking to him alone or first, did not dare to speak with him, but at night threw notes about the platform and the chair on which he did business as praetor, saying: "Are you asleep, Brutus?" and "You are no Brutus." Cassius too spurred him on. Many signs are said to have come to Caesar showing his death, of which this is one. Sleeping beside his wife, he noticed her uttering indistinct sounds and inarticulate groans; for she dreamed she was weeping over him, holding him murdered in her arms. In the day she begged her husband not to go out to the senate. When the seers too, having sacrificed, said the omens were bad, he decided to send Antony to dismiss the senate. But Brutus Albinus, who was trusted by Caesar but shared in the conspiracy with Marcus Brutus and Cassius, mocked the seers and attacked Caesar for bringing slanders on himself of contempt for the senate. For it had come at his command, and all were ready to vote that he be proclaimed king of the provinces outside Italy, and wear a diadem as he went over the rest of land and sea. Saying this, Brutus took Caesar by the hand and led him. A slave belonging to someone else, eager to meet him as he went, and unable to, gave himself up to Caesar's wife to keep, saying he had great matters to report to Caesar on his return. A sophist, Artemidorus of Cnidus, having written a paper about the conspiracy, came near him and said: "Read this, Caesar, alone and quickly; for it tells you great things that concern you." Caesar took it and set out to read it, but being prevented by those meeting him, held it in his hand and so went into the senate. The senate rose to him. Of Brutus's party some stood round behind his chair, and others met him as if pleading for some exile. Brutus Albinus kept Antony, who was loyal to Caesar and strong, back outside. blocks: So Gaius Julius Caesar perished through his ambition and love of power. For those who flattered him, perceiving his love of the first place and of glory, did not stop voting him one thing after another. The things voted were such as these: that he should always wear the triumphal dress, sit on the curule chair, always have lictors bearing laurel, be named father of his country and be stamped on the coinage; that his birthday should be kept as a public festival, and that his statues should stand in the temples of Rome and in all the cities. On the rostra they set up two statues of him, one as having saved the citizens, the other as having delivered the city from siege; and both were crowned with the crowns customary for such deeds. They ordered a new senate house to be built, to be called the Julian after his name. They voted that he should be censor for life and alone, and have the privileges of the tribunes; and they decreed that if anyone insulted him in deed or word, he should be sacred and liable to the curse. What being sacred meant I have already explained. Seeing him pleased with this, they gave him a gilded chair and the robe that the kings of old had worn, and a guard of knights and senators; they enacted that prayers be offered for him publicly, that men swear by his fortune, and that everything he would do should be valid; they called him Jupiter Julius, and voted him many other things, which we pass over so as not to weary the hearer by counting each. From these he seemed an object of envy, or rather of retribution, and he provoked many against himself, until he came to the end that befell him.

So he lay slain; and all who were there were thrown into confusion, not knowing the purpose of the murderers, and fled as if they would be in danger at once, terrified those they met, and filled the city with laments. While the city was in this state, the murderers, afraid that someone might attack them, went through the forum with their swords bare and bloody and ran up to the Capitol, and spent the day and the night there. Lepidus, learning in the camp what had happened, occupied the forum by night with the soldiers and harangued the people against the murderers. Antony, when Caesar was killed, hid in fear; but learning that Lepidus had come and the murderers were on the Capitol, he took courage and came out, gathered the senate, addressed it, and brought in proposals about what had happened. Cicero, speaking to the people, persuaded all not to bear grudges against one another, but if anyone had done wrong, to overlook it, so that there might not be civil war again and destruction of the citizens at one another's hands, but that they should be of one mind, being of one race and kin. He added that what Caesar had done, whether in gifts or honours or offices, must be kept, and none of it meddled with or overturned. Persuaded by him, they voted to bear no grudge against anyone. The murderers too, speaking to the soldiers from the Capitol, promised to annul nothing that Caesar had done and to take from no one anything given to each; and so they came to reconciliation. Those on the Capitol did not come down until they had received the son of Lepidus and the son of Antony as hostages.

After this, when Caesar's will was read and the people learned that he had adopted Octavius, and had left gifts to the city and to each man thirty drachmas, as Octavius writes, or as others say seventy-five, they were stirred. Antony set out the body, covered in blood, in the forum, and by giving a speech over the dead man roused the multitude to anger. For he said much in praise of the man and stirred his hearers to pity at his suffering; then, listing the names voted to him, he added: "But this father, this high priest, the inviolable, the hero, the god, is dead, alas, not overpowered by disease, nor withered by old age, nor wounded somewhere abroad in war, nor carried off by some divine power of itself, but plotted against here within the wall; he who campaigned safely even into Britain, ambushed in the city; he who enlarged its pomerium, slaughtered in the senate house; unarmed, the great warrior; naked, the peacemaker; beside the courts, the judge; beside the magistracies, the magistrate; by the citizens, he whom none of the enemy could kill even when he was cast into the sea; by his comrades, he who often pitied them. Where, Caesar, is your kindness, where your inviolability, where the laws? You made many laws so that no one should be murdered even by his enemies, and you your friends have so pitiably killed; and now you lie slain in the forum through which you often went in procession crowned; and on the rostra you are thrown down covered with wounds, from which you often addressed the people. Alas for the grey hairs dabbled with blood; O the torn robe, which you took, it seems, only for this, to be slain in it."

At this the people, enraged, searched for the murderers, snatched up Caesar's body and burned it in the forum, rushed to the murderers' houses, and killed Helvius Cinna, a tribune, misled by the likeness of name; for it was not he who plotted against Caesar, but the praetor Cornelius Cinna. The multitude set up an altar where they had burned Caesar's body, to sacrifice on it to Caesar as to a god. But the consuls overturned it, and brought in a law that no one should ever again become dictator, setting death as the penalty if anyone proposed it or anyone anywhere accepted it. Antony at that time did many things on his own authority, giving offices, land, freedom and exemption from taxes, and bringing back exiles, as if he were the successor of Caesar's power; and he raised much money from this.

blocks: Gaius Octavius, who was surnamed Caepias, was the son of Caesar's sister, who was married to Octavius of Velitrae in the Volscian country; he was brought up by his mother, having been left an orphan. When he grew up he lived with Caesar, who had no children. So Caesar loved his nephew and had great hopes of him. For his mother Atia, when pregnant with him, dreamed that her entrails were carried up to heaven and stretched over all the earth, and her husband on the same night seemed to see the sun rising from her womb. When the child had just been born, Nigidius Figulus, a senator, who was believed to understand the motions of the stars best, asked Octavius, who had come late to the senate, the reason for his lateness. When he said it was because of the birth of a child, Nigidius cried out: "You have begotten a master for us." While the child was being brought up in the country, an eagle snatched a loaf from his hands, flew up, and then flew down and gave it back to him. When he was a boy and staying in Rome, Cicero dreamed that he saw him let down by golden chains from the sky to the Capitol and being given a whip by Jupiter. Catulus too dreamed that Jupiter had put the image of Rome in the bosom of Octavius while he was still a child. From these things, then, Caesar formed great hopes of him, adopted the boy and left him his heir, and educated him carefully in rhetoric in both the Latin and the Greek tongue, and trained him for campaigns and for the management of civil and governmental affairs.

This Octavius, then, when Caesar was slain, happened to be at Apollonia, sent there for his education. Learning there what had happened, he crossed to Brundisium. Learning of Caesar's will and that the people were stirred, he took the name of Caesar, accepted the inheritance and took hold of affairs, being eighteen years old. As he entered Rome a rainbow, many-coloured and large, encircled the whole sun, foretelling the disturbance that was to come. Having entered, he tried to become tribune, but was prevented by Antony's party. He did not keep quiet, but won over the tribune, was brought before the people by him and addressed them, promised to pay at once the gift left them by Caesar, and held out hopes of other things too. Having drawn the people to himself in this way, since a star then appeared from the north towards the west, which some called a comet foretelling what such stars usually do, while others assigned it to Caesar as enrolled among the stars, the one formerly Octavius, now called Caesar, and afterwards Augustus too, took courage and set up in the temple of Venus a bronze statue of Caesar with a star above its head. When no one prevented this, out of fear of the people, he did other things too in Caesar's honour.

Antony insulted and wronged this young Caesar. Because of this a murmur once arose among the multitude, and almost all were very indignant. So Antony in fear came to terms with him; and they seemed to be reconciled, but quarrelled again over some suspicion. Antony, seeing Caesar growing, tried to draw the crowd to himself by granting them favours. For he was powerful, being consul himself, with one of his brothers tribune, namely Lucius, and the other, Gaius, praetor. The affairs of the city were unsettled. Antony seemed to have the advantage, being consul. But Caesar was most favoured by the multitude, both because of his father and because of the promises he made, and above all because they resented Antony's great power and wished to humble him.

blocks: When Antony went off to Brundisium to the soldiers who had crossed over from Macedonia, Caesar sent friends ahead there with money to win them over, and himself, going as far as Campania, collected a crowd from various places, saying he was avenging his father, giving money and promising more; and with them he hurried to Rome before Antony came back, spoke to the people and won praise, and went away again to gather a force. The soldiers at Brundisium received Antony kindly; then, when he treated them harshly, so that he even killed many of them, they mutinied, and many went over to Caesar. Antony set out from Rome for Gaul, afraid that it might make some revolt; and Caesar followed. Decimus Brutus, one of those who had conspired against Caesar, then governed Gaul; and he, out of hatred for Antony, did not yield to him. Learning this, Caesar made Brutus his associate; for he did not yet see the time for avenging his father's murderers.

In Rome the senate deliberated in alarm because of the war. Many brought in one proposal or another, but Cicero said that they ought to vote Antony an enemy, praise Caesar and Decimus Brutus for opposing him on their own initiative, help them and give them authority for the future, and send both consuls to the war to fight him without delay or hesitation. When Cicero had advised this, Quintus Calenus, opposing him, advised them to send to all, with the senate ordering them all alike to lay down their arms and put themselves and their soldiers at its disposal, and to praise them if they obeyed, but if they disobeyed, to entrust the war to the consuls. He said this, but those acting for Caesar prevailed. Some men were sent from the senate to Antony, ordering him to give up the legions and Gaul and go to Macedonia, and ordering those serving with him to go home within a stated day, or know that they would be counted as enemies. Before learning Antony's answer, they entrusted the war against him to the consuls and to Caesar, giving him the rank of praetor.

Learning this, Antony reproached those sent to him, and sending others back, turned the blame for the war, by the reasons he put forward, onto those who had voted against him. Those in Rome again voted Antony an enemy, and those serving with him if they did not leave him, fixing another day for this. He besieged Decimus in Mutina, but achieved nothing worth mention. Decimus at first defended himself strongly against Antony, then was completely walled in. So Caesar, afraid that he would either be taken or give in from lack of supplies, marched with Hirtius against Mutina. They could not cross the river near it because of the guard on it; but eager to let Decimus know of their presence, they signalled from the tallest trees. When he did not understand, they made a very thin sheet of lead, wrote on it, rolled it up like paper and gave it to a diver to carry across; and so Decimus learned of their presence and wrote back to them in the same way.

Antony, seeing that Decimus would not give in, left his brother Lucius against him, and himself set out against Caesar and Hirtius. At first the battles were even, but later Antony got the upper hand. Perceiving that Junius was coming near, he set off against him secretly by night, ambushed him, wounded him, killed most of his soldiers, and shut the rest up in their entrenchments; and then he turned against Caesar and the others. And Hirtius, straight from his march,
