blocks: met him unexpectedly as he was worn out from the battle and defeated him heavily. The senate, learning of Antony's defeat, named Hirtius, Junius and Caesar imperatores, though Junius had fared badly and Caesar had not even fought; for he had stayed to guard the camp while Hirtius set out against Antony. So Antony was defeated; and Titus Munatius Plancus too, who was of Antony's side and was fighting Pontius Aquila, Decimus's legate, was beaten. From this Antony's soldiers were not disposed towards him as before, and some of the peoples attached to him were in revolt. For a while he was dismayed and kept quiet, but when a force came to him from Lepidus he took heart again and made a sudden sally; and when there had been great slaughter on both sides, he was routed and fled.

The senate, learning what had been done, rejoiced at Antony's defeat, declared all who had been found with him enemies, and took away their property and his. They thought Caesar worthy of nothing great and even tried to bring him down, giving to Decimus all that Caesar had hoped to receive. So that he might not be able to do any harm, they voted his enemies into commands, entrusting the fleet to Sextus Pompey, Macedonia to Marcus Brutus, and Syria and the war against Dolabella to Cassius. Contriving to set Caesar's soldiers against one another, they praised some and gave them money and crowns of olive, and voted the others nothing. But even so they remained of one mind, Caesar leading them to this. So those in the city, learning this and afraid, still did not declare him consul, but voted him other honours. When he paid no attention to these, they voted him praetor first and after that consul too.

They thought they were handling Caesar as a boy and a youth, which they kept saying; but he, terribly angry both at the rest and at being called a boy, turned to arms, secretly negotiated with Antony, gathered those who had escaped from the battle, whom the senate had voted enemies, and accused the senate and people before them. Those in office for a while made light of this, but when they learned that Antony and Lepidus had come to an understanding, they began to court Caesar and entrusted him with the war against them, not knowing of the talks he had had with Antony. This meant not to take the field against either Antony or Lepidus; for very many of their men had served with them. So he sent four hundred envoys from among the soldiers themselves to the senate. This was a show of an embassy, but in fact the whole thing was the exacting of what had been voted them and an effort to have Caesar declared consul. When the senators put off their answer, the soldiers were angry; and one of them went out of the senate house and took up his sword (for they had been ordered to go in unarmed), and said: "If you do not give Caesar the consulship, this will give it."

Caesar made a grievance of the fact that they had been forced to lay down their arms when they went into the senate, and that someone had asked whether they had been sent by the legions or by Caesar; and he hastily sent for Antony and Lepidus, and himself set out for Rome with the soldiers, as if forced by them. They killed some of the knights as spies. The members of the senate, learning of their approach, sent them the money before they came near and voted Caesar consul. But the soldiers, knowing they had done this under compulsion, both frightened them and grew bold. At this the senate changed and forbade the army to approach the city, and entrusted its guard to the praetors. But when Caesar with the army was before the town, some of the senators and many of the people came over to him, and the praetors surrendered themselves and their soldiers to him; and having taken the city in this way without a fight, he was put forward as consul by the people too, without even coming to the assembly, so as not to seem to force them. Quintus Pedius was given to him as colleague, if one should call him that and not a subordinate.

Chosen consul in this way, Caesar arranged affairs in the city as he thought fit and gave money to the soldiers, in word from his own means, in fact from the public funds, and acknowledged his gratitude to them. Many honours were voted him by the senate, willingly in appearance, but in truth forced by fear. Among other things he was adopted into Caesar's family according to custom, and took the name. For even before he had called himself Caesar, as having inherited the name along with the estate, but he did not hold it securely before confirming it according to ancestral custom. From then on he was called Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus; for it is the custom for those adopted to take the rest of their name from the one who adopts them, but to keep one of their former names.
text: met him unexpectedly as he was worn out from the battle and defeated him heavily. The senate, learning of Antony's defeat, named Hirtius, Junius and Caesar imperatores, though Junius had fared badly and Caesar had not even fought; for he had stayed to guard the camp while Hirtius set out against Antony. So Antony was defeated; and Titus Munatius Plancus too, who was of Antony's side and was fighting Pontius Aquila, Decimus's legate, was beaten. From this Antony's soldiers were not disposed towards him as before, and some of the peoples attached to him were in revolt. For a while he was dismayed and kept quiet, but when a force came to him from Lepidus he took heart again and made a sudden sally; and when there had been great slaughter on both sides, he was routed and fled. The senate, learning what had been done, rejoiced at Antony's defeat, declared all who had been found with him enemies, and took away their property and his. They thought Caesar worthy of nothing great and even tried to bring him down, giving to Decimus all that Caesar had hoped to receive. So that he might not be able to do any harm, they voted his enemies into commands, entrusting the fleet to Sextus Pompey, Macedonia to Marcus Brutus, and Syria and the war against Dolabella to Cassius. Contriving to set Caesar's soldiers against one another, they praised some and gave them money and crowns of olive, and voted the others nothing. But even so they remained of one mind, Caesar leading them to this. So those in the city, learning this and afraid, still did not declare him consul, but voted him other honours. When he paid no attention to these, they voted him praetor first and after that consul too. blocks: When he had won over the soldiers and enslaved the senate, he made the distribution to the people of what his father had left them, so that he might draw them too to himself and not have them opposing him when he turned to avenging his father's murderers. He set up courts, so as not to seem to act by force in anything, and that while most were absent, and some held governments of provinces. If some were present, they did not appear out of fear, but even slipped away secretly somewhere. So not only those who had struck the blows or conspired were condemned in their absence, but many others too who had had no part in the plot, and some who were not even in the city at the time, among them Sextus Pompey; and they were banished from fire and water and their property was confiscated.

Having done this, Caesar marched, as it seemed, against Lepidus and Antony; but he did nothing, not because he had come to an understanding with Antony, and through him with Lepidus, but because he saw them strong and of one mind, and hoped through them to overcome Cassius and Brutus, who had already become very powerful, and after that to subdue them too through each other. For this reason Caesar kept the agreement even against his will, and managed their reconciliation with the senate and the people, not proposing it himself so as to avoid suspicion, but arranging for Quintus to advise it. When those in the city consulted him about it, he pretended to consent to the measure unwillingly, as forced by the soldiers. When the reconciliation had been voted them, both set out to meet Caesar, bringing the largest and best part of their army. For they did not trust him firmly, nor did they wish to seem to have had their safety and return voted through him, but through themselves and their own strength; and they hoped to get what they wanted through the legions. Caesar too met them with a host of soldiers. They came together for a conference, and having talked quietly, they conspired in sum for power and against their enemies, and openly they agreed together that the three should be overseers and managers of affairs for five years, so that they might not seem to aim at oligarchy. Privately they also assigned themselves governments of provinces, so that they might not be thought to appropriate the whole empire. And they gave one another the slaughter of their enemies in exchange. To Lepidus they entrusted the guard of Rome and the rest of Italy, and Caesar and Antony agreed to march against Marcus Brutus and Cassius. They confirmed what they had decided with oaths, called the soldiers together and made such speeches as were fitting. Antony's soldiers, at his prompting, asked Caesar to take the daughter of Antony's wife Fulvia, whom she had by Clodius. He did not refuse, though another had already been betrothed to him.

From there they hurried to Rome. Some unlucky signs befell Antony and Lepidus, but for Caesar an eagle settled on his tent and killed two crows that attacked it and tried to pluck some of its feathers; this foretold his victory over both his partners. So they came to Rome with the armies, and at once carried out what they had decided; and many were slaughtered, so that the city was filled with dead. Some were killed in their houses, some in the streets, in the market places and by the temples, and their heads were set up on the rostra for them, while the rest of the bodies were either thrown out on the spot as food for dogs and birds or cast into the river. Not only their enemies but also their friends perished. For the others counted as enemies all who had helped or worked with each of the three. So it happened that the same men were friends of one of them and enemies of the others, so that while each privately took vengeance on those who had plotted against him, they destroyed their dearest friends together in common. For no one could punish his own enemy who was another's friend without giving in exchange someone counted as his own friend, or even more, if the man asked for slaughter was honoured for virtue or birth or rank. They also killed the rich, even if they had nothing to charge them with, since they needed much money to satisfy the desires of the soldiers.

blocks: These things were done mostly by Lepidus and Antony. For having been honoured by the elder Caesar, and having held offices and commands longest, they had the most enemies. They seemed to be done by the young Caesar too, because of his share in the power. For he did not kill many himself, being not cruel by nature and brought up in his father's ways, and he nursed no fierce hatred for many and took pains to be loved. Not only did he destroy few, but he even saved very many; and he dealt most gently with those who hid anyone, though death had been proclaimed for them too.

Lepidus was implacable, and Antony killed cruelly and pitilessly even those who tried to help those being killed, and he looked at the heads of the slain even while dining, and glutted himself with the unholy sight. His wife Fulvia too put many to death, out of enmity and for money, some of them not even known to her husband. Once, when Cicero's head was brought (for he was caught fleeing and slain), Antony, after much abuse of him, ordered it to be displayed more conspicuously than the others on the rostra, so that where he had been heard speaking against him, there he might be seen with his right hand; for it had been cut off with it. Fulvia took the head in her hands, and in her bitterness spat on it, set it on her knees, opened its mouth, pulled out the tongue and pierced it with the pins she used in her hair, uttering many foul jests.

Many perished, but some were also saved. For slaves put on their masters' clothes, hid them, and were slain as if they were the masters. And one branded slave not only did not betray the master who had branded him, but saved him. For as he was running away with his master and found they were being pursued, he killed a man who met them, gave his clothes to his master and let him go; and himself lit a pyre and put the corpse on it, and meeting the pursuers with his master's clothes and ring, said that he had killed his master as he fled; he was believed because of the spoils and his brand-marks, and saved his master and was himself honoured. Quintus Cicero, Marcus's brother, was smuggled away by his son, who was tortured for it and did not speak. His father, learning what was happening and pitying his son, gave himself up to the slayers of his own accord. Many escaped secretly and went to Brutus and Cassius. But most went over to Sextus. For having earlier been chosen admiral, and having been powerful on the sea for some time, he had built up a strength of his own, though he was later deprived of the command by Caesar, and had seized Sicily. Then, when a price was put on his head too and the other slaughters took place, he greatly helped those in the same case, receiving those who came to him and aiding them in every way; so many came to him.

Such things happened about the slaughters; and many outrageous things also happened about the property of others. The houses of the well-off were sacked, and they exacted a year's rent from all the houses in the city and in the rest of Italy, the whole of it for rented houses, and half for those in which the owners lived, according to the value of the dwelling; they took from the owners of land half of their income, and gave the properties of the slain to the soldiers, some as a gift, others selling them cheap; for no one else was allowed to come to the auction to buy, since they set death as the penalty for anyone who came. They gave offices, honours and priesthoods, wiped out some laws and wrote others in their place, and did everything as they pleased, so that the monarchy of the murdered Caesar was thought a good one.

blocks: This, then, is what they did that year. In the following year, when Marcus Lepidus and Lucius Plancus were consuls, taxes that had already lapsed were revived and others newly imposed; many were levied on land and many on slaves. What grieved everyone more than the rest was that the property of every man and woman of any means at all was tithed. In word a tenth of the property was exacted from each of them, but in fact not even a tenth was left to anyone. Something else too was devised. Anyone who wished was allowed to give up all his property and afterwards ask back a third of it; that is, to get nothing and have trouble besides. For those who openly robbed the two parts by force, how would they give back the third? Very many other things were also laid on people at that time, driving them into poverty, and only those who held the arms became exceedingly rich.

So those three men acted; and at the same time they glorified the elder Caesar and voted him many and varied honours. Having done this, Lepidus stayed in Rome to manage the city and the rest of Italy, and Caesar and Antony marched against Brutus and Cassius. For they, learning that Caesar Octavius was taking hold of affairs and winning the crowd to himself, had given up hope of the free state and, afraid of him, had gone to Athens. The Athenians received them splendidly and voted them bronze statues, as having emulated their own tyrant-slayers, I mean Harmodius and Aristogeiton. Then, learning that Caesar was rising higher, Cassius set out for the Syrians, who knew him, and Brutus won over Greece and Macedonia. People attached themselves to him both because of the glory of what he had done and because he had taken on many soldiers, some who had been wandering there after the battle at Pharsalus, others left behind from those who had gone out with Dolabella; and money had been sent to him from Asia by Trebonius. He won over the Greek world without effort, and after this, adding all Macedonia and Epirus, he wrote to the senate reporting what he had done. They, being at that time suspicious of Caesar, praised him and told him to govern everything there. From this he became more eager himself, and had his subjects yielding without excuse. When Caesar made himself master in Rome and was openly punishing his father's murderers, Brutus considered how to defend himself against him when he came, and beat off some plots made against him by certain men. He withdrew into upper Macedonia with the strongest part of the army, and from there sailed to Asia, so that the soldiers might not change sides on learning of what was being done in Rome, reported in a more frightening form. Then he hurried back to Europe again, afraid that there might be some revolt.

At the same time Cassius too crossed to Asia to Trebonius, and taking from him money and many horsemen and many others from the Cilicians and the Asiatics, he brought the people of Tarsus, even against their will, into alliance. Coming into Syria, he won over everything, peoples and armies alike, without a fight. Having taken over Syria, he set out for Judaea, learning that the soldiers left in Egypt by Caesar were coming. He readily won them over, and the Jews too. So Cassius too quickly became strong, and wrote to the senate as Brutus had; and the senate confirmed his command of Syria and voted the war against Dolabella. For Dolabella had been appointed to govern Syria, but learned of the decree while staying in Asia; and he did not go to Syria, but stayed where he was, killed Trebonius by treachery at Smyrna and took all Asia. Having become master of Asia in this way, he came into Cilicia while Cassius was in Palestine, won over the people of Tarsus, who joined him willingly, and defeated Cassius's guards at Aegae; then he invaded Syria, was beaten off from Antioch, but won over Laodicea. The fleet came over to him too; and becoming strong from this, he went off to Aradus, where, left with few men, he was in danger. Escaping, he met Cassius, engaged him and was defeated, and was besieged in Laodicea. Forced by lack of supplies, and afraid of being taken alive, he killed himself. His legate Marcus Octavius did the same.

Cassius, when he had settled affairs in Syria and Cilicia, came to Brutus in Asia. For when they learned of the conspiracy of the three men, knowing that they were doing everything against them, they themselves deliberated and acted on everything in common more eagerly. Going round themselves and sending others, they won over those who did not side with the three, and gathered money and soldiers; and when some would not be persuaded to fight with them, they turned against them. Cassius defeated the Rhodians in a sea battle and took their ships and money, and after this seized Ariobarzanes and put him to death; Brutus overcame the Lycians, won over most of the cities without a fight, laid siege to Xanthus, took it and burned it. Then he came to Patara and invited them as friends; and when they did not obey, he sent them the captives from Xanthus, who were their kin, hoping to win them over through them. Not even so did they give in. So he sold some of the captives and set the rest free. Seeing this, the people of Patara at once joined him as a man of virtue. The people of Myra did the same, since he had taken their general at their port and released him. And he soon won over the rest too.

Not even so did they give in. So he sold some of the captives and set the rest free. Seeing this, the people of Patara at once joined him as a man of virtue. The people of Myra did the same, since he had taken their general at their port and released him. And he soon won over the rest too.

blocks: From there both came into Asia, and hurried to Macedonia. Gaius Norbanus and Decidius Saxa had been sent into Macedonia by Caesar and Antony, and encamping near Philippi they had seized the short road first. So Brutus and Cassius went round by another, longer way, forced the guard there, came to the city by the heights and encamped there. Being superior in numbers to their opponents, they occupied the mountain called Symbolum, brought in supplies from the sea, and took them by raiding the plain. Norbanus and Saxa did not dare to engage them, but sent for Caesar and Antony. They left part of the army to guard Italy and crossed the Ionian Sea with the greater part. Caesar fell ill and stayed at Dyrrhachium, while Antony drove on to Philippi, and was tripped up when he ambushed some of the enemy bringing in grain. Caesar, fearing both outcomes, whether Antony should get the worse by engaging alone, or should win (for from the one he thought Brutus and Cassius, and from the other Antony at any rate, would become strong against himself), hurried on though still ill; and Antony's men took heart.

While the opponents sat facing each other, there were sallies from both sides, but no pitched battle, though Caesar and Antony were eager to engage. But Cassius and Brutus put it off, not shrinking from the battle, but in the hope of winning somehow without dangers and loss of men. But the armies were weighed down by the delay and came to despise their opponents, since Caesar's and Antony's men had held the purification that is made before battles inside their fortification, as if afraid; Brutus's men set off for battle and let it be known that if he put it off any longer they would leave the camp and scatter; and so, even against their will, they engaged.

This contest plainly became the greatest for the Romans. One might judge this from the signs that came both in Rome and in Macedonia. For in the town the sun sometimes grew small and sometimes appeared large, and once it even shone at night; torches seemed to dart here and there; sounds of trumpets, clashing of arms and shouts of armies were heard at night from the gardens of Caesar and of Antony, which bordered each other by the Tiber; a child was born with ten fingers on each hand, and a mule gave birth to a monster, whose front parts were like a horse and the rest like a mule. These and other things happened in Rome; and in Macedonia many bees swarmed round Cassius's camp, at the purification the lictor brought him his wreath upside down, in a procession a boy carrying a golden Victory slipped and fell, and many vultures and other carrion birds went about their camps and screeched in a dreadful and terrifying way. A doctor of the young Caesar dreamed that Athena told him to take Caesar out of his tent and set him in the battle line, though he was still badly ill; which saved him, as will be told.

They did not fix the day of battle, but as if by some agreement they armed at dawn and came out, and drew up in order and quiet. Then they met with much pushing, much swordplay and great eagerness; and none used retreats or pursuits, but stood where they were and wounded and were wounded, killed and were killed. Brutus, fighting against Caesar's men, won, but Cassius, drawn up against Antony's, was beaten, and the camps on both sides were taken. Yet the beaten did not know of the others' victory, nor the victors of the defeat; for the camps were far apart, and a vast dust having arisen, they did not know the outcome of the battle. Meanwhile the entrenchment of Caesar and Antony was sacked, and everything in it taken, so that if Caesar had not slipped out of the camp in accordance with the doctor's dream, he would have been caught in it and in danger.

Cassius escaped from the battle, but since his fortification too had been sacked, he withdrew to a hill that had views over the plain, and suspecting that Brutus too had been overthrown, he sent a centurion to look and report to him where Brutus was and what he was doing. When the man sent met horsemen whom Brutus had sent to learn about Cassius, and was surrounded by them as they greeted him and welcomed him, Cassius thought those coming were enemies and that the centurion had been caught by them, and ordered a freedman named Pindarus to kill him.

So he had such an end; and the centurion, coming back and learning what had happened, blamed himself for his slowness and killed himself too. Brutus, learning of Cassius's defeat and death, wept for him, and gathering the surviving soldiers of Cassius, comforted them with words and gifts of money. About eight thousand of these fell in the battle, and of Caesar's and Antony's more than twice as many. So they were downcast, until a servant of Cassius named Demetrius came to Antony in the evening, bringing his cloaks and sword. When these were brought they took heart so much that at daybreak they led out the force armed for battle. Brutus did not wish to fight a pitched battle, but tried to harass and disturb the enemy by night. Once he even turned the river aside and flooded much of their fortification. But when he learned that some of his men were deserting to the other side, afraid that there might be some greater revolt, he decided to engage them. Since there were many captives in his camp, and he had no way of disposing of them during the battle, he ordered the slave crowd to be killed, but of the free he released some openly and saved others by hiding them and sending them away, seeing that the commanders were implacable, although the enemy had killed those of his soldiers they had taken alive.

blocks: In the evening, when they were to fight the next day, the phantom appeared to Brutus that he had seen before at night when crossing from Asia; it was like this. It was deep night and a light not very bright was burning in his tent; he was awake, considering and reckoning something. He thought someone came into the tent, and looking towards the entrance he saw a terrible and strange sight, a monstrous body standing silently by him. When he asked, "Who are you, or with what purpose have you come?" he heard from it: "I am your evil genius, Brutus, and you will see me at Philippi." And Brutus said undismayed: "I shall see you." So he saw this phantom again, showing the same appearance, but saying nothing, and going away. They say that two eagles also met and fought then in the space between the camps, and the one on Brutus's side gave way and fled.

So engaging the enemy, he too was defeated. For his infantry, after fighting evenly for a very long time, gave way, and from this his cavalry too, though fighting nobly, gave in. There Marcus, the son of Cato, ranked among the best and noblest of the young men, did not yield when worn out nor flee, but using his hand and declaring who he was and naming his father, fell on many enemy dead. The bravest of the others too fell, running risks for Brutus. Lucilius, a good man, seeing some barbarian horsemen riding hard at Brutus, said that he himself was Brutus and asked to be taken to Antony, as if afraid of Caesar. They brought the man, sending messengers ahead. When they were near, Antony was at a loss how he should receive Brutus, but Lucilius, brought before him, said: "No enemy, Antony, has taken Marcus Brutus or would take him. May fortune never so far prevail over virtue. He will be found alive, or else lying dead in a manner worthy of himself." Antony, in wonder, said to the soldiers bringing him: "Perhaps you take the deception hard, fellow soldiers; but know that you have taken a better prize than the one you sought; for seeking an enemy you bring us a friend."

Brutus, having come to a wooded place when it was already dark, with few officers about him, looked up to heaven and cried out: "Zeus, let not the cause of these evils escape you." Plutarch records that he spoke this line; but Dio records that Brutus then said: "O wretched virtue, you were only a word after all; I practised you as a deed, but you were a slave to fortune." When someone said they must flee, he said: "We must indeed flee, but with our hands, not with our feet." Saying this, he fell on his bare sword and died. Antony found his body and covered it with the most costly of his own purple cloaks.

Porcia, the wife of Brutus and daughter of Cato, was guarded and not allowed to kill herself, but she snatched live coals from the fire, swallowed them and died. Plutarch wrote of her that before the slaying of the elder Caesar, seeing her husband thoughtful and full of unusual disquiet, and perceiving that he was nursing some plan hard to unravel, she did not ask him about the secrets before she had made a test of herself. For, he says, she took a small knife and secretly made a deep cut in her thigh, so that soon violent pains came on and shivering fevers broke out from the wound. When Brutus was anxious, she said to him, at the height of her pain: "I, Brutus, was not given to you like a concubine, to share only your bed and table, but to be a partner in good and in bad. Your part in our marriage is all without fault; but what proof or thanks is there from me, if I am to bear with you neither a secret suffering nor a care that needs trust? I know that a woman's nature is thought too weak to keep a secret; but good upbringing and worthy company have some strength for character. And I have the advantage of being Cato's daughter and Brutus's wife. Before, I trusted in these less, but now I have learned that I am unconquerable even by pain." Saying this, she showed him the wound and told him of the test. He, amazed, prayed the gods to grant that, succeeding in the deed, he might show himself a husband

blocks: worthy of Porcia.

So Brutus's life ended in the way that has been told; and of the notable men who had been with him, most killed themselves at once or perished when taken, and the rest, escaping to the sea at the time, later joined Sextus. So Brutus and Cassius perished, slain by the swords with which they had made away with Caesar; and Caesar and Antony at once divided the empire between them. To Caesar were allotted Iberia and Numidia, and to Antony Gaul and Africa, on the agreement that if Lepidus was indignant at this, they would give up Africa to him. They divided only these, because Sextus held Sardinia and Sicily, and the parts outside Italy were still in confusion. On this Antony went off to Asia to settle those who had fought against them and to raise money; and Caesar set out for Italy, to stop Lepidus if he made any trouble, and to face Sextus. Being ill and so travelling more slowly, he reached Rome, performed the customary rites for the victory, and turned to the management of affairs. For Lepidus kept quiet out of fear and sluggishness, but Antony's wife Fulvia and Lucius Antonius, who was consul, took hold of affairs and quarrelled with Caesar, so that Caesar sent Fulvia's daughter back to her, dissolving the kinship that came from the marriage.

For this, then, and because of the famine that was then oppressing the Romans, Caesar was at a loss. For the sea about Sicily was held by Sextus, and the Ionian Gulf by Gnaeus Domitius, who was one of Caesar's murderers, and having escaped from the battle at Philippi had got together a fleet, held the gulf for some time and damaged his opponents' interests. Because of this famine and for other reasons the people and the soldiery rose against each other, and the strife turned to fighting, so that men on both sides were wounded and died, and many houses were burned. Afraid from this, Caesar wished to be reconciled with Fulvia and the consul Lucius. When he achieved nothing by sending many others to them, including veterans, he sent senators, showing them the agreement he had made with Antony and making them judges of the differences. When they too could achieve nothing, he turned to the soldiery again. The soldiers, coming together in Rome as if to consult with the people and senate about something, paid no attention to them, but gathered on the Capitol, ordered the agreement made by Antony and Caesar to be read to them, ratified it, and set themselves up as judges of the disputes. Since Caesar was ready to be judged on the appointed day, but Fulvia and the consul did not appear, they condemned them as being in the wrong and took up Caesar's cause. A battle was fought between them in which Caesar prevailed, so that many of the senators and knights perished, and the consul Lucius was taken, but released. Fulvia escaped to Antony with her children.

Caesar, having dealt with affairs in Italy, and the Ionian Gulf having been freed (for Domitius had given up and sailed to Antony), prepared to set out against Sextus. But because of his power, and because Sextus had come to an understanding with Antony through Antony's mother, he feared he would have to make war on both at once; and preferring Sextus, as more trustworthy and stronger than Antony, he sent him his mother Mucia, and married the sister of Sextus's father-in-law Lucius Scribonius Libo, in case he might make him a friend by kindness and kinship. For Sextus, deprived earlier by the elder Caesar of the command he held, but keeping hold of the fleet, hoped, since he had had no part in that Caesar's murder, to be brought home by the young Caesar too. But when he learned that a price had been put on his head too, he despaired and prepared for war, building triremes, receiving deserters and making allies of the pirates. In a short time he became strong and mastered the sea about Italy. As his affairs went forward he sailed to Sicily, seized it, and gathered more soldiers from there and a very strong fleet. For this, and so that he might not become friends with Antony, Caesar longed to be reconciled with him. Failing in this, he sent Marcus Agrippa to make war on him, and himself went off to Gaul. Learning this, Sextus sailed up to Italy and kept on plundering it. Caesar took control of Gaul, and sent Lepidus to Africa, so that, receiving it as from him and not from Antony too, he might owe gratitude to him alone.

blocks: Marcus Antonius, coming to Asia, going round some places himself and sending others to others, raised money from the cities and sold the principalities. When Cleopatra appeared to him in Cilicia, out of love for the woman he no longer gave any thought to what was honourable, but was a slave to the Egyptian; and he did other outrageous things because of this, and killed her brothers; and at last he went off to Egypt.

From this the Parthians, who had been stirring before, then attacked the Romans more than ever, Labienus provoking them to it. He had served with Brutus and Cassius, and had been sent by them to the Parthians to ask for an alliance; and when he learned of their defeat he stayed among the barbarians, and then promised to become leader of the war, and undertook to bring many of the peoples over. So he received a large force from Orodes, king of the Parthians, and was sent out with his son Pacorus. Pacorus subdued Syria except Tyre and invaded Palestine, while Labienus seized Cilicia and the mainland cities of Asia. Antony learned this, as he learned the other things being done in Italy, but because of his love and his drinking he cared neither for the citizens nor for the allies, but lived in luxury with Cleopatra and the Egyptians, until he was utterly ruined.

At last, late, he roused himself and sailed to Tyre; but making the war with Sextus his excuse, he left them, and coasting along the mainland as far as Asia, passed over into Greece. There he met his mother and his wife, made Caesar his enemy and made a treaty with Sextus. Then, crossing into Italy, he seized some of it and besieged other parts. Caesar gathered his forces. When they had broken into war, the rest of Italy was disturbed, and Rome most of all. Meanwhile Fulvia, who was staying at Sicyon, died. When this was reported, both laid down their arms and were reconciled. Caesar was allotted Sardinia, Dalmatia, Iberia and Gaul, and to Antony fell all the rest that the Romans held beyond the Ionian Sea, both in Europe and in Asia; Lepidus held the peoples in Libya, and Sextus Sicily.

So they divided the empire again in this way, and shared the war against Sextus; and to mark the reconciliation they entertained each other in the camps about Brundisium, Caesar in Roman and soldierly fashion, Antony in Asiatic and Egyptian. When they were reconciled, as it seemed, the soldiers who were then with Caesar surrounded Antony and demanded from him the money promised them after the battle at Philippi, for which he had been sent to Asia to gather as much as he could. And they would have done him some harm, as he gave nothing, had Caesar not restrained them, buoying them up with hopes.

After this they took up the war against Sextus. Since famine, with Sextus master of the sea, was pressing those in Rome, and many taxes of all kinds were imposed on them, they were terribly vexed and no longer kept quiet, but urged them to make a treaty with Sextus. When they did not persuade them, they turned to Sextus, drove the magistrates out of the forum with stones, threw down the statues of Caesar and Antony, and rushed at them as if to kill them. So they were forced, even against their will, to open negotiations with Sextus. First they talked with him through their associates, then they came to a conference themselves. They made peace on these terms: that the slaves who had deserted should be free; that the exiles, except the murderers, should return, and some of them be given tribuneships, praetorships and priesthoods at once; that Sextus himself should be chosen consul and appointed augur, receive seventeen and a half million drachmas from his father's property, and govern Sicily, Sardinia and Achaea for five years, receiving no deserters, acquiring no more ships, holding no forts in Italy, but himself maintaining peace on the sea and sending a fixed amount of grain to those in the city.

Having written down these terms and deposited the documents with the Vestal Virgins, they gave one another their right hands and kissed one another; and at this an immense shout went up from the mainland and from the ships, so that the mountains echoed. After this the others received one another and returned one another's hospitality, and so did these men themselves, first Sextus on his ship, and then Caesar and Antony on the mainland. Though Sextus could have killed both, since they were in his ship with few men, as his freedman Menas advised, saying he would cut the cable, if he wished, and sail away, he would not, but even betrothed his daughter to Marcus Marcellus, Caesar's nephew.
text: Marcus Antonius, coming to Asia, going round some places himself and sending others to others, raised money from the cities and sold the principalities. When Cleopatra appeared to him in Cilicia, out of love for the woman he no longer gave any thought to what was honourable, but was a slave to the Egyptian; and he did other outrageous things because of this, and killed her brothers; and at last he went off to Egypt. From this the Parthians, who had been stirring before, then attacked the Romans more than ever, Labienus provoking them to it. He had served with Brutus and Cassius, and had been sent by them to the Parthians to ask for an alliance; and when he learned of their defeat he stayed among the barbarians, and then promised to become leader of the war, and undertook to bring many of the peoples over. So he received a large force from Orodes, king of the Parthians, and was sent out with his son Pacorus. Pacorus subdued Syria except Tyre and invaded Palestine, while Labienus seized Cilicia and the mainland cities of Asia. Antony learned this, as he learned the other things being done in Italy, but because of his love and his drinking he cared neither for the citizens nor for the allies, but lived in luxury with Cleopatra and the Egyptians, until he was utterly ruined. At last, late, he roused himself and sailed to Tyre; but making the war with Sextus his excuse, he left them, and coasting along the mainland as far as Asia, passed over into Greece. There he met his mother and his wife, made Caesar his enemy and made a treaty with Sextus. Then, crossing into Italy, he seized some of it and besieged other parts. Caesar gathered his forces. When they had broken into war, the rest of Italy was disturbed, and Rome most of all. Meanwhile Fulvia, who was staying at Sicyon, died. When this was reported, both laid down their arms and were reconciled. Caesar was allotted Sardinia, Dalmatia, Iberia and Gaul, and to Antony fell all the rest that the Romans held beyond the Ionian Sea, both in Europe and in Asia; Lepidus held the peoples in Libya, and Sextus Sicily. So they divided the empire again in this way, and shared the war against Sextus; and to mark the reconciliation they entertained each other in the camps about Brundisium, Caesar in Roman and soldierly fashion, Antony in Asiatic and Egyptian. When they were reconciled, as it seemed, the soldiers who were then with Caesar surrounded Antony and demanded from him the money promised them after the battle at Philippi, for which he had been sent to Asia to gather as much as he could. And they would have done him some harm, as he gave nothing, had Caesar not restrained them, buoying them up with hopes. After this they took up the war against Sextus. Since famine, with Sextus master of the sea, was pressing those in Rome, and many taxes of all kinds were imposed on them, they were terribly vexed and no longer kept quiet, but urged them to make a treaty with Sextus. When they did not persuade them, they turned to Sextus, drove the magistrates out of the forum with stones, threw down the statues of Caesar and Antony, and rushed at them as if to kill them. So they were forced, even against their will, to open negotiations with Sextus. First they talked with him through their associates, then they came to a conference themselves. They made peace on these terms: that the slaves who had deserted should be free; that the exiles, except the murderers, should return, and some of them be given tribuneships, praetorships and priesthoods at once; that Sextus himself should be chosen consul and appointed augur, receive seventeen and a half million drachmas from his father's property, and govern Sicily, Sardinia and Achaea for five years, receiving no deserters, acquiring no more ships, holding no forts in Italy, but himself maintaining peace on the sea and sending a fixed amount of grain to those in the city. Having written down these terms and deposited the documents with the Vestal Virgins, they gave one another their right hands and kissed one another; and at this an immense shout went up from the mainland and from the ships, so that the mountains echoed. After this the others received one another and returned one another's hospitality, and so did these men themselves, first Sextus on his ship, and then Caesar and Antony on the mainland. Though Sextus could have killed both, since they were in his ship with few men, as his freedman Menas advised, saying he would cut the cable, if he wished, and sail away, he would not, but even betrothed his daughter to Marcus Marcellus, Caesar's nephew.

blocks: So this war was put off; and Antony, going back from Italy to Greece, stayed there a very long time, satisfying his desires and harming the cities, so that they might be handed over to Sextus as weak as possible; he lived in many other ways contrary to ancestral custom, called himself the new Dionysus and wished to be so named by others. When the Athenians for this reason betrothed Athena to him, he said he accepted the marriage, and exacted from them a dowry of a million.

He was busy with these things, and sent Publius Ventidius ahead into Asia. He engaged Labienus, who drew up with his Romans and the Parthians, and routed them; many of the Parthians were slaughtered by the enemy, and more perished at one another's hands, trampled in the flight, and the survivors fled into Cilicia. Labienus prepared to come to grips with him again. But his soldiers, disheartened by the flight of the barbarians, tried to run away by night. Ventidius learned of this in advance from a deserter, ambushed and killed many in the retreat, and drew the rest over to himself. Labienus escaped at the time, but was later caught by Demetrius, who was a freedman of the elder Caesar and had then been sent by Antony to Cyprus. Ventidius recovered Cilicia and sent Silo ahead with horsemen to Amanus (this is a mountain on the borders of Cilicia and Syria, with a very narrow pass); and there Silo would have been in danger from those posted by Pacorus to guard it, had not Ventidius by chance come upon him fighting and helped him. So he took over Syria, except the Aradians, and then seized Palestine too.

When Appius Claudius and Gaius Norbanus were consuls, the multitude, weighed down by the exactions, rose against the tax collectors, and came to blows with them and with the attendants and the soldiers who helped them collect the money.

Caesar married Livia. She was the daughter of Livius Drusus, who killed himself after the defeat in Macedonia, and the wife of Nero, and was in her sixth month of pregnancy by him. When Caesar hesitated for this reason to marry her while she was with child, the priests called pontiffs, asked whether this was not unholy, said that if the pregnancy were in doubt the marriage ought to be put off, but since it was admitted nothing prevented it from taking place; perhaps they really found this so in the ancestral rules, or if they did not find it, they said so for Caesar's sake. Her husband himself gave her away like a father. When the woman was already living with Caesar she gave birth to Claudius Drusus Nero, and Caesar sent him to his father; who, dying much later, left Caesar himself as guardian to him and to Tiberius.

Meanwhile Caesar and Sextus went to war; for having made the agreement not willingly but under compulsion, they did not keep it. They would have fought even if they had had no pretext. Still, some causes gave them handles for the fighting. For Menas, who was a freedman of Sextus and was in the island of Sardinia, was suspected for other reasons and because he had come to an understanding with Caesar, and when summoned by Sextus to give account of his administration, he killed those sent and handed over to Caesar the island, the fleet, the rest of the army and himself. Caesar honoured him greatly; for he adorned him with gold rings and enrolled him among the knights. The matter of the rings is like this. None of the Romans of old, not only of the freedmen but not even of the freeborn, except the senators and knights, was allowed to wear gold rings, unless the one in power permitted it. When Sextus asked for this man to be handed over to him, Caesar did not hand him over, charging Sextus in return with receiving deserters, building triremes contrary to the agreement, and other things. Sextus, blaming Caesar over Menas and for other reasons, sent forces and plundered much of Campania. Learning this, Caesar sent for Lepidus and Antony. Lepidus did not obey at once, and Antony came from Greece to Brundisium, but before meeting Caesar, alarmed because a wolf had come into his headquarters and killed soldiers, he sailed back to Greece, giving the Parthian affairs as an urgent excuse.

Sextus pressed on with affairs more eagerly, sailed against Italy, and did much harm, but suffered no less in return. When sea battles took place, Sextus's men had rather the better, since many of Caesar's ships were destroyed in the battles and many were endangered by violent winds; so that Caesar, wishing to invade Sicily, gave this up and was content to guard the coast of the mainland. Sextus was elated still more, and himself harmed Italy, and sent Apollophanes to Libya. Caesar built many ships, collected rowers from the senators, the knights and the commons, enlisted heavy infantry and gathered money from everywhere; and he himself arranged affairs in Italy and Gaul, and entrusted the preparation of the fleet to Agrippa, ordering him to work it up and train it. He gathered the ships and rowers, armoured the ships, and trained the rowers to row on benches set up on land.

Those in Rome were disturbed by the quarrels of the magistrates with one another, and signs alarmed them, among others that an eagle snatched a white hen carrying a sprig of laurel with berries and dropped it into Livia's lap; which seemed no small sign. She took care of the hen and planted the laurel, and the laurel took root and grew, and Livia was to hold the power of Caesar in her bosom and prevail over him in everything.

blocks: At this time Antony came from Syria to Italy, as if to share with Caesar, because of what had befallen him, the war against Sextus; but he did not stay, but gave him ships and promised to send others, received heavy infantry in return, and himself went off as if to march against the Parthians. Before he left they blamed each other; then they were reconciled, Octavia bringing about the reconciliation. Octavia was Caesar's sister, who after Fulvia's death had been joined to Antony by her brother, the husband she had before having died. Since the time of mourning had not yet passed, the penalty was removed by a vote of the senate. Then too, so that there might be a greater bond of kinship between them, Caesar betrothed his own daughter to Antyllus, Antony's son. They feigned and pretended these things because of the circumstances they were then in. They took the priesthood and the consulship from Sextus, and gave themselves the command for another five years; for the first had already run out.

Antony hurried to Syria, and Caesar prepared for the war against Sextus. Menas deserted back to Sextus, being faithless and always courting the stronger side. When spring came, Caesar set out against Sicily, hoping to surround it with his fleet, trusting in the number and size of the vessels and the towers they carried, so that they might fight from them as from a wall, from above. As he went a very heavy storm came on and destroyed many ships, and Menas, falling on the rest while they were in disorder, burned many and took others in tow. Had he not gone over to Caesar again and betrayed the fleet he commanded, Caesar's expedition would have come to nothing then too. Menas deserted because he was suspected in every way by Sextus; but Caesar did not trust him any more either.

When Caesar had recovered his fleet, he went back to the mainland, intending to take the infantry of his army across to Sicily when the time came. Sextus watched for his crossing at Messana. He ordered Demochares to lie at anchor at Mylae against Agrippa, who had been left by Caesar at Lipara with the ships. They spent a long time there, but at last Agrippa went off with the best of his ships to spy on the enemy. When he neither saw them all nor would any of them put out, he came back, and prepared to fight the next day. The same happened to Demochares, and he too prepared to attack the enemy, and sent for Sextus. Day was already dawning, and both fleets sailed against each other and began the sea battle. For a very long time they fought evenly, but at last, late and towards night, Caesar's men won; but they did not pursue.

Caesar, since Sextus had left Messana because of the sea battle, crossed safely to Tauromenium. When the sea battle had ended, Sextus came hurriedly to Messana, and learning that Caesar had crossed, engaged him by land. Caesar lost most of his fleet and was nearly destroyed himself; but for the moment he got safely to the mainland. He was distressed because his army was cut off on the island, and did not take heart until a fish leapt up out of the sea of its own accord and fell at his feet; for the seers explained this as showing that he would enslave the sea. Caesar's army was besieged, and since supplies ran out and there was no one to help, Cornificius, its commander, burned the vessels that had survived the sea battle, and led the army off himself towards Mylae. They suffered much harm from the enemy following them, both on the rest of the march and more at the crossings of the rivers. They suffered so for three days, and on the last the enemy harmed them in every way, Sextus too having joined them. And all would have perished, had not the enemy been forced to leave them alone against their will. For Agrippa, having won the sea battle, crossed to Sicily and sent grain and help to the army. Sextus, expecting Agrippa himself to come there and afraid, withdrew in haste, so that he left some baggage and supplies in his fortification; fed on these, Cornificius's men went off to Agrippa; and Caesar won them back with praise and gifts.

blocks: After this, when Caesar came to Sicily, Sextus encamped facing him near the Artemisium. While they sat facing each other and skirmishing, Gallus joined Sextus with forces, and Lepidus joined Caesar. Gallus strengthened Sextus, but Lepidus quarrelled with Caesar, wishing to manage everything jointly with him on equal terms, while Caesar treated him in everything as a subordinate. So he inclined to Sextus and negotiated with him in secret. Suspecting this, Caesar hurried to come to battle with Sextus before anything new arose. A sea battle broke out on the sea, and on land the infantry of both stood drawn up; while the sea battle went on for a long time evenly balanced, both infantry armies watched in anguish; when Sextus's men were routed, the one side raised the paean, the other lamented. Sextus's infantry went towards Messana, as having been beaten along with the fleet, while Caesar received those of the defeated who came ashore and burned the vessels that ran aground. Meanwhile Demochares killed himself, and Apollodorus went over to Caesar. Others did this too, and Gallus and all the horsemen with him, and some of the infantry.

Sextus, despairing after this, took his daughter and others, put his money and the most valuable of his other things into the best of the surviving ships and sailed away by night; and no one pursued him, both because he sailed off secretly and because Caesar was in great confusion. For Lepidus went against Messana, was received into it, and burned some things and plundered others; then, afraid when Caesar came up, he encamped on a strong hill, complained of everything in which he thought himself slighted, demanded what had been given him under the first conspiracy, and laid claim to Sicily as having subdued it; and he dealt with Caesar about this through messengers, having the forces he had brought from Libya and all those left behind in Messana. Caesar, trusting in his arms, at once set out against him with a few men. Thought to be coming on some peaceful business because of the fewness of those with him, he was received into the camp. But when he said nothing about reconciliation, Lepidus's men were provoked and killed some of his men, and he himself escaped by getting help. After this he came against them again with his whole army, and besieged them, shutting them up in their entrenchment. Afraid of being taken, out of respect for Lepidus they did not go over to Caesar all together, but came over to him a few at a time. And so Lepidus too came to him as a suppliant in dark clothing, as if of his own will. He was deprived of his power and had to live under guard in Italy. Of those who had served Sextus, Caesar punished some and let others go; and of the cities he pardoned those that had come over to him willingly, and punished those that had resisted him.

The soldiers mutinied and grew bold, and gathering together each demanded what he wanted. When Caesar paid little attention to them, since there was no enemy present, they threatened him. When they achieved nothing, they demanded with anger and shouting to be discharged from service; for they hoped to get what they asked by threatening to desert. Caesar, thinking that a ruler ought not to yield to his subjects under compulsion, said their request was reasonable, and discharged first those who had served with him against Antony, and when the others too pressed him, he discharged those who had served ten years, saying that he would no longer make use of any of them, however much they wished it. Hearing this, they said nothing more, but began to obey him.

Then he settled affairs in Sicily, and sending forces won over both Libyas without a fight, and those in Rome voted him many honours. Sextus, putting out from Messana, and suspecting he would be pursued or even betrayed by those with him, gave out that he would sail across the open sea, but put out the beacon that flagships show so that the others may follow them, and sailed to Cephallenia; where the rest, driven ashore by a storm, by chance joined him again. So he called them together, took off his general's dress, and said among other things that if they stayed together they would not escape notice, but scattered they would escape more easily. From this, as they went off in different directions, he himself crossed to Asia, meaning to go to Antony. But learning in Lesbos that Antony had marched against the Medes, and that Caesar and Lepidus had gone to war, and hoping to succeed to Antony's command, he put on his general's dress again and prepared to seize the opposite coast. When Antony then learned of his doings and promised him safety and goodwill if he laid down his arms, he agreed, but did not do as he had promised, but kept hold of affairs as before and negotiated with the Parthians. Learning this, Antony sent the fleet against him with Marcus Titius. He in fear sent envoys to Antony. When Antony said he would not make a treaty unless he received his ships and the rest of his force, he put the heavier baggage into the ships, burned them, and set off inland. Antony's men pursued, caught him and took him alive. Learning this, Antony at once in anger wrote that he should be killed, but later repented and wrote that he should be saved. The second letter-bearer arrived before the first, and the man holding him, receiving later the order for his death, and either thinking it really was the second or pretending not to know the truth, put Sextus Pompey to death.

From this, as they went off in different directions, he himself crossed to Asia, meaning to go to Antony. But learning in Lesbos that Antony had marched against the Medes, and that Caesar and Lepidus had gone to war, and hoping to succeed to Antony's command, he put on his general's dress again and prepared to seize the opposite coast. When Antony then learned of his doings and promised him safety and goodwill if he laid down his arms, he agreed, but did not do as he had promised, but kept hold of affairs as before and negotiated with the Parthians. Learning this, Antony sent the fleet against him with Marcus Titius. He in fear sent envoys to Antony. When Antony said he would not make a treaty unless he received his ships and the rest of his force, he put the heavier baggage into the ships, burned them, and set off inland. Antony's men pursued, caught him and took him alive. Learning this, Antony at once in anger wrote that he should be killed, but later repented and wrote that he should be saved. The second letter-bearer arrived before the first, and the man holding him, receiving later the order for his death, and either thinking it really was the second or pretending not to know the truth, put Sextus Pompey to death.

blocks: Such was his end; and Antony defeated the Parthians through Ventidius. For their king Pacorus fell in the war, and of the barbarians some were killed in the battle and others fled, and Ventidius brought the cities of Syria under him. Then he marched against Antiochus, who reigned over Commagene. While he was there Antony suddenly came upon him, and not only was not pleased at his successes, but envied him and removed him from his command, and himself attacked Antiochus and shut him up in Samosata. When he achieved nothing by besieging him, he made terms of peace and set off for Italy.

Orodes, king of the Parthians, having become very old, and giving up the kingship in his grief for Pacorus, handed the rule to Phraates, the eldest of his other sons. He, being most impious, treacherously murdered his brothers, killed his father himself when he was distressed over them, and destroyed the best of the others.

Antony sent envoys to the Parthians about peace, but prepared for war, so that he might catch them unprepared because of their hope of a settlement. Learning that the Mede had gone to help the Parthian as an ally, he left the baggage and much of the army behind with Statianus to follow, and himself hurried on with the horsemen and the light infantry, as if to subdue the Medes' land at once. But the Parthian and the Mede fell on Statianus and the army with him unexpectedly and slaughtered them all; Antony hurried to help them, but came too late and found only the dead. Not long after he engaged the barbarians and routed them, but did them no great harm. Besieging the Mede's royal city, he was rather besieged himself, since supplies ran out for his army, and when they went out to gather them they were badly harmed by the barbarians lying in wait for them.

While Antony was in this state, Phraates prompted some men and through them persuaded him to send to negotiate for terms; and the Parthian, after heaping reproaches on those sent, said he would make no treaty unless they broke camp at once. And Antony withdrew. While he was waiting for the treaty, the Medes burned the siege engines and scattered the earthworks. The Parthians fell on them suddenly and did much terrible harm. So when he knew he had been deceived, he tried to go off to Armenia. Going away through unknown country, he met many difficulties. And all those with him would have perished, having fallen into an ambush and being shot at with thick showers of arrows, had they not formed the tortoise by locking shields.

The tortoise is made like this. The baggage and the light-armed are placed in the middle of the army; of the heavy infantry, those using oblong, hollow shields are placed round the outside, and encircle the others facing outwards with their arms held about them, while those carrying flat shields crowd together in the middle and raise them above themselves and the rest, so that nothing but shields can be seen over the whole formation, and all are under shelter from the missiles because of the closeness of the arrangement. It is so close-packed that men can even walk on top of it. Such is the shape of this formation, and for this reason it got the name of tortoise, because of its strength and its good cover. They use it in two ways: either they advance with it against some fort and assault the wall, or, surrounded by archers, they sometimes all crouch so as to seem exhausted, and when the enemy come near they suddenly rise, and so terrify and confuse them. This is what happened then. For being shot at with many missiles, as has been said, they formed the locked shields of the tortoise and rested their left knees on the ground. The barbarians, thinking they had fallen from their wounds, laid aside their bows, drew their swords and came at them to cut them down. But the Romans rose up and fell on them, armed men on the unprotected, prepared men on the unsuspecting, heavy infantry on archers, Romans on barbarians, and cut them down.

Antony suffered nothing more terrible from the enemy, but was worn down by cold. For it was winter, and the borderlands of Armenia through which he went are always icy; so that many of his men perished. So he made up to the Armenian and flattered him, though he was angry with him. Distributing money to the survivors of the army, he went off to Egypt to Cleopatra. For her sake he was greatly slandered by his countrymen, both because he had children by her and because he had given her many lands. For he was so enslaved to his love of her and her spells that he even ordered his wife Octavia, who was coming to him from Rome, to go back and not come to him.

blocks: Caesar went to Sicily, but having been delayed there by the winter, and learning that some of the peoples subject to the Romans had revolted during his absence, he came back and prepared against them, and won over and subdued some himself and others through others. Then he marched against the Pannonians too, who live near Dalmatia along the Ister itself from Noricum to Moesia in Europe. They live a hard life, being badly off for land and climate, growing neither wine nor olive oil, but eating and drinking barley and millet alike; but they are thought the bravest of men. Some of the Greeks called them Paeonians, not knowing the truth; for the people of the Paeonians is near Rhodope and Macedonia itself, while these are called Pannonians both by others and by themselves. Caesar marched against them then, came to battle with them many times, and later won them over by agreement.

Antony, contriving to take vengeance on the Armenian, left no stone unturned, as the proverb has it, until he induced him to come into his camp. When he came in, he seized him and kept him under guard unbound, and took him round the forts where his treasures were stored, eager to get them. When he achieved nothing (for the Armenians chose instead the eldest of his sons, Artaxes, as king), he bound him in silver chains, as if granting him this honour as a king; and he seized all Armenia, since Artaxes withdrew to the Parthians after being beaten in battle. Antony left the armies in Armenia, and himself went back to Egypt, taking the Armenian there with his wife and children; and he gave the plunder to Cleopatra and brought the Armenian with his family to her in golden chains. They neither begged her nor bowed down to her, but addressed her by name.

After this Antony ordered Cleopatra to be called queen of kings, and called her Caesar's wife, and her son truly his child, so as to discredit Caesar Octavius as his adopted and not his legitimate son; and he assigned lands to them. To his own children by Cleopatra, called Ptolemy and Alexander, he allotted many others. While doing this he wrote to the senate that he would lay down his command and put affairs in its hands and the people's, not meaning it, but so that by the hopes he raised they might either force Caesar, who was present, to lay down his arms, or hate him if he disobeyed.

Going as far as the Araxes, as if marching against the Parthians, he was content with an agreement with the Mede. For they agreed to fight as allies of each other, the one against the Parthians, the other against Caesar, and exchanged soldiers. The Mede received part of Armenia, newly acquired, from Antony, and Antony his daughter Iotape, to marry his son Alexander. On this he set out for Ionia and Greece for the war with Caesar. The Mede, with the Romans fighting alongside him, defeated the Parthians and Artaxes when they attacked him. But when Antony called back his own soldiers and kept the Mede's, he was beaten in turn and captured. And so Armenia was lost along with Media.

The Romans had been robbed of the free state, but they did not slide into open monarchy until Sextus perished, the peoples that had revolted were enslaved, and the Parthian made no move. For then Antony and Caesar openly turned against each other, and the people were utterly enslaved. These were the causes of the war they put forward. Antony charged Caesar with having appropriated the land and the force of Lepidus, and those of Sextus, and demanded half of these and of the soldiers he had enlisted from Italy, which was his too; and Caesar charged him with holding Egypt and other places that had not been allotted to him, and with killing Sextus, whom he said he would willingly have spared himself, and with having seized the Armenian by deceit and put him in chains, and so brought disrepute on the Romans; and he too demanded half of the spoils, and brought up before all Cleopatra and her children and the gifts made to them, and above all he blamed him for bringing Caesarion into the family of

blocks: Caesar. These, then, were the charges they brought against each other. For a while they did not openly arm against each other, until Gnaeus Domitius and Gaius Sosius, who were of Antony's party, became consuls. Then they were openly at war. For Sosius on the first of the month said much in praise of Antony and much against Caesar. At that time Caesar left the city, making up another reason; but afterwards he came back, set a guard of soldiers about himself, spoke moderately on his own behalf, made many charges against Antony and Sosius, and promised to convict Antony by documents. So the consuls, neither daring to answer nor bearing to keep silent, left the city and went off to Antony, and not a few of the other senators went with them. And again others left Antony and came over to Caesar, because he had given up his marriage with Octavia and because they resented Cleopatra. Learning from them both Antony's other affairs and about his will and with whom it was kept, Caesar took it and read it in public, doing a most lawless thing. Because of what was written, even those most attached to Antony showed such anger that they took from him the consulship and all his other power, and voted safety and praise to those with him if they deserted him; and they declared war openly on Cleopatra, which was really aimed at Antony; for they knew he would endure anything for her.

For she had so enslaved him that she was called queen and mistress by him, had Roman soldiers in her bodyguard, and all their shields had her name written on them. She went into the forum with him, arranged festivals with him, examined lawsuits with him, and rode with him; and in the cities she was carried in a litter, while Antony followed on foot with her eunuchs. He was painted and sculpted with her, he being called Osiris and Dionysus, and she Selene and Isis. So he seemed to have been driven out of his mind by her through sorcery. And she bewitched and bound not him alone but also those powerful with him, so that she even hoped to rule the Romans, and made it her greatest prayer and oath to give judgement on the Capitol. Antony sometimes wore a scimitar at his side, and used dress contrary to ancestral custom. For him, then, as consul and general of the Romans, dress outside ancestral custom was counted a charge; but how could one free the present emperors of the Romans from blame and accusation, who change their dress contrary to ancestral custom, and not sometimes, but always wear barbarian clothing?

So matters fell out between Caesar and Antony; and they prepared for the war, each taking on many allies. Much was rumoured among the people, and many signs too occurred. A monkey came into the temple of Ceres during some rite and threw everything inside into confusion; many boys in Rome gathered with no one ordering it and fought one another, some as Caesar's men, others as fighting for Antony, and those bearing Antony's name were beaten; a stone statue of him gave out blood; fire destroyed the temple of Ceres and another temple of Hope; and other such things happened. None of these frightened them; but Antony set out as if to make war on them in Italy unexpectedly, but coming to Corcyra and sailing from there to the Peloponnese, he wintered at Patrae himself, and sent his soldiers off in every direction; while Caesar put out from Brundisium, but meeting a storm and suffering from it, he went back.

blocks: When spring had begun, Antony made no move anywhere; for his rowers, being a mixture from many peoples and wintering far from him, had not been trained and had been reduced by disease and desertions; and Agrippa, having taken Methone by assault, watched for the landings of the merchant ships, and making descents now here, now there, on Greece, disturbed him greatly. Caesar gathered at Brundisium all the soldiers, and all the senators and knights of any influence, the former so that they might help him, the latter so that they might not make any revolt when left on their own, and so that he might show that he had the greatest and strongest part of the Romans of one mind with him. With them he crossed the Ionian Sea, took Corcyra, which had been abandoned by its guards, and put in at the harbour called Sweet (it is so called because it is made sweet by the river flowing into it), and from there sailed to Actium. When no one sailed out against him or came to talk with him, though he challenged his opponents either to battle or to an agreement, he occupied the place where Nicopolis now is, and from there lay in wait against Actium by land and sea. Antony's men had seized Actium first and fortified it with towers on both sides.

When Antony learned of Caesar's arrival, he hurried with his men to Actium; but he did not fight at once, though Caesar tried in every way to draw him into battle, but used skirmishes for many days, until he had gathered his armies. Caesar sent an army into Greece and Macedonia, so as to draw Antony off there even against his will. Agrippa sailed suddenly against Leucas and the vessels in it and took them, captured Patrae and won over Corinth. Marcus Titius and Statilius Taurus made a sudden sally and caught Antony's cavalry, and won over Philadelphus, king of Paphlagonia; and Gnaeus Domitius and others went over to Caesar. So Antony, afraid that all those he had sent into Macedonia and Thrace might join Caesar, set out towards them.

Meanwhile a sea battle took place, and in the first attack Antony's men routed Caesar's, who were few; but when Agrippa, to whom Caesar's whole fleet had been entrusted, happened to arrive, Antony's men not only got nothing out of their victory but were destroyed. For this reason Antony came back, and was defeated in a cavalry fight with Caesar's advance guard. And since his supplies too had begun to run out, he held a council whether they should stay where they were and risk all, or move away and draw out the war in time. Others advised other things, but Cleopatra prevailed with her advice that the most important places be given over to garrisons and the rest sail away with them to Egypt. She came to this opinion alarmed by signs and fearing the despondency and sickness of the army. And she frightened Antony too. Yet they planned to sail off neither secretly nor openly as fugitives, so as not to throw the allies into fear, but as if preparing for a sea battle; and so they chose the best of the vessels, since the rowers had been reduced by death and desertion, burned the rest, and at night secretly put all the most valuable things aboard and made them ready to sail. Antony addressed the soldiers and encouraged them for the sea battle. And so he put all the leading men of those with him aboard the ships, so that they might not start anything, as Dellius and some others had done by deserting, and put aboard great numbers of archers, slingers and heavy infantry. For he had few triremes; the rest of his ships were quadriremes and ten-banked ships.

Caesar watched their preparation and made ready, and learning their purpose from others and from Dellius, he gathered the army and urged them to battle with a speech. Meanwhile, when a violent rain and a great squall fell on Antony's fleet, Caesar took heart and watched for their sailing out. When Antony's men drew up but did not advance, he set out as if to attack them where they stood or to make them withdraw; and when they neither sallied nor turned back, but stayed where they were packed close in formation, he held off for some time; then they closed and fought at sea.

The sea battle was evenly matched and undecided for a long time, when Cleopatra's sixty ships, at a signal given by her, raised their sails to sail away and made for the open sea. Antony, seeing Cleopatra's ship sailing off, forgot everything, went across into a quinquereme and pursued the woman who had ruined him and would ruin him further. She, recognising his ship's signal, waited; and taken up into her ship, he went alone to the prow and sat in silence. He spent three days like this, but when they were at Taenarum, her women friends brought them together and persuaded them to dine and sleep together. Antony's fleet, after his withdrawal, held out until the tenth hour; then fire was brought against the vessels on Caesar's order, and some were burned and others taken; for about three hundred ships are said to have been taken.
