And so he put all the leading men of those with him aboard the ships, so that they might not start anything, as Dellius and some others had done by deserting, and put aboard great numbers of archers, slingers and heavy infantry. For he had few triremes; the rest of his ships were quadriremes and ten-banked ships. Caesar watched their preparation and made ready, and learning their purpose from others and from Dellius, he gathered the army and urged them to battle with a speech. Meanwhile, when a violent rain and a great squall fell on Antony's fleet, Caesar took heart and watched for their sailing out. When Antony's men drew up but did not advance, he set out as if to attack them where they stood or to make them withdraw; and when they neither sallied nor turned back, but stayed where they were packed close in formation, he held off for some time; then they closed and fought at sea. The sea battle was evenly matched and undecided for a long time, when Cleopatra's sixty ships, at a signal given by her, raised their sails to sail away and made for the open sea. Antony, seeing Cleopatra's ship sailing off, forgot everything, went across into a quinquereme and pursued the woman who had ruined him and would ruin him further. She, recognising his ship's signal, waited; and taken up into her ship, he went alone to the prow and sat in silence. He spent three days like this, but when they were at Taenarum, her women friends brought them together and persuaded them to dine and sleep together. Antony's fleet, after his withdrawal, held out until the tenth hour; then fire was brought against the vessels on Caesar's order, and some were burned and others taken; for about three hundred ships are said to have been taken.

blocks: Such was the end of the sea battle, on the second of September; and then all power came round to Caesar alone, so that from this time his monarchy is reckoned. He founded a city on the site of his camp, calling it Nicopolis. He also set up bronze statues of a man and a donkey. For it is said that while it was still night on the day the sea battle took place, as he came out of his tent and went round the ships, a man driving a donkey met him, and when asked his name said: "My name is Eutychus, and the donkey's Nicon." These statues were later brought to Byzantium and set up in the hippodrome.

Antony's infantry and cavalry held together for seven days after his flight, and at last went over to the victor. Some, especially of the Romans, went off to Antony, and the allies went home. Caesar hurried to Italy, afraid that there might be some revolt; but coming to Brundisium he went no further; for the senate, the knights, most of the people and others gathered there. Having done there what he thought fit, he set out again for Greece. Taking his ships across the Isthmus of the Peloponnese because of the winter, he quickly reached Asia.

Cleopatra in her flight hurried to reach Egypt, afraid that there might be some revolt. Arriving there she collected money from every quarter and gathered forces. Antony sailed off to Libya. When the army he had there too revolted from him, he set out to kill himself, but was stopped by his friends, and went back to Alexandria. They prepared as if to make war, but also sent men to Caesar with proposals for peace, and money for those with him. And Cleopatra, without Antony's knowledge, sent him a golden sceptre, a crown of the same and a royal chair, as if giving him the rule through them. He took the gifts, making them an omen, but gave Antony no answer, and told Cleopatra that if she killed Antony or drove him out he would give her safety and leave her rule untouched. Meanwhile the Arabians burned the triremes that had been built for Cleopatra in the Arabian Gulf, and the peoples and princes all refused their help.

Antony and Cleopatra, hearing what Caesar had sent them, sent again, she promising to give him much money, he reminding him of their friendship and kinship; and he offered to kill himself, if by this Cleopatra might be saved. But again no answer was given to Antony, while to Cleopatra Caesar again made many threats and promises. Afraid that Cleopatra might destroy the money, which was very great, and which she had gathered into the tomb she had built in the palace (for she threatened to burn it all with herself if she failed to get what she wanted), he sent Thyrsus, a freedman of his own, to say many kind things to her, and that Caesar was in love with her. So Caesar took Pelusium too, by force in appearance, but in secret betrayed by Cleopatra. For hearing that he loved her, and longing for this, she at once gave up Pelusium to him.

Antony, who was away, learning of the capture of Pelusium, came back and met Caesar before Alexandria, and engaging his horsemen, who were tired from the march, he won. Taking heart from this, and having shot notes into Caesar's camp with arrows promising the soldiers much money, he engaged the infantry too, and was defeated. Worsted, he turned to the fleet and prepared to fight at sea or to sail to Iberia; but Cleopatra, learning this, made the ships desert, and herself suddenly went into her tomb, as if afraid of Antony, who suspected that he was being betrayed by her. Two maids and one eunuch were there with her. Going in, she shut the doors securely, and sent men to tell Antony that she was dead. Believing it, he told one of those present to kill him. When that man drew his sword and killed himself, he said: "Well done, Eros (for this was the man's name), for teaching me what I must do"; and striking himself through the belly, he let himself fall on the couch. The wound did not bring a quick death. When there was an uproar, Cleopatra heard it. She did not open the doors, but leaning out from above (for the part near the roof had not yet been finished), and learning what had happened, she ordered him to be brought to the tomb. He, learning that she was still alive, asked to be carried there, and being carried he was hauled up with ropes and cords by her and two of her maids. Receiving him smeared with blood and dying hard, she tore her robes over him, beat her breast and tore it with her hands. He asked for wine to drink, and having drunk and spoken a little with Cleopatra, he died.

Caesar, when Antony's death was reported to him, wept, and reading Antony's letters to his friends, he condemned himself, since Antony had asked for what was fair and just, while he had been harsh and arrogant in his answers.

blocks: He sent Proculeius to Cleopatra, wishing to take her alive, thinking it a great thing for his glory to lead her in the triumph. She talked with him standing inside doors that were securely shut. When he had studied the place and reported to Caesar, Gallus was sent to talk with her, and he drew out the talk at the doors on purpose, while Proculeius got in through a window by a ladder without being noticed, with two servants. When one of the women shut in with her cried out, "Wretched Cleopatra, you are taken alive," she set out to stab herself (for she wore a small dagger at her side), but Proculeius ran to her, held her, took away the dagger, and searched her in case she was hiding some poison. Caesar sent Epaphroditus, a freedman, ordering him to keep her alive, taking great care. Caesar himself drove into the city. Antony was buried by Cleopatra lavishly and royally.

When she got fevers (for her breast was inflamed and ulcerated), she refrained from food, so as to be released from life by this. Suspecting this, Caesar threatened her and made her afraid for her children, and at these, as at siege engines, she gave way, and accepted food and care. A little later Caesar himself came to talk with her. She was lying simply on a pallet in a single tunic, and leapt up and fell at his feet, her voice trembling and her face wasted. When Caesar told her to lie down and sat beside her, she begged him like one clinging hard to life; at last she handed him an inventory of her treasures. He, thinking she loved life, was pleased, and saying he would treat her more splendidly than she could hope, thought he had deceived her, but rather was deceived himself. For learning that Caesar had decided to go away by land through Syria, and would send her to Rome after three days, she begged Caesar to let her pour libations for Antony. When he allowed it, she was carried to the tomb and lamented much; then, having garlanded the coffin and kissed it, she ordered a bath to be made ready for her. Having bathed and lain down, she ate a splendid meal. And someone came from the country bringing a basket full of figs. When the guards asked what he was carrying, he showed them the figs; and they told him to take them in. After the meal Cleopatra sent Caesar a sealed tablet. When Caesar read it, with her prayers asking to be buried with Antony, he quickly understood what had been done, and sent men in haste to see what had happened. They ran and found her dead on a golden couch, adorned royally. Of her women, Iras was dying at her feet, while Charmion, already heavy-headed and reeling, was arranging the diadem about her head. When someone said, "This is fine, Charmion," she said: "Very fine indeed, and fitting for the descendant of so many kings." Saying this, she too fell beside the couch.

She is said to have died by the bite of an asp brought with the figs. Others say the asp was kept in a water jar, and when Cleopatra provoked it and enraged it with a golden distaff, it sprang and fastened on her arm. It is also said that she had poison in a hollow scraper and hid the scraper in her hair. Dio says it was a pin with which she bound up her hair, smeared with a poison that has the power, if it touches blood, to kill very quickly and painlessly. So she perished, but the truth was not known, except that two small, faint punctures were seen on her arm, while no sign of poison broke out on her body, nor was the creature found, unless, as some said, they saw some tracks of it by the sea, where the room looked out and had windows. It has been guessed that she died of an asp because she had earlier been collecting many deadly poisons and trying them on those condemned to death; and she found that the quick ones brought a painful death, while the gentler ones worked over time; and only the bite of the asp, without convulsion, brought on a sleepy torpor with a soft sweat and a dimming of the senses, and easily deadened the body.

Caesar, hearing of her death, was amazed, and applied remedies and Psylli to the body. The Psylli are men (for a woman is not born with this power), who can suck out every poison of every reptile before the one bitten or wounded dies, and are not harmed themselves, and cure the one poisoned. They are born of one another, and test their children either by throwing them in with snakes, or by throwing their swaddling clothes on some venomous creatures; for these do the child no harm and are numbed by his clothing. Caesar was grieved at the woman's death and admired her nobility, and ordered her to be buried with Antony lavishly and royally. Her maids too received an honourable burial at his order. Cleopatra died at thirty-nine, having reigned twenty-two of these years, and having ruled with Antony more than fourteen; Antony, some say, was six years past fifty, others three. Caesar put to death Antony's son Antyllus, the son of Fulvia, and Cleopatra's son Caesarion.

So Antony and Cleopatra departed; and Caesar saw the body of King Alexander and touched it. But he would not look at the bodies of the Ptolemies, though the Alexandrians wished to show them to him too, saying: "I wished to see a king, not corpses." Nor was he persuaded to visit Apis, saying: "I am used to worshipping gods, not oxen." He made Egypt tributary, found a vast amount of money and took it all. Having managed affairs there as he thought fit, he went off through Syria to Asia and wintered there. The Romans, both then and earlier, when he won the sea battle, voted many things in his honour. In the summer he crossed to Greece and to Italy. When he entered the city the Romans offered sacrifices, and the consul sacrificed oxen, which had never before been done for anyone else. He celebrated the victory for three days. All the processions were splendid; for so much spoil had been gathered that it sufficed for all. An image of Cleopatra on a couch was carried by, with an asp clinging to her arm, and with the other captives her children, Alexander, also called Helios, and Cleopatra, also called Selene. After them all Caesar drove in. And there were shows for many days.

blocks: At this time Marcus Crassus, sent into Macedonia, Thrace and Greece, made war on many peoples, and conquered some and won over others. These peoples were of old called Moesians and Getae, living in all the land between the Haemus and the Ister; but as time went on some of them were called by other names too. After this, all that the river Savus, which flows into the Ister above Dalmatia, Macedonia and Thrace, divides from Pannonia came to bear the name of Moesia. Among them are many other peoples, and those called Triballi and those called Dardanians.

These, then, were the deeds and sufferings of the Romans in seven hundred and twenty-five years under the kingship, the free state and the dynasts; and from this they began again to be ruled strictly by a monarch, though Caesar planned to lay down his arms and entrust affairs to the senate and people. But sharing his intention with Agrippa and Maecenas, to whom he entrusted his secrets, he found Agrippa's opinion turning him away from monarchy; but Maecenas advised the very opposite, saying that he had already been managing the monarchy for a long time, and that one of two things was necessary, either to remain as he was or to perish by giving it up. For it was impossible for those who had once ruled alone to live safely as private men. He also suggested how he might rule safely and justly, and inoffensively too, stretching out a long speech on the subject. To all this he added: "If whatever you would wish another ruling over you to do, you do yourself of your own accord, you will make no mistake and will succeed in everything, and you will live most pleasantly and most safely."

So they advised Caesar thus; and he admired and praised both, but chose the advice of Maecenas; and he did not lay down the monarchy, and he took the title of imperator, not that given in the old way to some for victories (for he had often been called by this), but the one signifying royal power. The next year he was consul for the sixth time, with Agrippa as his colleague, whom he honoured exceedingly, and married to his sister Octavia. Caesar was called leader of the senate, as was the custom in the strict free state; he did many other things in honour of Rome and the citizens, gave money generously to many of the senators who had become poor, and burned the old bonds of those owing to the public treasury; and all that had been done unjustly under Lepidus and Antony he annulled by a single edict. Being praised for this, so that he might be honoured the more, he desired to receive the monarchy from willing men, so as not to seem to rule the unwilling. Having prepared those most attached to him, he came into the senate in his seventh consulship; and saying that he renounced the monarchy and was putting everything under the best men, he begged them to accept his laying down of the monarchy. Of the senate, some knew his intention and others suspected it; some did not wish to expose him, others were afraid. So some pretended to believe him and others were forced to; and they compelled him, as it seemed, to rule alone.

So he confirmed his leadership from the senate and the people, and took on the whole care of public affairs. Of the provinces he gave back to the senate the weaker, as peaceful and without wars, and kept the stronger himself, as perhaps dangerous and risky, in appearance so that the senate might enjoy the finest part of the empire and the labours might lie on him, but in truth so that they might be unarmed and unable to fight, while he had arms and maintained soldiers. So that he might not seem to have monarchical ideas, he accepted the command of the provinces assigned to him for ten years. For he promised to settle them in that time, making this promise in word. For when the ten years were over, another five years, then five again, after this ten, and another ten again, were voted him five times, so that by the succession of ten-year terms he ruled alone for life. And from this the emperors after him, though appointed for life, still always held a festival every ten years, as if then renewing their leadership.

Many things were voted then too in Caesar's honour, and he was surnamed Augustus. For he wished to be called Romulus, but perceiving that he was suspected from this of desiring kingship (for the Romans endured in fact the condition of those ruled by kings, but resented the name), he refrained from the name and chose to be called Augustus, as being something more than human. For all the most sacred and venerable things are called augusta. From this they also called him Sebastos, from sebazesthai, rendering it in Greek somehow, as one revered. The residence of the emperors was named the palace, because Caesar lived on the hill called the Palatine, where Faustulus, who brought up Romulus, lived, and had his headquarters there. For this reason, even if the emperor lodges somewhere else, his lodging has the name of palace. All the power given of old to the consuls, the tribunes, the censors and all the others has been given to the emperors; and besides this it was granted them to be released from the laws, that is, to be free from every constraint of the laws and liable to none of them.

For all the most sacred and venerable things are called augusta. From this they also called him Sebastos, from sebazesthai, rendering it in Greek somehow, as one revered. The residence of the emperors was named the palace, because Caesar lived on the hill called the Palatine, where Faustulus, who brought up Romulus, lived, and had his headquarters there. For this reason, even if the emperor lodges somewhere else, his lodging has the name of palace. All the power given of old to the consuls, the tribunes, the censors and all the others has been given to the emperors; and besides this it was granted them to be released from the laws, that is, to be free from every constraint of the laws and liable to none of them.

blocks: When Caesar was named Augustus, no small sign happened that night; for the Tiber flooded and covered the whole plain of Rome, so that it was sailed over. The seers foretold from this that he would grow great and would hold the whole city in his hand. He did the other business of his office more eagerly, as ruling willing men, and made laws. Yet he did not make all his laws on his own judgement, but some he set out in public, so that he might correct them if anything did not please; and he urged anyone who knew something better than he to advise him on everything. He took as counsellors for six months the consuls, one from each of the other magistracies, and fifteen from the body of the senators, so that through them what was deliberated might be shared with all. Sometimes he also judged with them. For the senate judged by itself too, and dealt with embassies and heralds. The people gathered for the elections, but nothing was done that did not please him. Of those who were to hold office, he himself nominated some, and put others to the public, taking care that they were not appointed unfit, or through canvassing or bribery. And he brought peoples under the empire of the Romans, some through himself and some through others.

Aelius Gallus, the governor of Egypt, marched at this time against the Arabia called Happy, of which Sabus was king. No one of the enemy stood before him, yet he did not advance without toil. For the desert, the sun and the water, which had a strange nature, wore them down greatly, so that most of the army perished. The disease, attacking the head, dried it up, and killed many at once, while in the survivors it went down to the legs, passing over all the body between, and maimed them. There was no remedy except anointing with olive oil mixed with wine; and very few had these; for the land bears neither, and they had not provided plenty of them beforehand. In this distress the barbarians too attacked them, recovered the places they had lost before, and drove the survivors out of the country.

Augustus, in his eleventh consulship, fell so ill that he had no hope of recovery, and made his arrangements as if about to die; he appointed no successor, but gave Piso the forces and public revenues written in a book, and handed his ring to Agrippa. One Antonius Musa restored him from this bad state by cold baths and cold drinks. For this he received money from him and from the senate, and was allowed to wear gold rings, though a freedman, and exemption from taxes was granted to him and to those of his profession, both living and to come. Having recovered in this way, he brought his will into the senate and offered to have it read, showing that he had left no successor to the rule; but no one read it.

The next year there was famine and plague in all Italy, and the Romans, thinking these had happened for no other reason than that they did not have Augustus as consul then too, wished to appoint him dictator, and shut the senate in the senate house and forced it to vote this. They came to him begging him to be named dictator and overseer of the grain supply. He accepted the care of the grain, but would not take the dictatorship, and when neither by reasoning with them nor by begging could he persuade them, he tore his clothes; for rightly and wisely he guarded against the hatred and envy of the title, having power and honour above the dictators. When some formed a plot against him, they and their fellow conspirators were condemned in their absence as if to be exiled, and not long after were slaughtered.

blocks: After this he went to Sicily. While he was there the Roman people, electing the consuls, fell into strife, so that it was shown from this too that they could not be saved under popular government. For they caused such an uproar and threw everything into such confusion that Augustus was called back by the sensible. Augustus, indignant at this, and neither able always to give his time to Rome nor daring to leave it without a ruler, looked for someone to set over it. He judged Agrippa most fit for this, but wishing to give him greater dignity too, so that he might rule them more easily, he forced him to leave his wife and marry his own daughter Julia, and sent him at once to Rome for the marriage and to manage the city; among other reasons because Maecenas said to Caesar: "You have made him so great that he must either become your son-in-law or be killed." Agrippa, finding affairs in Rome swelling, settled them. Augustus, having managed affairs in Sicily, crossed to Greece, went through the Greek lands and sailed to Samos; wintering there, he went to Asia in the spring, arranged affairs there and in Bithynia, and enslaved the people of Cyzicus because they had scourged and killed some Romans; and he did the same to the Tyrians and the Sidonians when he was in Syria. Julia gave birth to Gaius. Augustus, having given governments of provinces to some, went back to Samos, wintered there again and managed much business; for very many embassies came there; and the Indians then made friends, sending gifts, among them tigers, then seen by the Romans for the first time.

Again there was strife in Rome and slaughter over the consular elections. Learning this, and seeing that there would be no end to the evil, Caesar hurried to Rome and appointed a consul himself. Since everyone was preparing to go out to meet him, he entered the city by night; which he did often both in leaving the town and returning, so as to be a trouble to no one. Then, being asked, he was elected overseer of morals and censor for five years, and received the honour of the consuls for life. When some were accused of plotting against him and Agrippa, he punished some others, but Lepidus, though he hated him for other reasons and because his son had plotted against him, he would not kill, but insulted and mocked him in one way or another.

He made other laws too, and that those who had bribed anyone for office should be barred from office for five years; he set penalties for unmarried men and women, and rewards for marriage and the begetting of children. And since the males were far more numerous than the females of good birth, he allowed any who wished, except senators, to marry freedwomen, ordering their children to be legitimate. When some, by betrothing themselves to infant girls, enjoyed the privileges of married men but did not perform the work of them, he ordered that no betrothal should be valid after which a man did not marry within two years, that is, the girl must be at least ten when betrothed; for twelve years is reckoned the full age of marriage for girls.

Agrippa had another son by Julia, named Lucius; Augustus adopted him and his brother Gaius, and at once declared them successors to the rule, so that he might be less plotted against. Once, when he was dining with Pollio, a very rich man but very cruel and harsh, and Pollio's cupbearer broke a crystal cup and was sentenced by his master to be thrown to the lampreys (for he kept such fish in tanks, trained to eat men, and threw them the slaves he put to death), Caesar asked to be let off the cupbearer's punishment; and when he did not persuade Pollio, he said: "Bring all the cups of this sort you have, or any other precious ones, so that I may use them." When they were brought he smashed them, saying it was so that men might not be punished like this because of them. Pollio, in view of the number lost, forgot the one cup, and unable to punish the cupbearer, since Augustus had done the same thing to many, kept quiet against his will.

Agrippa fell ill in Campania and died; Caesar came there, brought his body to Rome, set it out in the forum and read a speech over him, gave him a lavish funeral and buried him in his own tomb. Agrippa's death became a common grief for the Romans. For he was the best man of his time in other respects, and used Augustus's friendship for Augustus's good and the common benefit, and giving all his wisdom and courage to Caesar for the most useful ends, he spent all the power and honour he had from him on benefiting others; so he was neither burdensome to him nor envied by the others. When he died, since Augustus needed a helper in affairs, he took Tiberius even against his will; for Agrippa's sons, his grandsons, were still counted children. He took Tiberius's wife from him, who was a daughter of Agrippa by another wife, and betrothed Julia to him. Then through him, through Drusus and through Lucius Piso he brought many peoples under him. When the senate and people contributed money for statues of him, he set up none of himself, but made statues of Public Health, Concord and Peace. On the first day of the year itself, people came to him and gave, some more, some less, and he gave back as much again or more, not only to the senators but to the others too. His sister Octavia also died then, and he himself and Drusus spoke funeral speeches over her as she lay in state in public; and the senators put on mourning clothes, making the mourning public.

blocks: In the following year Drusus, as consul, marched out against some peoples. Having subdued some, he tried to go further. As he was going away a woman larger than human nature met him, who seemed to say to him: "Where are you hurrying, insatiable Drusus? It is not fated for you to see all these things. Go away; for the end of your life and of your deeds is already at hand." As he returned from there a disease fell on him, of which he died. The emperor, learning that he was ill, sent Tiberius in haste; he found him still breathing, and when he died brought him to Rome. He was set out in the forum, and Augustus and Tiberius praised him in funeral speeches.

After this Caesar brought in laws and allowed the senators to read them, so that they might say if anything did not please them or they thought of something better. He wished to be so much a man of the people that when one of those who had served with him asked him for help in court, he sent one of his friends to speak for him, as having no leisure himself; but when the man asking for help said in vexation, "But whenever you needed help, I did not send another in my place, but ran risks for you myself," he went to the court and spoke for him. When some magistrates were accused of having got their offices by bribery, he did not investigate and pretended not even to know of it; for he wished neither to punish anyone for this nor to pardon them if convicted. Though he gave up the leadership, as he said, when the second ten years had passed, he took it again, as if unwillingly, intending to march against the Celts. He himself stayed at home and sent Tiberius against them. When he came back he proclaimed him imperator, appointed him consul again and honoured him with a triumph. He renamed the month called Sextilis August.

When Maecenas died he grieved; for he had been helped by him in many other ways, and above all he was freed from his anger, when he gave way to it too much, and turned to greater mildness. A proof: once when he was judging and had pronounced many death sentences, Maecenas tried to push through those standing round and come near him, and being unable, wrote on a small paper, "Get up, executioner," and threw it into his lap; on reading it he at once rose and cancelled the sentences he had passed then. For he was not vexed at being corrected by his friends, but was glad. The greatest proof of Maecenas's virtue is that, while resisting Augustus's impulses, he was close to him and pleased all the others, and that, having very great power with him, so that he gave many honours and offices, he himself lived out his life in the rank of the knights and was not arrogant.

Augustus, seeing that Gaius and Lucius, his grandsons, whom he had also adopted, did not imitate his ways (for they not only lived too luxuriously but were also insolent), and wishing to make them more sober as private persons, gave Tiberius the tribunician power for five years and assigned him Armenia, which was being estranged after the death of Tigranes. He gained nothing from this. For the boys took it hard, thinking themselves slighted, and Tiberius feared their anger; so he did not go to Armenia, but went to Rhodes. The next year Augustus, consul for the twelfth time, enrolled Gaius among the youths, brought him into the senate house at the same time, declared him leader of the youth, and allowed him to become commander of a squadron. A year later Lucius too received all the honours that had been given to his brother Gaius. When the people gathered and asked for something to be set right, and sent the tribunes to Augustus about it, he came and considered with them what they asked; and at this all were pleased.

Discovering that his daughter Julia was living licentiously, he was exceedingly angry; he sent her away to an island beyond the borders, where her mother Scribonia sailed with her of her own accord; and of those who had had to do with her, he put to death Iullus Antonius and some other notable men, as aiming at the monarchy, and banished the rest to certain islands.

blocks: When the Armenians revolted and the Parthians helped them, Augustus, grieved at this, was at a loss what to do. For he was not able to campaign himself because of his age, Tiberius, as has been said, had already gone away, and he did not dare to send any other of the powerful men; and Gaius and Lucius were young and inexperienced in affairs. Under the pressure of necessity he chose Gaius, gave him proconsular power and a wife, so that he might gain some dignity from this too, and assigned him advisers. He set out, received with honour by all as the emperor's grandson or even thought his son; and Tiberius, coming to Chios, paid court to him, rubbing away suspicions, and for this reason cringing and humbling himself. Going to Syria, Gaius achieved nothing great and was wounded. For one Addon, who held Artagira, drew Gaius to the wall as if to tell him a secret, and wounded him. Addon was besieged and taken, but Gaius fell ill from the wound, and since he was not healthy anyway, and his mind had been weakened by it, he grew much duller, and asked to live as a private man; so that Augustus, deeply grieved, urged him to come to Italy and do what he wished. He sailed along to Lycia in a merchant ship, and there he died. His brother Lucius had died before him, suddenly of a disease.

Livia was suspected over their deaths, and so was Tiberius, who not long before had come back from Rhodes to Rome. For he himself was very skilled in divination by the stars, and he had Thrasyllus, a man of the highest skill in astrology; so that he knew what would befall himself and them. It is said that once in Rhodes Tiberius wished to push Thrasyllus off the wall, as the only one who knew all he was planning, and seeing him downcast, he asked why he was gloomy; and when he said he foresaw some danger hanging over him, Tiberius wondered at it, and wished to keep him for himself because of his hopes.

So much for this. Augustus, when he was called master by the people, forbade anyone to use this title to him, and having lent fifteen million drachmas without interest to those in need for three years, he was praised and exalted by all. Among the Romans twenty-five drachmas are worth one gold coin; among the Greeks, Dio says, the gold coin exchanges for twenty drachmas.

After this, when a Celtic war had broken out, and he himself, his body worn out by age and disease, was not able to campaign, partly forced by circumstances and partly persuaded by Julia (for she too had now been brought back from exile), he adopted Tiberius and entrusted him with the campaign against the Celts. Suspecting that Tiberius might grow proud and start something new, he adopted Germanicus, the son of Drusus, too. While he was doing this, others plotted against him, and Gnaeus Cornelius, a grandson of Pompey the Great. Neither wishing to kill them (for he saw that nothing was gained for his safety from those who were put to death), nor daring to release them, so as not to draw others against himself by this, he could neither be free of care by day nor rest at night. Livia, seeing this, asked him why he did not sleep. He said: "Who, wife, could rest even a little, having so many enemies and being plotted against so constantly?" She spoke to him much about this, and at last gave the opinion that he should punish none of such men with death, but correct them in some other way, so that they would not commit such an offence again, and above all by pardon and kindnesses. "For the sword," she said, "cannot persuade or force anyone to love; it destroys the one punished, and estranges the souls of the others from the punisher, since they do not love him because others have been punished, but rather hate him because fear hangs over them too from it." When Livia had said many such things, Augustus was persuaded by her, and let all the accused go, admonishing them with words; and he even appointed Cornelius consul. Augustus's remaining grandson, born to Agrippa by Julia, whom he also called Agrippa, was enrolled among the youths.

Suspecting that Tiberius might grow proud and start something new, he adopted Germanicus, the son of Drusus, too. While he was doing this, others plotted against him, and Gnaeus Cornelius, a grandson of Pompey the Great. Neither wishing to kill them (for he saw that nothing was gained for his safety from those who were put to death), nor daring to release them, so as not to draw others against himself by this, he could neither be free of care by day nor rest at night. Livia, seeing this, asked him why he did not sleep. He said: "Who, wife, could rest even a little, having so many enemies and being plotted against so constantly?" She spoke to him much about this, and at last gave the opinion that he should punish none of such men with death, but correct them in some other way, so that they would not commit such an offence again, and above all by pardon and kindnesses. "For the sword," she said, "cannot persuade or force anyone to love; it destroys the one punished, and estranges the souls of the others from the punisher, since they do not love him because others have been punished, but rather hate him because fear hangs over them too from it." When Livia had said many such things, Augustus was persuaded by her, and let all the accused go, admonishing them with words; and he even appointed Cornelius consul. Augustus's remaining grandson, born to Agrippa by Julia, whom he also called Agrippa, was enrolled among the youths.

blocks: Tiberius managed the wars, and kept coming to Rome, afraid that Augustus might prefer someone else while he was away. When the Dacians, the Sarmatians and other Pannonian peoples stirred, Tiberius turned back against them from Celtic country. Augustus sent Germanicus there too, as if Tiberius could have overcome them quickly but was wasting time on purpose, so as to be in arms because of the war. He sent Germanicus because Agrippa had been disowned as incorrigible; his property was assigned to the military treasury, and he was confined to an island. The Romans, having done much in the wars with these peoples and suffered no less, at last won over some by agreement and defeated others in battle. Tiberius came back to Rome, and was sent again by Augustus to Dalmatia, where some were in revolt; and he subdued them, though with difficulty and danger, and Germanicus likewise subdued others.

This war had this end; but news brought from Germany stopped those in Rome from celebrating the victory. For the Romans held some of Celtic country, not lying together, but scattered as it had happened to be conquered. Soldiers were there, cities were being founded, and the barbarians were being remoulded to Roman customs and good order. As long as they were being brought from their ancestral ways little by little and methodically, they did not take the change in their life hard; but when Quintilius Varus, receiving the command of Germany, hurried to change them all at once, gave them orders as if they were slaves and exacted money, they would not bear it, but received Varus as if they would do what was ordered, led him far from the Rhine, and gave him assurance that they would be subject even without soldiers. He believed it, neither kept the armies together as in enemy country, and sent others to other places. So while he was confident and suspected nothing terrible, they rose, killed the soldiers among them, and came upon him while he was in forests hard to get out of with the army about him, and suddenly surrounded them through the thickest woods, which they knew well. They did them very much harm many times; and at last, since the Romans had lost many and others of the same race kept joining the barbarians, the Romans were slaughtered more easily as they were surrounded, so that Varus and the rest of the most notable men were wounded; and they, afraid of being taken alive, killed themselves. When the rest learned this, some imitated their commander, and others laid down their arms and let anyone who wished kill them. So they were cut down without fear, and the barbarians took all the forts except one, and being busy about it they neither crossed the Rhine nor invaded Gaul. But they could not take it either, since they did not know how to besiege, and the Romans had many archers, by whom they were beaten back and very many perished.

After this, learning that the Romans had set a guard on the Rhine and that Tiberius was coming with a heavy army, most of them left the fort, while those left behind, standing away from it so as not to be harmed by sudden sallies of those inside, watched the roads, hoping to take them by lack of food. The Romans inside, as long as they had plenty of food, stayed where they were, expecting help; but when no one helped them and they were gripped by famine, they watched for a stormy night and came out (there were few soldiers, but many unarmed), and passed the first and second outposts of the barbarians, but at the third they were discovered. And all would have perished or been taken, had not the barbarians turned to seizing the plunder, and the trumpeters, sounding a quick march together, given the impression that help had come for the besieged; and then they really were helped. Tiberius decided not to cross the Rhine, but stayed quiet, watching that the barbarians did not do so. Nor did they dare to cross, knowing he was there. After this he and Germanicus invaded Celtic country and overran some of it, but neither won a battle nor brought any people under them, since no one came to grips with them, and they themselves did not go far from the Rhine, afraid of being tripped up again, but spent the time there until autumn and came back.

blocks: Augustus, managing the affairs of the monarchy and having now become very old, commended Germanicus, who had been consul before being praetor, to the senate, and the senate to Tiberius. When horse races were being held on his birthday, a madman sat in the chair dedicated to Julius Caesar and put on his crown; which disturbed everyone, as signifying something about Augustus. And more portents tending to this occurred. For the whole sun was eclipsed, much of the sky appeared fiery and seemed to burn, and comets and blood-red stars were seen; when a meeting of the senate was called because of his illness, so that they might offer prayers, the senate house was found shut; and a thunderbolt fell on a statue of him and wiped out the first letter of the name Caesar. These things appeared while he was still alive; and he fell ill at Nola and died on the nineteenth of the month August, having lived seventy-six years less thirty-four days, and ruled alone forty-four years from his victory at Actium.

Livia was suspected over his death, because Augustus had secretly sailed across to Agrippa on the island, where he had been exiled with his mother Julia. For fearing that, having been reconciled, he would bring him back to the monarchy, she is said to have poisoned some figs still on the trees, from which Augustus used to pick figs with his own hand, and she herself ate the unpoisoned ones and gave him the poisoned. Whether so or otherwise, falling ill then, he gathered his companions, and having told them what he wished, he said at last: "I took over Rome of clay, and leave it to you of stone," the word indicating the strength of the empire. Livia did not reveal his death at once, afraid there might be some revolt while Tiberius was in Dalmatia, but kept it hidden until he arrived.

When his body had been brought to Rome, Drusus took his will from the Vestal Virgins, the priestesses of Vesta, with whom it had been deposited, and brought it into the senate; those who had sealed it examined the seals, and it was read in the hearing of the senate. Four books of his were also brought into the senate, of which one gave instructions about his funeral, another set out the deeds he had done, in the third he arranged the affairs of the soldiers and of the public revenues and expenditures and the amount of money in the treasuries, and the fourth contained instructions for Tiberius and charges to the community. When these had been read the funeral took place and funeral speeches were given by Drusus and Tiberius; then his body was burned. At the time not many mourned, but later all did, remembering that he was easy of access to all, helped many with money, honoured his friends greatly, and was grateful to those who corrected him when he went wrong; as to Athenodorus, a wise man, for such a reason as this.

He was prone to sexual pleasures, and the women he wished were brought in covered litters and so carried into his bedroom, and he brought them out and used them. Once he fell in love with a woman and sent to fetch her. Meanwhile Athenodorus, who was an acquaintance of the woman's husband, happened to go to see his friend, and finding both him and his wife in distress (for they could not resist), he asked the cause of their grief. Learning it, he told them to keep calm; for he said he would go to Augustus himself and turn aside his desire. When the covered chair was brought for the woman to get into, Athenodorus got in, took a sword, ordered the chair to be closely covered, and so was carried to Augustus's bedroom. When Augustus uncovered the chair, he leapt out sword in hand, saying: "Are you not afraid, then, that someone coming in like this may kill you?" Augustus was not only not angry and did not abuse Athenodorus, but even thanked him and became more self-controlled. For these reasons, then, and many others they missed him, and found Tiberius, who ruled alone after him, not like him.

In the forty-second year of Augustus's sole rule our Lord and God Jesus Christ was born, made man, according to Eusebius son of Pamphilus, who in his Church History records that Augustus ruled alone fifty-seven years, while the others count the years of his sole rule as forty-four. The disagreement arises from this, that the others reckoned Caesar's sole rule from the time he defeated Antony in the sea battle at Actium, when he truly ruled alone, having become sole master of Roman affairs, while Eusebius adds to the sole rule the time he ruled with Antony too, since even then Augustus did what he wished, while Antony busied himself with Egypt and was a slave to his love of Cleopatra, through which he also perished. So in this way Eusebius recorded that Christ was born in the flesh in the forty-second year of Caesar's sole rule. For if we say that the years of Caesar's sole rule were forty-four, the appearing of our Lord and Saviour did not take place in the forty-second year, but the Lord turns out to have been born in the twenty-ninth year. For, as the divine evangelist Luke records, John baptised Christ in the fifteenth year of the rule of Tiberius Caesar; and he was thirty years old when he was baptised, according to the same evangelist; so that fifteen of the thirty years must be taken from the years of Tiberius's sole rule, and the other fifteen counted from the forty-four of Augustus. So the remainder of these comes to twenty-nine. In the twenty-ninth year, then, of the strict sole rule of Caesar Augustus, the Lord is found to have been born in the flesh of the ever-virgin and holy Mary, the Mother of God.

blocks: So Augustus died, as has been told, and Tiberius succeeded to the monarchy. He was of noble birth and educated, but most intricate in his mind, making his words the opposite of his intention. For he said the opposite of what he wished, hiding one thing in his heart and saying another; he pretended to be angry where he was not, and put on a show of mildness where he was enraged; he looked on his worst enemy as his closest friend, and treated his dearest as a perfect stranger. He did not think it right for others to know his mind, holding this to befit a sole ruler. And whether anyone opposed what he said or agreed with it, he was hated.

For the time, he at once wrote to all the legions and provinces as emperor, while saying he was not emperor; for when this too was voted him with the other names he did not accept it. While managing all the business of the rule, he said he had no need of it, and made a show of giving it up, both because of his age (for he was fifty-six years old) and because of weak sight; for he saw very well in the dark but very little by day. Then he asked for partners and colleagues in the rule, with no intention of doing any of this, but because he had a deceitful character, and because he suspected the armies in Pannonia and in Germany, and feared Germanicus, who was then governing Germany and was loved by the soldiers. For these reasons he did nothing openly as emperor, but pretended to be ill, stayed at home and delayed, so that in the hope of his giving up the rule willingly no one might start a revolt, until he had become master of all the government. He at once sent and killed Agrippa, who was Augustus's grandson by Julia and Agrippa, as has been said; and he greatly feared Germanicus.

The army in Pannonia too made an uproar, so that they even rushed at their commander. Then, when the boldest and chief culprits had been punished, the rest settled down. Those in Germany abused Tiberius and hailed Germanicus as emperor. When he drew his sword as if to kill himself, one of the soldiers held out his own sword and said: "Take this; it is sharper." So Germanicus refrained from killing himself, so that they might not mutiny further, and forging a letter as if sent by Tiberius, granting them gifts and promising other things, he stopped the mutiny for the time. Later, when envoys were sent by Tiberius, they learned of Germanicus's stratagem, and suspecting that the envoys had come to overturn what he had promised, they rioted again and rushed at the envoys. They seized Germanicus's wife Agrippina, who was the daughter of Caesar's daughter Julia and of Agrippa, and his son Gaius; they let Agrippina go to him, since she was pregnant, but kept the son. When they achieved nothing, they too quieted down. So the man who could have taken the imperial power did not wish to; while Tiberius praised him in appearance before the senate, but in himself greatly suspected and feared him as one entrusted with armies.

When no more revolt was reported, he took up the rule, no longer pretending. As long as Germanicus lived he did nothing on his own, but brought everything before the senate, and did not think it right to be called emperor by anyone except the soldiers alone, but was named Caesar, Germanicus and leader of the senate; he prayed to live and rule only as long as was good for the state, was eager to seem a man of the people in everything, and spending very little on himself spent very much on the public. Restoring and adorning buildings that had suffered, he inscribed on them the names of those who had built them in the first place; he helped cities and private persons, enriched many senators who were poor, and had his gifts counted out at once in his presence, so that the givers might not embezzle any of them, knowing that this had happened under Augustus. He neither killed anyone for money nor confiscated anyone's property at that time, nor raised money outside what was customary. When Aemilius sent him more money than had been ordered, he wrote back: "I want my sheep shorn, not shaved." He was easy of access and affable, honoured the magistrates as in a free state, rose for the consuls, kept company with his friends as in private life, visited them when ill, bringing no guard; and when one of them died he read the funeral speech himself. He ordered his mother Livia to behave in the same way to all. But she was very puffed up; for some time Tiberius's letters bore her name too; she tried to manage everything else as if ruling alone, and wished not to rule on equal terms with him but even to rank above him, boasting that she had made him emperor. He was vexed with her at first; then he removed her from public affairs, but left her to manage the household; and when she was oppressive in this too, he went away and kept clear of her. For some time he lived most temperately, punished others who were licentious, and rebuked his son Drusus, whom he had by Agrippina, his former wife, and who was licentious and cruel, and was vexed with him. Once he said to him: "While I live you will do nothing violent or insolent; and if you dare anything, not even when I am dead."

blocks: He did these and other things like this as long as Germanicus lived; after that he changed many of them. When the bequests left by Augustus to the people had not yet been paid, and a corpse was being carried out through the forum, a man went up and whispered in its ear, and when asked what he had said, said he had told it to tell Augustus that they had not yet received anything; Tiberius killed him at once, saying in mockery that it was so that he might take the message himself, and distributed the bequests to the others. When his grandson, whom he had by Drusus, died, he refrained from none of his usual business, saying that the business of the living must not be given up because of the departed.

One Clemens, who had been a slave of Agrippa and looked like him, pretended to be Agrippa himself; going to Gaul he won over many there and many in Italy, and at last set out for Rome to recover his grandfather's monarchy. But Tiberius caught him through some men who pretended to be on his side, and tortured him to learn something about accomplices; and when he revealed nothing, he asked him: "How did you become Agrippa?" And he answered: "The same way as you became Caesar."

His wife Julia he not only did not bring back from the exile to which her father Augustus had condemned her for licentiousness, but even shut her up, so that she perished of ill treatment and hunger. When many asked him to have the month of November, on the sixteenth of which he had been born, called Tiberius after him, he said: "And what will you do if there are thirteen Caesars?"

Meanwhile Germanicus died at Antioch, bewitched and poisoned by Piso. For human bones were found buried in the house where he lived, and lead tablets bearing curses together with his name. That he had also been destroyed by poison was shown by his body, which was brought into the forum and shown to those present. At his death Tiberius and Livia were pleased, but the others were most deeply grieved. For he was most handsome in body and most excellent in soul; renowned for both learning and courage in war, he treated those under him most gently, and having great power, as a Caesar, he was as modest as the weakest; he did nothing to rouse Drusus's envy or to plot against Tiberius, and though he could have received the imperial power from the soldiers, the senate and the people willingly, he would not. Piso, brought back to Rome some time later, and brought into the senate by Tiberius himself for the murder of Germanicus, to clear away the suspicion of having destroyed him, asked for a postponement and killed himself. Germanicus died leaving three sons, whom Augustus had named Caesars in his will. The eldest of these, Nero, was enrolled among the youths at that time.

Up to this time, then, Tiberius did very much good and little wrong, but when Germanicus was out of his way, he changed little by little. For he ruled savagely in other ways, treated harshly as guilty of impiety those who did or said anything unfitting against him or his mother or Augustus, and was implacable towards those suspected of plotting against him. Now he even showed some men that he wished certain others dead, and killed them through those men, and was not unnoticed in doing so. He inquired into the day and hour on which each of the powerful men had been born, and so searched out the fate of each; so that meeting Galba, who later ruled alone, he said: "You too will one day taste the rule." But he spared him, saying that he would rule in old age and long after his own death.

Then Tiberius was consul with Drusus, so that many foretold Drusus's destruction from this; for there was none of his colleagues in the consulship who did not die by violence. And after this he perished by poison. For one Sejanus, who had great power with Tiberius and had become overbearing, once squared up to Drusus with his fist, and afraid from this of both him and Tiberius, and at the same time expecting that if he did away with Drusus he would more easily handle Tiberius, gave him a poison through some of his servants and through his wife, whom some write was Julia and others Livia (for he was committing adultery with her). So he perished in this way; and Tiberius came into the senate, lamented him, and commended Nero and Drusus, the sons of Germanicus, to the senate; and the body of Drusus was set out on the rostra; and Nero, who was his son-in-law, spoke praises over him. His death became the cause of death for many, as having rejoiced at his destruction. For many others perished, and Agrippina with her children, except the youngest. For Sejanus provoked Tiberius much against her, expecting that if she perished with her children he would marry Livia, Drusus's wife, whom he loved, and would have the power, since Tiberius would have no successor; for he hated his grandson as a child of adultery. And he exiled and destroyed many others on one charge or another, most of them made up; he punished one man because he had written the history of Caesar and Augustus, though he had written nothing against them, and burned the work wherever it was found, because it did not glorify them. He destroyed more as having reviled him. One Sabinus, accused on such a charge, was shut up in prison, then also murdered, and his body thrown into the river. This was terrible to all in itself, but a dog of Sabinus made it more terrible still, going into the prison with him, staying by him when he was dead, and jumping into the river with him when he was thrown in. So these things happened, and few out of many have been recorded.

Livia, having become very old, died, having lived eighty-six years. Tiberius neither visited her when ill nor honoured her when dead, except with a funeral and some statues. But to Tiberius's discredit the senate voted the women mourning for her for a whole year; and because she had saved many of them, brought up the children of many and given dowries to more girls, they assigned her other honours too. Tiberius paid none of the bequests she had left to anyone. Some of her sayings should be recorded. It is said that once, when some naked men met her and were going to be put to death for it, she saved them, saying: "To chaste women such men are no different from statues." When someone asked her, "How and by what conduct did you gain mastery over Augustus?" she answered: "By being strictly chaste myself, doing gladly whatever pleased him, not meddling in any of his affairs, and pretending neither to hear of nor to notice his amorous playthings."

Tiberius raised Sejanus to great glory, and made him his son-in-law by betrothing him to Julia, Drusus's daughter, but later put him to death, the senate having condemned him to death at his urging. His body lay thrown out for three days while the crowd insulted it; then they threw it into the river. His children were put to death by decree, and his wife killed herself. Others too perished because of him, some killing themselves, others killed by others.
text: He did these and other things like this as long as Germanicus lived; after that he changed many of them. When the bequests left by Augustus to the people had not yet been paid, and a corpse was being carried out through the forum, a man went up and whispered in its ear, and when asked what he had said, said he had told it to tell Augustus that they had not yet received anything; Tiberius killed him at once, saying in mockery that it was so that he might take the message himself, and distributed the bequests to the others. When his grandson, whom he had by Drusus, died, he refrained from none of his usual business, saying that the business of the living must not be given up because of the departed. One Clemens, who had been a slave of Agrippa and looked like him, pretended to be Agrippa himself; going to Gaul he won over many there and many in Italy, and at last set out for Rome to recover his grandfather's monarchy. But Tiberius caught him through some men who pretended to be on his side, and tortured him to learn something about accomplices; and when he revealed nothing, he asked him: "How did you become Agrippa?" And he answered: "The same way as you became Caesar." His wife Julia he not only did not bring back from the exile to which her father Augustus had condemned her for licentiousness, but even shut her up, so that she perished of ill treatment and hunger. When many asked him to have the month of November, on the sixteenth of which he had been born, called Tiberius after him, he said: "And what will you do if there are thirteen Caesars?" blocks: Besides other things, Tiberius was slandered for his lusts, which he indulged licentiously and shamelessly with the most nobly born, both male and female, and was reviled for cruelty because of the deaths of Agrippina and Drusus. For people, thinking that everything against them had earlier been done by Sejanus, were exceedingly grieved when they learned that they had been killed after his destruction. He appointed Gaius, the younger of Germanicus's sons, quaestor. For his grandson Tiberius he passed over, both because he was a child and because he was suspected of not being Drusus's son, and paid attention to Gaius as the one who would rule. For he knew everything about Gaius, and once said to him when he was quarrelling with Tiberius: "You will kill him, and others will kill you." But having no one else so closely related to him, and knowing that Gaius would be most wicked, he gladly gave him the rule, as they say, so that his own deeds might be hidden by the excess of Gaius's wickedness, and the greatest and noblest part of the senate might be destroyed after his own death. He is said often to have uttered that old line, "When I am dead, let earth be mixed with fire," and to have called Priam happy because he perished utterly together with his country and his kingdom. So great a number of the senators and others had been destroyed that those holding the governments of provinces had no successors for lack of men to succeed them.

The others were killed for various reasons, false and true, but Aemilius Scaurus died because of a tragedy. The play was Atreus, and it advised one of the subjects to bear the folly of the ruler. Learning this, Tiberius thought the line had been written against him, and said: "Then I shall make him an Ajax," and forced him to kill himself. Meanwhile a young man claiming to be Drusus was seen about Greece and Ionia. The cities received him gladly, and he would have gone on into Syria and taken over the legions, had not someone recognised him, seized him and brought him to Tiberius; who was celebrating Gaius's wedding at Antium.

Then the Tiber flooded much of Rome so that it was sailed over, and countless things were destroyed by fire. If Egyptian matters have anything to do with the Romans, the phoenix was seen in that year. These things seemed to foretell Tiberius's death. He had been ill for a long time, but neither changed his way of life nor used doctors, because of the word of Thrasyllus, who knew very exactly the day and hour on which Tiberius would die, but said he would live another ten years, so that, thinking to live longer, he might not hurry to kill many. As happens in old age and an illness that is not acute, he was sometimes worn down and sometimes recovered. From this the others and Gaius were sometimes glad, thinking he would die, and sometimes afraid that he would live. So Gaius, fearing that he might recover, did not give him food when he asked, as though it would harm him, and threw many thick clothes on him as though he needed warmth, and so smothered him, having lived seventy-seven years, four months and nine days, of which he ruled alone twenty-two years, seven months and seven days. He died on the twentieth day of March.

In the fifteenth year of his reign our Lord Jesus Christ was baptised, and in the eighteenth he was betrayed, crucified and rose again. Eusebius records that Pilate, who was then procurator of Judaea, wrote to Tiberius about the Lord, since it was the custom for the governors of provinces to report any new things among them to the one who steered the monarchy, so that nothing happening in any of the provinces might be unknown to him. For, he says, when the resurrection of our Saviour from the dead had already been noised abroad to all in all Palestine, Pilate communicated it to Tiberius the emperor; and he, learning of his other wonders, and that after death he had risen from the dead and was already believed by very many to be God, referred this to the senate. But the senate rejected the proposal, because it had not first approved it itself, since an old law prevailed that no one should be made a god among the Romans except by the vote and decree of the senate. But when the senate had rejected the proposal about our Saviour, Tiberius, keeping the opinion he had held before, planned nothing harmful against the teaching of Christ. As witness to this Eusebius brings forward Tertullian, a Roman and one of the distinguished men in Rome, in a work he set out in the Latin language and that was translated into Greek, saying this: "There was an old decree that no god should be consecrated by anyone before he had been approved by the senate. So Tiberius, in whose time the name of the Christians had come into the world, when this teaching was reported to him from Palestine, where it first began, communicated it to the senate, making it clear that he was pleased with the teaching. The senate, since it had not approved it itself, rejected it. But he kept to his own opinion, threatening death to the accusers of the Christians." Eusebius records that Tiberius did this on learning of the divinity of our Saviour and his resurrection from the dead, having taken it from Tertullian's work.

blocks: So Tiberius died, and he was succeeded by Gaius, the son of Germanicus and Agrippina, whom they also called Germanicus and Caligula. For though Tiberius had left the sole rule to his own grandson Tiberius too, Gaius sent his will to the senate and had it declared void, as made by a man out of his mind, since he had entrusted the rule of the Romans to a boy who was not even allowed to enter the senate house. So he at once removed him from the rule in this way, and afterwards adopted him and killed him, as if he had prayed for his death; and he distributed much money to the soldiers and the people, partly from Tiberius's will and partly from Livia's, which Tiberius had not paid. And had he spent the rest properly, he would have seemed high-minded and magnificent; but as it was, spending insatiably on dancers, horses, gladiators and other things of the kind, he quickly emptied the treasuries, which had become great, and proved besides that he had done the former things too from carelessness and lack of judgement. Not even into the third year did he save any part of it, but at once he needed a great deal more.

He behaved in the same way in other things too. For having become the most adulterous of men, seizing one woman as she was being given to a husband and tearing away others already married and living with men, he hated all but one; and he would surely have hated her too if he had lived longer. Having shown much piety towards his mother, his sisters and his grandmother Antonia, he afterwards forced his grandmother, when she rebuked him for something, into a voluntary death, and having seduced all his sisters, he shut two of them up on an island; for the third had died before. He did many other such things. He attacked Tiberius as licentious and bloodthirsty, so that others too, thinking to please him by this, used too reckless a freedom of speech; then he praised and exalted him, so that he even punished some for what they had said against him; he reviled those who abused him and hated those who praised him as his friends; and he killed very many of those who had stirred up Tiberius against his father, his mother and his brothers, though he said he had forgiven them his anger and burned their papers. He ordered temples and sacrifices to be made to himself as to a god. He was angry when asked for something, and again resentful at not being asked; he rushed hotly at some deeds and handled others most sluggishly; he spent money most unsparingly and raised it most meanly; he was vexed and pleased alike with those who flattered him and those who spoke freely. He punished many who had done great wrongs, and killed many who had done no wrong at all. Of his companions he flattered some to excess and insulted others to excess.

In short, the Romans were then handed over to such an emperor that the deeds of Tiberius, though they seemed very harsh, surpassed those of Gaius as much as those of Augustus had seemed better than Tiberius's. For Tiberius ruled, and used his other servants for his own will, but Gaius was ruled by the charioteers and gladiators, and was a slave to the dancers and the rest of the people of the stage. At first he was a spectator and hearer of them, taking sides with some and against others; then he drove chariots himself, fought as a gladiator, danced and acted in tragedy. blocks: this. Then he was consul, taking his uncle Claudius as colleague. He, being a knight, then for the first time was consul and a member of the senate, being forty-six years old. Gaius's father-in-law Marcus Silanus, since he was a burden to him both by his virtue and by the relationship, was insulted and outraged, and killed himself, though he had been greatly honoured by Tiberius. Gaius cast out Silanus's daughter and married Cornelia Orestina, whom he snatched away at the very wedding he was celebrating with Gaius Calpurnius Piso, to whom she was betrothed. Though he was like this, he did some things worth praise. For having put out a fire with the soldiers, he helped those who had suffered loss; when the order of knights was short of men, he sent for the leading men from the whole empire and enrolled them; he gave the elections back to the people; and he did some other such things. But he did many times more things worthy of blame. He killed many; and it was not so much the number of those who perished that was terrible, though it was terrible, but that he rejoiced exceedingly in their murders and was insatiable for the sight of blood. Once, when out of cruelty those condemned to be given to the beasts ran out, he ordered some of the crowd pressed against the benches to be seized and thrown to them. And so that they could neither cry out nor make any accusation, their tongues were cut out first. He murdered many for their property, charging them with other things. The death of his sister Drusilla destroyed no fewer. She was married to Marcus Lepidus, who was at once Gaius's favourite and his lover, and Gaius too lived with her. When she died he granted her many honours and then even deified her. A little later he married Lollia Paulina, forcing her husband himself to betroth his wife to him, so that he might not break the law by taking her without betrothal.

Once, seeing much mud in a narrow street, he ordered it to be thrown into the clothes of the man who was then aedile and in charge of cleaning the streets. Vespasian was then aedile; so that later, when he took over affairs in confusion and turmoil and set them right, what happened then seemed not to have happened without the gods, but that the city had plainly been handed over to him by Gaius to be set right.

Gaius kept murdering many, and there was nothing besides murders. Nor did he do the multitude any favour, and they hated him greatly; for they said and did many other things that did not please him, and above all he was terribly indignant because, extolling him, they shouted, "Young Augustus!" For he did not think himself called happy because he ruled alone while young, but reproached because at such an age he held so great a rule. He made money in every way, finding now one and now another handle for gain; and no one of those who had anything, man or woman, was left unharmed. And if he allowed some of the older people to live, he called them fathers, grandfathers, mothers and grandmothers, milked them while alive, and inherited their property when they died.

He wished in a way to drive and ride across the sea, and bridged the space between Puteoli and Bauli. This place is opposite the city, twenty-six stades from it. Of the ships for the bridge some were built and others gathered; from which a famine became severe in Italy and above all in Rome. This bridge too became a cause of death for many. For having spent untold money on it he plotted against many more because of their property. So one Junius Priscus, a praetor, was accused of other things, but died because he was rich; and when Gaius learned that he had owned nothing worth death, he said: "He deceived me and perished for nothing; for he could have lived." Domitius Afer, having come near to danger, was unexpectedly saved. For bringing him into the senate on some charge, Gaius read a long speech against him (for he thought it right to beat all the orators, and was eager to surpass Domitius, who was a most able speaker); but he neither answered nor made a defence, but pretended to wonder at Gaius's skill and to be struck with amazement, and pleaded and begged, saying he feared the orator more than the Caesar. Gaius, pleased at this, and believing he had beaten him by the power of his words, stopped his anger.
text: this. Then he was consul, taking his uncle Claudius as colleague. He, being a knight, then for the first time was consul and a member of the senate, being forty-six years old. Gaius's father-in-law Marcus Silanus, since he was a burden to him both by his virtue and by the relationship, was insulted and outraged, and killed himself, though he had been greatly honoured by Tiberius. Gaius cast out Silanus's daughter and married Cornelia Orestina, whom he snatched away at the very wedding he was celebrating with Gaius Calpurnius Piso, to whom she was betrothed. Though he was like this, he did some things worth praise. For having put out a fire with the soldiers, he helped those who had suffered loss; when the order of knights was short of men, he sent for the leading men from the whole empire and enrolled them; he gave the elections back to the people; and he did some other such things. But he did many times more things worthy of blame. He killed many; and it was not so much the number of those who perished that was terrible, though it was terrible, but that he rejoiced exceedingly in their murders and was insatiable for the sight of blood. Once, when out of cruelty those condemned to be given to the beasts ran out, he ordered some of the crowd pressed against the benches to be seized and thrown to them. And so that they could neither cry out nor make any accusation, their tongues were cut out first. He murdered many for their property, charging them with other things. The death of his sister Drusilla destroyed no fewer. She was married to Marcus Lepidus, who was at once Gaius's favourite and his lover, and Gaius too lived with her. When she died he granted her many honours and then even deified her. A little later he married Lollia Paulina, forcing her husband himself to betroth his wife to him, so that he might not break the law by taking her without betrothal. Once, seeing much mud in a narrow street, he ordered it to be thrown into the clothes of the man who was then aedile and in charge of cleaning the streets. Vespasian was then aedile; so that later, when he took over affairs in confusion and turmoil and set them right, what happened then seemed not to have happened without the gods, but that the city had plainly been handed over to him by Gaius to be set right. Gaius kept murdering many, and there was nothing besides murders. Nor did he do the multitude any favour, and they hated him greatly; for they said and did many other things that did not please him, and above all he was terribly indignant because, extolling him, they shouted, "Young Augustus!" For he did not think himself called happy because he ruled alone while young, but reproached because at such an age he held so great a rule. He made money in every way, finding now one and now another handle for gain; and no one of those who had anything, man or woman, was left unharmed. And if he allowed some of the older people to live, he called them fathers, grandfathers, mothers and grandmothers, milked them while alive, and inherited their property when they died.
