blocks: Then he set out for Gaul as if the Celts were stirring, and did no harm at all to the enemy, but very much to the subjects, the allies and the citizens. Once when he was playing dice and found he had no money, he asked for the census lists of the Gauls. Ordering the richest of them to be put to death, he went back to his fellow players and said: "You are playing for a few drachmas, but I have gathered a hundred and fifty million." So everything was done without judgement. He killed Lepidus too, that lover and beloved, the husband of Drusilla, whom he had honoured exceedingly and promised to have as successor to the rule; and he sent his own sisters to the Pontian islands as having been corrupted with him; and he did many other such things. Then he cast out Paulina, on the pretext that she bore no children, but in truth because he had had his fill of her, and married Milonia Caesonia, with whom he had committed adultery before, and whom he then wished to have as wife too, since she was pregnant, so that she might bear him a child in thirty days.

Those in Rome were disturbed, and disturbed too because very many lawsuits were brought against them for friendship with his sisters and with those murdered, and they expected that Gaius's cruelty and licentiousness would grow still more if the time of his rule were longer. They were so disposed towards him; and he sent for Ptolemy, the son of Juba, and killed him too as rich.

Living in this way he was bound to be plotted against. He discovered the attempt, seized Anicius Cerialis and his son Sextus Papinius and tortured them; and when Cerialis revealed nothing, he persuaded Papinius, promising him safety and immunity, to denounce some men, whether truly or falsely, and at once killed him and the others before his eyes. He forced the father of one of those being killed to be present while his son was murdered; and when the father asked whether he permitted him to close his eyes, he ordered him to be slain too. That man, in danger, pretended to be one of the conspirators and promised to reveal all the rest, and named Gaius's companions and the partners of his licentiousness and cruelty. And he would have destroyed many, had he not been disbelieved because he also accused the prefects, Callistus and Caesonia.

He died, but this very thing brought about Gaius's destruction. For calling the prefects and Callistus aside, he said: "I am one, and you are three; and I am unarmed, while you are armed. If, then, you hate me and wish to kill me, murder me." From then, thinking that they hated him and were vexed at what was being done, he suspected them, wore a sword even in the city, and set them against one another, so that they might not agree together, talking to each alone as most trustworthy about the others, until, understanding the scheme, they gave him up to the plotters.

When the senators were in great fear because they had not condemned some men, one Protogenes, who served Gaius in his harshest deeds, so that he carried two books, one of which he called the sword and the other the dagger, came into the senate, and when all greeted him, as was natural, he looked sharply at one Scribonius Proculus and said: "Do you too greet me, when you hate the emperor so?" Hearing this, those present surrounded their fellow councillor and tore him to pieces; at which Gaius was pleased and said he was reconciled with them.

blocks: When people flattered him, some calling him a hero and others a god, he went terribly out of his mind. For even before he had claimed to be thought more than human, pretended to keep company with the Moon and to be Jupiter, and for this reason above all made it his excuse for lying with his sisters; and he played all the gods, even the female ones themselves, and became Juno, Diana and Venus, and changed his whole appearance to match the change of names, so that he was seen now as an effeminate man carrying a mixing bowl and a thyrsus, now as a manly figure wearing a club and a lion skin, and again shown beardless or bearded. He held a trident and brandished a thunderbolt, made himself like a hunting maiden, and played the woman again, decked out precisely with dress and with things attached and put on, and wished to seem an emperor anything rather than a man. Once a Gaul, seeing him doing business on a high seat in the form of Jupiter, laughed. Learning this he called him and asked: "What do you think I am?" And he said: "A great piece of nonsense." He suffered nothing terrible; for he was disregarded as being a cobbler. Gaius greeted few with a kiss, and held out his hand or his foot for the others, even senators, to do obeisance to. All flattered him. Once he asked Lucius Vitellius, a man of good birth and sound sense, saying that he was keeping company with the Moon, whether he saw the goddess with him. He, looking down as if amazed, and speaking low and trembling, said: "Only you gods, master, can see one another."

Gaius went so mad that he even ordered those in Asia to raise a precinct for him at Miletus. And in Rome two temples were set up for him; one he built for himself on the Palatine, the other was voted him by the senate and built. He also complained against Jupiter for having occupied the Capitol first. He sent statues of himself to every part of the world, ordering them to be worshipped. He was converting the temple in Jerusalem into a shrine of his own, so that it might be called the temple of Gaius, the new manifest Jupiter, though Josephus passed over this in his Antiquities. From this the revolt of the Jews took its beginning. He appointed many priests for himself, and was his own priest. He thundered back at the thunder with a machine, and flashed back at the lightning. Whenever a thunderbolt came down, he threw stones back, adding at each the line of Homer: "Either lift me, or I you."

In his time, as Eusebius records, saying he has gathered this from those who wrote down the Olympiads, Pilate fell into such misfortunes that he was forced to become his own murderer, divine justice pursuing him.

Since he raged in every way (for to count each thing would be a matter of much talk and distaste), Cassius Chaerea and Cornelius Sabinus plotted against him. More men conspired, and those about him knew of what was being done; and those who did not conspire, when they knew, did not reveal it and were glad to see him plotted against. The plot came while he was putting on a show. For Chaerea and Sabinus, though grieved at the shameful things being done, still endured them for five days. But when Gaius himself wished to dance and act in a tragedy, and for this announced three more days, they watched for him as he came out of the theatre, surrounded him in a narrow passage and killed him; and when he fell, none of those present held back, but they wounded him even when dead. They also at once slaughtered his wife and his daughter. So Gaius, having done these things in three years, nine months and twenty-eight days, learned by the deeds themselves that he was not a god. When his death was announced, all except the few who had shared in his debauchery rejoiced, remembering what he had once said when, angry with the people, he said, "Would that you had one neck," and adding: "You have one neck, but we have many hands." When a few ran about making an uproar and shouting, "Who killed Gaius?" Valerius Asiaticus, a man of consular rank, went up to a conspicuous place and cried out: "Would that I had killed him!" And so those making the uproar were struck dumb and quieted down.

blocks: So Gaius perished; and when the senate gathered on the Capitol, some thought they should have popular government, others decided they should be ruled by one man again; and of these some chose one man and some another. Meanwhile some soldiers, bursting into the palace to plunder something, found Claudius hiding in a dark corner (for he had been with Gaius as he came out of the theatre, and fearing the disturbance had hidden himself), and dragged him out not knowing who he was; but recognising him, they hailed him emperor and took him to the camp, and with no one hesitating, all gave him the power, as being of the royal family and thought to be reasonable. For though he shrank back and objected, the more he stood aside and resisted, the more the soldiers strove in turn not to receive an emperor from others, but themselves to give one to all. So, against his will as it seemed, he submitted. When the consuls and senators learned that the rule had already been seized, they too agreed.

So Tiberius Claudius Nero Germanicus, the son of Drusus, the son of Livia, received the imperial rule, being in his fiftieth year. In soul he was not bad, but was trained in learning, so that he even wrote some works; but in body he was sickly. He was much ruled by women and by slaves, since from childhood he had been brought up in sickness and great fear, and so pretended to more simplicity and slackness of character than was true, which he himself admitted in the senate; and having lived a long time with his grandmother Livia, a long time with his mother Antonia, and with freedmen, he showed nothing befitting a free man. The women and freedmen got hold of him in his drinking and his love affairs; for he was most insatiably given to both. Besides, he was cowardly. Yet, being of such a nature, to put it briefly, he did not a few things properly whenever he was free of the passions mentioned and master of himself.

He did not go into the senate at once, but after thirty days, both because he feared Gaius, who had perished as he had, and because some better men than he had been named for the rule by the senate. He guarded himself carefully in other ways and had all who came to him searched in case they had a dagger, and had soldiers with him at dinners. This went on afterwards too; but the searching for daggers was stopped by Vespasian. He put Chaerea and some others to death, not for Gaius's sake, but providing for his own safety; and Sabinus died willingly, not thinking it right to survive when Chaerea had been punished. He brought Gaius's sisters Agrippina and Julia back from exile and gave them back their property, and likewise brought back the others who had been banished. Examining carefully those bound in prisons, he released those who were falsely accused and punished those who had done some wrong. He burned the poisons, many of which were found among Gaius's things, and the books of Protogenes, whom he also put to death. The papers that Gaius said he had burned, but which were found to exist, he showed to the senators and gave to be read by those who had written them and those against whom they had been written, and after this burned them. When the senate wished to dishonour Gaius, he himself prevented its being voted, but by night he made away with all his statues, and overturned what had been wrongly done by Gaius and by others because of him. When statues were voted him he refused them; and he forbade sacrifice or obeisance to him in images. He did many other such things, being modest and doing them by judgement and not for show. For he betrothed his daughters, one to Lucius Junius Silanus and the other to Gnaeus Pompeius Magnus, and did nothing extravagant, but judged cases himself on those days, and the senate met. He did these things reasonably; and when the consuls in the senate came down from their seats to speak with him, he rose too and went to meet them. He lived mostly as a private man, and he and those about him lived in Greek fashion.

He was admirable in money matters. For he forbade money to be offered to him, which had happened under Augustus too. He also forbade anyone who had kin to leave him an inheritance. Of the property confiscated earlier under Tiberius and Gaius he gave some back to the owners if still alive and some to their children; and to many who had been deprived of their realms and lands by Gaius he restored them. He did other such deeds for which he was praised. But other things of a different kind were done by his freedmen and his wife Valeria Messalina.

When a severe famine came, he took thought not only for plenty at the time but also for the future. For since almost all the grain of the Romans was imported, the coast at the mouths of the Tiber, having neither safe landings nor suitable harbours, made their mastery of the sea useless to them; for nothing could come in during the winter season. Seeing this, he built harbours and completed a work worthy of the spirit and greatness of Rome. Being moderate in everything, when a son was born to him, who was then named Claudius Tiberius Germanicus and later Britannicus as well, he did nothing else conspicuous, nor allowed himself to be called Augustus or Messalina Augusta.

blocks: He constantly held gladiatorial games, delighting in them greatly, and from this many men perished, condemned on some charges. So becoming used to filling himself with blood and slaughter, he turned more readily to other killings too. The cause of this was the imperial freedmen and Messalina. For if they wished to kill anyone, they frightened him, and were allowed to do whatever they wished. Often, suddenly struck with alarm and ordering someone to be put to death in his immediate terror, he afterwards came to himself and recovered his senses, and learning what had happened was grieved and repented.

Since he was doing such things, the Romans no longer had good hope of Claudius. So he was plotted against by others and by Annius Vinicianus, who sent to Furius Camillus Scribonianus, governor of Dalmatia, and persuaded him to revolt. When the soldiers would not obey him, he killed himself; and Claudius, though so terrified that he was ready to give up the power to him of his own accord, took heart on learning of his death, rewarded the soldiers with various things and with money, and searched out the fellow plotters and punished very many. Many others, and Vinicianus, killed themselves. For Messalina and Claudius's freedman Narcissus and his fellow freedmen, seizing this occasion, held back from none of the most terrible things. So many men and women were punished; and some of those quite guilty were saved, some by money and some by favour. When Narcissus came forward in the senate house and said to Galaesus, a freedman of Camillus, "What would you have done, Galaesus, if Camillus had become sole ruler?" he answered: "I would have stood behind him and kept quiet." Arria, the wife of Caecina, a consul, though very close to Messalina, would not bear to live when her husband was dying, but even strengthened her husband when he lost heart. For she took the sword, stabbed herself and handed it to him, saying: "See, Paetus, it does not hurt." These were praised for this; but Claudius was so disposed towards punishments that he constantly gave the soldiers this line as a watchword: "A man must defend himself when someone first does him harm."

Messalina and his freedmen so sold and peddled citizenship, military posts, procuratorships, governorships and everything else that all goods became scarce, and from this Claudius was forced to fix their prices from the tribunal.

Aulus Plautius made an expedition to Britain and suffered some things and did others, and then reported what had happened to Claudius; who entrusted affairs at home to Lucius Vitellius, who had been his colleague as consul, and set out on campaign. Reaching the Ocean and crossing to Britain with greater preparation and elephants, he joined the armies. Engaging the barbarians with them, he won and took their royal seat. He came back to Rome, having sent the news ahead through his sons-in-law Magnus and Silanus. Learning this, the senate named both him and his son Britannicus, and voted them many other things.

Messalina fell in love with a dancer named Mnester, and since she could not persuade him to lie with her by promises or by threats, she arranged for Claudius to order him to obey her, as if she needed him for something else; and when Claudius told him to do whatever he was ordered by Messalina, he lay with her, as if ordered to do this too by him. She did this with many others too. For she committed adultery as if her husband knew what was happening and allowed her to be licentious. Vinicius, because he would not be corrupted with her, was destroyed by her with poison. The Romans were vexed to see him a slave to his wife and freedmen.

In the following year, which was the eight hundredth year of Rome, Claudius was consul for the fourth time. Then he hastily sent for one Gallus, who was qualified to be a senator but had moved to Carthage, saying: "I shall bind you with golden fetters." And so, fettered by the rank, he stayed where he was. When a plot against Claudius was reported, he despised the man reported and took no account of him, saying: "One must not defend oneself against a flea and a wild beast alike." Many others accused by Messalina he put to death, and Asiaticus, and his son-in-law Magnus; Asiaticus for his property, Magnus for his birth and the connection. Yet they were convicted as if on other charges. Since many masters thought their sick slaves worth no care, but even pushed them out of their houses, he made a law that all who survived such treatment should be free. When a grandson was born to him by his daughter Antonia, whom he had married to Cornelius Faustus Sulla, Messalina's brother, after the death of Magnus, he allowed nothing to be voted, out of modesty. Messalina and his freedmen were puffed up. There were three who most shared the power among them: Callistus, who had been put in charge of the books of petitions; Narcissus, who was over the letters, and so even wore a dagger at his side; and Pallas, to whom the management of the money had been entrusted.
text: He constantly held gladiatorial games, delighting in them greatly, and from this many men perished, condemned on some charges. So becoming used to filling himself with blood and slaughter, he turned more readily to other killings too. The cause of this was the imperial freedmen and Messalina. For if they wished to kill anyone, they frightened him, and were allowed to do whatever they wished. Often, suddenly struck with alarm and ordering someone to be put to death in his immediate terror, he afterwards came to himself and recovered his senses, and learning what had happened was grieved and repented. Since he was doing such things, the Romans no longer had good hope of Claudius. So he was plotted against by others and by Annius Vinicianus, who sent to Furius Camillus Scribonianus, governor of Dalmatia, and persuaded him to revolt. When the soldiers would not obey him, he killed himself; and Claudius, though so terrified that he was ready to give up the power to him of his own accord, took heart on learning of his death, rewarded the soldiers with various things and with money, and searched out the fellow plotters and punished very many. Many others, and Vinicianus, killed themselves. For Messalina and Claudius's freedman Narcissus and his fellow freedmen, seizing this occasion, held back from none of the most terrible things. So many men and women were punished; and some of those quite guilty were saved, some by money and some by favour. blocks: Messalina, not content with committing adultery, also wished to have many husbands; and she would have married all her lovers with contracts, had she not been caught with the first and perished. For as long as all the imperial freedmen were of one mind with her, there was nothing they did not do by common consent; but when she accused and killed Polybius, though she was intimate with him too, they no longer trusted her, and deprived of their goodwill she was destroyed. For she enrolled as her husband Gaius Silius, the son of the Silius who was slain by Tiberius, feasted the wedding lavishly, and gave him a royal house, gathering into it all the most precious of Claudius's treasures; and at last she declared him consul. These things, plain to the others, escaped Claudius. When he was once away from home and alone, Narcissus revealed everything that was happening through the concubines. So he went back to Rome, killed many others and the dancer Mnester, and after this slaughtered Messalina herself.

When she had perished in this way, he married his niece Agrippina through the efforts of the freedmen, because she had a son, Domitius, already nearly of age, so that by bringing him up as a reserve for the rule they might suffer nothing terrible from Britannicus, as having caused his mother Messalina to be killed. When the marriage had already been decided, fearing Silanus, who was honoured by Claudius as a good man, and at the same time seeking his daughter Octavia, who was betrothed to Silanus, for Agrippina's son Domitius, they persuaded Claudius to kill Silanus as plotting against him. When this had been done, Vitellius made speeches in the senate that it was for the public good that Claudius should marry. He declared Agrippina suitable for this, and advised them to force him into the marriage. Spurred by this, the senators went to Claudius and compelled him, as it seemed, to marry, and made a decree that Romans might marry their nieces; for before it had been forbidden.

When the marriage was completed, she made Claudius her own, being most clever at managing him, and won over those he favoured, some by fear and some by kindnesses. At last she had his son Britannicus brought up like any ordinary boy (for the other son had died), and made Domitius at that time Claudius's son-in-law, and later had him adopted, and having had him adopted by Claudius she trained him for power and had him educated by Seneca. She gathered untold wealth, missing not even the slightest handle for gain, and murdering many for money. She also killed some women out of jealousy. When she had killed Lollia Paulina and did not recognise her head when it was brought, she opened its mouth with her own hands and inspected the teeth, which were peculiar in some way.

After this Claudius named Agrippina Augusta, and adopting her son renamed him Tiberius Claudius Nero Drusus Germanicus Caesar, paying no heed to the fact that the sky seemed to be on fire that day. And after this, bringing his daughter Octavia into another family, so as not to seem to be marrying brother and sister, he betrothed her to him. Agrippina exiled Calpurnia, a woman of the first rank, or, as is said, even killed her, because Claudius admired and praised her beauty. When Nero (for this name prevailed for him) was enrolled among the youths, on the day he was enrolled the divine power shook the earth greatly and struck all alike with fear at night. So Nero grew, while Britannicus had neither any honour nor any care; for Agrippina drove away some of those who looked after him and killed others; and she slaughtered Sosibius, to whom his upbringing and education had been entrusted, as plotting against Nero. Handing him over to those she wished, she allowed him neither to be with his father nor to appear in public. She could do everything, ruling Claudius and having won over Narcissus and Pallas; for Callistus, having risen far in power, had died.

The astrologers were driven out of all Italy, and those who kept company with them were punished. Caratacus, a chief of barbarians, was taken and brought to Rome, and was pardoned by Claudius; then, going round the city after his release and seeing its splendour and size, he said: "And then, owning these and such things, you covet our little huts?" Vexed with one Julius Gallicus who was pleading a case, Claudius ordered him to be thrown into the Tiber. At which Domitius Afer, who was the most powerful advocate of his time, made a very fine jest; for when someone asked for his help, since he had been left in the lurch by Gallicus, he said to him: "And who told you that I swim better than he does?"

blocks: After this, when Claudius fell ill, Nero went into the senate and promised horse races if Claudius recovered. For Agrippina moved in every way so that he might please the multitude and be thought the sole successor to the rule. So she had Nero promise the horse races, to which they were most devoted, for the health of Claudius, which she was praying against; and having caused some disturbance over the selling of bread, she persuaded Claudius to make known to the people by edict and write to the senate that, even if he died, Nero was already able to manage public affairs. From this he was much talked of and on everyone's lips, while many did not even know whether Britannicus was alive, and the rest thought him mad and epileptic, since Agrippina put this about. When Claudius got better, Nero held the horse races magnificently, and then married Octavia too, so that from this as well he might now seem a man. Nothing seemed enough to Agrippina; though all that Livia had had had been given to her, and some more had been voted. She wished to be called openly Claudius's equal in power. Once, when a great fire was spreading over the city, she went with him to help.

Claudius, vexed at what was being done, which was coming to his knowledge for a while, and meeting Britannicus kindly whenever he came upon him, would not bear what was happening, but prepared to put an end to her power, to bring his son among the youths, and to declare him successor. Learning this, Agrippina hurried to forestall him with poison before anything of the kind could be done. When the poison achieved nothing, because of the wine, of which Claudius always drank much, and because of the rest of his regimen, which all who hold power generally use to protect themselves, she sent for Locusta, a notorious poisoner who had recently been convicted for this very thing; and having prepared through her another poison that could not be escaped, she put it into some of the things called mushrooms, and ate from the others herself, but had him eat from the one containing the poison, which was the largest and finest. Plotted against in this way, he was carried out of the dinner as if very much overcome with drink, which had often happened at other times; and worn down by the poison, he died during the night without being able to say or hear anything, having lived sixty-three years, two months and thirteen days, and ruled alone thirteen years, eight months and twenty days.

Agrippina did this after sending Narcissus ahead to Campania, as if to use the waters there for his gout; for she could never have done such a thing while he was present; such a guardian of his master was he. When Claudius died, he too was at once destroyed, having had very great power. Before he was slain he did a splendid deed. For all Claudius's secret papers against Agrippina and some others, which he had as manager of his letters, he burned beforehand. He was slain by the tomb of Messalina, which, falling out by chance, seemed to have happened as vengeance for her. A comet was seen for a long time, a rain of blood, a thunderbolt fell on the standard of the guard, and other things happened which were reckoned as signs of Claudius's death.

In his reign Theudas too appeared, whom the divine Luke mentions in the Acts, and Josephus records in the nineteenth book of the Antiquities that he was a sorcerer who deceived many, until Fadus, the procurator of Judaea, sent a squadron of horsemen, killed many of his followers and took many alive, and when Theudas himself was taken alive, cut off his head. Simon the sorcerer too, staying in Rome under this emperor, deceived many of those living in Rome with his sorceries and won them over. Justin, the philosopher and martyr, shows this in his Apology for our teaching addressed to Antoninus, writing this: "And after the ascension of the Lord into heaven the demons put forward some men who said they were gods, who were not only not persecuted by you, but were even thought worthy of honour; of whom one was Simon the Samaritan, from the village of Gitta, who under Claudius Caesar, having worked magical powers by the operation of the demons in your royal city of Rome, was thought a god and has been honoured by you with a statue standing in the river Tiber between the two bridges, inscribed in Latin letters, Simoni deo sancto"; which rendered into Greek means "To Simon the holy god."

Peter too first came to Rome under Claudius, sowing the saving message in it and lighting up the minds of those in it with the light of truth, so that many of the Romans believed, and were so taken by the teaching of the chief of the apostles that they were not content with his words alone, but used entreaties with Mark too, the apostle who was Peter's follower, to set out for them a written record of the chief apostle's teaching, and so became the cause of the writing of the Gospel according to Mark. So Eusebius records these things.

blocks: Claudius departed from among men in the way that has been told, and Nero appropriated the leadership through Agrippina's efforts, being her son and having become Claudius's adopted son, since Claudius's will was suppressed and Britannicus, who was the dead man's legitimate son and still a boy, was pushed aside. When Nero had been proclaimed emperor and Augustus by the senate and the army, Agrippina managed all the business of the rule in his name, making a trade of everything. As time went on, Seneca, who was prefect of the guard, and Burrus, Nero's teacher, stopped her, and themselves conducted the rule as well as they could. For Nero, being very young when he became sole ruler (for he was then in his seventeenth year), and not fond of business, lived in luxury, made love, caroused, got drunk, and spent his time on gladiators and horse races. He was lavish and not small-minded, but rather prodigal. A proof: when he ordered two and a half million in silver to be given to one of his companions, and Agrippina had the money gathered and set before him, so that he might change his mind on seeing it all together, he understood, asked how much the heap was, and on learning said, "I did not know that I had given so little," and ordered it doubled. So he quickly drained the royal treasuries, quickly needed new resources, and collected unaccustomed taxes from every side.

When Agrippina, being most greedy for money, was furiously angry because she could not raise money, and threatened to make Britannicus emperor, Nero in fear killed him with poison. He died on the spot and was carried out as if in an epileptic fit; and at the funeral, since he had turned livid from the poison, he was smeared with gypsum and carried through the forum; but heavy rain fell while the gypsum was still wet and washed it all off, so that the horror was not only heard of but also seen.

Later he made away with his mother Agrippina too, sending his freedman Anicetus. She, seeing the man sent and knowing why he had come, tore her clothes, bared her belly and said: "Strike this, Anicetus, strike it; it bore Nero." She was slain, and Nero even became an eyewitness of the bold deed, stripped her and saw her whole body and counted the wounds. At night he was so disturbed that he leapt out of bed in terror. In Rome in many places some people secretly wrote: "Nero, Orestes, Alcmaeon, matricides."

He also sent away the Augusta Octavia, the daughter of Claudius, his wife. For being in love with Sabina, he wished to live with her as his wife. Sabina, afraid that Octavia might some time be called back, procured accusers against her of adultery and false sorcery, and caused her first to be exiled and then also slain. Then Sabina herself was killed by Nero; for he jumped on her with his heel when she was pregnant. He mourned her long when she was dead. He missed her so much that first he sent for and kept a woman like her, then castrated a freedman boy whom he called Sporus, since he too looked like Sabina, and married him, though he himself had been married to one Pythagoras, a freedman. And Pythagoras kept company with Nero as a husband, and Sporus as a wife. He played the lyre in public, though he had a thin and husky voice, and drove a chariot in the hippodrome. He crossed to Greece too, not at all as his ancestors had, but for dancing, playing the lyre, acting as herald and acting in tragedies. For Rome was not enough for him, but he needed an expedition too, so that he might become, as he said, a winner of the circuit of games.

But why should one tell each of the things done by him? For simply everything that ordinary actors play, he too said, did and suffered, except that he was bound with golden chains; for it was not fitting for an emperor of the Romans to be bound with iron ones. A soldier who saw him bound was indignant, ran up and freed him. Another, when someone asked what the emperor was doing, answered: "He is giving birth"; for he was playing some such part then. He also tried to dig through the Isthmus of the Peloponnese, though people hesitated. So taking a mattock himself and digging a little, he persuaded the others by compulsion to imitate him. When the first touched the earth, blood is said to have gushed up, groans and bellowings were heard, and many apparitions appeared.

He died on the spot and was carried out as if in an epileptic fit; and at the funeral, since he had turned livid from the poison, he was smeared with gypsum and carried through the forum; but heavy rain fell while the gypsum was still wet and washed it all off, so that the horror was not only heard of but also seen. Later he made away with his mother Agrippina too, sending his freedman Anicetus. She, seeing the man sent and knowing why he had come, tore her clothes, bared her belly and said: "Strike this, Anicetus, strike it; it bore Nero." She was slain, and Nero even became an eyewitness of the bold deed, stripped her and saw her whole body and counted the wounds. At night he was so disturbed that he leapt out of bed in terror. In Rome in many places some people secretly wrote: "Nero, Orestes, Alcmaeon, matricides." He also sent away the Augusta Octavia, the daughter of Claudius, his wife. For being in love with Sabina, he wished to live with her as his wife. Sabina, afraid that Octavia might some time be called back, procured accusers against her of adultery and false sorcery, and caused her first to be exiled and then also slain. Then Sabina herself was killed by Nero; for he jumped on her with his heel when she was pregnant. He mourned her long when she was dead. He missed her so much that first he sent for and kept a woman like her, then castrated a freedman boy whom he called Sporus, since he too looked like Sabina, and married him, though he himself had been married to one Pythagoras, a freedman. And Pythagoras kept company with Nero as a husband, and Sporus as a wife. He played the lyre in public, though he had a thin and husky voice, and drove a chariot in the hippodrome. He crossed to Greece too, not at all as his ancestors had, but for dancing, playing the lyre, acting as herald and acting in tragedies. For Rome was not enough for him, but he needed an expedition too, so that he might become, as he said, a winner of the circuit of games. But why should one tell each of the things done by him? For simply everything that ordinary actors play, he too said, did and suffered, except that he was bound with golden chains; for it was not fitting for an emperor of the Romans to be bound with iron ones. A soldier who saw him bound was indignant, ran up and freed him. Another, when someone asked what the emperor was doing, answered: "He is giving birth"; for he was playing some such part then. He also tried to dig through the Isthmus of the Peloponnese, though people hesitated. So taking a mattock himself and digging a little, he persuaded the others by compulsion to imitate him. When the first touched the earth, blood is said to have gushed up, groans and bellowings were heard, and many apparitions appeared.

blocks: He was the first to begin the persecution of the Christians, and he killed Peter and Paul, the chief of the apostles, at the same time, as Eusebius records, bringing forward testimonies from older writers. Others say that both apostles were perfected on the same day, but in different years. After Peter, Linus became the first high priest of Rome.

While Nero was still in Greece, the Jews revolted openly; and he sent Vespasian against them. Those in Britain and the Gauls, weighed down by the levies, had long been vexed and inflamed. Gaius Julius Vindex, a man whose father had been a Roman senator, seeing his countrymen the Gauls eager for revolt, roused them with a speech, and made them swear to do everything for the senate and people of the Romans, and to kill him himself if he did anything contrary to this. He put forward as emperor Servius Sulpicius Galba, who was of the nobility and then governor of Iberia. He accepted the leadership, but did not wish then to take the titles of the sole rule. As the revolt dragged on, Vindex slew himself, deeply grieved that the soldiers with him had been in danger, and indignant with heaven because, having reached out for such a thing, to overthrow Nero and free the Romans, he had not accomplished it. For he showed such eagerness for this that when Nero proclaimed a reward of two and a half million to anyone who brought him Vindex's head, he said: "Whoever kills Nero and brings me his head shall receive mine in return."

Nero, learning that Petronius too, whom he had sent ahead with the larger part of the army against the rebels, had taken Galba's side, no longer had any hope in arms, but planned to kill the senators, burn the city and sail to Alexandria, remarking: "Even if we fall from the rule, our little art will keep us there." As he was about to do this, the senate called away Nero's guard, went into the camp, declared him an enemy and chose Galba as emperor instead. When Nero perceived that he had been deserted by his guards, he put on mean clothing, mounted a horse no better, and with his face covered so as to escape notice, fled by night with Epaphroditus and Sporus. When he was recognised, so that he was even hailed as emperor by one of those who met him, he turned off the road and hid in a reedy place.

The people in Rome, when day came, rejoiced exceedingly and filled the city with garlands, and some wore caps as if freed; and the senate voted Galba all that belonged to the rule. The crowd jeered at Nero and murdered and dragged about many of those who had had power with him. The soldiers and others searched for him, and learning where he was, sent horsemen after him. Perceiving them approaching, he ordered those present to kill him and themselves. When they would not obey, he groaned aloud. Then wishing to kill Sporus and being unable, he said: "I alone have neither friend nor enemy." When the horsemen were already near, he struck himself, saying: "O Zeus, what an artist perishes in me!" As he was dying hard, Epaphroditus finished him off. So he died in the month of July, having lived thirty years, five months and twenty days, of which he ruled thirteen years and eight months less two days. In the eighth year of his reign Anianus became the first bishop of Alexandria after Mark the apostle and evangelist.

blocks: Galba, when Nero had perished and the senate had voted him the rule and Rufus had come over to him, took heart, yet did not take the name of Caesar before the senate's envoys came to him; nor had he before written the title of emperor in any letter. He punished those who had falsely accused anyone under Nero or given false witness. Slaves who had done or said anything against their masters were handed over to those very masters for punishment. The money and property that some had received from Nero were demanded back. He brought back those whom Nero had exiled as having committed some impiety against him, moved the bones of those of the royal family who had been slain to the tomb of Augustus, and restored their statues.

The soldiers in the Germanies put Aulus Vitellius at their head and revolted. Galba, learning of the revolt, adopted Lucius Piso, a young man of good birth, reasonable and sensible, and declared him Caesar. But Marcus Salvius Otho, indignant that he had not been adopted by Galba himself, rose against him, having prepared only thirty soldiers. For when Galba was sacrificing and he alone of the senators stood by him, and he heard the soothsayer say that Galba would be plotted against and advise him to stay at home and go out nowhere, he at once ran off as if going to the camp on some other business, was brought inside the wall by the soldiers who had conspired with him, and having persuaded the other soldiers too, or rather bought them with many promises, he received the rule from them on the spot and from the others.

Galba, learning what was being done, sent some men to the camp, thinking he could win back those in it. Meanwhile a soldier came up to him holding up a bare and bloody sword, saying: "Take heart, emperor; for I have killed Otho." Believing him, Galba set out for the Capitol to sacrifice. In the middle of the forum horse and foot met him, and there, before many eyes, they cut down the old man, the consul, the high priest, the Caesar, the emperor; and cutting off his head they stuck it on a pole. So he was murdered, saying only: "And what harm have I done?" Piso too died, and many others. Having done this, the soldiers cut off their heads and brought them to Otho in the camp and into the senate, so that the senators, struck with dismay, pretended to rejoice and voted Otho all that belonged to the rule. But it was plain that he was forcing the senate, and that he would rule more licentiously and harshly than Nero.

blocks: and twenty-three days, and ruled nine months and thirteen days, had this end; and Otho repented of what he had done, since bad omens appeared in the victims when he sacrificed and other signs came to him, but having entered on the rule he could not back out of it. He held on to it and paid the penalty.

Meanwhile someone, pretending to be Nero because of his likeness to Nero, threw almost all Greece into confusion, and gathering a band of criminals he set out for the legions in Syria. But as he was crossing at the Cydnus, Calpurnius seized him and killed him.

Otho secretly sent many men to Vitellius for a reconciliation. When he was not persuaded, he sent envoys openly. But Vitellius neither gave them any answer nor sent them back. Then Otho sent forces by land and sea, but was defeated through a divided command, not through weakness. He set out from Rome and took the leading men out with him. Giving part of the force to Proculus, he himself withdrew, saying he could not bear to see a battle of men of the same race. From this the soldiers and commanders, condemning his softness, did nothing of what was needed, but were defeated, sent heralds to Vitellius's men and mingled with them. A horseman reported this to Otho, and when he was not believed, said, "Would that this were false, Caesar," and having said this killed himself. When all believed from this and were ready to fight again (for the guards were many, and not a few others were present), and begged him not to betray either himself or them, for "we shall all gladly die for you," they said, Otho said: "It is much more just for one to perish for all than many for one"; and that he did not wish the Roman people to be at strife and so great a crowd of men to be destroyed because of one man. Having said this he withdrew to his room, and having written to his family and to Vitellius on their behalf, he burned the letters some had written him against Vitellius, so that no one might be in danger by being found out from them; and calling each of those present he embraced them and gave them money. Meanwhile, when a disturbance of soldiers arose, he went out, and having calmed them he did not withdraw until he had sent them off to safety, some to one place and some to another. And so, when there was no longer any disturbance, he killed himself. The soldiers buried his body, and some slew themselves over him.

This was the end of Otho, who lived thirty-seven years and ruled ninety days; from this he even overshadowed the impiety and wickedness of his life; for having lived most wickedly of men, he died most nobly. The soldiers were at once thrown into disorder, and many were killed by one another; then they came to agreement and went over to the victors.

blocks: Those in Rome, learning of Otho's fate (for he was away from the town, as has been said), proclaimed Vitellius emperor. Otho's death was reported to him while he was in Gaul. His wife and child came to him too, and he named the child Germanicus and emperor from the tribunal, though it was six years old. Being fond of divination and doing not even the slightest thing without it, he nevertheless drove out the astrologers then, and later the sorcerers too, ordering them to leave all Italy before a certain day. They in turn put up notices by night, and ordered him in turn to leave life before the day on which he did in fact die.

He was given to luxury and licentiousness. From the beginning he was the sort to be devoted to taverns, dice dens, dancers and charioteers, spent untold sums on such things, and for this reason had many creditors; and then he was more insolent still, spending most of the day and night gorging himself insatiably and constantly vomiting, so as to be nourished only by the passage of the food. By this he was able to hold out. Those who dined with him fared very badly. So one of them, who fell ill and for this reason missed the common table for some days, said: "If I had not fallen ill, I would surely have perished." The whole time of his sole rule was nothing but drinking bouts and revels. And why should one list each of them, when it is agreed by all that during the time of his rule he spent nine hundred million on dinners? He was often entertained by others too, and on the same day some gave him breakfast, others lunch, others dinner, and others some after-dinner comforts for his gorging.

Living in this way, he was not wholly without good deeds. For he kept the coinage struck under Nero, Galba and Otho, not vexed at their images, and maintained whatever they had given anyone, taking nothing from anyone; he neither demanded arrears of taxes nor confiscated anyone's property, putting to death very few of those who had served Otho, and not depriving their relatives of their property either. He gave the families of those put to death earlier all that was still found in the treasury. Nor did he challenge the wills of those who had fought against him and fallen in the battles. He forbade senators and knights to fight as gladiators or put on any show in the orchestra. For this he was praised.

After this the revolt in Judaea against him was reported to him. He was terribly afraid of it, since other signs had occurred, and the moon seemed to be eclipsed twice contrary to the regular order; for it was darkened on the fourth day and on the seventh. Two suns were seen at once, from the east and from the west, the one weak and pale, the one from the east strong.

The revolt happened like this. Vespasian was staying in Judaea (for, as has already been told, he had been sent there by Nero because of the revolt of the Jews); he sent his son Titus to greet Galba when he became sole ruler; and when Titus came back, since he had learned on the way of the rising of Vitellius and of Otho, Vespasian too set out for the monarchy, according to Dio. But as Josephus says in his history of the capture, the soldiers with him, learning that the Gauls in Europe had revolted and put forward Galba as emperor, that those serving in Germany had chosen Vitellius instead, and that those in Rome had put forward Otho, themselves voted the monarchy to their own general, and urging one another on they proclaimed Vespasian emperor and called on him to save the empire of the Romans, which was in danger. When he refused, the commanders pressed him, and the soldiers surrounded him with drawn swords and threatened to kill him. So he was persuaded, and first wrote about his affairs to the man governing Egypt; and he at once proclaimed him emperor. Vespasian, learning this, sent Mucianus, the governor of Syria, into Italy against Vitellius.

At that time he also called to him Josephus the Hebrew, who had dared to hail him as emperor while Nero was still alive and was still a prisoner and captive with him, and ordered him to be freed, as having foretold the rule to him. When Titus told his father Vespasian that it was just for the disgrace too to be taken from Josephus along with the iron, and that this would happen if the bonds were not untied but cut through, which is done for those who have been bound wrongly, Vespasian agreed, and someone came forward and cut through the chain with an axe. For Josephus, as he himself recorded, having found an oracle in the sacred writings showing that someone from their country would rule the world, supposed, because of the strife in Rome and the constant changes of its rulers there, that the oracle pointed to Vespasian, and foretold the power to him. Appian too mentions this oracle in the twenty-second book of his Roman History. But it would be thought more just, and indeed most true, to take the oracle as referring to the Saviour of the race of men, the Lord Jesus Christ; for Vespasian did not reign over the whole world, as in the oracle, but only over the part under the Romans; and much of the world was outside the Roman empire; but the Lord reigned and reigns over the whole world, to whom it was said by the Father: "Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations for your inheritance, and the ends of the earth for your possession."

Vespasian set out for Alexandria, where good news came to him from Rome too, that Vitellius had been slaughtered, that he himself had been proclaimed emperor by the people and the senate, and that his son Domitian had been advanced to the leadership until his own arrival in Rome.

Vitellius's death happened in this way. Vespasian's soldiers had already come near Rome, and bursting into it they did every kind of terrible thing. While the city was being sacked, Vitellius in fear put on a ragged tunic and hid in a dark room in which dogs were kept, meaning to escape by night to his brother at Tarracina. But the soldiers searched him out and seized him, covered with filth and blood (for he had been mauled by the dogs), tore his clothes, bound his hands behind him, put a rope round his neck, and some slapped him, others plucked his beard, and all jeered at him, among other things for his prodigality. When he was ashamed at this and looked down, the soldiers pricked him under the chin with daggers, so that he would look up even against his will. A Celt, pitying him, said: "I will help you in the only way I can." He wounded him and slew himself; but Vitellius did not die of the wound, but was dragged towards the prison. Deeply pained at what he suffered and what he heard, he said: "But I was your emperor." The soldiers in anger cut him down, cut off his head and carried it round the whole city; he had lived fifty-four years and eighty-nine days, and ruled a year less ten days.

Deeply pained at what he suffered and what he heard, he said: "But I was your emperor." The soldiers in anger cut him down, cut off his head and carried it round the whole city; he had lived fifty-four years and eighty-nine days, and ruled a year less ten days.

blocks: When this had been done, Mucianus arrived and managed affairs with Domitian; Vespasian was hailed as emperor by the senate too, and Titus and Domitian were named Caesars. Mucianus was called brother by Vespasian, and received authority to do and write whatever he wished, only adding the emperor's name; and for this reason he wore a ring that had been sent to him, so that what he ordered might receive the imperial seal. So he and Domitian gave offices and procuratorships to many, and appointed one prefect after another and consuls, as if they were sole rulers themselves. So Vespasian wrote to Domitian: "I thank you, my son, for letting me rule and not yet having deposed me."

Vespasian, coming to Alexandria, raised much money from there, making money also from many taxes, reviving those that had lapsed, increasing those customary, and adding new ones too. He did the same afterwards in the rest of the empire, in Italy and in Rome itself. He settled Egypt in a short time, and sent much grain from it to Rome; and having left his son Titus at Jerusalem to sack it, he waited for its capture, so as to return to Rome with his son. But as time was spent in the siege, he left Titus in Palestine, and himself boarded a merchant ship and sailed to Lycia, and from there went partly on foot and partly by sea to Brundisium.

Coming to Rome he gave gifts to the soldiers and the people, took in hand the precincts and public works that had suffered, repaired those already ruined, and when they were completed inscribed on them not his own name but that of those who had first built them. The property of those who had opposed him and fallen in the battles he left to their children or other relatives, and he also destroyed the old bonds owed to the treasury. Spending magnificently on the public, he lived most frugally, and spent nothing beyond necessities. He was neither of noble birth nor rich. He received all who came to him. He kept company with his friends even before dawn, lying in bed; the doors of the palace were open all day, and there was no guard at them. In sum, in his care for public affairs he was thought an emperor, but in everything else he was common and lived on equal terms with the rest.

When Jerusalem had been taken, Titus came back to Italy, and he and his father held the triumph in a chariot; and Domitian, who was consul, joined them in it on horseback. After this Vespasian appointed teachers in Rome of both Latin and Greek learning, drawing a salary from the treasury. Mucianus, making a long accusation against the philosophers, persuaded Vespasian to drive them out of Rome; and all except Musonius were driven out. He was thought fond of money, because when some voted to set up a statue to him, the cost of which was two hundred and fifty thousand, he held out his hand and said: "Give me the money; for this is its base." And to Titus, who was indignant at a tax he had introduced, he said, taking gold coins that had come from it: "See, my son, whether they smell." He was plotted against by Alienus and by Marcellus. When they were found out, Alienus was slain in the palace on Titus's order, and Marcellus, tried in the senate and condemned, killed himself by cutting his throat with a razor.

Vespasian fell ill with fevers and died; or, as some said, falsely accusing Titus, having drunk poison at a dinner. When the doctors rebuked him in his illness for doing all the business of the rule while ill, he said: "An emperor must die standing." He died having lived sixty-nine years, eight months and eight days, and ruled alone ten years less six days.

blocks: When he died Titus succeeded to the rule. Ruling alone, he did nothing murderous or amorous, either because he changed or because he lived a very short time, as rulers go. For he lived two years, two months and twenty days after becoming sole ruler, at the age of thirty-nine years, five months and twenty-five days. So they put him on a level with the many years of Augustus, because neither would Augustus have been loved if he had lived a shorter time, nor Titus if longer; the one because, having been rather harsh at the beginning because of the factions and wars, he was later able to shine by his benefactions over a long time, the other because, having ruled mildly, he died at the height of his glory, and would perhaps have been shown, had he lived long, to have had more good fortune than virtue. He put no senator to death during his leadership, and issued letters confirming everything given to anyone by the former emperors. He was careful with money and did not spend it in vain; yet he never punished anyone for money.

In his time the false Nero appeared, who was an Asiatic called Terentius Maximus, resembling Nero in looks and voice; for he too sang to the lyre. He won over some people from Asia, and advancing to the Euphrates attached many more to himself, and at last fled to Artabanus, the leader of the Parthians; who, being angry with Titus, received him and prepared to bring him back to Rome.

In the first year of his leadership a great fire suddenly broke out in Campania in the autumn. For Mount Vesuvius, which is near Neapolis, has abundant springs of fire; only the middle is on fire, while the outside parts are without fire. So, as the parts in the middle are being parched and turned to ash, the peaks round about keep their ancient height, while the middle, consumed by the fire, has become hollow by settling. Flame comes up from it by night, and smoke by day, sometimes more and sometimes less; sometimes it also throws up ash, when it suddenly settles, and sends up stones, when it is forced by wind; it roars and bellows, having outlets that are not compressed but loose and free. Such is Vesuvius; and then a tremendous crash was suddenly heard, as if the mountains were falling together, and first huge stones leapt up, then much fire and boundless smoke, so that the sun was hidden and darkness came out of light. And untold ash was blown up, so that the land, the sea and the whole air were covered, the fish and birds perished, and two cities, Herculaneum and Pompeii, were buried while their people were sitting in the theatre. The ash was so great that some of it came even to Africa, to Syria, to Egypt and to Rome itself; and from it a plague later broke out.

Titus sent settlers to the Campanians and gave them money, among other things the property of those who had died without heirs. He himself accepted nothing from anyone, though many offered; and he restored many of the public works from his own means. He held wonderful games, at which he threw down from above small wooden balls bearing a token, one of some food, another of clothing, another of gold, horses, pack animals, cattle, slaves; those who snatched them took them to the givers and received what was written on them. His too is that famous saying: "Today I have not reigned, since I have done good to no one."
In his second year Linus, the first bishop of the church of the Romans, dying, handed the high priesthood to Anencletus.

blocks: In the following year Titus died, as the prevailing report has it, plotted against by his brother, or as some write, of illness. Yet while he was still breathing and perhaps able to recover, Domitian put him into a chest full of snow, as if the illness needed some cooling. As he breathed his last he is said to have said: "I have done only one wrong"; but what this was he did not make clear. Some say that he had had Domitia, his brother's wife; others that he had not killed Domitian, who was plainly plotting against him, but was himself destroyed by him and handed over the rule of the Romans to such a man.

While Titus was still breathing, Domitian rode off to Rome, went into the camp and took the title and power of emperor. He was bold, quick to anger, treacherous and secretive; he truly loved no human being except some women, but pretended to love the man he most wished to kill. He was faithless even to those who did him favours and served him in the most terrible things. Whenever some provided him with very much money or falsely accused many, he put them to death, so that the wrongs might seem to proceed from them alone. Being most wicked, he held the friends of his father and his brother in dishonour, and destroyed some of them. He sent away his wife Domitia for adultery, having murdered Paris the dancer in the middle of the street because of her, and lived openly with his niece Julia as his wife. Then, at the people's request, he was reconciled with Domitia, but went on with Julia no less.

After this he set out for Gaul, and having plundered some of the treaty peoples beyond the Rhine, he swelled as if he had achieved something great, and increased the soldiers' pay, perhaps because of the victory. For when each received seventy-five drachmas, he ordered a hundred to be given. Repenting, he did not reduce the amount, but cut down the number of those serving. And he harmed the treasury greatly both ways, making those who defended him both insufficient and highly paid. He was vexed alike with those who courted him and those who did not, with the one as flatterers and the other as despising him. Pretending to false victories, he was elected consul for ten years and censor for life.

Many of those tributary to the Romans revolted, since money was being exacted from them by force, as the Nasamones did. For they killed the money collectors and so defeated Flaccus, the governor of Numidia, when he came against them, that they even sacked his camp. Finding in it other supplies and wine, they filled themselves and fell asleep. Learning this, Flaccus attacked them, destroyed them all and killed all the non-combatants. Elated at this, Domitian said to the senate: "I have stopped the Nasamones from existing." For he already thought it right to be considered a god, and exulted in being called master and god. These things were not only said but also written. At a show, when much rain and a violent storm suddenly came on, he let no one leave the show, but himself changing his cloaks, he did not allow them to change at all; and from this many fell ill and died.

No one could count those punished by him. Many men and women of the rich were punished for adultery; some of the women had been seduced by him himself. On other charges too many were fined and put to death. For a woman was murdered because she undressed in front of his image, and another man as having kept company with astrologers. One Mettius, whom rumour proclaimed as about to rule alone, he exiled and murdered, charging him with having the world painted on the walls of his bedroom. A sophist, because in practising he wrote a declamation against tyrants, he punished with death. Many perished too as philosophers, and the rest were driven out.

Doing such things, he was plotted against by Parthenius and Sigerus, his chamberlains, Entellus, who managed the books of the rule, and Stephanus, a freedman. Neither his wife Domitia nor the prefect Norbanus nor his fellow consul Petronius was ignorant of the plot. For Domitia, hated by him, feared she would die, and the others no longer loved him. It is said that Domitian, suspecting them all together, was planning to kill them, and having written down their names, put the list in his bed under the pillow; and a little child took the list and carried it off, not knowing what it was carrying. Domitia came upon it, read what was written, and told them; and from this they hurried on the plot.

Many unfavourable signs came to him too. One Larginus Proculus, who had foretold in Germany that Domitian would die on such a day, was arrested for this and sent to Rome; and when questioned by him he said then too that it would be so. He was condemned to death, but it was put off, so that he might be killed after the day on which he had said Domitian would die; and when Domitian was slain on that day, he was saved. Another, who told him when and how he would perish, was asked by what manner he himself would die; and when he said he would be eaten by dogs, he was condemned to be burned alive and thrown on the fire. But a heavy rain burst down and the pyre was put out, and dogs found him lying on it with his hands bound behind him and tore him to pieces.

When Domitian was resting at midday, Parthenius sent in Stephanus, as stronger than the others. Domitian was struck, though not mortally, but was thrown down by him and lay there; then he was finished off by him and others. So he was slain, and Stephanus too perished, those who had had no part in the conspiracy running together against him.

Apollonius of Tyana, who was a Pythagorean philosopher but above all a sorcerer, was then at Ephesus speaking to the crowd at the very hour Domitian was being killed, as was later established exactly from what happened on both sides; he stood speechless for some time, then cried out: "Well done, Stephanus, strike the wretch; you have struck, you have wounded, you have killed!" Philostratus, who wrote the life of Apollonius, recorded this so.

Domitian lived forty-four years, ten months and twenty-six days, and ruled alone fifteen years and five days. In the fourth year of his reign the first high priest of the church of the Alexandrians after Mark the apostle died, and Abilius succeeded him, becoming the second bishop of Alexandria. In the twelfth year of his leadership, when Anencletus died, Clement received the high priesthood of Rome, being its third bishop, according to Eusebius.

This most hateful emperor after Nero stirred up again the persecution of the Christians, becoming the successor of his war against God; he confined the apostle and evangelist John on the island of Patmos for his preaching, and ordered the descendants of David to be put to death. Recording this, Eusebius brings forward Hegesippus, who says this: "There still survived grandsons of Jude, who was called the Lord's brother according to the flesh, whom some reported as being of the family of David. When they were brought to him, Domitian asked them whether they were of David; and they admitted it. Then he asked further how much property they owned and how much money they had; and they said that they had only nine thousand denarii, and that they held this not in silver but in the value of land, from which they supported themselves by their own labour and paid their taxes; and they showed the roughness of their hands as evidence of their labour. When they were asked about the kingdom of Christ, what kind it was and where and when it would appear, they answered that it was not of the world nor earthly, but heavenly, and would appear at the end of the age. At this Domitian despised them as of no account, let them go free, and stopped the persecution by an order."

blocks: So this most wicked man broke off his life by violence, as would that he had done before his monarchy too; and the leadership passed to Nerva, a man most nobly born and most reasonable. For those who plotted against Domitian did not set to work until they had secured the successor to the sole rule. So they went to Nerva; who would nearly have perished when the astrologers said he would rule alone. For Domitian, examining the days and hours in which all the leading men had been born, did away beforehand with not a few of those who were expected from this to be in some power. And he would have killed Nerva too, had not one of the astrologers who was well disposed to him said that he would die in a few days; for believing this would really happen, he did not wish to murder him too, since he would surely die soon. For this reason they more easily persuaded him to agree to accept the leadership. When Domitian had perished he at once took the sole rule. By decree he allowed those driven out by Domitian to return and get back their property. The senate voted that Domitian's honours be torn down. At that time, then, the story goes, the great apostle John too came back from his exile in Patmos to Ephesus.

Nerva loved justice and was not overcome by money. For in his reign Atticus, the father of Herodes the sophist, as Philostratus recorded in his Lives of the Sophists, found a treasure of untold value in his house. Afraid, he wrote to Nerva: "A treasure has been found in my house; what then do you order about it?" And he wrote back: "Use what you have found." Still cautious, he wrote again: "But what has been found is beyond me." And the emperor wrote back to this: "Then misuse it."

In his reign Abilius, the second bishop of Alexandria, departed this life, and Cerdon presided over the church there. The church at Antioch was then led by Ignatius the God-bearer, who is also known as the second bishop there after Euodius. Likewise Symeon led the church of the faithful in Jerusalem, he too having received the bishopric second, after his kinsman James, who was called the brother of the Lord.

By this emperor gladiatorial fights and the watching of them were forbidden. He did nothing without the opinion of the leading men of the senate. He made a law that no one among the Romans should have the generative parts cut out, nor marry a niece. Discovering that Calpurnius Crassus and others were plotting against him, he seated them near him at a show while they did not yet know they had been found out, and handed them swords, supposedly so that they might see whether they were well made and sharpened, but in truth so that they might know that he despised death. He said: "I have ruled so that I can lay down the rule and live safely as a private man." Being despised for the goodness of his ways and his great age, he went up to the Capitol and cried out: "With good fortune for the senate and people, I adopt Marcus Ulpius Nerva Trajan." Then he also proclaimed him Caesar, and wrote with his own hand to the man, who was then governing Germany: "May the Danaans pay for my tears with your arrows." So Nerva, having ruled one year and four months, fell ill and departed this life, having put forward Trajan as emperor.

For Domitian, examining the days and hours in which all the leading men had been born, did away beforehand with not a few of those who were expected from this to be in some power. And he would have killed Nerva too, had not one of the astrologers who was well disposed to him said that he would die in a few days; for believing this would really happen, he did not wish to murder him too, since he would surely die soon. For this reason they more easily persuaded him to agree to accept the leadership. When Domitian had perished he at once took the sole rule. By decree he allowed those driven out by Domitian to return and get back their property. The senate voted that Domitian's honours be torn down. At that time, then, the story goes, the great apostle John too came back from his exile in Patmos to Ephesus. Nerva loved justice and was not overcome by money. For in his reign Atticus, the father of Herodes the sophist, as Philostratus recorded in his Lives of the Sophists, found a treasure of untold value in his house. Afraid, he wrote to Nerva: "A treasure has been found in my house; what then do you order about it?" And he wrote back: "Use what you have found." Still cautious, he wrote again: "But what has been found is beyond me." And the emperor wrote back to this: "Then misuse it." In his reign Abilius, the second bishop of Alexandria, departed this life, and Cerdon presided over the church there. The church at Antioch was then led by Ignatius the God-bearer, who is also known as the second bishop there after Euodius. Likewise Symeon led the church of the faithful in Jerusalem, he too having received the bishopric second, after his kinsman James, who was called the brother of the Lord. By this emperor gladiatorial fights and the watching of them were forbidden. He did nothing without the opinion of the leading men of the senate. He made a law that no one among the Romans should have the generative parts cut out, nor marry a niece. Discovering that Calpurnius Crassus and others were plotting against him, he seated them near him at a show while they did not yet know they had been found out, and handed them swords, supposedly so that they might see whether they were well made and sharpened, but in truth so that they might know that he despised death. He said: "I have ruled so that I can lay down the rule and live safely as a private man." Being despised for the goodness of his ways and his great age, he went up to the Capitol and cried out: "With good fortune for the senate and people, I adopt Marcus Ulpius Nerva Trajan." Then he also proclaimed him Caesar, and wrote with his own hand to the man, who was then governing Germany: "May the Danaans pay for my tears with your arrows." So Nerva, having ruled one year and four months, fell ill and departed this life, having put forward Trajan as emperor.

blocks: Trajan drew his family from Iberia, and was in his forty-second year from birth when he obtained the sole rule, so that he was at the height of both soul and body, neither filled with rashness by youth nor dulled by age. He honoured the good, and being well disposed to all, he neither feared anyone nor hated, nor heeded slanderers, nor was quick to anger, and kept equally from others' money and from unjust killings. Yet being high-minded and generous in spirit he spent much on roads, harbours and public buildings. When he rebuilt the hippodrome in Rome, which had been ruined, larger and more beautiful, he inscribed on it that he had made it big enough for the Roman people. He delighted more in being loved than in being honoured, and wished to be dear to his subjects and fearsome to his enemies. He had no share in literary learning, but he understood and practised its work. Though fond of wine, he was sober, and though keen on boys, he hurt no one. Being warlike and having had very many successes, he did not let the soldiers grow arrogant, so firmly did he rule them. His wife was Plotina.

He marched against the Dacians, or Dacoi as the Ionians say, as Appian says in the twenty-third book of his Roman History, not bearing to give them the money they received every year, and longing to exact punishment for what they had done. Decebalus, who ruled the Dacians, learning of Trajan's onset against the nation, was afraid, knowing the man to be a most skilful general. When war broke out between them, the Romans killed many of the enemy, and no fewer of their own were wounded. The wounded were so many that when the bandages ran out Trajan did not spare even his own clothing. When he had taken the heights, though with difficulty, and come near their royal seat, Decebalus sent envoys, agreeing to hand over the arms, the engines and the engine makers, and to do anything else that was demanded; and coming to the emperor he threw himself on the ground and did obeisance to him. Then Trajan went back to Italy, bringing Decebalus's envoys with him. They were brought into the senate, and laying down their arms and clasping their hands in the posture of captives, they said much and begged; and so, obtaining peace, they received back their arms. Trajan held a triumph and was named Dacicus. He was not, as a warlike man, neglectful of other things or less given to judging, but judged cases from the tribunal in many places and often.

When it was reported to him that Decebalus was making trouble again and not keeping to the treaty, he marched against him once more. Decebalus, beaten by force, planned to overcome him by guile. Knowing that Trajan was easy of access and received anyone who wished into conversation, he sent false deserters, so that they might make away with him if they could. One of them was suspected and arrested, and under examination revealed the secret. The emperor bridged the Ister, accomplishing a work that cannot be admired worthily or described, and crossing the river by this bridge, he overcame the Dacians, with difficulty and danger, but he overcame them. Decebalus in despair killed himself. From this the nation of the Dacians and their country became subject to the Romans. He also found the treasures of Decebalus, though they were hard to find. For the barbarian had diverted a river that flowed past his palace, dug the earth over which the water had passed to a great depth, laid in the trench a great deal of gold, more silver, and other precious things that do not perish from moisture, paved the earth there with slabs, heaped soil on them, and so turned the water back into its first course; and he stored much in a cave too. He did this with no one else present except captives who toiled at it; and after the hiding he killed the captives, so that they might not make known what they had done. But one companion of Decebalus who knew about the hoard showed it to Trajan.

He loved Licinius Sura, a rich man, and was loved by him; and when some slandered the man as plotting against him, he went to him uninvited for dinner, and sending away his guards he called Sura's doctor and had his eyes treated by him, and had his beard shaved by Sura's barber; then he bathed and dined. And the next day he said to those slandering Sura: "If Sura wished to kill me, nothing stopped the man from doing so yesterday." When he appointed a prefect of the guard, and held out to him the sword he had to wear at his side, he said: "Take this, and if I rule well, use it for me, but if badly, against me." He also built libraries.

After this he marched against the Parthians and the Armenians, because the Armenian had received his diadem not from him but from the king of the Parthians. This was the pretext; but the whole of it was ambition and love of glory. So he subdued Armenia. The senate voted him many things, and among other things named him Optimus, which in Greek means best, and then also gave him the surname Parthicus. He took more pride in the title of Optimus than in the others,
