blocks: In this way, then, as has been said, Valentinian was voted emperor. He was brought, proclaimed, and put on the imperial insignia. Sallustius, because he had shown zeal for his proclamation, asked as a reward to be released from the cares of the prefecture. And the emperor said: "Did you load me with the burden of so many affairs for this, that you yourself should not even touch it?" Valentinian came from Pannonia. He was pious towards God; for this reason Julian condemned him to exile; and then, recalling him from exile, made him tribune of a numerus. He was very vigorous in strength and very just in mind. So he punished many of those then holding office as wrongdoers, saying that the ruler is required to care for justice before all else. He took his brother Valens as partner in rule, and entrusting the eastern part to him, he himself stayed in the west, and having fought many wars against barbarians he set up trophies over them. Before his reign he had a son named Gratian, born to him by his wife Severa; and he proclaimed him emperor. He also married a second wife while the first was still alive. The second was Justina, by whom he begot the younger Valentinian and daughters Justa, Grata, and Galla.

Under him, when Eudoxius, the heterodox high priest of New Rome, died, Demophilus was put in his place, being of the same belief as his predecessor; he held the church for twelve years. This emperor also appointed the great Ambrose bishop of the city of Milan. Learning about his brother Valens that he was championing the Arian heresy and forcing everyone to assent to it, he rebuked him by letter and urged him to depart from the heresy. But he did not depart from his own will, and raged all the more against the orthodox.

A certain Rhodanus, a praepositus, had great power with Valentinian. A woman called Berenice came to the emperor Valentinian against him, charging the praepositus with wronging her. The emperor investigated, and learning that the woman was not lying, he summoned the praepositus and ordered him to remedy the wrong to the woman. He, trusting in his freedom of speech with the emperor, took no account of the wronged woman. So the woman came to the emperor again; and he, learning that the praepositus had taken no notice of the woman, at once stripped him of his rank, and ordered him to be led round the theatre in bonds while a horse race was being held, with heralds going before him crying out the wrong done to the woman and the disobedience to the imperial command; and after being led round and proclaimed, to be burned there on the spot. So he met such an end; and all his property was given over to the woman by imperial letter. This emperor died while staying in the Gauls, having enjoyed a long life; for he lived eighty-four years, of which he reigned eleven. And he left his son Gratian as successor to the rule of the west.

blocks: Valens, championing the Arianisers as one of their opinion, persecuted the orthodox and brought many terrible things upon them, persuaded by his own wife Domnica. Once, when he was staying in Nicomedia, eighty men of the priesthood came to him on an embassy from the body of the orthodox, and he ordered them all to be burned with the ship that carried them. And they were all burned up in the middle of the sea with the ship, which lasted as far as Dacibyza. Gregory, great in theology, mentions them too, saying: "burnings of priests at sea". He not only punished the orthodox, but also handed all the churches over to the Arians, driving the orthodox bishops out of them.

It is said, then, that when those of the right belief had been driven out of the catholic church at Nicaea too, they went to the great Basil, and he interceded about this with Valens, but Valens would not be persuaded, and the great Basil said: "We must leave the judgement of this, emperor, to God. Let the church be securely locked, and let those who hold the views of Arius stand outside and pray to God. And if the church opens for them of its own accord, let them have it; but if it does not open, we too must be allowed to pray to God. And if the gates are thrown open of their own accord, it must be thought that the divine precinct has been allotted to us by God; but if the sanctuary does not open for us either, let it in that case be given up to the Arianisers." This pleased the emperor, and he allowed it to be done so. So the church at Nicaea was locked on every side. The Arianisers prayed and babbled for a long time, but the church did not open. At last, late, when the heretics had withdrawn, the orthodox, with the great Basil leading them, began their prayer; and at once the bolts and bars burst, the gates parted from each other, and gave entry to the faithful. This emperor allowed the Hellenes to make sacrifices and favoured the Jews; he opposed only the orthodox.

When the Scythians overran the Thracian and Macedonian country, he went out to stand against them. At that time the great father Isaac, meeting him as he rode, said: "Give back the churches to the orthodox, emperor, and know that you will return victorious; but if you campaign against God, you will not return from there." The most impious emperor was angered by this, and ordered the saint to be kept under guard until he returned. And he said: "If you return, God has not spoken in me." And Valens saw in a dream a man saying to him:
"Go quickly to great Mimas, where a terrible doom snatches you, wretch."

Waking, then, he asked who Mimas might be. And one of those who had devoted themselves to letters (for such men followed the emperors and were their intimates, as I wish they did now too) told him that Mimas was a mountain of Asia lying by the sea, and that Homer mentions it in the Odyssey, saying "past windy Mimas". And he said: "What need have I, then, to go to this mountain and die there?" So campaigning against the Scythians and engaging them near Thrace, he was shamefully defeated, and fleeing he hid in a building, beside which a heap of chaff and sweepings was piled up. When after the emperor's defeat the Scythians plundered that country and also set the houses on fire, that building too was burned down, and Valens perished in it. But Saint Isaac, though shut up, knew in the spirit of Valens' burning, and told those who happened to be there that Valens was at that moment dying by fire. The day was noted, and afterwards it was learned that the saint had not been mistaken. After the barbarians had withdrawn from there, when some were searching for the emperor's body, a tomb was found in the house in which he had been burned, with an epitaph of an ancient man: "Here lies Mimas, Macedonian general."

Against this emperor Procopius, the cousin of Julian, rose up and took Byzantium. But betrayed by his own men, and tied by the legs to two trees bent down by force, when the trees were let go the wretch was torn apart. At that time the walls of the city of Chalcedon were also pulled down, as its citizens had favoured Procopius. As they were being pulled down, a slab was found in their foundations with this written on it:

"But when the Nymphs, delighting in a sacred dance through the city, take their stand along the well-garlanded streets, and a wall becomes a lamentable defence for baths, then countless tribes of far-scattered men, wild, raging, clad in evil strength, crossing the stream of Cimmerian Ister with the spear, will destroy both the Scythian country and the Mysian land. And setting foot on the Thracian land with frenzied hopes, there they would meet the end of life and their doom."

Valens used the material of the walls of Chalcedon to build a channel of water, which common speech calls an aqueduct, and named it after himself, Valens; by it he had water brought into the city, so that it should have plenty of water both for other uses and for baths. And the prefect of the city built a Nymphaeum in the place called the Taurus, displaying through it the benefits of the water channel. These things were followed by the barbarians' invasion too, as written on the slab; they plundered Thrace, and were later destroyed in it.

Under this Valens, it is said, Libanius the sophist and Iamblichus, the teacher of Proclus, practised divination by a cock, seeking to learn who would reign after Valens. It is, as the story goes, of this kind. The twenty-four letters are written in dust, and a grain of wheat or barley is put on each of them. Then a cock is let loose, while certain incantations are sung over them, and it is watched from which letters it takes the grains. And these, put together, are thought to reveal what is sought. When they did this then, they saw the cock take the grain on the theta, and the one on the epsilon, the one on the omicron and the one on the delta. So what was revealed seemed ambiguous: it seemed to mean either Theodorus, or Theodosius, or Theodotus. Learning this, Valens suspected and destroyed many of those called by such names. He also sought those who had made the divination. So Iamblichus, fearing his cruelty, drank a deadly poison, as some have recorded, and took himself out of life. For Valens was hard to appease in his anger; so he used to say that a man who quickly put aside his anger would very quickly put aside justice too. He reigned thirteen years and four months, and perished as his impiety deserved.

Valens used the material of the walls of Chalcedon to build a channel of water, which common speech calls an aqueduct, and named it after himself, Valens; by it he had water brought into the city, so that it should have plenty of water both for other uses and for baths. And the prefect of the city built a Nymphaeum in the place called the Taurus, displaying through it the benefits of the water channel. These things were followed by the barbarians' invasion too, as written on the slab; they plundered Thrace, and were later destroyed in it. Under this Valens, it is said, Libanius the sophist and Iamblichus, the teacher of Proclus, practised divination by a cock, seeking to learn who would reign after Valens. It is, as the story goes, of this kind. The twenty-four letters are written in dust, and a grain of wheat or barley is put on each of them. Then a cock is let loose, while certain incantations are sung over them, and it is watched from which letters it takes the grains. And these, put together, are thought to reveal what is sought. When they did this then, they saw the cock take the grain on the theta, and the one on the epsilon, the one on the omicron and the one on the delta. So what was revealed seemed ambiguous: it seemed to mean either Theodorus, or Theodosius, or Theodotus. Learning this, Valens suspected and destroyed many of those called by such names. He also sought those who had made the divination. So Iamblichus, fearing his cruelty, drank a deadly poison, as some have recorded, and took himself out of life. For Valens was hard to appease in his anger; so he used to say that a man who quickly put aside his anger would very quickly put aside justice too. He reigned thirteen years and four months, and perished as his impiety deserved.

blocks: Gratian the son of Valentinian and the younger Valentinian his brother became masters of the Roman empire; for Gratian alone had been proclaimed by his father, as has already been related. But when Valentinian died, Gratian was not present at his father's death. So the army at that time proclaimed the younger Valentinian emperor, who was then four years old. Gratian, returning from abroad, reproached the soldiers and even ill-treated some of them, punishing the ringleaders of his brother's proclamation for having proclaimed another without the consent of himself, who was emperor. But he did not refuse his brother himself as co-ruler, but took him as partner in the rule. This emperor emulated his father in piety. So when his uncle Valens once asked him for help against the Scythians, he did not give it, writing to him that one must not fight alongside the enemy of God. And to the shepherds who had been driven out of their own churches he granted by decree their return to them.

When after the defeat of Valens the Scythians had swollen in their pride, and were plundering Thrace and the parts around it and could not be checked, he summoned Theodosius from Hispania (Hispania is the most distinguished city of European Iberia), a man very brave and very pious. He sent him as general with an army against the barbarians; and he engaged them, won, and raised a trophy, a great multitude of Scythians being slaughtered in the war, and the rest turning to flight, some perishing as they were caught, others destroyed by one another in the flight. When nearly all those barbarians had perished, Theodosius left the army there and came himself to bring the news of the victory to Gratian, who was then staying in Pannonia. When he reported the victory to the emperor and announced the good news of the barbarians' destruction, he was disbelieved, because of the speed of the deed and the Scythians' being so very hard to fight. But when the emperor learned the truth and was fully assured of the barbarians' destruction, he admired the man for his speed and his prowess, and praised him. As the share of Valens had now been added to him after his death, he looked at the almost boundless extent of the empire, and realising that he could not by himself alone govern so great an empire, he proclaimed Theodosius emperor of New Rome, at once rewarding him for his prowess, and at the same time judging that no one else would be better than him for partnership in the rule. So he assigned all the east and Thrace to him, and allotted the west to himself. And when he had come to the Gauls he was killed by treachery by Andragathius the general, having reigned six years after his father's death.

blocks: When Gratian had died, the younger Valentinian was left as sovereign emperor of the west, not yet having reached manhood. He, corrupted by his mother Justina, who was an Arianiser, assented to the doctrine of the Arians and opposed the orthodox. When Maximus rose against him and attempted a usurpation and got the upper hand in battles, he wrote to the emperor Theodosius what had happened, asking for help. And he wrote back that one should not wonder if the slave gets the better of the master when he has risen against one who rejects his own Master and calls the Creator, who is of one substance and equal honour with the Father, a creature and a slave. But he went to his aid, and he captured and killed Maximus, and Andragathius the general, who had murdered Gratian. Then again Eugenius rose against the younger Valentinian and set about a usurpation. Valentinian, afraid, took himself out of life by hanging. And learning of Eugenius' usurpation, Theodosius took the field against him.

When he came to Thessalonica with the army, he was insulted by the Thessalonians, and the prefect was murdered, the people having rioted for certain reasons. At the time, then, the emperor seemed to bear the people's disturbance with patience; but afterwards he proclaimed a horse race, and when the people had gathered in the theatre he set the armies round them, and they shot the people with arrows and javelins, so that up to fifteen thousand of them died. And having sated his anger in this way, Theodosius set out from there and came to the city of Milan. There he was rebuked by the great Ambrose and not allowed to enter the church. And he did not allow him entry to the divine precinct until he made a law that sentences of death should not be carried out until thirty days had passed after the sentence. He did this because of the emperor's quickness to anger, so that, with his anger calmed over the thirty days, he might review the sentences dispassionately and confirm the lawful ones, and condemn to idleness those voted perhaps in anger. Theodosius engaged the usurper Eugenius in the Gauls, defeated him, captured him, and killed him.

This emperor, while a private man, had a wife who was pious, chaste, and a friend of the poor, Placilla, by whom Honorius and Arcadius were born to him; and he made her Augusta. When she died after his accession, he married Galla, the daughter of Valentinian the Great.

While the emperor was away in the west, the Jews, winning over the prefect of the city, Honoratus, built a costly synagogue in the Chalkoprateia, with his permission; for he championed the cause of the Hellenes. The people of the city, angered at this, reviled the prefect; and he took no account of their abuse. So the people, not bearing it, set fire to the synagogue at night and burned it. The prefect then wrote to the emperor Theodosius about this. And he imposed on those who had dared to burn the synagogue the repayment of what had been spent on it, and allowed it to be built again. The great Ambrose learned of this, and when the emperor was staying in the city of Milan and came to the church on one of the feasts of the Lord, he began to say: "Why, emperor, do you yourself insult the one who made you emperor from a private man, and put into your hands his own flock, which he acquired with his own blood, and crowned your head that was once unkempt, by putting those who reject him above those who acknowledge him, and exacting penalties from Christians on behalf of Jews, and forcing them, in the middle of a city where Christ is preached and the cross worshipped, to build a synagogue for the killers of Christ?" And the emperor, abashed at the rebuke, said: "And shall we allow the people to do what they like, disorderly and shamelessly, in well-governed cities, bishop?" "But neither should this be allowed, emperor," the holy Ambrose retorted, "that the Jews have synagogues in the middle of a pious city and send up blasphemous prayers in the hearing of the God-fearing. Do not you decree this, most orthodox Augustus." Softened by this, Theodosius both let the Byzantines off the penalty and forbade the Jews to have a synagogue within the queen of cities.

When new taxes were imposed on the Antiochenes, the people, moved to indignation by the novelty of the levy, pulled down the images of the emperor Theodosius' former wife standing in the market-place of their city and dragged them through the public streets. Angered at this, he took away the city's rights and made it subject to neighbouring Laodicea, and threatened to treat its citizens badly; and he would have done so, had not Flavian, then high priest of Antioch, come to the emperor and interceded and made him give up his anger. At that time too the great father John Chrysostom, who was a presbyter of the church in Antioch, wrote the speeches entitled On the Statues.

blocks: At that time also Gregory, great in theology, who had formerly taught the orthodox in secret in the church of Saint Anastasia because of the shamelessness and boldness of the heretics, when the emperor Theodosius had given back the churches to the orthodox and driven out the Arianisers, openly proclaimed the Son of one substance with the Father and the Holy Spirit as God, worshipped and glorified together with both. For Macedonius, who had been patriarch of Constantinople for a short while, as has already been related, would not allow it to be called God, nor equal in power with the Father and the Son, nor yet of one substance. So the second council was convened at that time, at the emperor's order, a hundred and fifty God-bearing fathers being gathered in the queen of cities. Leading them in the contests were the Theologian, and the great Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, and the holy Amphilochius, head of the church of Iconium. They decreed the Holy Spirit both God and of one substance and of equal power with the Father and the Son, cut off Macedonius and those who held his opinion from the catholic church, added to the holy creed the clause about the Holy Spirit, from "And in the Holy Spirit" to the end, and confirmed what had been decreed at the first council. At that time also some of the bishops, envious of the Theologian because of the throne of Constantinople, said that he had not mounted the throne canonically, since he had previously been proclaimed for another see. So the saint wrote his farewell speech, read it publicly, stepped down from the throne, and returned to his own homeland, Nazianzus. Nectarius was ordained patriarch of Constantinople, a man of senatorial rank who had held civil offices. At that time too the throne of New Rome obtained the second rank, placed after elder Rome but preferred to the others.

The great Amphilochius too at that time asked the emperor to have the Arians driven out of the city, as blaspheming the Son of God, or at least not to be allowed to hold meetings. When he saw that Theodosius was slow about this, he watched for an opportunity, when Arcadius too was sitting with his father, and went in and gave the emperor the fitting greeting and obeisance, but said carelessly to Arcadius: "Greetings to you too, child." When the emperor was angry at the slight to his son, the saint then said: "You, a man, did not bear calmly the dishonour to your son. Do you think that God does not loathe and hate those who blaspheme his only-begotten Son, and is not angry with those who allow them to mix with the orthodox and corrupt many?" The emperor, admiring the saint's method, forbade the heretics' assemblies by decree.

When this emperor had brought down Eugenius, the last usurper, the whole empire of the Romans came round to him, and he proclaimed his two sons emperors. Wishing them to share in education both in letters and in character, he brought from Rome the great Arsenius, who was a deacon of the church there, famous for wisdom and virtue; and he handed the boys over to him, instructing him to treat them not as emperors but as private persons and ordinary boys, and to whip them if he saw them negligent or straying from what was proper, and to deal with them as with his own children. He held Arsenius in great honour and enriched him with money. Arsenius took the boys and seated them on thrones, while he himself stood to give them their lessons. And once the emperor came upon them suddenly, and finding them sitting and Arsenius standing, he was angry; and making the boys get up from the thrones and seating Arsenius, he ordered him to teach them like that. And from then on they stood by the teacher, while the one teaching sat. Once, then, when Arcadius had made a slip, the teacher gave him a whipping. He, resenting it, made a plot against him because of this, resolved to kill the man, and made ready the assassin. Arsenius, learning what was planned, withdrew secretly from the palace, and going to Scetis he entered the solitary life and became equal to the angels. The emperor Theodosius made a great search for him but did not learn where on earth he was.

This emperor fell ill in Milan and departed this life, having governed the empire for seventeen years and five months. He divided it between his two sons, assigning to Arcadius New Rome and the eastern part, and allotting to Honorius elder Rome and the west.

blocks: So each of them ruled the part allotted to him; and learning that the great Arsenius was living as a monk in Scetis, they wrote to him very many times asking him to pray for them. Arcadius also wrote to the saint privately, begging him to grant him pardon for the plot against him, and offered to let him take the tribute of all Egypt for that year and use it as he wished. But the great Arsenius would not write back to the emperors; he told those sent to him to say to them: "God will forgive you and will make you do his will; but to me, already dead to the world, money is useless."

This emperor Arcadius built a city in Thrace and named it Arcadiopolis, and he raised the column in the Xerolophos and set up a statue of himself on it. When Nectarius, patriarch of Constantinople, died, he brought John of the golden tongue from Antioch the Great and put him forward as patriarch of New Rome. But being sluggish and soft in mind beyond what was proper, he was ruled by his wife Eudoxia. She was a reckless woman and a slave to love of money, and for this reason most unjust. So, being checked in her impulses by the great father, and sometimes even rebuked, she was roused to anger and was eager to take revenge on the saint. Finding Theophilus of Alexandria as a partner in her wickedness, she persuaded Arcadius to condemn the saint to exile. And he was thrown out of the church and led away into exile. Of the people of the city, some lamented, others rioted. When the sluggish Arcadius learned this, he sent in haste recalling John, and he was brought back and restored to the church again. But he, being unenslaved, did not stop moving his tongue against wrongdoers. The empress Eudoxia, applying to herself the teachings about injustice (for her conscience convicted her of being such), was furious, and inflamed her wrath against the great father. And again, to pass over what happened in between, she persuaded her husband, leading him as though by a halter, to condemn the saint to exile. And he was thrust out of the church tyrannically and led away to dangerous lands and to the most distant frontiers, having experienced many hardships on the road, which one can hear his golden tongue relating in his letters. Having reached Cucusus, and being led away from there to Pityus, when he was at Comana he measured out his life there, aged fifty-two, having held the high priesthood of the queen of cities for five and a half years. Divine justice did not slumber, however, but quickly pursued that thrice-wretched empress. For not yet three months had passed after the death of father Chrysostom when she met a violent death. For while she was carrying, the foetus died, and sharp pains gripped her; and when it rotted inside, the empress's womb also took part in the rot, and so she departed this life wretchedly. When that golden-mouthed father had been thrown out of the church, one Arsacius was put in his place, and after being bishop for two years he died; after him Atticus was ordained.

Eudoxia had died before her husband and emperor, and Arcadius himself followed her not long after, having reigned after the death of his father Theodosius for fourteen years and three months and three days. The column standing at the place called the Pittakia is said to be Eudoxia's. Dying, Arcadius left as successor to the throne his son Theodosius, called the Little to distinguish him from his grandfather, or because he was at a very childish age when his father died; for he was then only seven years old. But let the account of him be put off; let the narrative go through the affairs of Honorius in summary.

blocks: He was left by his father as emperor of elder Rome at a very young age (for he was ten years old), and was under the guardianship, by his father's decision, of Stilicho, a man who was first among those in Rome and had been entrusted with the administration of public affairs. He took Stilicho's daughter Maria as his wife. When she died he is said to have married her sister Thermantia, who was not yet of full age. And she too died quickly. Being simple-minded he was hated by the powerful men in Rome, and learning that he was being plotted against he moved to Ravenna, and is said to have sent to Alaric, the ruler of the nation of the Vandals or Goths, asking him to march against Rome, wishing in this way to take revenge on the citizens of Rome for their hatred of him. And Alaric, they say, attacked Rome, but did not sack it; he made a treaty with the Romans, took all the money found in the palace and Honorius' sister Placidia, and went back. He handed the girl over to a certain count Constantius to be guarded; and the man who had received her ran away and brought her to her brother, and he married her to him, having honoured him with senatorial rank, and then even proclaimed him emperor; for Honorius had no offspring of his own. And shortly afterwards Constantius was slain, Placidia having borne him children, Valentinian and Honoria.

Some, then, record these things in this way; but others say that Stilicho was slain, that those in Rome were hostile to Honorius, and that he moved to Ravenna; that Alaric, despising his simple-mindedness, marched on Rome and took it by siege; and that when it was taken someone in tears came to Honorius reporting that Rome had been taken by Alaric. He, shaken in his body by a spasm at the news and striking his thighs with his hands, said: "Rome was here just now. How then has it been taken?" The messenger, understanding, and groaning greatly, said: "I am speaking of the city and not of the bird." For this emperor had an enormous hen, in which he delighted, which he called Rome; and he cried out because of it, thinking it had been taken.

Honorius fell into dropsy and died, having lived forty years and reigned ingloriously thirty of them. A certain John, usurping in Rome, drove out from there his sister Placidia with her two children, Valentinian and Honoria.

blocks: The little Theodosius, living in Constantinople, was brought up by his own sister Pulcheria, carefully nurtured and educated, no one rising against them, out of fear of Isdigerdes, who was king of the Persians. For Arcadius, when he was dying, wrote Isdigerdes in his will as guardian of his son, who was still a child, as has been said. When the will was brought to him, he sent Antiochus, the most honoured of the eunuchs at his court, to be guardian and protector of the emperor Theodosius, urging the officials by letter to submit to their emperor; and threatening them that if they did not do so, he himself would come to avenge the boy.

When he had now begun to be counted among the youths, his sister Pulcheria betrothed him to Eudocia of Athens, who was of extraordinary beauty and had a share of every kind of learning. She was the daughter of one Leontius, a philosopher from Athens, and was named Athenais. He, knowing from his science that his daughter was going to have brilliant good fortune, when making his will left his property to his sons (there were two, Valerius and Gesius), and ordered that only a hundred gold pieces be given to his daughter, writing that her fortune was enough for her. So when her brothers had appropriated their father's estate, Athenais demanded her own lawful share; and she asked her brothers not to act according to their father's will, which was unjust. But they even drove her out of her father's house. Her aunt on her mother's side took her in and went up to Constantinople, and they petitioned Pulcheria, telling her the case. She, seeing that the girl was very beautiful and young, asked whether she was still untouched by a man; and learning this, she baptised her, as she was still uninitiated, and renaming her Eudocia she married her to her brother Theodosius, crowned her with a diadem, and called her Augusta.

Having married her, Theodosius got rid of Antiochus, who was the most powerful of the imperial eunuchs and stirred up everything, holding power himself, not merely sharing in it. And so Antiochus was removed from the honour of praepositus; all his property was taken away, and he himself was tonsured as a cleric at the church of the all-praised martyr Euphemia in Chalcedon, and died not long after. The empress Eudocia summoned her brothers, and bearing them no grudge, but rather acknowledging thanks, since she would not have obtained the throne if she had not been driven out by them and for that reason gone to Constantinople, she had Gesius made prefect of Illyricum through the emperor, and honoured Valerius as magister.

The patriarch Atticus, having brought a paralysed Jew to the knowledge of Christ by his exhortations, granted him the divine bath and brought him out of the font healed. He also entered the name of the holy Chrysostom in the church's diptychs, where it had not been entered before; for that most pious father was both called and thought an Origenist. When Atticus died, who had headed the body of the faithful for twenty years, Sisinnius was ordained, and having held the high priesthood for two years he measured out his life, in the twenty-second year of the reign of Theodosius. And Nestorius was put in his place. Having held the high priesthood for three years, he taught people not to call the holy Virgin Mary Theotokos, decreeing that Christ was a mere man and babbling that the Son of God dwelt in him as in one of the prophets. Dividing him into two, he insisted that the Word of God did not take flesh from the pure blood of the Mother of God, but that the Son and Word of God was one, and Christ, made a son by adoption and deified by grace, was another. When the heads of the other patriarchal thrones learned this, Celestine of Rome, Cyril of Alexandria, John of Antioch, and Juvenal of Jerusalem, they referred it to the sovereign Theodosius and Pulcheria, asking for a council to be assembled and for what Nestorius was teaching to be examined. So a council of two hundred fathers was convened at Ephesus, led by the most holy Cyril, who also held the place of Celestine of Rome, as he had been unable to attend because of illness. The doctrines of Nestorius were examined and rejected as heterodox; the holy Virgin was shown to be Theotokos, to be believed and called so, and the one incarnate from her without a man was proclaimed by those holy fathers to be Son of God and God. For a clearer confession of the faith and a plainer refutation of the impiety of Nestorius, the most holy Cyril also composed twelve chapters and handed them to the church as memorials of the right belief. Nestorius was deposed and removed from the company of the right-believing high priests.

Three days after the council, John of Antioch, Theodoret bishop of Cyrrhus, Ibas of Edessa, and others arrived at Ephesus; and because the members of the council had not waited for their arrival too, they were angry with the great Cyril as the leader of the rest, found fault with the deposition of Nestorius, and taking his side voted the deposition of the divine Cyril and of Memnon of Ephesus. Theodoret also attacked Cyril's twelve chapters, and composed others to overturn them, against which the great Cyril contended in turn, proving that Theodoret did not teach rightly. The bishop of Antioch and the rest were condemned by the council and estranged from the orthodox. With matters standing so, and the bishops set against one another, and a schism among them, the emperor Theodosius ordered them all to come to Constantinople; and when they had arrived in the emperor's presence, the inquiry took place, and Nestorius was deposed and exiled to the east, the bishop of Antioch and Theodoret agreeing with the holy council, as having opposed it before out of vexation and rivalry. When Nestorius was perverting many, John of Antioch made a report about this to the emperor, asking that he be moved elsewhere. And the wretch was carried off to Oasis, a barren land of Arabia, blown over by destructive winds.

Maximian, a presbyter of the church, was put in his place in the pastorate of New Rome. And after him, when he had held the high priesthood for two years, Proclus, the disciple of Chrysostom, was appointed patriarch. He had earlier been ordained bishop of Cyzicus by the patriarch Sisinnius, but had not been accepted by the people there, who chose another high priest, and had been without office in the meantime. Enthroned, then, on the throne of Constantine's city, he asked the emperor that the body of Chrysostom be brought back from Pityus, and that the saint not remain in exile even in death. The emperor was persuaded by him, and the saint's body was brought back, received with surpassing honour, and laid within the sanctuary of the famous church of the Holy Apostles.

The emperor Theodosius, wishing to move the walls of the city and make its circuit larger, entrusted the work to Cyrus the prefect; and he, using great zeal and eagerness, raised the land wall from sea to sea in sixty days. So the people of the city, pleased at the work and greatly admiring the prefect for his speed, cried out publicly: "[Constantine] built, Cyrus renewed." For this he was envied and suspected by the emperor, and was tonsured a cleric against his will, and then became bishop of Smyrna.

blocks: When the patriarch Proclus died, in the twelfth year after he had headed the orthodox people in Constantinople, the divine Flavian was installed on his throne. At that time also Eutyches, who was an archimandrite, taught that our Lord Jesus Christ did not keep the two natures after the incarnation, but that both were mixed and blended together into one nature. When he remained uncorrected, Flavian cut him off from the body of the church, so that he would not pass on his corruption to what was healthy. So Eutyches went to Chrysaphius the eunuch, who shared his belief and had very great power with the emperor; and he persuaded Theodosius to allow Dioscorus, who held the throne of Alexandria after the departure of Saint Cyril, to come to Ephesus with other bishops and examine the case of Eutyches, with Flavian also present. This Dioscorus, then, being of the same belief as Eutyches, and having taken with him other bishops of the same mind, came to Ephesus and confirmed what Eutyches was introducing. When the most holy Flavian spoke against it, Dioscorus leapt up like some wild ass and jumped with his heel on that pious man's chest, and beating him on the temple with his fist did not let up until he had pushed him out of the assembly. And the saint, two days later, departed this life from the blow to his chest, having adorned the high-priestly throne of the younger Rome for two years. Dioscorus forced the bishops present there to subscribe to the definition he had set out. For the power of the eunuch mentioned had caused armed soldiers to be present there and to frighten those who objected. Domnus, the bishop of Antioch, subscribed too, being swept along, but then denounced Dioscorus and attacked the definition as full of impiety.

When the emperor Theodosius learned of this and came to know about Flavian, he held Chrysaphius to blame and was angry with him. Dioscorus, afraid, advised him to persuade the emperor to appoint as patriarch of Constantinople Anatolius, his own apocrisiarius, so that he would receive Eutyches into communion and the affair of the blessed Flavian would remain uninvestigated. So the eunuch persuaded the emperor, who was easily led, and Anatolius was ordained patriarch. This Chrysaphius, taking advantage of the ruler's compliance, also persuaded him, with the empress Eudocia as his helper, to remove Pulcheria from the administration of affairs. And she withdrew from the palace and lived by herself and kept quiet at the Hebdomon. But the emperor, coming to himself late and with difficulty, and reckoning up the bloody murder of the blessed Flavian and the affair of Pulcheria, and finding that profane eunuch to be the cause of everything, was moved to just anger against him, and condemned him to exile and confiscated his property, and summoning his sister he asked her pardon, and put the administration of affairs in her hands again.

Pulcheria was very intelligent, and of her brother's many shortcomings she corrected some and covered up others. It is said, then, that this emperor signed documents without paying attention; and she advised him not to confirm everything put before him, but to look over what was written first. He insisted that he was not being cheated by anyone; for he maintained that he knew what was being written. So, to prove her brother's sluggishness of mind, Pulcheria thought of something like this. She drew up a document of sale in his name, as though he had sold the Augusta Eudocia to her, and putting the deed of purchase before him as something else, she persuaded him to confirm it with his signature; then, when Eudocia was summoned by him, she would not let her go. When the emperor asked the reason, Pulcheria showed him the bill of sale, and so proved to him that he signed many things he neither knew nor perhaps wished to happen. At the time, then, as that pretended sale had no force, the empress was restored to the emperor.

But afterwards, when a certain cause arose, the emperor fell out of love with the Augusta. The cause: an apple of extraordinary size was brought to the emperor. He, marvelling at it, sent it to the empress, and she gave the apple to Paulinus. The man was learned, and for that reason close to the empress. He, admiring the size of the apple and knowing nothing about it, presented it to the emperor. He recognised what was presented, and hiding it he asked his wife where the apple sent to her was. She said she had eaten it, afraid that her husband would suspect what he already suspected. He asked again more insistently; and she again insisted with an oath that she had eaten the apple. The emperor, full of anger, brought it out. And she was caught in the act not telling the truth. And for him the suspicion was confirmed. And so Paulinus was killed on a false suspicion, and Eudocia was hated. She asked to go to Jerusalem, and going there with great wealth she built churches and gave much to the poor and to the monasteries there. Returning from there, she went there again after her husband's death, and died there. What she was like in letters is shown by the so-called Homerocentra. For when one Patricius had attempted the work but left it unfinished and, so to speak, unarranged, she brought it to completion and arranged it, as the inscription in heroic verse which she gave the work shows those who read it.

The emperor Theodosius died at the age of fifty, having reigned almost all the years he lived, a very few with his father and the others on his own. As to the cause of his death, some say it was illness, others have recorded that while he was riding in a hunt his horse fell with him, and that, having been struck in vital parts, he died shortly afterwards. He was not unacquainted with literary education, but had also had a share of the other mathematical books and had a taste of astronomy itself; he was trained to the highest degree in riding and archery, and was skilful at painting and modelling. Being mild in character he was soft in the handling of affairs; so the eunuchs who had power with him did many things they should not have, Antiochus and after him Amantius, and lastly Chrysaphius.

In the times of this emperor, when the patriarch Proclus was holding a procession of prayer with the clergy and a very large part of the city's population, suddenly a child was lifted up into the air. As the people were amazed and cried "Lord, have mercy" for a very long time, the child was brought down again, saying it had been taught that "who was crucified for us" must not be added to the Trisagion.

blocks: So Theodosius died. Pulcheria, before the emperor's death was yet known to many, sent for Marcian, a man already old, but good in character and self-controlled, and told him of the emperor's death, and said: "I have chosen you before all for emperor, if you will give me assurance that you will keep my virginity untouched, which I have dedicated to God." When he agreed, she summoned the patriarch and the senate, and proclaimed him and crowned him with a diadem.

Marcian had not been one of the distinguished men before, nor of those of brilliant family, but simply a soldier. Once, going off on campaign with his own regiment, he fell ill in the province of the Lycians and was left behind by his comrades. He was given hospitality there by two brothers, one named Julius and the other Tatianus, and when he had recovered from his illness he went out hunting with his hosts. In the course of the hunt they became tired out and lay down on the ground to rest, and fell asleep around midday. Tatianus shook off sleep before the others, and saw an eagle with its wings spread out shading Marcian and keeping off from him the heat of the sun's rays. Marvelling, he quietly woke his brother and showed him the strange sight; and he too was astounded. Both men, then, thought that what the eagle had done to Marcian signified the throne, and when he woke from sleep they foretold the throne to him, and asked him to remember them when he obtained the rule; and giving him two hundred coins they let him go. Again, campaigning with Aspar, who had undertaken a war against the Vandals, he was taken prisoner with very many others, and was kept under guard in a courtyard with his fellow captives. The leader of the Vandals, leaning out from above, was looking over the captives, and he too saw Marcian asleep, and an eagle above him with its wings raised making shade for him. He too, then, took the sight as an omen pointing to the throne, and sending for Marcian he demanded of him that if he became emperor he would not make war on the Vandals; and when he agreed he released him from prison. So in this way God signified the throne to him long before. And then what had been foretold came to pass, and at once he summoned the brothers who had been his hosts and had announced the good news of the rule to him, and he appointed Tatianus prefect of the city and entrusted Julius with the government of Illyricum. He was good to everyone.

In these times Pulcheria built the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae, and the fourth council took place, Leo the pope of Rome and Anatolius the patriarch of New Rome having asked the emperor Marcian that the affair of Dioscorus of Alexandria and Eutyches, and all that they had dared against the most holy Flavian, should not remain uninvestigated. So it was decided that a council should take place, and six hundred and thirty God-bearing fathers gathered in the church of the holy martyr Euphemia in Chalcedon. Their leaders were Leo the pope of Rome, Anatolius of Constantinople, and Juvenal of Jerusalem. The multitude of fathers was assembled against Dioscorus and Eutyches, who told the fable that our Lord Jesus Christ wore flesh of another substance than ours, and that he was one nature, so that the sufferings were thereby attached to the Godhead. The divine fathers deposed and anathematised them, since they would not renounce their heterodoxy. They received Theodoret and Ibas, once they had anathematised Nestorius and the chapters they themselves had published out of rivalry; and they confirmed the three earlier councils and strengthened the holy creed, bringing under anathema those who introduce a pair of sons, and those who teach that the Godhead can suffer, and those who dare to think and say that there is a mixture and confusion of the two natures, or who invent that there were two natures in Christ before the union but one after the union, and those who tell the fable that the form taken by the Lord from us was heavenly or of some other substance. And they decreed that our Lord Jesus Christ is perfect in Godhead and perfect in manhood, truly God and truly man, of a rational soul and body, of one substance with the Father in his Godhead and of one substance with us in his manhood, and like us in all things except sin; one and the same, made known in two natures, without confusion, without change, without division, without separation, the properties of each nature being preserved and coming together into one person and one hypostasis.
text: So Theodosius died. Pulcheria, before the emperor's death was yet known to many, sent for Marcian, a man already old, but good in character and self-controlled, and told him of the emperor's death, and said: "I have chosen you before all for emperor, if you will give me assurance that you will keep my virginity untouched, which I have dedicated to God." When he agreed, she summoned the patriarch and the senate, and proclaimed him and crowned him with a diadem. Marcian had not been one of the distinguished men before, nor of those of brilliant family, but simply a soldier. Once, going off on campaign with his own regiment, he fell ill in the province of the Lycians and was left behind by his comrades. blocks: When these things had been decreed by all those God-inspired fathers, with the pious emperor Marcian also present, Dioscorus was sent into exile at Gangra by imperial order; for Eutyches had died miserably before. In place of Dioscorus, Proterius, a most holy and most orthodox man, was ordained bishop of Alexandria. When the heretics of the party of Eutyches and Dioscorus went about the city mocking what had been decreed by the council, and saying that the council had prevailed through the imperial power and not through the truth, and still trying to establish their own heterodoxy, the patriarch Anatolius called an assembly of those of his own opinion and those of the opposing belief, and said to his opponents: "Since you still hold to your own opinion and are not persuaded that you do not believe rightly, but accuse us of accepting the doctrine of Nestorius because we proclaim two natures in the Saviour, each keeping its properties unconfused, we must, if you agree, leave the decision about this to God. Let your view of the faith be written by you in a volume, and ours will be written by us; and let both volumes be placed in the coffin of the all-praised martyr Euphemia, and let the judgement between those who teach rightly and those who teach perversely be given to her." This pleased the heretics too; and the volumes were written, and the stone closing the coffin was lifted, and the papers were laid on the martyr's breast, and the stone was put back on the coffin again and sealed by both parties. After that there were supplications to God and prayers all night, that he would reveal which of the opinions seemed to him pleasing and which to be rejected. And on the third day they came together, the emperor not being absent either; and when the coffin was opened (O your wonders, Lord!) the volume of the heretics was found lying at the martyr's feet, and the other held in her right hand, which she is said to have stretched out to the emperor and the patriarch, handing them the volume. Those who championed the right doctrine broke into applause, while those of the other opinion went away downcast and covered in a darkness of shame; and some of them even changed over to orthodoxy.
At that time the empress Pulcheria also died, piously and gloriously and with good hopes. For she distributed all her wealth to the poor, and by her mercy to them she gained the mercy of God.

Valentinian, the nephew of Honorius, of whom we made mention somewhere above as born of his sister Placidia, while reigning in elder Rome, took as his wife Eudoxia, the daughter of the younger Theodosius. But living dissolutely and licentiously, he left his own wife alone, though she was very beautiful, and debauched himself with other men's wives; he also resorted to divinations and sorceries. Living in this unholy way, he died pitiably. For Maximus, one of the patricians in Rome, a grandson of the Maximus who had usurped long before and whom Theodosius the Great defeated in war, got into the palace and slaughtered Valentinian in it, and took Eudoxia by force, and seized the throne. She, since her father Theodosius had died and Pulcheria had measured out her life, and she hoped for vengeance from no other quarter, sent to Gizericus, who was called rex of the Vandals, and begged him to free her from the tyranny of Maximus; and he attacked Rome with a fleet and a large force. Maximus fled from it, and was killed by those with him. Gizericus took Rome without effort, and having gathered up all its wealth, and the offerings of the divine churches made of gold and adorned with stones, and some of the vessels of the temple there which Titus had carried off from Jerusalem, these too made of gold, and taking Eudoxia with her two daughters, he returned to Africa. He married one of her daughters, Eudocia, to the elder of his own sons, Honorichus; and learning that Placidia was betrothed to a husband, the patrician Olybrius, he kept her with her mother Eudoxia. The empress Eudoxia, having spent two years there, returned to Byzantium with her daughter Placidia while Marcian was reigning. For Eudocia was left with her husband; and having lived with him for sixteen years and borne a son, Ilderichus, because her husband was of the Arians' belief she was distressed at living with him. And seizing an opportunity, she too moved to Constantinople, her mother having already died; then she went off to Jerusalem and died there.

Marcian died having reigned six years and some months, as some say, from illness, as others, poisoned at the nod of the patrician Aspar, having become an old man and lived long. Being mild in mind and good to his subjects, he used to say that an emperor must not take up arms as long as it was possible to be at peace. The patrician Aspar, who then had great power, was not chosen to be emperor by the people of the city, because he belonged to the heresy of Arius. So he himself made Leo emperor, as some have recorded, on his own initiative, as others, having received the authority from the people. Leo, it is said, was the manager of his estates, and Aspar demanded of him that he crown one of his sons Caesar. And when he had promised this, Aspar brought him up to the height of the throne. Some say he was a tribune and commander of the units at Selymbria. And some say he drew his descent from the Thracians, others from the Dacians in Illyricum.

blocks: As soon as Leo had been made emperor, Aspar pressed him, forcing him to make one of his sons Caesar according to his promise. When he put it off, Aspar took hold of the imperial purple and said: "Emperor, the man who wears this must not lie." And he answered in turn: "Nor must he be forced and led like a slave." Unable to hold out to the end, he yielded to necessity and made Aspar's son, the brother of Ardaburius, Caesar from patrician. This seemed hateful to the senate too and stirred the people of the city to riot. For they feared that if power came round to Aspar's family, the Arians, taking freedom of speech again, would show greater evils to the orthodox than before. So the clergy, the monks and as many of the people of the city as were sound in the faith gathered and begged the emperor to appoint a Caesar of their own belief. He then calmed the riot by what he said and did. When some time had passed, learning that Aspar's party was plotting against him, he killed him and Ardaburius.

Isocasius the quaestor, a learned man, was accused of other things and of paganism; Leo stripped him of his rank and handed him to the prefect for examination. As he was brought into the court in the guise of a condemned man, the prefect said to him: "Do you see, Isocasius, what state you are in?" And he said: "I see, and I am not surprised that, being a man, I have fallen into human misfortunes; but judge my case as you used to judge with me." Hearing this, the people acclaimed the emperor, and snatching Isocasius away took him to the church; and the ruler was pleased when he learned that he had been baptised.

This emperor had a wife called Verina, by whom two daughters were born to him, Ariadne and Leontia; the one he betrothed to Zeno, and Leontia he joined to the patrician Marcian, the son of Anthemius, who reigned in Rome. Under this emperor there was a most dreadful fire in New Rome, which girded the city from sea to sea, that is from the northern part to the southern, and in length went from the Bosporion as far as the church of Saint John the Hut-dweller, and to the south from the church of the holy apostle Thomas as far as the church of the great martyrs Sergius and Bacchus; and in the middle of the city it burned everything between from the Lausos to the Taurus. At this time Aspar is said to have run through the streets carrying a vessel full of water on his shoulders, urging the people to do likewise so as to put out the fire, and giving each a silver coin as pay. That fire went on consuming the city for four days, and besides the rest it burned the very great hall in the place called the Senate, in which the senate and the chosen men met for counsel, and the emperor himself when he put on the consular robe, a famous and most splendid work; and the place called the Nymphaeum, another hall facing the one mentioned, used for the weddings of those who have no houses that hold a crowd; and another royal hall in the Taurus, costly and very large; and besides these most famous churches and many private houses of the more distinguished.

In his reign there is also said to have been a most violent earthquake at Antioch, so that almost that whole city fell down. And it is said that much ash rained on Byzantium, so that it rose a palm's breadth; and that from this the emperor in fear left the city and stayed for a long time at Saint Mamas. On becoming emperor he appointed Rusticius, a noble and most able general, commander of the army; and when he died, he chose instead Basiliscus, the brother of the empress Verina. He marched against Gaiseric in Africa with a large fleet and was most shamefully defeated and lost most of the fleet; as some record, through bad judgement and not conducting the war like a general, but as others say, through treachery; for they say he received a great deal of money from Gaiseric, and when battle was joined turned his flagship, backed water and took to flight, and from this gave courage to the enemy and broke the spirit of his own men; and he came back ingloriously with a few, while the rest fell in the sea battle.

A grandson was born to this emperor by his daughter Ariadne and Zeno, whom he named Leo and crowned with the royal diadem at a very infant age. For he judged Zeno unfit for the empire, since he had neither a royal mind nor a form worthy of rule, but was most hideous to look at and had a soul worse than his looks. For this reason some record that Aspar and Ardaburius were put to death by the emperor Leo, since he wished his grandson the little Leo to reign, and feared them as having great power, lest, despising his infancy, they should seize the rule.

Under this emperor the precious robe of the all-holy Mother of God was brought to Constantinople from Palestine, and laid in a silver casket in the church he built at Blachernae; and from this the church is called the Holy Casket. When the patriarch Anatolius died, who had presided over the church for eight years, Gennadius was ordained. When he had steered the church for thirteen years and come to the end of his life, Acacius was brought in in his place. The emperor Leo fell ill and died, having reigned eighteen years, leaving the little Leo as successor to the empire. He was adorned with other virtues, but compassion shone out in him most of all; he used to say that as the sun gives a share of its warmth to those it shines on, so the emperor must think those he looks on worthy of pity.

blocks: The little Leo, left still an infant, survived in the empire for one year, and died an infant after his grandfather, leaving his own father Zeno as emperor, having put the diadem on his head with his own hands. Zeno was of the most shameful nation of the Isaurians, and was himself most shameful both in form and in soul. And he carried on the rule not as an emperor but plainly as a tyrant. He also had a brother called Conon, who outdid his brother in wickedness, delighting in blood and taking pleasure in the slaughter of men. Against this Zeno, Basiliscus, the brother of the empress Verina, mentioned above, who was staying in Thrace, raised his hand, with Verina and some of the senate helping him. Zeno, being cowardly and unmanly, at once fled with his wife Ariadne to his countrymen in Isauria.

Basiliscus was proclaimed emperor at the Campus, crowned his own wife Zenonis Augusta, and appointed his son Marcus Caesar. He was no better than Zeno in character, and not rightly disposed in religion. For he too belonged to the heresy of Eutyches and Dioscorus, led into it by his wife, and he did great harm to the churches of the orthodox, and decreed by a tyrannical letter that the council at Chalcedon was void. He tried to force Acacius, the patriarch of New Rome, to vote this in synod. But the orthodox multitude of the city gathered in the church, reviled Basiliscus and called the council at Chalcedon holy. For this, then, Basiliscus was hated by the people and the senate.

He sent Illus and Trocundus with a force against Zeno; they came and besieged him. But since Basiliscus had promised them much and not fulfilled his promises, and the senate, weighed down by Basiliscus because of his wickedness, wrote to these men about what he was doing, they joined Zeno, became his friends and helpers instead of his enemies, and taking him with them went back. Basiliscus sent his own nephew Harmatius with the Thracian legions against Zeno; and he met him near Nicaea, and corrupted by money, and besides by a promise that his son Basiliscus would be crowned Caesar, went over to Zeno. From there Zeno came to Constantinople and was received by the senate and the people. Basiliscus fled to the church with his wife and children, and came out from there when he received an assurance that he would not be deprived of life. They were taken to a fort, where he is said to have been shut in a tower with his dearest and to have perished of hunger. Others say they were killed as they were being taken away. Zeno also exiled his own mother-in-law, the empress Verina. So Basiliscus, whether as has been said or otherwise, perished after holding tyrannical power for two years.

In his reign a very great fire broke out in Constantinople, beginning from the Chalkoprateia and consuming and turning to ash everything next to it, the porticoes of the public squares and the buildings standing on them, and also the place called the Basilica itself, in which there was a library holding a hundred and twenty thousand books; among which is recorded to have been the gut of a serpent, a hundred and twenty feet long, with the poems of Homer, the Iliad and the Odyssey, written on it in gold letters; Malchus too mentions this in writing about these emperors. That fire also destroyed the splendour of the city in the Lausos, and the statues set up there, the images famous for their art of Hera of Samos, Athena of Lindos and Aphrodite of Cnidus, and it ran as far as the Forum.

Zeno, having grasped power again, appointed Harmatius's son Caesar, fulfilling his promise, and Harmatius himself general; and a little later he killed Harmatius, saying that as he had not kept faith with Basiliscus, he would certainly not keep it with him either. He made his son, the Caesar, a cleric. He also put to death Illus the master of offices, who had attempted a usurpation because he knew he was being plotted against by the empress Ariadne with Zeno's knowledge; and also Pelagius the patrician, a most learned and most just man, in appearance charging him with paganism, but in truth avoiding his rebukes; for being of a free mind he rebuked his unholy deeds. The most hateful Zeno destroyed very many other notable men too, and inclined to heresies, lawless deeds and a corrupt life; and living so, he was torn from life by violence.

The manner of his death is disputed. For some say that he used to gorge and get drunk, go out of his mind and fall down no different from a corpse. And since he was hated even by his wife Ariadne, once when he was drunk like this he was put by her in one of the imperial coffins as if already dead, and at once the very great stone that served as its lid was put on it; and when he came to, he shouted and lamented from inside, but with no one paying attention, he died there pitiably. Others say that he fell ill, and being struck by most violent pains gave those who saw him the impression that he was dead, and so was put in the tomb, and died in it groaning and calling on his household, since Ariadne allowed no one to open the tomb or pay him any attention at all.

When Zeno had died most pitiably in this way, Ariadne raised Anastasius Dicorus, who was a silentiary (this is one of the humble ranks), to the empire, with the agreement of the senate and the army, and with Urbicius the eunuch, who was then very powerful, working for his proclamation. Anastasius was called Dicorus because the pupils of his eyes were unlike each other; for the right was darker in colour, while the left was coloured more blue-grey. When he was about to be crowned, the patriarch Euphemius demanded from him a written confession of faith, and that he would change nothing of the doctrines of the church. For after Acacius, who had been most wicked to the orthodox and had held the church for seventeen years and died, Fravitas had been ordained patriarch, of the same belief as Acacius and Zeno. After three and a half months he too departed life, and Euphemius presided over the church of Constantinople, a holy and most orthodox man. When one Peter the Hoarse had seized the throne of great Antioch like a bandit, Euphemius struck him from the diptychs as a heretic. In his place he wrote in the name of Felix, pope of Rome, an orthodox man who had attacked the letters of Zeno and Acacius because they were in communion with Peter the Hoarse, who was of the heresy of Eutyches and Dioscorus, and above all had sent Acacius a document of deposition, for which Acacius had struck his name from the diptychs. So this patriarch Euphemius, having received a document in Anastasius's own hand that he accepted the doctrines of the church and would keep everything defined by the council at Chalcedon, crowned him. He at once sought Ariadne in marriage, and issued an imperial letter remitting what was owed to the treasury by anyone up to that time. When the fortieth day after Zeno's burial had passed, he celebrated the marriage too. Since a tax called the chrysargyron was oppressing his subjects, he abolished this too.
text: The little Leo, left still an infant, survived in the empire for one year, and died an infant after his grandfather, leaving his own father Zeno as emperor, having put the diadem on his head with his own hands. Zeno was of the most shameful nation of the Isaurians, and was himself most shameful both in form and in soul. And he carried on the rule not as an emperor but plainly as a tyrant. He also had a brother called Conon, who outdid his brother in wickedness, delighting in blood and taking pleasure in the slaughter of men. Against this Zeno, Basiliscus, the brother of the empress Verina, mentioned above, who was staying in Thrace, raised his hand, with Verina and some of the senate helping him. Zeno, being cowardly and unmanly, at once fled with his wife Ariadne to his countrymen in Isauria. Basiliscus was proclaimed emperor at the Campus, crowned his own wife Zenonis Augusta, and appointed his son Marcus Caesar. He was no better than Zeno in character, and not rightly disposed in religion. For he too belonged to the heresy of Eutyches and Dioscorus, led into it by his wife, and he did great harm to the churches of the orthodox, and decreed by a tyrannical letter that the council at Chalcedon was void. He tried to force Acacius, the patriarch of New Rome, to vote this in synod. But the orthodox multitude of the city gathered in the church, reviled Basiliscus and called the council at Chalcedon holy. For this, then, Basiliscus was hated by the people and the senate. He sent Illus and Trocundus with a force against Zeno; they came and besieged him. But since Basiliscus had promised them much and not fulfilled his promises, and the senate, weighed down by Basiliscus because of his wickedness, wrote to these men about what he was doing, they joined Zeno, became his friends and helpers instead of his enemies, and taking him with them went back. Basiliscus sent his own nephew Harmatius with the Thracian legions against Zeno; and he met him near Nicaea, and corrupted by money, and besides by a promise that his son Basiliscus would be crowned Caesar, went over to Zeno. From there Zeno came to Constantinople and was received by the senate and the people. Basiliscus fled to the church with his wife and children, and came out from there when he received an assurance that he would not be deprived of life. They were taken to a fort, where he is said to have been shut in a tower with his dearest and to have perished of hunger. Others say they were killed as they were being taken away. Zeno also exiled his own mother-in-law, the empress Verina. So Basiliscus, whether as has been said or otherwise, perished after holding tyrannical power for two years. In his reign a very great fire broke out in Constantinople, beginning from the Chalkoprateia and consuming and turning to ash everything next to it, the porticoes of the public squares and the buildings standing on them, and also the place called the Basilica itself, in which there was a library holding a hundred and twenty thousand books; among which is recorded to have been the gut of a serpent, a hundred and twenty feet long, with the poems of Homer, the Iliad and the Odyssey, written on it in gold letters; Malchus too mentions this in writing about these emperors. That fire also destroyed the splendour of the city in the Lausos, and the statues set up there, the images famous for their art of Hera of Samos, Athena of Lindos and Aphrodite of Cnidus, and it ran as far as the Forum. Zeno, having grasped power again, appointed Harmatius's son Caesar, fulfilling his promise, and Harmatius himself general; and a little later he killed Harmatius, saying that as he had not kept faith with Basiliscus, he would certainly not keep it with him either. blocks: The chrysargyron tax was like this: all, beggars and poor men, every harlot and all freedmen living in the country and in the cities, were forced to pay a yearly tax to the treasury. A levy was also exacted for horses, mules, oxen, donkeys and dogs, a silver coin for each man, and the same for a horse, a mule and an ox, and six folles for a donkey, and likewise for a dog. From this there was crushing of men and lamentation everywhere. But the emperor Anastasius abolished this levy and burned the registers of it before the people in the Hippodrome; and in this he was generous and managed civil affairs well. For civil offices, which before had been sold, he gave without payment. But in his belief about the divine he was not good; for inclining to the heresy of the Confounders, who hold that there is one nature in the Saviour after the union of the two natures, he did much harm to the churches of the orthodox and was pitiless to those who presided over them. For he exiled the patriarch Euphemius, who would not be persuaded to anathematise the council at Chalcedon, having first taken back his own document by guile, or by force, as others say; and he banished his successor Macedonius, a holy man, who would not agree with him, to Euchaïta. After him Timothy, of the same mind as the emperor, was brought in.

Longinus, the brother of Zeno, attempted a usurpation, was subdued by Anastasius, and was confined at Alexandria, where he was ordained a priest and died. He also drove out of the queen of cities the many Isaurians staying in it; and taking them up, Longinus the master of offices, not the brother of Zeno but another, revolted and plundered much of the east; but he was defeated, and the barbarians with him perished. At that time Theoderic, the ruler of Africa, being an Arian, is said to have killed an orthodox deacon who was very close to him and had gone over to Arianism to please him, saying: "Since you did not keep faith with God, still less will you keep it with me."

When Anastasius, pope of elder Rome, died, and the people were divided, some voting for one Laurentius, the orthodox for Symmachus, and they were at strife with one another, Theoderic, mentioned above, who then ruled Rome, came to it, gathered a council, confirmed Symmachus as bishop of Rome and drove away Laurentius. At this time the nation of the Bulgars, not known before, is recorded to have overrun Illyricum and Thrace. When the Hagarenes were plundering the east, Anastasius made a treaty with them.

When the Thracian Vitalian attempted a usurpation, taking the Moesians and Scythians as allies, plundering with them the parts about the queen of cities, and even coming against it with a fleet, Anastasius opposed him through Marinus the prefect; and when a sea battle took place, by a device made by the famous Proclus (for he was then flourishing in philosophy and in machines, having gone through all the works of Archimedes, famous in these things, and made further discoveries of his own), the enemy fleet was defeated. For Proclus is said to have forged burning mirrors and hung them from the wall facing the enemy ships, and when the sun's rays struck them, fire flashed out from them like lightning and burned the enemy's sea-borne army, and the ships themselves; which Dio recorded that Archimedes devised long ago, when the Romans were besieging Syracuse.

Anastasius, being a zealot for the heresy of Eutyches, wished to add to the Trisagion "who was crucified for us." So for this he sent the logothete and the prefect to the church; they stood on the ambo as on a stage and began to announce the imperial order. As much of the multitude as was orthodox was stirred, and set out to tear the men apart. They barely escaped the people's frenzy, but the multitude, inflamed with fury, went for the houses of these men. They pulled them down, plundered what was in them, killed many, insulted the emperor and acclaimed Vitalian as emperor; they burned many houses and murdered very many; and they killed a monk who lived near the cistern built by Anastasius called the cistern of Mocius and was held in honour by this emperor, and also put to death a nun walled up near the gate of the Xylokerkos, as one in whom too the emperor had faith; and they bound the two bodies together, dragged them about, and then burned them.

blocks: In this emperor's time Alamundarus, the phylarch of the Hagarenes, was instructed by the orthodox, believed and was baptised. Severus sent two bishops to him, eager to draw him into his own heresy. When the bishops taught him that the two natures of Christ were fused into one nature, and from this it followed that the Godhead too suffered with the flesh of the Lord, he, wishing to expose them as saying absurd things and teaching unbelievable ones, arranged for one of his men, in the presence of those unholy bishops, to give him a message in his ear. When the man had done as he was told, Alamundarus looked gloomy and pretended to be grieved. When the bishops asked why he was troubled and what the news might be, he said it had been reported to him that the archangel Michael had died. When they insisted that the news was false, since it was impossible for the archangel to die, the phylarch took them up and said: "If, then, an angel does not die, how by your account did the Godhead suffer and die, blended with the flesh and made into one nature?" At this the bishops wondered at his understanding; and despairing of ever being able to bring him over to their belief, they withdrew.

When the Bulgars again overran Illyricum, some of the Roman commanders drew up against them with the units under them. But since the Bulgars used incantations and sorceries, the Romans were shamefully defeated, and all but a few perished. Their destruction was foretold by a comet, by crows flying over them and going before them as they marched, and by the trumpeters, who sounded something mournful and full of lament instead of the war note.

When the Timothy mentioned above, who had done the orthodox much harm, died, John the Cappadocian was entrusted with the leadership of the church, and led it for two years. The empress Ariadne died too.

It is said that in the years of Anastasius's reign a statue of the Fortune of the city, made of bronze in the form of a woman, with one of her feet inside a ship standing before her, worked in the same material, stood somewhere in the city. Some parts of this image of the ship, either worn by time or broken by malice, had been taken away. So merchant ships no longer put in at Byzantium, but when they came near were kept off by violent winds, and had not long ships driven by many rowers brought their cargoes into the city, those in it might have been consumed by famine. This lasted for a time and became a worry to those caring for public affairs. Someone then guessed the cause and reported it to those entrusted with the care of the city; and the fragments of that ship were searched for and found, and were put back and fitted to it, and the voyage was unhindered for the ships, and the sea full of them sailing in. To learn whether this had been the hindrance to the ships' sailing in, they took away the parts of that ship again; and all the ships still sailing in were driven back again by force of wind. From this they were assured that the breaking of that bronze ship was the hindrance to the merchant ships' sailing into the city, and thinking that ship worthy of care they restored it.

A little before his death, when a plot against him was reported, Anastasius seized many, among them Justin and Justinian, and meant to destroy them; but he was prevented in a dream, in which a fearsome man seemed to stand by him and say: "Do no harm to Justin and Justinian; for each of them is to serve God in his own time." So he let them off the charge of treason. The emperor Anastasius is also said to have seen in a dream a fearsome man holding a volume and saying to him: "See, because of your false faith I wipe fourteen years from your life." Anastasius, having had an oracle that he would die by a thunderbolt, built the place called the Tholotos and stayed in it, but got no good from it. For once, when most dreadful thunders burst and many lightnings flashed, he in fear moved from room to room and slipped from chamber to chamber. And so he was found lying dead in one of the royal bedchambers, having lived eighty-eight years, of which he reigned twenty-seven years and three months.

In this time a most dreadful earthquake took place, and in Byzantium collapses happened in various places; but great Antioch fell down almost entirely, and its inhabitants were buried in the ruins. This Anastasius built the wall called the Long Wall, reaching from the great sea to Selymbria, because of the attacks of the Moesians, that is the Bulgars, and the Scythians. He also set up a bronze statue of himself on the column of the Taurus, since the one that formerly stood on it, which was of Theodosius the Great, had fallen. So he reigned, and so he ended his life.
