blocks: Justin the Thracian was proclaimed emperor, born of humble and obscure parents, and himself formerly a labourer, or a cowherd and swineherd; then he changed to a soldier's lot, reached the command of a unit, and became a count. After the death of Anastasius, when a council was held about choosing an emperor, Amantius the eunuch, who was praepositus and very powerful, wishing one Theocritus, a man close to him, to reign, gave Justin money to distribute to the soldiers, so that they would choose him emperor. But Justin distributed the money and won the empire for himself, and was raised by the soldiers and the people to the height of sole rule. Amantius took Justin's trick hard and plotted against him with others of the more notable men; and when this became known Justin killed him with Andrew the chamberlain and Theocritus. This Amantius, at the time when Anastasius saw in his sleep the man carrying the volume and wiping out some of the years of his life, dreamed that as he stood before the emperor a great pig came at him, threw him to the ground and consumed him. He built the church of the holy apostle Thomas; so it keeps his name, being called the church of Amantius.

Justin, being most orthodox, issued a decree that all should honour the council at Chalcedon, and that the six hundred and thirty holy fathers who had formed it should be written in the sacred diptychs of all the churches. Having a wife called Lupicina, he crowned her and proclaimed her Augusta, renaming her Euphemia. Vitalian, who had revolted under Anastasius, became very close to him, was appointed general and was even consul, and had great power with Justin. Being orthodox, Justin ordered Severus to be driven from the throne of Antioch and put to death; learning this, Severus fled to Egypt with others of the same mind, and they threw it into confusion by bringing in the question of the corruptible and the incorruptible. When Severus had escaped, Paul, the warden of the hostel of Eubulus, was appointed bishop of Antioch; and Justin brought back all who had suffered unjust exile under Anastasius.

In his time a comet appeared in the east, letting its rays fall downwards, which those who study the heavens call bearded; and Vitalian was treacherously murdered by the people of Byzantium, who resented him for having killed many when he rose against Anastasius. Others say he was put to death in the palace by order of the emperor Justin and of Justinian, since he wished to rule over even the ruler himself; and Justinian was appointed general of the armies. When John the Cappadocian, who was patriarch of Constantinople, died, Epiphanius, a priest of this church, was ordained; and when Hormisdas, pope of Rome, departed life, John succeeded to the helm of the church of the Romans.

When there was enmity between the Romans and the Persians, the emperor Justin sent envoys and gifts to the king of the Huns, asking for an alliance against the Persians; and he agreed. When Cavades, the king of the Persians, asked the same king for an alliance, he promised to fight with him; and he went off to the Persians with his people to draw up against the Romans. But the emperor Justin, sending an embassy about peace to the king of the Persians, wrote to him not to trust the Huns, since they had sworn oaths with the Romans about an alliance, had taken much money, and wished to betray the Persians in time of war. Cavades asked the king whether he had taken money from the Romans; and when he admitted it, he concluded that Justin was telling the truth and at once killed him, and almost all the Huns, except a few who escaped and were saved. He made peace with the Romans and made Justin guardian of Chosroes, the younger of his sons. For he was leaving the kingdom of the Persians to him, passing over the older ones. But the emperor declined the guardianship.

Tzathus, the leader of the Lazi, revolted from the Persians and came over to Justin, and being baptised, named son of the emperor, proclaimed king of the Lazi and married to the daughter of one of the senators, he went back to his own country. This again became a cause of war between Romans and Persians, as the emperor of the Romans was taking for himself those who were subject to them. At that time too the events concerning Saint Arethas happened in the city of Negra. Cavades murdered all the Manichaeans in his realm, and their bishop, and burned their books, because they had taught one of his sons their heresy and made him think as they did.

The city of Anazarbus or Anazarba, the metropolis of Second Cilicia, then collapsed in an earthquake; and Edessa, a famous city of the province of Osrhoene, was flooded, when the river flowing through it, called the Scirtus, overflowed, threw down and swept away the houses of the city, and buried some of its inhabitants in the ruins and drowned others. When the water went down some days later, a stone slab was found on the bank of the river with these words carved on it in hieroglyphic letters: "The river Scirtus will leap evil leaps for the citizens." Half of Pompeiopolis was swallowed up when the city split in the middle, and many of the people, still alive in the chasm, lamented, and no one could take them up. A woman from Cilicia then appeared who was a giant in the height of her body and her whole build; for she stood a full cubit above any tall man; she was very broad in the shoulders and chest, and had the rest in proportion to her height and breadth, I mean her appearance and her voice, the strength and size of her arms and forearms, the thickness of her fingers and everything that goes with these.

When Justinian had been appointed general after the death of Vitalian, as has been said, the whole management was given over to him. Once, when those holding commands asked the emperor to choose the general as partner in the empire, he took hold of his purple and said: "Pray that no younger man put this on." So he then put off their request. But not long after they passed a decree voting Justinian the rank of nobilissimus, and asked the emperor to ratify what had been voted; and he gave way and ratified it in a letter of his own. When he got a wound in the shin he was bedridden. As the illness grew strong and his life was in doubt, he called the patriarch Epiphanius, sent for the men in office, and declared his nephew Justinian emperor, putting the diadem on his head himself. When the people of the city had gathered in the hippodrome, Justinian went out to them crowned, and acclaimed by all went back to the palace, being then forty-five years old. At once his wife Theodora too was proclaimed Augusta, and a little later Justin's life ended, having reigned nine years and twenty days.
text: Justin the Thracian was proclaimed emperor, born of humble and obscure parents, and himself formerly a labourer, or a cowherd and swineherd; then he changed to a soldier's lot, reached the command of a unit, and became a count. After the death of Anastasius, when a council was held about choosing an emperor, Amantius the eunuch, who was praepositus and very powerful, wishing one Theocritus, a man close to him, to reign, gave Justin money to distribute to the soldiers, so that they would choose him emperor. But Justin distributed the money and won the empire for himself, and was raised by the soldiers and the people to the height of sole rule. Amantius took Justin's trick hard and plotted against him with others of the more notable men; and when this became known Justin killed him with Andrew the chamberlain and Theocritus. This Amantius, at the time when Anastasius saw in his sleep the man carrying the volume and wiping out some of the years of his life, dreamed that as he stood before the emperor a great pig came at him, threw him to the ground and consumed him. He built the church of the holy apostle Thomas; so it keeps his name, being called the church of Amantius. Justin, being most orthodox, issued a decree that all should honour the council at Chalcedon, and that the six hundred and thirty holy fathers who had formed it should be written in the sacred diptychs of all the churches. Having a wife called Lupicina, he crowned her and proclaimed her Augusta, renaming her Euphemia. Vitalian, who had revolted under Anastasius, became very close to him, was appointed general and was even consul, and had great power with Justin. Being orthodox, Justin ordered Severus to be driven from the throne of Antioch and put to death; learning this, Severus fled to Egypt with others of the same mind, and they threw it into confusion by bringing in the question of the corruptible and the incorruptible. When Severus had escaped, Paul, the warden of the hostel of Eubulus, was appointed bishop of Antioch; and Justin brought back all who had suffered unjust exile under Anastasius. In his time a comet appeared in the east, letting its rays fall downwards, which those who study the heavens call bearded; and Vitalian was treacherously murdered by the people of Byzantium, who resented him for having killed many when he rose against Anastasius. Others say he was put to death in the palace by order of the emperor Justin and of Justinian, since he wished to rule over even the ruler himself; and Justinian was appointed general of the armies. When John the Cappadocian, who was patriarch of Constantinople, died, Epiphanius, a priest of this church, was ordained; and when Hormisdas, pope of Rome, departed life, John succeeded to the helm of the church of the Romans. When there was enmity between the Romans and the Persians, the emperor Justin sent envoys and gifts to the king of the Huns, asking for an alliance against the Persians; and he agreed. When Cavades, the king of the Persians, asked the same king for an alliance, he promised to fight with him; and he went off to the Persians with his people to draw up against the Romans. But the emperor Justin, sending an embassy about peace to the king of the Persians, wrote to him not to trust the Huns, since they had sworn oaths with the Romans about an alliance, had taken much money, and wished to betray the Persians in time of war. Cavades asked the king whether he had taken money from the Romans; and when he admitted it, he concluded that Justin was telling the truth and at once killed him, and almost all the Huns, except a few who escaped and were saved. He made peace with the Romans and made Justin guardian of Chosroes, the younger of his sons. For he was leaving the kingdom of the Persians to him, passing over the older ones. But the emperor declined the guardianship. Tzathus, the leader of the Lazi, revolted from the Persians and came over to Justin, and being baptised, named son of the emperor, proclaimed king of the Lazi and married to the daughter of one of the senators, he went back to his own country. This again became a cause of war between Romans and Persians, as the emperor of the Romans was taking for himself those who were subject to them. At that time too the events concerning Saint Arethas happened in the city of Negra. blocks: So he departed, having reigned piously. When Justinian began to rule, the empire did not become a monarchy, but the power was divided in two; for his partner in life had no less power than the ruler, if not more. This emperor was very easy to approach and had his ears wide open to slander, quick to retaliate, unsparing in draining money and more unsparing in gathering it. For he spent some on buildings, some so that whatever he wished might be accomplished, and some on wars and quarrels with those who opposed his wishes. So, always needing money, he collected it by unholy means and was grateful to those who found him pretexts for raising money. And while he was so disposed, the empress fell short of the emperor in nothing, either in power or in acquiring money by every means. For she was far more powerful than her husband, and most resourceful in finding newer and many-sided schemes. From this misfortunes came on the subjects from two sides; for the yearly taxes were raised higher and new ones were devised besides. Some were punished and deprived of their property as not rightly disposed in their belief about the divine, others as living licentiously, others because of their disputes with one another, and others for other reasons. To count them all would need a long history.

In the fifth year of his reign the light of a comet was seen, which is called a torch, as sending its rays upwards, and it lasted shining for twenty days. He also made a treaty with the Persians. Affairs in the east were at peace, but civil wars wore down the city, and destroyed its beauty and splendour, as much as had been left after the fire that happened in the reign of Leo. For hatred having grown in the factions against the emperor and the empress for the reasons given, both parties, the Blues and the Greens, though always opposed to each other, came to agreement and began a riot. The ruler tried to stop the riot by letting loose on them a body of the barbarians called Aeluri. But it blazed up more; for when fighting broke out between the factions and the barbarians at the place called the Milion, and many fell on both sides, the clergy of the church, eager to stop the riot and the war, took up the all-holy books of the divine gospels and the venerable images of our Saviour and pushed into the midst of the fighters, thinking that out of respect for the holy things they would lay down their arms and stop fighting; but the barbarians, caring nothing at all for the holy things, cut down the factions and spared neither the sacred things nor those carrying them. This provoked those of the city to riot, and as if defending God himself, they were inflamed to greater madness, and not only men but women too fought from the upper storeys, pelting that barbarian crowd from above with stones, tiles and anything that came to hand. The barbarians, seized with frenzy and wishing to punish the women, set fire to the houses from which they were being pelted. As a violent wind was blowing then, the flame quickly rose into the air and burned to ashes many very large and very beautiful buildings, and burned statues of ancient men famous for wisdom and courage and for brave deeds of hand and wise counsel, and above all the divine precinct itself of the Great Church, which the emperor Constantius built, and that of Saint Irene, the hostel of Eubulus, the Bronze-roofed hall of the palace, which is now called the Chalke, and which serves as a prison, the bath of Severus called the Zeuxippus, and much else that gave the city and the empire adornment and wonder.

Then the emperor planned to put down the riot another way; he decided to go up to the hippodrome and speak to the factions, and sent there to summon the people. But they would not come, and urged one another to beware of the hippodrome, so that they might not be shut in it as in a prison and become a by-product of the rulers' anger. From there they ran to the Market and planned to choose another emperor for themselves; and seizing one Hypatius, a relative of the emperor Anastasius, partly unwilling and partly persuaded, they took him to the Forum of Constantine the Great, raised him high on a shield and proclaimed him emperor, and from there took over the hippodrome, acclaiming him, and looked for a purple robe and a crown. While the factions were busy with this, those about the emperor managed by distributing a great deal of money to draw away many of the Blues, and so, breaking up the factions' agreement, they made them turn against each other. Then suddenly the rulers' chamberlains leapt out of the palace armed, and other soldiers from the city, and the barbarians burst in too, and mowed down the crowds like grass without mercy, now at strife with one another; for the hippodrome was full of men, some of the rioters' party, but most gathered to watch what was happening and the proclamation of Hypatius. They seized Hypatius and his brother Pompeius and brought them to the emperor, and they were put to death and their property confiscated. The number of the people killed was reckoned at about forty thousand. Not only the property of these two men was confiscated, but also that of many other senators; and they too were punished in many ways.

Since in this riot, as has been said, the Great Church, whose builder was Constantius, had burned down, the emperor Justinian began to build another, much greater and more splendid, the building being begun in the year six thousand and forty, in the fifteenth indiction, in the month of February. That emperor began the building not only of this sacred house but of many others too, and needing untold money for them, on the advice of the prefect he cut off the salaries that had been fixed of old to be given in each of the cities to the teachers of the liberal arts there, and so, as the schools in the cities fell idle, rusticity prevailed among their people.

In the seventeenth year of his reign the great column set up in the forecourt of the Great Church was completed, on which this emperor set up an equestrian statue of himself, where before another column of Theodosius the Great had stood, bearing a statue made of silver by his son Arcadius, weighing seven thousand four hundred pounds; Justinian took it down with the column, took away the silver, and raised the column now seen with his own statue. He also destroyed a very large conduit made of lead, by which water was brought into the city, needing much of this material for his buildings. A most violent shaking of the earth also happened then, from which half of Cyzicus collapsed.

It is recorded that someone then came to Byzantium leading a wonder-working dog; for when many had gathered to see it, several of them gave their rings, and all were put down together before the dog. It was ordered by its master to give each his own, and taking them one by one in its mouth it gave each man his own without mistake. Again it was ordered to show who was rich, who poor, which of the women was a harlot, which a widow, which married to a husband, and other such things, and it showed everything without error, holding in its mouth the cloak of each person in answer to the question.

blocks: In the tenth year of Justinian's rule, when the patriarch Epiphanius died, Anthimus of Trebizond was transferred to the priestly throne of Constantinople. This emperor also breathed hard against those mad for men, and punished very many for this reason, cutting off their private parts. When someone asked, "Why do you punish corrupters of boys in this way?", he said: "If they had robbed a temple, would I not have cut off their hand?" He also raised the great church of the Mother of God at the Spring and the shrine of the revered martyrs Sergius and Bacchus, put up many other buildings, and built a bridge over the river Sangarius, on which this epigram by Agathias was made: "You too, Sangarius, after the proud West and after the nations of the Medes and the whole barbarian herd, your streams fettered by strong arches, have been so enslaved by a sovereign hand; you who were once not to be crossed by boats, once untamed, lie bound in a stone shackle." The empress Theodora then built the famous church of the Holy Apostles. There had been a church to the Apostles there before, built by Constantius, the son of Constantine the Great, but not like the present one, falling far short of it in beauty and size.

Once, when Honorius was reigning over elder Rome, the nation of the Vandals migrated and came into Spain, and crossing from there into Libya, seized it with their own king Godigisclus. When he died leaving two sons, one called Gontharis and the other Gaiseric, the rule came round to Gaiseric alone, since Gontharis died. This Gaiseric took Carthage and Rome itself, and having led the Vandals for thirty-nine years paid his debt to nature. His son Huneric succeeded him, by whom very many terrible things were brought on the orthodox, since he forced all to follow Arian ways. He ruled eight years and died leaving his grandson Gundamund as successor. He too was harsh to the orthodox, and ended his life after holding the rule for twelve years. Then Thrasamund became leader of the Vandals, he too an Arian, not punishing the orthodox but only shunning them; and when he had spent twenty-seven years in the rule and come to the end of his life, the leadership fell to Hilderic, who was Gaiseric's grandson by his son Huneric. He did not treat Christians harshly and was mild to all, having by nature a soft character, from which he was also sluggish in war. This Hilderic became an acquaintance of Justinian while he was still a private man. But one Gelimer, a kinsman of Hilderic, an ill-natured man, but energetic and most able at making trouble, attempted a usurpation; seizing his own master he handed him over to prison, with all who were close to him. Rubbing off, as it were, the charge of usurpation, he wrote to Justinian that he had seized this rule not from love of it, but because Hilderic was unfit to manage it. The emperor wrote back to Gelimer that he would not bear it unless he helped the one overthrown and punished the usurper.

So, sending for the patrician Belisarius from the east (for the man was there fighting the Persians), he sent him to Libya with a heavy force and a large fleet, setting him over all the forces as commander-in-chief with full powers; and Procopius of Caesarea went with him, who recorded the wars there at greater length. Belisarius sailed to Libya and pitched a camp. Gelimer, learning this, ordered his brother Ammatas to kill at once Hilderic and his kinsmen, whom he held under guard. And they were put to death. Gelimer engaged Belisarius, was routed and driven out of Carthage, and Belisarius became master of the rest and of all Libya and subjected it to the empire of the Romans, after the Vandals had ruled it for ninety-five years. He also took Gelimer himself alive, with his wife and children. It is said that while he was besieged with his followers in the wretched country of the Moors, his provisions ran out, and he wrote to the commander whom Belisarius had set over the siege, asking him to send him one loaf, a lyre and a sponge. Not able to understand why Gelimer was asking for these things, the commander asked the bearer of the letter; and he said that he asked for the loaf wishing to see one, since he had not seen one since he was driven out of Carthage, the barbarians he was with living poorly; the sponge so that he might wipe the tears from his eyes with it; and the lyre so that with it he might lament his misfortunes. Yet he surrendered himself to the besiegers with those with him, was brought to Belisarius, and laughed as he was led in to him, so that to those who saw him he seemed to have gone out of his mind from the excess of his suffering. But what was happening was something else. For reckoning from what fortune to what he had come, and judging human affairs worthy of laughter, he laughed at them.

Belisarius kept him and the leaders of the Vandals in honour, to be brought to the emperor. He also took over Sicily and Sardinia (this too is an island), brought the parts as far as Gades under himself, and so returned to Byzantium and was thought worthy of great honour by the emperor, bringing Gelimer himself with his wife, children, kin and all his household. Then he also led a triumph for the victory, while a horse race was being held in the hippodrome, with the ruler himself presiding, as was the custom, and the senate and the whole people present. The commander-in-chief came forward from the starting gates holding by the hand the purple robe of Gelimer, who followed; and with him went the generals of the regiments, commanders and captains, and Gelimer's kinsmen. When Belisarius had come before the ruler, he persuaded Gelimer to throw himself to the ground and so pay obeisance to the emperor. He did what he was told, shedding tears. And Belisarius himself threw himself on the ground, showing Gelimer that he had been asked to do this not as a captive, but because it is the custom to do obeisance so to the emperors of the Romans, and as if lightening his misfortune for him. When Gelimer had paid the same obeisance to the empress, a splendid lodging and royal service prepared for him received him.

Some days later, when another horse race was being held in the hippodrome, the spoils of the war were carried through the middle of the city and brought into the Stadium: javelins, thrones and covered litters for women, all made of gold and adorned with precious stones, a couch of the same, carpets worked with gold, vessels for the service of tables, some made of gold, some of silver, cups of gold set with stones, purple garments and robes of the same kind, royal crowns, women's ornaments set with stones and pearls, and very many other things almost past counting, and above all seven chests full of gold and books of the divine gospels gleaming all over with gold and decorated with all kinds of stones. Such were the things of the triumph. Belisarius was also thought worthy of the consulship.

He also took Gelimer himself alive, with his wife and children. It is said that while he was besieged with his followers in the wretched country of the Moors, his provisions ran out, and he wrote to the commander whom Belisarius had set over the siege, asking him to send him one loaf, a lyre and a sponge. Not able to understand why Gelimer was asking for these things, the commander asked the bearer of the letter; and he said that he asked for the loaf wishing to see one, since he had not seen one since he was driven out of Carthage, the barbarians he was with living poorly; the sponge so that he might wipe the tears from his eyes with it; and the lyre so that with it he might lament his misfortunes. Yet he surrendered himself to the besiegers with those with him, was brought to Belisarius, and laughed as he was led in to him, so that to those who saw him he seemed to have gone out of his mind from the excess of his suffering. But what was happening was something else. For reckoning from what fortune to what he had come, and judging human affairs worthy of laughter, he laughed at them. Belisarius kept him and the leaders of the Vandals in honour, to be brought to the emperor. He also took over Sicily and Sardinia (this too is an island), brought the parts as far as Gades under himself, and so returned to Byzantium and was thought worthy of great honour by the emperor, bringing Gelimer himself with his wife, children, kin and all his household. Then he also led a triumph for the victory, while a horse race was being held in the hippodrome, with the ruler himself presiding, as was the custom, and the senate and the whole people present. The commander-in-chief came forward from the starting gates holding by the hand the purple robe of Gelimer, who followed; and with him went the generals of the regiments, commanders and captains, and Gelimer's kinsmen. When Belisarius had come before the ruler, he persuaded Gelimer to throw himself to the ground and so pay obeisance to the emperor. He did what he was told, shedding tears. And Belisarius himself threw himself on the ground, showing Gelimer that he had been asked to do this not as a captive, but because it is the custom to do obeisance so to the emperors of the Romans, and as if lightening his misfortune for him. When Gelimer had paid the same obeisance to the empress, a splendid lodging and royal service prepared for him received him. Some days later, when another horse race was being held in the hippodrome, the spoils of the war were carried through the middle of the city and brought into the Stadium: javelins, thrones and covered litters for women, all made of gold and adorned with precious stones, a couch of the same, carpets worked with gold, vessels for the service of tables, some made of gold, some of silver, cups of gold set with stones, purple garments and robes of the same kind, royal crowns, women's ornaments set with stones and pearls, and very many other things almost past counting, and above all seven chests full of gold and books of the divine gospels gleaming all over with gold and decorated with all kinds of stones. Such were the things of the triumph. Belisarius was also thought worthy of the consulship.

blocks: When the Vandal war had been ended, he was sent by the emperor to Rome, to win it and all Italy for him, which was held by the Goths, whose leader was Theodahad. Learning this, Theodahad sent Agapetus, the great high priest of Rome, a godly man, to the emperor as his envoy. He reached Byzantium and met Justinian, and first talked about God and faith in him, and blamed the raising of Anthimus to the throne of New Rome, both because he had been moved uncanonically to Constantinople from Trebizond, which is the metropolis of the cities lying in Polemoniac Pontus, and because he shared in the false belief of Severus. The emperor, having thought Anthimus worthy of the high priestly see of Constantinople through the efforts of the empress, held to his own act. When the divine Agapetus still pressed him, he even threatened him, saying he had the power to do what he wished. But when the high priest laughed at the emperor's threats and answered that he would gladly accept slaughter and would be blessed if thought worthy of such an end, the emperor was ashamed, changed his mind and put the matter under inquiry. Some of the high priests spoke against Agapetus, pope of Rome, to please the empress, by whom they had been corrupted with money. But he, pleading for the truth, prevailed over them all, and Anthimus was thrown out of the throne of Constantinople, having enjoyed it one year, the emperor himself respecting the most holy pope and the truth. Menas was brought in instead, a most pious man, who boasted Alexandria in Egypt as his country, was born of one of the notable men there, and was not unversed in letters, and above all in the more divine.

When the divine Menas had obtained the high priesthood, or rather it had been fortunate in obtaining him, he held a local council with Pope Agapetus, and put under anathema Severus, Eutyches, Peter, Julian of Halicarnassus, and Anthimus as of one mind with them. While still staying in Byzantium the most holy Pope Agapetus departed life. Menas, having steered the church piously for sixteen years, ended his life; and Eutychius was raised to the high priestly see of New Rome, presiding over the church with right belief for twelve years. In his time the fifth council of the hundred and sixty-five holy fathers was gathered, led by Vigilius, pope of Rome, the Eutychius mentioned, and Apollinarius of Alexandria. It was gathered against Origen and his strange beliefs, and against those who championed his views, Didymus and Evagrius, who taught the pre-existence of souls and spoke of an end of punishment and the restoration of the demons to their former state, and many other things; and it put them under anathema with their doctrines, and also Theodore of Mopsuestia, who held the views of Nestorius, or rather had been his teacher; the emperor Justinian was present at the council and agreed with what those divine fathers arranged in a God-loving way.

So these things fell out. Belisarius, sailing to Italy, first took Naples by siege, then coming to Rome itself, partly by force and partly by the goodwill of the citizens, he got inside it too; for Theodahad, the ruler of the Goths, happened to be staying in Ravenna. The city of Milan too was taken by the Romans. When the Goths besieged it again, the emperor sent Narses with a force to help Belisarius. Narses was a eunuch, but otherwise noble and most able as a general, and close to the rulers. Since these two generals did not agree with each other (for Belisarius wished to ascribe all the successes to himself, while Narses would not bear to seem placed under him), they separated, and conducted the war one in one place, the other in another, and so they failed in some things. For the imperial troops guarding Milan, pleading lack of necessities, gave it up to the Goths; and the quarrel between the two would perhaps have ended in some greater evil, had not the emperor called Narses to him by letter.

blocks: From then Belisarius, commanding alone again, brought all Italy and its cities under him, and became so fearsome and so loved by the barbarians that they thought him worthy of their rule and begged him to become their king, giving themselves and all they had over to him. But he said: "I shall never bear to be called king myself while Justinian lives," as Procopius of Caesarea, who served with him then, wrote of these matters. From this, then, having become envied, he was slandered to the emperor as desiring the throne, and the emperor called him back from there, as if to campaign in the east and be entrusted with the Persian war.

The Augusta Theodora died, having lived twenty-one years and three months of the reign. When the Great Church had already been finished and consecrated, the great eastern semi-dome of the church fell in an earthquake, and in falling it crushed the canopy of the holy table, that all-holy table itself and the ambo; for this reason the dome is said to have been taken down by the emperor's order and raised again twenty-five feet higher, and consecrated a second time by the patriarch Eutychius.

Under this emperor the sea monster was also caught that had troubled the people of Byzantium for more than fifty years, which they called Porphyrius; it did not always appear, but at intervals. When it appeared, it sank many ships and caused the destruction of many men; they used many devices against it, but all remained useless; yet it was caught while chasing dolphins. For they, fleeing it, came near the land, and it did not check its rush against them, until, having come very close to the land, it fell into deep, marshy mud. There it was stuck fast in the clay and could no longer get out of the marsh. When this became known to those living round about, it armed them against this sea beast, and cutting it with axes and hatchets they killed it. Then they fastened the stoutest ropes to it and dragged it out of the sea with yokes of oxen. Its length was thirty cubits, and it was ten broad, as Procopius of Caesarea recorded about this too.

In the time of this emperor, according to the same writer, the threads of the Seres, that is silk, began to be made among the Romans. For the stuff of silk was brought to the Romans from the Persians, bought through merchants, but they knew neither how it was made nor that it was the thread of worms. But two monks who came to Byzantium from India described its production, and promised to bring eggs, the offspring of those worms, which are very small in size, and to show the Romans how they come to life when warmed and change into worms, and how they make silk, having nature as their teacher. The emperor Justinian encouraged these monks to the work with gifts for the present and splendid promises for the future. They brought the eggs of the Seres to Byzantium, changed them into worms by putting them in dung and warming them with it, fed them on mulberry leaves and produced silk through them; and from this the Romans knew thereafter how silk is made.

When a plot planned by many was reported to the emperor, the patrician Belisarius too was accused of sharing in it, and the emperor took away all his guards and left him under watch in his house; and when he died his property was assigned to the imperial treasuries.

Towards the end Justinian was taken by the heresy of the Aphthartodocetae, who teach that the Lord took on flesh not corruptible but incorruptible from the moment it was assumed, and he was eager for all to believe so; and when the patriarch Eutychius spoke against him and opposed him, he banished him to Amaseia, and John Scholasticus, who was the representative of Antioch, was appointed patriarch. Justinian died holding this belief, having reigned thirty-eight years, seven months and thirteen days, leaving the empire to his nephew Justin, who had been honoured as curopalates.

blocks: He was an Illyrian by birth, very able by nature in everything, and great-souled in mind. Being pious, he adorned the churches built by Justinian, added both new apses to the church at Blachernae, so that it was cross-shaped, lavishly built the church of the chief Apostles at the Orphanage, the church of the divine Unmercenaries in the quarter of Basiliscus, and that of the holy protomartyr Thecla, and the Golden Hall of the palace, restored the great aqueduct of Valens, and much else. His wife was Sophia, whom he also crowned Augusta, and in whose name he built the harbour of Sophia and a palace before the city, naming it and the place Sophianae after her; on which this epigram was made by Agathias: "Where the wandering strait opens the sea, splitting the land in two along the sea-washed shores, the divine lord set this golden palace for his consort, the queen, the most glorious Sophia. Fitting, O mighty Rome, that the beauty opposite you looks from Europe on Asia."

This empress Sophia, having made an exact account of all the lenders and of what anyone owed them, whether by written bonds or by pledges, paid off the loans to them from her own means, took the pledges and the bonds, gave back the pledges to their owners and destroyed the bonds.

This emperor, having a sickly body and so not going out often, made those who wished to do wrong bolder, as though there were no one to avenge it. Once when he went out he was beset by many complaining of wrongs. So avenging the wronged became a care to him. As he was thinking about this, a man came to him promising that if he were made prefect and given power over all for a fixed time, no one would be found wronged. Pleased at this promise, the emperor appointed that man prefect. When he had taken his seat, and someone came and accused one of the more notable senators, he summoned the accused; but he did not appear. Then he sent him a second message; but he, despising this too, went off to the imperial banquet; for he happened to have been invited to it. When the prefect learned this, he too went to the palace, found the banquet already going on, and said to the emperor: "I promised you, emperor, to leave no one wronged within such a time; and this I shall surely accomplish, if I have the help and support of your majesty; but if you yourself rather take the side of the wrongdoers and, being friendly to them, have them at your table, nothing will be achievable for me; so either do not give them such licence, or remove me from office." And the emperor said: "If I myself am the wrongdoer, raise me from here." At once, then, the prefect raised the accused man from the feast, set him in the court and tried him with his accuser, and finding him in the wrong, punished him with blows on his body and restored the wrong to the injured man many times over from his property. From this those with a grasping disposition were afraid, held back from wrongdoing, and came to terms with those they had wronged.

The treaty with the Persians was broken under this emperor; for the Romans were giving them a yearly tribute of five hundred pounds so that the forts of the Roman empire next to them might be kept unharmed, and this Justin, saying it was disgraceful for Romans to pay tribute to Persians, stopped the gold. Sending an embassy to Arethas, king of the Ethiopians, he persuaded him to overrun and plunder the parts of the Persian dominion near the Ethiopians; and so war was kindled again between Persians and Romans. So the emperor appointed the patrician Martinus general of the east and sent him against them, and in the fourth year of his reign a war took place, and many fell on both sides, but the Romans won. Hormisdas, the ruler of the Persians, sent Ardamanes with a heavy force to plunder the Roman lands; he went over much Roman country, carried off very much plunder from it and went back, since the patrician Martinus did not dare to go out against him. The emperor, learning this, took it as a calamity, took the command from Martinus and entrusted it to Archelaus, and made a treaty with Hormisdas again.

From the grief over this he fell into a disease of the mind, and suffered also in his feet. Having no children of his own, he first adopted Tiberius, the count of the excubitors, and proclaimed him Caesar. When his illness let up, he called the patriarch Eutychius (for when John Scholasticus died, he had been brought back and restored to the high priestly throne), and gathering the senate and the clergy of the church, proclaimed Tiberius emperor, charging him in the hearing of all to be pious towards God, to do good to his subjects, to avenge the wronged, not to let the soldiers be greedy, not to be proud of the purple, to allow the well-off to enjoy their own without envy, to help those who had nothing as far as he could, and to honour fittingly the empress, his former mistress. Having given Tiberius this advice and counsel, Justin died, having reigned thirteen years.

blocks: The empire was left to Tiberius, who was crowned by the patriarch Eutychius. Having a wife, Anastasia, Tiberius proclaimed her Augusta; she bore him two daughters, Charito and Constantina. Sophia, the former empress, withdrew from the palace and settled in the palace named after her, Tiberius giving her royal service as his own mother.

This emperor sent an embassy to Hormisdas too, renewing the treaty. But he would not accept the renewal; so Tiberius prepared a large army for the war against the Persians, and put forward Justinian, one of the notable men, as general of the east; he advanced against the Persians, and when he had encamped near them, came to a parley before the battle and persuaded them to make a treaty with the Romans for three years. When the third year was running out, Hormisdas, the ruler of the Persians, advanced with his forces into Armenia. This threw the Roman armies there into fear. But their general, speaking to them, gave all courage, and they stood up to battle with Hormisdas; and for a while the Persians, using volleys from their bows, seemed to have the upper hand, while the Romans fenced themselves with their shields and did not go out against them. But when the Romans knew that the enemy's quivers had already been emptied, they locked shields, raised the war cry, and came at the Persians at close quarters, fighting them with hand-to-hand weapons. They did not stand their charge even for a little, but were routed, and most were killed; their camp was plundered; the royal tent of Hormisdas, all his baggage and the elephants were set aside for the emperor, and the rest left to the soldiers. The Romans advanced into the interior of Persia and plundered much of its country.

At that time Tiberius also began to build the bath of Blachernae, restored many churches and public houses, I mean hostels and homes for the old, and further adorned the Golden Hall built by Justin. When the patriarch Eutychius, having graced the throne of Byzantium a second time for four years, died, John the Faster, a deacon of the Great Church, a most holy man, was ordained patriarch. All the Persian captives brought into the queen of cities the emperor clothed magnificently and let go home; and their relatives, seeing them beyond hope, wondered greatly and praised the emperor.

Under this emperor the Chagan, the leader of the Avars, asked for builders to be sent to him to build him a bath. When they were sent, he built a bridge over the Danube, forcing them to it, so that crossing by it without trouble he might plunder the lands under the Romans. Tiberius, gathering from the nations a host amounting to twelve thousand young and vigorous men, formed them into an army in his own name, and setting over them as general Maurice, the count of the foederati, and as second in command Narses the chamberlain, sent them against the Persians. When war broke out the Roman army prevailed and took cities and much country from the barbarians. When Maurice came back the emperor received him with honour and made him his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter Constantina. The other, Charito, he joined to the general Germanus, and honoured both as Caesars. Falling into a wasting disease, he was carried on a litter to the tribunal and there had his own son-in-law Maurice proclaimed emperor in the presence of the patriarch John and the senate. He was so worn down by the disease that he could not even speak to those gathered; so he set out his wishes to them in writing. Going back from there to the palace he came to the end of his life, having reigned three years, ten months and eight days.

But their general, speaking to them, gave all courage, and they stood up to battle with Hormisdas; and for a while the Persians, using volleys from their bows, seemed to have the upper hand, while the Romans fenced themselves with their shields and did not go out against them. But when the Romans knew that the enemy's quivers had already been emptied, they locked shields, raised the war cry, and came at the Persians at close quarters, fighting them with hand-to-hand weapons. They did not stand their charge even for a little, but were routed, and most were killed; their camp was plundered; the royal tent of Hormisdas, all his baggage and the elephants were set aside for the emperor, and the rest left to the soldiers. The Romans advanced into the interior of Persia and plundered much of its country. At that time Tiberius also began to build the bath of Blachernae, restored many churches and public houses, I mean hostels and homes for the old, and further adorned the Golden Hall built by Justin. When the patriarch Eutychius, having graced the throne of Byzantium a second time for four years, died, John the Faster, a deacon of the Great Church, a most holy man, was ordained patriarch. All the Persian captives brought into the queen of cities the emperor clothed magnificently and let go home; and their relatives, seeing them beyond hope, wondered greatly and praised the emperor. Under this emperor the Chagan, the leader of the Avars, asked for builders to be sent to him to build him a bath. When they were sent, he built a bridge over the Danube, forcing them to it, so that crossing by it without trouble he might plunder the lands under the Romans. Tiberius, gathering from the nations a host amounting to twelve thousand young and vigorous men, formed them into an army in his own name, and setting over them as general Maurice, the count of the foederati, and as second in command Narses the chamberlain, sent them against the Persians. When war broke out the Roman army prevailed and took cities and much country from the barbarians. When Maurice came back the emperor received him with honour and made him his son-in-law by marrying him to his daughter Constantina. The other, Charito, he joined to the general Germanus, and honoured both as Caesars. Falling into a wasting disease, he was carried on a litter to the tribunal and there had his own son-in-law Maurice proclaimed emperor in the presence of the patriarch John and the senate. He was so worn down by the disease that he could not even speak to those gathered; so he set out his wishes to them in writing. Going back from there to the palace he came to the end of his life, having reigned three years, ten months and eight days.

blocks: Maurice took up the management of public affairs, crowned by the patriarch John the Faster. When he came to the sole rule he was forty-three years old. He was written in contracts as Maurice Tiberius.

The Chagan, the leader of the Avars, having subdued Sirmium, sought to have another twenty thousand added to the eighty thousand given him yearly; and the emperor, wishing to keep peace, made this addition. He also asked for an elephant, never having seen the animal. So the emperor sent him the largest of those he had. But the Chagan, being insatiable or looking for pretexts not to keep peace, demanded that another twenty thousand be added to the hundred. When the emperor would not accept this addition, he marched against the Romans and subdued many cities of Illyricum; and he threatened to overthrow the Long Wall too. So Maurice sent envoys to the barbarian and made a treaty. But the Chagan, being insatiable and faithless, worked against the Romans by guile, keeping quiet himself, but arranging for some peoples of the Sclaveni to plunder the lands under the Romans, and they came as far as the Long Wall. The emperor put forward Comentiolus as general, and attacking the barbarians suddenly through him, drove them from the Roman borders, many being killed, and recovered all the plunder they had taken and the captives.

Having married his own sister to Philippicus, he sent him against the Persians with a heavy army. He came close to Nisibis and from there invaded Persia, drove much plunder from there, and coming back attacked the country of the Medes, and having plundered no less of it, came back into Roman territory. Again he attacked the Persian borders and was likewise successful. Falling ill, he came to Martyropolis, and from there went back to Byzantium. A son was born to Maurice, whom he named Theodosius. Philippicus again marched against the Persians, and asked the army with him whether they were eager to fight the Persians. They confirmed their eagerness even with oaths. So when they engaged the enemy, the barbarians held out for a while; but when the general urged his men to strike their horses, and many of the horses fell when struck, the Persian army was routed, was heavily defeated, and a great part of it perished; the Romans won brilliantly and took about two thousand of the enemy alive.

Hormisdas, the ruler of the Persians, appointed Bahram general and ordered him to engage the Romans. He engaged and was defeated; learning this, Hormisdas sent him a woman's dress, took away his command and ordered his second in command by letter to put Bahram to death. Bahram, realising what trouble he was in, forged a letter as if sent to him by Hormisdas, showing anger against the whole army, and gathering it had the letter read aloud, and himself reminded them of Hormisdas's harshness and cruelty, and by this stirred them to raise their hands against their ruler. So they came at him suddenly, seized him and threw him into prison. He asked to advise them about the rule of the Persians what he knew to be good for the nation, and advised them not to prefer his son Chosroes for the rule, since he was insatiable and unjust, insolent and most boastful, but to appoint another son of his to rule the nation. When some of those in high position opposed his words and maddened the Persians against him, the son he had preferred for the rule and that son's mother were killed by the crowd before his eyes, and he himself had his eyes put out, and so was imprisoned. Chosroes was chosen for the rule by the whole nation. For a while he was kindly disposed to his father, not releasing him from custody, but giving him every care there. But he accepted none of the things his son sent him, but rather repaid his kindnesses with insults. So, seized with anger at this, Chosroes ordered his father to be beaten to death with clubs on the flanks. This made hatred grow among the Persians against Chosroes.

He marched against Bahram, and suspecting some of the grandees with him of siding with Bahram, put them to death. When the army rose against him, he in fear ran away with a few men and came to the Romans. Learning this, Maurice ordered the general of the region to receive Chosroes with royal attentions and welcomes. He sent Narses with armies to fight alongside Chosroes and restore him to his own rule. So Narses engaged Bahram and won a famous victory, killing many of the Persians and taking about six thousand alive, whom he brought to Chosroes; and he had them all shot down with javelins. Those among the captives who were of the nation of the Turks, fighting with Bahram, he sent up to Maurice; many of them bore crosses on their foreheads, their brows having been pricked in the form of a cross and ink poured into the marks. When asked about this, they said that a good while before their race was being destroyed by plague, and some of the Christians among them suggested this to them, and none of those who had done it was endangered by the plague. Bahram, defeated, sought safety in flight. Chosroes went back to his own rule and country.

It is said that before the victory, when the Roman general was considering conducting the war another way, Chosroes insisted on not joining battle as the general thought, but proposed another way; the general said it would be unprofitable to fight so, and Chosroes did not give up his aim, so that the general, provoked, mocked Chosroes, calling him no general and ignorant of the art of war. Chosroes, stung by the mockery, and having knowledge of the movement of the stars, and so boasting that he knew the future, said: "If we were not under the tyranny of circumstances, general, you would not have dared to pelt the great king with mockery. But since you are proud at present, hear what the gods have planned for later. Terrible things, be sure, will flow back on you Romans. The Babylonian race will hold the Roman country for three cycles of seven years. After this, for a fifth seven years, you Romans will make slaves of the Persians." And when these things were accomplished, the day without evening would come to dwell among men. But so much for this.

The emperor Maurice proclaimed his son Theodosius emperor, crowned at Easter by the patriarch John. He completed the church of the holy Forty Martyrs, which had earlier been begun by Tiberius but left unfinished. When peace had been made with the Persians, he moved the forces from the east to Thrace, and himself went out of Byzantium to see what had been ruined by the barbarians. At that time too the sun was eclipsed, and a woman in Thrace bore a child that had neither eyes nor eyelids, neither hands nor arms, but a fish's tail projecting at its hip.

When the Chagan came against Thrace with a countless host, the Roman general Priscus in fear shut himself in the fort of Tzurulon. The barbarian prepared to besiege it. Then Maurice outgeneralled him in this way. He composed a letter to Priscus urging him to hold out; for in a little while the barbarians would withdraw in disgrace. For ships were being sent to their country with an army to plunder their houses and take their wives and children captive. He gave this letter to someone, charging him to fall into the hands of the barbarians as if on his way to Priscus. When this happened, the barbarian read the letter, and fearing for his own people, made a treaty with Priscus for a few gifts and went away. Philippicus built a monastery in Chrysopolis in the name of the Mother of God, and in it a most splendid house, so that he might receive Maurice in it.

blocks: John the Faster, patriarch of Constantinople, left life and passed to the eternal dwellings, having adorned the high priestly throne for more than thirteen years. So Cyriacus, priest and steward of the Great Church, was appointed patriarch. By him the church of the all-holy Mother of God, which is called the Deaconess's, was built. And Peter, Maurice's brother, raised the church called Areobindus's to the Mother of God. The empress Sophia and the Augusta Constantina presented the emperor with a crown adorned with precious stones and enormous pearls. He took it and dedicated it to God, bringing it to the church.

The Chagan again advanced against the Roman lands. As the Roman armies drew up against him, he sometimes won and sometimes was beaten. In one day seven sons of his died of a pestilential disease and fever. The emperor sent Comentiolus against the Chagan with a very large army, and is said to have ordered him to betray the soldiery to the enemy, bearing a grudge against them for some mutinies and disorders. Comentiolus engaged the barbarians in disorder, and he himself with those about him turned to flight, having prepared for this beforehand. Of the rest some fell and others were taken alive. They say those taken alive were about twelve thousand. The Chagan, swollen by this victory, came as far as the Long Wall. The emperor gathered people and sent them out to guard the wall. Not only the Chagan's sons, as has been said, died of the pestilential disease, but also a great number of the Avars; so the barbarian, losing heart, was eager to go back home. So he sent to Maurice to ransom the captives, giving one coin for each. The emperor did not agree. The Chagan then asked to receive half a coin for each of the captives. But not even so would he buy those taken, partly out of stinginess, for he was a slave to money, and partly bearing a grudge against the soldiers. So the barbarian in a frenzy mowed them all down with swords, and went away. From this hatred grew in all against the emperor, and he was reviled by all.

The army made a complaint against Comentiolus, as having betrayed the soldiery in the war. With those making the complaint was the soldier Phocas, who spoke to the emperor so shamelessly that he was beaten by some. The emperor, paying no heed to the charges against Comentiolus, sent away his accusers with nothing done. When the emperor was in a procession, a riot was raised by the people, and stones were thrown at him by some; the emperor searched for them, found some and punished them. He betrothed his son Theodosius to the daughter of the patrician Germanus, the patriarch Cyriacus performing the marriage rite. A monk holding a bare sword went from the Forum as far as the Chalke, saying that Maurice would die by the sword.

The emperor, reckoning up his crime over the captives, begged God to pay the penalty for it in the present life, and sent everywhere asking all to ask God for this. When a rumour prevailed that the name of the one who would succeed him began with the letter phi, he thought this was his son-in-law Philippicus. And the man was under suspicion with him, and though he swore he had never thought of any such thing, he did not persuade him; but a dream once seen by the emperor removed his suspicion of Philippicus. The dream was this: a great crowd seemed to stand by the image of Christ the Saviour above the Chalke gate and cry out against the emperor, and a voice came from the image to bring Maurice too; and he was brought at once and asked where he wished to pay the penalty for the crime he had committed against the captives, in this age or in the age to come. He said: "Here, merciful master." And he heard a voice saying: "Then hand him over with his whole family to Phocas the soldier." Waking from the anguish, the emperor called Philippicus, and first asked his pardon for having suspected him for nothing, then asked whether he knew a soldier Phocas in the Roman regiments. He answered that he knew him, and that he was the one sent a little before by the army, "who spoke to you rather insolently." The emperor asked further what the man was like in age and character; and Philippicus said that Phocas was young, but bold and cowardly in character. To this the emperor answered: "If cowardly, also a murderer," and told him the dream. At that time too the comet called the sword appeared.

The emperor wrote to his brother Peter, who was then general, to cross the Ister with the army and provide for its needs from there. This was arranged out of love of money, so that the army might feed itself by plundering and he might save the soldiers' rations. This raised a mutiny in the army, and at once Phocas was proclaimed emperor by them; he happened to be a centurion. The general Peter, learning this, fled, and brought the news of what had happened to the emperor himself. When those in the city too rose, Maurice slipped out of the palace, boarded a dromon with his wife and children and fled; and he sent his son Theodosius to Chosroes, so that, remembering what he had received from Maurice, Chosroes might show the like to him. When the emperor's departure became known to the multitude, it raised the riot higher and caused Maurice to be reviled through the market.

blocks: When Phocas was not far from Byzantium, those of the Green faction went out acclaiming him. He came with them to the Hebdomon, and there his head was crowned by the patriarch; and going into the palace he at once proclaimed his wife Leontia Augusta in the presence of the factions; at which, when a dispute arose between the Greens and the Blues about the places where they were standing, they began to riot against each other. Phocas sent some men and tried to calm their riot. When one of those sent insulted the demarch of the Blues and pushed him, the faction would not bear it and shouted: "Go away, learn your station; Maurice is alive." From this the tyrant was stirred to the murder of Maurice, and when he had been brought to the harbour of Eutropius at Chalcedon, his sons were first killed before his eyes. At each he said, "You are just, O Lord, and your judgements are right," bearing the misfortune nobly. His last child, still at the breast, showed the man's nobility and patient endurance of the trial still more; for when the nurse, so that Maurice's line might not perish altogether, stole away the child she was nursing and gave her own in exchange for slaughter, Maurice asked for his own to be brought. Then he himself received the slaughter great-heartedly.

It is said that his son Theodosius too was caught as he was going away to Chosroes, was brought to Phocas and put to death, and the empress Constantina and her three daughters too, and that they were buried in the church of Saint Mamas near the wall, which Pharasmanes the eunuch built, who had been chamberlain to Justinian. These heroic elegiacs were inscribed on her tomb: "I, thrice wretched, daughter of the emperor Tiberius and wife of the emperor Maurice, the queen blessed with many children, who had learned that glory and many rulers are a good thing, lie here with my children and my husband, by the folly of the people and the madness of the army. I have suffered far worse than Hecuba and Jocasta; alas, I am a living corpse more than Niobe; yes, yes, the father; why did they kill the newborn for nothing, who knew nothing of men's wickedness? New Rome is shaded by our leaves no more; for the root has been broken by Thracian winds." Maurice died at sixty-three, having reigned twenty years.

When Phocas held power, Narses revolted and seized Edessa. By Phocas's order Germanus was defeated by Chosroes, who was fighting as Narses's ally; and being wounded he died some days later. After this Narses fled to Hierapolis, and receiving sworn pledges from Phocas's brother, the magister Domentziolus, was sent to Phocas. He, not at all deterred by the oaths, handed him over to the fire. This Narses built the church of Saint Panteleemon and that of the holy martyrs Probus, Tarachus and Andronicus, and the hostel there. Phocas killed not only him, but also Maurice's brother Peter, and Germanus, the father-in-law of Maurice's son Theodosius, and Germanus's daughter, and all Maurice's kin. Philippicus was tonsured a cleric and lived in his monastery in Chrysopolis. Phocas killed many others too and punished them with cruel penalties.

When the patriarch Cyriacus died eleven years after his appointment, Thomas, sacellarius and deacon of the Great Church, became patriarch. Evils of many kinds then took hold of the Romans. For in the east the Persians brought Syria, Palestine and Phoenicia under them. They overran Armenia, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia and Galatia, and came as far as Chalcedon, plundering everything. In Europe the Avars ravaged Thrace, and the Roman armies in both parts were destroyed; and besides there was a great death of men, failure of crops and destruction of animals from the hardest winters. Above all, the avenging fury Phocas, maddened when the factions mocked him in a horse race, killed many, maimed many, drowned some, and handed very many to the prefect to punish them; they were shut up in the praetorium. The crowds came together, set fire to the praetorium, and those imprisoned escaped. The Hebrews in Antioch rose against the Christians and killed many of the Antiochenes, and the patriarch of the city himself, Anastasius, and burned his body in the market. Phocas sent men and killed some, maimed others and drove them out of the city. The patriarch, having presided over the church for three years and two months, died, and Sergius, deacon of the Great Church, was brought in in his place.

Phocas married his daughter Domentia to Priscus the general, and after the wedding, holding a horse race, he saw statues of Priscus and his wife Domentia standing with his own statues, and in a frenzy ordered the demarchs to be beheaded. When the factions begged, he barely let them go. So for this reason Priscus, fearing for his life, and at the same time hating Phocas's tyranny over all, sought to overthrow the tyrant. Phocas, being mad for women, a drunkard, cruel and bloodthirsty, was hated by all. And while Heraclius, the father of the Heraclius who later reigned, was general in Africa and Libya, those of the senate and Priscus the general himself sent to him, begging to be freed from the tyranny of Phocas. The said general Heraclius had as second in command one Gregoras, a notable man. These two, agreeing, sent their own sons against the tyrant, Heraclius his son Heraclius sailing with many ships and a host of soldiers, and the patrician Gregoras his son, marching by land with many horsemen and an infantry army, on the terms that whichever first took the queen of cities and overthrew the tyrant should be thought worthy of the empire. Learning this, Phocas seized Heraclius's mother and his betrothed Eudocia, to whom he had been betrothed from Africa, the daughter of the leading man of that land, and shut them up in a monastery.

Heraclius got there first and anchored in the harbour of Sophia, and when battle was joined he prevailed over Phocas's men. For he was helped by Crispus, who held the office of prefect. Photius, one of the notable officials, whose wife the tyrant had seduced by force, took the palace with a host of soldiers and dragged the tyrant from his throne (for those about him had given up and withdrawn from the palace), stripped off his purple, put dark clothing on him, and brought him in chains to Heraclius. Seeing him, he said: "Is this how you managed the affairs of the city, wretch?" And Phocas, possessed by madness, answered: "And will you manage them better?" Angry, Heraclius jumped on him with his heel and ordered him to be beheaded. Some recorded that he was put to death at once, but others say his hands and feet were first cut off, then also his private parts, because of his licentiousness and because he had shamed the wives of many, and so his head was cut off, and his wretched body burned at the Bous, where there was, as is said, a furnace made of bronze in the shape of an ox, which had been brought from Pergamum, from which the place was named. His brothers and others close to him were put to death. Such was the end of the tyranny of the most wicked Phocas, who had trampled on the empire for eight years.
text: When Phocas was not far from Byzantium, those of the Green faction went out acclaiming him. He came with them to the Hebdomon, and there his head was crowned by the patriarch; and going into the palace he at once proclaimed his wife Leontia Augusta in the presence of the factions; at which, when a dispute arose between the Greens and the Blues about the places where they were standing, they began to riot against each other. Phocas sent some men and tried to calm their riot. When one of those sent insulted the demarch of the Blues and pushed him, the faction would not bear it and shouted: "Go away, learn your station; Maurice is alive." From this the tyrant was stirred to the murder of Maurice, and when he had been brought to the harbour of Eutropius at Chalcedon, his sons were first killed before his eyes. At each he said, "You are just, O Lord, and your judgements are right," bearing the misfortune nobly. His last child, still at the breast, showed the man's nobility and patient endurance of the trial still more; for when the nurse, so that Maurice's line might not perish altogether, stole away the child she was nursing and gave her own in exchange for slaughter, Maurice asked for his own to be brought. Then he himself received the slaughter great-heartedly. It is said that his son Theodosius too was caught as he was going away to Chosroes, was brought to Phocas and put to death, and the empress Constantina and her three daughters too, and that they were buried in the church of Saint Mamas near the wall, which Pharasmanes the eunuch built, who had been chamberlain to Justinian. These heroic elegiacs were inscribed on her tomb: "I, thrice wretched, daughter of the emperor Tiberius and wife of the emperor Maurice, the queen blessed with many children, who had learned that glory and many rulers are a good thing, lie here with my children and my husband, by the folly of the people and the madness of the army. I have suffered far worse than Hecuba and Jocasta; alas, I am a living corpse more than Niobe; yes, yes, the father; why did they kill the newborn for nothing, who knew nothing of men's wickedness? New Rome is shaded by our leaves no more; for the root has been broken by Thracian winds." Maurice died at sixty-three, having reigned twenty years. When Phocas held power, Narses revolted and seized Edessa. By Phocas's order Germanus was defeated by Chosroes, who was fighting as Narses's ally; and being wounded he died some days later. After this Narses fled to Hierapolis, and receiving sworn pledges from Phocas's brother, the magister Domentziolus, was sent to Phocas. He, not at all deterred by the oaths, handed him over to the fire. This Narses built the church of Saint Panteleemon and that of the holy martyrs Probus, Tarachus and Andronicus, and the hostel there. Phocas killed not only him, but also Maurice's brother Peter, and Germanus, the father-in-law of Maurice's son Theodosius, and Germanus's daughter, and all Maurice's kin. Philippicus was tonsured a cleric and lived in his monastery in Chrysopolis. Phocas killed many others too and punished them with cruel penalties. When the patriarch Cyriacus died eleven years after his appointment, Thomas, sacellarius and deacon of the Great Church, became patriarch. Evils of many kinds then took hold of the Romans. For in the east the Persians brought Syria, Palestine and Phoenicia under them. They overran Armenia, Cappadocia, Paphlagonia and Galatia, and came as far as Chalcedon, plundering everything. In Europe the Avars ravaged Thrace, and the Roman armies in both parts were destroyed; and besides there was a great death of men, failure of crops and destruction of animals from the hardest winters. Above all, the avenging fury Phocas, maddened when the factions mocked him in a horse race, killed many, maimed many, drowned some, and handed very many to the prefect to punish them; they were shut up in the praetorium. The crowds came together, set fire to the praetorium, and those imprisoned escaped. The Hebrews in Antioch rose against the Christians and killed many of the Antiochenes, and the patriarch of the city himself, Anastasius, and burned his body in the market. Phocas sent men and killed some, maimed others and drove them out of the city. The patriarch, having presided over the church for three years and two months, died, and Sergius, deacon of the Great Church, was brought in in his place. Phocas married his daughter Domentia to Priscus the general, and after the wedding, holding a horse race, he saw statues of Priscus and his wife Domentia standing with his own statues, and in a frenzy ordered the demarchs to be beheaded. blocks: Heraclius, crowned by the patriarch Sergius, at once crowned his betrothed Eudocia too, and they received the royal crowns and the wedding crowns together, so that on the same day they were proclaimed both emperors and bridegrooms. The Persians overran the east, brought some of the lands under them and plundered others, and the Roman army attacking them was defeated and destroyed, a few being saved by flight. And the Avars and Scythians made Europe desolate. So the emperor Heraclius was at a loss what to do. For examining the army rolls he found them very short, almost all having been consumed in the wars. For of those who under Maurice had proclaimed Phocas, numbering many thousands, only two soldiers were found to be left. So he enlisted men, put forward Crispus as general of Cappadocia, and sent him there.

A daughter, Epiphania, was born to him by the Augusta Eudocia, whom he also named Fabia. Then a son too was born, the little Heraclius, also called the new Constantine, and he crowned both children with the royal diadem. A little later his wife the Augusta Eudocia left life. As her body was being carried out royally through the market, a barbarian girl leaning out happened to spit, and the spittle fell on the bier on which the Augusta was being carried, and the girl was seized and burned, offered to the dead woman as a very pitiable funeral gift. Heraclius married Martina, his niece, and proclaimed her Augusta.

Since Chosroes and the Persians were rushing on unchecked and plundering everything, the emperor sent envoys to him, asking him to have his fill at last of the destruction of men and make a treaty on terms of yearly tribute. He would not accept the embassy. So again another embassy went to him asking for peace. But the Persian made arrogant and blasphemous answers, saying he would never spare the Christians unless they denied the Crucified and worshipped the sun. Despairing of peace, the emperor planned to campaign against the Persians; so he was eager to make a treaty with the Chagan, who did not stop plundering Thrace. So he sent to him asking for peace; and the barbarian did not refuse. Pleased, the emperor went out of the city and camped outside the Long Wall with royal splendour and a guard and much money, which he was bringing the Chagan as gifts. But the barbarian, disregarding the oaths and the treaty, set out to seize the emperor. He did not succeed in this, for the emperor escaped in time, but having taken the royal baggage, the guard, the money and many thousands of captives with complete impunity, he went back. Again Heraclius sent an embassy to him, charging him with faithlessness and drawing him towards peace; and he made a treaty.

The emperor set out from the queen of cities and came to Caesarea, where Crispus was general; and since he was ill or pretended to be, the emperor went to him to visit him and take counsel about what was to be done. He received him slightingly, neither going to meet him nor rising from his bed, and in conversation behaving rather boastfully. Heraclius understood what was happening and was vexed at being despised, but pretended neither to be vexed nor to understand Crispus's slight towards him. At this moment it was reported to him that the Augusta had borne a son. He left the armies to Crispus and went back to Byzantium himself. When Nicetas, the son of the patrician Gregoras, came into the queen of cities, the emperor held him in great honour, calling him brother. Crispus too came back from the campaign. So when an assembly of the senate was held, and the patriarch was present as about to baptise the emperor's son, the emperor said to those present: "What does one who insults the emperor deserve?" They answered: "He does not deserve to live; for he has made himself unworthy of all kindness." The emperor then listed what concerned Crispus, while he was present; then turning to him he said: "You who did not make a son-in-law your friend will never make one of anyone." So he ordered him to become a cleric. By Martina, his niece, he had two sons, Fabius, whom he also named Heraclonas, and the other, David.

As Chosroes plundered and destroyed everything, and had brought Palestine under him, and Jerusalem by siege, a countless multitude of Christians is said to have been killed. For the Jews bought them cheaply and slaughtered them, and they say their number amounted to about ninety thousand. The Persians took the patriarch of the holy city of Jerusalem and the precious wood of the cross and brought them to Persia. The emperor, lacking an army equal to the enemy, and money besides, borrowed silver and gold from the Great Church and the other holy houses, and struck coin with it. He gathered people from the themes, trained them in experience of war, and called in allies. So he went out of the city after the feast of Easter, and attacking Sarbarus, Chosroes's chief satrap, who had been sent against the Romans with a heavy force, he routed him, cut down his armies and made them the work of the sword.
