blocks: Meanwhile the Chagan broke the treaty and came against Byzantium, and his forces encamped by the wall, ravaging everything outside. So those of the city, the patriarch and the patrician Bonus (for Heraclius, going abroad, had left both of them as guardians of his son Constantine and managers of public affairs), prepared a host of brave men and sent them out unexpectedly against the barbarians, who were careless as if no army were present, and destroyed many thousands of them. The survivors fled shamefully and went back to their own homes.

Heraclius again engaged another satrap sent against him by Chosroes with thirty thousand men, routed him too, and sent almost all those with him to Hades. The survivors went back, reported what had happened to their countrymen, and provoked them, who had already hated Chosroes, to hate him more. Heraclius invaded the interior of Persia too, pulled down the cities and destroyed the precincts of fire together with the very fire honoured by them. Learning that the envoys he had sent had been killed, he was angry, and did not hold back from killing, burning and overthrowing whatever lay before him.

Chosroes, as the emperor plundered Persia and he was in difficulties, fled to Ctesiphon. When Sarbarus, his chief satrap, was slandered to him as siding with the Romans and abusing him, he wrote to his second in command to put Sarbarus to death. The man carrying this letter was seized by the Romans on his way and taken to Byzantium; the managers of public affairs, learning what was written in it, sent it and its bearer to Sarbarus; and he, reading what was written, questioning the letter carrier and learning the mind of Chosroes, forged another letter ordering himself and many satraps and the chiefs of the army to be put to death. He also persuaded the man who had brought Chosroes's letter to say that he had received this letter from Chosroes. So gathering the leaders of the regiments, he had the letter read in the hearing of all. Filled with fury, the commanders of the regiments agreed together to go over to the emperor.

Besides this something else happened that destroyed Chosroes. Having many sons, he wished to push aside Siroes, the eldest of them all, and make another, called Merdasan, successor to the rule. Learning this, Siroes won over some of the satraps, attacked his father, bound him, and set before him much gold and heaps of precious stones, saying: "For these you made the Persians enemies of the Romans and forced them to fight and destroy one another; enjoy, then, what you desired." Then he killed his son Merdasan, to whom he was handing the rule of the Persians, before his eyes, and also his other children, and after all of them the father himself. Having become master of the rule of the Persians, he sent to Heraclius, bringing him the good news of Chosroes's destruction, and having made a treaty with him he set free all the Roman captives in Persia and gave him back the precious wood of the saving cross and Zacharias, the patriarch of Jerusalem. The emperor in turn let all the Persians held by the Romans go back to their own people. Heraclius, having accomplished these things in six years, and having restored the precious wood and the patriarch himself to Jerusalem, came back to the palace in the seventh, received with acclamations, applause and splendour by the senate and the multitude of the city.

blocks: When the emperor Heraclius was at Jerusalem, the catholicos of the Jacobites, whom they called patriarch, came to him. The emperor charged him with not accepting the council at Chalcedon nor confessing two natures united in Christ, saying that if he accepted the council and confessed two unconfused natures in Christ the Saviour, he would consider him of the same belief and appoint him patriarch of the church of Antioch. He, being clever and full of wickedness, so as not to miss the emperor's promise, pretended to accept the council and agreed to say there were two natures united in Christ. But he asked about the wills and the operations, whether they should be called two, or single and one. The emperor wrote about this question to Sergius of Constantinople. He, having long championed the heresy of the Monothelites, wrote back to the emperor that they must teach one natural will and one operation in Christ. And asking Cyrus of Phasis too, he found him of the same mind as Sergius. Led on by these, Heraclius himself came to this belief, and was given muddy overthrow to drink by those hirelings, not shepherds.

When the holy Sophronius, high priest in Jerusalem, gathered the high priests under him and showed in synod that those who speak of one will and operation in the two natures of Christ plainly proclaim one nature too, and had John, who governed the throne of elder Rome, voting with him in this, the emperor put out an edict that neither a single nor a double operation should be taught in Christ; which seemed ridiculous not only to the orthodox but also to those of one mind with Severus. When Sergius, who held the throne of Constantinople, ended his life, Pyrrhus succeeded him, holding the same views as he, and revering and confirming the views of Severus and Cyrus.

As this emperor was returning from Persia in triumph, Mahomet, the phylarch of the Saracens, came to him; he had not got the rule of the tribe by birth, for he was of the obscure, but had acquired it by wickedness. For being poor he served a rich widow, whom he married, leading her into love of him by sorceries. He was gripped by the disease of epilepsy, and when the affliction attacked him from time to time he fell down and went out of his mind, and became a cause of dismay and shame to his mistress and wife. He, being wicked himself and having met a monk more wicked than he, who had been exiled from Byzantium for false belief, was taught by him, and told his wife that the archangel Gabriel came to him from heaven and initiated him into divine and secret things, but that he could not bear the sight of him and for this reason grew dizzy, was gripped by fear and fell to the ground. He had that crafty monk too bearing witness for him and telling the woman that truly this Gabriel is sent to all the prophets. From this the woman, casting off the reproach and rather boasting that she lived with a prophet, spread this story to the other women, and so that foul man acquired the name of prophet among his countrymen. When that woman died he became heir to her property, and was proclaimed phylarch, teacher and lawgiver of the nation of the Ishmaelites, deceiving some, and raising the sword against those who did not readily obey him and forcing them to submit to him. For he had already gathered a sizeable band about him. So he came out of Aethribus and went to the emperor, asking for land to live in, and received it. Having outwitted the whole nation in the way that has been told and brought it under him, he overran and plundered Syria and sacked many of the Roman lands, and from then the race of the Ishmaelites has not stopped overrunning and plundering all the land of the Romans.

Heraclius, having rolled into the heresy of the Monothelites, as has been said, fell into a dropsical illness. It is said that his private part turned and sent the urine upwards, and unless a board was put on his belly, what came out went up onto his face; which seemed to happen because of his lawless union with his niece. So this emperor died in the thirty-first year of his reign.

He, being wicked himself and having met a monk more wicked than he, who had been exiled from Byzantium for false belief, was taught by him, and told his wife that the archangel Gabriel came to him from heaven and initiated him into divine and secret things, but that he could not bear the sight of him and for this reason grew dizzy, was gripped by fear and fell to the ground. He had that crafty monk too bearing witness for him and telling the woman that truly this Gabriel is sent to all the prophets. From this the woman, casting off the reproach and rather boasting that she lived with a prophet, spread this story to the other women, and so that foul man acquired the name of prophet among his countrymen. When that woman died he became heir to her property, and was proclaimed phylarch, teacher and lawgiver of the nation of the Ishmaelites, deceiving some, and raising the sword against those who did not readily obey him and forcing them to submit to him. For he had already gathered a sizeable band about him. So he came out of Aethribus and went to the emperor, asking for land to live in, and received it. Having outwitted the whole nation in the way that has been told and brought it under him, he overran and plundered Syria and sacked many of the Roman lands, and from then the race of the Ishmaelites has not stopped overrunning and plundering all the land of the Romans. Heraclius, having rolled into the heresy of the Monothelites, as has been said, fell into a dropsical illness. It is said that his private part turned and sent the urine upwards, and unless a board was put on his belly, what came out went up onto his face; which seemed to happen because of his lawless union with his niece. So this emperor died in the thirty-first year of his reign.

blocks: The sole rule passed to his son Constantine, who enjoyed it a short time. For having ruled alone one year he perished by poison mixed for him by Martina, who was at once his stepmother and his cousin; his wife was Gregoria, the daughter of the patrician Nicetas, by whom a son, Constans, was born to him. Constantine was right in faith, having received the empire from his father, but not his false belief. So Pyrrhus, the president of Constantinople, is said to have shared in the plot against him too. When he had ended his life in this way, Martina with her son Heraclonas held on to the empire, but they too quickly fell from the rule. For Martina was hated by the senate for the murder of Constantine, and was dragged from the palace when the senate rose against her; her tongue was cut out, and Heraclonas's nose, though he was still ten years old, and exile was voted for both. And Pyrrhus was thrown out of the church and condemned to exile.

blocks: Constans, the grandson of Heraclius and son of Constantine, was set on the imperial throne by the senate, and Paul was set on the high priestly throne instead. He too was of one mind with those before him, that is Sergius and Pyrrhus. The emperor Constans was not a useless emperor in other respects, but in religion he was like his grandfather. For he too held the heresy of the Monothelites. So he punished most cruelly both that most wise man, the most divine Maximus, and his disciples, and condemned Martin, the most holy pope of Rome, to exile, in which he died. Martin, with the celebrated father Maximus, who had come to Rome, gathered a council of high priests and put those who held the views of the Monothelites under anathema; and Constans punished many others of the orthodox who would not bow to his monothelete will.

When the Saracens had already become very powerful and had taken for themselves many lands and islands tributary to the Romans, their leader Mauias built very many warships and planned to attack the empire of the Romans. Learning this, Constans too prepared a fleet and put in at the dockyard of Lycia called Phoenix; and when the Hagarenes too arrived there, a sea battle was to take place the next day. That night the emperor saw a dream that he was in Thessalonica. When he shared it with one of the learned, he heard that the dream was a sign of defeat, meaning "give the victory to another"; which also happened. For when the sea battle took place the enemy prevailed, and there was such a slaughter of Romans that the sea was dyed purple with blood. The emperor put on mean clothing, got into a boat that happened to be there with a few men and escaped, and got safely to Byzantium. The Hagarenes, with no one opposing them any longer, went against everything together. Then they also brought the island of Rhodes under them and pulled down the famous Colossus in it, the bronze of which a Jewish merchant is said to have bought and carried away on nine hundred camels.

But for a time the attack of the Hagarenes against the Romans was somewhat checked; for they fell to quarrelling with one another about a leader. For some chose Mauias, others Alem, who had become the son-in-law of Muchumet. Then they also made a treaty with the Romans for two years, agreeing to pay tribute. While Constans ruled alone there was a shaking of the earth and many lands of the Roman empire suffered badly, and at another time a violent wind blew and threw down many buildings. When the patriarch Paul had presided over the church unholily for twelve years and then died, Pyrrhus was brought back to the pastorate of the people of Constantinople, in the twelfth year of Constans's reign. For this Pyrrhus, driven out of the church as has been said, came to Rome, and when he was shown by Saint Maximus to hold wrong beliefs, he pretended to change from the belief of the Monothelites. Asked by the pope of that time for a statement of faith, he gave it and was received. Then he withdrew from Rome and went to Ravenna, and it became known that he had not left the heresy. So the pope, learning this, gathered the bishops under him and voted his complete deposition. So, having held the throne of Constantine's city for four months the second time, he died, and Peter was appointed patriarch, he too of the same belief as those before him, and having ruled the church for twelve years he died. After him Thomas presided over the orthodox, holding to the right belief, who departed life after two years and seven months and had John as successor.

This emperor Constans killed his own brother Theodosius, and was hated by those of the city for this and for what had been done to Pope Martin and the great Maximus. So he left Byzantium and put in at Sicily, staying about Syracuse, wishing to move the empire to elder Rome. For he said one should honour mothers rather than daughters. So he summoned the empress and his sons to him; there were three, Constantine, Heraclius and Tiberius. But some of those close to him prevented this. Others say that the multitude of the city did not allow them to go to him. Constans, having spent six years in Sicily, did not come back from there; for he was plotted against by those about him, and while bathing was struck mortally on the head with the bucket from which the hot water was being poured over him, and died, having ruled the Romans twenty-seven years.

blocks: When he died, the army with him at once chose as emperor an Armenian named Mizizius, a statue of a man and most handsome. Hearing this, the elder of the sons of Constans, called Pogonatus, who had already been adorned with the diadem of the empire, crowned by his father, reached Sicily with a great fleet, subdued Mizizius and put him to death, and those who had murdered his father, and among others the patrician Justinian, the father of Germanus the patriarch, and made Germanus himself a eunuch, though he was already past youth and beyond the age at which castration is thought proper. This emperor was smooth-chinned when he went abroad to avenge his father's murder, but came back with his beard grown long; so from then he was called Pogonatus by the citizens.

Those of the theme of the Anatolics came to Chrysopolis and cried out that Constantine's other two brothers too must be crowned, saying: "As we believe in the Trinity, so we must be ruled by three." Constantine sent to them promising to fulfil their request, and summoned the leaders of the people, so that the proclamation of his brothers might take place before them. When they came to Byzantium he put them to death as seditious; learning this, the others went back home full of fear. And he cut off the noses of both his brothers.

The descendants of Hagar did not stop ravaging and plundering all the empire, both on foot and by sea. Then with a heavy fleet they came against the queen of cities itself, and made an anchorage for their fleet from the western headland at the Hebdomon as far as the Kyklobion. The emperor Constantine, arming a fleet in turn, drew up against them every day, and sea battles took place from spring to autumn. When the barbarians achieved nothing, they sailed off and took Cyzicus, and having taken it spent the winter in it. At the start of spring they again came to Constantine's city, and again there were many sea battles. As the time wore on and autumn came, the sons of Hagar again anchored their fleet at Cyzicus; and they did so for seven years. So, despairing, and above all having lost a great number and suffered the loss of most of their ships (for at that time the liquid fire was devised, when one Callinicus, an architect, came from Syria and made it), they turned back with shame and great grief. When what was left of the barbarian fleet was off Syllaeum, a fierce storm of winds fell on it, sinking some ships and smashing others against the shore. When the general of the Cibyrrhaeots attacked it too, all of it perished. On land again another army of the Arabs attacked a Roman army and was defeated, so that not fewer than thirty thousand, it is said, fell.

From this the Saracens, knowing that none of their hopes could be achieved, and even more afraid that the Romans would attack them, wished to make a treaty, and Mauias sent envoys to the emperor asking for peace. The emperor agreed to it, and sent the patrician John, called Pitzigaudes, as a sensible man with a nimble tongue for speaking, to complete the terms of the treaty. He went off to the Arabs, was received most hospitably, arranged the terms of peace, and confirmed it in writing for thirty years, the Arabs agreeing to give the empire of the Romans a yearly tribute of three thousand pieces of gold, eight slaves and as many of their finest horses. So the sons of Hagar obtained peace in this way. The enemies of the Romans in the west, learning this, also made efforts to end their wars, sent envoys with gifts to the emperor, and peace was ratified with them.

blocks: And there was a lull of wars both in the eastern region and in the western. When the patriarch John died, Constantine was appointed, and died after two years, and Theodore was raised to this high priestly throne. He was thrown out after two years and had George as successor. Constantine, being orthodox, was eager to unite the churches, which had been split by the heresy of the Monothelites since the time of the reign of his great-grandfather Heraclius. So he ordered an ecumenical council to be gathered in Constantinople, which was led by the representatives of Agatho, pope of Rome, George of Constantinople and Theophanes of Antioch. For there was no patriarch of Alexandria or of Jerusalem, since these cities were under the Saracens. This council, the sixth, ratified that two wills and two operations are to be spoken of and believed in Christ the Saviour, the emperor too being present, and those who held one will and operation were anathematised: Theodore, bishop of Pharan, Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, Paul and Peter of Constantinople, Macarius of Antioch and Stephen his disciple, and the old man long in wickedness and childish in mind.

The nation of the Bulgars, having come into the Roman lands beyond the Ister, did them unchecked harm. So the emperor Constantine marched out against them by land and by sea, bringing a large fleet from the sea into the Danube. The barbarians, seeing the Romans' preparation, lost heart, and shutting themselves in a stronghold ringed with rivers and marshes, kept quiet; but the Roman army did not attack them either. When the two sides had been placed like this for some days, the barbarians condemned the Romans for softness. Something else happened too that gave them a courage opposite to their earlier cowardice. For the emperor, sick with gout and struck by sharper pains, sailed off with five dromons and his household to Mesembria (this is a place belonging to the Romans) to use the baths, leaving the army and the generals there and charging them to skirmish with the barbarians, so as to draw them into battle in this way. When a rumour went round the camp that the emperor was running away out of fear of the enemy, all fled shamefully with no one pursuing. This, happening unexpectedly for the Bulgars, breathed spirit into them and whetted them for valour, and pursuing from behind they killed many and took no fewer alive, and having crossed the Ister they pitched their tents in Roman territory, and from then did not stop plundering all the land under the Romans. So the ruler was forced to make a treaty with them on terms of paying them a yearly tribute, to the shame of the empire of the Romans. And so the affairs of the Romans were at peace on every side until the death of this emperor. He died leaving his son Justinian as successor, having reigned seventeen years.

blocks: Justinian, when he came to the rule, was a youth of sixteen years. So, using his own judgement in managing the empire, he surrounded the empire of the Romans with many evils. For the Mardaites, having seized the heights of Lebanon while Pogonatus was in power, were fearsome to the Arabs; so they asked the Romans for a treaty, and obtained it, as has been said. When this emperor had just taken the sceptre, Abimelech, then leading the Arabs (for Mauias had already died), sent asking for the peace to be confirmed, asking that the Mardaites move out of Lebanon, and promising that if this were done he would give the Romans a daily tribute of a thousand gold coins, a slave and a horse of their choicest. When the treaty had been renewed on these terms, and the Mardaites, numbering twelve thousand fighting men, had moved out of Lebanon, the nation of the Arabs, freed from fear of them, filled the empire of the Romans with many misfortunes.

Justinian sent the general Leontius and through him subjected Iberia, Albania and other lands. This emperor also broke the treaty with the Bulgars, not bearing to pay them tribute. Marching out into the western parts he brought many of the Slav peoples under him, some willingly, some by the law of war; and from them he formed a new corps. For picking from them brave and young men, to the number of thirty thousand, he called them the special people. Delighting in them and trusting in them, he also broke the agreements with the Arabs, taking as his reason that the coin sent for the yearly tribute bore not the Roman stamp but a new Arabic one. For it was not allowed for any other stamp to be struck on a gold coin than that of the emperor of the Romans. So he marched against them, trusting not so much in the Roman units as in this new special people. When the Arabs asked him not to set aside the treaty nor break the written agreements, calling to witness God, who had been taken as mediator and had confirmed them, and calling on him as avenger against those responsible for the battle, the emperor stopped his ears to this and prepared for battle. So the Arabs fastened the written treaty to a spear, and raising it like a standard to go before their army, they clashed with the Romans; and at once twenty thousand of the special people deserted to the Arabs, which caused fear among the Romans and put courage into the enemy, and the Romans were defeated, while victory smiled on the Arabs; who, following the fugitives, killed those they caught, so that almost more than could be counted of the Roman armies fell. The emperor, having shamefully escaped destruction with a few, when he was at Leucate ordered all those left of the special people of the Slavs to be put to death.

Coming to Byzantium, he busied himself with buildings. For he built the very large Triclinium in the eastern part of the palace, which is called by his name, being called the Justinianeios to this day. The sons of Hagar from then on came into the Roman lands without fear, and the patrician Sabbatius, who was over Armenia, learning of the emperor's defeat, went over to the Arabs and handed Armenia over to them. And they did not stop ravaging the whole east and taking Christians captive.

This emperor had a eunuch, Stephen, who drew his descent from barbarians, but was harsh beyond barbarians and very cruel indeed. He had very great power with him and was appointed sacellarius, and was oppressive to all, not only in exactions but also in punishments, and he punished not only ordinary people but also laid hands on those very high, so that he even once beat the reigning emperor's mother. The emperor also appointed one Theodosius, a monk who had formerly been a recluse, logothete of the general treasury, and he was no less than the eunuch Stephen in wickedness. So, since many terrible things were brought on the state by them, Justinian seemed hateful to all.

He had imprisoned the general Leontius for two years on suspicion of aiming at the empire, and later released him and made him general of Hellas. Leontius said to one Paul, a monk who practised astrology and had foretold the empire to him: "I am now going away to Hellas; and I know that the emperor will send men after me to kill me. What you foretold me is gone." He said: "Do not lose heart, but set about the deed, and you will not miss what you desire." So Leontius took those he trusted, broke open the public prisons, and brought out those imprisoned, who amounted to a great number; they went into the great church of God, many others streaming in with them, insulted Justinian and acclaimed Leontius, the patriarch Callinicus helping. From there they went over to the hippodrome and did the same, and taking Justinian out of the palace they cut off his nose at the Sphendone, and exiled him to Cherson, after he had held the empire for sixteen years. They seized the eunuch Stephen, that is the sacellarius, and the monk Theodosius, the logothete, tied ropes to their feet, dragged them through the Market, took them to the Bous and burned them.

He had very great power with him and was appointed sacellarius, and was oppressive to all, not only in exactions but also in punishments, and he punished not only ordinary people but also laid hands on those very high, so that he even once beat the reigning emperor's mother. The emperor also appointed one Theodosius, a monk who had formerly been a recluse, logothete of the general treasury, and he was no less than the eunuch Stephen in wickedness. So, since many terrible things were brought on the state by them, Justinian seemed hateful to all. He had imprisoned the general Leontius for two years on suspicion of aiming at the empire, and later released him and made him general of Hellas. Leontius said to one Paul, a monk who practised astrology and had foretold the empire to him: "I am now going away to Hellas; and I know that the emperor will send men after me to kill me. What you foretold me is gone." He said: "Do not lose heart, but set about the deed, and you will not miss what you desire." So Leontius took those he trusted, broke open the public prisons, and brought out those imprisoned, who amounted to a great number; they went into the great church of God, many others streaming in with them, insulted Justinian and acclaimed Leontius, the patriarch Callinicus helping. From there they went over to the hippodrome and did the same, and taking Justinian out of the palace they cut off his nose at the Sphendone, and exiled him to Cherson, after he had held the empire for sixteen years. They seized the eunuch Stephen, that is the sacellarius, and the monk Theodosius, the logothete, tied ropes to their feet, dragged them through the Market, took them to the Bous and burned them.

blocks: After this Leontius held the empire, in whose time the Arabs, overrunning the Roman lands, took many captives, and then brought Africa too under them. Learning this, the emperor Leontius sent one of the patricians, John, an energetic man, with the whole fleet to recover Africa for the empire of the Romans; and he routed the Arabs there in war, freed Africa from them, and wintered there, writing to the emperor what had been done and waiting to be told what to do. The protosymboulos of the Hagarenes (for so they called their leaders), learning what had happened in Africa, and taking its loss hard, prepared a very heavy fleet and sent it to recover Africa again. The patrician John, not being strong enough to fight it at sea, left the harbour and went back to the emperor to ask for a greater force. When the Roman fleet was off Crete, the leaders of the people, partly ashamed at having withdrawn from Africa and given it up to the enemy, partly afraid of the emperor's anger, persuaded the fleet to turn to revolt, revile Leontius, and acclaim as emperor Apsimarus, who was drungarius of the Cibyrrhaeots, and whom they at once renamed Tiberius. So he reached Byzantium with the fleet and anchored the vessels at Sycae. Leontius took care to guard the city. But some officials of the prefecture, allotted to guard the wall at Blachernae, let Apsimarus in from there, and that though they had been entrusted with the keys of the gates of that wall under dreadful oaths. Having come in this way, the men of the fleet plundered the houses of the citizens. Apsimarus deprived Leontius of his nose and put him under guard, after he had reigned three years, and beat those of the officials who had sided with him, stripped them of their property and exiled them.

blocks: So Apsimarus, or Tiberius, held the empire in this way, and at once appointing his own brother Heraclius sole general of all the cavalry and infantry armies, sent him to the east to face the Hagarenes. The Romans overran Syria and came as far as Samosata, plundering everything round about, killed very many of the Hagarenes, and taking very many captives and other untold plunder, put great fear into the Arabs. Baanes, surnamed Seven Devils, betrayed Fourth Armenia to the Arabs. Then the leaders of Armenia rose against the Hagarenes and killed them, sent to Apsimarus and received the Romans into the country again. But Moamed came against them, brought Armenia under the Hagarenes again, and burned the chief men of the Armenians alive. At that time too the Hagarenes marched against Cilicia. Engaging them, Heraclius, the emperor's brother, made most of them the work of the sword, and taking the rest alive sent them in chains to the ruler. Philippicus, the son of the patrician Nicephorus, who aspired to the throne because he had dreamed that his head was shaded by an eagle, he exiled to Cephallenia.

Justinian, exiled in Cherson as has been said, managed to escape from there and go to the Chagan, the leader of the Khazars, and being received by him most hospitably, married his sister Theodora, and a little later went from there to another country and stayed there with his wife; and Apsimarus sent to the Chagan promising to give him much money if he sent him Justinian's head. He agreed, and sending two of those close to him, ordered them in secret to kill Justinian; which Theodora learned through a slave and reported to her husband. He called each of those ordered to kill him aside, deprived him of life by strangling, sent Theodora to Khazaria, and himself boarded a fishing boat and sailed off, going to Tervel, the ruler of the Bulgars. When a great storm caught him as he sailed, the little boat was in danger of sinking. When those sailing with him advised him to promise God that if he were saved and recovered the rule he would do no harm to those who had acted against him, he said: "If I spare any of them, may I be drowned here at once." So he was saved, went to the ruler of the Bulgars, gave him very much and promised to give more if he were brought back by him to his ancestral empire, and promised to marry his daughter to him; and with him and a heavy barbarian force he reached the queen of cities, and encamping before the walls he tried the citizens, talking to them as they leaned out from the wall. They not only did not admit him, but even poured offensive insults on him. So at night he slipped in through the aqueduct, came up inside the city, and became master of it. Apsimarus fled to Apollonias and was caught.

blocks: He gave the ruler of the Bulgars many gifts, made terms of peace with him, and arranged for him to go away. When Apsimarus and his brother Heraclius were brought to him, and Leontius too, he hung Heraclius with many others on gibbets by the walls; Apsimarus and Leontius he led in chains round the Market and made a show of them while a horse race was held, and when they had been thrown under his feet he trod on their necks, and then ordered their heads to be cut off in the Kynegion, Apsimarus having reigned seven years. The patriarch Callinicus he first blinded and then exiled to Rome. He put forward as patriarch one Cyrus, a recluse monk, who had foretold his restoration to the empire. This emperor then destroyed a great number of both the common people and the soldiery, some openly and some secretly. Sending to Khazaria, he brought his wife, who had already borne him a son, whom he named Tiberius, and thinking both her and the child worthy of the imperial title, he crowned both.

Breaking the treaty with the Bulgars, he marched out against them with cavalry and infantry forces and with a large fleet, and went off to Anchialus. At first the Bulgars in fear ran up into the mountains, but from there, seeing the Roman army camping in disorder and scattering carelessly to gather fodder, they took courage, came at them, killed many, took no fewer captive and seized many horses. The emperor with the survivors shut themselves up in the fort there. Then, hamstringing all the horses so that the enemy might not take them, they boarded the ships of the fleet and went back to Byzantium in great shame.

Angry with those in Cherson, because when he was exiled there they learned that he was planning a revolt and wished to kill him, he sent triremes and dromons and other cargo ships with a very large army and two generals, ordering them to spare none of those there but to cut them all down with swords. Without any trouble (for the inhabitants of the cities in Cherson did not resist) they took them and killed almost all of them, sparing only the young, up to boys. Justinian, learning this, was enraged because they had not killed these too, and ordered them to be sent to him. As they were being sent, most of them happened to be drowned in the sea, and this seemed pleasing to the emperor. Not even so was he sated in his madness against them, but threatened to send again and so to make the country desolate as to pull down the cities and plough them. For this reason those still left in Cherson and their neighbours revolted, and proclaimed emperor Philippicus, the son of Bardanes, whom the narrative has recorded was exiled by Apsimarus to Cephallenia, who had just been recalled from exile and was returning to Constantinople, and had come there; Elias, their governor, helping. Learning this, Justinian slaughtered Elias's children in their mother's lap, and married her to her own slave, an Indian cook. Then, preparing a fleet, he sent it against Cherson, ordering the commander of the fleet to kill all of every age. When the fleet had already reached Cherson and was besieging it, Khazars came to help the people of Cherson. From this the siege was broken off, and the men of the fleet, not daring to go back to the emperor, poured abuse on him and acclaimed Bardanes as emperor.

When a long time had passed and nothing had been reported to him from the fleet, the emperor, suspecting that something had happened against him, set out from Byzantium, and coming as far as Sinope saw the fleet sailing straight for the city; at once he too turned back. Philippicus, having a good voyage, took the great city first, and Justinian camped at Damatrys. Elias, mentioned above, was sent against him and managed to persuade the army with Justinian to leave him and go over to Philippicus. So, deserted by the soldiers, Justinian was taken, and at once Elias cut off his head with his own hands. His son Tiberius, with his maternal grandmother Anastasia (for his mother Theodora had already died), fled to the church at Blachernae, went into the divine sanctuary, and getting under the all-holy table, holding one of the little columns that support it, begged not to die. But those sent to search for him dragged the boy out of the sanctuary and cut his throat with a knife like a beast's, cruelly.

blocks: Having obtained the empire, Philippicus armed himself against the sixth ecumenical council, and the fool gathered a council and through it annulled, as far as lay with him, that holy council. For it is said that when Leontius had just taken the sceptre, a monk who was a recluse in the monastery of Callistratus foretold to this Philippicus his rise to the imperial throne, and asked as payment for the prophecy the setting aside of the sixth council (for that monk was of the heresy of the Monothelites), and Philippicus promised it. So he annulled the sixth ecumenical council, as it seemed. Finding in the palace heaps of money stored up by earlier emperors, he used them for nothing needful and scattered most of them in a short time; and he might have spent it all, had he stayed longer in the empire. For in speaking he seemed most eloquent and not without understanding, but in action he was the most foolish of all and altogether unskilful. Driving the patriarch Cyrus out of the church, after he had spent six years in it, he appointed John, of the same belief as himself.

The Bulgars, having plundered all Thrace, overran everything up to the city, and went home taking much plunder and captives almost beyond counting. And the sons of Hagar did the same in the east. When two years and some months had passed since he took the empire, having held a horse race and bathed after the race in the bath of Zeuxippus, he made some of the senate his fellow diners, or, as some say, those who had won in the horse race. As he lay at the banquet he was seized by some of the senate and blinded. This was done on the Saturday of Pentecost. The next day, that is on Pentecost itself, the members of the senate and the common crowd gathered and appointed Artemius, the protoasecretis, emperor, renaming him Anastasius.

blocks: This emperor was conversant with all kinds of learning and most practised in the management of affairs. He dragged the patriarch John from the high priestly throne as not orthodox, after he had held the church three years, and moved Germanus from Cyzicus to the holy see of the queen of cities, whom the narrative has recorded somewhere above was deprived of his generative parts by Constantine Pogonatus. Learning that ships from Alexandria had put in at Phoenicia to bring shipbuilding timber from there, he prepared a fleet and sent it against them, ordering the fleets of the themes too to put in at the island of Rhodes, join there, and so sail out against the enemy, appointing as commander of the whole fleet John, deacon of the great church of God and general logothete. When all had gathered at Rhodes the deacon John was ready to sail out, but the men of the fleet, and above all those of the theme of the Opsikion, were not obedient, for they were not well disposed to the ruler, since he had not treated the naval forces well either. When the deacon behaved too commandingly towards their disobedience and treated them more harshly, he provoked them to revolt, and reviling the emperor they killed him at once. Giving up going further, some went off home and others set out for Byzantium; and at Adramyttium they took one Theodosius, a collector of public taxes, a private man, against his will, and proclaimed him emperor.

Learning this, Artemius prepared a fleet and set a guard on the city, and himself stayed at Nicaea, the metropolis of the Bithynians. The rebels came by land and sea to Chrysopolis, and for a while there were sea battles; then Theodosius crossed to Thrace and entered the great city through the wall of Blachernae by treachery, and when the fleet and army with him streamed into it, much of the property in the houses was plundered. Seizing those of the officials who held out for Artemius and taking the patriarch Germanus, they went off to Nicaea, showing Artemius that the city and the palace had already been taken. He put on the monastic habit, and receiving pledges that he would suffer nothing further, gave himself up to them, and was confined in Thessalonica, having reigned one year and three months.

Theodosius was of good character and dignified life, but an unbusinesslike man and very unfit for the management of affairs, and especially of an empire. Leo, also called Conon, who had been appointed general of the Anatolics by Artemius, pretending to be of Artemius's party, did not yield to Theodosius, having as his partner Artabasdus the Armenian, general of the Armeniacs. So setting out from there with the units under him, he came to Nicomedia, where, finding the son of the emperor Theodosius and seizing him with the imperial baggage, he came to Chrysopolis. Theodosius gave up the empire to him without trouble, being tonsured a cleric with his son, and receiving an assurance that he would suffer nothing else, he lived quietly the rest of his life, having reigned two years.

blocks: Leo was unworthily thought worthy of the imperial name. His country was Isauria, but he had been moved from there with his parents by the emperor Justinian, before he was driven from the rule, and lived in Mesembria in Thrace. When Justinian had been deposed from the rule and then was coming back with the Bulgars to take up the empire again, Leo met him and offered him gifts. Justinian at once honoured him as spatharius, and when he reigned the second time made him one of his close men. Then he was sent by him to the Alans, to stir them against the Abasgians, who had revolted from the rule of the Romans.

For the Abasgians, as Procopius of Caesarea records, were subject to two men of their own race, one ruling the eastern part of them and the other the part turned to the west. Both these rulers treated the nation badly out of love of money; for whatever boys they found handsome and fair of face and well made in the rest of their body, they dragged by force from their parents and deprived of their generative parts with iron, and sold them to the Romans for much money, who were always mad about eunuchs, and at once killed their fathers, so that they might never, resenting it because of their children, plot a rising against them. Among them it was the greatest misfortune to beget a son good to look at, since they exchanged their children's beauty for death. So the rulers of the Abasgians treated them. But Justinian the First, sending one of the eunuchs in the palace who was of their race (for many such moved about the courts of the Romans), forbade the leaders of the Abasgians to castrate anyone by force any longer; for the practice would end in nothing for them, since none of the Romans would wish to buy their eunuchs. This was most gladly received by the Abasgians, and trusting in the order of the emperor of the Romans they would no longer submit to their rulers in this business, and the rulers became more sluggish in the practice. Then they also deposed both their rulers and wished to live under their own laws. Up to then they had not been initiated into the faith of the Christians, but worshipped groves and woods, and in barbarian simplicity took the trees for gods. Justinian made it his aim to bring them over to piety, and sending holy men to them, through them brought them to knowledge of God. Then he also built a holy church of the Mother of God among the Abasgians and set up priests, and so brought them over to the ways of Christians from the wholly barbarian. From then, the Abasgians being ruled by no one, the emperors of the Romans sent governors, and their affairs were managed by them. When those sent turned to injustices and treated them too tyrannically, they, afraid of being wholly enslaved to the Romans, revolted and would no longer receive a Roman governor.

For this reason Justinian of the slit nose, wishing to punish them, sent the spatharius Leo to the Alans, whom Procopius writes as Albanians, who were neighbours of the Abasgians in very many places, wishing to arm them. Leo went there and spent many years, and came back late and with difficulty, finding neither Justinian, for he had been killed, nor Philippicus, for he had been deposed, having been blinded as has been said; so he went to Artemius, who was then reigning. He received him kindly and appointed him general of the theme of the Anatolics. Pretending, as has been said, to defend him, he raised his hand against Theodosius and became master of the sceptre (O unfathomable abyss of the judgements of God!), and at once married his daughter to Artabasdus, honouring him as curopalates.

Masalmas, the leader of the Arabs, crossed from Abydos into Thrace with a great army and plundered much of the Thracian country, and attacking the queen of cities pitched his camp by its land walls, and he himself besieged it from there, while the chief satrap Solimas besieged it from the sea with a great fleet. But the Romans routed their ships, both warships and cargo ships, with the liquid fire, so that many of the admirals, whose ships this liquid fire had not yet reached, despaired and went over to the emperor. So most of the Arabs' fleet perished in this way. Roman infantry armies, meeting those of them plundering in Bithynia, destroyed many, so that those too fled in fear. A strong famine pressed the Arabs in Thrace, so that they kept from none of the animals that died. It is said that they even touched human flesh. A pestilential disease also fell on them and destroyed vast numbers. And the Bulgars, coming against them, made many thousands of them, as some record, a by-product of the sword.
text: Leo was unworthily thought worthy of the imperial name. His country was Isauria, but he had been moved from there with his parents by the emperor Justinian, before he was driven from the rule, and lived in Mesembria in Thrace. When Justinian had been deposed from the rule and then was coming back with the Bulgars to take up the empire again, Leo met him and offered him gifts. Justinian at once honoured him as spatharius, and when he reigned the second time made him one of his close men. Then he was sent by him to the Alans, to stir them against the Abasgians, who had revolted from the rule of the Romans. For the Abasgians, as Procopius of Caesarea records, were subject to two men of their own race, one ruling the eastern part of them and the other the part turned to the west. Both these rulers treated the nation badly out of love of money; for whatever boys they found handsome and fair of face and well made in the rest of their body, they dragged by force from their parents and deprived of their generative parts with iron, and sold them to the Romans for much money, who were always mad about eunuchs, and at once killed their fathers, so that they might never, resenting it because of their children, plot a rising against them. Among them it was the greatest misfortune to beget a son good to look at, since they exchanged their children's beauty for death. So the rulers of the Abasgians treated them. But Justinian the First, sending one of the eunuchs in the palace who was of their race (for many such moved about the courts of the Romans), forbade the leaders of the Abasgians to castrate anyone by force any longer; for the practice would end in nothing for them, since none of the Romans would wish to buy their eunuchs. This was most gladly received by the Abasgians, and trusting in the order of the emperor of the Romans they would no longer submit to their rulers in this business, and the rulers became more sluggish in the practice. Then they also deposed both their rulers and wished to live under their own laws. Up to then they had not been initiated into the faith of the Christians, but worshipped groves and woods, and in barbarian simplicity took the trees for gods. Justinian made it his aim to bring them over to piety, and sending holy men to them, through them brought them to knowledge of God. Then he also built a holy church of the Mother of God among the Abasgians and set up priests, and so brought them over to the ways of Christians from the wholly barbarian. From then, the Abasgians being ruled by no one, the emperors of the Romans sent governors, and their affairs were managed by them. When those sent turned to injustices and treated them too tyrannically, they, afraid of being wholly enslaved to the Romans, revolted and would no longer receive a Roman governor. For this reason Justinian of the slit nose, wishing to punish them, sent the spatharius Leo to the Alans, whom Procopius writes as Albanians, who were neighbours of the Abasgians in very many places, wishing to arm them. Leo went there and spent many years, and came back late and with difficulty, finding neither Justinian, for he had been killed, nor Philippicus, for he had been deposed, having been blinded as has been said; so he went to Artemius, who was then reigning. He received him kindly and appointed him general of the theme of the Anatolics. Pretending, as has been said, to defend him, he raised his hand against Theodosius and became master of the sceptre (O unfathomable abyss of the judgements of God!), and at once married his daughter to Artabasdus, honouring him as curopalates. Masalmas, the leader of the Arabs, crossed from Abydos into Thrace with a great army and plundered much of the Thracian country, and attacking the queen of cities pitched his camp by its land walls, and he himself besieged it from there, while the chief satrap Solimas besieged it from the sea with a great fleet. But the Romans routed their ships, both warships and cargo ships, with the liquid fire, so that many of the admirals, whose ships this liquid fire had not yet reached, despaired and went over to the emperor. blocks: Sergius, the general of Sicily, learning of the Arabs' attack on the city and that the affairs of the Romans were in disorder, himself attempted a usurpation; and he did not think himself worthy of the imperial title, but had one Gregory, one of his servants, proclaimed emperor by the people, renaming the man Tiberius; and with Sergius's approval he advanced some to offices. When this was reported to Leo it roused him to oppose the usurper; and he honoured as patrician Paul, who was in charge of the imperial grooms (the Roman tongue knows to call him chartularius), named him general of Sicily, and sent him against the rebel, giving him orders to the governors of the lands commanding them to help Paul, and having also written a letter to the army in Sicily showing that the affairs of the Romans were going well, since the Arabs had now been defeated and routed, he sent this too to the soldiers by Paul. When Sergius learned that Paul had reached Sicily unexpectedly and entered Syracuse, he at once ran away and went to Lombardy. When Paul spoke to the soldiery and read the imperial letter in their hearing, they at once acclaimed the emperor and handed over Gregory and those about him to Paul in chains. He put Gregory to death, and flogged his shield-bearers, cut off their hair and condemned them to exile. Sergius, receiving an assurance that he would suffer no harm, came to Paul from Calabria. And affairs in Sicily quieted down in this way.

The Arabs besieging the city, having suffered more than they had done, set out to go back home, boarded the ships that were left and went away. But falling into a violent storm they all perished with their triremes, only ten ships being left, of which five were taken by the Romans, and the rest escaped the disaster and went off as messengers.

A whelp crueller than his father was born to Leo, and Leo crowned the mother, called Maria, and baptised the son in the Great Church, naming him Constantine. At this time he is said to have voided dung as he was dipped in the divine font, and from this to have been surnamed Copronymus; and the most holy patriarch Germanus is said to have said that this was a sign that this child would be a great evil to the church and to those who had chosen to be pious.

The magister Nicetas Xylinites, one of the very high men, suggested to Artemius, who was in Thessalonica, to go to the Bulgars and with their help recover the empire again. He was persuaded, and came to Byzantium with a host of Bulgars, thinking he would be received by the people. But when those of the city paid him no attention, the Bulgars betrayed him to Leo for much money. They went away; and he was put to death with Xylinites, and Xylinites's property, which was great, was all confiscated. Others of Artemius's fellow conspirators were also killed, and among them the high priest of Thessalonica.

Then Leo made his son Constantine emperor, the rite of crowning being performed by the most holy Germanus. From then Leo began to fight against God and raged against the revered images. Summoning the patriarch Germanus, he said that the images ought not to be honoured; for he called their veneration idolatry. That divine man said: "Speak no evil, emperor, and do not think so; for the thought is plainly impious; and I know it is said that this heresy is to be stirred up. But may it not be you who brings it in; for one called Conon is said to be going to begin it." And he took him up at once and said: "I am he; for I was named Conon by my parents from infancy." So the celebrated Germanus, who would not be persuaded to agree with his opinion, but rather most nobly spoke against it and exposed his false belief, he drove out of the church, after he had steered it fifteen years, and appointed as patriarch one Anastasius, of the same mind as himself. I come now to tell the cause of Leo's coming to think so and going so far in impiety.

blocks: Izith had just become leader of the Arabs; and two Hebrews came to him, sorcerers by trade, who said they practised astrology and from it knew the future, and promised the Arab the rule and a long life if he threw out of the churches of the Christians the images of Christ and of her who bore him. The barbarian did not delay, but did away with the revered images in all the churches in the land under him. And divine justice pursued him before long. For not a year had passed and the wretch lost his life. His son, succeeding to the rule, sought those false prophets, eager to punish them for their deceit of his father. But they had already fled from there and reached Isauria. There, coming upon this Leo, then a young man, a craftsman by trade, they foretold to him the empire of the Romans. When he looked at his own fortune, which stood very far from such a rule, and disbelieved their oracles, they insisted strongly that the prophecy would come true, and demanded that he assure them by an oath that when he obtained the empire he would give them whatever they asked. And he swore that indeed, when he obtained the empire, he would fulfil their request.

He then became master of the empire of the Romans in the way that has been told. Those who had foretold it to him came to him when he was already in the ninth year of his sole rule, and asked him to pay them the reward for the prophecy. Leo was ready for this, and asked them to say what they asked for. And that profane pair of Jews said: "We ask to be given neither wealth nor to be raised to a height of glory nor any other of the splendours of empire, but only that the images of the Nazarene and of her who bore him be removed everywhere." And he, being unstable in faith, agreed to do this as if it were something trifling and very easy; and having just begun the tenth year of his tyranny, he began to fight against God and went against the revered images with a dreadful roar, raised a most severe persecution, punished many who opposed his abominable opinion, and made them martyrs.

Besides the other things he did against the pious, he did this too. There was a royal house in the place called the Basilica, very near the Chalkoprateia, in which many books of both outside wisdom and the nobler and more divine were stored. It had from of old been the dwelling of the man foremost in learning, whom they called the ecumenical teacher, who also had twelve others living with him, sharing in the highest degree of literary education. Public allowances were granted to them, and those who cared for learning and knowledge went to them, and the emperor made them counsellors in what had to be done. So he judged that if he won these over and brought them to his opinion, he would achieve the whole. Summoning the men, he shared with them his wicked opinion about the revered images. They not only did not agree with him, but tried to turn him altogether from this opinion, partly stroking the beast with the lion's name and charming him with saving words, partly opposing more nobly and exposing his impiety. But he, like an asp, stopped his ears and did not hear the voice of the charmers, nor was he charmed by the wise. So having talked with them many times and despairing of changing them, he let them go off to their own abode, that is the royal house, and himself ordered a great deal of fuel that catches fire easily to be gathered, placed round the house and lit at night, and so burned the house with the books and those wise and revered men.

blocks: For this reason Gregory, who was then steering the church of elder Rome, broke off communion with the president of New Rome and those of one mind with him, put them and the emperor under a synodal anathema, and stopped the tributes that until then had been brought to the empire from there, making a treaty with the Franks. For the Franks are not of the race of the Romans, but Procopius of Caesarea, who composed the varied history, says they are a Germanic nation, settled of old about the river Rhine and the Rhône and the lakes there. When Belisarius was general of the Romans under the first Justinian and was wrestling with the Goths over Italy and the cities in it and Rome itself (for they were held by the Goths), he records that these too then invaded Italy. The Goths, not being able to face both Romans and Franks, made a treaty with the Franks and ended the war with them, giving up to them as much of Gaul as had come to them. And at the Franks' request Justinian himself confirmed this act, arranging that the Franks should not oppose the Romans in their war with the Goths, but should be friendly to the Romans because of the confirmation. From this the Germans held Massalia, the colony of the Phocaeans, and all the places on the sea, mastered the sea there, and seized much of the Venetias too. So the Franks, having come close to the Italians, did not stop from then attacking the Romans there and plundering what was under them.

So Pope Gregory, having revolted from obedience to the emperor, as has been said, because of his false belief, made a treaty with the Franks, having first often tried by letters to turn Leo from his hatred of God and persuade him to revere the holy images; but it was like washing an Ethiopian. For not only did he think nothing right, but raging against the orthodox he punished many and gave them the crowns of confession. He weighed down the Calabrians and Sicilians with new taxes, decreeing that they should pay a poll tax like the Jews and that the male children born among them be registered. When his son Constantine was coming of age, he joined to him as wife a daughter of the Chagan, who led the Scythians, baptising her and naming her Irene. She was not drawn into her husband's false belief, but initiated into the pious doctrine she remained unchanged.

When a violent earthquake happened at Byzantium, many churches and houses fell and a crowd of men was buried in the ruins. At this time the statue of Arcadius set up on the column of the Xerolophos fell, and the statue of Theodosius the Great at the Golden Gate, and also the land walls of the city, and the city of Nicomedes and with it Nicaea, the Bithynian metropolises. The tyrant Leo, planning to make the fall of the walls a handle for gain, announced to the people of the city: "You could not quickly raise the walls again; and it is not good for you that the city should stay long unwalled. So we have ordered an addition to be made to the public taxes of twenty-four folles on each gold coin, so that when these are paid to the imperial treasury the parts of the walls that have given way may be renewed at imperial expense." From then until now this exaction has prevailed. So the wretched Leo, having reigned twenty-four years to the harm of the state, fell ill with dysentery and miserably spewed out his soul.

blocks: His ill-named son succeeded to the rule of the Romans along with his father's impiety; he not only raged against the revered images, but was also given to sorceries, the dissection of victims, necromancy and unspeakable practices, and in short kept from no evil, being many-coloured in wickedness and not of one form. For he was neither Christian, nor pagan, nor Jew, but a hotchpotch of impiety, like the Libyan beasts that are recorded to be born from the mixing of different kinds, born many-formed and mixed in shape and savagery; for this he was hated by all. In the second year of his tyranny (for I would not say reign), he marched out against the Arabs, and being in the theme of the Opsikion, of which theme his brother-in-law the curopalates Artabasdus held the command, he plotted against this kinsman of his. For the people and the senate, and the soldiery too, hating Constantine as has been said, were voting the empire to Artabasdus, who was orthodox. So Artabasdus, learning of the plot, spoke to the people and attacked Constantine. But Copronymus escaped first and fled to Amorium, and sending to Lancenus, the general of the Anatolic theme, and Sisinnacius, general of the Thracesian, persuaded them with splendid promises to fight for him. From this came civil wars, and the Romans were destroyed by one another. For each side held to its own emperor, since Artabasdus too had now been proclaimed emperor.

In the queen of cities the magister Theophanes had been left by Constantine as manager of public affairs; he, siding with Artabasdus and receiving a letter from him, proclaimed publicly that Constantine had died and that Artabasdus had been chosen emperor by the armies. And so the people of the city gathered in the Great Church, put Constantine under anathema and acclaimed Artabasdus, the patriarch Anastasius too approving. Artabasdus was received and proclaimed emperor by all, and at once set up the revered images everywhere. The patriarch Anastasius swore that Copronymus had said to him that Christ is not the son of God, but a mere man born of Mary, "as I was born of my mother Mary."

When Artabasdus went out of the great city, battles took place again. Constantine crossed from Chalcedon and besieged the city, pitching a camp by the land walls. Artabasdus attacked him, was defeated, shut himself inside the city and took care to guard it safely. Since Copronymus was master of the sea and did not let the merchant ships put in at the city, famine pressed those in it, so that many died from it. He captured Nicetas, Artabasdus's son, and showed him in fetters to his father. Then attacking the city again he took it. Artabasdus ran away and shut himself in a fort of the theme of the Opsikion, and being taken he was blinded with his two sons. Many of those who had fought for Artabasdus were put to death by Copronymus, and above the others the patrician Bactangius, a notable man, whose wife many years later the tyrant forced to go to the Chora, where he had been buried, dig up her husband's bones, carry them off herself and throw them into the Pelagiou, where the condemned were thrown. When a horse race was held, he led Artabasdus and his sons through the middle of the hippodrome in a triumph. He also ordered the patriarch Anastasius to be brought in from the Dihippion seated backwards on a donkey, so that he looked at its tail, and so led him too in triumph dishonourably, having first had him publicly beaten; so that the prophecy of the celebrated patriarch Germanus came true. For once when Anastasius was walking behind the said patriarch and trod on his omophorion, the holy Germanus turned and said: "Do not hurry; the Dihippion awaits you." Yet after the dishonourable procession he allowed him, as one of his own mind, to hold the church again and serve as priest.

Since Copronymus was master of the sea and did not let the merchant ships put in at the city, famine pressed those in it, so that many died from it. He captured Nicetas, Artabasdus's son, and showed him in fetters to his father. Then attacking the city again he took it. Artabasdus ran away and shut himself in a fort of the theme of the Opsikion, and being taken he was blinded with his two sons. Many of those who had fought for Artabasdus were put to death by Copronymus, and above the others the patrician Bactangius, a notable man, whose wife many years later the tyrant forced to go to the Chora, where he had been buried, dig up her husband's bones, carry them off herself and throw them into the Pelagiou, where the condemned were thrown. When a horse race was held, he led Artabasdus and his sons through the middle of the hippodrome in a triumph. He also ordered the patriarch Anastasius to be brought in from the Dihippion seated backwards on a donkey, so that he looked at its tail, and so led him too in triumph dishonourably, having first had him publicly beaten; so that the prophecy of the celebrated patriarch Germanus came true. For once when Anastasius was walking behind the said patriarch and trod on his omophorion, the holy Germanus turned and said: "Do not hurry; the Dihippion awaits you." Yet after the dishonourable procession he allowed him, as one of his own mind, to hold the church again and serve as priest.

blocks: While the Arabs were quarrelling with one another and busy with civil wars, Copronymus, taking the opportunity, marched against Syria and took Germanicea. When a very great earthquake happened in Palestine and Syria, many churches, monks' dwellings and houses fell, and tens of thousands of men perished. There was also a great destruction of men by disease in Sicily, Calabria, Hellas and other lands, which reached Byzantium itself; and the number of the dying was so great that the dead could not be carried out; so they put several on wagons and carried them out. The daughter of the Chagan bore Copronymus a son, whom he named Leo and proclaimed emperor, crowned by Anastasius, the patriarch of his belief. Constantine took Theodosiopolis and Melitene, and growing proud from this, breathed more violently against the church and the orthodox faith, setting out decrees by which he drew the rabble crowd to follow his most impious opinion.

At that time too the patriarch Anastasius, having trampled impiously on the church for twenty-four years, ended his life. Copronymus held a gathering of many bishops of his own mind, led by Theodosius of Ephesus and Pastillas of Perge, and through them decreed what he wished, with no one present from elder Rome or from the other sees; and he was not ashamed to call such a concourse of those unholy men an ecumenical council. With them he went to the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae, went up on the ambo and set there one Constantine, a monk who had been bishop of Syllaeum, and called out: "Many years to Constantine, ecumenical patriarch." A few days later this tyrant came to the Forum with his patriarch and the bishops of his mind, and before the whole people they forbade the veneration of the revered images, calling those who revered them idolaters, and put under anathema the celebrated Germanus, George from Cyprus, who had become patriarch of Constantine's city, and John of Damascus, great in wisdom and virtue, who had often exposed this fighter against God and his father as impious in letters.

Constantine marched out against the Bulgars, engaged them, lost many, not only ordinary soldiers but also notable men and generals, and came back defeated. From of old Christians among the Hagarenes had handled the tax books, for they do not know how to reckon, nor even to write small fractions, I mean thirds, quarters, eighths, twelfths and finer still; but at that time, out of envy, they were stopped from handling them. When the sons of Hagar could not accomplish such work by themselves, they were again entrusted with the management of these writings.

The ill-named tyrant scourged to death one Andrew, a monk called the Hut-dweller, a holy man, who exposed him and called him impious, and another Julian and Valens. The Bulgars, killing their leaders, who were descended in a line, chose another who did not belong to the rule, called Teletzes. The emperor marched against them by land and sea, and coming to Anchialus and engaging them there, the battle lasting from the fifth hour of the day until evening and many falling on both sides, he nevertheless won; the leader of the Bulgars ran away, there was great slaughter of the barbarians, no fewer were taken captive, and many went over to the emperor. Elated by this he held a triumph for the victory, himself passing through in full armour with the army armed, leading the captives in chains, ascribing the victory to his own arms and not to the divine power. After the triumph he ordered all the captives to be put to death.

blocks: In the days of his sole rule there was a great winter, so that not only were the rivers wholly frozen by the cold, but even the northern sea itself for very many stades, and the strait of the Narrows and the strait from the city to Chrysopolis. Then, when snow fell on the ice, and it too was packed and frozen by the cold, people crossed on foot the strait of the Narrows and that from the city to Chrysopolis, with pack animals carrying burdens and oxen drawing wagons with much load. This is said to have happened then in the other seas too. Then, when the air grew warm, the continuous ice was broken up and cut into pieces. A sudden, violent and forceful wind drove the pieces through the sea, not unlike great hills or islands of many plethra; and animals, wild and tame, were stuck fast on them, fettered by the ice and frozen to death. When some of these blocks of ice, rolled through the water by the force of the winds with a violent rush, dashed against the sea walls of the city, they at once threw down what they struck, and not only were the walls brought down, but very many houses were shaken down with them. Under him there was also a great drought, so that the ever-flowing rivers dried up and the springs failed completely.

None of this made his senseless soul any better, but calling his patriarch he said to him in secret: "Tell me, if we call Mary Mother of Christ, what harm will come of it?" He at once turned to supplication, saying: "Do not reveal this at another time or to another, emperor; for the thought is Nestorius's. Or do you not know how he is pilloried by every church of the faithful and condemned under anathema?" He answered him: "I did not say this as thinking so, but asked wishing to learn." He went so far in fighting against God that he handed the relics of the saints to the fire, and ordered that "saint" should be said neither of the Mother of God nor of any of those who had pleased God, but that one should say "the apostle Peter" and "Paul", and "the martyr George" or "Theodore", and likewise of the rest.

When the gathering of unholy high priests, of which I have already spoken, handed over in writing what they had impiously decreed, the most impious man called it a synodal tome and demanded that all the high priests and those monks famous for virtue should sign it. For though he had set on foot a most severe persecution against the monks, so that hardly any monk was left in the city or appeared in public, there were still many in hiding and others who had made their life outside the city. Those who out of fear bowed to his savagery and confirmed that godless writing were allowed to live and let go unharmed, but those who would not be persuaded were deprived of life by bitter punishments and violent deaths. At this time Stephen too, great among ascetics and famous among champions, would not be persuaded to receive and confirm what he called the tome, and after suffering much was at last cruelly put to death, and dragged from the prison of the praetorium as far as the Pelagiou was thrown there with the condemned, where there was a shrine of the martyr Pelagius, which the God-hater pulled down, and digging a very deep pit there ordered the condemned to be thrown into it. He punished many of the officials and of the senate too for honouring the holy images, and demanded an oath from all that none would pay reverence to the divine images; and he demanded this oath even from Constantine himself, whom he had set over the church, and he went up on the ambo and swore it.

Going out against the Bulgars with a large fleet, he anchored the ships at Anchialus, and when a violent wind blew almost all were smashed, and great numbers of both the fleet and the army perished in the waters; so he came back with nothing done. Raging against the monks, when a horse race was held in the hippodrome, he seized many of them and led them in triumph round the hippodrome, each holding a disreputable woman by the hand. Some of the notable officials he falsely accused of plotting against him, some out of envy for their good looks and strength, others because they told monks of his unspeakable practices; he cut off the heads of two of the more notable, and blinded the rest and shut them up within fixed bounds, where every year he sent and had each of them flogged with a hundred lashes of an ox-hide whip. He also said that the patriarch he had appointed, Constantine, talked with one of these officials and spoke against him, and arranged some accusers to convict him; and when he denied it, he made the accusers swear. When this had been done, the patriarch was exiled. The tyrant put forward as patriarch another, a eunuch Nicetas, not even of free birth but drawing his line from slaves, and not even able to read; for he had spent his time about the women's quarters. Then the tyrant ordered Constantine to be brought from exile, and, cruelly tortured so that he could not even walk, to be carried like a burden to the Great Church. While someone read out the charges against him, in the presence of a great crowd gathered for this, and with the new patriarch Nicetas sitting on the bench and listening to them, he was struck on the face, and so, after long abuse, was at last anathematised, and his head, beard and even his eyebrows were shaved, and seated on a donkey he was brought into the hippodrome while a horse race was being held, led in a dishonourable triumph, spat on and sprinkled with dust. After this the tyrant sent some of the officials and asked him what he thought of his faith and of the council. He, soothing his cruelty, answered that he believed rightly and that the council had decreed exactly; and having said this the thrice-wretched man was taken to the Kynegion and his head was cut off.
