blocks: Every day the profane man added to his madness against the churches and monasteries. Being licentious he married three wives, and by the first he had a son, Leo, whom he also thought worthy of the imperial title, and by the others Christopher, Nicephorus and Nicetas. The two he crowned Caesars, and Nicetas he honoured as nobilissimus. For his first son and emperor he brought a wife from Athens, betrothed her to him, crowned her Augusta and called her Irene; by her a son, named Constantine, was born to Leo.

Again Copronymus set out against the Bulgars with very many triremes and dromons, wishing to invade Bulgaria by the Ister. Then, losing heart, he planned to go back. But the Bulgars in fear sent to him and asked to make a treaty for peace, and they made it on terms that neither the Bulgars should plunder the Roman lands nor the Romans attack the Bulgars. On this he came back. Some of the Bulgars, drawn by gifts from this emperor, secretly told him what was being planned by their ruler; they informed Constantine that their leader wished to send people against one of the Roman lands to carry off plunder from there. He sent spies, and when the plunderers set out from Bulgaria, being ready he suddenly ran out against them, killed some and took others alive, came back with many captives, and again held a triumph in arms. Then he prepared many triremes and sent them against the Bulgars, and when they were off Mesembria a storm from violent winds fell on them and sank almost all.

Telerichus, the leader of the Bulgars, suspecting that his plans had been reported to the emperor by his own men, but not knowing who they were, outwitted the emperor's lightness and learned from him what he did not know. For he wrote secretly that he wished to come over to him, and asked him to tell him whether he had any friends among the chief men of the Bulgars, so that he might trust them with the secret and come to him with them. He, being dense, it seems, did not understand the barbarian's scheme, but foolishly at once revealed those attached to him. And the barbarian seized them all and made away with them cruelly and harshly.

And once more this emperor marched out against the Bulgars for the last time, and while he was encamped at [a gap in the text] in Thrace, his feet became like burning coals, from which violent and fiery fevers burned him, so that no remedy for them could be devised even by doctors. From there he was carried on a litter as far as Selymbria, from where he was taken by trireme, crying out: "I have been handed over to the fire while still alive." Just as he reached the Strongylon the wretch felt the divine razor made drunk, and there ended his life violently, having killed many thousands of the orthodox, above all monks, and having made their monasteries a by-product of fire, pulling down some and profaning others, as the monastery called Dalmatou, which was ancient and the oldest of all in Constantinople, from which he drove out the monks and made it a lodging for soldiers. He raged not only against the living, but did not stop abusing the martyrs of Christ and the others who had pleased him, saying they had no power and calling their intercessions a help of fig-wood, and burying some of their holy relics dishonourably, sinking others in the sea, and burning some to ash, as with the holy body of the all-praised martyr Euphemia.

Two stories are told about this. One says that that foul Copronymus seemed to have burned it, burning dogs and donkeys with it and scattering the ash, but that his plan did not come to pass; for the orthodox, learning of the plan, managed first to take the martyr's body from the coffin and move it, and put another corpse in it, and that this was handed over to the fire by that wretch. The other says it was not burned, but that the martyr's body was thrown into the sea with its coffin; and the coffin, steered by divine grace, ran ashore on the island of Lemnos, and being recognised by the faithful on the island was laid there, and under Irene and Constantine was brought back again to the queen of cities with honour and magnificence. So he, having lived so shamefully, died so violently, as has been recorded, having ruled alone thirty-four years and three months, counting with these the two years in which Artabasdus ruled, prevailing over him.

blocks: His son Leo, born of the Khazar woman, held the empire, sick with the same impiety, though at first he pretended to be pious and to honour the monks, so that some of the monks then became high priests of the leading metropolises. Finding much money in the public treasuries, which his father had wickedly gathered and stored up, he used it freely and won over his subjects, and by his feigned piety too. So those of the city, and many from the themes, gathered and asked, as if to please him, for his son Constantine to be proclaimed. He demanded, if they wished this, that they swear never to receive another emperor besides him and his son and their seed. And all swore, not only those of the senate and of the army, but also the common crowd, the merchants and the masters of workshops, and they issued written documents about this. This took place on the sixth day of the week of the Saviour's saving passion. On Holy Saturday the emperor appointed his own brother Eudocimus nobilissimus, and on Easter Sunday itself he crowned his son, the patriarch saying the customary prayer. When the patriarch Nicetas the eunuch died, who had presided over Constantinople for fourteen years, Paul the Cypriot was ordained patriarch, being a reader and orthodox.

Finding some of the notable men of the palace paying veneration to the divine images, he took off the fox skin and showed the lion hidden inside, tortured them most cruelly, led them round the market in a dishonourable procession, having first shaved them of their hair, and so put them away in the praetorium, where some of them gave up their souls to the Lord. He died having completed the fifth year of his sole rule. For he fell in love with the crown that Maurice had dedicated to God in the Great Church, took it and put it on his head, and at once was seized with a violent fever, and this took him out of life.

blocks: When he died, the Augusta Irene with her son Constantine, who was in the tenth year of his age, succeeded to the imperial rule. Both were venerators of the revered images, but before they had set their feet firmly in the empire some plotted against them, to make emperor the Caesar Nicephorus, the brother of the dead emperor Leo. When the conspiracy became known, the empress tortured those who had shared in the plot, cut off their hair and voted them exile, and had her husband's brothers, the Caesars and the nobilissimi, tonsured and thought worthy of the priesthood, and made them give the people communion at the feast of the Saviour's birth. She went out with her son with the guard usual for emperors, and coming to the Great Church presented the crown that her husband had taken from there, having adorned it with more ornament.

She also sent an army against the Arabs, to check their raids. The Hagarenes, going out to plunder, were met by the Roman army that had been sent, and were routed, and many were killed. In Thrace, at the Long Wall, someone digging then came upon a stone coffin holding a man's corpse and having letters carved on it saying: "Christ is to be born of a virgin, and I believe in him; and under the emperors Constantine and Irene you will see me again, O sun."

The empress Irene, wishing to find a wife for her son, sent to Charles, the king of the Franks, seeking his daughter for her own son. Then she gave this up out of fear and love of power, so that her son might not get the strength of the Franks through the connection, and brought a girl from the east; some say from the Armeniac theme, others from the Paphlagonians, being a granddaughter of Philaretus, famous for almsgiving; and she joined her to Constantine against his will, while he disliked the marriage, because he wished extraordinarily to marry Charles's daughter.

Aaron, the leader of the Arabs, marched against the Romans and came as far as Chrysopolis. Constantine sent an army and through it held the lake of Banes; and learning this, the Arabs asked to make a treaty with the Romans. The managers of public affairs went off to Aaron to make terms, and not taking care first to receive hostages from those important among them, they were seized by him and shut up in fetters. So the rulers, forced for the sake of the officials, made a treaty, agreeing to give tribute to the Arabs. On such terms they went away.

The empress appointed the patrician Elpidius general of Sicily; then, learning that he sided with the Caesars, she sent men to bring him from there. When the Sicilians did not allow those sent to take Elpidius, Irene, seized with anger, flogged his wife and children, cut off their hair and shut them in the praetorium; and she sent an army against him, setting over them a eunuch, one of those most faithful to her. When there were continual battles, Elpidius was routed, ran away to Africa and went over to the Arabs. They received him, put a royal headband on him, and he was proclaimed emperor by them, though nothing went forward for him according to his aim.

Freed from care about the Arabs by the peace, the empress went out with her son against Thrace, bringing a large force and musical instruments; and going to Beroe, she rebuilt the fort in it and named it Irenopolis, and having also built Anchialus and gone on as far as Philippopolis, she came back.
text: When he died, the Augusta Irene with her son Constantine, who was in the tenth year of his age, succeeded to the imperial rule. Both were venerators of the revered images, but before they had set their feet firmly in the empire some plotted against them, to make emperor the Caesar Nicephorus, the brother of the dead emperor Leo. When the conspiracy became known, the empress tortured those who had shared in the plot, cut off their hair and voted them exile, and had her husband's brothers, the Caesars and the nobilissimi, tonsured and thought worthy of the priesthood, and made them give the people communion at the feast of the Saviour's birth. She went out with her son with the guard usual for emperors, and coming to the Great Church presented the crown that her husband had taken from there, having adorned it with more ornament. blocks: When the patriarch Paul fell ill, withdrew from the church and was tonsured, the empress with her son came to him, blaming him for the withdrawal. He said: "Would that I had never sat on the throne of the high priesthood at all, when the church is under tyranny and there is a schism between it and the other catholic thrones." Then she sent picked men from the senate again, asking what might be arranged as needed. He answered: "Unless the error is corrected by a catholic council and the union of the churches comes about, there is no salvation for us." And the senators said: "Why then did you yourself agree, when you were ordained, not to venerate the images?" He answered: "Because of the madness of the rulers and your harshness. But for this too I lament, and through repentance I have fled to the mercies of God, asking not to be judged as a high priest." So he ended his life in this state.

The rulers put forward the celebrated Tarasius, who was an asecretis, as patriarch, and the whole people voted for him. But he refused, saying he could not preside over a church cut off from the other churches and put under anathema by them. When the emperors and the people pressed him, he said: "If you agree that an ecumenical council be gathered and a union of the churches come about, I too will accept the appointment." When all agreed to this, the divine Tarasius was ordained, and he and the rulers sent to elder Rome, where Hadrian presided, and to the other patriarchs, asking that some be sent from them to attend the council; and they were sent by all. When the other high priests and monks had gathered at Nicaea in Bithynia, the patriarch Tarasius too went out, and the seventh ecumenical council met there, and it was ratified that the revered images are to be venerated and revered, and the three who had presided over the church in Constantinople, Anastasius, Constantine and Nicetas, were condemned under anathema, and what had been decided by the holy council was written in a tome. The members of the council came from Nicaea to the queen of cities and, being in the palace with the rulers presiding, read the tome in the hearing of all; and it was ratified by the rulers, who signed it, and so the holy images were set up again in the divine churches, and all the churches were united.

Up to this point the affairs of the empire were steered by the empress and those close to her. But the emperor Constantine, having passed boyhood and beginning to be counted a young man (for he was twenty), and seeing everything managed by his mother, and the patrician and logothete Stauracius all-powerful, while he himself was thought worthy of no account, was vexed, and with some of the senate and of his servants planned to remove Stauracius from office and exile him. When the plan became known, the empress beat all the emperor's servants who shared in it, shaved them of their hair and exiled them to various places, and putting those of the senate in disgrace, ordered some not to leave their own houses and voted exile for others. She also tortured and abused her son and stopped him from going out. She forced the armies to swear not to accept her son in sole rule while she lived. The others swore even against their will, but those of the Armeniac theme did not submit, but said they knew Constantine as emperor, proclaimed from the beginning before his mother, and so wished him to be acclaimed again. Learning this, Irene sent the spatharius Alexius Mosele, drungarius of the Watch, to bring them over to her will. They put their own general under guard, chose Mosele as commander of the theme, and acclaimed Constantine alone as emperor. Spurred by this, those of the other themes too proclaimed Constantine alone as emperor, and gathering together proclaimed him alone as sovereign. Afraid of the agreement of the units, Irene let her son come forward. He at once tortured Stauracius and exiled the more honoured of his mother's servants, and himself brought his mother down from the palace with honour and ordered her to live in her house, which she had built in the quarter of Eleutherius.

blocks: So things stood. When a fire broke out, the great hall of the sacred palace called the Thomaites became the work of the fire, at which time the drafts of the commentary on divine scripture that John of the golden tongue wrote are said to have been burned, being stored somewhere there.

The emperor Constantine marched out against the Bulgars, whose nation Cardamus led; and after a small skirmish fear fell on both opposing sides. The emperor went back to the great city, and the Bulgars to their own homes. He set out against the Arabs too, but achieved nothing worth mention. Urged by his mother and by some of the men in office, he brought her back to the palace again, and allowed her to be acclaimed with him; and all the units of the themes accepted Irene's proclamation again, but those of the Armeniac theme opposed and rioted, and called on Alexius Mosele, who had been their general before, as has been said. For the emperor had already sent for him from there, honoured him as patrician and kept him with himself, since a rumour prevailed that the man would reign. For this, then, and because he was being called on by the rebels, the emperor in fear shut him up in the praetorium, having first beaten him and cut off his hair.

When the leader of the Bulgars set out against the Roman dominion, the emperor attacked him in disorder and was defeated, and lost a great number of soldiers, and many of the grandees too. The military units, gathered in the great city, planned to make emperor Nicephorus, who had been one of the Caesars, Constantine's uncle on his father's side. But the plan did not escape notice; so Nicephorus himself had his eyes put out, and Christopher, Nicetas, Anthimus and Eudocimus had their tongues cut out. The emperor also blinded Alexius Mosele, doing this at his mother's suggestion. Those of the Armeniac theme, learning of the blinding of Alexius, put their own general under guard. He was the patrician Camulianus. When this was reported to the emperor, he sent against them with a force Constantine Artaseras and Chrysocheir, who was general of the Bucellarii. When battle was joined many fell on both sides, but the imperial troops were routed, and both generals were taken alive, and the Armeniacs at once blinded them. Then the ruler himself marched out against them and subdued them, put the leaders to death, and punished the rest with confiscation of their property. He bound a thousand of those from their metropolis and brought them to the great city, and tattooed their faces with letters, ink being poured into the marks; the writing said: "Armeniac plotter"; and he scattered them in Sicily and other islands.

The emperor, turning against his own wife Maria, forced her to be tonsured, on the advice, as is said, of his mother, so that he might be hated by all and the management of the empire might come round to her. For though she lived with her son in the palace, she did not share in the power, but only in the acclamation, and she was very sick with love of rule. So when the ruler's consort had changed her dress and put on, against her will, instead of the imperial robe, the black garments of a nun, he married one Theodote, a lady of the bedchamber, crowning her Augusta. Marching against the Arabs he set up a trophy.

When Cardamus, whom the narrative has made known as leader of the Bulgars, demanded tribute to be paid him by the Romans, and sent about it to the ruler, threatening otherwise to plunder Thrace up to the city, he sent the barbarian the dung of pack animals, writing to him: "You are old, and do not trouble yourself coming here; I shall rather come to you." At once he gathered the Roman forces and went against the Bulgars, and when the armies were already near each other and the emperor was challenging the barbarians to battle, Cardamus lost heart with his armies and went off in flight. The Arabs too, advancing against Amorium, could achieve nothing against the city, but took plunder and went back.

blocks: Plato, the abbot of the monastery of Saccudion, would not bear to be in communion with the patriarch Tarasius, because he had received into communion the emperor, who had left his own wife and lived with another contrary to the church's laws; for he called what had happened adultery. The emperor brought him to the palace and imprisoned him; and the emperor's mother took Plato's side, because he had shamed her son. The ruler left the city with his mother and went to Prusa, and learning that a male child had been born to him, he left his mother there and came back in haste. She, taking the opportunity, won over the commanders of the units with gifts and promises and persuaded them to agree to depose her son and secure the sole rule for her alone. When they had agreed she looked for a good moment. The child born to the emperor, whom he named Leo, died, and was mourned by his father. Those who shared the plot against him with his mother, afraid that if time wore on and the deed were put off they would be found out, seized and destroyed, hurried and seized the emperor in the palace, and about the ninth hour gouged out his eyes most cruelly, taking care that he should be deprived not only of light but of life itself. At this time it happened that for seventeen days the sun did not shine, but those days were without light and dark; I do not know whether it happened so by chance or because of the blinding of Constantine, as men then thought, as if divine providence was indignant at the suffering, since it was done by a mother to her son. He had his eyes gouged out on the very day on which he had blinded his uncle Nicephorus and Mosele and cut out the tongues of the others, as has been said, five years having passed between. And Irene again took hold of the sole rule.

In elder Rome, when Pope Hadrian died, Leo was ordained, a reverend and most honoured man. The relatives of the dead Hadrian stirred the people to riot against him, seized him and maimed his eyes, but did not blind him. For those charged with the blinding spared the man out of pity, and harmed his eyes on the outside, but did not deprive him of light. He later went over to Charles, the king of the Franks, was restored by him to the throne of Rome, and took vengeance on his enemies; from which time Rome too came under the Franks, Charles being crowned by Leo and named emperor of the Romans. For under the first Justinian the Franks, who were of the race of the Germans, as has been said somewhere above, came into Italy and were enemies of the Romans. Under Leo the Isaurian, the pope of that time, Gregory, because of that emperor's false belief, ceased to obey that impious emperor, to pay tribute and to be in communion with those presiding impiously over the church of Constantinople, made a treaty with the Franks and ended the wars with them. Under Constantine and Irene Pope Leo received them into Rome too, and so they became masters of all Italy and of Rome itself.

When Irene ruled alone, as has been said, her husband's brothers, who were in confinement, managed to get to the Great Church, persuaded to this by some revolutionaries. So Aetius the eunuch, very powerful then with the empress, went off, gave them pledges that they would suffer nothing terrible, brought them out of the church, and they were taken away to Athens in exile. While they were living there, some of those of Hellas went to the ruler of the Slav peoples, asking him to bring them out, appoint one emperor and bring him up to the queen of cities. When this was reported to the empress, all were blinded at her order.

Charles, the leader of the Franks, having been proclaimed emperor of the Romans by Pope Leo, as has been said, sent envoys to Irene, seeking to be joined with her in married life. This did not seem unwelcome to her either, and it would have happened, had not the eunuch Aetius, who held power beside her, moved every device so that the marriage should not come about. For being very powerful in the palace he was planning to make his own brother Leo worthy of the empire; and this Leo, through Aetius's efforts, had been appointed sole general of Thrace and Macedonia; while Aetius governed the eastern themes of the Opsikion and the Anatolics, and from this, growing proud, he despised the men in office and treated them boastfully. They, vexed at this, formed a plot against the empress, and taking the patrician Nicephorus, the general logothete, came in the dead of night to the Chalke, while the empress Irene was ill and lying in her house in the quarter of Eleutherius; they told those guarding there that they had been sent by the empress to proclaim Nicephorus emperor, so that the patrician Aetius might stop forcing her to appoint his own brother emperor. The guards, believing the patricians, who were among the notable men, who said this, themselves acclaimed Nicephorus emperor with them, and so, being let through, they went into the great palace. Then that same night they gathered a mixed crowd and made the proclamation of Nicephorus through the whole Market before day, and set a guard round Irene's house, in which she was then living. When day was already dawning they moved her to the eastern palace and shut her up, and went to the Great Church, so that Nicephorus might be crowned there and proclaimed emperor; which was done.

blocks: The next day he came to the empress, who was under guard, saying he had been raised to the imperial rule against his will, for it was not of his choosing, and urging her to take heart, since she would lack nothing that a servant owes to his mistress. He asked her to show him all the imperial treasures. She said to him: "Having committed my affairs to God, I ascribe my fall from the empire to my sins, and reckoning your proclamation to be from God, I do obeisance to you as appointed by him, and ask you to spare my weakness and let me live in my house." And he said: "If you hide none of what has been stored in secret places, you shall have this too, and anything else that pleases you"; and he demanded an oath from her about this. She swore, and showed him very much. And he at once exiled her to the island called Prinkipo, in which she had built a monastery. For Nicephorus was most fond of money, extremely insatiable and most faithless, and, so to speak, a lodging of every wickedness. He could not bear even to pretend goodness to his subjects for a little while, but at once filled everything with every injustice. He took up Irene's son Constantine and won him over, so that he might show him hidden money. And he showed him much built into a wall. The emperor Nicephorus, understanding that all were vexed with him, and afraid that they would take Irene, who was near, and bring her back to the empire, exiled her to Lesbos and set guards over her, where, swallowed up by grief, she came to the end of her life.

Nicephorus also crowned his son Stauracius, who was very ugly and simple, and had neither looks nor nobility nor understanding worthy of rule. When the patriarch Tarasius departed life in the first week of the fasts, the celebrated Nicephorus, who was an asecretis, was ordained patriarch by common vote on Easter Sunday, while Plato and Theodore, who had become abbot of the monastery of Studius, rose against the ordination of that blessed man, because he had been appointed to the bishopric straight from the laity, though this had often been done. The emperor planned to drive them out of the city, but did not carry out the plan. Some say that their rising because the holy Nicephorus had become patriarch from the laity was a pretext, and the true cause love of rule. For they wished to become masters of the church, and set the greatest store on mounting the high priestly throne of Constantinople.

The emperor, wishing to bring his son Stauracius a wife, separated Theophano the Athenian, a relative of the empress Irene, who was already betrothed to a husband, from him unlawfully and joined her to Stauracius. This emperor, being a seed-bed of every kind of wickedness, did not stop devising one thing after another to crush his subjects. I shall mention a few, passing over the many, so that they may be like a taste from a full jar for those who read the history. He decreed that the poor from the themes should serve in the army, and that their arms and expenses should be supplied by their fellow villagers, and that the well-off should pay the taxes of the poor, which was called the allelengyon. He appointed inspectors, charging them to increase the public dues, and that two keratia on the gold coin should also be demanded for the cost of papers. They took the better pieces of real property from their owners and set them apart for the treasury. His too was the imposition of the hearth tax, a most wicked idea, laid on the tenants of churches, poorhouses, old people's homes and monasteries, and on everyone who had neither land nor tax liability; and the demand for money from those who had somehow passed from poverty to wealth, as finders of treasure; and that ship owners should be forced to buy land from the treasury, men who did not even know what farming is; and this was done to the shipmasters living in the themes. On the ship owners in Constantinople he imposed twelve pounds of gold each, so that they should pay interest to the treasury, beyond the other burdens laid on the ships. And whatever merchants or masters of workshops he learned were very well off, he sent and took their money, leaving them some small part, as he did with a seller of wax candles. For learning that that man was master of much money, he sent for him and said: "Put your hand on my head and swear by it how much gold you have." When he was forced to do this and swore he had a hundred pounds, he ordered them to be brought. When they were brought, he said: "You have no need of so much gold." So letting him take ten pounds, he took the rest himself, having then made him his table companion, so that he bought, against his will, the honour of lunching with the emperor for ninety pounds of gold.
text: The next day he came to the empress, who was under guard, saying he had been raised to the imperial rule against his will, for it was not of his choosing, and urging her to take heart, since she would lack nothing that a servant owes to his mistress. He asked her to show him all the imperial treasures. She said to him: "Having committed my affairs to God, I ascribe my fall from the empire to my sins, and reckoning your proclamation to be from God, I do obeisance to you as appointed by him, and ask you to spare my weakness and let me live in my house." And he said: "If you hide none of what has been stored in secret places, you shall have this too, and anything else that pleases you"; and he demanded an oath from her about this. She swore, and showed him very much. And he at once exiled her to the island called Prinkipo, in which she had built a monastery. blocks: Devising many such things against his subjects (for he was most resourceful in such matters), Nicephorus brought every harm on them and was hated by all. So once an unknown man took a sword in his hands and ran into the palace, seeking to kill this emperor. When some ran at him, he struck some with the sword, but was seized and handed over to tortures, revealed nothing against anyone, but pretending to be out of his mind was shut up. Nicephorus used Manichaeans and those called Athinganoi in oracles, auguries and secret rites. From this they spread corruptly into the Roman lands, and many of the simpler sort were corrupted in their faith by them.

The sons of Hagar, often marching against the Romans, harmed their lands, and took among others Euchaïta. They plundered the east, and the Bulgars the west. So the emperor planned to march against the Bulgars; and when one of those closest to him advised him to ease the harm to his subjects, "for all cry out against us," he said, "and if anything unlucky befalls us, all will rejoice at our fall," he said: "God has hardened my heart like Pharaoh's; so expect nothing good for those under my hand from me." So gathering the units from every side and coming into Bulgaria, where Krum led the nation, he at first had good fortune, so that he took Krum's aul (for so the Bulgars called the residence of their leader), put seals on his storerooms as already his own, and punished many of his own men for seizing spoils. When Krum lost heart and begged him to spare the nation and make a treaty with him on whatever terms he wished, he, swollen by his success, would not accept the treaty. So Krum, despairing, and thinking that he was now running for his life, gathered his forces and roused them with words of encouragement, and came while it was still night against the Roman camp, where all were sleeping without a guard; for they thought the barbarians would never dare to engage them, out of great madness; and at once they rushed at the imperial tent, and Nicephorus was killed, but how is not known. It is said that he was killed by his own men, either beginning his slaughter themselves, or the barbarians beginning and the Romans finishing off the murder of the avenging fury.

Stauracius too was wounded, between the right shoulder and the neck, and many were killed of those in high positions, in office, in commands, in ranks, and of the others serving in the army, and of those of the imperial service and the other servants beyond number. All the emperor's baggage and the whole Roman camp were plundered, and much wealth, many arms and countless horses fell to the barbarians. Stauracius was barely saved, and those whom the night allowed to escape notice by slipping into thickets and woods and such places. Krum took the body of the emperor Nicephorus and cut off the head, and for some days hung it on high, making a show of it and parading his success. Then, separating the bone of the crown and stripping it of skin and binding it in silver, he used it as a cup, and pouring wine into it gave it to those under him to drink. When the destruction of the Romans and the slaughter of the emperor were reported in Byzantium, there was great lamentation everywhere and the relatives of those killed wailed; but the destruction of the ruler made the calamity lighter, since all rejoiced at it.

blocks: So Nicephorus, having been most wicked, perished most shamefully. Stauracius, wounded, escaped by flight to Adrianople and was saved, and there he was proclaimed emperor through the zeal of some of those in office, and in a bad way from the wound he entered the great city. He plotted against the curopalates Michael, surnamed Rhangabe, who was his brother-in-law through his sister Procopia, wishing to leave the empire to his own wife. But the members of the senate, learning of Stauracius's design, and gathering those left of the units, proclaimed the curopalates Michael emperor at dawn, while it was still night; and at once Stauracius cut off his hair and put on the dress of a monk.

blocks: Michael came to the Great Church at daybreak and was crowned with the imperial diadem by the patriarch Nicephorus, who first demanded of him a written promise not to disturb any of the church's ordinances nor to stain himself with the blood of Christians. Some days later he proclaimed and crowned his wife Procopia Augusta; he was pious in mind and generous. He comforted with gifts of money those who had been wronged by Nicephorus and the wives of the soldiers who had fallen in the war. Stauracius's wife Theophano, who had cut off her hair and put on black dress, he gave much money, and assigned her besides a house to live in, which she turned into a lodging for nuns, where Stauracius too was buried, having died of the wound the narrative has shown, after ruling alone only two months and six days. That monastery was called after him the monastery of Stauracius, but as the name was mangled by the rabble crowd it is called Ta Braka, and by some who did not know the true name and changed it, forsooth, to something more Greek, it is named Ta Hebraïka. Finding the men who had led the monastery of Studius shut up, I mean Plato and Theodore, and also Theodore's brother the monk Joseph, archbishop of Thessalonica, and the more notable monks of that monastery, because they were not in communion, as has been told, with the patriarch and the church, he hurried to unite them, and did unite them. This emperor also thought his son Theophylact worthy of the imperial title and put the diadem on him through the patriarch. Then, marching out against the Bulgars, who were plundering the Thracian region, when one of the units rose against him, so that they even went as far as open insults, he calmed them with gentle words and generous gifts and returned to the palace.

When many sought to renew the madness against the revered images, he arrested some and punished them moderately, and through them frightened the rest and made them stop. Finding a monk, putting on a show of piety as it seems, who had scraped off an image of the Mother of God, he cut out his tongue. When the Hagarenes were again plundering the east, the general of the Anatolics, Leo the Armenian, engaged them, killed about two thousand, and carried off horses and arms in great numbers from them as spoil.

Krum, the ruler of the Bulgars, sent envoys to the emperor seeking peace on the terms made under Theodosius of Adramyttium and the patriarch Germanus. And if the emperor would not choose peace on these terms, he threatened to march on Mesembria, and said that the one who did not choose peace would be the cause of the destruction of the Christians. But on the advice of those about him the emperor did not accept the treaty on those terms, and Krum marched on Mesembria, bringing siege engines. For an Arab engineer, skilled in these, had once come over to Nicephorus and been initiated in divine baptism, but not receiving any provision worth mention because of that man's stinginess, and then complaining to him about the neglect, he was beaten most severely. So out of desperation he had gone over to the Bulgars, and through him the barbarians had learned to make every engine. So, well supplied with siege engines, they did not take long over the sack of the town of Mesembria. The emperor called the patriarch and some of the high priests and put before them the question of the treaty with the Bulgars, and whether they should hand over to Krum those who had fled from there to the Romans; for the barbarian demanded this too, besides the rest, in the treaty. The patriarch and the high priests advised that the refugees be handed over, judging it better for a moderate number to suffer than for countless multitudes to suffer. But those about the emperor and Theodore the Studite spoke against the treaty, saying the refugees must not be handed over. So from this the treaty with the Bulgars was prevented. For this emperor was good in character and right in faith, but sluggish in the management of affairs, and easily followed wherever he might be led by the most powerful of the officials.

blocks: A comet then appeared, shaped into various forms, among which, it is said, was the shape of a man without a head. The Bulgars, having taken Mesembria, found much in it, and among other things not the least amount of the liquid fire. When some captives returned, the emperor learned from them that Krum wished to plunder Thrace, and went out of the city. So the barbarian did none of what he planned, but lost many of his own men and went back; and the emperor, gathering the Roman forces from every side, went out again into Thrace, the Augusta too following him as far as Kidoktos. At this the soldiery was displeased and railed at the emperor. Then the Augusta went back, and Michael went about Thrace, doing nothing a general should, nor making any arrangement against the enemy; and the armies were no less a plunder for the inhabitants of the country than the barbarians.

Krum set out from his own haunts and encamped beside the imperial ranks. When battle was joined the Romans were defeated, the general of the Anatolics, Leo of Armenian descent, having become the cause of the defeat. For he, longing for the empire and slandering Michael to the army as unmanly and no general, as soon as the battle was joined ordered the units under him to follow him, deserted his post and went off in flight. This turned the others to flight too, so that Krum did not even believe what was happening because it was so unexpected, but thought it an ambush and held back those about him. But when he saw the Romans fleeing in disorder and without restraint, then he ordered his men to pursue, and made very great slaughter of soldiers and generals. The emperor was barely saved by flight with a few to Constantine's city, the camp and the imperial tent having become plunder for the barbarians.

From then Leo, seizing his freedom, and scattering those who shared his designs among what was left of the armies, saying that the Romans were being defeated through the simplicity of their rulers and that affairs needed a noble man, such as Leo the general of the Anatolics was, roused the soldiers to revolt; and they spoke ill of the emperor and thought Leo worthy of the imperial acclamation, standing round his tent. When he put on airs and, forsooth, refused the sole rule, Michael the Stammerer, commander of a unit, drew his sword, and suggesting to others who shared the conspiracy that they do the same, they persuaded Leo, unwilling as he seemed, to accept the proclamation. When this was reported to Michael, he at once neither set out to resist nor tried to lay claim to the empire, but sent the insignia of the empire to Leo. When Leo came to the palace, Michael with his wife and children ran as a suppliant into the church at the Pharos. Dragged away from there, Michael was taken off to the island called Prote, and having become a monk lived out his life there. His son Theophylact, who had been thought worthy of the proclamation too, as we have said, Leo deprived of his genitals and sent beyond the borders with his mother and his brothers.

blocks: So Michael's rule came to this end, after he had reigned two years. Leo, entering the palace, at once took off the cloak he was wearing and handed it to Michael the Stammerer, and he at once put it on, which many judged a sign that he would be Leo's successor in the empire. Not only did this sign of succession to power befall Michael, but also, walking behind Leo when he had changed into the imperial dress, he trod on its hem; this too seemed to Leo no good omen. The empire had also been foretold to both of them. For Bardanes, the general and patrician mentioned above, before attempting his usurpation, while he was turning it over in his mind, went to a monk living as an ascetic in Philomelium and believed to foretell the future, revealed the secret to him, and asked whether his plan would succeed. He forbade him the attempt, saying: "You will not gain what you desire, and you will be deprived both of your property and of your sight." At this he went away very sorrowful. This Leo, Michael the Stammerer and another, Thomas, brought up his horse for him. The monk, leaning out from above and seeing them, called the general back and said: "To you, as I have told you, God does not grant to obtain the empire; but of those who brought up your horse, know that two, Leo and Michael, will both hold the empire. The other will make the attempt and put a diadem on himself, but will not gain his aim, and will perish miserably." So he foretold this. Bardanes, disbelieving him, attempted usurpation; how he did not obtain the empire, but had his eyes gouged out and was deprived of his wealth, I have already told.

When Leo became emperor he honoured Michael the Stammerer as patrician and count of the corps of the Excubitors, and appointed Thomas, who was also one of those who had then brought up the horse for Bardanes, turmarch of the unit of the Federates. When the Bulgars were plundering Thrace, Leo sent envoys to their leader about a treaty. But he, swollen by his recent victory, did not accept the embassy about the treaty. So the emperor marched out against him, and again victory smiled on the barbarians; and when the Romans turned to flight, the barbarians pursued behind, and being contemptuous they did not pursue in order or in good formation, but scattered, some one way, some another. The emperor noticed this, for he happened to be standing on high ground, and sharpening those about him with words of encouragement and rousing them to battle, he charged against the barbarians with a noble presence of mind, and by the sudden change threw the enemy into panic fear; very many were killed, a great multitude was also taken captive, and Krum himself would nearly have been killed, being struck and falling from his horse, had not those about him stood round him, covered him with their shields and put him on another horse, and so he got away by flight.

After this the emperor reached the palace bearing a trophy and bringing much plunder, and not long after he began the frenzy against the revered images; how he became possessed by this madness I shall at once relate. To the monk I have already mentioned, who had foretold that he would become master of the empire, he sent gifts by one of those closest to him, paying a reward for the prophecy. The man sent did not meet him, for that monk had already departed this life, but finding another dwelling in his dwelling, he went to him as if to the other, not knowing the man. And he, since he championed the cause of the iconoclasts and was an ardent lover of the heresy, did not accept the gifts and sent back the man who brought them, saying he could not bear to take anything from a worshipper of idols, and threatening the emperor with the loss of both his empire and his life shortly, unless he refrained from worshipping idols, so calling the revered images. These things, reported to Leo by the man sent, made him anxious, and he shared what had been told with one of his intimates, Theodotus Melissenus, who happened to be a heretic of the iconoclast party. So he went after Leo with guile, and knowing a monk of his own belief, he advised him to share the matter with him and do whatever he suggested; for he said the man was full of spiritual graces and foresaw and foretold the future. When he saw that the emperor Leo agreed to his words, Theodotus went off to the monk, told him beforehand of the ruler's coming to him in the dress of a private man, and for what reason he would come, and instructed him in all he was to say to the emperor. Then the emperor went off by night to the monk, having changed his dress so that he might not be recognised as emperor; and Theodotus was with him. That monk, as if forsooth initiated beforehand by the Spirit into what was being contrived, addressed Leo as emperor, and said: "Do not hide your rank or try to deceive our nothingness. Know that you are not rightly disposed about worship, but plainly you and all your subjects worship idols. If then you remove the idols from the churches, your life and your reign will be long and happy; but if not, expect the speedy loss of both, and after it eternal punishments to succeed." So he said this. And Leo, marvelling at the monk for his supposed foreknowledge, for he did not know Theodotus's plotting, was caught by his words and breathed most violently against the divine images, voting by decree for their removal everywhere.

He wished, however, to have the patriarch of the same vote. But he spoke strongly against it, and exposed the doctrine as impious in words and in writings; this most divine man was Nicephorus. So the emperor condemned him to exile. It is said that the celebrated Nicephorus foresaw Leo's wickedness, and that he would be a thorn to the orthodox and an occasion of uproar to the churches. For when he was putting the diadem on his head he thought thorns were driven into his hand. So he was taken off into exile to Proconnesus. The confessor Theophanes, abbot of the monastery of Megas Agros, knowing in the spirit of his passing by, though he did not see the saint, lit candles and burned incense and greeted him; and he in turn from the ship returned the greeting with obeisances to the one sending him on his way, neither seeing nor being seen. When those sailing with the patriarch wondered and asked to whom he was paying obeisance, he said: "To the confessor Theophanes, the abbot of Megas Agros," foretelling his confession; for he had not yet been thought worthy of it then.
text: So Michael's rule came to this end, after he had reigned two years. Leo, entering the palace, at once took off the cloak he was wearing and handed it to Michael the Stammerer, and he at once put it on, which many judged a sign that he would be Leo's successor in the empire. Not only did this sign of succession to power befall Michael, but also, walking behind Leo when he had changed into the imperial dress, he trod on its hem; this too seemed to Leo no good omen. The empire had also been foretold to both of them. For Bardanes, the general and patrician mentioned above, before attempting his usurpation, while he was turning it over in his mind, went to a monk living as an ascetic in Philomelium and believed to foretell the future, revealed the secret to him, and asked whether his plan would succeed. He forbade him the attempt, saying: "You will not gain what you desire, and you will be deprived both of your property and of your sight." At this he went away very sorrowful. This Leo, Michael the Stammerer and another, Thomas, brought up his horse for him. The monk, leaning out from above and seeing them, called the general back and said: "To you, as I have told you, God does not grant to obtain the empire; but of those who brought up your horse, know that two, Leo and Michael, will both hold the empire. The other will make the attempt and put a diadem on himself, but will not gain his aim, and will perish miserably." So he foretold this. blocks: When the revered Nicephorus had been thus cast out of the church, Theodotus Melissenus was brought in in his place, who had two surnames, for he was also called Cassiteras. How he became known to Leo should not be left untold. When Michael Rhangabe was emperor, a woman of the women's quarters of the palace, who was seized by madness at the phases of the moon, would cry out to the emperor: "Come down, give up what belongs to others." This happened not once but very many times, and troubled the emperor. He shared the woman's cries with this Theodotus, who was his intimate, and he said: "When the woman is seized by the madness and cries the usual things, someone must ask her to whom the palace belongs, and what he is called, or what he looks like, and whether there is any other mark about him." He seemed to advise well, and he himself was entrusted with the questioning. The girl went mad again and cried out as usual. He questioned her. And she gave out like an oracle Leo's name and his appearance, and said: "If you go now to the acropolis, two men will meet you, and to the one of them whom a mule carries the palace belongs." Hearing this Theodotus revealed nothing to the emperor, but said the girl's words were words of madness, foretelling nothing clear. But he himself went to the acropolis, met Leo, and detecting the marks the woman had told, he took the man aside privately, and having given and received pledges, foretold the empire to him, as if he had been initiated into it by a more divine inspiration, and asked that after the outcome a reward for the prophecy should be laid up for him. This was the way that made Theodotus known and close to Leo, and he got as recompense for the prophecy the throne of Constantinople after the holy Nicephorus. O unfathomable abyss of God's judgements! Who after whom!

As soon as the unholy man had unworthily mounted the sacred throne, since he had the ruler of one mind with him, he carried on boldly and openly the outrage against the holy images. And Leo behaved like a wild beast towards those who wished to honour the revered pictures. For Theodotus himself made him savage, and so did the man who was then leader of the choir of those assigned to the imperial bedchamber, whom custom has come to call protopsaltes. For he, having drunk his fill of the muddy dregs of the iconoclast heresy, stirred the emperor on every side to remove the images. And once, when the divine words of Isaiah were being read in church, which say: "To whom have you likened the Lord? Did the carpenter make an image, or the goldsmith fashion a likeness of him?" and what follows, he came to the emperor and said in his ear: "Attend to the prophet, master, and obey him." From then Leo clung to the heresy without shame, and hastened to tear apart and devour those who would not bow to his impiety; and in other ways too he was harsh and inexorable in anger to offenders, and declared heavy punishments for moderate offences. Such was Leo towards the pious and those who had otherwise offended him.

Yet in the management of public affairs he was not sluggish, but very wakeful, and checked wrongdoers. When someone petitioned him that his wife had been carried off by one of the senate, adding that he had gone to the eparch but had not obtained justice, since the charge was proved, he at once removed the eparch from office and handed over the man who had committed the rape to be punished according to law. He appointed officials, both military and civil, by merit, and did not put up the governorships of the nations under the Romans for sale, nor give them as favours to men not fit for office or slaves of money, who would betray justice for it.

blocks: Michael the Stammerer from Amorium, raised to great fortune, and having, besides his other vices, an unbridled tongue, was denounced to the emperor as brewing and contriving evil against him. The denunciation came on the day before the one on which the church has received the custom of celebrating the Lord's birth in the flesh. At once, then, he was arrested; and the emperor sat in person as examiner of what was reported against him. Michael was convicted by his accusers, and himself confessed, and was condemned to death, and death by fire. He was being led off to be burned, and the place of punishment fixed was the furnace of the bath in the palace. The emperor too followed, either not trusting another with the execution of Michael or gloating over his destruction. But the empress, learning this, stopped the deed, partly begging her husband to put off the condemned man's punishment because of the feast, and partly approaching him more boldly and calling him godless, because he showed no regard for the day of the awesome mystery of the Saviour's birth. With this she softened his hardness and persuaded him to put off Michael's destruction for the time. And he said to his wife: "See, I have done as you ask; but you and your children will know what will befall you from this." So Michael thus escaped destruction.

One might wonder how Leo foretold what would happen; for he certainly did not know it beforehand from a more divine inspiration. How could he, a fighter against God, and otherwise a man of blood and of a life not clean of passions? It is said that it had been made known to him beforehand by some oracle that on the day of Christ's birth he would lose both his rule and his life. And they say too that a book was stored in the palace library in which there were oracles about the emperors, and figures of men and beasts were painted, and among the others there a lion was painted, on whose back the letter chi was marked; and there was a man behind the beast, driving a spear through the chi into the lion. The book contained this, and they were, as it seemed, Sibylline oracles. The painting, being hard to interpret, was explained, it is said, by the quaestor of the time, who said that an emperor would be killed on the day of Christ's birth. For the beast signified an emperor, the chi hinted at that day, and the spear fixed in the lion through the middle of the chi meant that the emperor would be slain on the very day of the feast. This troubled the emperor, and moreover his mother's dream frightened him. For she seemed to be in the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae and to see a woman escorted by men in white, and the floor of the church full of blood, and to hear the escorted lady order a vessel to be filled with blood and given to the emperor's mother. When she would not take what was offered, that resplendent woman said: "But your son fills those who honour me with blood, and does not understand that he is moving God and my Son to anger." Leo's mother saw this, reported the dream to her son, and begged him to stop the outrage against the revered images; but the wretch had stopped his ears and did not stop fighting against God. The divine patriarch Tarasius, who had already passed from this perishable life, was also seen in a dream by someone calling on a certain Michael and urging him to attack Leo and kill him. The prophecy of the monk in Philomelium too, and some other things, disturbed and frightened Leo.

Meanwhile, then, having bound Michael's feet in fetters, he handed him over to the papias to be guarded, and himself kept the key of the iron bond. Spending the night anxious, he had no sleep settling on his eyes. So he went off to the papias's quarters, and saw Michael sleeping on a bed and the papias lying on the floor. The papias did this either honouring Michael or because he was, as it seemed, privy to the plot against the emperor. When he saw this, and Michael sleeping a sleep deep and sweet, such as suits a man without care, he went back in wrath and showed his anger by the movement of his hand. None of the others noticed the emperor's presence, but one of the papias's men both knew he had come and, pretending to sleep, saw all he did, and how he was angered and how he threatened, and reported everything to them. Seized with fear, they considered how they might escape the emperor's wrath. And Michael said to the papias: "If you are willing, we shall not only escape the danger, but what we have planned will also come to effect." And he said: "Do what occurs to you, and you will have me following wherever you wish." So at once he wrote a letter to those who shared his designs, threatening that unless they came quickly and carried out what had been planned (for this was easy, as he had arranged it), he would reveal them all to the emperor, and he would not share the danger alone. Handing this letter to the papias, he told him to send someone from his household; and he sent one to show the letter to the accomplices, naming each by name, and to suggest that they come to the palace by night, disguised in the dress of clerics and carrying hidden daggers. They came as they were told; and as soon as it was dawn, while still night, the imperial chanters came to sing the morning hymns. With them the papias brought in Michael's accomplices too, and they hid themselves together in a corner in the dark, while the chanters sang the hymns. When they were already past the middle, the emperor too came into the church; and having a piercing voice, very heavy and entering the ears with harshness, he thought he sang well and was most melodious, and was accustomed to lead the hymns. So then he stood and intoned: "For love of the King of all they scorned." And at once those who had plotted against him leapt out from the corner and the dark, drawing their swords. He, understanding what was being done, ran into the sanctuary, and his murderers followed, and there, wounded by them with many blows and his hand cut off, he was at last deprived of his head too, having reigned cruelly and impiously for seven years and five months. His corpse was dragged into the Hippodrome and thrown there. And Michael, his feet still bound in iron, for the key of the bonds had not been found, since Leo carried it at once in his bosom, was acclaimed and given obeisance

blocks: as emperor. Then, when the irons had been broken, he came to the Great Church to be crowned with the diadem, counting the bloodshed as nothing. Leo's wife and his sons, of whom there were four, Sabbatius, who was renamed Constantine when he was proclaimed, Basil, Gregory, and a fourth, Theodosius, he brought down from the palace; her he shut up in the monastery of the Despots, and the sons he confined on the island called Prote and deprived them all of their manhood. Theodosius died, and Constantine was seized by loss of speech; for which he prayed most fervently to God, and also to the great father Gregory the Theologian, constantly visiting his image, that his loss of speech might be taken away; for with the fall from the empire Leo's sons had also fallen away from their father's false belief. Once, then, the saint seemed to stand by him, ordering him to rise and read "Again my Jesus". He, believing the word, went into the church and read, with nothing hindering his voice. And though he confined Leo's wife, as has been said, and his sons within fixed bounds, he did not leave them unprovided, but assigned them some of their own possessions, so that they might get from them what they needed; and he also gave them some people for their service.

This Michael came from Amorium, a city of upper Phrygia, in which Jews, Athinganoi and a crowd of other impious people had settled, and there was there a mixed heresy made from these, which this Michael too is said to have shared. This heresy receives divine baptism, but teaches the keeping of the Mosaic ordinance, except for the circumcision of the foreskin. He also had a Jew at home who trained him as a boy. So nothing pure was to be found in him, but the man was, so to speak, a seed-mixture of heresy. For this reason too he hated learning, since it served to overturn his false belief. Living in poverty, he served in the army from youth. Once, then, he went to the commander of his unit and asked him for something. An Athinganos happened to be standing by him, and said to the general, speaking in secret, that "this man who is asking you now will reign over the Romans." He at once, trusting the prophecy, made Michael his friend and his son-in-law, through his daughter.

As soon as Michael had leapt into the sole rule, as has been told, the most holy Nicephorus, who was in exile, wrote to him, asking that the images be set up again. He said he would make no innovation in the faith nor alter the state of the church, but also would not force anyone about the divine, but let him believe as he wished. But this stayed in words. For not long after he showed his own mind and went against the orthodox, and brought many others into terrible things, and besides the others sent into exile the divine Methodius and Euthymius, high priest of Sardis, for their honour of the holy images. Then he shut Methodius up at Akritas, and brought the celebrated Euthymius to a martyr's death, having him flogged without mercy through his son Theophilus. He emulated Copronymus in everything and was devoted to the Jews, and ordered fasting on the Sabbaths. Not believing in the resurrection, he mocked the good things to come, ridiculed the prophets and declared that demons do not exist; he did not think fornication a sin, and ordered people to swear by the God over all. He proclaimed salvation for Judas, and decreed that Easter was not celebrated at the right time. These few out of many marks of his wickedness, or rather folly, have been set down.

Let the narrative now give the history what happened then; these were civil wars. The one who began them was Thomas, who happened to be one of the three men about whom the monk in Philomelium foretold to Bardanes that two would mount to the imperial rule, while the third, who was this Thomas, would attempt usurpation and put a diadem on himself, but would not obtain the empire. This man, then, having been appointed by Leo over the unit of the Federates, as I have already said, when he learned that his benefactor had been killed by Michael, rose against Michael, in appearance avenging him, but in truth looking eagerly for the empire, and gathering no contemptible force, made almost the whole eastern region his own and arranged for the public taxes to be brought to him. Having grown great from this, he also attacked the Hagarenes, who were then plundering every land, and the islands themselves, with less fear because of the civil war. He attacked and checked their onrush, and having checked it encamped beside them, and came to talks with them, and in the talks made a treaty on terms that he would give up the Roman borderlands to them if he became master of the empire. text: as emperor. Then, when the irons had been broken, he came to the Great Church to be crowned with the diadem, counting the bloodshed as nothing. Leo's wife and his sons, of whom there were four, Sabbatius, who was renamed Constantine when he was proclaimed, Basil, Gregory, and a fourth, Theodosius, he brought down from the palace; her he shut up in the monastery of the Despots, and the sons he confined on the island called Prote and deprived them all of their manhood. Theodosius died, and Constantine was seized by loss of speech; for which he prayed most fervently to God, and also to the great father Gregory the Theologian, constantly visiting his image, that his loss of speech might be taken away; for with the fall from the empire Leo's sons had also fallen away from their father's false belief. Once, then, the saint seemed to stand by him, ordering him to rise and read "Again my Jesus". He, believing the word, went into the church and read, with nothing hindering his voice. And though he confined Leo's wife, as has been said, and his sons within fixed bounds, he did not leave them unprovided, but assigned them some of their own possessions, so that they might get from them what they needed; and he also gave them some people for their service. This Michael came from Amorium, a city of upper Phrygia, in which Jews, Athinganoi and a crowd of other impious people had settled, and there was there a mixed heresy made from these, which this Michael too is said to have shared. This heresy receives divine baptism, but teaches the keeping of the Mosaic ordinance, except for the circumcision of the foreskin. He also had a Jew at home who trained him as a boy. So nothing pure was to be found in him, but the man was, so to speak, a seed-mixture of heresy. For this reason too he hated learning, since it served to overturn his false belief. Living in poverty, he served in the army from youth. Once, then, he went to the commander of his unit and asked him for something. An Athinganos happened to be standing by him, and said to the general, speaking in secret, that "this man who is asking you now will reign over the Romans." blocks: When Thomas was in Thrace, as has been said, he had everyone coming over to him. So when the emperor again engaged him by land and by sea, the usurper routed and scattered both armies, and adopted another son, since the first had been killed, as has been said, one called Anastasius, who was a monk, and who took off the divine habit and put on worldly dress. Michael came to such straits that he stretched an iron chain from the acropolis to the little town opposite, so that what lay inside might be kept inaccessible to the usurper's men. But Thomas attacked the city by land and sea at once, breaking that iron chain very easily, and thought that if he only appeared, those in the city, because of their hatred for the ruler, would give him easy entry. But when he found those inside strong to guard the city and was cheated of his hopes, he withdrew for the time and pitched a camp at the most holy precinct of the divine Anargyroi; the place was called Ta Paulinou. Some days later he again brought war on the city by land and sea, bringing up siege engines and ladders. When he saw that his efforts were fruitless on every side, then, avoiding cold Thrace, for it was winter, he distributed his army among the districts, to rest there and escape the sharpness of the winter. As soon as spring came he brought his army against the city again from both sides and surrounded the walls with both the foot army and the fleet. Now Michael too had a fleet and an army ready. So the emperor, encouraging his men with words of exhortation, led them out all together from several gates and clashed with the usurper's people. They, losing heart at the suddenness and boldness of the attackers, turned their backs, and many fell, and the victory belonged to those from the city. So things went thus for the rebel on land; nor did things go better for him at sea. For the usurper's navy, seeing the imperial triremes coming against it, did not stand, but at once, not daring to engage, made for the shore with hard rowing, and some ran away, while others came over as deserters to Michael.

The rebel still clung to his usurpation, and did not break up his camp, and sent for the navy made ready for him in Hellas, and this arrived and was beached at Byrida. Learning this, the men of Michael's fleet attacked them by night, captured some of the enemy ships, and burned others with the liquid fire. On land there were frequent attacks, with Theophilus, the emperor's son, leading the people; but affairs were evenly balanced with the enemy, and victory smiled clearly on neither side. Meanwhile something happened that overthrew Thomas's affairs. For when rumour had proclaimed everywhere Thomas's revolt and the siege of the city, Mortagon, the leader of the Bulgars, who had made a thirty-year treaty under Leo and was then friendly to the Romans, came of his own accord to fight for the emperor and encamped at Kidoktos. This alarmed the rebel. Judging it not to his advantage to besiege and to make war on the Bulgars at the same time, for with his force divided he thought himself a match for neither, he went against the Bulgars with his whole army, engaged them and was defeated, and lost many of his men, some killed and some captured. Those who escaped the barbarian sword and avoided captivity kept quiet, waiting for what would come. The Bulgars, bringing the captives and much plunder, went back exulting in their victory. Learning of this defeat of the rebel, what was left of his fleet deserted to Michael.

In such a state, and wholly weakened, the usurper still did not give up the siege, but achieving nothing he withdrew from the blockade of the city and went farther off, and finding a suitable place he pitched a camp in it, and setting out from there plundered the suburbs of the city and ravaged their charms. Michael then attacked him, and when battle was joined Thomas's men willingly turned to flight, and some flowed over to the emperor, while the others each went off home. The usurper went off with very few to Adrianople, and Michael followed on his track and besieged the city, not with siege engines but with want of necessities. The people of the city, pressed by famine, asked the emperor for an amnesty for their offences, and having obtained it, bound Thomas and handed him over to Michael. He cut off his hands and feet, set him on a donkey and led him in the dishonourable triumph. Then he asked him about accomplices, and he would have revealed many, had not the patrician Exabulius checked the emperor's impulse, saying that one must not believe enemies against friends. Thomas, subjected to one punishment after another, ended his life most violently. His adopted son too fled to the little town of Bizye, was bound by those who lived in the fort and brought to the emperor, and punished violently like his pretended father, he too broke off his life. So Thomas's rising was put to rest in this way. The coastal cities of Thrace still held to the revolt even after he had passed away, and above the others Panium and Perinthus, for so Heraclea was called of old, out of hatred for the emperor. But Panium was taken when its wall fell in an earthquake, and Heraclea was taken from the sea. Having succeeded in this, Michael came back bearing a trophy, and when a horse race was held he brought into the theatre those who had helped Thomas in the usurpation, seated on donkeys, and condemned them to exile, punishing them no further, except two, Choereas and Zagorenus, who would not hand over the forts they held even after Thomas's fall; these he captured, impaled and killed.

blocks: While the Roman forces were busy with Thomas's revolt and the civil wars, the western Hagarenes, who live in the gulf of Iberia and are called Spaniards, finding full freedom, came to their leader, whom they call Amermumnes, and asked to send out a colony, being cramped by their numbers. He agreed, and taking them sailed off with triremes, going round the islands under the Romans and plundering them. When he came to Crete too and learned its great fruitfulness, he sent most of them out for plunder, while he himself, left behind with a few, forsooth to guard the ships, threw fire on them and burned them all. When the Hagarenes were thrown into confusion by this and asked the reason, Apochaps, for so their leader was named, said: "You asked for a colony; see then a land flowing with milk and honey; take it and live in it." When they said: "And where are our dearest ones?", Apochaps answered: "Here there are women, from whom you will soon have children too." Persuaded by this, the sons of Hagar brought the island under themselves and enslaved the natives. At that time Cyril, bishop of Gortyn, contended for Christ and won the crown of martyrdom.

When the emperor's wife died, he pretended openly that he did not wish to enter a second marriage, but secretly sent to the leading men of the senate that they should ask him to bring home another partner of his life. And the pretext was as if a seemly one; for they said it was a terrible thing that they should be ruled by him, while their wives were deprived of an empress. He at first, putting on airs, did not accept the request; but when they pressed him, he demanded pledges from them, if they wished him to bring in an empress, that they would have her as empress even after his death and honour the children who would be born to him by her as emperors. When the members of the senate had promised him this in writing, he pretended to be persuaded by them and brought home a woman said to be the daughter of the emperor Constantine, whom his mother had blinded, as has already been said earlier. She had long been tonsured and had been enrolled from her first hair among the nuns living as ascetics on the island of Prinkipo, and the woman's name was Euphrosyne.
When the patriarch Theodotus died, who had held the church impiously for six years, Antony, surnamed Cassimatas, was appointed, and he too was perverted in his belief about the faith.

The emperor sent a fleet against the Hagarenes who had seized Crete. But it was defeated, and those left came back as messengers of their own defeat. Then again he made ready another large navy and sent it, setting over it as general Craterus, who engaged the Hagarenes in Crete and at first had good fortune, capturing and killing many of them. Then he and the people under him, made bold by the victory, as though the enemy were already unnerved and would never dare to attack them, gave themselves over to ease and drinking without a guard, and slept that night in great carelessness. Noticing this, the enemy came on them by night with a very great war cry and destroyed them all, so that hardly a messenger of the disaster was left. For Craterus himself, the commander of the fleet, going off in flight in a merchant ship, was caught and impaled. Again another, called Ooryphas, entrusted with another navy, went round the islands, engaged the pirate ships of the Hagarenes, checked their rush for plunder, and restrained those in Crete from their former boldness.

In Sicily too another revolt was set in motion. For a man, Euphemius, commander of some body of troops, was seized with a mad love for a nun, and carried her off. So the general demanded him, to be punished for the offence. For this reason he fled to the emir of Africa, and promised to betray Sicily to him and to pay him much tribute, if he were proclaimed emperor of the Romans. He fulfilled his desire and gave him a heavy force. And Euphemius betrayed Sicily to him. So it came under the Hagarenes in this way. Euphemius not long after paid the penalty for his lawlessness and madness, and was deprived of life, killed most violently.

The emperor Michael, having enjoyed the empire for eight years and nine months, ended his life by a disease of the kidneys and retention of urine, or by dysentery, for both are said, leaving the empire to his son Theophilus. Under him Dalmatia too broke away from the rule of the Romans. It is said that there was also an ancient oracle running something like this: "A beginning of evils will fall upon the land, when there rules over Babylon a dragon of stammering tongue and very fond of gold." And he truly was very fond of gold.
