blocks: When Theophilus became sole ruler, his first work was the punishment of those who had helped his father obtain the empire and had killed Leo. And so that none of them might escape notice, he gathered the whole senate at the palace and said he was fulfilling his father's command. For his father, he said, had wished to reward worthily those who had worked with him and helped him to the empire, but had not had the chance to carry out his wish, being first busy with wars, and then falling ill and leaving life. But he had charged him to pay them the debt generously. And he urged those who had worked with his father at the overthrow of Leo to stand apart from the others. They, not understanding the trick, stood apart and said: "We are the ones who fought for your father." And he at once took off the mask of pretence and said: "Why did you lay murderous hands on the Lord's anointed, and become not only killers of men but murderers of an emperor with your own hands?" At once, then, turning to the eparch, he said: "Take these men and give them a worthy reward for their bold deed." And they, punished by the eparch, paid the penalty of murderers. Theophilus also drove his stepmother from the palace and took her to her former monastery on the island of Prinkipo, she having gained nothing from the oaths that Michael had demanded from the senate about her.

When Theophilus wished to bring home a wife, he gathered many beautiful girls from many places, among whom was Icasia, a virgin beautiful in looks and surpassing the rest, versed in letters and of distinguished family. He went round, then, looking at them, holding a golden apple, so that he might give it to the one who seemed pleasing to him. When in going round he came to Icasia, marvelling at her beauty, he said: "From a woman flowed the evil things." And she, quietly and with a modest blush, answered rather aptly: "But through a woman spring the better things too." He, as if thunderstruck by the virgin's word, passed her by and gave the golden apple to Theodora from Paphlagonia. Icasia, having missed the empire, built a monastery, which took her name as its name, and living as a nun in it she lived for herself and for God, not neglecting learning in letters. So writings of hers are found that do not lack the graces of good learning. So she arranged her own affairs, and having failed to win a perishable emperor she betrothed herself to the King of all, and gained the heavenly kingdom in place of an earthly one. The emperor Theophilus made Theodora his wife, crowned her at once with the marriage crown and the imperial diadem, and held the wedding.

Pursuing justice, he was grievous to wrongdoers and an inexorable punisher of them. So every week he went through the Market on horseback with the imperial guard to the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae. For though he gave no honour to the divine images, he kept faith, as he said, with Christ the Saviour and the Mother of God. Going off, then, and appearing in public in this way, he made himself easy of access to those who approached, and took care about goods for sale, and busied himself in finding out how each of them was sold. And if he found some things being sold dear, he examined the eparch about it, and either condemned him and removed him from office, or reproved and corrected him. Once, then, as he was going through, a woman came to him saying she was being wronged by the drungarius of the Watch, who was the brother of the Augusta, named Petronas; for she lived next door to him, and he, raising his dwellings, was darkening her house. So she brought this charge against Petronas. He, summoned by the emperor and asked what the woman might be saying, said she was talking nonsense. And the emperor said: "Let her never again petition me about this, or it will not be to your good." And he ordered the woman to go to Petronas, and if the damage were not put right, to come to him again. The woman went to Petronas, but he did nothing to put the harm right. She, despairing, again became a nuisance to the emperor; and he at once ordered some of the senate to go and inspect whether the woman was being harmed. They went at once, saw the damage, and reported it. And the emperor, still going forward in the Market, stood still there and ordered Petronas to be stripped and beaten on chest and back, and what he had built to the woman's harm to be pulled down, and the materials and the site itself to be assigned to her. This has been told as a mark of Theophilus's zeal for justice.

Let something else too be told, a sign of his just dealing and of his care for his subjects. Once a cargo ship put in at the harbour by the palace, laden with a weight of goods, and with this sunk down to its topmost wale. The emperor happened to lean out from above, and marvelling at the ship, asked through one of his attendants whose it might be. When he learned it was the Augusta's, and that it had just come in from a trading voyage that those sent by the empress had made in the parts of Syria, he ordered that if anything belonged to the ship's crew they should carry it out at once, but that no one should touch anything of the Augusta's. When this had been done and he had driven the men away from there, he brought the liquid fire against it and burned it, cargo and all, and railed at the empress, saying: "God has shown me emperor, and you force me to become a shipmaster. Know that trading has been assigned to private people, so that they may get from it the means to live. But if we, besides imperial abundance, try to get the gains of trade for ourselves too, where will those of private fortune find their living?"
text: When Theophilus became sole ruler, his first work was the punishment of those who had helped his father obtain the empire and had killed Leo. And so that none of them might escape notice, he gathered the whole senate at the palace and said he was fulfilling his father's command. For his father, he said, had wished to reward worthily those who had worked with him and helped him to the empire, but had not had the chance to carry out his wish, being first busy with wars, and then falling ill and leaving life. But he had charged him to pay them the debt generously. And he urged those who had worked with his father at the overthrow of Leo to stand apart from the others. They, not understanding the trick, stood apart and said: "We are the ones who fought for your father." And he at once took off the mask of pretence and said: "Why did you lay murderous hands on the Lord's anointed, and become not only killers of men but murderers of an emperor with your own hands?" At once, then, turning to the eparch, he said: "Take these men and give them a worthy reward for their bold deed." And they, punished by the eparch, paid the penalty of murderers. Theophilus also drove his stepmother from the palace and took her to her former monastery on the island of Prinkipo, she having gained nothing from the oaths that Michael had demanded from the senate about her. When Theophilus wished to bring home a wife, he gathered many beautiful girls from many places, among whom was Icasia, a virgin beautiful in looks and surpassing the rest, versed in letters and of distinguished family. He went round, then, looking at them, holding a golden apple, so that he might give it to the one who seemed pleasing to him. When in going round he came to Icasia, marvelling at her beauty, he said: "From a woman flowed the evil things." And she, quietly and with a modest blush, answered rather aptly: "But through a woman spring the better things too." He, as if thunderstruck by the virgin's word, passed her by and gave the golden apple to Theodora from Paphlagonia. Icasia, having missed the empire, built a monastery, which took her name as its name, and living as a nun in it she lived for herself and for God, not neglecting learning in letters. So writings of hers are found that do not lack the graces of good learning. So she arranged her own affairs, and having failed to win a perishable emperor she betrothed herself to the King of all, and gained the heavenly kingdom in place of an earthly one. The emperor Theophilus made Theodora his wife, crowned her at once with the marriage crown and the imperial diadem, and held the wedding. Pursuing justice, he was grievous to wrongdoers and an inexorable punisher of them. So every week he went through the Market on horseback with the imperial guard to the church of the Mother of God at Blachernae. For though he gave no honour to the divine images, he kept faith, as he said, with Christ the Saviour and the Mother of God. Going off, then, and appearing in public in this way, he made himself easy of access to those who approached, and took care about goods for sale, and busied himself in finding out how each of them was sold. And if he found some things being sold dear, he examined the eparch about it, and either condemned him and removed him from office, or reproved and corrected him. Once, then, as he was going through, a woman came to him saying she was being wronged by the drungarius of the Watch, who was the brother of the Augusta, named Petronas; for she lived next door to him, and he, raising his dwellings, was darkening her house. So she brought this charge against Petronas. He, summoned by the emperor and asked what the woman might be saying, said she was talking nonsense. And the emperor said: "Let her never again petition me about this, or it will not be to your good." And he ordered the woman to go to Petronas, and if the damage were not put right, to come to him again. The woman went to Petronas, but he did nothing to put the harm right. She, despairing, again became a nuisance to the emperor; and he at once ordered some of the senate to go and inspect whether the woman was being harmed. They went at once, saw the damage, and reported it. blocks: The empress's homeland was the country of the Paphlagonians, and her parents were Marinus and Theoctiste, of the well-born in their country, both pious and venerators of the revered images. When Theodora was married to the emperor, her mother Theoctiste, who was also surnamed Florina, was honoured as zoste and patrician. She lived at the monastery of the Gastria, and as some say she herself built the monastery. Once, then, the emperor's little daughters were taken to her as to their grandmother; there were five, and their names were these: Thecla and Anna, Anastasia, and Maria with Pulcheria. She welcomed the girls with gifts, and taking them aside urged them to revere the holy images, and bringing revered likenesses out of a chest, she had her granddaughters venerate and kiss them, and put them on their heads and faces. Once, when the girls came back from there, the emperor asked them what they had had from their grandmother and what she had said to them. The others were silent, but Pulcheria, still a little child, told the rest in her lisping voice and added that grandmother had dollies in a chest, so calling the images, "and she puts them on our heads and faces and gives them to us to kiss." Learning from this that his daughters were being taught by their grandmother to venerate the revered images, he no longer allowed the girls to be taken to her, but did nothing else painful to Theoctiste, respecting her for the kinship and still more for her virtue; she often rebuked him because he punished the orthodox and outraged the holy images, and assured him that for this all his subjects were hostile to him.

Something of the same kind happened about the empress. There was in the palace a little man suffering from derangement of mind and tongue, and he was like a plaything for the emperor; and being such, the women's quarters too were open to him. Once he went into the Augusta's chamber. She happened then to be kissing and venerating holy images, for she honoured them exceedingly without her husband's knowledge, and that little man, seeing the divine likenesses, asked the empress: "What are these?" And she said to him simply: "These are my pretty dollies." Going out from there, that deranged little man found Theophilus at dinner. So the emperor asked him where he had come from. He answered that he had been with Manna, for so he called the mistress, and said she had pretty dollies. The emperor, guessing the dollies were images, was enraged, and breathing wrath against the empress he poured insults on her and called her an idolater, relating what had been said by Denderis; for so that deranged little man was called. But she cleverly outwitted her husband. "Denderis did not see images," she said, "but as I was gazing into my mirror he saw the forms reflected from it and called them dollies." So, putting the story together convincingly, she softened the emperor's anger and calmed his wrath.

He was very harsh to the pious, hurrying to make all partners of his own impiety, and as he was an ardent zealot for justice, so too for piety, as he thought it, and strove madly to turn his subjects from the honour of images. From this he punished very many, trying to turn them, as he said with his unbridled tongue, from idol-madness, and made many confessors.

He sent John the synkellos, who had been his teacher and was a partner in his impiety, to the Hagarenes, wishing to display to them the wealth of the empire of the Romans. He sent him with very much money, some of which he sent as gifts to the leader of the Hagarenes, and some he assigned for the service of the man sent, among which were two ewers and basins of gold set with jewels and showing the graces of exact craftsmanship. Beyond all these he is said to have given him forty centenaria of coined gold, so that he might give to whichever of the Hagarenes he wished, generously and lavishly, and from this astonish the barbarians, who would reckon that if the ruler's men were so well supplied, how much wealth the ruler himself must be master of. So the synkellos came to the city of Baghdad, which is the ancient Babylon, came into the presence of the leader of the Hagarenes, talked with him and presented the gifts from the emperor; and for these and for the power of his speech, for he was very skilful in discussion, he was honoured and admired. He astonished the barbarians still more by being most generous towards them. For if any came to him, either sent by their own ruler or on some other business, he welcomed them with great sums of money, so that those receiving them both rejoiced and were amazed. Once, when the Amermumnes made him his table companion, he had one of those golden ewers and basins there, with which water was poured over his hands; and this, left lying carelessly, for he had ordered his servants to do so, so that it might be lost, was stolen by someone. When it was looked for and was not there, the barbarians raised an outcry, marvelling at its great value and its beauty. He, saying he did not care about what was lost, struck the barbarians with amazement, as they saw him unconcerned about such a thing, and told his servants to bring the other, which, when brought, threw the barbarians into greater amazement. The leader of the Hagarenes, vying with him in generosity, welcomed John with many gifts, and on top of all gave him a hundred captives, dressing them in rather splendid clothes. John, coming back from there and telling the emperor of things there, and of the shapes and variety of the royal houses, moved him to a desire to build such things. And he ordered a palace to be built for him at Bryas like those in Syria in every respect; and John, supervising the builders, and teaching them the shapes and the measures of breadth, length and height, quickly finished the buildings.

blocks: This emperor also renewed magnificently the sea walls of the city, which were then in a bad state both from the passage of time and from some other accidents, raising them higher than they had been before, and built a very large hostel in his own name, in a place where there had formerly been a lodging of courtesans. He was also continent in matters of love, so that only once was he caught by love for a girl serving the empress, outstanding in beauty. When Theodora was grieved at this, they say he swore he would never again have to do with another woman, was stung by remorse for the slip, and asked her forgiveness. But his madness about the revered images made all this count for nothing. For he raved outright and was more mad than those before him, and was a crueller punisher of those who honoured the sacred likenesses, and also of those who painted them. So he cruelly abused a monk Lazarus, then famous for painting, and shut him in prison; and when he recovered from the blows and again gave his hands to painting holy images, the tyrant ordered red-hot iron plates to be put on Lazarus's palms, so that the pious might not have the labours of his hands to venerate. He endured this punishment for the revered images, but the tyrant was cheated of his hopes. For it is said that after the punishment that confessor was thrown out of prison and, still bearing the wounds on his hands, with divine grace helping him, painted revered images, and after the tyrant's fall painted the likeness of the Saviour at the Chalke, and set it up as it is seen now, the divine image formerly there having long before been scraped off.

He also first cruelly abused the two brothers and confessors Theophanes and Theodore, who had exposed his impiety from prophetic sayings and from the scriptures, and then tattooed their faces and poured ink into the marks; and the marks formed letters, which were these iambics: "When all were longing to run to the city where the all-pure feet of God the Word stood for the establishment of the world, these men were seen in the revered place, wicked vessels of superstitious error. There, from unbelief, they did many shameful and terrible things with impious mind. From there they were driven out as apostates, and fleeing to the city of the empire they did not give up their lawless follies. So, written on as evildoers, they are condemned in their faces and driven out again." This persecutor made many others confessors too and handed them over to a martyr's end; to count them would be the work of another treatise and another occasion.

He was ambitious to compose hymns too; other poems of his are mentioned, and besides the others the sticheron sung at the feast of the palms, "Go forth, nations, go forth, peoples." He became the father of five daughters, but had not yet had a male child. Of his daughters he loved most the youngest, named Maria, and through her he made his son-in-law Alexius, called Mosele, a man of Armenian descent of the family of the Krenitai, in the prime of life and full of grace in his looks, whom he first honoured with other ranks and then also proclaimed Caesar. Having joined him to his daughter and honoured him so, he sent him with armies to Longobardia. Raised so high, he was not going to escape envy. So he was slandered by the envious as longing for the empire; but the slander did not take effect against the Caesar while the emperor's daughter was numbered among the living. But when a son, Michael, was born to the emperor, and the Caesar's wife had died, he at once changed his course, cut off his hair willingly, put on a worn cloak and was enrolled among the monks, and built the house of ascetics called that of Anthemius, where he lived out his life and was buried.

When the Arabs attacked the Roman lands, Theophilus marched out against them, having with him Theophobus and Manuel. These two were men both noble and good at war, of whom Manuel was known to all, even to the enemy themselves, having often been general and fought bravely, and having been protostrator of the emperor Michael Rhangabe. Theophobus was of Persian descent, but was brought up in the queen of cities and lived there, being obscure and not even known. It is said that his father sprang from the royal tribe among the Persians. When those of the royal family had died out among the Persians, they learned that there was a man among the Romans drawing his line from the royal family, and came making search for him. When the one they sought was found, he became known from this to the emperor too, and was raised to great fortune, honoured as patrician and married to the emperor's sister. Trusting in both these men, Theophilus went out against the enemy. When the armies had pitched their camps very near each other, the leader of the Saracens, Imbrael, left one of the generals under him with eighty thousand men drawn up against the Roman army, and himself withdrew with the rest, either from cowardice or from boastfulness. When the armies engaged, many fell on both sides, but at last the scholae gave way to retreat, and the emperor himself would have been taken, had not Theophobus with the Persian army about him helped with his hand and outwitted the sons of Hagar with stratagems. So then the emperor returned to the capital.

blocks: The next year he marched out again, and engaging the sons of Hagar he got the upper hand; a great multitude of them fell, and more were taken captive in war, among whom was a man known to the domestic of the scholae and vouched for by him as brave of hand, very skilful, a fine horseman, and able to handle two spears. When a triumph was held for the victory with a horse race, the ruler ordered that much-praised Hagarene to ride and handle the two spears. He, as ordered, showed the onlookers his skill with both hands. And the emperor praised and admired him. Theodore Craterus, who soon after was adorned with the crown of martyrdom, being one of the forty-two martyrs, was then standing by Theophilus and mocked the Hagarene. Filled with anger at the mockery, the ruler said: "And you, you womanish creature," for Craterus was a eunuch, "will you show anything like this?" And Craterus said: "I have not practised turning two spears, since battle needs not toys but earnest; but handling one, with God's help be it said, I shall throw this man down." The emperor, maddened at the word and swearing by himself, said: "Truly you shall die if you do not throw him down at once." And he, without delay, fought with the Hagarene and threw him from his horse.

Again, then, the emperor marched against the Hagarenes, and again there was a battle, and the end of the battle was not good for the Romans. For the emperor too would nearly have been carried off captive, surrounded by the Ishmaelites. When Manuel learned this, he shouted to those about him, drove into the midst of the enemy, and said to the emperor: "Follow me"; for he was standing still, having given up hope from cowardice. He, colouring over his cowardice, said he did not wish to flee and leave the people. But when, though often urged to leave the battle, he stood as if fettered by terror, Manuel drew his sword and said: "If you do not follow me, I shall kill you at once; for it is better for you to die than to be taken captive by the enemy and bring such a disgrace on the state of the Romans." By these threats of Manuel's he was barely freed from the numbness of fear, followed him and was saved; from this he called the man his saviour and paid him a lavish reward for his rescue. But not long after, the tongues of the envious turned the emperor's mind against Manuel. For they slandered him as attempting usurpation, and Theophilus was already persuaded by the slanders and had resolved to blind Manuel. Learning what was planned, he ran away, and coming near the Hagarenes made known to their leader who he was, and that if he received pledges that he would not be forced to forswear his own religion, he would come over to him. He at once gave pledges and received him with great joy. And Manuel, being there and entrusted with an army, did many brave deeds against the Persians and set up great trophies, and was loved and admired by the sons of Hagar.

Theophilus both grieved for Manuel and considered how to call him back from there. So, sending him pledges by oath and by a gold-sealed document with a monk, he urged him to come back. And he came back; how, must be told, for it is not unpleasant to tell. Meeting the monk who brought him the pledges from the emperor and agreeing to return, he went to the leader of the Ishmaelites and asked for an army to be given him, so that he might go into Cappadocia and pay back those who had denounced him to the emperor, for he said his accusers lived there; and he asked the leader of the Hagarenes to send his son out with him too, saying: "so that I may train him for you in warfare." He was persuaded and sent his own son out with him; for he trusted Manuel and had confidence in him. So he went off, and when he was already near the Roman borders, taking with him the ruler's son, the son of Hagar, with a few Saracens, he went out as if to hunt, with many servants following him. When he was inside the land of the Romans, he embraced the Ishmaelite's son and said: "You, child, go back to your own; I shall go to the Romans." Coming back to the great city, he was received with great joy by the emperor and at once honoured as magister, and he received from holy baptism the emperor's son Michael, whom his father crowned with the diadem and proclaimed emperor of the Romans.

When the patriarch Antony ended his life, who had held the church for ten [a gap in the text] years, John, whom the narrative has already said was Theophilus's teacher and fellow heretic, was appointed patriarch; the people of the time also called him Jannes, both for his heresy and for his sorceries, for he was practised in them. The most holy Methodius, who later adorned the patriarchal throne too, when he would not be persuaded to agree to his false belief, the impious Theophilus, after many floggings, the crushing of his jaws and the uprooting of his teeth, exiled to the island of Panormus, which is now called that of Antigonus, and shut him inside a tomb with two robbers; when one of them died, no words could describe adequately the violence and disgust the saint endured from the stench of the dead man. While that celebrated father was shut up there, the two brothers Theophanes and Theodore, being sent into exile after the tattooing of their faces and lodging at the harbour of Karta, sent this to Methodius through a fisherman known to him: "To the living dead and the life-bearing dead, who dwells on the earth and walks the heavens: the written-on, bound, write to the bound." To them the holy man wrote back through the same fisherman: "To those whose names are written in the books of heaven, and who are branded on the forehead in sober wisdom, the one buried alive speaks as to fellow prisoners." The saint spent seven years in the tomb, and then, cast out from there, was shut up in the palace, with no one seeing him except the one who served him and the emperor. For Theophilus, being studious and reading, asked the holy Methodius about what he was in doubt about; so he also always had him with him on his journeys.
text: The next year he marched out again, and engaging the sons of Hagar he got the upper hand; a great multitude of them fell, and more were taken captive in war, among whom was a man known to the domestic of the scholae and vouched for by him as brave of hand, very skilful, a fine horseman, and able to handle two spears. When a triumph was held for the victory with a horse race, the ruler ordered that much-praised Hagarene to ride and handle the two spears. He, as ordered, showed the onlookers his skill with both hands. And the emperor praised and admired him. Theodore Craterus, who soon after was adorned with the crown of martyrdom, being one of the forty-two martyrs, was then standing by Theophilus and mocked the Hagarene. Filled with anger at the mockery, the ruler said: "And you, you womanish creature," for Craterus was a eunuch, "will you show anything like this?" And Craterus said: "I have not practised turning two spears, since battle needs not toys but earnest; but handling one, with God's help be it said, I shall throw this man down." The emperor, maddened at the word and swearing by himself, said: "Truly you shall die if you do not throw him down at once." And he, without delay, fought with the Hagarene and threw him from his horse. Again, then, the emperor marched against the Hagarenes, and again there was a battle, and the end of the battle was not good for the Romans. For the emperor too would nearly have been carried off captive, surrounded by the Ishmaelites. When Manuel learned this, he shouted to those about him, drove into the midst of the enemy, and said to the emperor: "Follow me"; for he was standing still, having given up hope from cowardice. He, colouring over his cowardice, said he did not wish to flee and leave the people. But when, though often urged to leave the battle, he stood as if fettered by terror, Manuel drew his sword and said: "If you do not follow me, I shall kill you at once; for it is better for you to die than to be taken captive by the enemy and bring such a disgrace on the state of the Romans." By these threats of Manuel's he was barely freed from the numbness of fear, followed him and was saved; from this he called the man his saviour and paid him a lavish reward for his rescue. But not long after, the tongues of the envious turned the emperor's mind against Manuel. For they slandered him as attempting usurpation, and Theophilus was already persuaded by the slanders and had resolved to blind Manuel. Learning what was planned, he ran away, and coming near the Hagarenes made known to their leader who he was, and that if he received pledges that he would not be forced to forswear his own religion, he would come over to him. He at once gave pledges and received him with great joy. And Manuel, being there and entrusted with an army, did many brave deeds against the Persians and set up great trophies, and was loved and admired by the sons of Hagar. Theophilus both grieved for Manuel and considered how to call him back from there. So, sending him pledges by oath and by a gold-sealed document with a monk, he urged him to come back. And he came back; how, must be told, for it is not unpleasant to tell. Meeting the monk who brought him the pledges from the emperor and agreeing to return, he went to the leader of the Ishmaelites and asked for an army to be given him, so that he might go into Cappadocia and pay back those who had denounced him to the emperor, for he said his accusers lived there; and he asked the leader of the Hagarenes to send his son out with him too, saying: "so that I may train him for you in warfare." He was persuaded and sent his own son out with him; for he trusted Manuel and had confidence in him. So he went off, and when he was already near the Roman borders, taking with him the ruler's son, the son of Hagar, with a few Saracens, he went out as if to hunt, with many servants following him. blocks: When spring came the emperor again took up arms against the Hagarenes, sacked much of Syria and mastered cities, and Sozopetra itself, which happened to be the native city of the Amermumnes, though he begged much that he spare his native city. So the emperor returned with good fortune. Theophobus, left behind to manage the affairs of the armies, when the pay of the Persians fell behind (for the emperor had a Persian army), and the Persians were very aggrieved at this, was proclaimed emperor by them, even against his will, or rather while he begged them to give up their madness, lest they bring themselves and him into the worst evils; but he did not persuade them. So he sent to the emperor, hiding this from the Persians, making known what had happened and assuring him that he should suspect nothing against him. And coming back he went to the emperor, and was received most kindly and got back his former prosperity. The Persians too were all granted pardon, and nothing else was laid on them except that they were not allowed to be all together, but, numbering thirty thousand, they were divided, and two thousand were assigned to each theme, so as to be under the generals of the themes and obey them. So matters concerning the Persians and Theophobus stood thus.

The sacking of his native city touched the Amermumnes so deeply that life was not bearable for him unless he avenged it on Theophilus. Learning, then, that Amorium was Theophilus's native city, he resolved to march against it. The emperor, learning this, fortified it, among other ways by sending armies, led by Theodore Craterus, whom the history mentioned a little before, and the rest, who also finished the race of martyrdom among the Hagarenes, forty-two in all. The emperor too went out to meet the sons of Hagar, and engaging the son of the Amermumnes, who came with an army a match for him, he was put to flight. When night came on, Manuel, going round the guards of the camp, heard some of the Persians talking of betraying them to the Hagarenes, for he understood their language, and reported this to the emperor, and persuaded him to rise and leave the camp about dawn. And he went off, giving his horse its head. From then the Amermumnes, free of care, undertook the siege of Amorium and made attacks on the city most continuously; but he achieved nothing, since those inside fought back strongly, so that the Hagarenes even despaired of taking it, and they would have gone away and the city would not have been sacked, had not one of those inside, maddened over some quarrel, become its betrayer; his surname was Boïditzes. When the town was taken, how many people were killed it is not possible to say. Women, children and boys, numbering many thousands, were carried off captive, and the leading men among those in command there, the patricians Callistus, Constantine and Theodore Craterus, and many others of those distinguished in commands and illustrious from the honour of their ranks.

Learning this, Theophilus, who was at Dorylaeum, sent envoys to the leader of the Ishmaelites, asking that the notable men among the captives and those related to him by birth be given back to him for twenty-four centenaria. But he sent the envoys away insolently, saying: "I would be a fool if, when the expense of the campaign has come to about a thousand centenaria, I gave back the captives for so little." When the envoys came back without success, the calamity reached Theophilus's soul so deeply that no consolation could be found for him against it, but he even kept from food and would take no drink except only very cold water, like that from snow; using this constantly, he was struck in his inward parts, and the disease of dysentery fell on him. Reaching the palace, and already knowing his recovery hopeless, he called the senate, and asked them to show faith to his wife and son and to keep the imperial rule for them; and they agreed. When this had been done,

blocks: the emperor, who had held Theophobus suspect even before, ever since he was proclaimed emperor by the Persians, was confirmed still more in his suspicion by the betrayal that the Persians had planned to make, as I have already written, since those who slandered the man insisted that the Persians did this at his suggestions. When the emperor's body was already wasted by the disease and his strength had failed, afraid that after his death he would attempt usurpation, he shut him up at the palace, and when he knew that his life hung by a thin thread and was about to fail, he ordered Theophobus to be killed and his head to be brought to him; and when it was brought, the story is that the emperor laid his hand on it and, touching its hair, said: "From now on neither am I Theophilus nor you Theophobus." And on this he breathed out his soul, having reigned twelve years and three months, after urging his wife much, and Theoctistus of the Kanikleion, who then held power beside her, not to allow the revered images to be set up again, nor the patriarch John to be driven from the church.

blocks: So Theophilus died on this, and the rule of the empire passed to his son Michael, who was still a child, and for whom his father left as guardians the magister Manuel and the patrician Theoctistus. The management of affairs was handled by the empress Theodora, and her first concern was to end the persecution of the orthodox over the revered likenesses, the patrician Theoctistus too agreeing. For Manuel did not agree to the putting down of the heresy; so the deed was put off. But providence broke him with disease, and the disease was strong and his life was despaired of. Some monks came to visit him and asked how he was, and he answered in a thin, feeble voice, as one already failing. They said: "If you agree to consent to the honour of the images and to urge the empress to it, before long you will have both health of body and salvation of soul." He promised, and the disease weakened and Manuel grew strong again. When he had recovered his health he went to the empress, spoke about the revered images and pressed for their restoration, while her mother and her brothers, the patricians, also championed this. And she was a razor to the whetstone. First she released all those sent into exile by Theophilus, those shut up, and those struggling with other ill-treatment. Then she ordered an inquiry to be held about the heresy, and when it was held the multitude of the orthodox prevailed. Before the inquiry she dragged down from the high priestly throne the falsely named patriarch, the sorcerer John, who had mounted it lawlessly for six years, and brought in in his place the holy and divine Methodius. With him presiding over the body of the orthodox the inquiry took place, and the public veneration and restoration of the holy likenesses. At that time, they say, the empress also begged most fervently the patriarch and the other high priests and monks to offer a common prayer to God that the emperor, her husband, might obtain salvation; and that they did pray to God most fervently, and he did not overlook the request of his servants, but granted pardon to the emperor Theophilus. This is sung, and is accepted and believed by those who look to the love of God for men. For no one will disbelieve it except one who does not think the prayers of the saints to God have great power, nor knows how to weigh the goodness of God against human ignorance. So the restoration of the holy images came about in this way.

The deposed patriarch John, or Jannes, confined in a monastery, and finding there an image of Christ the Saviour and of her who bore him without seed, dug out the eyes of the revered likenesses. When the empress learned this, burning with divine zeal, she ordered that impious man's eyes to be cut out; but the order was not carried into effect, since some calmed the empress's just anger. But she sent and had him flogged with a strap, the blows being stretched to two hundred. Yet even so the sorcerer and those of his belief who had been put down with him could not bear to keep quiet. They put together a plot against the holy Methodius worthy of their madness, or rather their malice. For they corrupted a shameful woman with a gift of much gold and persuaded her to accuse that celebrated man of having been corrupted with her. The leading men of the senate were present as examiners of the charge. The woman was brought in, saying all she had been schooled in beforehand by those impious slanderers, and forsooth convicting the saint to his face. He kept quiet for a while; but when he saw the body of the church downcast, and above the others the magister Manuel, he stood up, raised with his hands the hem of his garment in the sight of all, and bared his private parts; they were wholly withered and had suffered wasting from some accident, so that it was plain they could not act for love. This was a cause of joy and amazement to the right-minded, and of shame and great dismay to the slanderers. When the saint was asked how the wasting of his parts had come about, that truly modest man said: "I was once sent to Rome on some business, and while I was living there the demon brought on me a burning of the flesh, and the passion was most violent, and the inflammation of desire did not stop, but burned more fiercely every day. Fearing for my chastity, I went to the chief pair of the apostles, Peter and Paul, and begged them to help me in my danger. Sleeping, then, at night, I saw the two men standing over me, and Peter seemed to touch my private parts with his fingers and tell me not to be afraid, and fire seemed to feed on my organs of generation, so that from the pain I even woke from sleep. Since then these parts have been dead in me and the burning has troubled me no more." The magister Manuel, having seen and heard this, at once set the woman before him and asked her what had moved her to the slander against the saint, and threatened, unless she made the truth plain to all, to hand her over at once to tortures, by which she would be forced to uncover the plot clearly. She hid nothing, but reported the first authors of the play, her own deceit, and of the gold, the giving of part and the promise of the rest. So the evildoers were about to be subjected to the penalties for slanderers, but the great Methodius saved them from punishment; and so this happened.

blocks: The ruler of the Bulgars, learning that the empire of the Romans was governed by a woman and a young child, sent some of his men threatening to withdraw from the treaty and take up arms against the dominion of the Romans. To this the empress made known to him: "I shall certainly set myself against you too; and if by God's gift I prevail, you will have been beaten by a woman, and reckon how ready to hand your shame will be; but if perhaps you win, there will be no glory for you in the success, having beaten a woman." When this was reported to the barbarian, it checked his impulse, and he judged it to his advantage to renew the treaty, and it was renewed. A sister of the ruler of Bulgaria, who had once been taken captive and was living in the palace, had been initiated in divine baptism and had become instructed in letters. Her brother asked that she be given back to him, and she was given to him; and he gave in return a man of the notable sort, Theodore Cupharas. The sister of the ruler of the Bulgars, coming to her brother, drew him towards the religion of the Christians, talking with him about it all the time and extolling the mysteries of the Christians. He had also been instructed in this beforehand by Cupharas, but had not yet been persuaded to give up his ancestral customs. A famine that befell the Bulgars changed both him and the nation to piety. For it pressed the whole nation, and there was no escape from the evil, but the nation was being destroyed, and their leader was grieved at this, and at a loss he fled to the God proclaimed to him by his sister, and called on him as deliverer from the famine and the destruction of the nation. When the invocation took effect and they were freed from the evils, he knew the power of the one called on, and asked that someone be sent to him to initiate him into the mystery of the Christians and perform divine baptism on him. A high priest was sent to him; and he was initiated and baptised. The Bulgars, since he had given up the ancestral belief, rose against their leader and sought to kill him. But he, trusting in the sign of the cross going before him, defeated those who rose against him, and so all chose the ways of the Christians.

Then their ruler sent envoys to the empress, asking that Roman land be granted to him, since his nation was cramped, and promising everlasting peace with the Romans and alliance in arms; and the empress fulfilled the request and granted him the land from the place called Sidera, which formerly divided the lands of the Romans and the Bulgars, as far as Develtus; having received this the Bulgars have called it Zagora. And from then there was peace in the west.

In the east the race of the Manichaeans was very numerous; they are called, rather boorishly, Paulicians by the common crowd, their name being made from Paul and John; these two men became famous among the Manichaeans, though they were not founders of the heresy or begetters of the false belief, but exceptional zealots, students and heralds of it. The empress took it into her head to bring these too over from the heresy to orthodoxy, and sent some of the more distinguished men to press this. But they, handling the matter clumsily and without skill, not only made the effort fruitless, but also forced the whole race, numbering many tens of thousands, to break out in revolt. Mixing with the sons of Ishmael, it campaigned with them against the Romans, and became for them the cause of many disasters.

The emperor Michael, having passed boyhood and just being counted among the young men, and seeing the management of the empire in others' hands, was also stirred to desire for sole rule by his uncle on his mother's side, Bardas; he too was one of Michael's guardians. Once, when a quarrel arose between the magister Manuel and the logothete of the drome Theoctistus, both of whom were fellow guardians of the emperor, Manuel withdrew from the palace, where he had been living, moved to his own house, and going from there to the palace kept up his work of administration. This seemed most welcome to Bardas; so he was eager to get rid of Theoctistus too; for longing for the empire, he feared him as one who would stand against him in the deed. The emperor had a tutor, a mean and wicked little man, whom the emperor desired to honour with some of the more splendid ranks, and he made a request about this to his mother. But Theoctistus said that the tutor ought not to be honoured with an honour greater than his station, so that the ranks might not be dishonoured. From this Theoctistus was hated by the tutor. Bardas, then, put this forward as the foundation of his own design, and through the tutor poured various slanders into the emperor's ears, and pricked his light-mindedness against Theoctistus, and at last suggested that he put him out of the way. This could not be done otherwise, he said, unless the man were killed; for while he lived the empress would hold on to him and keep him close. So when the man's death had been settled, he was watched for as he came out of the empress's chambers, for he was reporting to her about reports and administration; and as he came out from there they let loose the slayer on him. He, seeing the bare sword raised against him, crept under a bench, and the slayer drove the sword into his belly, Bardas too having drawn his sword and brandishing it, and threatening to strike anyone who would help the dying man. So Theoctistus was killed as has been said. The empress, when she learned what had happened, leapt out of her chamber wailing and railing at her son and her brother, and praying that both might go out of life by such an end. Bardas, joining evil to evil and arranging matters for his own design, advised that the empress Theodora herself be brought down from the palace. She, understanding what was planned, chose not to resist, so that no slaughter of men might happen. Sending for the members of the council, she said: "I myself am leaving the palace; but so that the emperor may not be able to say that he found the treasuries of the palace empty of treasure, I am showing you what has been stored up." And at once she ordered the treasurers to state the amount of gold and silver. They declared that there were one thousand and ninety centenaria of gold, and about three thousand centenaria of silver. And the empress said: "Besides these, much other wealth of every kind has been stored up." And having said this she left the palace.
text: The ruler of the Bulgars, learning that the empire of the Romans was governed by a woman and a young child, sent some of his men threatening to withdraw from the treaty and take up arms against the dominion of the Romans. To this the empress made known to him: "I shall certainly set myself against you too; and if by God's gift I prevail, you will have been beaten by a woman, and reckon how ready to hand your shame will be; but if perhaps you win, there will be no glory for you in the success, having beaten a woman." When this was reported to the barbarian, it checked his impulse, and he judged it to his advantage to renew the treaty, and it was renewed. A sister of the ruler of Bulgaria, who had once been taken captive and was living in the palace, had been initiated in divine baptism and had become instructed in letters. Her brother asked that she be given back to him, and she was given to him; and he gave in return a man of the notable sort, Theodore Cupharas. The sister of the ruler of the Bulgars, coming to her brother, drew him towards the religion of the Christians, talking with him about it all the time and extolling the mysteries of the Christians. He had also been instructed in this beforehand by Cupharas, but had not yet been persuaded to give up his ancestral customs. A famine that befell the Bulgars changed both him and the nation to piety. For it pressed the whole nation, and there was no escape from the evil, but the nation was being destroyed, and their leader was grieved at this, and at a loss he fled to the God proclaimed to him by his sister, and called on him as deliverer from the famine and the destruction of the nation. When the invocation took effect and they were freed from the evils, he knew the power of the one called on, and asked that someone be sent to him to initiate him into the mystery of the Christians and perform divine baptism on him. A high priest was sent to him; and he was initiated and baptised. The Bulgars, since he had given up the ancestral belief, rose against their leader and sought to kill him. But he, trusting in the sign of the cross going before him, defeated those who rose against him, and so all chose the ways of the Christians. Then their ruler sent envoys to the empress, asking that Roman land be granted to him, since his nation was cramped, and promising everlasting peace with the Romans and alliance in arms; and the empress fulfilled the request and granted him the land from the place called Sidera, which formerly divided the lands of the Romans and the Bulgars, as far as Develtus; having received this the Bulgars have called it Zagora. And from then there was peace in the west. In the east the race of the Manichaeans was very numerous; they are called, rather boorishly, Paulicians by the common crowd, their name being made from Paul and John; these two men became famous among the Manichaeans, though they were not founders of the heresy or begetters of the false belief, but exceptional zealots, students and heralds of it. The empress took it into her head to bring these too over from the heresy to orthodoxy, and sent some of the more distinguished men to press this. But they, handling the matter clumsily and without skill, not only made the effort fruitless, but also forced the whole race, numbering many tens of thousands, to break out in revolt. Mixing with the sons of Ishmael, it campaigned with them against the Romans, and became for them the cause of many disasters. The emperor Michael, having passed boyhood and just being counted among the young men, and seeing the management of the empire in others' hands, was also stirred to desire for sole rule by his uncle on his mother's side, Bardas; he too was one of Michael's guardians. Once, when a quarrel arose between the magister Manuel and the logothete of the drome Theoctistus, both of whom were fellow guardians of the emperor, Manuel withdrew from the palace, where he had been living, moved to his own house, and going from there to the palace kept up his work of administration. This seemed most welcome to Bardas; so he was eager to get rid of Theoctistus too; for longing for the empire, he feared him as one who would stand against him in the deed. The emperor had a tutor, a mean and wicked little man, whom the emperor desired to honour with some of the more splendid ranks, and he made a request about this to his mother. But Theoctistus said that the tutor ought not to be honoured with an honour greater than his station, so that the ranks might not be dishonoured. From this Theoctistus was hated by the tutor. blocks: Michael, having become master of sole rule, quickly scattered so much wealth, throwing it away on mimes, flatterers and charioteers, and emptying it out, as the saying goes, by whole wagonloads. When the treasuries had been emptied, and the time came for the distribution owed to the ranks, and he had nothing from which to make it, he melted down the golden plane tree, the two lions, the many griffins and the organs, all made of gold, which were an ornament of the empire and struck amazement into those from foreign nations, and gave them to have coins struck from them. He also did this with imperial robes, some of which, still surviving when he perished, Basil, who reigned after him, recovered, finding only three centenaria of the counted amount. Michael did not let his mother, after she had withdrawn from the palace, live in peace, but at Bardas's suggestion sent and had her and his sisters tonsured, confined them in the house of Carianus, and took away all they had. Theodora, struck in her soul by this, moved to the monasteries there, living only a little while after the calamity. Her daughters, the emperor's sisters, drained the evils brought upon them; Basil the Macedonian, after he took hold of the empire, later took them to the monastery of their grandmother on their mother's side, which is called Gastria. When the emperor's mother had left the palace, as has been said, the whole management of the empire came under Bardas, who was honoured as curopalates by his nephew.

Then Michael, just growing his first beard, marched out against the Hagarenes, and undertook to besiege their city Samosata, which is one of the cities by the Euphrates. The Ishmaelites barred the gates of the city against the besiegers and stayed inside, giving them the impression that from cowardice they had shut themselves in within the circuit wall. This brought the Romans to boldness, and they encamped carelessly and scattered without a guard. After pretending cowardice for three days, the sons of Hagar suddenly threw open the gates and fell on the Roman camp with a violent rush and a war cry, and no one withstood their onset, but all looked to flight, and as they were caught some were killed and others taken alive. At that time the Manichaeans too, fighting with the Ishmaelites, took alive many of the notable generals and sold them for great sums. Then the emperor himself would nearly have been taken, had he not escaped the enemy by the speed of his horse and got away safe. The camp was taken, and the imperial tent, and the baggage for the emperor's service, and everything else was plundered. Then Michael went back. Again, learning that the Hagarenes were attacking the lands of the Romans, he went out against them with a heavier force. They came through difficult but short ways unexpectedly on the Roman army and routed it. The emperor too would have been taken, had not the magister Manuel, who was domestic of the scholae, saved him.

The enemy did not stop harming the Roman lands. So the emperor's uncle on his mother's side, Petronas, was sent against them with Roman forces to set himself against them. He did not dare an engagement, but was afraid of the war. Learning, then, of a monk living as an ascetic on a mountain, famous for virtue and foreseeing the future, he went off to him and asked whether he should undertake the war; and he allowed it and promised him victory. So Petronas went off and attacked the enemy, and the army of the Hagarenes was defeated, and its commander Amer fell. His son, who was away from the battle, for he happened to have gone off for plunder, learning of the defeat and the death of his father, ran away, but he too was caught in his flight and handed over to the general. It is said that before this battle Amer asked one of the captives what the place where our camp is was called, and what the river flowing by was called, and what name that whole country had. When he said the country was called Lalakaon, the place of the camp Ptosas, and the river Gyres, he, taking an omen from these names, said that these names showed the end of the war would not be favourable for him. For he called Lalakaon "harm to the people", said Ptosas meant "fall", and from the name of the river divined that they would be surrounded by the enemy. So the victory went thus for Petronas; and he came back to Byzantium bearing a trophy, was received with honour, and was appointed domestic of the scholae. For Manuel had already died. Not long after he too paid his debt to nature.

blocks: Having shaken off all these, Bardas arranged the management of affairs as he wished. For Michael paid attention to nothing, but spent his time only on theatres and horse races, not with others driving, but the emperor himself, the Augustus, driving the chariot, the emperor competing, having put on a charioteer's dress in place of the imperial robe. Nor was this alone the terrible thing, but also that he forced those who were eminent in rank and honours to compete, some on his side and some against him, in the horse races, and to drive chariots. Once, then, he himself had put on the blue colour, the logothete of the drome the green, and others of the more notable the other colours; and they had already mounted the chariots. At that moment a letter was handed to the protonotarius of the drome by someone just arrived, announcing that the Saracens had encamped at the Melangeia; these are what are now more rustically called Malagina. The protonotarius, gloomy at the news, came to the emperor, told him this and showed him the letter. He, glaring at him angrily and madly, said: "When I am in such a contest, and am hurrying to take the middle place on the left, do you, you fool, talk to me about an inroad of Saracens?" Such was that wonderful emperor, and so did he care for public affairs and for the empire.

While he was in this state, Bardas turned everything and led it wherever he chose, and rose to the honour of Caesar, and courted the empire for himself, and sought an opportunity to obtain it. He did nothing good except that he took great care for learning. For philosophy had been neglected and almost wholly extinguished, so that not even a spark of it was left. The folly of the rulers had done this. He set apart schools for each of the sciences, put teachers over them, and assigned public allowances to each of them; and over all he set as teacher the philosopher Leo, whose fame for wisdom was great, and who had also become honoured by the emperor Theophilus in the following way. He had many students, and it happened that one of them, who had been initiated exactly into geometry, was captured by the Saracens, and he was assigned to serve one of the notable men among the barbarians. The man then presiding over the sons of Hagar was fond of learning and listened carefully to philosophical studies, and was devoted more than to the others to geometrical methods. The captive's master too used to go to the lecture hall, and once the captive followed him, and hearing the teachers and seeing them drawing geometrical figures and teaching that the triangle is the beginning of every figure, so that every figure is made up from it and resolved into it, and that of all figures of equal perimeter and equal sides the circle has the greatest capacity, and other such things, the captive asked his master whether he might question the teachers about what they were teaching; and he allowed it. He asked them to make clear the reasons for what was being taught. They were at a loss at this, and the leader of the Hagarenes called the captive and said: "Could you give the reasons for these things?" He agreed. "Speak, then," he said. And the captive began and made each thing clear, gave the reasons and listed the causes. And the hearers came to understand what was said and applied themselves more keenly to the theorems, and their minds were broadened, and they marvelled at the man and asked whether Constantine's city had others like him. He said: "It has many better than me, and one, the teacher of all, a man without rival in every branch of philosophy." Hearing this, the leader of the Hagarenes was caught by love for that teacher, and wished to come to see and hear him, and writing a letter to the man asking him to come and share his wisdom with him, he sent it by the captive, having treated him generously. When the letter was brought to him, Leo, afraid of being accused of receiving a letter from enemies, handed the letter to the logothete of the drome and presented the captive, and he related the matter. From this the philosopher Leo became known to Theophilus, was rewarded and urged to teach publicly, and then was also ordained high priest of Thessalonica. But when Theophilus died and the iconoclast high priests were deposed, Leo too was deposed with them, because he gave no honour to the divine images. So Bardas, finding him at leisure, set him over the other teachers, and so made learning flourish again, and brought it before long to growth. He also made the civil laws young again, himself attending the courts, when knowledge of them too had almost wholly failed. So Bardas's zeal for the sciences and studies deserves praise, but the rest was very blameworthy and despicable.

When the holy Methodius, having directed the church for four years, had moved to the eternal mansions, the monk Ignatius presided over the church. He was the grandson through his mother of the emperor Nicephorus, the former general logothete, and son of the emperor Michael Rhangabe, and after his father's fall from the empire, having been made a eunuch by Leo, he cut off his hair and for a long time subdued his flesh with ascetic sweat; the empress Theodora, when she directed the empire, brought him up to the high priestly throne of Constantinople. This divine man, then, forbade the Caesar Bardas, who had sent away his wife without cause and was said to be corrupted with his own daughter-in-law, to enter the sacred precincts. For this Bardas removed the high priest from the church, and after ill-treating him much shut him at last in a tomb. Then, bringing him out from there, he exiled him to the island of Mitylene. And he treated not only him so, but also many other high priests, as many as had voted with Ignatius when he excommunicated him; and he appointed as patriarch Photius, one of the notable men of the time and most famous in learning. When it happened that legates of the pope of Rome were also present, sent against the iconoclasts, Bardas persuaded them too to be of his mind. So, gathering in the church of the Holy Apostles, they brought the most holy Ignatius from exile and put him under deposition. And this happened somewhat in this way.

blocks: The nation of the Rhos, a Scythian nation of those around the Taurus, overran the regions of the Euxine Sea with a fleet and planned to attack Byzantium itself. But their plan was not carried into effect, since providence from above prevented it, and arranged that they should go away unwillingly and with nothing done, or rather after experiencing divine wrath. The Hagarenes from Crete were also plundering the Cyclades islands and the coastlands. Very violent earthquakes also happened, of which the most fearful shook the earth on the day of our Saviour's ascension. None of these drew Michael away from the horse races and his zeal for them, while he himself drove the races at the place in the Narrows called that of Saint Mamas.

So he also stopped the beacons that the emperors of old had devised, so that the sons of Hagar, invading the lands of the Romans suddenly, might not plunder what lay in their way and carry the people off captive. For this reason they had built a fort near Tarsus on a high hill, called Lulon, and those in it lit a beacon when they learned of an inroad of Ishmaelites; seeing this, those on Mount Argaeus made another beacon, and those on Isamus another, and when those on Aegialus saw this another was raised, and by those on Mimas another, and those on Cyrizus again made signal fires, and those on Mocilus likewise lit a beacon, and last of all a beacon was raised on the hill of Saint Auxentius. Seeing these, those in the countryside shut themselves up quickly in strongholds and avoided the plundering of the barbarians. And from the hill of Saint Auxentius knowledge of the enemy's inroad was given to the reigning emperor. So, so that he might not be interrupted in the horse races, since these beacons were often raised during them, he voted that the beacons near the capital should stop.

He also found fault with those who had reigned before, that they did not delight in simplicity, but laid claim to pomp and imperial grandeur. So he, thinking he was pursuing moderation, once met a woman who had just bathed and was going home, and getting off his horse he went off with the woman with a few young men who shared his secrets, and having been in her house and shared her table, he went off on foot to the palace. In such things he swaggered as if achieving something great, but by others he was judged to be acting foolishly, and they nursed hatred against him. Not least he seemed hateful because of the accursed young men kept about him, who fired him to every evil; they also made themselves out to be high priests and pretended to perform the bloodless rite, having Michael himself forsooth officiating with them, jesting in things not to be jested with, mixing vinegar and mustard and pouring the mixture into gold vessels set with stones, supplied by him, and giving a share of it to their fellow initiates and fellow players. But to list all the doings of such a troupe, of which the emperor himself was a fellow reveller, would be a matter of much talk and of no little disgust. The narrative has come to tell of the death of Bardas and of the ruler himself, and before these, of how Basil the Macedonian came to be close to Michael,

For this reason they had built a fort near Tarsus on a high hill, called Lulon, and those in it lit a beacon when they learned of an inroad of Ishmaelites; seeing this, those on Mount Argaeus made another beacon, and those on Isamus another, and when those on Aegialus saw this another was raised, and by those on Mimas another, and those on Cyrizus again made signal fires, and those on Mocilus likewise lit a beacon, and last of all a beacon was raised on the hill of Saint Auxentius. Seeing these, those in the countryside shut themselves up quickly in strongholds and avoided the plundering of the barbarians. And from the hill of Saint Auxentius knowledge of the enemy's inroad was given to the reigning emperor. So, so that he might not be interrupted in the horse races, since these beacons were often raised during them, he voted that the beacons near the capital should stop. He also found fault with those who had reigned before, that they did not delight in simplicity, but laid claim to pomp and imperial grandeur. So he, thinking he was pursuing moderation, once met a woman who had just bathed and was going home, and getting off his horse he went off with the woman with a few young men who shared his secrets, and having been in her house and shared her table, he went off on foot to the palace. In such things he swaggered as if achieving something great, but by others he was judged to be acting foolishly, and they nursed hatred against him. Not least he seemed hateful because of the accursed young men kept about him, who fired him to every evil; they also made themselves out to be high priests and pretended to perform the bloodless rite, having Michael himself forsooth officiating with them, jesting in things not to be jested with, mixing vinegar and mustard and pouring the mixture into gold vessels set with stones, supplied by him, and giving a share of it to their fellow initiates and fellow players. But to list all the doings of such a troupe, of which the emperor himself was a fellow reveller, would be a matter of much talk and of no little disgust. The narrative has come to tell of the death of Bardas and of the ruler himself, and before these, of how Basil the Macedonian came to be close to Michael,

blocks: who was from Macedonia, and was born of obscure and undistinguished parents, though one of those who have written his history tells the marvellous tale that he descended from the family of the Arsacids. When Krum, who was leader of the Bulgars, seized Adrianople, his parents too were taken captive and carried off to their country, bringing him newborn and still at the breast. After Krum had died, another took hold of the rule of the Bulgars, who, having often been broken in wars with the Romans, made a treaty with the then ruler of the Romans and agreed to free the captives, and did so according to the terms. Basil had then reached the age of youth. From infancy, they say, many signs happened foretelling the empire to him, of which one was the following. Basil was an infant, his parents were busy with the harvest, and the infant lay sleeping in the sun; and an eagle, flying low with its wings spread, made a shade for the baby. When the mother saw the eagle coming near the child, she raised her voice, ran to her son and drove the eagle off with stones. When she went back to her work, the eagle again came to the sleeping baby, performing its service. And the mother was again alarmed and drove it off. When this happened many times, she came to understand and took the thing for a good omen.

When he had passed boyhood, his father ended his life, and his mother was pressed by poverty besides the evils of widowhood. He, not being well supplied with the necessities of life, decided to hire himself out for service to someone; and setting out he went to the great city. Entering late in the evening by the gate of the city called the Golden, he lodged by the church of Saint Diomedes, which was not yet a monastery then; and lying down outside the precinct he fell asleep. In the night the martyr stood over the sacristan of the church in a dream, and ordered him to bring the emperor inside. He went out, and finding Basil sleeping on the bare ground, took the dream for an empty phantom. When the saint again seemed to order the same thing, and he again went out and found no one but Basil, he went back taking it the same way. So for the third time the martyr stood over the sacristan and urged him to bring in the man lying outside, saying: "For this is the emperor." So the sacristan went out, roused Basil, gave him hospitality in his dwelling, and shared with him what he had. The sacristan had a brother who practised medicine and served Theophilitzes. This Theophilitzes was related by birth to the Caesar Bardas and the emperor Michael, and because of his very small stature was called by the pet name Theophilitzes. The sacristan, revealing the secret dream to this brother, asked him to recommend this man to one of the officials for service. And he recommended him to his own master. But first both brothers revealed to Basil the prophecy about the empire given through dreams, and bound him beforehand by oaths to remember them in his reign.

Theophilitzes, pleased with Basil, for he was handsome and tall, brave and very skilful of hand, wearing his hair thick and curly, set him over his own grooms; common speech is accustomed to call this protostrator. A brave groom, well suited to this service, was being looked for by the emperor too. For a horse had been brought to the emperor Michael from somewhere, fit for every excellence becoming a horse, but stiff-necked and not easily mounted. Coming to see it, the emperor told someone to mount it. When many had tried, it grew bold and spirited and threw off the rider. The emperor was annoyed at this and vexed that he had no skilful groom. Theophilitzes, who was present, said he himself had such a man, and said: "If you wish, emperor, let him come forward." And he allowed it, and Basil was called, and taking hold of the horse's bridle, clicking to it and stroking it, he lifted himself lightly and mounted, and after cantering round a little, then gave it full rein and rode it out. The emperor was pleased at this, took Basil on, enrolled him among the imperial grooms, and as time went on also honoured the man as protostrator; the rank is one of the notable ones and of those close to the emperor. And the emperor's goodwill towards Basil grew every day, and so much that it even moved the Caesar to envy.

blocks: Once, when the emperor's mother was dining with the emperor, the protostrator Basil was called in at the emperor's order. And the empress gazed at him continually and looked the man over rather closely, and then declared like an oracle that he was the destroyer of her family, knowing this, as she said, from some signs made known to her long before by her own husband. But this seemed nonsense to Michael, and nothing drew him from his goodwill towards Basil, and he had already appointed him parakoimomenos. This too increased the Caesar's envy of Basil, and he plotted against the man and was plotted against by him in return. When a campaign was proclaimed by Michael against the Hagarenes holding Crete, the Caesar went to the church of the Mother of God called that of the Hodegoi, to take his leave of the Mother of God, and as he was already approaching the altar his cloak slipped from his shoulders for no evident cause. This sign seemed ill-omened both to the Caesar and to those who saw it. When many blamed the emperor because he had given all authority to the Caesar, so that he did whatever he wished and much that was improper, through the persistence of the reproaches that stupid man once seemed to sober up a little from his very deep stupor, and corrected and undid some of the Caesar's arrangements; this Bardas could not bear, but was very heavy at heart at it.

When the emperor marched out, as has been said, the Caesar marched out with him, and Basil and those about him made frequent slanders against him to Michael, and because of these the plot against him was confirmed. But since the Caesar was surrounded with great power, those preparing the plot were afraid. One morning, when Bardas had come out from his own tent with splendour and a large guard, and had come to the emperor, sat down with him and was talking with him, Basil, standing behind him, shook his hand, as if threatening the Caesar. He, suddenly turning round for some other reason and seeing Basil's hand and understanding what was meant, threw himself at the emperor's feet. Those sworn against him hesitated over the attempt, until Basil himself first brought his sword against him. So the others too took courage, surrounded Bardas and cut him limb from limb, and such was the end of his life that befell him.

The emperor gave up the campaign and returned to Byzantium, and joined to Basil Eudocia the daughter of Inger, who had earlier been the ruler's own concubine; then he proclaimed him emperor too, coming himself to the Great Church and having the diadem put on him through the patriarch Photius. A male child, Leo, was born to Basil by Eudocia, who was said rather to be Michael's, since Eudocia was pregnant when she was married to Basil.

Michael, always spending his time on horse races and drinking parties, and constantly getting drunk and losing his wits, which he did not have sound even when sober, provoked Basil to his own murder. For after a horse race held at Saint Mamas, in which he himself drove, and his grandees, and he won, when he lay down to dinner Basil and Eudocia too lay down with him. One Basilicinus, who had earlier been a rower of the imperial trireme, but had been taken up by the ruler for his bodily beauty and become close to him, standing by the emperor then at dinner, praised him to the skies, as having driven very skilfully and artfully. And he, already drunk and with his mind clouded, pleased by the praises, gave him the purple shoes and ordered him to put them on, and proclaimed him emperor. When he hesitated and looked at Basil, the emperor grew angry. Basil nodded to him to obey and put them on; and he took them and put them on. And the emperor said to Basil in a rage: "These imperial insignia suit this man better than you. Or may I not, as I made you emperor, make another too?" From this Basil, fearing for both his empire and his life, planned to act before he suffered, and shared the plan with others. When again Michael at dinner had indulged in unmixed wine and was already stupefied, and, led by the hand, had lain down in his own bedchamber in the palace at Saint Mamas and was seized by very deep sleep, first Basil went out and broke the bolts of the imperial bedchamber, so that those who moved about the chamber could not lock the doors, then took the conspirators and went off. Since those sleeping before the chamber were few and tried to stop them, a commotion arose and the emperor woke up. When one of those with Basil came in and raised his sword against Michael, he raised his hands, and the swordsman struck and cut off both of them, and went back to the others. He, not able to flee, walking unsteadily from the wine and hampered by drunkenness, lay lamenting terribly; and another of Basil's men, seeing him still alive, leapt in and, thrusting the sword into his chest, drove it down to the belly, so that even his entrails fell out.
