blocks: So Michael's life left him in this way, worthily of his way of living. Basil came at once to the palace, and having become master of it sent one of the chamberlains to bury Michael. He went off and found the wretch wrapped in a horse blanket, and taking him away buried him in the monastery at Chrysopolis. He had reigned with his mother fourteen years, and ruled alone himself eleven. Basil, having now taken hold of the empire and been proclaimed sovereign by all, opened the imperial treasuries in the presence of the chosen men of the senate, in which nothing else was found except only three centenaria of gold. So a council was held and it was voted by all that those who had received money on no reasonable ground should give it back, or at least, more moderately, half. In accordance with the vote half was exacted, and from this not less than three hundred centenaria came into the imperial treasury.

When Basil went to the Great Church on a feast and wished to share in the bloodless sacrifice, he was prevented by the patriarch Photius, who called him a murderer. Angered at this, he gathered a council and thrust Photius out of the church, on the ground that Ignatius had been dragged down from the high priestly throne unlawfully by the Caesar Bardas, and that Photius had mounted the divine seat uncanonically while Ignatius was alive, putting this forward as a pretext, a Patroclus. So he brought the divine Ignatius back again to the eminence of the high priesthood. As soon as he had taken hold of the sceptre, some of the patricians, George and Symbatius, raised a hand against him, who were caught and punished with bodily penalties. He crowned his sons Constantine and Leo as emperors, and afterwards also the third, Alexander. The fourth, Stephen, wishing to appoint him patriarch, he enrolled in the clergy of the church of God while he was still very young. His daughters, who were four, he placed in the imperial monastery of Saint Euphemia.

Marching out against the Hagarenes in Crete, he was defeated, and many fell, and he himself would have been taken, had not Theophylact Abastactus, the father of Romanus Lecapenus, who later reigned, saved him. Coming back to the great city he sent his son-in-law Christopher against the Hagarenes to Crete, who engaged them, routed them and humbled their boldness. The sovereign Basil also marched out against the Hagarenes in the eastern region and against the Manichaeans, whose leader was the man called Chrysocheir, and having seized some forts and driven off plunder, he undertook to besiege their metropolis Tephrike too, but learning that it needed a long blockade and was in any case hard to take, he set out from there and went off; and finding the Euphrates running high, he bridged it with boats and crossed, plundered much there, took other forts, made a treaty with some of the barbarians and received others who came over to him, and came back to the first of cities, and after a triumph through the middle of the city returned to the palace.

Chrysocheir, the head of the Manichaeans, attacked the Roman lands and plundered them. So the emperor sent the domestic of the scholae against him. Since he did not bring a force fit for battle, he judged he ought not to engage him in close combat. But wherever opportunity offered, engaging his men as they scattered and made raids, he harmed them and did not let them make their raids and plundering without fear. So Chrysocheir, bringing the plunder he had already been able to take, turned back home. The domestic of the scholae ordered two generals to follow him with the units under them and not let the barbarians scatter and plunder. In the evening, when Chrysocheir and his men had camped at the foot of a mountain, and the Romans had seized the heights first, a quarrel arose among the soldiers of both generals about first place and which were better in strength. When each side boasted that they were stronger than the others, one man, wishing to end their quarrel, said: "Why, fellow soldiers, are we boasting in vain, when it is possible to show now, not in words but in deeds, which are the brave men, with the enemy present?" The man's advice seemed good, and they at once attacked the enemy. They, struck by the suddenness, turned their backs to those striking them, and as the pursuit went on a long way the plain between was strewn with corpses, and Chrysocheir himself fell then, and many were taken alive and sent bound to the emperor, and Chrysocheir's head itself.

When the patriarch Ignatius passed to the mansions there, having steered the helm of the church eleven years in all, Photius was brought up by Basil to the throne of the high priesthood for the second time. A plot being put together against the emperor did not escape notice. So its leader, Romanus Curcuas, had his eyes gouged out, and those sworn with him were beaten, had their hair cut off and were condemned to exile.

blocks: When spring was already shining he marched out against Syria, having with him one of his sons, Constantine, and took some of the forts, while others came over to him, afraid because of the capture of the others. Then he attacked Germanicea, and having ravaged its suburbs he came to the city of Adata and besieged it. When its citizens showed little concern about the siege, Basil asked them in what they trusted that they did not come over to him, when the city was already being taken. And one of those advanced in age said: "I know exactly that it is not fated that the city be taken by you now, but by another of those descended from your loins, Constantine by name." When the emperor pointed out his son and said: "This is Constantine," that old man said: "This is not the Constantine by whom our city will be taken, but another of your descendants." Angered at the old man's prophecies, Basil pressed the siege more strongly. But when he achieved nothing, and the cold that came on troubled the army greatly, he left the siege and turned his mind to returning, ordering the captives to be killed, so that they might not need guarding or start some rising if they got the chance.

The Hagarenes from Tarsus and Melitene overran the Roman lands, and the stratelates Andrew, going against them, checked their onsets. When the emir of Tarsus wrote to him: "The son of Mary will not help you at all when I attack you," he hung the blasphemous letter on an image of the Mother of God, saying: "Pay back to the boaster, mistress, the wages of his insolence." And having said this he went against the blasphemer, and when battle was joined the enemy were routed, and there was great slaughter of them, and the emir himself was slain, a moderate number escaping. But the stratelates, being envied, was slandered as having been able to take Tarsus too and not having wished to. So the emperor took the command from him and gave it to Stypiotes, who promised to sack Tarsus and boasted that he would achieve much else; he not only achieved none of what he boasted, but even fell into misfortune from negligence and careless encamping. For the barbarians, learning that his camp was unguarded, attacked it by night and killed many, and more perished trampled by one another, and so the sons of Hagar prevailed.

So matters in the east went in this way, but those in the west were in a worse state. For both the Italy subject to the emperors of the Romans and most of Sicily had become tributary to the Carthaginians in the reign of Michael, and many other of the nations too. For the Hagarenes from Carthage fitted out a fleet and took many towns, and at last were besieging Ragusa too. So the Ragusans sent an embassy to the emperor Basil, asking help from him, and he sent them a hundred warships; learning that these were coming against them, the besieging Hagarenes broke off the siege of Ragusa and attacked Longobardia, and took the town of Bari, and using it as a base mastered all Longobardia. The other nations too, which were pressed by these Hagarenes, as has been said, learning what had happened at Ragusa, and that the enemy, fearing the alliance from the emperor, had given up the siege, also sent embassies asking for alliance and putting themselves under the leadership of the Romans. The emperor accepted the embassy and helped those who asked, both through the fleet mentioned before and through the king of the Franks. For he wrote to him to help the Roman army in the war against the Hagarenes, and by them the army of the Hagarenes was overcome, and their leader, called Sultan, was taken, whom the king of the Franks carried off to Capua.

Spending two years there he was never seen to smile by anyone, so that the king marvelled and promised to give a reward for the news to anyone who reported to him the barbarian laughing. So someone once said he had seen the Sultan laugh. The king called the barbarian and asked the reason for his laughter. He said he had seen the wheel of a wagon, part of which was on the ground and part raised aloft, and then the part aloft was brought down to the ground and the part on the ground was raised aloft. "So, comparing human affairs too to this moving and changing, I burst out laughing, reckoning that it was not impossible for my own affairs to be so disposed, and that as I was brought down from a height to lowliness, so perhaps I might again be raised from the ground to a height and be lifted up." So he spoke. And the king, taking the truth of his words to heart and pitying the Sultan for his change of fortune, made him his friend and gave him freedom of speech, and thinking the man intelligent, shared his counsels with him. But he, being crafty, went after the king with guile. For the king, having newly acquired the cities of Capua and Beneventum, feared that they might lay claim to their freedom. That barbarian, learning this, came to the king and said: "If you wish your rule over these cities to be secure, move the more notable men in them elsewhere, and the multitude, left to itself, will no longer plan anything rebellious." The king, thinking the advice would be useful, adopted the plan, and fetters were forged in secret. Then that wicked man talked with the leading men in the cities, and behaving as if in a more friendly way, told them in secret that the king wished to put the more notable of the citizens in fetters and move them to his own country, and, he said, the proof of his words was the forging of iron chains, handcuffs and other bonds. Finding this true, they supposed he was well disposed to them, and when the king went out hunting they barred the gates of the cities against him, and no longer received him inside. And he went off to his own land, and the Sultan found his freedom from those citizens as his reward. So, going off and recovering his former rule, he marched against the cities mentioned, Capua and Beneventum. They, pressed by the siege, sent to the king, begging him fervently to forgive them and to fight for them. When he did not accept the embassy, saying he rejoiced at their destruction, they sent another embassy to the emperor Basil, begging him to help them in their danger. And he promised, and the envoy was going back to urge his fellow citizens to take heart. But he was caught by the enemy, and the Sultan, learning where he had been and what good news he was bringing to the townsmen, said to him: "If you wish to live, report to those who sent you, as they lean out from the wall, that the emperor refuses the alliance; for if you do not do so, know that you will die at once." He agreed to do as he was told, and standing before the wall, held in bonds, he said that he had accomplished the embassy and that help from the emperor would come very soon; and saying this he was cut down by the swords. And the Sultan, despairing of taking the city, withdrew.

The emir of Tarsus, Esman, attacked the city of Euripus with large ships, which the sons of Hagar call kumbaria; but he achieved nothing, but was himself killed, struck a mortal blow, and the greater part of his army with him. Moreover, the ruler of Crete, Saet Apochaps, made ready another fleet and set over it one Photius, an active man, who harmed the coastlands of the Aegean and the islands. The Roman fleet met him, whose admiral was the drungarius of the fleet, the patrician Nicetas Ooryphas, and burned many of the enemy ships with the liquid fire, and those sailing in them, put many to the sword, and sent more to the bottom. Those who escaped this great danger saved themselves by shameful flight. Yet they were not content with being saved; but making ready pirate ships they overran the Peloponnese and the islands there. But the drungarius of the fleet mentioned came against them again; for putting in at the harbour of Cenchreae, and learning that the enemy ships were lingering about Methone, Pylos and Patrae, he quickly took the triremes across the isthmus at Corinth over dry land, attacked the enemy unexpectedly, and while they were struck by the surprise he burned some of the pirate ships and sank others with their crews, Photius himself, the commander of the enemy, being killed. So the fleet of the Cretans too perished in this way.
text: When spring was already shining he marched out against Syria, having with him one of his sons, Constantine, and took some of the forts, while others came over to him, afraid because of the capture of the others. Then he attacked Germanicea, and having ravaged its suburbs he came to the city of Adata and besieged it. When its citizens showed little concern about the siege, Basil asked them in what they trusted that they did not come over to him, when the city was already being taken. And one of those advanced in age said: "I know exactly that it is not fated that the city be taken by you now, but by another of those descended from your loins, Constantine by name." When the emperor pointed out his son and said: "This is Constantine," that old man said: "This is not the Constantine by whom our city will be taken, but another of your descendants." Angered at the old man's prophecies, Basil pressed the siege more strongly. But when he achieved nothing, and the cold that came on troubled the army greatly, he left the siege and turned his mind to returning, ordering the captives to be killed, so that they might not need guarding or start some rising if they got the chance. The Hagarenes from Tarsus and Melitene overran the Roman lands, and the stratelates Andrew, going against them, checked their onsets. When the emir of Tarsus wrote to him: "The son of Mary will not help you at all when I attack you," he hung the blasphemous letter on an image of the Mother of God, saying: "Pay back to the boaster, mistress, the wages of his insolence." And having said this he went against the blasphemer, and when battle was joined the enemy were routed, and there was great slaughter of them, and the emir himself was slain, a moderate number escaping. But the stratelates, being envied, was slandered as having been able to take Tarsus too and not having wished to. So the emperor took the command from him and gave it to Stypiotes, who promised to sack Tarsus and boasted that he would achieve much else; he not only achieved none of what he boasted, but even fell into misfortune from negligence and careless encamping. For the barbarians, learning that his camp was unguarded, attacked it by night and killed many, and more perished trampled by one another, and so the sons of Hagar prevailed. So matters in the east went in this way, but those in the west were in a worse state. For both the Italy subject to the emperors of the Romans and most of Sicily had become tributary to the Carthaginians in the reign of Michael, and many other of the nations too. For the Hagarenes from Carthage fitted out a fleet and took many towns, and at last were besieging Ragusa too. blocks: Again another sixty very large ships set out from Africa, and these too ravaged the land under the Romans, and came as far as Cephallenia and Zacynthus. So a navy was sent against them, with Nasar as admiral. But since many of those who laboured at the rowing ran away, the triremes were half empty; so the admiral judged he ought not to engage the enemy in this state, but reported what had happened to the emperor, and the deserters were looked for and quickly caught. So that he might strike fear into the navy and yet punish no Christian, the emperor ordered thirty of the Hagarenes kept in prisons to be brought out by night, their faces smeared with soot so that they might not be recognised, then beaten and led round through the Market, and taken to the Peloponnese and impaled. When this was done the sailors of the fleet were terrified, and so they attacked the enemy by night and raised a trophy, some of the enemy being killed and others taken. Then they also crossed to Sicily, and harmed and sacked the cities there that belonged to the Carthaginians.

The Arabs from the south, learning that the Roman fleet was idle, sailed with ships against the coastlands of Phoenicia and Syria and harmed them. For the emperor, because he had killed Michael, who reigned before him, as if propitiating God, built churches anew to the archangel Michael in many places in the queen of cities; and in the palace itself he built him a costly and expensive sanctuary, which he called the New Church. So, with the seamen busy on these buildings, their backs never free from lifting and their hands slaving at the baskets, the fleet was idle; so the Hagarenes, as has been said, plundered the coastlands without fear, and not only harmed these, but also sacked Syracuse. The emperor wore out the seamen of the fleet on his buildings, also raising a church to the prophet Elijah the Tishbite; for he honoured him exceedingly, and thought that some day he would be taken up by him and carried up with him in the fiery chariot. Yet when he learned of the capture and razing of Syracuse, he sent men to stand against the accursed Hagarenes; but nothing was achieved. Then he sent out Nicephorus Phocas with a force fit for battle, a man most noble and a most able general, who set up many trophies against the descendants of Hagar.

When this emperor was serving Theophilitzes, as has been said, he went down with him to the Peloponnese, and went into the church of the holy apostle Andronicus with his master. There was there one Prosmenon, a monk who laid claim to virtue, who paid no attention to Theophilitzes, but on seeing Basil he rose, did obeisance and greeted him warmly. A widow in that country, foremost among the natives and overflowing with much wealth, who was acquainted with the monk, learned what had happened, sent for him and asked how it was that he had not thought Theophilitzes, a distinguished official related by birth to the emperors, worthy of any greeting or welcome, while he addressed the man who served him and gave him an honour not suited to his station, but far exceeding it. For, knowing the monk, she guessed that he had not done this without reason. He said: "I saw Theophilitzes as a private man, but Basil as emperor, and for this I honoured the man as emperor. For know that he has been marked out as emperor by God." Hearing this, the woman, when Basil fell ill and was left behind there after his master set out from there, took him into her house and thought him worthy of care, and when he recovered she persuaded him to become an adopted brother to her son, gave him money, and then also foretold the empire to him, and asked that when he obtained the rule he should not forget her son, nor herself, if she were still numbered among the living. So Basil went off on these terms. And she, as soon as he became emperor, came to the queen of cities with her son, bringing many costly gifts; the emperor received her with honour, and honoured her son, whom he had as a brother by spiritual bond, as has been said, as protospatharius.

When various earthquakes happened, by which many churches were cracked, the emperor set them up again; moreover, the great western arch of the Wisdom of God the Word, which had cracked and was expected to fall, he bound together and made firm by the devices of craftsmen. He also persuaded many of the Jews to become Christians by gifts of money and promises, and having made a treaty with the nation of the Rhos, he brought them to knowledge of our mystery. For when they agreed to be baptised, a high priest was sent to them by the sovereign. But they, about to change from their own religion to ours, hesitated and wavered, and said to the high priest: "Unless we see some wonder, such as the many you teach were done by Christ, we could never be persuaded to accept your doctrine." And he said: "Ask what you wish." And they said: "The book that teaches the things about Christ must be thrown into fire; and if it stays unharmed, it will be proof to us that the one you preach is truly God." The bishop agreed to do this. A fire was lit; the high priest raised his hands and eyes to heaven and said: "Glorify your name, Christ our God." He put the holy Gospel into the fire; and it stayed a long time in the flame and remained unharmed. The barbarians were amazed, believed the preaching, and pressed to be initiated in divine baptism. So this happened in this way.

blocks: One of the emperor's sons, Constantine, whom he loved more than the others, fell ill and died, and the sovereign bore his death heavily and was inconsolable, and sought to have him appear to him alive. There was a monk Theodore, surnamed Santabarenus; he had become close to the emperor, who believed he had reached the height of a virtuous life, so that he even worked signs from it; this Santabarenus, then, who was also styled president of the metropolis of Euchaïta, is said to have shown the emperor his dead son forsooth alive. For in a thicket he made a phantom of Constantine on horseback meet his own father; and the emperor, thinking he embraced and kissed him, no longer saw him. By doing other such things too, and amazing the emperor with them, Santabarenus brought him wholly over to himself, so that he had faith in him and distrusted him in nothing. So the emperor was disposed thus towards Santabarenus.

Leo, the second of the emperor's sons, already a young man, married to the daughter of Martinacius and proclaimed emperor by his father, did not like Santabarenus, but called him a poisoner, a sorcerer and a deceiver of the sovereign. He, stung by this as if by goads, rose to retaliate. And pretending goodwill towards Leo, he said: "Being a young man, emperor, and hunting and riding with your father, you ought to carry a dagger too, so that you may use it against a wild beast when needed, and perhaps hand it to your father at the right time, or even defend him against plotters." He, not detecting the trick, was persuaded to carry a little sword inside his boot according to the advice. Santabarenus used this dagger against Leo for his revenge, and said to the emperor: "Your son is plotting against you, and the proof of this is that when he hunts with you he carries a hidden dagger." So Basil went out hunting and Leo followed his father; the dagger was found hidden under his shoe. The informer seemed to speak the truth. The accused made his defence but it was not accepted; the father was enraged against his son, shut him up in one of the imperial chambers and took away the insignia of power, and, as some record, he also planned to put out his son's eyes, being stirred to this by Santabarenus; and the plan would have become deed, had not the patriarch and the leading men of the senate, begging much, turned the emperor from his intention.

Meanwhile the anger remained, Leo was under guard, and much time passed, and the emperor feasted with some of the senate; this happened at fixed times by old custom. In the house where the feast took place there was hanging in a cage one of the mimicking creatures, called a parrot; hearing someone constantly lamenting and calling on Leo, it imitated the voice and often cried "Leo, Leo." Those dining with the emperor, finding in these cries of the bird an occasion for pleading for Leo, rose from the feast and, filled with tears, said: "Will not this creature, emperor, be an accusation against us, since it calls on its own master, while we, enjoying the banquet with your majesty, forget him, who has now been shut up for a long time? Let go, master, your anger against him, release him from guard, and look on him kindly, or rather look on him as a father." With this the emperor slackened his anger against his son, was reconciled with him and gave back the imperial honour.

Going out hunting, he met a stag of extraordinary size, carrying horns raised up high, and he chased it, and coming near it raised his hand with a sword, wishing to strike the creature. But it defended itself against its pursuer with its horns, and when one of the tines growing on them caught in the emperor's belt, he was carried off aloft, hanging from the creature's horns; and he would perhaps have perished, had not someone got there first and, cutting the belt with a sword, saved him; and the man saved by him gave him a fine reward for the rescue, the cutting off of his head, and the pretext was as if a seemly one, that, he said, he had bared a sword against the emperor, not reckoning that the man had raised the sword for the emperor and was rather worthy of reward and imperial gifts. So he got this profit from his zeal for the emperor. And he, struck in the body by the horn and his inward parts wrenched, lived on, but not for long; he died from this, having reigned with Michael one year and ruled alone nineteen, leaving the empire to his son Leo, who was the elder of his surviving sons.

blocks: When Leo became sovereign he at once set about revenge on Santabarenus. Suspecting that the patriarch Photius, who was friendly to him, would take his part, he invented charges against the patriarch, thrust him out of the church and confined him in the monastery of the Armeniacs, and appointed his own brother Stephen patriarch, and since the high priest of Heraclea was not there, he was ordained by the protothronos. He ordered Santabarenus to be brought from Euchaïta; for he presided over the church there. Sending to the monastery of Philippicus at Chrysopolis, where the emperor Michael had been buried, he brought his body out of the coffin, and with a great procession and imperial honour laid it in the church of the Holy Apostles in a marble chest, his brothers too, Alexander and the patriarch, being present at the procession. Being corrupted with the daughter of Zautzes while his wife Theophano was still alive, he honoured her father as magister and logothete of the drome, and afterwards also as basileopator, himself inventing the name. When the church of the holy apostle Thomas was burned with others in a fire, this emperor renewed it. Santabarenus had now been brought and was guarded in the palace at Pegai, where the emperor sent and had him flogged without mercy, and put him in exile at Athens. Not long after he sent there and gouged out his eyes; but after several years of exile he brought the man back and granted him a provision.

The duke of Longobardia, Hagion, who was son-in-law of the king of Francia, when he learned of Basil's death, broke the treaty with the Romans and took the whole country for himself. So the emperor sent the master of the table against him with the western units, who engaged him and was defeated; and he lost almost all he had brought, barely escaping himself. When the patriarch Stephen died, Antony, named Cauleas, was appointed patriarch.

When the Bulgars were at peace by treaty and trading with the Romans, those in charge of the customs exacted unjust dues from them. This served as a pretext for their ruler Symeon, who was looking for occasions to make war on the Romans. And he did make war, and a Roman army armed against him, and many of the Romans fell, and [the text is corrupt here]; many were taken, whose noses Symeon cut off and let them go back to Byzantium. Grieved at this, the emperor persuaded with gifts the Turks about the Ister, who are also called Hungarians, to go against the Bulgars and harm them as much as they could, and the emperor himself made ready to move arms against the Bulgars by sea and by land, entrusting the war against them to the patrician Nicephorus Phocas, appointing him domestic of the scholae. Before the war the sovereign sent the quaestor to Symeon to treat for peace. But the barbarian, suspecting he had come with guile, shut him up and bound him, and fought against Phocas. While he was busy with him, the Hungarians plundered his country. So, leaving Phocas, he set out against them, engaged them and was defeated, many Bulgars being slain and more taken, and Symeon himself barely escaping into Dorostolum; this is Dristra. The emperor bought the Bulgar captives from the Hungarians, and Symeon begged for peace. Trusting his words, the emperor sent Choerosphactes to make a treaty, whom the barbarian held and bound. He himself attacked the Turks, routed them and ravaged their country. Then he wrote to Leo that he would never make peace unless he first received the Bulgar captives; and having received them he did not make peace. So the emperor used the eastern and western units, gathered together, against the Bulgars, but all were defeated when they attacked Symeon. So the affairs of the Bulgars went in this way.

The emperor, staying in the country with Zautzes's daughter Zoe, was plotted against by some. Zoe, noticing the plot from a noise, woke the sleeping emperor, and he at once came back to the palace, and so escaped the plot. As soon as the empress Theophano had died, the emperor proclaimed this Zoe Augusta and made his former concubine his lawful wife; she enjoyed her good fortune only a little while; for she lived one year and eight months in the empire and died. Another plot was again reported to the emperor, which Basil the epiktes, who was the nephew of Zautzes, was planning. He shared the secret with the eunuch Samonas, who first confirmed with oaths that he would keep what would be said unrevealed. Samonas was of Hagarene descent, and learning of the plan against the ruler, he at once carried the secret to him. And Basil and those privy to the plan were arrested, and Samonas was honoured as protospatharius and became close to the emperor.

blocks: Leo also took a third wife, who was called Eudocia, drew her family from the Opsikion and was outstanding in beauty. But she too lived only a short time with the emperor. For she conceived and, coming to give birth, died with the child born. This sovereign longed to have a son, the more so since he had had an oracle about it; for he was a lover of every kind of wisdom, and of the secret kind too, which divines the future through incantations, and he spent time on the movements of the stars and pursued the science of the effects that come from them, and he found that he would have a son as successor to the empire. So he took a fourth wife, Zoe Carbonopsina. He did not, however, give her the imperial rank at once, but she lived with him a good while uncrowned, until a child was born of her to the emperor, who was granted divine baptism by the patriarch Nicholas. For when Antony had lived on the throne of Constantinople [a gap in the text] years and departed life, Nicholas the mysticus was ordained patriarch. After the birth of his son, whom the emperor named Constantine, he also proclaimed his wife. For the fourth marriage Leo was excommunicated by the patriarch.

Honouring his first wife, the blessed Theophano, he raised a sanctuary in her name very near the church of the Holy Apostles, in which he also laid her body. He built another church in the name of Saint Lazarus, in which he stored his holy body, brought over from Cyprus, and also that of Mary Magdalene. While the seamen were busy with the buildings and the fleet was not sailing, the navy of the Hagarenes sacked Tauromenium and seized the island of Lemnos, and great destruction of people happened in them.

When the emperor's procession at Pentecost took place, this emperor made his procession to the church of Saint Mocius according to custom, and as the sovereign was already approaching the screen of the sanctuary, someone rushed out from the ambo holding a very heavy staff and brought it down on the imperial head, and would have crushed it, had not the staff struck the hanging lamp and so lost the force of its blow. Still, blood running down from the emperor's head threw the officials into confusion; and since Alexander, the emperor's brother, was not present there, the supposition prevailed among most that he was not without a share in the plot. The man who did the bold deed was put to tortures, and naming no accomplice, had his hands and feet cut off, and was at last given to the fire. The monk Mark, who completed the four-ode canon of the great man, being present, said to the emperor: "This was foretold by David, who said: 'How much the enemy has done evil in your sanctuary, and those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast.' Know then, emperor, that from now you will reign ten years." And the word became deed. For Leo died ten years later, on the very day on which he was then struck on the head.

Samonas, already mentioned, being very powerful with the emperor and having got abundant wealth, took it and ran away to the Hagarenes, from whom he sprang. But he was caught crossing the Halys; he said he was going to the cross at Siricha, having made a vow to it; Constantine, the son of the duke Andronicus, took him and brought him back to Byzantium. The emperor, still keeping his former affection for Samonas, ordered Constantine, if he were asked before the senate about Samonas, not to say that he was running away, but that he was going off to the cross at Siricha. The next day, with the senate present, the emperor asked Constantine, putting him on oath, whether Samonas was fleeing; and he, not wishing to lie because of the oaths, said that he was going off to his own homeland, Melitene. The emperor sent Constantine away in anger, but afterwards granted Samonas his former intimacy, then also honoured him as patrician and appointed him parakoimomenos; and he led the sovereign on to many improper things, one of which was forcing the patriarch to receive him and release him from the excommunication. So the emperor sent for the high priest and begged to be received. When he could not be moved, he was at once taken across from the palace to Hieria, and from there they led him on foot to the monastery at Galakrenai, which he himself had built, having presided over the church eleven years. The synkellos Euthymius, a holy man, was appointed patriarch, who also with all zeal prevented the emperor when he wished to decree by law that whoever wished might take two wives at the same time, or three, up to four.

blocks: When the Hagarenes were plundering the lands of the Romans with ships, the emperor appointed Himerius, the logothete of the drome, leader of the fleet and sent him against the sons of Hagar, ordering him also to take the duke Andronicus with him. But the crafty Samonas, having an implacable hatred against the duke's family, suggested to one of Andronicus's friends that he should tell him not to sail with Himerius, since he was going to gouge out his eyes by imperial order. So Andronicus was not persuaded to go with Himerius, and so he alone fought at sea, won, and overcame the enemy's navy. From this Andronicus, despairing, took his relatives and slaves and seized Kabala, a strong fort lying not very far from Iconium. Samonas did not stop provoking the emperor and moving him to anger against the man. He, learning also of the thrusting out of the patriarch Nicholas from the church, and despairing on every side, went over with his whole household to the Hagarenes. When the emperor learned this he was greatly grieved, fearing he would have the man as an enemy instead of a champion. So he wrote an imperial letter, by which an amnesty for what had been done was granted to Andronicus, his return was permitted, and the gift of many good things was promised. They put this letter in wax and, shaping the wax like a candle, handed it to a Saracen, one of the captives brought out of prison, ordering him to give it to Andronicus. Samonas called this Hagarene and said to him in secret: "Do you know that you are carrying in your hands the destruction of all Syria? So, to save your homeland and your kinsmen, hand this wax to the vizier." He did as he was told, and the sons of Hagar, learning the meaning of the letter, bound Andronicus and all those with him. So Andronicus ended his life in bonds, and some of those with him, not bearing the ill-treatment of the bonds, forswore their faith. Constantine and some of those with him escaped from prison and went off to the Roman lands, and bravely routing the Hagarenes who pursued them, they were saved. The emperor received him with great joy, welcomed him magnificently and honoured him exceedingly; then he said to him: "Do not let your name deceive you, Constantine, and do not think you will gain the empire, because a Constantine is going to rule the Romans; for know exactly that this is my son. If you adorn the Sparta that has fallen to you, it will be well with you; but if you make trouble and attempt usurpation, be sure that through this gate," pointing out to him the one on the west of the Chrysotriklinos, "your head will be brought in without the rest of your body." And this later happened.

When some came from Melitene, among whom was Samonas's father, the emperor received them with honour, and brought them into the Great Church, though improperly, since they were unbelievers. Samonas's father, seeing the honour his son had in the palace and the wealth he had about him, wished to live with him. But he was prevented by him, since he advised him to keep his own religion and return to his homeland, saying: "If I too find an opportunity, I shall come back to you." When the feast of Pentecost came, the emperor crowned his son and proclaimed him emperor.

The abominable Samonas had a eunuch servant named Constantine, from Paphlagonia, and gave him to the empress for her service. When Constantine became very close to the empress and to the ruler himself, the profane Samonas was stirred to envy and denounced him to the emperor as the empress's lover. So Leo, jealous, ordered him to be tonsured a monk, and not long after brought him back, ordered him to take off the monk's garments and put on worldly dress, and made him closer to himself than before. This was not bearable for Samonas. So he had an abusive pamphlet written through one of his men, and threw it where the emperor was going to pass; he found it and read it, was grieved, and looked for the one who had done it. One of those who knew of this deed of Samonas's made known to the ruler that he was the author of the abusive pamphlet. At that time an eclipse of the moon happened, and the emperor sent for the metropolitan of Synada, to ask about it. Samonas took him aside privately and asked about the eclipse; and he said: "The affliction of the moon signifies a misfortune of yours; but if the thirteenth of July passes before you suffer it, you too will escape the misfortune." Then the bishop of Synada, asked by the emperor too, answered that the harm would fall on the second person after you. The emperor judged the second person to be his brother Alexander, but he was mistaken in the judgement; for at some time things had to go badly for the most wicked Samonas. So, learning that he was the father of the abusive pamphlet, he thrust him out of the palace, tonsured him and shut him up within fixed bounds. And this happened before the thirteenth of July had passed. Constantine, whom he had envied, was appointed parakoimomenos in place of Samonas, and the emperor also built a monastery for him at Nossiai.

Leo fell ill with a disease of the bowels, and was so worn down in strength that he could not even give the senate the customary address about fasting, which is called a silention. Yet, having said a few things to it and asked them to remember him and keep faith with his wife and his son, and saying that this was his last address to it, he did not die at once, but lasted until May. Then, dying, he left the sole rule to his brother and handed his son over to him, asking him to take care of him, bring him up royally and leave him as sovereign; seeing him coming to him when he was already failing, they say, he said: "See, the bad time after the thirteen months." Leo reigned twenty-five years and three months.

blocks: As soon as Alexander had set his feet firmly in the rule, he brought the patriarch Nicholas from Galakrenai and brought him up to the throne of Constantinople, bringing Euthymius down for the second time, and holding his deposition on the bema, the partisans of Nicholas insulting the man much, and then exiling him. Having become sole ruler, this emperor did nothing fitting for an emperor, but gave himself up to luxury, hunting and debauchery, and entrusted the affairs of the empire and the state to charlatans and men from the crossroads, whom he had had as partners in shameful doings before his sole rule; one of them, called Basilitzes, he intended to make successor to the sceptre too; for he wished his nephew Constantine to be a private man and to deprive him of his genitals. And had not the end of his life come on him quickly, and so his plans been frustrated by providence above, they might, as far as it lay with him, have been carried into effect. Asking sorcerers whether his life would go on to length, he heard from them that his life would be long if he put teeth and genitals on the boar in the theatre, which is made of bronze. "For this," they said, "is your stoicheion, standing opposite the Lion, your brother," judging nothing sound except that the sovereign was like a boar, because he gaped after his belly and banquets and was given constantly to licentiousness. So, believing their words, he who was more foolish than swine had the missing parts made on the bronze work.

When Symeon, the leader of the Bulgars, asked through some men sent by him whether he welcomed peace, Alexander received the men sent with dishonour, spoke arrogantly and threatened them excessively. So Symeon, not bearing the insult, took up arms against the Romans. Alexander, wasting away wholly in banquets and drinking, once lunched after a bath, stuffed his belly and drank insatiably of unmixed wine, and set out to play ball, and straining his body with the riding and the twistings of the ball game he suffered a rupture, and voiding blood through his nose and his private parts, he died after one day, having written as guardians of his nephew and administrators of the empire the patriarch Nicholas, the magister Stephen, the magister John Eladas, the rhaiktor John, and two of those raised by him from a vagabond's fortune to senatorial rank and the patriciate, Basilitzes and Gabrielopulus.

Alexander, wasting away wholly in banquets and drinking, once lunched after a bath, stuffed his belly and drank insatiably of unmixed wine, and set out to play ball, and straining his body with the riding and the twistings of the ball game he suffered a rupture, and voiding blood through his nose and his private parts, he died after one day, having written as guardians of his nephew and administrators of the empire the patriarch Nicholas, the magister Stephen, the magister John Eladas, the rhaiktor John, and two of those raised by him from a vagabond's fortune to senatorial rank and the patriciate, Basilitzes and Gabrielopulus.

blocks: So Alexander, having played at the imperial rule for one year and one month, ended his life; and power came round to Constantine the son of Leo, who was still quite a child; for he was completing the seventh year of his age. Constantine, the son of the duke Andronicus, who was domestic of the scholae, when he heard of Alexander's death, for he was away from the queen of cities, partly uncovering and fanning the spark of desire for the imperial rule that he had kept hidden under the ashes, and partly stirred to it by others, of whom the patriarch Nicholas is said to be one (for since Alexander's will had not yet been read he did not know that he himself had been left as a guardian), attempted usurpation, and taking the picked men of the armies came to Byzantium, and entering by a postern at night seized the gate of the Hippodrome with torches, and having won over some of the senators too, a great crowd of the common people having gathered, they acclaimed and proclaimed him as emperor. When those inside would not open the gates, Constantine's protostrator, trusting in his hands, struck the gates more boldly and tried to break them down by force, but was pierced with a spear through some gap by one of those inside. And he was at once dead. Constantine went off from there to the theatre of the horse races, then came to the place called the Chalke, and went on as far as the Excubitors. One of the guardians, the magister John Eladas, gathered some men from the hetaireiai and the seamen and sent them out to stand against the usurper. When they clashed many fell on both sides; Gregoras, the duke's son, was slain, and his nephew Michael, and Curticius the Armenian. Grieved at this, Constantine, eager to strengthen his own company, drove his horse on, wishing to engage those in front; but since the ground was paved with slabs, the horse slipped, fell and brought its rider down, and someone at once came at him, cut off his head and brought it to the emperor Constantine, entering by the western gate of the Chrysotriklinos, fulfilling the prophecy of the late emperor Leo. That the duke Constantine would not obtain the empire was also known to those about the emperor from elsewhere. For there was a tax collector Nicholas, who, having become a debtor to the treasury for much money, fled to the Ishmaelites, forswore the faith and pursued astrology. He had sent a note to the logothete of the drome, the gist of which was this: "Do not fear the duke; for he will rebel senselessly and be destroyed at once." And the revolt was ended. Constantine's father-in-law, the magister Gregoras, and Leo Choerosphactes fled to the Great Church; the guardians brought them out of the divine precinct and tonsured them as monks in the monastery of Studius. Others they beat and led in triumph, the eyes of others they put out, they cut off the heads of some, and others they impaled from Chrysopolis as far as Leucates. And many others would have become a by-product of the guardians' power, had not some of the judges checked their inclination to punishments, saying: "How do you do these things without an imperial command, when the emperor, being a child, does not consent to what is being done?" The guardians also tonsured Constantine's wife and made his son Stephen a eunuch, and sent them to their house in Paphlagonia.

The emperor's guardians, the patriarch and the rest, taking affairs into their own hands, did much that was improper, and also quarrelled with one another, some bringing in one thing, others the opposite, and their management was a kind of rule of many, not a monarchy. The Bulgar Symeon, hoping to master the queen of cities easily since no emperor was in charge of affairs, came against it with a very large force, encamped outside its walls and intended to besiege it. But seeing the strength of the walls, the crowd on them and the abundance of engines on the walls, he grew dizzy and moved off to the Hebdomon, seeking a treaty. So the patriarch and the rest of the guardians took the emperor and came to the palace at Blachernae, where Symeon too came, having given and received hostages, and bowing his head to the patriarch was blessed by him and dined with the emperor. Then, not pleased with the terms, he went back without agreement, he and his sons having been welcomed with gifts.

Since the emperor kept calling for his mother all the time and weeping for her (for Alexander had already brought her down from the palace), the guardians were forced to bring her back. On coming back she took hold of the management, taking with her the parakoimomenos Constantine and the two brothers Gongylius, and first she removed the patriarch from the palace, then thrust out Alexander's servants, the rhaiktor, Basilitzes and Gabrielopulus, and the rest too. The parakoimomenos Constantine had all power.

The Bulgar Symeon overran and plundered Thrace, and pitched a camp at Adrianople, hoping to take it by siege. When he saw that his attempt was a vain effort, he went after the capture of the city another way. For he corrupted some of the guards with money and sacked it by betrayal. But the empress's efforts later brought it under the Romans again. Not bearing Symeon's frequent attacks on the Thracian country, she made a treaty with the sons of Ishmael, and gathering the eastern and western units, entrusted the war against Symeon to the magister Leo Phocas, who was domestic of the scholae. He joined battle, defeated the Bulgars conspicuously and made great slaughter of them. Worn out and drenched with sweat, and fainting from it, he got off his horse at a spring and refreshed himself. Meanwhile his horse escaped from the hands of the man holding it and ran about the plain of the camp without a rider. Being well known, it threw the armies into fear, since they thought the domestic had fallen, and they stopped fighting and halted the pursuit, and confusion seized them. Symeon, seeing from a lookout what had happened in the armies, gave orders to those about him and rushed against the Romans, and falling on them in their confusion turned them all at once to flight, and some the Bulgars pursued and killed, while others perished trampled by one another. The domestic of the scholae was barely able to escape to Mesembria; and many of the generals and unit commanders perished then.

blocks: John Bogas was sent to bring the Patzinaks into alliance against the Bulgars, and the patrician Romanus Lecapenus, drungarius of the fleet, was ordered to sail along with the fleet, partly to work with the domestic of the scholae, and partly to ferry the allies across, if they were brought by Bogas. So Bogas came with the allies. But when a quarrel arose between him and Lecapenus, the Patzinaks, seeing them squabbling with each other and careless about their crossing, went back to their own land. Some, then, tell it this way, and that the defeat of the Romans happened from their not getting the alliance, but others have told the matter differently; for they say that when Phocas had defeated the barbarians and was pursuing, a rumour arose that the drungarius of the fleet was going off with the fleet to take over the empire; this fell on the domestic so as to throw him into confusion, so that he gave up the pursuit and went back to the camp to make sure about the rumour, and from this the war turned the other way; for the Romans fled, thinking the domestic's departure to the camp was a flight from the battle, and the Bulgars turned back from their flight and pursued them. The domestic's return to the camp was caused by desire for the empire. For, being in love with it, he hurried, if it was true that the drungarius was going off, to seize the rule first and make it his own. After the defeat, when Lecapenus and Bogas came back, the matter between them was examined, and Romanus was condemned to be blinded as having been the cause of the defeat, either by malice or by carelessness; but some who had great power with the empress snatched him from this sentence.

The Bulgar Symeon, puffed up by the victory, came against the reigning city. The domestic of the scholae, Phocas, again stood against him, and when battle was joined at Katasyrtai the barbarians were defeated. While many, and these distinguished men, nursed a desire for the empire, more than the others the domestic of the scholae, Phocas, burned with desire for it, trusting in himself because of his family and his strength, and not least in the parakoimomenos Constantine, the eunuch, who then had all power in the palace, and whose brother-in-law he was through his sister. Seeing this, then, the emperor Constantine's tutor, afraid for him, persuaded him to make the drungarius of the fleet, the Romanus mentioned, his friend and take him as a guard. So the emperor wrote a letter in his own hand and sent it to the drungarius. He, receiving it, promised to bring down the power of the parakoimomenos if possible. Once, when the parakoimomenos came to where the fleet lay at anchor and was urging him to sail out, the drungarius met him rather like a slave, talked with him submissively and quietly led him on round the triremes. When he came near the flagship, having ready many brave men following him, he said: "Take him up." They seized him and put him in the trireme, while those about him at once scattered. When this reached the empress's ears it threw her and those in office into confusion. So she sent to Romanus asking what might have happened. But the seamen drove off those sent with stones. The next day the emperor called the patriarch and sent the magister Stephen to bring his mother down from the palace. When she clung to her son with tears, he was moved to pity and let her be, but transferred the authority to himself, and appointed the magister John Garidas domestic of the scholae. The drungarius Lecapenus, fitting out the fleet as if for a sea battle, sailed to the palace at the Boukoleon on the day of the Annunciation. The patriarch and the magister Stephen at once left the palace, and Romanus, having sworn most awesome oaths never to plan against the emperor nor to attack the empire, went up to the palace, went into the church at the Pharos together with Constantine, gave pledges and was appointed great hetaireiarch. The emperor wrote to Phocas not to lose heart or despair, but to wait a little, as provision would be made for him shortly. Romanus betrothed his own daughter Helena to Constantine, and on the third day of Easter the wedding was held, the patriarch Nicholas performing the sacred service, and at once Romanus was honoured as basileopator, and his son Christopher as great hetaireiarch.

Learning this, Phocas attempted usurpation, taking with him the parakoimomenos Constantine and other officials, and declaring that he was acting on behalf of the emperor Constantine. Romanus wrote a letter exposing Phocas's pretext, and confirming it with the emperor's signature and gold seal, sent it to the army with Phocas by a woman of the courtesan sort. And she, secretly showing the gold-sealed letter to many, made many leave Phocas and come over to the emperor. Phocas, coming to Chrysopolis and left by the crowd with him, which went over to the emperor, turned to flight, and coming to a place called Goeleon by the natives, was caught, blinded and brought into the reigning city; and this was the end of his usurpation. Another plot too was formed against the emperor; for some sent young men against him while he was hunting, so that they might attack him at the hunt. But the plan became known, and the authors were punished. The emperor's mother Zoe too was thrown out of the palace, as forsooth plotting against the basileopator, and tonsured in the monastery of Saint Euphemia. On the twenty-fourth of the month of September Romanus was raised to the rank of Caesar, and in December he was crowned with the diadem of the empire by the patriarch Nicholas, forsooth at Constantine's bidding.

blocks: So Romanus Lecapenus obtained the proclamation in this way, but he was not content with obtaining it, but shortly after he crowned his own wife Theodora too, and then his son Christopher, by the choice of Constantine in appearance, but in truth with him forced, vexed before those he trusted and counting what was done a calamity, but not daring to resist. When a plot was made against Romanus, whose first author was the sakellarios Anastasius, forsooth as avenging Constantine, the details of it became known, and the accomplices were punished as Romanus thought fit, and the sakellarios was tonsured. Romanus took this as a pretext for putting Constantine below himself, who until then had been acclaimed first in the proclamations.

Symeon sent an army against the city; and so that they might not come and destroy the beauties before the city, Romanus too sent men to stand against them, and when the Bulgars attacked them many of the officials fell, and of the soldiers some, hurrying to board the triremes sailing alongside, slipped into the sea and were carried off by the waves, others were destroyed by the enemy, and others taken alive. When the Roman army had been treated thus at Pegai, the Bulgars burned the palace there and everything else on the shore of the strait opposite the city. When Romanus's wife, the Augusta Theodora, died, Sophia, the wife of the emperor Christopher, was granted the name of Augusta. Symeon, the leader of the Bulgars, attacked Adrianople and besieged it. He would have achieved nothing, had not the supplies of those inside failed; for, forced by famine, they handed over themselves and the city to the enemy. At that time Leo of Tripoli too went against the Romans with a naval force; but Roman triremes attacked him near the island of Lemnos, destroyed almost all the Hagarenes and sank their ships, the Tripolitan barely managing to escape.

The Bulgar Symeon plundered the lands of Macedonia and Thrace with a heavy army, and coming to the city made his camp near Blachernae, and sought to meet the emperor Romanus, and the emperor chose the meeting, and the emperor came with the fleet to the shore of Cosmidion, and Symeon arrived with his own army, and they talked, and the emperor gave Symeon magnificent gifts. But they parted from each other without agreement, which a pair of eagles also seemed to show. For they say these flew over them and met each other with screaming, then at once parted, one flying off to the city and the other moving its wings towards Thrace.

The emperor Romanus, insatiable for the rule of the empire, and as if forgetting the oaths he had sworn on sacred things, and not content with having made himself and the elder of his sons worthy of the diadem, crowned his other two sons too as emperors, and then also the grandson born to him from Christopher, and changed the rule of the Romans from a kingship into a rule of many. His last son, Theophylact, for whom he was courting the high priestly throne of the queen of cities, he had tonsured a cleric, and he was appointed synkellos through the patriarch. When the patriarch Nicholas, having held the church for thirteen years the second time, departed life, Stephen, metropolitan of Amaseia, was transferred to the throne of Constantinople.

The ruler Symeon, being a man of blood, never at all chose to keep quiet, so he marched against the nation of the Croats, but was defeated by them, and lost his own army in the difficult ground of the mountains. Meanwhile someone came to the emperor Romanus, saying that the statue set up above the arch at the Xerolophos and looking to the west was the stoicheion of Symeon the Bulgar, and that if someone cut off its head, the destruction of Symeon would follow the cutting. So he said this, and not long after the head of the statue was cut off, and at that very hour Symeon's life failed him, seized by a heart attack, as was afterwards known to the emperor, who found out exactly the time of his death. When Symeon had departed from among men, the rule of the Bulgars came round to Peter, born to him by his second wife, who, since the nation of the Bulgars was pressed by famine and he feared that the nations round about might attack him, and the Romans above the others, sent to the emperor to make a treaty, and, if he chose, a marriage alliance with himself. When both requests seemed agreeable to the emperor, Peter himself came, and terms of peace were made, and the emperor's granddaughter, born of the elder of his sons, Christopher, was joined to him in married life.

blocks: The emperor Romanus, not thinking it enough that he had put the emperor Constantine below himself, looked for an occasion to put Christopher before him too, and arranged that the crowd of Bulgars at the time of the wedding should riot, demanding that Christopher be proclaimed before Constantine, and as if forsooth managing things he allowed what was asked to be done. Then, neither fearing God, who had pledged his promises, nor respecting his subjects, he made his other two sons too be acclaimed before Constantine, and the first became fifth, and had not the little Romanus, his son's son, died first, he too would have been honoured before him. So the native-born emperor, to whom the empire belonged by inheritance, was like something written in the margin. But justice did not slumber over this; let the account of it be put off.

Stephen of Amaseia, having spent three years on the throne of the first of cities, died, and a monk, Tryphon, was ordained on terms that after a fixed time he would willingly give up the throne to the emperor's son Theophylact; for he was still a boy. In these times there were an unbearable winter, a very severe famine and a most dreadful fire. At that time the emperor Christopher too measured out his life. When the fixed time had passed, the patriarch Tryphon did not give up the high priestly throne according to the agreement, but held on to the high priesthood with both hands. And the emperor was vexed at the deceit, as having been mocked. So the bishop of Caesarea, eager to please the emperor, went after the patriarch's simplicity with guile, and putting on a friend's mask said to the patriarch: "The ruler's attack on you is violent, but charges to put you under deposition fail him, and so those who surround you now plan to accuse you of not knowing letters at all. But hurry to beat off those plotting against you in this too. You will undo their effort if, before many people, you take a paper and write your name and the rank of your high priesthood. When this is brought to the emperor, no charge against you will be left." So he gave this advice, and the other was persuaded, and before many people he wrote this on a blank paper: "Tryphon, by the mercy of God archbishop of Constantinople, New Rome." And the bishop of Caesarea took the paper and went off to show it to the emperor. So a document of resignation, as if from the patriarch, was worked into it above the signature, and as having resigned he was thrown out of the church, and the emperor's son was ordained patriarch.

A fleet of the Rhos came against the city, and the fleet was not of a thousand ships, as is said, but its boats were counted at fifteen thousand. When these anchored near the Pharos, a Roman fleet stood against them prow to prow, at once turned the barbarians to flight, and burned many of the boats to ash with the liquid fire. Those that were left crossed to the east and fell in with the patrician Bardas Phocas, who commanded a military company, and who, catching many coming out of the boats to gather necessities, killed them. The domestic of the scholae, Curcuas, too, meeting others going out of the ships in search of supplies, took them alive and put them to the sword. Having suffered badly thus by sea and by land, they no longer went out from the boats. When their food had wholly failed, they decided to go back home and had already begun to sail out. But the triremes attacked them again, and twice the barbarians were beaten at sea, so that very few of their ships escaped and returned to their people, as messengers to them of the disaster. And the Rhos, having suffered worse than they did, gave up the attack on the Romans.

blocks: The Hagarenes too, through the domestic of the scholae John Curcuas and his brother Theophilus (Theophilus was the grandfather of John, who later held the empire), were often defeated and humbled and lost not the fewest of the cities they held. The emperor Romanus, seeming perhaps to come to a sense of his perjury and of his breaking of the agreements he had made with the emperor Constantine, hurried to propitiate God by good works. He made various distributions, and besides these he paid off to the lenders what was owed by those in the city and released the debtors from the weight of their debt, and taking the bonds burned them with fire in the middle of the Market; the debts were counted at nineteen centenaria. He also paid the rents of those living in hired houses in the great city. These things helped the debtors, but to Romanus, I think, they were of little or no profit, both because what was given belonged to others, for it was public money, and because, having seized the empire and holding it, enjoying it and depriving the one it belonged to, he allotted himself the whole of the imperial fortune and drew off a little drop for good works, doing something like a man who, having driven off his neighbour's ox and slaughtered it, gave the tips of the feet to the poor and feasted on the whole body himself. But this is by human judgement; if one looks to the divine goodness, perhaps one would not call even these things without effect.

While he held the sceptre, the image of Christ the Saviour not made by hands, the divine towel, was brought to the first of cities. Edessa had held it until then; but it was in danger of being taken by the Romans besieging it, so, to escape the sack, the people of Edessa gave the divine image as its ransom. At that time too a pair of boys joined together came from Armenia; when one died, the joining was cut by doctors; but it helped the survivor nothing, and living a little after his brother he too breathed his last.

How Romanus appropriated the empire, which in no way belonged to him, and granted his sons the imperial honour and title, and how he gave himself and his sons first place, while putting Constantine, the native-born successor to the empire, below all as one of many, I have already told. The narrative has now come to add what followed, and to show that even if providence goes after wrongdoers perhaps more slowly, measuring out to them a time for repentance, yet if they do not keep from evil it goes after them with slow foot and exacts justice. Romanus was completing the sixth year of his sole rule. Constantine was turning over in his mind all the time how to recover the empire for himself, and to achieve his desire he stirred up the sons, through others, against the father, or rather one of them, Stephen. For Constantine, being of steadier mind, did not accept the approach. But Stephen, taking others as partners, attacked his father, seized him, confined him on the island of Prote and tonsured him, while he himself laid claim to the imperial management with his brother-in-law and his brother; but the three could not agree. So they differed in some things and contradicted one another; and from this they suspected one another, and Stephen took thought to drag Constantine down from the empire, and Constantine in turn Stephen. But Constantine was much quicker to act, his wife Helena too urging him to it. So, taking also some of the military officials, he seized both brothers while they were lunching with him, and at once sent one to the island of Panormus, which is that of Antigonus, and the other to the one called Terebinthus, and had both tonsured clerics. Then, as they were being moved from there, they came into their father's sight, and seeing them he said: "I have begotten and raised up sons, and they have rejected me." From there Stephen was confined at Proconnesus, and from there moved to Rhodes, and from it to Mitylene; for Constantine Samothrace became the fixed bound. He, often trying to run away, and for this having killed the chief of his guards with poison, was killed by the others. Stephen died in Lesbos, having spent nineteen years there. Their father measured out his life on Prote, and so justice went after each of them.

blocks: As soon as Constantine had obtained the monarchy he put the diadem on his son Romanus too, and paying rewards to those who had helped him to the overthrow of the reigning emperors, he honoured Bardas Phocas as magister and appointed him domestic of the scholae of the East. Of Bardas's two sons, he appointed Nicephorus, who later reigned, general of the Anatolics, and Leo general of Cappadocia, and rewarded the others in other ways. He made Romanus, the son of the emperor Stephen, a eunuch, and also Basil, the bastard son of the old Romanus, whom he had begotten after being corrupted with a slave woman. Christopher's son Michael he had tonsured a cleric.

He was pious towards God and devoted to learning, as can be learned from his writings, and also from his letters, which, even if they were not worked out exactly according to the art of rhetoric, are yet adorned with its figures and some of its styles. He also gave himself to rhythms and metres of every kind; one could know this from the verses in which he lamented his wife when she died. He also took care of philosophy itself, which was already almost forgotten, and also of the sciences, setting teachers over them and rekindling them when they were failing. These things were on the better side of him. But in the management of the empire he was rather soft, quick to anger and slow to forgive towards offenders and an inexorable punisher, and used more wine than was enough. And in appointing to office he did not set worthy men over the commands or the offices of the state, but the more worthless and unfit, and those whom the empress and the parakoimomenos Basil brought in, putting the offices up for sale. But so the affairs of the empire were managed, even if not well in everything.

Plots were planned against the ruler, one by the parakoimomenos Theophanes, who had many others privy to it and wished to bring Romanus back from Prote to the palace; the other by others who planned to take Stephen from Lesbos and restore him to the empire. But Constantine detected both plots, punished the conspirators and put those who longed for the empire under safer guard. When the Turks (we said before that the Hungarians are so called) were plundering the Roman lands, it happened that the nation kept quiet for a time. For their leader, called Bulosudes, and another, Gylas, also ruler of a part, came to the emperor; and each of them was granted the divine bath of rebirth and initiated into our mystery, and each was honoured as patrician and drenched with money, and so they went back to their own haunts, taking a high priest too, through whom many were brought to knowledge of God. Gylas stayed in the faith and kept the peace. But the other, breaking his agreements with God, armed himself again against the Romans, and trying to do this to the Franks too he was caught and crucified. Elga, the wife of the Rhos who had sailed against the Romans, when her husband died, came to the emperor, and having been baptised and honoured as was fitting, went back.

The sovereign, since the daughter of Hugo, the king of the Franks, who had been married to his son Romanus, had already died, took thought to bring him another wife, and joined to him a girl of low or even vulgar fortune, some might say, for they say she was born of tavern keepers, but most comely in looks, simply a statue shaped by nature, who was called Anastaso and renamed Theophano.

blocks: In the twelfth year of Constantine's sole rule the patriarch Theophylact died, having been high priest for twenty-three years; he was sixteen years old when he was lawlessly granted the high priesthood. So the patriarch was under tutors while his father reigned; then, shaking them off, he did much that was improper, or, to put it more properly, forbidden, being mad for horses, keeping dogs, devoted to hunting and doing what goes with these. He nursed a very violent love of horses, and had very many mares. One of them, more notable than the rest, being in foal, happened to give birth on the holy day of Maundy Thursday, and while the patriarch was then celebrating the liturgy someone came bringing good news of the birth; he was overjoyed, cut short the divine service, went off in haste to Cosmidion, for his horses had their quarters there, and having seen the newborn foal came back to the church and performed the rite of the holy sufferings of Christ the Saviour. He ended his life from riding; for riding most recklessly and being dashed against one of the sea walls, he brought up blood through his mouth, and from this he was ill for two years, and then, falling into dropsy, died. And Polyeuctus was appointed patriarch, a monk and eunuch, outstanding in learning and virtue, who was ordained by the bishop of Caesarea. For the bishop of Heraclea, having offended the emperor in some matter, was barred from his privilege; and this was found by the mockers as a charge against the patriarch. When he had been ordained, he met the emperor and made an attack on the relatives of the old Romanus and urged him to check their greed. The emperor himself did not hear this with displeasure, but the empress Helena, prompted by the eunuch Basil, of whom more later, stirred the sovereign against the patriarch, and looked for an occasion by which she might take the high priesthood from him.

At that time too the precious hand of the Forerunner was brought to the first of cities from Antioch by a deacon, Job. When the Hagarenes in Crete were plundering the coastlands of the Roman dominion, the emperor made ready a fleet, made up of very many warships, and sent it against them. But the fleet's affairs failed through the inexperience and carelessness of its admiral. Most of the ships' crews perished, some captured, some put to the sword, and very few were saved. The admiral himself would have been taken, had not his servants stood round him and, pushing back the Hagarenes with locked shields, given the general room to board the flagship and so escape. But things did not go so for Bardas Phocas, the domestic of the scholae, against the eastern Hagarenes; managing the wars against them with a general's skill and experience, he took many of their towns and made plunder of whatever he met.

The emperor's son Romanus, having begun to be counted among men from beardless youth and longing to bring power round to himself, plotted against his father's life, his wife too helping him, and they prepared the plot with a deadly poison, which they secretly mixed into a purging drink that the sovereign was to drink. Just as it was about to be given to the emperor to drink, whether by providence or by chance, most of it was spilled, and the little that was left, drunk by the emperor, brought on him pains and no small fears of danger, but did not put his life in danger. So for the time he escaped it with difficulty. In the fifteenth year of his reign this emperor went out to the mountain of Olympus, in word so that he might be armed against the Hagarenes by the prayers of the ascetics there, but in truth, as is said, so that he might meet Theodore of Cyzicus and consider with him how to thrust Polyeuctus out of the church. Having been there, he came back to the palace in a bad way, and soon after measured out his life, as it seems to some from a bodily disorder, but as others believe from being again plotted against by his son. The whole span of his life was fifty-four years and two months; he reigned with his father Leo, his uncle Alexander and his mother thirteen years, and with Romanus, who seized the empire, twenty-six years, and finally ruled alone fifteen years. Right up to his death he took great care for the deposition of the chief shepherd Polyeuctus. It is said that some days before his death stones were thrown at night with a great whizzing against his chambers, and that this happened for several nights, and that the emperor thought he was being stoned by some men, and set many round the palace, by whom what was happening was watched; no one was seen sending the stones; so the deed was not thought to be done by men.

blocks: So Constantine died when the thread spun for him broke at the time fixed for his life, and his son Romanus, who was also called the child, took hold of the sole rule. He was called the child, not because he held the empire at a child's age, for he was already counted among men, but to distinguish him from his grandfather on his mother's side, Romanus, who was old and aged. But if anyone were to say he was called the child because his life too was childish, this too would fit his character very well. As soon as he became master of the sceptre he crowned his son Basil and granted him the imperial title. Then a second son too was born to him, who got the name of his grandfather Constantine. Romanus himself gave himself up to luxuries and pleasures and a dissolute life, and kept company with corrupt and pestilent men, and put the management of the empire under the praepositus and parakoimomenos Joseph Bringas.

So the magister Nicephorus Phocas, the domestic of the scholae, was sent against the Saracens in Crete with an army fit for battle, and for seven months he often engaged the barbarians, brought every siege engine against their towns and brought them under himself, then sacked their metropolis Chandax too, and subdued the leader of the Saracens in Crete, called Curupes, and the one first among the others after him, named Anemas. And had not Phocas been called back from there because of a prevailing rumour that the Roman who drove the Saracens out of Crete would in any case take hold of the Roman sceptre, the island might have been wholly subdued and the Saracens driven from it. Romanus also sent Leo Phocas, Nicephorus's brother, with a force against Chambdan, who ruled Aleppo; and he engaged Chambdan and defeated the barbarian by force, so that the greater part of his army fell in the battle, the rest was captured, and the commander himself was barely able to escape with a few that could be counted. Leo came back, was received magnificently and honoured with a triumph for victory. A plan of some men against the sovereign was detected, and those who stitched it together and their accomplices were arrested, but they were not punished harshly.

The magister Nicephorus Phocas, called back from Crete, was not allowed to hurry back to Byzantium, but was ordered to go to the east with the whole army; for Chambdan was expected to go against the Romans again. When Nicephorus Phocas had gone off to his house in Cappadocia, the parakoimomenos regretted that he had allowed him leave to go home; and he took great thought to get rid of the man.
