text: So Constantine died when the thread spun for him broke at the time fixed for his life, and his son Romanus, who was also called the child, took hold of the sole rule. He was called the child, not because he held the empire at a child's age, for he was already counted among men, but to distinguish him from his grandfather on his mother's side, Romanus, who was old and aged. But if anyone were to say he was called the child because his life too was childish, this too would fit his character very well. As soon as he became master of the sceptre he crowned his son Basil and granted him the imperial title. Then a second son too was born to him, who got the name of his grandfather Constantine. Romanus himself gave himself up to luxuries and pleasures and a dissolute life, and kept company with corrupt and pestilent men, and put the management of the empire under the praepositus and parakoimomenos Joseph Bringas. So the magister Nicephorus Phocas, the domestic of the scholae, was sent against the Saracens in Crete with an army fit for battle, and for seven months he often engaged the barbarians, brought every siege engine against their towns and brought them under himself, then sacked their metropolis Chandax too, and subdued the leader of the Saracens in Crete, called Curupes, and the one first among the others after him, named Anemas. And had not Phocas been called back from there because of a prevailing rumour that the Roman who drove the Saracens out of Crete would in any case take hold of the Roman sceptre, the island might have been wholly subdued and the Saracens driven from it. Romanus also sent Leo Phocas, Nicephorus's brother, with a force against Chambdan, who ruled Aleppo; and he engaged Chambdan and defeated the barbarian by force, so that the greater part of his army fell in the battle, the rest was captured, and the commander himself was barely able to escape with a few that could be counted. Leo came back, was received magnificently and honoured with a triumph for victory. blocks: As soon as rumour had proclaimed in Byzantium what had happened about Phocas, the parakoimomenos Joseph was in anguish. The usurper's father, Bardas Phocas, fled to the great church of God. Nicephorus's brother Leo was able to run away and join his brother. This brought the parakoimomenos into great helplessness; being hard of access he was hated by all, so all rejoiced if the affairs of the empire passed to another and he were removed from the scene; so all ran together to the great sanctuary of God. Learning this, Bringas, when he should have approached the crowd with mild words and softened its impulse, rather roughened it with threats, saying: "I shall stop their impulses by arranging that when they buy grain they carry the coin's worth in their own lap." Hearing this maddened the crowd. Basil, the former parakoimomenos, who was hostile to this Bringas and had a large body of servants about him, when evening had already come, armed his servants and sent them out to various parts of the city, and they, joined by a crowd of townsmen, pulled down many houses of those on the other side, and that of Bringas himself among them, and many people were killed. They did this, and at the same time acclaimed Nicephorus sovereign everywhere. From this fortune changed places for Bardas Phocas and Bringas. For the one came out of the church with confidence, and Bringas went into it as a pitiable suppliant. The parakoimomenos Basil and those about him made ready triremes, and the imperial one too, and going with them to Chrysopolis brought Nicephorus from there to the Hebdomon, and from there they came with a public procession to the Great Church, and the patriarch Polyeuctus crowned the man. The empress Theophano was at once thrust out of the palace and taken off to the Petrion; the parakoimomenos Joseph was confined in Paphlagonia and died after two years. Bardas, Nicephorus's father, was honoured as Caesar.

A few days later the emperor made Theophano his wife, and though he had kept from meat ever since his son Bardas died, struck unintentionally by a spear by his own cousin Pleuses while playing with him, from then on he ate this too. When the sacred marriage service was being performed in the New Church in the palace by the patriarch Polyeuctus, at the entrance to the sanctuary, when the emperor had already come near the screen, he was prevented by the patriarch from going in with him, as was his custom, the patriarch saying that unless he first served the penances of those who marry a second time, he must not dare the entrance to the sanctuary. The ruler bore this with difficulty, and was angry with the patriarch. There was also a story because of which the patriarch did not allow him to set foot on the sacred floor at all. For it was said that Nicephorus had been godfather of Theophano's children at holy baptism, and the patriarch demanded that he either separate from the empress or keep far from the holy things. But he would not give up Theophano; for his love for her was still burning; so he shared the question with the high priests present and the more learned of the senate. They, ascribing the canon about this to Copronymus, said that the legislation of such a man ought not to be reckoned in force, and all gave him a written permission about this. But the patriarch still held to his objection, until the emperor's father, the Caesar Bardas, gave him sworn assurances that the emperor had not been godfather of Theophano's children, and Stylianus, the protopapas of the palace, who was said to have been the first herald of this rumour, swore before a synod that he had neither seen nor spoken to anyone about it. When this had been done, the patriarch received Nicephorus.

The Saracens in Sicily exacted tribute from the Romans by old agreements, and this emperor thought it unbearable that while he reigned the Romans should pay tribute to the Hagarenes; so he sent against them the patrician Manuel, a bastard son of his father's brother Leo, who, having become domestic of the scholae under the old Romanus, attempted usurpation and was blinded. This Manuel, then, putting in at Sicily with a splendid navy, not only achieved nothing, but failed badly from inexperience and youthful arrogance, or rather recklessness; for both he himself and all the army with him perished. So matters in Sicily went thus. Against Cilicia, which the Hagarenes also held, the emperor sent the magister John Tzimisces, who had been appointed domestic of the East. He came to Adana, engaged the Hagarenes in it and set up a trophy against them. And from this rumour proclaimed him greater in generalship than before.

blocks: When Nicephorus was already completing his second year in the rule, he himself went out against Cilicia with a heavy hand, bringing Theophano with her children too. He left her before Cilicia at Drizion, which is a fort, and he, attacking Cilicia, took Anabarza, Rhosus and Adana, which are cities of the Cilicians, and also several forts. He judged he should not attack Tarsus and Mopsuestia because of the winter, or because his love for Theophano drew him back to her; for he went off with her to Cappadocia. And from there, when spring began, he returned to Cilicia, and himself besieged Mopsuestia, and set his brother Leo over Tarsus. Mopsuestia is divided in the middle by the river Sarus, and one part of it was taken by siege, and the Hagarenes in it moved to the rest, throwing fire into the part they left; then the other part too was taken, and no one escaped from there. Those in Tarsus, learning of the sack of Mopsuestia, called on the emperor and handed over the city. Three days later a fleet sailed out from Egypt to help Tarsus, but it was not allowed to put in at the shore; so it sailed off again; and falling in with violent blasts of wind and with Roman triremes, the greater part perished. The emperor returned to Constantinople bringing the gates of Tarsus and of Mopsuestia, made of bronze and showing exactness of craftsmanship, which he adorned and fitted, some to the eastern wall at the acropolis, and the others to the western wall. And paying God, as it were, the first fruits of his campaign, he dedicated in the divine sanctuary of the Wisdom of God the Word the precious crosses which the barbarians had taken when Stypiotes, being domestic of the scholae and besieging Tarsus, fell into misfortune through bad counsel. Through him the Roman dominion also gained Cyprus, which was held by the Hagarenes. Then he attacked Syria, and having sacked cities and taken lands lying by Lebanon and the coast, he came to Antioch. When the people of Antioch resisted rather strongly, and the supplies of the soldiers were already failing, and a great swamp had formed from rain, he gave up the siege and came back to the first of cities, bringing the holy and divine likeness of Christ the Saviour which he found on a tile at Hierapolis in Syria, and a lock of hair of John the Baptist stained with blood.

Such was this sovereign in generalship, and he greatly increased the borders of the Romans and extended the measured lines of their dominion. But for some reasons he was hateful to all. The reasons were these: when the soldiers who had joined him in the revolt ill-treated whomever they met, he paid no attention to those wronged, and when many houses of both distinguished men and commoners were plundered he behaved as if no harm had happened, or rather he even revelled in the drunken outrages against the townsmen, and this against those who had helped him obtain the empire; and because, on the pretext of the continual wars, he wore out his subjects with new levies, increases of the old ones and the exaction of every kind of goods, and the soldiery treated those of his subjects among whom it was quartered no better than enemies. Besides this, pretending that he lacked money because of his frequent campaigns, he reduced bit by bit the imperial gifts distributed to the senate, and wholly stopped the yearly grants assigned from of old to sacred sanctuaries and charitable houses. Then he also made an imperial decree that churches should not be enlarged in real property, and the pretext was that in his view the property of the churches was not spent properly by the high priests. Then, when the high priests of the time and the chief shepherd Polyeuctus disagreed about elections, the former drawing to themselves the freedom to elect whomever they approved, and he finding fault with the elections as not made without passion nor with uprightness of judgement, and hurrying to have the high priests share with him about those to be elected, the emperor seized an occasion from this and moved the whole appointment of bishops into his own power, ordering that no one be sent to any church whatever without his judgement; and when a bishop died, he sent an imperial servant to the widowed church, and while the necessary expenses were met stingily by him, he himself took what was left over.

While he reigned there was no end of registrars, inspectors, recruiting officers and those called protonotarii sent into all the lands, who squeezed the subjects with every kind of ill-treatment and drove them to the utmost want, not sparing even the wholly destitute, but enrolling these in the courier services, moving those formerly subject to these to the naval service, transferring the seamen to foot soldiers, enlisting former foot soldiers among the horsemen and changing the horsemen into cataphracts, and laying a heavier military burden on each. For he seemed to set his name wholly to the handling of the soldiery; so, as far as lay with him, he also decreed that soldiers killed in wars should be honoured equally with the martyrs, receive like hymns and be celebrated in the same way. And had not the patriarch and some of the high priests, and also some of the chosen men of the senate, nobly resisted, saying: "How could those who kill and are killed in wars be reckoned by anyone martyrs or equal to the martyrs, when the divine canons put them under penance, keeping them for three years from the awesome and holy communion?", that godlike decree might perhaps have been ratified.

Besides the rest he was also, it seems, a slave of money; for until his time every coin had drawn the weight of an exagium, but he devised the tetarteron, clipping it in weight, and made the collections in the heavier coin, but the payments and all the expenses in the clipped one. And when an old custom prevailed that every stater bearing an imperial image was of equal value with the one newly struck by the reigning emperor, he ordered his own coin to be preferred. Why? So that it alone, sought by the merchants, might bring him profit, with large exchange fees exacted for each coin. While the citizens were thus harmed by these things, there was no provision by the market overseers about goods for sale; each of the merchants had his own will as law; and those buying necessities became poorer every day.

blocks: These and many other things, for it is hard to count them all, maddened everyone against Nicephorus, and all prayed to be rid of his tyranny. Not least the walling of the palace also grieved people. For having had an oracle that he would be killed in the palace, he thought he was getting himself safety by the wall, when he should have reckoned that if the oracle were true, what was fated, or, to put it so, what was fixed by God, would also be inescapable and unchangeable; but if it can be prevented by some device, it is not wholly true and the devices are superfluous. But he, reckoning none of this, at great expense crowned the palace with the wall that is now seen; the citizens judged this an acropolis and a tyrant's stronghold built against them. So when he had finished the fortification and thought he had got himself a safe guard, then he knew the device had profited him nothing, suffering his destruction inside it. But not yet about this; let the narrative still go through his deeds.

Returning from Antioch on the Orontes, this emperor built a fort on the mountain of the Taurus, which most people now call the Black Mountain, in which he left Michael Burtzes, honouring him as patrician and naming him general of the Black Mountain, ordering him to harm the people of Antioch. And he left Peter, one of his own servants, a eunuch but active and weighty and knowing how to command soldiers, naming him stratopedarch, so that he might give the army a place in Cilicia to spend the winter. The emperor came to Byzantium, and Burtzes, constantly riding out, harmed the Hagarenes in Antioch and looked for a way to take the city, if he could, and win fame. So once he secretly took the measure of the height of one of the towers, and made ladders to fit that height. Watching for a wintry night, moonless and snowy, he quietly approached the wall of the city, set the ladders against it and climbed up with three hundred men, for he had brought so many, without anyone noticing, and killed the guards of that tower and of others nearby, and at once sent to the stratopedarch, making known to him what had happened and calling him to help. He hung back; for it is said the emperor had ordered him not to attack Antioch, because it was rumoured among all that the destruction of the ruler would follow the capture of Antioch. The people of Antioch, learning of the capture of the towers, gathered there, eager to drive the Romans out of them. So the stratopedarch, having his reasoning fighting between two opposites, the imperial order and the destruction of Burtzes and the three hundred men with him, resolved not to let so many men perish, and setting out with the whole army attacked the city of Antiochus. At once the enemy lost heart in hand and soul, while Burtzes's men and he himself, who had already given up, came to life again, and Burtzes, cutting through the bolts of the gates with an axe, gave the stratopedarch free entry, and so the famous Antioch came quite easily under the Romans. This, reported to the emperor, caused grief, not joy, and he was angry with the stratopedarch, and gave Burtzes insults and threats as reward for his zeal and his brave deed, took his command from him and ordered him to stay at home without going out.
text: These and many other things, for it is hard to count them all, maddened everyone against Nicephorus, and all prayed to be rid of his tyranny. Not least the walling of the palace also grieved people. For having had an oracle that he would be killed in the palace, he thought he was getting himself safety by the wall, when he should have reckoned that if the oracle were true, what was fated, or, to put it so, what was fixed by God, would also be inescapable and unchangeable; but if it can be prevented by some device, it is not wholly true and the devices are superfluous. But he, reckoning none of this, at great expense crowned the palace with the wall that is now seen; the citizens judged this an acropolis and a tyrant's stronghold built against them. blocks: Something else too happened which maddened the people against the emperor and the sovereign against the people. By an old custom, on one of the Lord's feasts the emperor made a procession to the divine church at Pege, and a quarrel happened to arise between Armenians and seamen, and from it a clash with each other, noise, great din and killing of men on both sides. When rumour announced what had happened to those in the city before the emperor's return, the reckless among the people gathered in bands in many places, and meeting the Armenians as they came back beat them with clubs. When the emperor too reached the market of the bakers, they poured insults on him too, and uproar arose, shouting and running together, and some threw stones at the emperor, others sprinkled dust on him, and they reviled him as far as the market that is paved with slabs and carries the round porphyry column. And had not some of the more honoured citizens received the emperor there, checked those following and reviling him and otherwise behaving disorderly, and surrounding him acclaimed him and so brought him safe to the palace, perhaps some great evil would have happened. From this a story was spread that the emperor, bearing a grudge against the people, would take revenge on it at a horse race. So when a horse race was being held, the emperor at an untimely moment brought armed soldiers into the middle of the theatre, perhaps to show the people, as in a model of war, what the clash of battle is like, as if forsooth providing them pleasure from it, or perhaps wishing to shake fear over them. When the soldiers bared their swords, the people in the theatre, thinking this was what had been rumoured, rushed to run away from the theatre, and crowded at the exits and trampled by one another, not a few perished. Perhaps many more would have been in danger, had not the emperor been seen unmoved on his own seat. For the people, seeing him not moving from his seat at all, stopped their flight. Those related to the dead then, lamenting their kin, jeered at the emperor publicly. Knowing, then, that he was hated by the citizens for these things, he girded the palace with a wall; but when this had been finished and the keys of the gates had been brought to him, then the fear he feared came on him, and he got no profit from the safety he had devised.

When the Turks, that is the Hungarians, were plundering the Thracian lands, the emperor Nicephorus wrote to the ruler of Bulgaria not to allow them to cross the Ister and ravage the land of the Romans. But he did not obey, saying: "When these men marched against us, you would not help us when asked. And now, when under compulsion we have made a treaty with them, you ask us to break the treaty, take up arms against them and start a war without pretext." Rebuffed from this quarter, he sent an embassy to the ruler of Rhosia, Sphendosthlavus, urging him against the Bulgars; so he sent Calocyrus, the son of the leading man in Cherson, to Rhosia. So a Rhos force marched against the Bulgars, plundered much of their country and drove off from there plunder not easily counted. And in the following year the Rhos harmed the lands of the Bulgars no less than before.

blocks: While Phocas reigned there was also a most fearful earthquake, from which Constantine's city did not suffer much, but other cities suffered very badly. Winds also blew in the month of May, by which the crops were destroyed and a severe famine came, which Nicephorus turned to his own profit, raising the price of grain and selling it dear to the starving, not caring that he was cursed by the people, but rather boasting that he was a benefactor of his subjects because he sold two medimni for a coin, and this with the example of Basil the Macedonian, who not very long before had shown magnificence in such a want. For that sovereign once went off making his customary procession to the church of the Holy Apostles, and seeing some men of the city who showed a rather dignified bearing looking gloomy, he asked the reason for their gloominess. They said: "And how should we not be gloomy, master, seeing death hanging over us, we who buy two medimni of grain for a gold coin?" Hearing this, he groaned aloud, and relieved their dejection with money, and railed at and cursed those entrusted with the civil offices because they had not told him of the want, and at once ordered the imperial granaries opened and twelve medimni of grain sold for one coin. But for him this deed was royal, while for the emperor now being written of it was very much a huckster's, who, seeing his subjects pressed by famine, did not help, but even revelled in their misfortunes, and scratched the wounds of those wounded by the famine. And the emperor's brother Leo oppressed no less both the people of the city and the inhabitants of the countryside, pursuing trade himself too. So they were disposed thus towards the sufferers, and the sufferers jeered at the ruler for this. For once, when the emperor was inspecting newly enrolled soldiers, since a grey-haired man too was counted among them, the sovereign said to him: "How, fellow, do you enrol yourself among the soldiers, being old?" And he at once answered cleverly: "I am much stronger now, master, than when I was in my prime. For then I could not have carried on my shoulders a coin's worth of grain, even half; but now I shall more easily lift on my shoulders two coins' worth." The emperor understood the irony, but bearing it calmly passed on to another.

Nicephorus, who had before been very much in love with Theophano, afterwards kept from intercourse with her, either sated with her or keeping from intercourse out of self-control. For not even when young was he very prone to love. She, hating the man for his unsociableness, or fearing for her sons (for it was whispered by some that Nicephorus wished to deprive the little emperors of their genitals and make his brother Leo emperor), came secretly to talks with Tzimisces, either caught by love for the man, for he was outstanding in beauty and gave off the graces of good looks, or reckoning him a fit counterweight to Nicephorus; and, as some say, she also came into intercourse with the man, stirred him against Nicephorus and, as the proverb has it, let the ball roll downhill. For John was in any case angry with the emperor, because he, persuaded by his brother, who envied John, thought the man suspect, and, removing him from his military command, moved him to a civil one, appointing him logothete of the drome, which was reckoned for him not power but punishment, and a heavy one. Then, adding to the man's ill-treatment, he also ordered him to stay at home; for these reasons John was angry. And when he found that wanton woman sharpening him on, and she had also obtained his return by imperial order, he set about the usurpation, having the empress working with him, and at the same time revealed the secret to those he trusted and set about the deed, and taking them in the dead of night he came to the southern sea of the palace; the place is called Boukoleon, because there is a stone lion in it mounted on a bull of the same, and holding its horn with its left foot it twists the bull's neck. Coming there, he saw a basket let down from above, and he and those with him were drawn up by it by Theophano's maids. They were Michael Burtzes, who was also bearing a grudge against the emperor because of his unreasoning anger, as has been said, Leo Abalantes, and the dark Theodore, whom they called Atzypotheodorus because of his rather dark looks, and two others. Slipping without a sound into the imperial bedchamber, for Theophano arranged this for them too, they found Nicephorus sleeping on the ground, and one of them leapt on him with his heel, insulted him and woke him. When, woken, he raised his head, he at once received a mortal blow on it, which terribly shook both his body and his soul. Then Tzimisces sat down on the imperial bed, and they set Phocas, already enfeebled, beside him, holding him up on either side. He asked him the reasons for which he had been ill-treated by him. When he answered nothing, but only uttered "Lord, help," John ordered those about him to strike his jaws with the hilts of their swords and break or knock out his teeth. Then someone from behind struck him in the back with a spear, and the spear came out through his chest. And when a commotion arose from those sleeping before the chamber, for they had now become aware of the plot, they cut off the head of the man, who had just breathed his last, and showed it through a window to the bodyguards, and so stopped their onset. It is said that a few days before, Nicephorus found a writing in his bedchamber revealing the plot. The emperor Nicephorus's brother Leo, learning what had happened, fled to the Great Church with his son Nicephorus. The murdered emperor was fifty-seven years old, of which he held the Roman sceptre six years and as many months. And so he paid his debt.

blocks: Tzimisces, having become master of the empire, made the sons of Romanus, who were still children, partners in the rule, and taking on the parakoimomenos Basil, whom Phocas had honoured as proedros, a rank that did not exist before, as one practised in public affairs, he entrusted him with their whole management. He removed those related to Nicephorus or otherwise suspected of keeping goodwill towards him, confining the curopalates Leo and his son Nicephorus in Lesbos, setting Amaseia as the fixed bound for Leo's other son Bardas, and dealing with and arranging others in other ways. He brought back those exiled by Nicephorus, among whom high priests too were counted, as many as had not stooped to sign the tome by which it had been decreed that no high priest should be appointed without him. Then John went off to the Great Church to be crowned. But he was not allowed by Polyeuctus to enter the church, as being defiled by murder. Tzimisces bore the rebuke mildly and pleaded that he had not been the murderer with his own hand, but said that Abalantes and Atzypotheodorus had made away with Nicephorus at Theophano's bidding. So the patriarch demanded that Theophano be driven from the palace and confined, that Nicephorus's murderers be driven out, that the tome we mentioned be torn up, and that John himself accept penances. He promised to do everything, and at once sent and brought the empress down from the palace, tore up the tome when it was brought there, and promised to distribute to the poor the property he had while he was a private man. When this had been done, at the feast of the birth of our Saviour and God, he was both allowed entry into the church and crowned with the diadem, and he confined Theophano at Proconnesus.

Proclaimed in this way, since great Antioch was widowed of a high priest, he appointed a monk Theodore, who had foretold to him that he would gain the empire, and told him not to hurry or seize it, but to wait as it were for the appointment from God. He, accepting the high priesthood, made a request to John to move the Manichaeans from the east to the west, since they were corrupting many with their abominable heresy. Fulfilling his request, he moved the race of the Manichaeans to Philippopolis. The patriarch Polyeuctus, living thirty-five days after Tzimisces's proclamation, departed life, and in his place the monk Basil Scamandrenus was brought in to the high priestly throne of the reigning city.

The sons of Hagar, thinking it unbearable to be deprived of the cities already taken from them, gathered from every side, made agreements for alliance, gave the leadership to the Carthaginians, and marched against Antioch by Daphne and besieged it. When those in the city resisted them rather strongly, the gathering of the nations was reported to the emperor. He ordered the general of Mesopotamia to help the besieged; and when war broke out with the Hagarenes, the barbarians, though many times more than the Romans, were routed and scattered.

The Rhos, having brought the nation of the Bulgars and its country under themselves, and the leaders of the nation, Boris and Romanus, no longer remembered their homes, but wished to stay there holding the country. Calocyrus too stirred them to this, saying: "If I am proclaimed emperor of the Romans by you, I shall give up the country of the Bulgars to you, make with you a peace for ever, and pay what has been promised many times over." They, charmed by the excellence of the land and puffed up by Calocyrus's words, were not persuaded when the emperor wrote that he would fulfil everything Nicephorus had promised them, and spoke rather boastfully to the envoys. So he was forced to take up arms against them, and setting over the Roman forces as commander, whom he named stratelates, the magister Bardas Sclerus, the brother of his wife, who had already died, he ordered him to set out against the Rhos. He went off; and the barbarians and their leader Sphendosthlavus, learning this, armed the Bulgars and took as allies the Scythians who are called Patzinaks and the Turks who live in Pannonia, and putting together an army counted at three hundred thousand, plundered all Thrace. Sclerus, not daring to engage them and fight in close battle, for the soldiery with him was very small against their multitude, overcame the barbarians by a general's methods. First he set ambushes, attacked the Patzinaks alone, and cleverly drawing them round into the ambushes, killed some and took others alive; then, when he engaged the others too, the battle was evenly balanced for a while; but one of the Scythians, who seemed brave in bulk of body and presence of mind and to surpass all his kinsmen, seeing Sclerus riding through the ranks under him and rousing them to valour, rushed at him and brought his sword down on the man's head; but because of the strength and smoothness of the helmet it did not touch him. Sclerus in turn struck the Scythian on the head, and the blow of the sword was so effective that the barbarian was cut in two and the halves of him fell from the horse. The barbarians, struck by the deed, fell into fear and at once turned to flight, and the Romans, driving after them, killed many and took many alive. Night coming on stopped Sclerus's men from the pursuit; and all who were left were wounded.

First he set ambushes, attacked the Patzinaks alone, and cleverly drawing them round into the ambushes, killed some and took others alive; then, when he engaged the others too, the battle was evenly balanced for a while; but one of the Scythians, who seemed brave in bulk of body and presence of mind and to surpass all his kinsmen, seeing Sclerus riding through the ranks under him and rousing them to valour, rushed at him and brought his sword down on the man's head; but because of the strength and smoothness of the helmet it did not touch him. Sclerus in turn struck the Scythian on the head, and the blow of the sword was so effective that the barbarian was cut in two and the halves of him fell from the horse. The barbarians, struck by the deed, fell into fear and at once turned to flight, and the Romans, driving after them, killed many and took many alive. Night coming on stopped Sclerus's men from the pursuit; and all who were left were wounded.

blocks: So matters with the Rhos stood thus. Bardas Phocas, the son of Leo, escaping from Amaseia, where he had been confined, seized Caesarea of the Cappadocians, having won over many, and attempted usurpation, putting on himself the insignia of the empire. His father Leo, with his other son Nicephorus, planned to cross from Lesbos to Thrace, having the archbishop of Abydus working with him; but being found out he was condemned to be blinded, with his son Nicephorus. It is said that the emperor secretly ordered those entrusted with the blinding of the men not to gouge out their eyes, but to give the appearance of blinding, while keeping the men's sight unharmed. When this had happened thus, an imperial letter reached Sclerus, who had just routed the Scythians, to cross to the east and stand against Bardas Phocas. And he went off at once and came to Caesarea, and Phocas's men left him and flowed over to Sclerus, and he, left alone with his servants, fled to the fort of Tyropoion. When he was already near that fort, horsemen sent by Sclerus caught up with him, one of whom, Constantine Charon, bolder than the others, it seems, outstripping his fellow soldiers, came at Phocas with a more violent rush; he was bringing up the rear and protecting those with him, and Charon pelted him with insults. And Phocas said: "You ought not to rebuke a man who has come into such misfortunes." When at this Charon came near Bardas and tried to strike him, he raised his club and struck Constantine on the helmet, crushing it together with the man's head, and at once purple death seized the stricken man, killed by one blow. Those driving behind, seeing him fallen, gave up the pursuit, and Phocas slipped into the fort. Then Sclerus too arrived and persuaded him to come over to the emperor; and when he came Tzimisces made him a cleric and confined him on Chios. And Sclerus was ordered again to move to the west.

The emperor took as his wife, through the efforts of the parakoimomenos Basil, Theodora, the daughter of Constantine Porphyrogenitus. In the second year of his reign, when spring shone out, he marched against the Rhos with many armies and a splendid fleet, and as he went envoys, forsooth, of the Scythians met him; but they were spies and scouts of the strength of the Romans, which did not escape the emperor. So he ordered them to be led round the whole camp and to learn it well, and told them to go. When they had gone, he himself took lightly armed foot soldiers, about five thousand, and four thousand horsemen, and went after the envoys, and suddenly came near great Persthlava and pitched a camp, which threw the Tauroscythians into helplessness. Calocyres, the first author of the evils, who was there then, learning that the emperor had arrived, ran off to the camp of the Rhos; and they, learning of the emperor's presence from him, were thrown into confusion, but nevertheless encamped beside the Romans. The emperor's men, coming to the town of Persthlava, as has been said, caught about eight thousand training outside, and engaged them. They held out a little, then turned their backs and fled. Those inside, arming themselves as each could, came out to help their fellow tribesmen, and the Romans, meeting them as they came on in disorder, killed many, and the others went back again into the city. But some horsemen rode out and walled off the path leading into the city, and the barbarians scattered over the ground outside the town; there some were taken alive, others killed, and those in the city shut the gates and were besieged. The next day, when the parakoimomenos Basil came with the whole army, the emperor set about the siege more strongly, and some climbed the wall by ladders, cut down with swords the barbarians caught there, opened the gates and gave the whole Roman army easy entry. And so the town of Persthlava was taken by the Romans, where Boris, the king of the Bulgars, was also taken, whom, and all the Bulgars, the sovereign treated mildly, letting them go free, saying he had taken up arms not against the Bulgars but against the Rhos.

When many Scythians had fled to a stronghold, the emperor ordered it too to be taken. The soldiers were unwilling because the place was hard to take. Learning this, John himself went on foot before the others to the stronghold, and from this all ran together there; and by their zeal the stronghold too was taken, and of those in it some were destroyed and some taken by the Romans. In this town the emperor set a garrison fit for battle, and he went off to Dorostolum, which is also called Dristra, and taking some cities on the way and sacking forts he reached Dorostolum. Before this city the leader of the Rhos, Sphendosthlavus, was encamped. When the armies saw each other, they at once clashed with each other, and for much of the day they fought on even terms, but towards late afternoon the Rhos, worn out, turned to flight, and the Romans pursued; very many of the barbarians perished, no fewer were taken alive, and the rest went back into Dorostolum. And the emperor, pitching a camp before the city, waited for the triremes to guard the Ister, so that the Rhos might not run away. Sphendosthlavus put in fetters all the Bulgars he held, who were twenty thousand, it is said, fearing they would rise against him or go over to the emperor. When the fleet too arrived, the emperor besieged the city. Envoys came to the emperor from Constantia and other forts, asking pardon and handing over themselves and the forts to him. The Romans took these over, and the siege of Dorostolum lasted many days, the barbarians resisting stoutly. But when from the continual battles many had become wounded, and their means of life were already failing them, their spirits began to break. But Sphendosthlavus, watching for a moonless and stormy night, put about two thousand men into dugout boats, embarked with them himself, and went off to forage, and having collected what they needed they went back to Dorostolum. And seeing some Roman servants scattered about the river on various tasks, they got out of the boats, killed some, and went back again to Dorostolum unnoticed. This grieved the emperor greatly, and he was angry with the commanders of the fleet, and threatened that if the barbarians again sailed off without their notice, death would be their penalty. Having besieged the city for sixty whole days and not yet taken it, he decided to overcome those inside by famine, and sat round it, watching closely so that nothing they needed might be brought to them from anywhere. The barbarians made many sallies and were defeated; and since they were pressed by famine and had no hope of a supply of necessities, nor yet of alliance, some advised running away by night, others entrusting themselves to the Romans and so returning home, and others suggested something else.

blocks: But Sphendosthlavus urged them to fight the Romans once more, and either prevail and be saved or prefer a glorious death to an unhappy life. He said this, and the multitude approved, and the next day, ready to die, they engaged the Romans, and for a long time sometimes the Romans got the better of the Scythians, and sometimes the barbarians of the Romans. When the emperor noticed that the narrowness of the place was to the advantage of the enemy, since the Romans could not attack them in mass, he suggested to the generals that the units should withdraw quietly to the plain, moving little by little. This gave the barbarians the impression of cowardice and flight on the part of the Romans, and they followed with a war cry. When they came to a wider plain, the emperor gave the Romans the signal to turn, and turning they attacked the barbarians, and the battle became dreadful. The emperor sent the magister Bardas Sclerus with the units under him to shut the barbarians off from the way into the city. The battle was evenly balanced for a long time. It is said that the Romans then received more divine help. For a storm struck the Scythians in the face, and a horseman was seen by many of the Romans fighting for them and throwing the phalanxes of the barbarians into confusion. On the day of that battle the memory of the stratelates Theodore, famous among martyrs, was being celebrated. So the Scythians were routed and rushed for the city; but it could not be entered by them, for the entry to it had already been shut off by Sclerus, and so they scattered over its suburbs, and as they were caught they were destroyed, and they perished by one another, pushed and trampled together, so that those killed were hard to count. Those who were left were all wounded. It became known that it was the stratelates Theodore who then helped the Romans and fought with them against the barbarians. For a woman who lived in piety and dignity in Byzantium seemed, one day before this battle, to see in her sleep the holy Mother of God going forth escorted by many, and to hear the Mother of God say to one of those going before her: "Lord Theodore, my John and yours is in heavy struggles; hurry, then, help him." The woman made the dream known to some. They noted the day, and it was the one before the last battle. The emperor, repaying the martyr for his help, built him a very beautiful church at Euchaneia or Euchaïta, pulling down the former one, in which he laid his body of many contests, and named the city Theodoropolis in place of its former name.

The barbarian Sphendosthlavus, despairing on every side, sent envoys to the emperor, asking pardon, begging to go back home, to be enrolled among the allies of the Romans, and that any Scythian who wished might go to the Roman lands and trade in them. And the emperor accepted the requests and fulfilled them all; then Sphendosthlavus himself came to the sovereign and talked with him, and asked him to make known to the Patzinaks that they should not prevent the Rhos, going home, from passing through their country. And the emperor asked them to do this, and to be his allies, and not to cross the Ister and plunder Bulgaria. They agreed to the rest, but refused the passage of the Rhos.

blocks: When the war with the Rhos had been ended in this way, the emperor returned to Byzantium and was received splendidly by the whole citizen body. For the patriarch met him with the whole clergy, and the members of the senate and the people, bringing crowns and a four-horse chariot, whose horses were white, and they begged him to mount the chariot and hold the triumph. He accepted the crowns, and held the triumph on a riding horse, this too white, and on the four-horse chariot he placed the royal robes of the Bulgar kings, and above them an image of the Mother of God, and the chariot went ahead. Coming to the market called the Plakote, he stripped Boris of the insignia of the kingship among the Bulgars and honoured him with the rank of magister. Sphendosthlavus, going home with the Rhos, fell into ambushes of the Patzinaks, and all perished together.

This emperor built magnificently the church of Christ the Saviour at the Chalke. When the patriarch Basil was accused on some charges and deposed by a synod four years after his appointment, Antony the Studite was ordained patriarch. Since the cities gained by the Romans in the east had turned to revolt, shaken off the yoke of slavery and broken the bonds of the Roman dominion, the emperor marched out against them, and brought them under the yoke of the Roman dominion again, some submitting without trouble, others by the sword and great force. Returning from there, and coming to Anabarza and Podandus, and seeing there and in many other lands well-peopled and very fruitful estates, he asked whose they were. And learning that they belonged to the parakoimomenos Basil, some gained for the empire by the emperor Nicephorus Phocas, some by himself when he was domestic of the scholae, and some by others, and given to him, he was grieved and said it was a terrible thing that one eunuch should enjoy the public lands, for which many good men had fallen and many had suffered hardship. These words, reported by someone to the parakoimomenos, stirred him to plot against the emperor, and mixing a deadly poison, not quick or swift to kill, but slow and working on the drinker over time, and winning over with gifts the man who used to pour the emperor's wine, he poured it into the ruler's cup; and drunk, it harmed little by little the drinker's strength and destroyed the state of his body, until it drove the sovereign to his death. So John Tzimisces, passing from things here in this way, left the empire to its heirs, that is to Basil and Constantine, the sons of Romanus, having reigned six and a half years.

I have come to relate something that almost escaped notice. But they were detected and arrested, one of the conspirators having revealed the plan, and were no longer granted kindness, but had their eyes dug out without pity, and this was the end of their good fortune and of their desire for the empire.

blocks: So the sceptre of the Romans was restored to those to whom it belonged by birth, I mean Basil and Constantine, of whom the one was completing the twentieth year of his age, and Constantine the seventeenth. But while they wore the symbols of the empire, the proedros Basil simply had the power girded about him. Basil put up with this, not yet trusting himself, and attended to the parakoimomenos as to a trainer and shaped himself on his handling and management of public affairs, so that when the time called he too might handle the military rolls and the good order of the state. For he was wakeful and active in character, not easygoing like his brother and given to the idle life. As soon as power came round to these brothers, the proedros brought their mother back from exile and restored her to her sons.

Suspecting the magister Bardas Sclerus, who was stratelates and had all the eastern forces under him, he took from him the command of stratelates and appointed him duke of Mesopotamia. This grieved Sclerus greatly, and, as he always nursed a desire for the empire in any case, stirred him to revolt. So, taking up the command to which he had been appointed, he revealed the secret to many. Being loved by the whole army for his deeds of valour, he had almost all obedient. Since his son Romanus was in the queen of cities, he hurried to have him with him too, and secretly sending someone he was able to get his son away unnoticed, and at once set about the usurpation, bound his head with the imperial headband and put purple shoes on his feet, was acclaimed as emperor, took pains to collect money, and took as allies the emir of Amida, for so Emet is called, and the emir of Martyropolis, which is named Mieferkeim, and also Arabs. Taking these with him he pressed on towards Constantine's city, buoyed up by good hopes, which he nursed from elsewhere too, but above all from a dream of a monk who practised virtue. For he seemed to see Sclerus come to a woman sitting on a high lookout, and she put the imperial whip into his hand. The whip, it seems, was a symbol of the divine anger and of the destruction of the Romans from the civil wars, which Sclerus thought signified the empire, judging the vision by his own desire.

When the rumour of Sclerus's usurpation reached the rulers, what was left of the soldiery was made ready to stand against the rebel. Meanwhile the high priest of Nicomedia was sent to him as envoy, and said much to him to lead him to peace, but did not persuade him. For Sclerus, showing him the scarlet shoe, said it was impossible for one who had once put it on to throw it off easily. When those in the palace learned this answer, they set out of necessity for battle. The commander of the imperial force was the eunuch Peter, Phocas's man, whom we mentioned before. When the armies had encamped opposite each other at Lipara, which was also named Lycandus, and clashed with each other, for a time the imperial troops held out bravely, then they were routed and many were killed, and the camp fell to the enemy and was plundered. Then, having taken Tzamandus, a very populous city, by the coming over of its inhabitants, he gathered a swarm of money from it. Having thus prevailed over the imperial army, he drew many from it over to himself, who had already given up hopes of safety with the emperors, and not only nameless soldiers but many famous ones too flowed over to him.

When this was reported to the parakoimomenos, Leo the protovestiarius was sent again, entrusted with unmixed authority and given licence to do all that is permitted even to emperors; one might call the man a dictator in the Latin tongue. Joining the stratopedarch, the protovestiarius tried to draw Sclerus's men over with promises and honours; but when he saw he was attempting what could not be achieved, he passed Sclerus by night and went towards the East. From this fear for their dearest seized Sclerus's men, and leaving the rebel they came over to the protovestiarius. Afraid at this, Sclerus sent the magister Michael Burtzes, who had come over to him, and the patrician Romanus Taronites with an army against the protovestiarius. They attacked him and were defeated. When the defeat of those sent became known to Sclerus, he himself went against the protovestiarius with the whole army under him, clashed with the army with him and won. The stratopedarch Peter was killed, and the protovestiarius was captured. This victory raised Sclerus's affairs high and brought those of the emperors to despair, all the more because the rebel was also master of the sea. So the parakoimomenos made ready a fleet and sent it against the rebel's fleet, and in the sea battle Sclerus's fleet was beaten and scattered.

When things at sea were quiet, the parakoimomenos arranged things on land, and sent Eroticus to Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, to guard it; Sclerus attacked it and was beaten off, and hoped that famine would make those in it betray it, and indeed he spent a long time there, and brought those inside to be pressed by want of grain. So Eroticus decided to outwit the enemy by deceit, filled the granaries with sand and coloured the sand over with grain, so that the whole mass seemed to be grain. Having some captives from the enemy's camp, he showed them the granaries, not even half empty, and through them made known to Sclerus that he did not fear a siege by famine. "But if you give me pledges," he said, "allowing me to leave with whom I wish, I shall give up the city to you, being on your side." Sclerus heard this with great joy and gave him pledges, and he, taking most of the city's people and the soldiers with him, left the city and went off to the great city, and Sclerus went into Nicaea, and then knew he had been outwitted.

The parakoimomenos, when Sclerus set out from there and came near the reigning city, was at a loss. So, changing his mind, he called Bardas Phocas back from exile, and binding him with awesome oaths and most dreadful curses never to attack the empire nor to plot against the reigning emperors, he set the man over the remaining forces, honouring him as magister, giving him abundant money and entrusting him with the battle against Sclerus. So Phocas went off. Sclerus, learning this, then knew he would have to fight an opponent worthy of him, and setting out he went off, and near Amorium he engaged Phocas, and a battle of the armies took place, and Sclerus's men got the upper hand, and Phocas's men turned their backs. So this battle went thus. The next day the leaders of the armies chose to fight each other themselves and take on the contest for the whole. So they came at each other, and Sclerus was first to strike Phocas, as some say with a club on the head, but as others say he raised his sword against him, and when Phocas leaned to the other side and avoided the blow, the tip of the sword cut off the ear of Phocas's horse. Phocas struck back at Sclerus with a club on the head, and the stricken man, growing dizzy, fell on his horse's neck; those about him, seeing him in a bad way and stained with blood from the blow, surrounded him, held him and took him off to a spring, to revive the fainting man with the water and wash off the blood that had run down, and having got him down from the horse they did this. Meanwhile Sclerus's horse escaped from the man holding it, and bolting without a rider ran about the camp with its mane drenched in blood; Sclerus's armies, seeing it, for the horse was well known and was called Aegyptius, and thinking their leader had fallen, rushed headlong to flight. Phocas, noticing what was happening, encouraged his men and attacked the fleeing, and many were killed by their opponents, many were taken, and more were killed by one another, trampled together. From this Sclerus, at a loss, fled with those who were left to Chosroes the Babylonian. The man sent also carried to Sclerus and those with him documents confirmed by the imperial hand, offering them an amnesty for what they had done, if they gave up the attempt and submitted to the emperor. When the Babylonian learned of these imperial letters to Sclerus and those with him, he shut up both the man carrying out the embassy and Sclerus and the soldiers with him. So Sclerus's revolt ended there at that time.
text: So the sceptre of the Romans was restored to those to whom it belonged by birth, I mean Basil and Constantine, of whom the one was completing the twentieth year of his age, and Constantine the seventeenth. But while they wore the symbols of the empire, the proedros Basil simply had the power girded about him. Basil put up with this, not yet trusting himself, and attended to the parakoimomenos as to a trainer and shaped himself on his handling and management of public affairs, so that when the time called he too might handle the military rolls and the good order of the state. For he was wakeful and active in character, not easygoing like his brother and given to the idle life. As soon as power came round to these brothers, the proedros brought their mother back from exile and restored her to her sons. Suspecting the magister Bardas Sclerus, who was stratelates and had all the eastern forces under him, he took from him the command of stratelates and appointed him duke of Mesopotamia. This grieved Sclerus greatly, and, as he always nursed a desire for the empire in any case, stirred him to revolt. So, taking up the command to which he had been appointed, he revealed the secret to many. Being loved by the whole army for his deeds of valour, he had almost all obedient. Since his son Romanus was in the queen of cities, he hurried to have him with him too, and secretly sending someone he was able to get his son away unnoticed, and at once set about the usurpation, bound his head with the imperial headband and put purple shoes on his feet, was acclaimed as emperor, took pains to collect money, and took as allies the emir of Amida, for so Emet is called, and the emir of Martyropolis, which is named Mieferkeim, and also Arabs. Taking these with him he pressed on towards Constantine's city, buoyed up by good hopes, which he nursed from elsewhere too, but above all from a dream of a monk who practised virtue. The whip, it seems, was a symbol of the divine anger and of the destruction of the Romans from the civil wars, which Sclerus thought signified the empire, judging the vision by his own desire. When the rumour of Sclerus's usurpation reached the rulers, what was left of the soldiery was made ready to stand against the rebel. Meanwhile the high priest of Nicomedia was sent to him as envoy, and said much to him to lead him to peace, but did not persuade him. When those in the palace learned this answer, they set out of necessity for battle. The commander of the imperial force was the eunuch Peter, Phocas's man, whom we mentioned before. When the armies had encamped opposite each other at Lipara, which was also named Lycandus, and clashed with each other, for a time the imperial troops held out bravely, then they were routed and many were killed, and the camp fell to the enemy and was plundered. Then, having taken Tzamandus, a very populous city, by the coming over of its inhabitants, he gathered a swarm of money from it. Having thus prevailed over the imperial army, he drew many from it over to himself, who had already given up hopes of safety with the emperors, and not only nameless soldiers but many famous ones too flowed over to him. When this was reported to the parakoimomenos, Leo the protovestiarius was sent again, entrusted with unmixed authority and given licence to do all that is permitted even to emperors; one might call the man a dictator in the Latin tongue. Joining the stratopedarch, the protovestiarius tried to draw Sclerus's men over with promises and honours; but when he saw he was attempting what could not be achieved, he passed Sclerus by night and went towards the East. From this fear for their dearest seized Sclerus's men, and leaving the rebel they came over to the protovestiarius. Afraid at this, Sclerus sent the magister Michael Burtzes, who had come over to him, and the patrician Romanus Taronites with an army against the protovestiarius. They attacked him and were defeated. When the defeat of those sent became known to Sclerus, he himself went against the protovestiarius with the whole army under him, clashed with the army with him and won. The stratopedarch Peter was killed, and the protovestiarius was captured. This victory raised Sclerus's affairs high and brought those of the emperors to despair, all the more because the rebel was also master of the sea. So the parakoimomenos made ready a fleet and sent it against the rebel's fleet, and in the sea battle Sclerus's fleet was beaten and scattered. blocks: When the patriarch Antony resigned the priesthood, which he had held for six years, and died soon after, the church was widowed of a high priest for four and a half years, then Nicholas Chrysoberges was appointed. The affairs of the Bulgars were stirred up again; for when Tzimisces's death was announced, they entrusted their rule to four brothers, David, Moses, Aaron and Samuel, who were named Cometopuli, because they were sons of one of the notable men among them called counts. For those of the royal family had died out for them, only one of Peter's sons being left, I mean Romanus, who was a eunuch. Of the four brothers, the Cometopuli, David very soon measured out his life, and Moses, besieging Serrae, was struck by a stone and died at once. Aaron, with his whole family, was taken out of life by his brother Samuel, either because he was getting the rule for himself alone or because he favoured the Romans, for both are said, only one of his sons being saved, who was called by two names, Sphendosthlavus and John. And the rule of Bulgaria came round to Samuel alone, who, finding freedom while the Roman armies were busy with the civil wars, went round all the western parts of the Roman dominion, not only plundering but also making the lands and the cities his own.

When, as has been told, the emperor had shaken off Sclerus's usurpation, he was eager for revenge on the barbarian, and decided to make the campaign in person. So he went out without sharing the matter with the magister Bardas Phocas, though he was domestic of the scholae of the East, nor with any other of the commanders of the eastern forces. When he was already entering the Bulgar lands he ordered the magister Leo Melissenus to stay behind and guard the difficult passes; and he himself went in and made ready to undertake the siege of Sardica, which is Triaditza. Stephen Contostephanus, who was domestic of the western units, reckoning that if the campaign went well for the emperor he would never stop conducting the wars in person, and neither he himself nor the other commanders would any longer be thought by him worth much account, planned to frustrate his attempt and check his drive. So he came to him and said that Melissenus was attempting usurpation and was going off in haste to Byzantium to seize the empire, and asked him not to delay, but to march back and not put it off. This troubled the emperor, and he signalled the return to the people. Samuel, who was lingering on the mountain tops, for he did not dare to fight in close battle, seeing the sudden withdrawal, judged what was being done to be cowardice, and attacked the Romans, threw them all into confusion by the surprise and put them to flight, and mastered the camp, the imperial tent and the insignia of the empire. The emperor was barely saved at Philippopolis, and finding Melissenus there, he was enraged against Contostephanus and poured insults on the man. He, chafing, grew harsh, and the emperor, boiling with anger, leapt up from his throne, seized Contostephanus by the hair and the beard and dashed the man to the ground.

From this the leaders of the Roman forces, angry with the emperor, Phocas because his hopes were slipping away and, as the proverb says, going the way of Mandrabolus, others because he treated them arrogantly and did not share his counsels with them, and others for other reasons, gathered at Charsianon, put a diadem on Bardas Phocas and made him worthy of the empire. And they arranged the affairs of the revolt well, as it seemed to them.

Sclerus, kept under guard in Babylon, was brought out of prison unexpectedly. For since the rule of the Persians had been overthrown by the Saracens, a Persian man named Inargus, stirring the Persians with words, persuaded them to revolt from slavery to the Saracens and take up arms against them, Inargus himself being their general. Chosroes fought the Persians many times, and was defeated as many times as he engaged them, and despairing he fled to the Romans in prison, released them from prison, talked with Sclerus about the war and asked him not to bear a grudge for his ill-treatment. He at first refused the war, then, when the Babylonian pressed him, agreed, but promised to undertake the war with the Romans alone. So the prisons were searched, and all the Romans found in them were brought out and armed, and about three thousand were gathered; taking them, he went against the Persians, engaged and won; but neither he nor those with him judged it right to go back to Chosroes any more; for they feared that the barbarian would shut them up again, all the more since he had made trial of their bravery. So they took to flight, and Chosroes sent a multitude in pursuit of them, and those sent caught up with the fugitives, being many times more than them, but fewer than the fugitives were able to escape, the rest falling there, overcome by Roman hands.

blocks: So Sclerus and those with him came back to the Roman borders. Learning that Phocas was already longing for the empire and had begun a usurpation, he made overtures to Phocas, asking to be his partner both in the war and in the empire itself. He accepted the partnership, and if they gained their desires, he allotted himself the queen of cities and power over most of the nations and lands, and assigned to Sclerus Antioch, Coele Syria, Phoenicia, Palestine and Mesopotamia, and pledged the agreements with oaths on sacred things. Trusting in this, Sclerus came to Phocas. He, having caught him in his nets, took from him the imperial dress, shut him up and set a guard round him. And bringing the army with him under himself too, he held to the usurpation more strongly. Sclerus, however, providing for himself some safety in the future in case of failure, before he was seized by Phocas had arranged for his son Romanus to flee secretly, as if deserting to the emperor; he was received with great joy by the ruler and at once honoured as magister.

Phocas, putting a portion of the army under the patrician Delphinas, sent him to Chrysopolis opposite the capital, while he himself came with the rest of the force to Abydus. But the emperor suddenly attacked Delphinas, encamped at Chrysopolis, with a Rhos people; for having made a marriage alliance with Vladimir, their ruler, through his sister Anna, he had received an allied force from there; and he mastered the enemy quite easily, and having subdued Delphinas himself he impaled him. Then he went off to Abydus with his brother Constantine. And now the opposing armies stood face to face, and Phocas was drawn up before his own, while the emperor Basil, riding round on horseback, encouraged the opposing army; seeing him, Phocas drove his horse against him, giving it full rein, judging that if he brought him down he would have won the contest. But he had not yet gone far from his own men, and some say he rolled off his horse, others that he turned aside to a hill, got off his horse, stretched out on the ground and at once his breath left him. Some said the man was struck a mortal blow by someone. And the emperor Constantine claimed the killing of him for himself; but this was idle talk; for his body was found wounded nowhere. Others believed he had been done away with by a deadly poison, which seemed more likely; the poison, they say, Basil prepared, and Phocas's wine pourer, secretly won over by the emperor, gave it to him. When Bardas fell, the army with him was scattered, and some were killed as they were caught, others taken alive, and those seized were punished as the emperor thought fit.

But he was rather different from before. For he had become haughty and reserved in character, suspected everyone, and was inexorable in anger, and he showed his haughtiness not only to others but also to the parakoimomenos himself; he was vexed with the man and hurried to bring the management of affairs round to himself, and indeed he removed him from the administration of the state, ordering him to stay at home without going out, then shortly after sent him into exile, and examining each of his acts he voted most of them void, and took away most of the monastery he had built, and touched not only fields or estates and houses, but also offerings, slabs and costly columns. So he, covered for this by a cloud of despondency, lost the use of his limbs and was seen as a breathing corpse, and after a short while ended his life pitiably.

Then for the first time he became truly sovereign, and knowing how many cares the management of the empire needs, he scorned imperial luxury, kept from splendid robes and shook off all sweetness of temper, though before he had not lived so, but had been overcome by love affairs and given himself to revels and luxuries and delighted in imperial extravagance. Allotting the power to himself alone, he gave his brother a share only in the name of emperor and the distinguished colour, and assigned him a bodyguard, small however and not excessive. He bore it and did not dispute with his brother, having, I think, an easygoing character and delighting in a softer life and a luxurious way of living, and in hunting and the company of the companions of his age with whom he had been brought up. So the two brothers were thus.

Sclerus, released from prison when Phocas died, again took up his former attempt and did not put off usurping again. The emperor, in letters written to him, urged the man to stop his madness at last and not to wish always to be the cause of wars for his kinsmen and to stain the earth with blood, and that of Christians. He, worn down by old age by now and dizzy about the future, made peace and came to the ruler. He sat under an imperial tent, and Sclerus came slowly to the tent, held up on either side, partly because of old age, partly because of the bulk of his body, for he was very large; at which time the emperor Basil is said to have spoken the much-repeated words: "The man I feared is brought to me led by the hand." Others say that Sclerus was struck with blindness as he went to the sovereign, and for this was led by the hand. When the man came near the tent, the emperor, noticing his feet still shod in purple shoes (for Sclerus had taken off the other marks of the empire, but had not put off the shoes, either because he forgot or did not notice), at once turned his eyes away, not bearing to meet him except in a private man's dress. He threw off the envied shoes before the tent and so went into it, and the emperor rose and welcomed the man, and they talked with each other, shared a table and drank from the same cup. In this way Sclerus's usurpation too was ended, he himself being honoured as curopalates, and those who had helped him being allowed to keep whatever each had received from him while he was usurping, whether in ranks, offices or possessions.

The emperor, having shaken off the cares of the revolts, went out to Thrace and visited Thessalonica, giving thanks to the famous martyr; and leaving there a distinguished commander with a heavy force, to stop Samuel's raids, he came back to Byzantium, and went off to Iberia, having been left heir by the curopalates David at his death of the rule that belonged to him. Coming there and taking hold of the country left to him, and having brought David's brother George, who ruled inner Iberia, to keep quiet and be content with his own, and having taken his son as hostage, he went against Phoenicia, and checked the rulers of Tripoli, Damascus, Tyre and Berytus, who by agreement were attacking Antioch by Daphne and harming the land under it, and persuaded them to keep their subjection to the Romans, and taking hostages from them too he returned. But so things stood.

When the man came near the tent, the emperor, noticing his feet still shod in purple shoes (for Sclerus had taken off the other marks of the empire, but had not put off the shoes, either because he forgot or did not notice), at once turned his eyes away, not bearing to meet him except in a private man's dress. He threw off the envied shoes before the tent and so went into it, and the emperor rose and welcomed the man, and they talked with each other, shared a table and drank from the same cup. In this way Sclerus's usurpation too was ended, he himself being honoured as curopalates, and those who had helped him being allowed to keep whatever each had received from him while he was usurping, whether in ranks, offices or possessions. The emperor, having shaken off the cares of the revolts, went out to Thrace and visited Thessalonica, giving thanks to the famous martyr; and leaving there a distinguished commander with a heavy force, to stop Samuel's raids, he came back to Byzantium, and went off to Iberia, having been left heir by the curopalates David at his death of the rule that belonged to him. Coming there and taking hold of the country left to him, and having brought David's brother George, who ruled inner Iberia, to keep quiet and be content with his own, and having taken his son as hostage, he went against Phoenicia, and checked the rulers of Tripoli, Damascus, Tyre and Berytus, who by agreement were attacking Antioch by Daphne and harming the land under it, and persuaded them to keep their subjection to the Romans, and taking hostages from them too he returned. But so things stood.

blocks: When the patriarch Nicholas Chrysoberges had distinguished himself in the high priesthood for twelve years and eight months, and then ended his life, the magister Sisinnius, a man brought up in learning, was appointed patriarch. And when he too had directed the church for three years and died, Sergius was ordained patriarch, who was abbot of the monastery of Manuel and was related by birth to the patriarch Photius.

When Samuel, the leader of the Bulgars, was plundering not only the lands of Thrace and Macedonia, but also Hellas and the Peloponnese itself, the emperor sent out the magister Nicephorus Uranus, governor of the west, who, while Samuel was encamped by the river Spercheius, made camp on the land opposite. Since it had then rained much and the river was not passable from this, the approach of the Romans seemed beyond hope to Samuel. But Uranus, searching by night and noticing the river passable at a certain place, crossed it quietly with the army and fell on Samuel's men while they were off their guard, and the barbarians, struck by the surprise, fell without even raising their hands, and wounds were dealt to Samuel and his son Romanus, and they would have been taken had they not mixed themselves among the dead bodies, and so escaped unnoticed.

Then the emperor too marched against the Bulgars, and having overthrown some of the forts at Sardica, came back to Mosynopolis. He also took great Persthlava and little Persthlava and Pliscova through generals. Berrhoea too was handed over to him by Dobromerus, who came over to the Romans. Servia was taken by siege, and Nicholas, who had been entrusted with guarding it, whom they called Nicolitzas as being small in stature, who, though honoured as patrician, ran away again and went off to Samuel. Then again the emperor marched against Vidin and took the city. While the emperor was besieging it, Samuel suddenly attacked Adrianople, and when a fair was being held outside, he made plunder of the merchandise, took a multitude of captives and went back. The emperor, having brought Vidin under himself and coming back, caught Samuel camped by the river Axius. The Vardar was so named among the ancients. Since the river was running high, the barbarians had encamped carelessly; for they hoped the Roman force could never cross the river. But a ford became known, and by it the emperor crossed and the army too, and many of the Bulgars perished, and Samuel escaped, his tent and the whole camp being plundered. The emperor also took over the city of Scopia, given him by Romanus, the son of Peter, who had ruled the Bulgars, to whom its guarding had been entrusted by Samuel.

Then, coming back to Constantine's city, he decreed that the tax payments of the humble who had perished should be exacted from the powerful; this was called the allelengyon. When many begged about this, and the patriarch Sergius himself, that this unjust and unreasonable exaction might stop, the emperor could not be moved. For lifted up above all by time and his victories he showed himself contemptuous towards all, and wished his subjects not to be well disposed to him but to fear him, and wished to manage both the military and the civil affairs not according to prevailing custom, which the lawgivers decreed should count as law, but according to his own judgement and his own will. So he paid no attention to learned men either, but thought learning something superfluous and not useful; so he picked for himself men distinguished neither in birth nor in learning, entrusted them with the imperial letters and shared his counsels with them, and himself dictated the documents to them plainly, as it happened. He also blocked the outlets of money from the treasuries and made them full. They say that two hundred thousand talents of gold were stored up by him. For no one could bring the rest of his wealth under number, since when his treasuries were filled he stored the rest underground, digging winding, labyrinthine passages. The chests overflowed with costly stones, both others and the white ones whose special name is pearls. But they were not for his use, but a few of them adorned his purple, so that he might have the distinction he used in processions, and when he gave audience to envoys, and when he held any other public festival. The rest, stored in the treasuries, were a useless burden.

In times of war he was a varied man and many-sided in mind towards those under his hand, but in times of quiet and peace he was more of a ruler; he stored up his angers and, holding them within himself, made them public at the right times and paid back the offenders. Being firm in mind, he did not easily change what he had decided. So towards those against whom he happened to nurse some anger, he did not quickly change his disposition. But these things illustrate the character of this sovereign; let the history keep to what was done under him and relate what followed.
