blocks: The ruler of Egypt, breaking the treaty with the Romans, threw down the church in Jerusalem in which is the Lord's tomb, and the monasteries there. The emperor, continually attacking Bulgaria, harmed and ravaged it. Samuel, unable to draw up against the Roman army, tried to shut off the entrances to him with trenches, blocking the difficult passes with buildings and setting guards on them. So the emperor came again and tried to force the passage, but was beaten off, the guards resisting rather strongly; yet he did not give up the attempt, but he himself waited, still testing the defence, and sent out one of the generals with the unit under him from somewhere else, to see if he could go round and contrive something for the passage. He went through mountains and many difficult places, escaped the notice of the Bulgars and fell on the guards of the defence from behind; and they, terrified by the suddenness, no longer cared for guarding the barrier, but set most store on guarding themselves from destruction. Then the Roman army, seizing its chance, broke the barrier, went through and pursued, killed many and took more alive, Samuel barely escaping. The emperor cut out the eyes of all the captives, numbering fifteen thousand, leaving one one-eyed man to each hundred, so that he might lead them, and so ordered them to go off to their leader. He, seeing them and not bearing the suffering, grew dizzy and fell fainting to the ground, and, recovering a little, he was seized with a heart attack and died.

The rule of the Bulgars came round to his son Gabriel, also called Romanus, whom, before he had ruled a year, the son of his uncle Aaron, Vladisthlavus John, for he too had two names, killed. The sovereign, having passed through the defence in the difficult passes, as has been said, subdued other strong forts and the Bulgars in them, and came to Mosynopolis, where Samuel's death was reported to him. So at once he set out and attacked Bulgaria, and took cities and forts of it. Samuel's son Romanus, also called Gabriel, for he had not yet been killed, sending to the emperor, promised subjection; but some time later a servant of John Vladisthlavus, who had killed this Gabriel, came, announcing the killing of Samuel's son and bringing letters promising subjection to the emperor, and many of the notable men among the Bulgars flowed over to him. But the emperor, learning that Vladisthlavus did not intend to keep his promises, again attacked Bulgaria, plundered many of its lands, and taking again by siege the city of Achrida, in which the palace had been built for the leaders of the Bulgars, and other forts through generals, he returned to Constantine's city. And again he marched against the Bulgars, and again took forts, and of the many barbarians destroyed some and held others alive.

The ruler of the Bulgars, John or Vladisthlavus, set out against Dyrrachium, and while besieging it fell, having ruled two years and five months. Learning this, the emperor at once went out, and when he came to Adrianople some notable men of the Bulgars came to him, handing over to him Pernicus and thirty-five other forts, and many others of these barbarians flowed over to him. John's wife Maria sent to the emperor the archbishop of Bulgaria, David, with letters promising to leave Bulgaria if she obtained what she wished. And shortly after the woman came to the sovereign, bringing three sons and six little daughters, and three other sons of hers became fugitives in the mountains, but they too, forced because the mountains were guarded, came to the emperor. These were Prusianus and his two brothers, of whom he honoured Prusianus as magister and the rest as patricians.

Having brought all Bulgaria under himself, overthrowing some of the forts and strengthening others and leaving them sufficient garrisons, he himself came to Athens, to offer thanks to the Mother of God, and having dedicated many costly things to the church he returned to the first of cities and held a triumph, crowned with an upright tiara, which the common crowd calls the toupha, named, I think, from typhos, pride, as making those crowned with it puffed up; and so he came as far as the Wisdom of God the Word, giving thanks to the Lord in it. When he was there, the patriarch, begging much that he abolish the allelengyon, did not prevail on him, though he had promised to do this if he mastered the Bulgars. This patriarch Sergius, having shepherded the church for twenty years, departed life, and Eustathius, who was first among the priests of the church in the palace, was appointed high priest of the church in Constantinople.

When Bulgaria had been subjected to the dominion of the Romans, the nations of the Croats too submitted, and also Sirmium. Then the emperor marched against Abasgia, since its ruler had broken the treaty. When he was there, the patricians Xiphias and Nicephorus, the son of Bardas Phocas, revolted behind him, but their revolt was quickly quenched, Xiphias killing Phocas, and he himself being seized and taken in bonds to the reigning city. As soon as the emperor had got rid of the cares of this usurpation he clashed with the Abasgians, and in a strong battle many fell on both sides and the contest was evenly balanced; then, when battle was joined again, the Romans won, and George, the ruler of the Abasgians, ran off to the inner parts of Iberia, and shortly after, asking for a treaty, gave up to the emperor as much land as the sovereign wished, giving his son Pancratius as hostage; and having accomplished this the emperor returned. He also planned to set out for Sicily, but the plan did not come to effect; for his life had already come to its end, and he was ill. A little before he died the patriarch Eustathius died, having presided over the church of the orthodox for eight years. While the emperor was ill, Alexius, who then had the headship of the monastery of Studius, came to the emperor bringing him the holy head of the precious Forerunner, and at once the emperor appointed him patriarch, and that evening ended his life, having lived and reigned seventy-two years, and ruled alone for fifty years and more; for the rest he reigned with his father, then with Phocas, and after him with Tzimisces.

blocks: So Basil died an old man, and his brother at once took hold of power, I mean Constantine, who was a little short of him in years of life. Being of a lazy and easygoing nature, or having come into the habit of an idle life, for his brother had not shared any imperial business with him, when he ruled alone he too had this way of living: he put the management of public affairs under others, and these not men who had already given proof of themselves, but men who were not only not well born, but not even of free fortune, foreigners and unable to speak correctly, but speaking thoroughly barbarous Greek. He himself gave himself up to luxuries; for he was overcome by belly and sex, and was mad about dice and the theatres, and also about hunting. He was large in bulk of body and most noble in strength, but cowardly in the state of his soul, so he did not choose to calm the onsets of the barbarians by wars, but rather by gifts and ranks. He punished his subjects even on bare suspicion, readily gave ear to slanders, and was quick to anger, but he did not bear a grudge like his brother, nor stay in his anger, but quite easily changed to the opposite disposition and was grieved when he had treated someone badly. Punishing many, he deprived most of their sight, cutting out their eyes, and judged this punishment lighter than the others, and used it more, as making those condemned to it powerless.

When young he married a wife, Helena, the daughter of Alypius, a man of the very highest at the time, and had three little daughters by her, and lost her by death, and the girls were brought up in the palace. Of them the eldest, Eudocia, her beauty marred by a pestilential disease, was dedicated to God by her own will; the others were with their father when he ruled alone, he taking no thought about them such as befits a father. Being open of hand, he did not use the virtue rightly, so he fell into the opposite vices. For to those about him, who were barbarians, slaves whom he himself had acquired and made eunuchs and had as chamberlains and bedchamber servants, whom he also granted the first honours and offices, he supplied money by whole wagonloads, while to the others he stretched out his hand very sparingly. So the mind of this sovereign was thus.

Let the narrative go through what happened outside. The Patzinaks, who are Scythians as has been said before, crossed the Ister and did no small harm to the country of the Romans. But Constantine Diogenes, who held Sirmium and was also named duke of Bulgaria, attacked them, routed them and forced them to cross back over the Ister and keep quiet. When the emperor Basil died, the taxes of two years were uncollected; for he gave delays to the collections, sparing the taxpayers, but this man exacted without pity those of the past years and those of the three in which he himself ruled, and this when a great drought had happened through the whole time of his reign. So the poor were ground down. The general of Samos overcame a fleet of the Hagarenes that had sailed against the islands called the Cyclades, taking twelve ships with their crews and making the rest scatter.

When the sovereign had come to deep old age, and from the wasting of it a disease too had fallen on his body, he considered who would succeed to power. He decided, then, to make the patrician Constantine Dalassenus his son-in-law through one of his daughters and successor to the empire, and sent to bring him, as he had his dwelling in the theme of the Armeniacs; but before that man arrived Constantine changed his mind, and chose for the succession and for marriage to one of his daughters one of the men in office, of noble blood, who had been raised to the office of eparch. But the choice had something steep in its way to fulfilment; for that illustrious man was living with a wife; he was Romanus of the Argyroi. So what did the emperor contrive for this? He pretended an anger against the man, and a grievous and violent one, and sent men to take him off for punishment, and to cut the hair of his wife and move her to another life. She, not knowing the play being staged, readily gave herself up to leave her life; so she had her hair cut off and changed into black, and he was brought to the palace, and the second of Constantine's daughters was joined to him in married life. For the third, it is said, refused to live with him because his wife had been separated from him against her will. And he was joined to Zoe, and the emperor Constantine, living three days after their marriage, paid his debt, being seventy years old and more, having danced through the empire three years less one month.

blocks: Romanus, who was called Argyropulus, then took hold of the sceptre, and at once cut out the allelengyon tax from the roots, and increased by an addition the distribution of gold coins supplied from the imperial treasuries to the singers of God assigned to the Great Church, knowing that what was supplied to them was insufficient. For he had once been great steward of the Wisdom named after God the Word, since formerly the emperor was permitted to appoint the steward of this church; and he freed those shut up for public or private debts, paying the latter and remitting the public ones, and made a distribution of much money for the emperor Constantine, his father-in-law, and bought back very many captives, and those bishops who had been driven into want by the allelengyon tax were restored by him, and he consoled those ill-treated by the late emperor, either in the maiming of limbs or in confiscations of property or otherwise.

The magister Prusianus the Bulgar, suspected of conferring secretly with Theodora, the sister of the Augusta Zoe, and of casting eyes on the empire, was arrested and guarded, and then blinded, and Theodora was confined in the Petrion, and Diogenes, the emperor's son-in-law through his niece, was accused of planning usurpation, bound and shut in a tower. When George, the ruler of Abasgia, died, his wife sought a treaty and a wife for her son. The emperor renewed the treaty and sent Helena, the daughter of his brother Basil, as bride to Abasgia, having honoured the bridegroom Pancratius as curopalates.

The emperor wished and made ready to set out against Aleppo, which is also called Berrhoea. For though the emperors Nicephorus and John had brought many of the cities of Phoenicia and Syria under the dominion of the Romans, Basil after them, busy with the battles against the Bulgars, had no time to secure the captured cities; yet while he lived, they did not dare openly to shake off the yoke of slavery. But when Constantine had taken hold of the sceptre and was directing the empire easily, the descendants of Hagar, knowing this to be the right time for what they planned, attacked the garrisons of the cities, made away with them and became masters of the cities themselves. The leader of Aleppo, making continual raids, plundered Antioch itself and the nations neighbouring the land of the Syrians that were subject to the Romans. The duke of Antioch, drawing up against him while the sovereign Constantine was still alive, was shamefully defeated, and having lost most of those with him was barely able to escape himself. Romanus took his command from him and appointed another; and he too set out, and as he went envoys sent by the Aleppan came to him with costly gifts, asking to obtain pardon, to renew their subjection, to pay the contributions that had fallen behind, and to pay them yearly with good will in future. But he, though many men distinguished in generalship tried to turn him from going forward as unprofitable and advised making peace, was not held back from his impulse, but imagined he would quite easily master the Hagarenes, and thought that by achieving this he would get himself some great and overwhelming glory. So he went off into Syria and pitched a camp. The Arabs, men lightly equipped and daring riders, lay in ambush on swift-footed horses, unarmoured, on either side of the camp, and leaping out killed or seized those going off to gather fodder and to draw water, so that the soldiers and their horses gave out from thirst. Then the Arabs, growing more used to raids against the Romans and as if convicting them of cowardice, suddenly rushed down from the heights with a barbarian war cry, and giving an impression of numbers by not keeping a locked formation but running out scattered and coming at the camp in disorder, they terrified the whole army and turned it to flight, and the sovereign himself would have been taken, since the guard about him was thrown into confusion and had left the man it guarded unguarded, had not someone put him on his horse and strengthened him to flee, when he had almost breathed his last from fear. So the Romans went off in disorder, running as each happened to. The barbarians, amazed at the unexpected rout, did not run after the fleeing, but ran to the camp, taking a few of the more distinguished alive, plundered the imperial tent, which was full of every kind of wealth and imperial costliness, and loading the rest of the baggage on themselves they went back.

blocks: The emperor was brought safe to Antioch by the efforts of those about him, and from there hurried back to Constantine's city, no longer showing his former disposition of soul, but changed for the worse. For to gain the equivalent of what had been lost, he became a tax collector instead of a ruler, and a bitter accountant, exacting from sons debts of their fathers grown old, and kindling fires against his subjects which time, long past, had already put out or covered for a while under ashes. From this many were driven from their fathers' houses and fields, and stripped of their former prosperity were driven into conspicuous poverty. Of what was so exacted nothing was brought into the public treasury, but having set out to build a monastery and found a church to the Mother of God there, he spent this on them and used up other money from the imperial treasuries, now raising the building, now pulling down what had already been raised, and either building it up again higher or wider, or varying its design, or changing the new work in another way. He also assigned revenues to the monks, not proportioned to monks, but suited to men in luxury and leading a relaxed and dainty life, devoting to them whole public lands, and these the richest and most fruitful. But no more about this.

Amer, the son of the Aleppan, came to the queen of cities with many gifts, renewing the peace, and the emperor agreed to it. The empress Zoe, coming to the Petrion, had her sister Theodora tonsured a nun. When the emperor was away from the city, Constantine Diogenes was arrested as planning usurpation and about to run away to Illyricum, and under examination he threw himself down a precipice and died, so that he might not, overcome by force, reveal those who knew of it. At that time the Arabs overran Mesopotamia, the Patzinaks Bulgaria, and the Hagarenes the coastland of Illyricum. A Roman fleet attacked these last and burned and consumed most of their boats; and those escaping from the sea battle were destroyed by a storm in the Sicilian sea. And again about a thousand ships sailed out from Africa and ravaged many of the islands and some of the coastlands. But Roman ships, falling in with a part of them, killed many and took five hundred alive, who were brought in bonds to the emperor. Moreover the protospatharius George Maniaces, general of the cities by the Euphrates, mastered Edessa, where he also found the autograph letter of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ and sent it to the emperor. When famine pressed Cappadocia, the Armeniac theme and Paphlagonia, and again locusts ravaged the east, many were forced to leave their homelands, whom the ruler won back with distributions of gold and persuaded to return to the lands that bore them. When earthquakes happened, hostels were badly damaged, and the men's houses opposite Byzantium, which had been set apart from of old as a dwelling for those whose bodies were maimed by the sacred disease and for lepers. But the emperor renewed these too, and took care of the aqueduct bringing water into the great city when it was broken.

blocks: Now his life drew near its end, and how he died must be told. As soon as he gained the empire he measured out for himself long years both of life and of rule, and this though he was sixty when he took hold of the sceptre, and imagined he would leave a succession to the empire from his own loins, not being able to see even that the empress to whom he had been married was fifty, past her prime and with her womb too dry to receive seed. At first, then, he was zealous for sex, strained himself, used some ointments and hung little stones on his wife, as if they did something for conception. And she put up with amulets and charms and accepted incantations. But when the ruler knew that all that was done was in vain and gave up his effort, he was no longer disposed the same way towards his wife, but went to her less. For he was also by nature sluggish and rather soft for intercourse, and time too had now blunted his motion. When some years had been measured out for him in the empire, and he was averse to the empress, she, scorned, was stirred to hatred, and more so through longing for a man.

There was a eunuch, a servant of the emperor even before his reign, and he had brothers, one of whom was Michael, a man whose face nature had carved into exact beauty. After the accession his brother presented him to Romanus to be taken into his service; and he enrolled the young man among the chamberlains. The empress, caught by love for him, was burned in her soul, and his beauty, seen every day, kindled the fire. The eunuch, hated by her before, was then called to her and granted more intimate talk, and then was asked about his brother Michael. When this happened many times, being clever he understood the love, and suggested to his brother that he go to the empress, and if she made trial of him, not to shrink back, but to touch her, kiss her and cling to her. What need to say more? The love affair went as far as intercourse, and as time went on the passion for Michael broke out almost into the open, and was whispered not only by those in the palace but also by those at the crossroads, and was unknown only to the sovereign; so that when he lay with the empress in bed, Michael was called in and ordered to rub his feet. What then would one think but that he touched her feet too? And the emperor became as it were procurer for both and bedfellow. When his sister Pulcheria and others told him of the play and urged him to be on his guard, he did nothing else but call the suspected man and ask him whether he was loved by the empress. He denied it, and having denied it he was asked for assurances of his word and oaths on sacred things. When he swore the oaths falsely, the emperor thought the words of the others slander. It is said, however, that for the perjury a terrible disease fell on Michael. It was that at certain intervals he suffered derangement of mind, distortion of the eyes, shaking of the body and falling to the ground, and then came back to himself and was restored. He suffered this many times in front of the emperor too; and he, pitying Michael for the affliction, thought what was said all the more false, and held that one in such a state neither loved nor was loved. There are those who say that the emperor was not unaware of the love, [a gap in the text] but that, since the empress was lusty and mad for sex, he put up with her inclination for Michael, pretending ignorance, so that she might not consort with more men.

While things were so, the sovereign fell ill, and his face swelled, his breathing was continually laboured, his look was like a corpse's, and most of his head was bare; for the hair of it had fallen out. So it is said the man was worked on with poisons. In this state he went off to one of the baths in the palace to bathe, and he went neither led by the hand nor expected to die at once. When he had cleansed his body, he went down into the pool there, where the whole play is sung to have happened; for they say some held his head down under the water a good while, and so he was drawn out from there almost breathless and laid on the bed. When a commotion arose at this, the empress too came, as if lamenting something over the affliction, and having made sure of the emperor's death she went off at once. He, living a little while speechless, and then bringing up something rather black through his mouth, gave up the ghost, having reigned five and a half years, brought up in learning, having had a share of Greek education and not unacquainted with the laws of the state, but thinking and priding himself that he knew more than he truly knew.

blocks: Such was the end of life that overtook him. The empress was wholly bent on setting Michael on the throne of the empire, and when those about her, that is her father's servants, advised her to give the matter delay and consideration, she would not bear it, being urged to the accomplishment by the eunuch John, Michael's brother, who whispered secretly to her: "We shall perish at once if the outcome is delayed for a short time." So she at once took Michael, put an imperial robe on him, bound his head with the diadem herself, set him on the imperial seat, and sitting down beside him herself urged all then present to acclaim him and do obeisance. Some have recorded that the sacred marriage service was also performed for them at once then, at night, the patriarch Alexius having come to the palace and found Romanus dead and Michael already completing the rites of the empire. When what had happened had already spread to those outside, the whole city too proclaimed the new sovereign, partly pleasing him, partly because they were glad to have got rid of the one gone.

So the empress thought she had planned excellently, got all power for herself and would have Michael as a servant; but something different happened. For for a while he made a show of keeping his affection for the empress, pleasing her and doing what was agreeable to her, then, not bearing to stretch the pretence out long, he changed, suspected her, and afraid for himself removed from the palace the eunuchs who were her father's servants and separated from her the maids she was used to, putting others in their place to serve her. Besides this he blocked up the women's quarters for her and set a guard round, and no one was allowed to come to her unless the commander of the guard examined the visitor where he came from and on what business he came. For he was afraid, having the grounds of his fear from his own experience. Michael is said to have been led to this more by his brother John the eunuch. For the man was clever and active, reserved in character and changing colour towards those he dealt with, very energetic and tireless under a mass of cares, and neither gorging himself nor greedy for unmixed wine nor overcome by wine did he slacken his zeal for the public administration. So matters about the empress were arranged thus, and Michael held to the management of public affairs. Then his disease grew strong, which some called a demonic wrath that had fallen on him for the perjury and was choking the man, as once Saul, and others madness and derangement; and the eunuch John took over the whole steering of the empire, having long before put on the monastic habit, but keeping it only in the habit.

The patrician Constantine Dalassenus, living at home and learning about the new emperor, was vexed that the empire of the Romans had come round to such a man. This filled the emperor's men with confusion, afraid that Dalassenus might attempt usurpation. And John sent a man to assure him with oaths that he would experience nothing grievous and to persuade the man to come to the emperor. He came, and the emperor received him gladly, welcomed him with gifts, honoured him with a higher rank and ordered him to live in the city. Nicetas, the emperor's brother, appointed duke of Antioch by Daphne, was shut out of entry into the city by the people of Antioch. For the citizens of Antioch had killed a collector of the public taxes as having behaved oppressively towards them, and fearing they would pay the duke the penalty for their bold deed, they barred the gates of the city against him. He gave them assurances on oath that they would suffer nothing bad for the murder, and was allowed entry; then, counting the oaths as nothing, he killed many, and sent some of the notable men among them in bonds to the great city, writing to his brother John that the people of Antioch had shut him out of entry because of their goodwill towards Dalassenus. From this Dalassenus was confined on the island of Plate, and his son-in-law through his daughter, Constantine Ducas, crying out against the injustice and not keeping silent about the perjury, was shut up in a tower. Then Dalassenus was moved from Plate and shut in a tower.

At that time Myra was taken by the sons of Hagar, and the lands of the Mysians became plunder for the Patzinaks. When Nicetas, the duke of Antioch, ended his life, Constantine, who was also a brother of the emperor, succeeded the dead man at Antioch, and his other brother was appointed protovestiarius. A fleet of Hagarenes sailing from Africa and Sicily harmed the islands and the coastlands; but a Roman fleet sailing against them sank many of the boats with their crews and took many alive, and some they sent to the emperor, while others were impaled along the coast. Pancratius, the ruler of Abasgia, to whom the emperor Romanus had joined his own niece, broke the treaty with the Romans and took back the forts and cities he had earlier ceded to the Romans, as if exacting justice from the Romans for the emperor, his wife's uncle. The Patzinaks, often crossing the Ister, treated the lands of the Romans badly, killing those caught from youth up. And the Arabs besieged Edessa, and the city would have been taken had not the duke of Antioch, Constantine, the sovereign's brother, helped it; rewarding him for his zeal, the emperor appointed him domestic of the eastern units.

And the Arabs besieged Edessa, and the city would have been taken had not the duke of Antioch, Constantine, the sovereign's brother, helped it; rewarding him for his zeal, the emperor appointed him domestic of the eastern units.

blocks: When Amer, the ruler of Egypt, died, his wife, who was a Christian, sought to make a treaty with the Romans together with her son; and the emperor ratified a thirty-year treaty with her. Two Saracen brothers who ruled Sicily had differences with each other, and one of them fled to the emperor of the Romans, asking for alliance. So the patrician George Maniaces was sent to help him, appointed general of Longobardia. Before Maniaces had quite reached Sicily, its ruling brothers made peace with each other and planned to drive Maniaces from the island when he arrived, and sent for an allied force from Africa. When war broke out the Roman army prevailed, and after great slaughter of the Carthaginians they first sacked thirteen cities, then Maniaces, advancing little by little, brought all Sicily over to the dominion of the Romans.

Edessa would nearly have been taken, the Arabs having planned to subdue it by guile. For twelve of their chiefs came to Edessa bringing five hundred camels, each of which was loaded with two chests; and each of the chests had a soldier inside; they said they were going to the emperor bringing gifts, and they wished, if they were allowed to bring the chests inside, to bring out the soldiers in them by night and take the city. When the chiefs came in to the general of the city, he received them generously. Their servants with the camels were still outside the city. A beggar, an Armenian who knew the language of the Arabs too, came to the Arabs camped outside to beg. He heard someone in a chest asking where they were, and coming into the city reported the plot to the general. He left the chiefs of the Arabs feasting in the city, and going out himself with his men and breaking open the chests killed all the soldiers in them, and coming back into the city put the rest of their chiefs to the sword, and cutting off the hands, ears and nose of one, let him go, so that he might announce the disaster to those at home.

The Carthaginian, learning of the destruction of those he had sent to Sicily, himself too marched to the island with a larger force. And Maniaces encamped against the Hagarenes, and ordered the commander of the fleet, the patrician Stephen, the emperor's brother-in-law, for he too had been sent with him with the fleet, to guard the coast securely, so that the Carthaginian might not be able to run away if defeated. When battle was joined, a multitude of the Africans almost beyond counting was killed, but their leader escaped from the battle, boarded a small boat, escaped the notice of those in the fleet and got home safe. Maniaces counted this a disaster and railed at the commander of the fleet. When he, trusting in his kinship with the emperor, was vexed at the insults, Maniaces, seized with anger, even dealt him blows. He at once wrote to his brother John the eunuch, named orphanotrophus, that Maniaces was attempting revolt. From this Maniaces was brought from there in bonds and handed over to prison, and the whole command came under Stephen. And not long after, the island came round to the Hagarenes through the inexperience and carelessness of the commander, and before these through his greed for shameful gain, only Messene, a city of the Sicilians, being left to the Romans, and this through the generalship of its commander; he was Catacalon Cecaumenus; for he not only guarded the city but also killed thousands of the enemy.

The emperor's brother, the eunuch John, nursing a very keen desire to preside over the church, won over some of the high priests; and they promised him to depose the patriarch Alexius, as appointed not by common vote but by imperial authority. He answered: "If I have not become patriarch canonically, as you say, let all those ordained by me too be deposed with me." This stirred the rest of the high priests to rise against the patriarch's accusers, and the orphanotrophus's desire remained unfulfilled. He wore out the subjects with many unaccustomed exactions, being most resourceful in such things. So when his sister Maria, who was the mother of Michael Calaphates, who later reigned, went to Ephesus to pray, and coming back from there told how much the poor suffered in having the new taxes exacted, and asked that the great part of the burden be lifted from the subjects, the orphanotrophus, laughing aloud, answered her: "You think like a woman, not knowing how many expenses the state needs." He is said to have been plotted against by the empress Zoe. For when the doctor was about to give him a purging medicine, the empress persuaded the man preparing the medicine with gifts and promises, through some people, to give him a deadly drug instead of a healing one; but the attempt became known and he escaped the danger. So public affairs were managed thus by John the orphanotrophus; and his brothers did no less harm to all than he, or rather more, being most unjust and most fond of money; for this the emperor too hated them, but he was not allowed to check their wickedness by his elder brother, the eunuch John, who sometimes begged them off and sometimes covered up their doings and did not let them come to the sovereign's knowledge.

blocks: As the disease grew stronger in the emperor and derangements of his reason came on him often, he did not make processions continually, nor imperial parades, nor did he give audience on the steps, sitting freely on the imperial throne, but curtains were hung around him, and some men appointed to watch him stood round, who, whenever they saw any sign of the derangement of his mind, and many signs gave warning of it beforehand, at once drew the curtains over him, and covering the sufferer with them ordered those present to go out. The affliction came on him suddenly and left him suddenly. In this state Michael little by little kept from seeing the empress and from going to her, either ashamed that he had paid her back such things for such things, or because, as the affliction came on him often and very readily, he was ashamed to be seen by her suffering so, or because the state of his body was ruined and he was not fit for intercourse. Some say that, having confessed the sin of adultery and of the emperor's murder to spiritual men, he received other commands from them and to keep from sex; from this he made distributions of much money and built monasteries and went off to Thessalonica, praying the gloriously victorious martyr Demetrius that he might find some remedy for the affliction; and dropsy too came on him.

When John saw his brother in this state, fearing for the empire, lest if the sovereign died suddenly it should fall to Zoe as its heir, and from this he himself and the whole family should come to utter destruction, he went after the sovereign with persuasions and persuaded him to appoint his nephew Michael Caesar, so that he might be in reserve for the rule of the empire. Since he knew, as has been said, that Zoe was heir to the empire, he went after her too, and they made the well-born woman out to be the mother of the ill-born man. For both brothers, talking with her about this, named Michael her adopted son. She, neither daring to speak against their wishes, and being easygoing in any case and easily led in mind, agreed. And the senate gathered by proclamation in the divine church at Blachernae, and those filling the imperial ranks, and in the midst of them the empress, brought forward and standing at the screen of the sanctuary, adopted Michael from there and embraced him as a son. The sovereign at once appointed him Caesar, and the gathering acclaimed him. So John thought he had already accomplished everything and secured power for his own family; but it was the overturning of everything for him and for all his kin; how, the narrative will show in its time.

blocks: When the Bulgars, as has already been told, had been overcome by the emperor Basil and their kingship put down, the barbarians bore the yoke of slavery for a while. Then they planned to shake it off and were restless, but their lack of a ruler hindered the plan. A man of obscure family, called Dolianus, but full of guile and cleverness, gave himself out as the son of Aaron, who was the brother of Samuel, who had ruled the nation, having run away from Byzantium, as is said, and having persuaded the nation that he was a son of Aaron born to him by a concubine, not from a lawful bed, he was chosen king by the barbarians. From this the nation broke out into open revolt, set about robbery and overran the lands of the Romans. So a general was sent with a force to check the inroads of the robbers. But he, treating those under him badly, stirred them against himself, and would have perished had he not run away by night. So the army under him, afraid, went into revolt, and appointed as their leader one of themselves called Teichomerus, born of Bulgar family, and named him king of Bulgaria. And the Bulgars were divided, some flowing to Dolianus and some to Teichomerus. But Dolianus went after his rival with guile. For he called him to a partnership in the rule and in the battle against the Romans; and he was persuaded. So when both leaders had joined and the multitude of the Bulgars had gathered, Dolianus said to those assembled that the nation of the Bulgars would never be saved while steered by two leaders, and: "If you wish your salvation, put one of us out of the way; if then you know that I am of Samuel's family, get rid of Teichomerus; but if not, submit yourselves to him and put me out of the way." At this a shout arose, and all acclaimed the kingship for him, and Teichomerus was stoned. Dolianus, having become sovereign, took Dyrrachium and went against Hellas, and won over Nicopolis and the land under it, those in them coming over to him willingly, since they could not bear the greed and insatiability of the orphanotrophus. And so he made the lands of the Romans, as the saying goes, a Mysian prey.

When the news was brought to the emperor, he set out at once to catch the rebel, saying he thought it a terrible thing if, having added nothing to the empire himself, he should overlook a part of it being taken away. Since his life had been despaired of, for the dropsy had already mastered him and his body had swelled, his kin kept him from the campaign with entreaties and the leading men of the council did not approve the plan. But he, strengthened by zeal and setting eagerness against weakness, went against the Scythians, and the thing was worthy of wonder. For at night he was worn out by the disease and not expected to rise on the morrow, yet as soon as day shone he was seen on horseback and went before the army. When he came to the borders of these Scythians, he made ready to draw up for battle. The units had not yet clashed with one another when something happened that gave the emperor the victory, perhaps without toil. For the son of that Aaron, the patrician Alusianus, who was still among the Romans, having offended the ruler, had been condemned to stay at home and neither come to the palace nor enter Byzantium at all unless he were allowed entry. So he was despondent for this; and when he learned of the nation's revolt and the choice of Dolianus to rule it, he ran away from his house and changed his dress, putting on the dress of an Armenian and pretending to be a servant of Theodorocanus going off to the camp, escaped everyone's notice and reached Bulgaria. But he did not at once make himself known, but talking with some he reminded them of Aaron and said: "If one of his sons were here, would not the legitimate one have seemed to you more worthy of the rule of the nation than the bastard?" When all prayed to be ruled by a legitimate son of Aaron and that the kingship should come round again to an undoubted man truly belonging to the old royal family, he entrusted the secret to one of those who knew Aaron's family better. He, examining his looks rather closely with his eyes, and then knowing of a certain mark on him beyond doubt, asked to see this too. It was a black colour about the right elbow and thick hair on it. Seeing this too, and no longer in doubt, he threw himself down before the man and embraced his feet. And he told the others too that one of the royal family had come to them. And many, breaking away from the doubtful one, joined the legitimate one, and the rule was divided; but since the kingship would not stand at all if the leaders differed with each other, they joined in action and made a treaty, though they suspected and lay in wait for each other. But Alusianus was found quicker at plotting and anticipated Dolianus's guile. Preparing a drinking party and taking his fellow ruler as his drinking companion, he attacked him as he drank and dug out the wretch's eyes, and from this the Scythian people came round to one rule. Then he secretly made known to the emperor that he wished to come over to him, if he found him kindly and did not lack fitting rewards. He accepted the approach and promised to reward him worthily. And he at once came over and was honoured as magister. The emperor at once attacked the nation, and it, being leaderless and scattered, was overcome without difficulty and submitted again to the dominion of the Romans, and the emperor returned to Byzantium and held a triumph, leading through it many captives and Dolianus himself with his eyes put out.

The sovereign was in a bad way and already near the dissolution of his frame. So he scorned the rule, moved from the palace and went off to the house of ascetics he himself had founded before the walls of the city, which he named with the name of the wonder-working Anargyroi. Coming there he took off the purple and all the other marks of the empire, cut his hair and underwent the holy rite, put on the rag of humility in Christ and girded on the divine skin, the symbol of voluntary mortification, he who was already being mortified against his will. When what had happened was reported to the empress, she went out from the palace on foot and came to him. But he barred the doors against her and shut her out from entry to him, I do not know whether ashamed of how he had behaved towards her, or wholly given to repentance and not wishing to come to the memory of his old affection for her. So she went back without meeting Michael. He, living a little while after the change of his life, moved his life to the eternal mansions, lamenting to his last breath the bold deed he had done against the emperor Romanus; he had been a fair and good emperor, as far as lay with him, but his kin clung to him like a stain, somehow soiling his goodness. It is recorded by some that he held the Roman sceptre into the seventh year, and by others something beyond this.

blocks: The rule of the empire came to the Caesar, his mother's brother John accomplishing everything. For the emperor Michael had honoured him as Caesar, as has been written before, then, as if repenting, did not keep a good disposition towards him. So his lodging was fixed somewhere outside the city, and he was not allowed to visit the emperor unless ordered. When the sovereign went out of the palace, as has been said, his brothers forged an imperial letter allowing him access to the palace. And he went in; but the first of the brothers, the orphanotrophus, advised that they ought not to attempt any action without the empress's judgement. So they came to her and threw the Caesar at her feet, put forward the adoption, gave pledges and swore awesome oaths that Michael would share only the name of the empire, while the power would be hers, and she might use him, if she wished, as a slave bought with silver. With this, bewitching her, who was easily led in any case, and charming her with soothing words, they despoiled her and made her follow their will. And the sceptre was put into Michael's hands, and he was crowned with the imperial crown, though unworthy of it, not so much from his family, though he happened to be of a most ignoble and obscure one, for his father was one of those who caulk ships with pitch, as from the badness of his ways. For he was deceitful in mind, unfeeling and ungrateful in soul, respecting neither the laws of kinship nor of friendship. His tongue too was out of tune and at odds with the plans of his soul, hiding one thing in his heart and saying another, and besides this, if anyone, the man was envious, slavish and mean in difficult times, quick to anger and changeable, not changing more readily from anger to mildness, but from a kinder disposition to hatred on any chance.

Such a man, then, was brought up to the axle of the empire, and from this the crowning blow of misfortunes was brought on the orphanotrophus, his uncle, and on the whole family. For he did not keep up the act and the pretence for long, but for a very few days he called his uncle master, thought him worthy to sit beside him and put everything in his hands, then took away something of his honour, then was not obedient to him in most things, and at one time or another showed something that irritated his uncle. He regretted his zeal for this nephew, but had nothing he could do at once, but was brewing his attempt, while meanwhile he did not visit the emperor continually. When a quarrel arose between him and his brother Constantine, to whom alone of all his kin Michael was attached and whom he honoured as nobilissimus, and Constantine was harsh against John before the emperor, John, stung by the words, and more because the emperor had not rebuked Constantine for his railing against him, was offended and went off somewhere far from the town. When this became known it drew a great part of the senate after him, so that they visited him, not from goodwill, but so as to draw his favour on themselves. But the emperor, wary of the gathering of the many to him, reproached him by letter for his disdain and asked him, with malice, to come. And he went; but the emperor, not waiting for his uncle's arrival, went off to the theatre; for it was a day of horse races. When his uncle came and did not find the reigning emperor, boiling over with anger, as having been insulted, he went back. And the emperor broke out into open hostility to him, and sent a ship ordering him to come in it to give account of his disdain towards him. So he was sailing to the palace. But the emperor, from above, by a signal agreed beforehand with those bringing John, stopped the ship from passing to the palace, and at once a trireme came up, took him and sent him into exile. With such things did the man who through him had become Caesar, and then emperor too, repay his benefactor. When he had put him out of the way, he went after his kin, and men, not only in the sense that marks out the male nature, but in the sense that marks those who had married and reached the age of men, already bearded and fathers of children, he deprived of their genitals and made eunuchs.

So his lodging was fixed somewhere outside the city, and he was not allowed to visit the emperor unless ordered. And he went in; but the first of the brothers, the orphanotrophus, advised that they ought not to attempt any action without the empress's judgement. So they came to her and threw the Caesar at her feet, put forward the adoption, gave pledges and swore awesome oaths that Michael would share only the name of the empire, while the power would be hers, and she might use him, if she wished, as a slave bought with silver. With this, bewitching her, who was easily led in any case, and charming her with soothing words, they despoiled her and made her follow their will. And the sceptre was put into Michael's hands, and he was crowned with the imperial crown, though unworthy of it, not so much from his family, though he happened to be of a most ignoble and obscure one, for his father was one of those who caulk ships with pitch, as from the badness of his ways. For he was deceitful in mind, unfeeling and ungrateful in soul, respecting neither the laws of kinship nor of friendship. His tongue too was out of tune and at odds with the plans of his soul, hiding one thing in his heart and saying another, and besides this, if anyone, the man was envious, slavish and mean in difficult times, quick to anger and changeable, not changing more readily from anger to mildness, but from a kinder disposition to hatred on any chance. Such a man, then, was brought up to the axle of the empire, and from this the crowning blow of misfortunes was brought on the orphanotrophus, his uncle, and on the whole family. For he did not keep up the act and the pretence for long, but for a very few days he called his uncle master, thought him worthy to sit beside him and put everything in his hands, then took away something of his honour, then was not obedient to him in most things, and at one time or another showed something that irritated his uncle. He regretted his zeal for this nephew, but had nothing he could do at once, but was brewing his attempt, while meanwhile he did not visit the emperor continually. When a quarrel arose between him and his brother Constantine, to whom alone of all his kin Michael was attached and whom he honoured as nobilissimus, and Constantine was harsh against John before the emperor, John, stung by the words, and more because the emperor had not rebuked Constantine for his railing against him, was offended and went off somewhere far from the town. When this became known it drew a great part of the senate after him, so that they visited him, not from goodwill, but so as to draw his favour on themselves. But the emperor, wary of the gathering of the many to him, reproached him by letter for his disdain and asked him, with malice, to come. And he went; but the emperor, not waiting for his uncle's arrival, went off to the theatre; for it was a day of horse races. When his uncle came and did not find the reigning emperor, boiling over with anger, as having been insulted, he went back. And the emperor broke out into open hostility to him, and sent a ship ordering him to come in it to give account of his disdain towards him. So he was sailing to the palace. But the emperor, from above, by a signal agreed beforehand with those bringing John, stopped the ship from passing to the palace, and at once a trireme came up, took him and sent him into exile. With such things did the man who through him had become Caesar, and then emperor too, repay his benefactor. When he had put him out of the way, he went after his kin, and men, not only in the sense that marks out the male nature, but in the sense that marks those who had married and reached the age of men, already bearded and fathers of children, he deprived of their genitals and made eunuchs.

blocks: When he had raised such a trophy over his own blood, he thought one Herculean labour was still left to him, to get rid of the empress too, and for this he stripped for action, having his uncle Constantine too leading him on to the deed and sharpening him. So the most ill-born son made up stories against his most well-born mother and invented charges against her, called her a poisoner and accused the innocent woman of plotting against his life. What need to go round in circles? He thrust her out of the palace and confined her on the island called Prinkipo, and finally had his benefactress tonsured and changed her dress, and in place of the purple that belonged to her through five generations he dressed her in a worn cloak. And he, as if he had already accomplished everything, rejoiced and was seen exultant, and gave himself to games and luxuries.

But justice did not slumber, but at once went after the accursed man. For when what had happened to the empress was proclaimed to those in the city, dejection and gloom could be seen among all, and each was disposed as in his own calamity, and then they openly railed at the usurper. The women raised laments, calling on the empress. And at last all the people of the city broke out into open riot. And to punish the bold man, no one spared his own life, but each, arming his right hand with whatever came to hand, they ran together to the palace. At first the stirring of the multitude did not much disturb him, then, seeing the people raging and gathering into bands and the crowd flowing in, and noticing those about him uncertain in their minds, for they too hated the bold deed against the empress, he became very afraid and in anguish. But the nobilissimus lightened his anguish a little. For being at home and learning of the riot, he armed those about him, and many were kept by him, and passing through the middle of the Market went off to the palace, and at once they sent men to bring back the empress, and set some against the rioters to shoot arrows at them from out of sight and sling stones, by which not the fewest were killed. When the empress had been brought back, they set her on a height in the theatre and showed her to the rioters, so that forsooth their anger might be calmed now that their mistress had been called back. But this rather kindled their anger and fired their wrath. For when they saw her in changed dress, they broke out further into war, and hating the usurper for his malice they left the empress Zoe and turned to Theodora her sister, who had already had her dress changed before by her sister, as the narrative taught earlier, and taking some of her father's servants, they came to her, brought her out of her dwelling, and, as it were locking their shields about her, led her to the great sanctuary of the Wisdom of God the Word, and Theodora was proclaimed empress by all, by those of the council and those of the people and those of the church themselves.

This put out every hope for Michael and those about him, and fearing for his life he moved from the palace, and boarding one of the imperial ships he and the nobilissimus went off to the famous monastery of Studius, laying aside the marks of the empire and putting on a monk's garments. When this became known to the people, they could not hold themselves in for joy, and ran together against him. When the day was already declining, Theodora's party, fearing that the empress Zoe might call back the man thrown out, so that her sister might not share the empire with her, sent men to dig out the eyes of both. So they were dragged from the very altar of the monastery of Studius and led away. The multitude flowed together about them, insulted and jeered at them, and making up songs mocked them in tragic strains. When they came to the Sigma, a place so called, there their eyes were cut out, Constantine bearing the calamity bravely, Michael calling on God and wailing. When darkness had covered both, those who had carried out the blinding came back to Theodora, who was still waiting at the great sanctuary. Zoe was at the palace. It was her will not to accept her sister as partner of power; for she was jealous beyond measure. But the members of the senate, respecting both, the one as their empress of long standing, the other as just proclaimed and the cause of the overthrow of the tyranny, persuaded the elder to take her sister as partner of power. So Theodora too came to the palace and shared power with her sister. From then the men blinded in their eyes were condemned to exile, the empire having been cut short for them at four months and five days, and would it had been shorter still. So the rule of the

blocks: Romans had come down to the women's quarters, and no innovation was made about them, but all yielded to them, both the leading men of the senate and the most distinguished of the military. Both sat on the bema, and the whole imperial ceremony was performed about them, and the form used for emperors was kept in the bodyguard, and the members of the first council and those in office all stood by with reverence. Examinations of lawsuits, settlements of public disputes on either side, audiences of envoys, appointments to office and the other things belonging to the empire took place before them. But whether fear lest the rule should come round to her sister alone, for it was whispered by some that the rule belonged more to her, as being also the cause of the usurper's overthrow, or desire for a man and for intercourse persuaded Zoe to bring into the palace one who would reign and live with her. And Constantine Dalassenus was brought, as if summoned for something else. But using rather abrupt words and seeming a burdensome and difficult character, he was rejected. Then she inclined to another, neither of the very well born, nor of those enrolled in more splendid ranks, nor of those in distinguished offices, but with looks worthy of a tyrant's rule, and such as to draw to love even a soul not given to lust. So the empress blew towards him with all sails, but a disease, snatching the man suddenly from life, made her votes void. His wife too was suspected of having arranged his death and mixed a deadly poison for him out of jealousy, so that she might not be deprived of her husband while he still lived and see another woman sleeping beside him. So he fell from his hopes in this way, and the empress from her drive.

The votes inclined to Constantine Monomachus, a man of noble birth and of the notable sort, who had been the emperor Romanus's kinsman by marriage through his niece, for he had consorted with her in a second marriage, and of outstanding looks. The emperor Romanus had shown him no great favour, but because of his kinship with him he moved about the imperial courts, and from this he became familiar with the empress, and she was friendly to the man and made him close to her, and welcomed him with favours worth many talents, as she was unsparing of hand and royal in disposition, so that this gave the malicious an occasion for slander against them. So Michael, the sovereign after Romanus, not deaf to what was said, when he reigned confined the man in Lesbos on some invented charges, but the whole of it was jealousy. And he was in exile the whole time of Michael's reign, and he did not find the second Michael any kinder. But when power came back to Zoe, the man was released from exile and was being brought to the reigning city. When he was near, he was stopped from going further, and someone sent from the palace met him near the church of the archangel at Damocraneia, put an imperial robe on him, and setting out from there with an imperial bodyguard he entered the reigning city. And the sacred marriage service was performed for the rulers by one of the priests; for the patriarch Alexius shrank from performing the rite of union for them himself because of the third marriage. The next day he performed the rite of the imperial crowning, and Monomachus was crowned and the Roman sceptre put into his hands. From then the rule of the sisters came to an end,

blocks: having lasted into the third month, and the management of public affairs passed to Monomachus; and he at once, neither with reason nor with any sensible management, made the honours of the ranks and the distributions of money, but handed out the honours in heaps and gave them to those they did not suit, and if it happened that the imperial treasuries were emptied in a single day, he reckoned it no matter at all. To those who had offended him when he was a private man he remitted all charges, and bore a grudge against none of them; and he gave himself up to pleasures and luxuries, partly trying to spit out the disgust left by the storm of his misfortunes, having just put in, perhaps, at the imperial rule as at a sheltered harbour, and partly to please the empresses and court their good humour, since they were of easygoing character. He paid attention to learning, or rather to those who pursued learning and had a reputation for erudition, he himself having tasted learning only with the tip of his finger. So matters in the palace stood thus, but those outside did not go fortunately for the Romans.

For a Scythian man who ran away from Byzantium, named Boisthlavus, gathering a band about him and lurking in the Illyrian mountains like a wild beast, plundered the nations neighbouring these mountains and subject to the Romans, Triballi, Serbs and those of the same race as these. When this was reported to the emperor, he wrote to the governor of Dyrrachium to engage Stephen; for Boisthlavus was also called by this name. He, undertaking the battle against him without skill, for he had no share of generalship's experience, became the cause of great calamity to those campaigning with him, he himself barely being saved with a few, while he laid the whole rest of the army low there, not even able to use their hands and defend themselves against their slayers. So matters in Illyricum went in this way.

Monomachus (for let the narrative linger again on his domestic affairs), since his second wife too had died, judged he should not turn to a third marriage, but he was corrupted with a niece of his wife who was living in widowhood, secretly at first, and then openly too. She was of young age, had beauty of body in abundance and was of distinguished family; for she sprang from the seed of the Scleri. They were so melted in each other and love was so burned into them that if they were not together they seemed not even to live or to bear it. So when this emperor had been condemned to exile, as has been said, she too exiled herself from everyone, so that she might see her lover and beloved and not be exiled from him, and went off with the man, becoming everything to him, lightening his calamity as far as possible and supplying him from her own means, so that he might not be pressed by want besides his other griefs; for hope of rule nursed her too. When he was raised to the height of the empire, while her hopes had not come to pass, the emperor did not forget the woman even in his good fortune, but spoke to the empress about her and asked that the woman be called back and obtain some prosperity. She did not refuse; for time had carried away her jealousy, as she was already past her prime, and the trials that had befallen her had made her more moderate. So the Sclerena was brought up from Mitylene, and at first no distinguished dwelling was made ready for her, nor dainty service. But as time went on an imperial bodyguard was assigned to her and her house was changed into a palace. For Monomachus pretended he was building a house of his own at her lodging, so that he might go to her often, as if to see something of the buildings. For a while, then, he made a stage play of his love, and as it were blushed at what was happening. Then he laid aside both shame and play, and lived with the woman not as a concubine nor as a half-wife, but as openly his wife, and money flowed to her from the imperial treasuries every day in rivers and veins of gold were opened, and the emperor visited her without concealment. But thinking it a terrible thing if he did not live with her and share her house all the time, he moved the woman from there to the palace, having first conferred about this with the empress and persuaded her not to be vexed at what was done. More than this, oaths of friendship are said to have been sworn between the two women, the sovereign asking this. The woman was honoured as Sebaste, this honour being assigned to her first of those formerly imperial; and she was named mistress. And the empress was neither angry nor vexed at this, but with the emperor lodging in the middle, the empress and the Sebaste lived on either side in turn. The Augusta never went to the emperor unless she had made sure that he was alone without his beloved. But she, in this state and raised to such good fortune, and nursing still greater hopes within herself, was suddenly snatched away by disease, and died, leaving great grief to the emperor.
