blocks: So she departed, and a civil war came upon the emperor. For George Maniaces, a man most manly in soul, most noble of hand and most skilful at commanding, had been sent to Italy by the two empresses, when they were in charge of the affairs of the empire, to make war on those invading it and making parts of it their own, and to recover these for the dominion of the Romans, and he was standing against the enemies of the Romans. When the axle of the empire had rolled over to Monomachus, Romanus Sclerus, who was the brother of the emperor's beloved, became very powerful through his sister and was honoured as magister and protostrator; and bordering on Maniaces's house in the theme of the Anatolics, he harmed the man's affairs, bearing a grudge because he had formerly quarrelled with him and been worsted. It is said that he also climbed into Maniaces's bed. These things, reported to the man, moved him to anger and caused him much grief; then he was also deprived of his command, Romanus bringing this about too. So, reflecting that if he went back to Constantine's city the ruler would not treat him kindly because of Sclerus, he attempted usurpation. And as to the most eminent of generals and a warlike man, much of the soldiery came over to him. And he put the army into boats and crossed from Italy to the mainland opposite. This threw the emperor into confusion, and he wrote a letter to Maniaces, freeing him from every fear if he laid down his arms, and promising better things. But when he, having once thrown the die, would no longer let go of his arms, the emperor marched against him. He set over the army none of the brave men or those tried in generalship, fearing that he too might dare the same things, but a eunuch of the chamberlains, faithful to him however. He took the forces and went off, and Maniaces hurried to catch the eunuch's men unprepared. When the armies attacked each other, so far as it lay with the chief fighter, I mean Maniaces, the enemy's army was routed, but by the providence that directs our affairs the battle was suddenly turned the other way, and Maniaces's men were defeated. For as he went at the ranks and threw the phalanxes into confusion, and those he shouted at at once fell back and the locked shields broke up, he was suddenly found struck, and with a mortal blow, from which much blood running down spread a mist over him and brought slackness on his limbs, so that the bridle fell from his hand, and he slipped from his seat and was thrown from his horse to the ground. So he lay, at once dead, a little outside the space between the armies, and the imperial troops were for a time afraid to approach him. But when his men knew their leader had fallen, they were seized by terror and scattered. Then those of the other side ran to the man lying there, cut off the wretch's head and brought it to their general. He at once sent it to the sovereign, and he raised it aloft in the theatre; then, when the eunuch who seemed to have succeeded in the war came back with the army, a triumph was held, with the emperor presiding with great splendour in the forecourt facing the Market of the church of the Saviour in the place called the Chalke, and the empresses sitting with him on either side. So the affairs of Maniaces ended thus.

Another usurpation again was set in motion, whose author was Theophilus Eroticus. He, learning of the affairs of the second Michael, the nephew of the first, and that the empire had been entrusted to women, won over the Cypriots, for he happened to be their governor then, and attempted revolt. But Monomachus needed no delay to put him down. For sending a fleet he subdued Eroticus through it and brought the island into subjection quite easily. The patriarch Alexius died, having enjoyed the patriarchal throne for eighteen years, and Michael, called Cerularius, was set up in his place. Monomachus took twenty-five centenaria of gold from the monastery of the patriarch Alexius, stored there by that patriarch. The eunuch John, who had been orphanotrophus, the brother of the emperor Michael the Paphlagonian, moved to Mitylene when Monomachus came to power, was blinded there, as it seems to some, by the empress Theodora without the sovereign's judgement, but as to others, the ruler himself ordering it, angry with him because of the long and causeless exile. He, living a few days after the blinding, measured out his life.
text: So she departed, and a civil war came upon the emperor. For George Maniaces, a man most manly in soul, most noble of hand and most skilful at commanding, had been sent to Italy by the two empresses, when they were in charge of the affairs of the empire, to make war on those invading it and making parts of it their own, and to recover these for the dominion of the Romans, and he was standing against the enemies of the Romans. When the axle of the empire had rolled over to Monomachus, Romanus Sclerus, who was the brother of the emperor's beloved, became very powerful through his sister and was honoured as magister and protostrator; and bordering on Maniaces's house in the theme of the Anatolics, he harmed the man's affairs, bearing a grudge because he had formerly quarrelled with him and been worsted. It is said that he also climbed into Maniaces's bed. These things, reported to the man, moved him to anger and caused him much grief; then he was also deprived of his command, Romanus bringing this about too. So, reflecting that if he went back to Constantine's city the ruler would not treat him kindly because of Sclerus, he attempted usurpation. And as to the most eminent of generals and a warlike man, much of the soldiery came over to him. And he put the army into boats and crossed from Italy to the mainland opposite. This threw the emperor into confusion, and he wrote a letter to Maniaces, freeing him from every fear if he laid down his arms, and promising better things. But when he, having once thrown the die, would no longer let go of his arms, the emperor marched against him. He set over the army none of the brave men or those tried in generalship, fearing that he too might dare the same things, but a eunuch of the chamberlains, faithful to him however. He took the forces and went off, and Maniaces hurried to catch the eunuch's men unprepared. When the armies attacked each other, so far as it lay with the chief fighter, I mean Maniaces, the enemy's army was routed, but by the providence that directs our affairs the battle was suddenly turned the other way, and Maniaces's men were defeated. For as he went at the ranks and threw the phalanxes into confusion, and those he shouted at at once fell back and the locked shields broke up, he was suddenly found struck, and with a mortal blow, from which much blood running down spread a mist over him and brought slackness on his limbs, so that the bridle fell from his hand, and he slipped from his seat and was thrown from his horse to the ground. So he lay, at once dead, a little outside the space between the armies, and the imperial troops were for a time afraid to approach him. But when his men knew their leader had fallen, they were seized by terror and scattered. Then those of the other side ran to the man lying there, cut off the wretch's head and brought it to their general. He at once sent it to the sovereign, and he raised it aloft in the theatre; then, when the eunuch who seemed to have succeeded in the war came back with the army, a triumph was held, with the emperor presiding with great splendour in the forecourt facing the Market of the church of the Saviour in the place called the Chalke, and the empresses sitting with him on either side. So the affairs of Maniaces ended thus. Another usurpation again was set in motion, whose author was Theophilus Eroticus. He, learning of the affairs of the second Michael, the nephew of the first, and that the empire had been entrusted to women, won over the Cypriots, for he happened to be their governor then, and attempted revolt. But Monomachus needed no delay to put him down. For sending a fleet he subdued Eroticus through it and brought the island into subjection quite easily. The patriarch Alexius died, having enjoyed the patriarchal throne for eighteen years, and Michael, called Cerularius, was set up in his place. Monomachus took twenty-five centenaria of gold from the monastery of the patriarch Alexius, stored there by that patriarch. The eunuch John, who had been orphanotrophus, the brother of the emperor Michael the Paphlagonian, moved to Mitylene when Monomachus came to power, was blinded there, as it seems to some, by the empress Theodora without the sovereign's judgement, but as to others, the ruler himself ordering it, angry with him because of the long and causeless exile. He, living a few days after the blinding, measured out his life.

blocks: Another usurpation, more dreadful, rose against Monomachus. This was Leo Tornicius's, who was related to the sovereign by birth on his mother's side. Living in Orestias, as the city of the emperor Hadrian was called of old, he had the Macedonians attached to him, as to someone superior. For the man was not mean either in looks or in mind. He also had something else by which he drew most people to himself. For rumour prophesied about him, such as is said idly about others too, that he would one day be master of the Roman sceptre. The emperor was not disposed towards him as a relative, but was even hostile to the man. But the ruler's sister Euprepia made him her friend and welcomed him, a noble woman and most steady in mind, who had come to distinguished fortune and abundant wealth, and who was not loved by her brother, though he was wary of her because of her surpassing intelligence. She, getting none of the greater things from him, did not visit him often, and when she did visit she behaved arrogantly, refuting and reproaching him. And if at this she saw her brother angry, she took offence contemptuously. So the emperor, seeing his sister's closeness to Tornicius, suspected and was angry, and to set them far from each other, he entrusted to him the command of the lands among the Iberians that belonged to the dominion of the Romans, having voted for him an exile handsomely disguised. And he went off. But the rumour that raised him in hopes to great fortune did not stop. And from this some slandered the man to the emperor. He, shaken in mind by these words, sent and had Tornicius's hair cut, thinking to cut off his hopes with his hair, and clothed him in a black rag, thinking that so he darkened the expected splendour of his fortune, and when he came back so, he did not pity him, but laughed at him and let him go.

The Macedonians, who had been attached to the man before, as has been said, and nursed good hopes about him, secretly took him out of the queen of cities by night and brought him to their metropolis Adrianople, and by the efforts of his supporters most of the armies quickly gathered there, or else from hatred of the sovereign. For for some reasons he had not treated the soldiers well, but nursed suspicions against them, and for this they were stirred to enmity against him. When they had gathered, they at once granted him imperial acclamation and proclamation. And he at once set to work with them, and suddenly came against the reigning city, and as he came many soldiers and townsmen came over to him, and he was buoyed up by hopes, thinking that no one would stand against him, but rather they would easily open the gates of the city to him too, both because the eastern armies were busy with wars there and because the people of the city were angry with the sovereign, as one who did not treat them to their liking. Buoyed up by such hopes, he encamped before the city, to besiege it if it did not receive him very readily. So at dawn he drew up his army, and coming near the circuit wall of the city at Blachernae he asked those inside to open the gates for him, encouraging them to the deed with splendid promises. When they paid no attention to him, but mocked and jeered at him, he set about the attack. The emperor drew up against him with a few soldiers, a crowd of commoners and some other men, servants of some of the senate, all together not even exactly a thousand in number; and setting them before the circuit wall of the city facing the usurper's men, he thought he would strike terror into the enemy with them. The sovereign himself sat royally in one of the imperial chambers that projected beyond the others and faced the plain before the city, so that he might see the enemy and be seen by them. The Macedonians, being used to buffoonery, seeing the emperor, some insulted him outright, while others formed choruses and, making up songs of comedy, danced and sang them, beating the ground with their feet.

Then, when a part of the enemy attacked the imperial troops set before the wall outside, some rushed to the gates, while others fell into the ditch and perished. So great was the fear of all that those standing on the walls threw themselves down from there and fled, and those guarding the entrances of the city at once vanished, without even barring the gates. If, then, the war at that time had had one who knew how to win, nothing would have prevented Tornicius from being at once inside the town and putting an end to the attempt. But this, since it had not been decided by the management from above, escaped the usurper. The emperor would nearly have been in danger; for one of the enemy aimed at him and shot an arrow at him, and it missed the emperor and struck a youth among the chamberlains. But the wound from the arrow was not mortal for him either; but those about the emperor, afraid, at once moved, and he himself was carried with his seat somewhere else. Good fortune, having escaped Tornicius in the way described, turned his affairs the opposite way. For the city was again put under guard, and the usurper, attacking again at dawn and beaten off, nearly perished too. For as stones weighing a talent were being slung from an engine against the enemy, one went at the usurper, and did not reach him, but put fear into him and those about him, and breaking up their line they went back to their camp and no longer tried the siege. But the usurper, waiting a few days, when he saw some of his own men going over to the emperor and others scattering and running away, withdrew from the blockade of the town and went off as if to master the Thracian forts easily, but was beaten off from them too. Meanwhile the eastern forces called back by the sovereign arrived and were sent against the usurper. Those who were joining in the revolt with him, when they learned this, afraid for themselves, and since the commander of the eastern units had encamped beside the rebels and was persuading some by talks and others by letters to desert to the sovereign, almost all left the usurper and joined the imperial troops, and these were not only obscure soldiers but also distinguished men who had held commands and been made illustrious by offices, he being left with only one of the notable men, Batatzes. When Tornicius had been left by the rest, and his capture was inescapable on every side, he and Batatzes fled to a divine church. From there they were brought in fetters to Monomachus; he voted the loss of sight for both, and the lamps of their bodies were at once put out, and the revolt was wholly dissolved.

blocks: So far the narrative has related civil battles, and will now pass to battles with barbarians. Let the attack of the Rhos come before the others. This nation had also come against the Romans very many times at other times, but having been defeated at last it made a treaty with the Romans and a marriage alliance, so that through the kinship the races might be bound in harmony, and they visited each other trading. So at that time too many Tauroscythians were in Constantine's city, selling their own goods and buying ours. A quarrel happened to arise between some of the Scythians and some Romans, and blows followed it and wounds, and deaths followed these, and among the dead one of the notable men among them was counted. This became a pretext for the ruler of that country to stir against us, and at once he built very many boats, which among them are called monoxyla, put on them a multitude almost beyond counting, shook an undeclared war over the Romans and came inside the Propontis. When the ruler learned of the attack, he sent envoys to them that they should lay down their arms, as the emperor was ready to heal and make good anything that had happened to grieve them. But the barbarian received the envoys arrogantly, belched out boastful and haughty words, and sent them away dishonoured. So the ruler, despairing of a treaty, himself prepared for a sea battle, and since the navy happened not to be at home, but was very far away, busy guarding lands, he made ready some triremes and other cargo ships, put an abundance of the liquid fire on them and set them against the barbarian boats, the ruler himself being present and sitting somewhere above the harbour. When most of the day had passed and the barbarians stayed quiet and did not break their formation, the emperor ordered Theodorocanus to take three of the triremes and skirmish against the barbarians, to draw them into battle. But he did not try skirmishes, but a pure sea battle, and burned some barbarian boats with the liquid fire, sank others with their crews, and captured one himself, having leapt into it, cutting some down with the sword and taking others in bonds, as if overcome by fear. When the attack on the enemy had gone so well with the three triremes, the emperor gave the signal to other cargo ships too, and more put out; and the barbarians, seeing them come on, no longer thought of battle, but breaking their formation backed water and rushed to flight. Some weight from above also fought with the Romans then; for a hard wind suddenly blew from east to west and, raising a storm, fell on the boats of the barbarians, and swamped many and gave them to the deep, and dashed many against reefs and rocks and smashed them. Of their crews, some the water covered, and others a military force lying in wait on the shores destroyed. The multitude of the barbarians having been overcome in this way, the emperor returned to the palace bearing a trophy.

blocks: So one barbarian war has been related; let another stirring of a nation be told too, which then seized the east and feeds on it to this day, I mean the Turks. These are a Hunnic race living north of the Caucasus mountains, very numerous and independent. When the rule of the Persians, or rather of the Macedonians, which overthrew the kingdom of the Persians, had been overthrown by the Saracens, and then these too, quarrelling among themselves, were divided into opposing parts and fought one another, Muchumet, the son of Imbrael, ruler of Persis, of the Chorasmians, of Media and of some others, made war in the times of the emperor Basil on the Babylonians and the Indians, and being defeated he sent for an allied force from the Turks; the general of those who came to Muchumet's alliance was Tangrolipix Mucalet. With them Muchumet attacked his opponents and routed them, and returning home he would not let the Turks go back to their own land, but wished to hold them back, so that he might use them as allies against others too. They, unable to go off to their own land unless the bridge of the Araxes were opened to them (this river is not passable except by the bridge, and the bridge was towered on both sides, and guards stood on the towers), revolted, and fleeing to the mountains, for being three thousand they did not dare to fight many tens of thousands in close battle, they ran out from there and plundered the lands of the Saracens. So Muchumet sent armies of about twenty thousand against them, entrusting their command to ten men of his own race. The Turks attacked them by night and very easily cut down most of them. Those who were saved went back with their generals to Muchumet. He blinded the ten commanders of the army, and threatened to treat the surviving soldiers in the worst way. They, afraid, joined the Turks; and as many others too were already flowing to them, slaves and evildoers delighting in plunder and robbery, they became a very numerous army, and clashed with Muchumet near Aspachan, and when many Saracens had fallen Muchumet himself too died. So the armies agreed, and Tangrolipix was entrusted by all with the rule of the lands under Muchumet. Chosen for leadership, he sent and threw down the towers on the bridge of the Araxes. When the passage of the river had thus been opened to the Turks, a great multitude of these barbarians flowed to Tangrolipix, and the leader of the Turks, gaining a heavy hand from them, took the rule from the Saracens on every side, assigned it to himself and his kinsmen, and made the sons of Hagar subjects.

Then he himself gained the Babylonians by battle, and sent his nephew Cutlumus with an army against the Arabs; but he was defeated and turned back, and sent envoys to the ruler of Media, as Baasparkan was called of old, asking to be allowed to pass through his country. But he, who had been appointed by the emperor to rule this country, not only did not grant him passage, but drew up against him, and engaging him was defeated, lost many of his own men, and was himself captured. So Cutlumus, coming back to Tangrolipix, related the war in Media and praised the fruitfulness of the country, and added that it was easy to take, being held by women, so calling those who had fought him. Tangrolipix was angry with him for his defeat, and was going against the Arabs. And Cutlumus, afraid, ran off with those with him, and seizing Pasar, which is a city of the Chorasmians, revolted from the Sultan, for so Tangrolipix was named, and for a long time resisted his uncle, who besieged him but could achieve nothing because of the strength of the city. So the Sultan was busy with the siege of Pasar; and he sent Asan against Media with a force fit for battle. He attacked the country and engaged the Romans, and fell himself, and the soldiery with him was defeated, and all perished except a very few. Learning this, the Sultan lost heart, but hurried to make good the misfortune again, and entrusting an army numbering a hundred thousand to Alim Abramius, his half-brother, sent him against the Romans.

The general of Baasparkan made this known to the emperor by letter, asking for an allied force. And he wrote to Liparites, who was lord of a part of the Iberians, to join the Romans and help against the Turks. When the Turks were already at hand, the Romans judged they should not fight them unless they were joined by the Iberians too, according to the imperial order. Since the soldiers kept still, Alim, unable to engage them as they sat in a stronghold, attacked Artze, which was a country town, and a multitude lived in it, if I may say so, beyond number; the people were merchants, and they had abundant wealth. As the town was unwalled, the barbarians hoped to take it at the first assault, but they knew they had been beguiled by their hopes when they attacked it. For the inhabitants brought timber into the passages and blocked them with it, and from the houses they shot at the enemy and killed many, and this went on for six days. When Alim, the general of the Turks, knew that the people of Artze were holding out most strongly and were not easily taken by siege, he decided to overcome the men by fire; so at once it was kindled and set to the houses. When the fire was lit on every side, the natives were routed, and the barbarians mastered the town and found in it much gold and other wealth, as much as had not been consumed by the fire.

From there they rushed again against the Roman army. When Liparites with the Iberians too had arrived, the clash of the armies took place about the time of unyoking the oxen. Alim and Chorosanes, who was another general of the barbarians, with those under them, were routed and turned to flight, and the Romans drawn up against them pursued them far into the night. But Liparites, fighting on the other wing, was captured by the enemy. When the Romans stopped the pursuit, they waited for Liparites, not knowing what had happened to him. Meanwhile someone reported to them the capture of Liparites, and that his captors had taken him and were going off in haste. The Romans, learning this, were despondent. The barbarians brought Liparites to the Sultan. The emperor, learning of Liparites's capture, sent to the Sultan, asking him to grant Liparites his freedom, sending much ransom for him and gifts to the Sultan too, and asking for a treaty to be made between Romans and Turks. The Sultan sent Liparites as a gift, gave all the ransom to the man for whom it had been sent, and urged him no longer to take up arms against the Turks. He too sent an envoy to the emperor, whom they called the sherif. He is among them what among us was formerly called the synkellos; for as the synkellos took the patriarch's place when he died, so the sherif succeeded the caliph when he perished. So the sherif came into the great city, came to talk with the ruler, and having spoken arrogantly and demanded that tribute be paid to the Sultan, was sent away. From this the Sultan, heavy at heart, went against the Romans himself, and from then on the nation of the Turks, advancing, mastered the whole east and reached the mainland opposite Byzantium. So the affairs of the Turks went in this way.

So the Sultan was busy with the siege of Pasar; and he sent Asan against Media with a force fit for battle. He attacked the country and engaged the Romans, and fell himself, and the soldiery with him was defeated, and all perished except a very few. Learning this, the Sultan lost heart, but hurried to make good the misfortune again, and entrusting an army numbering a hundred thousand to Alim Abramius, his half-brother, sent him against the Romans. The general of Baasparkan made this known to the emperor by letter, asking for an allied force. And he wrote to Liparites, who was lord of a part of the Iberians, to join the Romans and help against the Turks. When the Turks were already at hand, the Romans judged they should not fight them unless they were joined by the Iberians too, according to the imperial order. Since the soldiers kept still, Alim, unable to engage them as they sat in a stronghold, attacked Artze, which was a country town, and a multitude lived in it, if I may say so, beyond number; the people were merchants, and they had abundant wealth. As the town was unwalled, the barbarians hoped to take it at the first assault, but they knew they had been beguiled by their hopes when they attacked it. For the inhabitants brought timber into the passages and blocked them with it, and from the houses they shot at the enemy and killed many, and this went on for six days. When Alim, the general of the Turks, knew that the people of Artze were holding out most strongly and were not easily taken by siege, he decided to overcome the men by fire; so at once it was kindled and set to the houses. When the fire was lit on every side, the natives were routed, and the barbarians mastered the town and found in it much gold and other wealth, as much as had not been consumed by the fire. From there they rushed again against the Roman army. When Liparites with the Iberians too had arrived, the clash of the armies took place about the time of unyoking the oxen. Alim and Chorosanes, who was another general of the barbarians, with those under them, were routed and turned to flight, and the Romans drawn up against them pursued them far into the night. But Liparites, fighting on the other wing, was captured by the enemy. When the Romans stopped the pursuit, they waited for Liparites, not knowing what had happened to him. Meanwhile someone reported to them the capture of Liparites, and that his captors had taken him and were going off in haste. The Romans, learning this, were despondent. The barbarians brought Liparites to the Sultan. The emperor, learning of Liparites's capture, sent to the Sultan, asking him to grant Liparites his freedom, sending much ransom for him and gifts to the Sultan too, and asking for a treaty to be made between Romans and Turks. The Sultan sent Liparites as a gift, gave all the ransom to the man for whom it had been sent, and urged him no longer to take up arms against the Turks. He too sent an envoy to the emperor, whom they called the sherif. He is among them what among us was formerly called the synkellos; for as the synkellos took the patriarch's place when he died, so the sherif succeeded the caliph when he perished. So the sherif came into the great city, came to talk with the ruler, and having spoken arrogantly and demanded that tribute be paid to the Sultan, was sent away. From this the Sultan, heavy at heart, went against the Romans himself, and from then on the nation of the Turks, advancing, mastered the whole east and reached the mainland opposite Byzantium. So the affairs of the Turks went in this way.

blocks: The nation of the Patzinaks was again stirred against the European region; the nation is Scythian and populous, pasturing beyond the Ister. The ruler of the nation then was Tyrach, a man splendid in family among the nation, but sluggish in character. Another, called Cegenes, obscure as regards descent, but a man of action and energy who had often shown valour in wars, was loved by the nation. So he was ambushed by Tyrach, who sought to kill him. Learning this, he won over two of the tribes, there being thirteen in all, crossed the Ister with them and came to the Roman borders, saying he came as a deserter to the emperor and would not be useless to him. This was reported to Monomachus, and the governor of the country was ordered to receive the Scythians. Cegenes came to the queen of cities, came into the emperor's presence, received saving baptism and was honoured as patrician. He also persuaded the Scythians with him to share in this divine bath. Spending his time in the lands by the Ister and suddenly crossing the river, he harmed Tyrach's people, killing and plundering. So Tyrach sent an embassy to the emperor and complained that he had received the rebel of the nation, and that unless he stopped the refugee from harming the nation, he would have the whole nation as an enemy. To this the sovereign said: "I shall neither become the betrayer of one who has come to me, nor prevent him from defending himself against those who plotted against him."

When these messages were brought to Tyrach, since winter had come and the Ister was frozen by the cold from one bank to the other, he crossed the river on foot with the whole nation and, seizing the Roman country, ravaged what lay in his way. The emperor, learning this, at once sent an army to help the governor of the country and Cegenes. But the Patzinaks, finding an abundance of food, wine and other drinks made from honey, and gorging themselves on them, fell into a disease of the bowels. Learning this from a deserter, Cegenes persuaded the Roman forces too to attack the enemy. So when the barbarians saw the Romans' attack on them, being worn out by the disease, they grew dizzy, lost heart, let go their arms, became suppliants and gave themselves up to their enemies. Of these, those who came under Cegenes were partly given to the sword and partly sold into slavery for gold. The rest of the multitude was thought likely to be useful to the Romans, if, deprived of its arms, it were settled in the country of the Bulgars, which was mostly empty, since that nation had been overthrown a little before. And this was done at the emperor's order. Tyrach with the leading men of the nation was brought to the ruler, and being granted divine baptism they were honoured with splendid ranks.

When the Romans had battles with the Turks in the east, the sovereign picked fifteen thousand Patzinaks, armed them, gave them horses, set commanders of their own race over them, and took them across at Chrysopolis, ordering them to go off to Iberia, and appointing them a guide for the road too. When they came to Damatrys, they halted and would not go on; turning back and reaching the strait, they ferried themselves across the sea with their horses at the monastery of Saint Tarasius, at once made a forced march and joined their kinsmen, and when they had gathered together they went off and pitched their tents in the plains by the Ister, and setting out from there overran the lands of Thrace. Though the emperor often sent armies against them, the barbarians had the upper hand, so that they scattered without fear over all Thrace and Macedonia and made everything plunder, not only what was far off but also what was at the city's doors. At last they made a thirty-year treaty with the Romans. And so the war of the Patzinaks ended.

blocks: The Sultan did not stop attacking the lands and cities under the Romans, plundering some and sacking and making others his own. In these times the sovereign also detected a plot which Romanus Boïlas had put together. He was a man of the obscure, and had a half-voiced tongue, unable to speak correctly, slipping in conversation and uttering sounds not to be made out by the hearers. This was partly a natural defect, and partly pretence and play, the play-actor straining nature's failing by his acting. The emperor delighted in such a man as in no one else, and if he heard him uttering mistaken and inarticulate sounds, he thought his babblings beyond all sweetness. And so for this he became so close to the emperor that every time was right for him to go in to him and meet him. Nor was it that the men's quarters were so open to him while the women's quarters were shut, but these too were free to him and could be entered when he wished, and wealth flowed to the man from both sides, and snatched up from the crossroads he was raised to the very summit of the senate. But he was not content with being so fortunate, but also loved the empire, and planned to assign it to himself by killing the sovereign. And he revealed the secret to those he knew were ill disposed to the emperor. Those who accepted the proposal he strengthened for the deed, raising them with great hopes. And if any were vexed at the approach, he said he had put the proposal to them as a test, to know their faithfulness to the sovereign, praised the men for their disposition and swore he would make known to the emperor that they were well disposed to him. So he went after most people in this way, and those sworn with him thought the plan would very easily be carried out. For not only was access to the imperial bedchamber free to him, whether the emperor happened to be sleeping or lying with the empress, but he had also been entrusted with the keys of the secret entrances. And the plan would have been carried into effect had not one of those who shared in the scheme revealed it to the emperor. So he was caught in the act, holding the very sword with which he was about to make away with the sovereign at once. But he, through the ruler's foolishness, suffered nothing grievous, while his accomplices in the plot did not remain unpunished.

This emperor, wishing to seem generous and liberal, but not pursuing the virtue as he should, turned it into a vice. For instead of magnificence he rolled into prodigality, giving the public money neither to those he should, nor as much as he should, nor when he ought. Building the monastery of the Mangana, and it is said he began the building because of his beloved, I mean the Sclerena, so that he might visit her continually, as she then had her dwelling in the house of the Kynegion, having the building of the monastery as a pretext, he drained the imperial or public treasuries; so, needing money, he did not keep even from forbidden sources of revenue. Moreover, there were lands which did not contribute taxes to the emperors, but instead of all tax-paying guarded the difficult passes and walled off from the barbarians the way into the lands subject to the Romans; he imposed taxes on these lands and stopped the guards. And from this the way into the Roman lands became very easy for the barbarians. So that man will be judged by those who reckon without passion the cause of the eastern region being mastered by the barbarian spear.

blocks: When the empress Zoe ended her life in deep old age, for her life stretched beyond seventy years, he mourned her not like a man but like a boy. It is said that he even made her equal to the angels, since a mushroom sprang up somewhere on her tomb from some moisture, and he called this a sign arranged from above, so that it might not go unknown that the empress had been enrolled among the intellectual powers. When she had died, as has been said, the emperor, still burning with love, brought into the palace a girl given to the Romans as a hostage from the Alans, the child of one of their rulers, and naming her Sebaste assigned her an imperial service and a supply of wealth. And had he not held the empress Theodora in respect, or rather been ashamed of the lawlessness of a fourth marriage, he would have called this beloved of his empress too and adorned her with a diadem. When he died, the good fortune did not stay with the Sebaste, but she went back to her former fortune as a hostage.

Now the end of this sovereign too must be told. Not long had been measured out since he became master of the dominion of the Romans when the disease of arthritis fell on him, which first brought the flow of that humour on his feet, so that his feet were powerless for walking and standing. If he ever needed to move, he either went forward with difficulty, supported by some, or was moved wholly by others. As time went on the cause flowed to his hands too; then it came on his shoulders, and at last his whole body was flooded by the humour, and was slackened and put out of joint, the humour being shut up in the hollows of the joints. So the emperor's body had suffered thus for a long time. Then something else happened besides, a stabbing in the side from wind, and made the end of his life expected by him and by those who held power beside him, of whom the first was the logothete John, a little eunuch, obscure in family or rather most ill-born, most unfit for handling affairs, and with so much share of the art of grammar that he could neither speak correctly nor spell without slips. To him the emperor gave the management of public affairs and showed him the most eminent of all the council. For formerly there had been over the imperial administration a man in every way a counterweight to this one, in family, in learning and in exactness in the management of the state. Being such, whenever the emperor ordered him to do something improper, he did not bend to the ruler's choice, but spoke against it and kept him from what was not fitting. He was annoyed, and as this happened often he was angry at that man's freedom of speech, and to unload the opposition he removed him from the management of public affairs, this was Lichudes, and brought in John in his place, and handed him the steering of civil affairs, so that he might not be held back by anyone in what he set out to do. This John, then, and others, who were also very powerful with the emperor, despairing of his life, persuaded the sick man to take thought for the succession, and suggested to him that Proteuon was fit for the rule; he had been girded with the command of Bulgaria and was away from the queen of cities. So a man was sent to call him; and the plan was hidden from the empress Theodora. But the plan did not escape the empress to the end. Knowing that the dying man was not putting power in her hands, she left him dying hard at the palace at the Mangana; and she, through the efforts of those who served her, boarded a ship and put in at the great palace. And the imperial bodyguard at once flowed to her, and the chosen men of the senate, and she was proclaimed sovereign by all, as the rule belonged to her by inheritance. This, made known to Monomachus, added to his pain, and living a little while, long enough to groan at what had happened and lose heart, he died, having reigned twelve years and eight months. And he was laid in the monastery of the Mangana, which he had built.

blocks: The empress Theodora, though past her prime when she took hold of the sole rule, would not set an emperor over affairs, but delighting in power, for as long a time as she lived on in the empire she herself was master of everything, being led to this by her servants too, whom she set over the greatest offices. She entrusted the management of civil affairs to the synkellos Leo, who was named Paraspondylus, who had served the emperor Michael long before. She presided on the bema, gave audience to envoys, appointed to offices, gave justice in lawsuits, delivered verdicts and arbitrated public and common matters, and her sole rule was prosperous. For no one raised a hand against her, nor were the subjects seen treating her decisions slightingly, nor was any nation stirred against the Romans then, but there was also good tempering of the seasons and the earth bore abundant fruits. Though this empress was past her prime, as has been said, and full of days when she held the sceptre, yet she measured out for herself many more years of life. She also had a rather strong body, not easily bent by toils. But when her end too pressed on her, even though some monks promised her ages more of life, and she had fallen into a terrible disease, which the Asclepiads call ileus, and those about her had given up their hopes for her, they gathered and considered whom they might bring into the rule in her place, who would keep their prosperity and good fortune for them. Michael the Stratioticus seemed suitable to them for this, a man born in Byzantium, but unfitted for handling affairs and so great a dominion, both from natural sluggishness and simplicity and through the length of time that had stretched out his life. For he was no longer an old man, as the common crowd called him, but very old. So they persuaded Theodora to set him in the empire in her place. And she at once crowned Michael with the imperial diadem, having first bound him with awesome oaths not to arrange anything in the administration of the empire without their judgement. On this the empress's breath failed, having ruled alone one year and nine months.

blocks: So the old Michael, proclaimed sovereign in the way described, was seen to be most generous, even beyond what was fitting, to those of the senate and to the common crowd, advancing each of them up the steps of the ranks and assigning honours unsuited to most. But towards the military rolls, and above all to their leading men, to whom commanding armies and cavalry squadrons had long been assigned, he behaved quite opposite to the others. For he showed no generosity towards them when they had just come to the queen of cities, nor welcomed them with mild words. The first of these were two men, both of them magistri, splendid in family, and no less distinguished for generalship's intelligence, strength of hand and boldness of soul. One of them was Isaac Comnenus, and the other Catacalon Cecaumenus, whose homeland was Colonea, whom, being duke of Antioch, he released from the command at the same time as his proclamation, appointing his own nephew Michael magister and duke of Antioch and giving him the surname Uranus, so that he might seem to trace his family to the ancient Uranus. This Cecaumenus, then, as having forsooth not used his command well, but having broken up the forces and been oppressive to those under his hand, he rebuked rather insolently, pelted with reproaches and did not spare insults, and when the other most splendid men who commanded units there set out to defend the man, he did not hold his tongue against them, nor did he respect Comnenus himself. This threw the soldiers into despondency, seeing Michael most generous to the others but not showing them goodwill even in words; yet they held back from making any rising, but decided to make a second attempt.

But let the narrative now relate another rising against the emperor before theirs. For the proedros Theodosius, the cousin of the emperor Constantine Monomachus, as soon as Michael had been proclaimed, taking his proclamation hard, took his own servants and some others who were sick with the same lightness of mind as he, and in late afternoon went through the Market escorted by them, saying that power belonged to him because of his kinship with Monomachus and crying out that he was being wronged. Coming to the public prison, which is called the praetorium, he broke the bolts and gave those shut up in it free exit. He did the same at the prison of the Chalke too, hoping through these to gain his aim. When he learned that a military force was gathering at the palace and was already being sent against him, he turned to the Great Church, and left alone with his son, as those following him scattered, he fled to the church; taken from there he was condemned to exile. When his attempt had come to this end, the common crowd, laughing at him, made up some words and sang them at him; they were: "The fool did what Monomachus would have done, if he had any sense." And so these things went.

This Cecaumenus, then, as having forsooth not used his command well, but having broken up the forces and been oppressive to those under his hand, he rebuked rather insolently, pelted with reproaches and did not spare insults, and when the other most splendid men who commanded units there set out to defend the man, he did not hold his tongue against them, nor did he respect Comnenus himself. This threw the soldiers into despondency, seeing Michael most generous to the others but not showing them goodwill even in words; yet they held back from making any rising, but decided to make a second attempt. But let the narrative now relate another rising against the emperor before theirs. For the proedros Theodosius, the cousin of the emperor Constantine Monomachus, as soon as Michael had been proclaimed, taking his proclamation hard, took his own servants and some others who were sick with the same lightness of mind as he, and in late afternoon went through the Market escorted by them, saying that power belonged to him because of his kinship with Monomachus and crying out that he was being wronged. Coming to the public prison, which is called the praetorium, he broke the bolts and gave those shut up in it free exit. He did the same at the prison of the Chalke too, hoping through these to gain his aim. When he learned that a military force was gathering at the palace and was already being sent against him, he turned to the Great Church, and left alone with his son, as those following him scattered, he fled to the church; taken from there he was condemned to exile. When his attempt had come to this end, the common crowd, laughing at him, made up some words and sang them at him; they were: "The fool did what Monomachus would have done, if he had any sense." And so these things went.

blocks: The eastern commanders who had been insulted made an attempt again, and went to the protosynkellos Leo, who managed public affairs, and tried through him to entreat the emperor that they alone should not be left without reward, when all had enjoyed the sovereign's generosity, and this when, while the others lived in comfort, they stood by the shield and fought in front of the dominion of the Romans. But he, being no less clumsy than the emperor at handling grieved men and calming the swelling grief had raised in them, not only did not smooth the men's harshness with words, but rather roughened them, belittling each and sending them all away dishonoured. So, having tried the second attempt too, they judged they should delay no longer, but each urging on his neighbour they hurried to bring their plan into the open. They decided to have Bryennius too as accomplice and helper in the attempt, who was one of the distinguished men, commander of the forces from Macedonia and girded with the command of Cappadocia, and who also had reasons for grief against the sovereign. When they found him too ready for their plan, they sought one of themselves to reign, and Comnenus was preferred above all by all. When they had agreed on this, they all went home, having taken leave of the emperor.

Bryennius too went off with the units under him, and coming to the theme of the Anatolics he arranged the distribution of the soldiers' pay there; for the patrician John Opsaras was with him, bringing gold. When the distribution had already begun, Bryennius added to the soldiers' allowances and increased the amount assigned to each. The man mentioned, the paymaster of the gold, said this had not been ordered him by the sovereign. And Bryennius rather insolently ordered him to be silent and do as he was told. When Opsaras still would not obey, but even spoke against him more boldly, Bryennius, seized with anger, leapt up from his seat, took the man by the hair and the beard, dashed him to the ground and put him in bonds. The commander of the Pisidians and Lycaonians, who was encamped somewhere near and learned of the affair of Opsaras, judging it the beginning of a usurpation, suddenly attacked Bryennius's tent with the units under him. And he bound him, freed Opsaras from his bonds and handed Bryennius over to him; and he at once cut out his eyes, and so sent the man to the emperor, writing to him also all he had dared. So this happened thus.

Comnenus and those sworn with him came together and set to work, the military rolls flowing to him from one place after another. For the whole soldiery desired that a soldier should be girded with the imperial rule. For it was vexed at being ruled by the civil part, but did not dare to bring its longing into the open, but hid its desire and was in labour with its aim in this. When they learned that Comnenus had attempted usurpation, and that he himself was the leader of the play, and that the strongest of the families were helping him in the attempt, thinking this was what they had planned, they seized the moment, and each hurried to get ahead of his neighbour. From this a heavy force gathered to Comnenus; so sending through the whole east he exacted the taxes, appointing receivers of them and registrars of what was brought in. Then setting out he went off to Nicaea, already proclaimed emperor by all those campaigning with him, wishing to become master of it, so that he might have the city as a base or a refuge, whichever way his fortune might incline; and he took it, and setting a sufficient garrison in it, he himself encamped twelve stades before it.

The emperor Michael, gathering the western forces, and any of the eastern ones that were left somewhere and had not been carried off with Comnenus, set over them as general the domestic of the East, the eunuch Theodore, the servant of the empress Theodora, yoking with him as fellow commander the magister Aaron, who was the brother of Comnenus's wife. They encamped opposite the enemy and joined battle at a place called Hades by the natives, and the left wing of the imperial troops defeated the right wing about Comnenus, and took alive Romanus Sclerus, who commanded it. But the enemy's left wing, which Cecaumenus commanded, routed the right of the imperial troops, and went into their very camp, tore down the tents and threw them to the ground. This put great boldness into Comnenus's men, and threw down the spirits of their opponents and persuaded them to flee. So there was great slaughter of the imperial troops, not only of common soldiers but also of commanders, and more were taken alive. And victory smiled openly on Comnenus.

blocks: Learning this, the emperor Michael despaired of the war and wished to lay down the rule, but this was not the wish of those about him, so he was not allowed to carry his wish into effect. So men from the chosen of the senate were sent as envoys to Comnenus; they were the proedros Constantine Lichudes, the proedros Leo Alopus, and Michael Psellus, the consul of the philosophers. What they announced was the adoption of Comnenus, who would be made the emperor's son, his elevation to the honour of Caesar, and for those who had planned the usurpation with him release and amnesty for the offence. They announced this to Comnenus in the hearing of the multitude, and it raised an uproar, saying it did not wish to see its leader in another dress, nor would it bear him to take off the imperial robe he had already put on. Most said this not because they thought so, but to flatter the usurper. When the gathering broke up, Comnenus took the envoys aside privately and said: "If you assure me that you will carry some secrets across to the sovereign, I shall tell you all that is in my heart." When they agreed to keep every secret unrevealed, he said: "I am content now with the dress of Caesar and do not seek the imperial one, but I ask assurance from the ruler that he will never give the sole rule to another, that he will keep for each of those with me whatever honour he has received from me, and that he will now give me some share of imperial authority, so that I may honour some with the lesser ranks and appoint some to military commands; and if this is carried out for me, I shall make peace and hold off. Since this displeases the multitudes, I shall write two letters to the ruler, and with one I shall win over the soldiery, and in the other I shall write the secrets." Besides this he asked that the man managing public affairs be removed from the administration, as ill disposed to him and to those with him. Having said this and handed them the letters, he urged them to go.

They went back to the old sovereign, bringing the letters and reporting by living voice all that Comnenus had said to them in secret. The emperor, pleased at this, promised to fulfil all he had asked, and added: "As he made known secret thoughts to me through you, so I in turn entrust something more private to him through you. Swear to the man, then, that the interval will not be long before I make him a partner in power, but now I put this off for certain reasons." On this the envoys went off again, and Comnenus received the messages gladly, and the messages seemed not unwelcome to the others, and more so because they had learned that the man entrusted with the administration had been removed from it, and all decided now to lay down their arms and keep from the usurpation.

The old emperor, before his agreement with Comnenus was made, getting for himself, as he thought, the goodwill of the civil part, wrote a document binding each one with oaths and curses neither to call Comnenus emperor nor to pay him imperial honour, and persuaded some of the senators with money, others with distributions of ranks, and others with other charms, to sign the document and confirm what was in it. When they heard that Comnenus was coming and would enter on the following day, some seditious members of the senate came at dawn to the sanctuary of the Wisdom of God the Word, and the commanders of the hetaireiai went with them, and with shouts they called on the patriarch to come out and see them. He, barring the doors against them on every side, sent his nephews out to them to ask what they were saying. They, making an uproar and already gathered into a multitude, as many flowed together there, seized the patriarch's nephews, and threatened to treat them badly unless the high priest came out to them at once. It is said that these were pretexts and things planned beforehand, so that the patriarch might seem to join the rioters unwillingly. So he came down from the upper rooms dressed in his priestly robe, forsooth complaining to those present that he was being forced. The bolder of the rioters, or rather those through whom the riot was formed, took him into their midst and asked him to become their envoy to the emperor, so that the document they had signed under force might be given back to them, since he had made peace with Comnenus. He agreed to fulfil their request; but it was all pretence. For when a short hour had passed they openly proclaimed Comnenus emperor and sovereign, the patriarch himself approving and helping, and making known to Comnenus that he should not delay but hurry, and asking rewards for the proclamation, while rather insolently ordering the man who was reigning till then to come down from the palace. When high priests brought the patriarch's messages to the old Michael, he said: "And what will you give me in place of the empire?" They answered: "The heavenly kingdom." At once, then, throwing off the insignia of the empire, he went out of the palace. Comnenus, honouring Cecaumenus as curopalates, sent the man with some force to take over the palace. The multitude of the city poured out to meet the new emperor, making his entry into the reigning city most splendid. So Michael, having ruled alone one year

blocks: fell from the empire, and having lived not long in the dress of a private man he paid his debt. Comnenus, established in the empire, ascribed his success in it to himself and not to God, and this is plain from his engraving himself on the coinage holding a sword, all but crying out: "This and nothing else won me the empire." He repaid those who had helped him most generously, and hurried to pay each his rewards and get him to go home, so that they might not cause some disturbance or rise against the people while staying in the town. He held the patriarch in great respect, and for his sake honoured his nephews with higher honours and set them over distinguished offices. Still pleasing the patriarch, he also assigned to the church the management of church affairs, the great steward having been appointed by the reigning emperor until then, and also the skeuophylax; he put both under the patriarch's authority, making both foreign to the public treasury. Then he proclaimed his wife Augusta, honoured his brother John as curopalates and named him great domestic.

Since the emperors before him, all who had mounted the empire after that Basil Porphyrogenitus, had not used public and common affairs well, but had squandered some on their own enjoyments and on the building of monasteries, and given some to whomever they happened, or rather to whomever they wished, the imperial treasuries had been emptied and the public treasuries were short of money. Comnenus, then, setting out to correct this, did not set about the correction quietly or little by little, but as he set himself up on the stater with his hand raised, holding the bare sword, so he brought himself to affairs and was ready to cut the swellings at once, not to soften or plaster over what was festering. So from the moment he mounted power and turned his former usurpation into lawful rule, he turned back and overturned the doings of the man before him, and if he had given anything to anyone, he took it away and deprived those who had received it; and he also put down and annulled many acts of those before him, and he did this not only to the common people, but did not spare those of the senate either. Then, going further, he also went against the divine, and cut off many of the gifts dedicated to the houses of contemplation built by them, or rather, subjecting those living as ascetics in them to reckonings and assigning them sufficient expense, he devoted the rest to the public treasury and took it back, and every day he made some such innovation after another. From this he was hated by all, by the common multitude and the senate, and also by the soldiery; for he did not keep from that either, but reduced their means too, and more than the others those who spent their life in monasteries. But nothing drew him from his undertakings, not reason, not fear, not hatred, not blame; so lifted up was his mind and so swollen the soul he had.

blocks: But the patriarch too was no less proud than he. So he wished to command him, and if he ever failed in his requests, he was vexed, threatened and rebuked, and then, as if he himself had given him the empire, threatened that he himself would also take it away from him again. The emperor was not going to bear this mildly; so he took care to act before he suffered anything. So when the patriarch went off to his own monastery, as the festival of the heavenly powers honoured in it was already at hand, so that he might celebrate it more splendidly, the ruler sent a band of soldiers there, for he did not wish to bring the man down from the Wisdom of God the Word, so that no disturbance might arise among the clergy or the people, and exiled him and his nephews who were with him. Then he took thought to subject him to deposition too, and used some of the high priests as helpers for this, and through them made known to the man that he should renounce the pastoral office, so that he might seem to resign it willingly, since if not, it would be taken from him against his will, charges being brought forward against him. When he would not yield to the emperor's will, the ruler took thought about his deposition. But death came first and released the patriarch's care. For shortly after the patriarch passed from things here, and someone brought Comnenus the good news of his death, as freeing him from cares. But he at once repented and cried aloud, and bringing back his body from exile with an honourable procession laid it in his monastery, and restored his nephews again to their former honours.

For the church he set in his place the proedros and protovestiarius Constantine Lichudes, a man who had long been distinguished in the administration of public affairs and had remained beyond reproach, to whom Monomachus had entrusted the care of the Mangana and the documents about its freedom. Wishing to bring these under himself, Comnenus contrived a scheme full of wickedness, the offspring of a wretched mind. For when Lichudes had been voted for and appointed and already ordained priest, he made known to him secretly that some things were being said against him that barred him from the priesthood, and unless these were discussed in a synod, he could not obtain the anointing of the high priesthood. "But if you give me the title deeds of the Mangana," he said, "I shall overlook what is said and allow you to be anointed." Lichudes, seeing that he could no longer return to his former position, and counting it a disgrace to remain as he was, brought and gave what was asked, and so was allowed to have the high priestly rite performed.

blocks: Comnenus, marching against the Hungarians and the Scythians who are called Patzinaks, made peace with the Hungarians when they asked for peace. When he set out against the Scythians, the others submitted and made peace, for they were not all ranked under one leader, but one of them, Selte, growing bold and engaging a part of the Roman force, was defeated, and having lost most of his own men ran off with those who were left. Returning from there, the emperor encamped at Dybistus, it being already near the end of the month of September. When a violent rain poured down and snow fell long before its season, most of the cavalry was destroyed and many soldiers were in danger from the cold, and the rivers, overflowing and becoming seas, suddenly swept away their supplies, so that the necessities failed both the soldiery and its pack animals. Then, when the rain and the snow had stopped for a little, the emperor came out of the imperial tent and stood under a very large oak that stood somewhere there; and some of those in high positions stood round him. When a cry arose in the place, the emperor and those about him moved away from the oak, and it at once was torn up by the roots and fell. The sovereign, returning to the great city and paying God thanks for this deliverance, raised a church within the palace to the protomartyr Thecla; for on the day on which her memory is celebrated he escaped the danger from the oak.
text: Comnenus, marching against the Hungarians and the Scythians who are called Patzinaks, made peace with the Hungarians when they asked for peace. When he set out against the Scythians, the others submitted and made peace, for they were not all ranked under one leader, but one of them, Selte, growing bold and engaging a part of the Roman force, was defeated, and having lost most of his own men ran off with those who were left. Returning from there, the emperor encamped at Dybistus, it being already near the end of the month of September. When a violent rain poured down and snow fell long before its season, most of the cavalry was destroyed and many soldiers were in danger from the cold, and the rivers, overflowing and becoming seas, suddenly swept away their supplies, so that the necessities failed both the soldiery and its pack animals. Then, when the rain and the snow had stopped for a little, the emperor came out of the imperial tent and stood under a very large oak that stood somewhere there; and some of those in high positions stood round him. When a cry arose in the place, the emperor and those about him moved away from the oak, and it at once was torn up by the roots and fell. The sovereign, returning to the great city and paying God thanks for this deliverance, raised a church within the palace to the protomartyr Thecla; for on the day on which her memory is celebrated he escaped the danger from the oak.

blocks: But now it must be told how he laid down the empire, even though those who have written about him do not agree. For Psellus, great in eloquence, says that the emperor, spending his time in hunting and often raising his right hand with a spear against bears and boars, was struck in the side by a cold wind, and from this a shivering came on him and a fever blazed up from deep within, and on the next day he had a stabbing in his side and his breathing was not strong, and from this, it being doubtful whether he would live, or rather having wholly given up on life, he set Constantine Ducas in the empire and changed to the better life. But the Thracesian says that the emperor was hunting near Neapolis, and that a boar fearful to see appeared from somewhere, and Comnenus, giving his horse its head, chased the boar, and it went into the sea and vanished, and meanwhile a flash as of lightning fell on the emperor, and the sovereign, thrown into confusion by its stroke, fell from his horse and lay on the ground, spitting foam from his mouth and sensing nothing of what was about him, and from there he was put in a skiff and brought to the palace, and having been ill a little while and then despaired of, he cut his hair and put on a rough worn cloak instead of the purple, appointing the duke Constantine emperor, and so put in at the monastery of Studius, and lived the rest of his life there, having recovered from the disease. He reigned two years and three months, being active and showing a haughty character, very quick in action, a most able general in war, not versed in learning, but attentive to it and welcoming its nurslings. When he was blamed for having attempted usurpation, he said: "I shrank from serving my fellow slave and not getting my due."

blocks: empire without trouble, as has been said, advanced many of the senate and the common multitude to higher steps of the ranks. And all whom Comnenus had deprived of their own honours, and these too were many, he restored to them again. When a plot was put together against him, he very nearly went to the bottom of the sea. For he was in the palace of the Mangana, and the conspirators reckoned that if a disturbance that had arisen in the city's Market were reported to him, he would at once go off by sea to the great palace. They had arranged beforehand that the imperial trireme and its helmsmen, whom common speech calls protokaraboi, should not be there. So when the emperor heard of the disturbance, he judged he must go off at once to the palace. When the imperial trireme was not found there, he boarded whatever skiff there was; and as he went the imperial ship appeared, and cutting the surge with much rowing and violent rush it was steered by the helmsmen towards the little boat the emperor had boarded. Their intention was to run the trireme over the little boat, so as to sink it and send it to the bottom with the emperor. When those sailing with the ruler saw the trireme bearing down, they shouted out and cried boldly to hold off and turn the helm. The men at the helm, as if thunderstruck by their cries, lost heart, and the whole was divine providence. And so the emperor escaped the danger and learned how and by whom the plot had been prepared, and punished those responsible only by loss of their property.

This emperor boasted of his descent from those of old called by the surname of the Ducas, that is Andronicus, Pantherius and besides them Constantine. But since their family had long ago been destroyed with its whole house, when Constantine attempted usurpation, as has been said before, in the reign of Constantine Porphyrogenitus, the son of the ruler Leo, I mean the philosopher, while he was still under guardians because of his infancy, and no male had been left, his ancestors were descended from some female, as the story goes; so he was not reckoned a pure Ducas, but mixed, having a counterfeit kinship with the Ducas.

The man was pious towards God, fair in character, a lover of justice, but sluggish and dull in mind, delighting in those witnessed to for dignity of life, but extraordinarily fond of money and devising means by which he might have many treasures. So above all he bent his zeal to these two things, to the increase of the public taxes, for which he offered for sale to those who wished the offices that audit the tax collectors, and the offices of the dues whose collection he entrusted on contract, and to the hearing of lawsuits. But in judging he did not pay much attention to exactness, but in places he acted on his own authority and changed the verdicts, making his decisions according to persons. Being stingy and sparing, he resolved within himself not to clash with the nations in battles, but to win them over with gifts and other kindnesses and reconcile them to the rule of the Romans, seeking two things for himself from this, not to spend more on campaigns, and to keep quiet himself and give his time as far as possible to collecting money; so he also neglected the military rolls, or rather struck many, and the braver, off the registers because of their heavy pay; so that it happened that the barbarians grew bold, while the armies of the Romans shrank and were humbled and the dominion of the Romans diminished. For at that time many of the eastern lands were plundered and went on to ruin, and others came under the enemy.

blocks: So matters towards the rising sun were thus in a bad state, and those in the west too suffered badly through want and uselessness of soldiers. For when the nation of the Uzes, who are Scythians preferred above the Patzinaks among the Scythian nations both for superiority of race and for excess of numbers, crossed the Ister with all their families, the governors of the cities by the Ister, who were the magister Nicephorus Botaneiates and the magister Basil Apocapes, tried to bar their crossing, but could not. But the barbarians engaged them, overcame the army with them and carried off both these men captive, and crossing the Danube filled all the country about it. For there were, as the story goes, sixty thousand who could bear arms. Setting out from there they plundered Macedonia and advanced as far as Hellas. This made the emperor despondent, but he shrank from gathering forces and put it off, so as not to give up an obol. He said that the nation could not be overcome. Sending envoys with gifts to their leaders, he tried with these to persuade the barbarians to make peace. When all railed at the emperor openly for not going out against the barbarians out of stinginess, he left the city and encamped at Choerobacchi, bringing no more than a hundred and fifty men with him, as is said, while taking thought for gathering an army. Meanwhile the destruction of the nation was reported to him. For a pestilence fell on it, and when it was very badly hurt by it, the Patzinaks and the neighbouring Bulgars attacked it in its weakness and destroyed it utterly, the leaders barely being able to cross the Ister with a few. The whole stratagem was of the divine power. For the emperor, despairing on every side, fled to God, begging him with tears and contrition of heart and calling on help from there. This was done in the sixth year of this sovereign's reign.

Before this there was a great earthquake on the twenty-third of the month of September, by which churches and houses were thrown down in many places. At that time the pagan temple at Cyzicus too fell, a very beautiful work and worthy of wonder, and the very great and famous church of the holy fathers at Nicaea was shaken down. In the month of May of the fourth indiction a comet was seen following the sun as it went to its setting. At first it was the size of a full moon, then, as if putting out hair, it diminished, and as far as its hair grew, its size lessened. It stretched its rays towards the east, appearing for forty days.

When the patriarch Constantine Lichudes, having directed the church for four years and six months, had passed to another life, John Xiphilinus was brought up to the high priestly throne of Constantine's city, who came from Trebizond, had been educated in learning of every kind and had been counted among the leading men of the senate. But leaving everything willingly, he went to the monasteries on Olympus, cut his hair and took up the monastic life, and having spent a long time there was judged worthy of the patriarchal throne.

The emperor, seized by disease, suffering from it a long time and in distress, and already worn down, and knowing that his end was coming on him inescapably, left the empire to his three sons whom his wife Eudocia had borne him, the two, Michael and Andronicus, while he was still a private man, and Constantine when he was reigning, and she herself had been proclaimed Augusta. So this one was also born in the purple, and he adorned him at once, before the others, with the imperial insignia, and then proclaimed the rest too. He set these over the rule, and left them their mother as empress, nurse and, to say it all, mistress, putting the handling of the empire in her hands, as she seemed to him prudent, skilful at bringing up children and fitted for managing affairs, having first demanded of her a written oath that she would not come to a second marriage. The document confirmed by her was given to the patriarch to be kept; and all the members of the senate also declared in writing that they would never proclaim another emperor except his sons. On this he died, having reigned seven and a half years, and lived sixty or something beyond. When he reigned he honoured his brother as Caesar and had him as adviser and sharer of his secrets. Not versed in learning, he loved it and respected the learned, and said he wished to be known for learning rather than for the empire. He used to say he would treat those who plotted against him badly in no other way than only by using them as men bought, since the laws had taken away their freedom.
