blocks: So according to the dead emperor's dispositions, the empress Eudocia and his sons were successors to the empire, and the empress took over the care of public affairs, ruling over her sons, and presided on the bema with them, she herself in the middle and seating them beside her on either side; so in appointments to office, so in examinations of civil matters, so they gave audience to envoys, so they went out in the customary processions. The barbarians plundering the east did not stop overrunning the lands under the Romans and harming them daily. For the soldiers, as I have already said, had been reduced and harmed through the emperor's stinginess. And if some still held to soldiering, they too were unwilling to go out against the enemy, being deprived of their customary pay. So the barbarians now lay in wait for Mesopotamia, now sacked the region about Melitene, now harmed Cilicia, at another time attacked the Cappadocians, and sometimes those in Coele Syria. These things, reported to the empress, caused alarm, and as many said affairs needed an emperor, she, fearing that the public would set up some emperor by itself, and so she and her sons would fall from the empire, decided herself to bring someone into the rule, so as to keep power for herself and her children and have it remain theirs without being taken away. For they say she did not join Diogenes to herself from licentiousness or overcome by pleasure, but to set him over the rule as a man of action, tried in war and unrivalled in strength, so that the barbarian onrush might be checked somewhat, with him setting his arms against them.

This man was of splendid family and of those famous for brave deeds. His father, having become a kinsman by marriage, through his niece, of the former emperor Romanus of the Argyroi, and being caught at usurpation, threw himself down a precipice. He himself had been honoured with the rank of vestarch. For having been made duke of Sardica by Ducas, and falling in with Patzinaks somewhere there and engaging them, he destroyed many and took no fewer alive, and sending those taken alive and the heads of the slain to the emperor, he was honoured as vestarch, the ruler writing to him: "The rank is not a gift, Diogenes, but the reward of brave deeds." So, staying there, he prepared to usurp, when he learned the sovereign had died. When the man's plan was made known to the empress, she sent and had him seized, and he was brought in bonds to Byzantium, and convicted as a plotter he was condemned, and meanwhile shut within fixed bounds. Then again he was brought as a condemned man before the imperial bema, so that the verdict against him might be ratified. So pity for the man came on those standing by and the soul of all was moved. For he was not only unrivalled in strength, but also fair to see. So the empress too felt for him with the others, and pity for the man came on her too, and whether love too I cannot say, and instead of the verdict fixing his punishment a decree was issued freeing him from punishment. And he, released from the charge, went off to the land of the Cappadocians, for it was his homeland, and the empress sent for him and appointed him magister and stratelates, and already planned to proclaim him emperor, judging the man most noble in her own mind. But she was held back by the oaths and the document kept by the patriarch. And it was her concern how to remove it.

So she devised a wicked and deep plan about this, and shared it with one of the eunuchs about her, and used the servant as a kind of go-between, suggesting what and how much he should say to the patriarch. He came to the high priest and said: "Know, master, that the empress loves your nephew," for he had a nephew Bardas, young, lusty and overcome by sex, and he added: "If you agree to give back to the empress the handwritten oath and persuade her that no danger hangs over her from this, she will at once take your nephew as her husband, and the imperial power will follow for him." When the patriarch, beguiled by this, gave himself up wholly, he was also asked to make trial of the members of the senate. He, calling each of them, said that affairs needed an emperor to take them in hand. For if they were still managed by a woman alone and little children, before long not only the distant parts bordering on the enemy would certainly be lost to the dominion of the Romans, but also those at the very doors. And besides this he made a great attack on the oaths and the document, and spoke ill of the dead emperor, as having taken no thought for the common good, but out of jealousy having demanded unlawful oaths and lawless documents. Having most agreeing with him in this, and persuading those who spoke against it to vote with him, some with gifts and some with promises, he sent the handwritten oath to the empress. She, taking it, carried her plan into effect, and took Diogenes and was joined to him, sharing the deed with the elder of her sons and with the Caesar, who were called to the palace, shared in the wedding and tasted the wedding cups, and Diogenes was proclaimed emperor, the empress Eudocia having ruled with her sons for seven months and some days.

blocks: Romanus Diogenes, having become master of the rule of the Romans, did not turn out according to the hopes of Eudocia, who had made him emperor. For she, having snatched him not only from open danger, when he was condemned and already saw the executioner standing over him, but having also made him worthy of so great a rule, thought she would have him yielding in everything and would herself rule the reigning emperor. But he, being boastful in any case and not to be enslaved, for a little while forced his character and submitted to the Augusta's wishes and acted out submission, then, not bearing the force, quickly went back to his own way, chafed at obedience and wished to bind on the power purely himself. With the east in a bad state, some parts already given up, others coming to it, he proclaimed a campaign, and pitched the imperial tent in the part of the east opposite Byzantium, aiming at these two things: to wall off the barbarians' approach and secure safety for the subjects as far as possible, and to get himself some glory and not yield in everything to the empress, but rule alone himself. So, setting out from the palace in full armour, he crossed to the east, not bringing an army fit for battle, and what he brought was worn down by want of arms, horses and necessities. For it was not easy to restore suddenly an army that had long been neglected, as has been said.

When the soldiers in this state had gathered in the theme of the Anatolics, which is in Phrygia, the enemy, learning that the emperor himself was coming against them, and that he was such as to run risks readily before his subjects, warlike and irresistible in his onset (for the barbarians did not know exactly how matters stood with his army), were cautious and shrank from fighting in close battle. So the Sultan turned back, and dividing the barbarian army into two parts ordered their leaders to set out, the one into the more southern upper Asia, the other towards the more northern. They, coming on and plundering what they met, fell suddenly on Neocaesarea, sacked it and went off from there filled with spoils. This, reported to the emperor, instilled despondency, and taking the more lightly equipped of the army he went off through difficult roads and mountains, hurrying to get ahead of the enemy. When he came on them unexpectedly, he threw them all into terror, and they at once looked to flight, leaving there both the plunder and the baggage. There was not much destruction of the barbarians, since the emperor's men were worn out from the march and not able to pursue far. But the captives taken and whatever else made up the plunder were all freed.

From there he took the road leading to Syria, and sent a phalanx to Melitene, while he himself set out for Aleppo and drove off much plunder of men and other animals. And from there he came to Hierapolis in Syria. Undertaking to besiege it, he took over the city by agreement. Then, when the barbarians attacked a part of the Roman army and defeated it, none of the others was eager to come to the help of the defeated. The emperor, being inside the captured city and learning what had happened, rushed out very quickly with those about him to help the defeated. The ruler of Aleppo, learning of the defeat of the Romans, joined the other barbarians himself too with his whole force, expecting to carry off the emperor captive at once. And they surrounded the Roman camp. But the emperor, bringing an undeclared battle on them, for he went out of the camp and led the army out with him without any sound of trumpets or any other clear signal, routed the enemy and forced them to look to flight. If, then, the Roman army had pursued far, it would have won a very great and famous victory. For the Arabs' horses are swift in the first rush and the fleetest of all, but they do not extend their running far, but tire very quickly. But being called back and giving up the pursuit, they saved the enemy and deprived themselves of great success and glory. Yet to the emperor it seemed sufficient good fortune that the Romans had dared at all to go against the enemy and had laid aside much of their former cowardice. The citadel of Hierapolis was settled at the emperor's order. Attacking other towns, passing some by as impregnable and seizing others, he came to the city of Cilicia called Alexandria. And as he went from there it was announced that Amorium had been plundered and many killed. The emperor was vexed at this, but unable to help those who had suffered, he arranged matters for his own army so that they might pass the winter season without lacking necessities, and himself went back to the queen of cities, rather boastful, as if he had achieved much, not only towards the others but towards the empress herself. She, perceiving that her hopes had turned the opposite way for her, was vexed and had her heart swelling, not bearing his rebukes.
text: Romanus Diogenes, having become master of the rule of the Romans, did not turn out according to the hopes of Eudocia, who had made him emperor. For she, having snatched him not only from open danger, when he was condemned and already saw the executioner standing over him, but having also made him worthy of so great a rule, thought she would have him yielding in everything and would herself rule the reigning emperor. But he, being boastful in any case and not to be enslaved, for a little while forced his character and submitted to the Augusta's wishes and acted out submission, then, not bearing the force, quickly went back to his own way, chafed at obedience and wished to bind on the power purely himself. With the east in a bad state, some parts already given up, others coming to it, he proclaimed a campaign, and pitched the imperial tent in the part of the east opposite Byzantium, aiming at these two things: to wall off the barbarians' approach and secure safety for the subjects as far as possible, and to get himself some glory and not yield in everything to the empress, but rule alone himself. So, setting out from the palace in full armour, he crossed to the east, not bringing an army fit for battle, and what he brought was worn down by want of arms, horses and necessities. For it was not easy to restore suddenly an army that had long been neglected, as has been said. When the soldiers in this state had gathered in the theme of the Anatolics, which is in Phrygia, the enemy, learning that the emperor himself was coming against them, and that he was such as to run risks readily before his subjects, warlike and irresistible in his onset (for the barbarians did not know exactly how matters stood with his army), were cautious and shrank from fighting in close battle. They, coming on and plundering what they met, fell suddenly on Neocaesarea, sacked it and went off from there filled with spoils. This, reported to the emperor, instilled despondency, and taking the more lightly equipped of the army he went off through difficult roads and mountains, hurrying to get ahead of the enemy. blocks: As soon as spring began to shine, the emperor again thought of another campaign. So leaving Byzantium and coming to Caesarea, he learned that a great multitude of Turks was overrunning the east, and partly sending a part of the army against them, partly engaging them himself, he routed the enemy, put all those taken alive to the sword, and set his course towards the Euphrates. Appointing Philaretus general, who was of the family of the Brachamii, a man who seemed sufficiently fitted for military experience, but whose life was not good, but quite the opposite of his name, he handed him half the army, while he himself turned towards the north. The enemy, appearing to those with Philaretus, threw them into terror, and when they left the places they had been appointed to guard and turned to flight, the enemy followed and took all their baggage. When this came to the emperor's knowledge it made him gloomy, and the enemy, setting their course against Cappadocia, sacked it and went for Iconium, which had a great multitude of people and flourished in all things thought good.

The emperor, coming to Sebasteia and learning of the Turks' drive against Iconium, himself too pressed his march after them. Learning that they had already sacked Iconium and, wary of his catching them, had set out, he sent a part of the Roman forces to Chatatures, the duke of great Antioch, and ordered him to go to Mopsuestia and engage the Turks as they passed there. But the enemy, coming into the plain of Tarsus, fell in with the Armenians and lost almost all their plunder. And hearing of the Romans lying in wait at Mopsuestia, they went off through the night and escaped. This became a cause of grief to the emperor, and giving up he set out for Byzantium; for autumn too had already come. At that time too the great church of Blachernae was burned, in the year six thousand five hundred and seventy-eight.

When spring came, he honoured the protoproedros Manuel Comnenus, the nephew of the late emperor Isaac, as curopalates and set him over the armies. He was young, but commanded like old men, and falling in with an army of barbarians engaged it and won. This is said to have moved Diogenes to envy, and for this he divided off no small part of the army with him and sent it against Syria. Then, when Comnenus with those left was at Sebasteia, a multitude of Turks appeared, and he attacked them. They pretended flight, and Comnenus's men pursued the fleeing. But by a signal the barbarians turned about and attacked the Romans as they were scattered, killed many, took no fewer, and the commander Manuel himself, and plundered the camp. The news of this troubled the sovereign, and also a rumour that arose that the city of Chonae and the famous sanctuary of the archangel there had been seized by the barbarians. So the emperor was wholly bent on going at once against the enemy and helping those in danger, but some advised him to hold back for the time. Meanwhile Manuel Comnenus came, together with the Turk who had captured him, who came over to the emperor. For the Sultan, having for some reason come to hate the man, had sent an army against him to seize him. So he, afraid, chose to flee to the emperor, who at once honoured him as proedros. He was very short in stature and most ugly in form.

blocks: When spring was shining, he boarded the imperial trireme; and as he was just crossing, a dove, not quite black in colour but inclining to the darker, flew round his trireme and did not stop fluttering about him until he caught it with his hands. He sent it to the empress, but the dove was judged no good sign either for the one who caught it or for the one to whom it was sent. Moreover, when the pole that stands in the middle and supports the imperial tent broke of itself, the tent fell down; and this too was thought an ill-omened sign. Yet nothing checked the emperor's eagerness, but he went on as far as the theme of the Anatolics, holding to stinginess beyond his custom. When he was lodging somewhere in some rooms, fire coming from somewhere burned the rooms themselves, and half burned some of the imperial horses, bridles and carriages; and this too seemed a bad omen. Moving from there, crossing the Halys and passing Caesarea, he pitched his camp at the place called Cold Spring, where he treated some of the Nemitzoi rather harshly for wrongdoings. When their unit revolted, he at once appeared himself on horseback, bringing the soldiery, and struck the rebels with terror and made them his allies again. Then he went off to Theodosiopolis, and there, ordering each man to bring food for two months, as he was going to march through uninhabited country, he divided the army and gave a part to Ruselius, who was a most warlike Latin, and sent him against Chliat. Another part he assigned to another, ordering him to sack Manzikiert; while the emperor himself was left with the rest, who were not fit for battle.

Manzikiert was handed over to the emperor by agreement, the Turks having lost heart, asked for assurance and left it. But the enemy suddenly attacked soldiers who had gone out to gather necessities. Learning this, the emperor sent the magister Nicephorus Bryennius against them with a company, who attacked the Turks and, seeing the force with him in difficulties, sent asking for help. The emperor, not knowing the strength of the enemy, convicted Bryennius of cowardice and was harsh towards the man. It happened that the priest was then reading the Gospel and saying: "If they have persecuted me, they will also persecute you." Yet he sent the magister Nicephorus Basilacius too with a part of the soldiers, and when these had been added to Bryennius the contest was evenly balanced for a while. Then, when Basilacius rushed in the front ranks against the enemy with those about him, the enemy turned their backs, and he pursued, Bryennius with those about him not pursuing. When he came near the enemy's camp, his horse was struck and he got off it, and being not easy to move because of the weight of his arms he was surrounded by the enemy, and being taken alive was brought to the Sultan; he neither approached him in too slavish a way, nor did the Sultan treat him as a captive, but often calling the man he questioned him about the emperor and showed him his own forces. And he praised and admired the Sultan's forces, but said it would not be to his advantage to draw up against the emperor.

The emperor went out of the camp with the rest to see what was happening, and standing on hills until evening he went back. And the Turks at once surrounded the camp, and riding round it they shot arrows and filled the army's ears with inarticulate cries and howls. So that night passed. At dawn a company of Uzes deserted to the enemy. And this made the remaining multitude of Uzes suspect too.

blocks: The emperor sent very quickly to Chliat and called back the armies there. When they did not come, for Tarchaneiotes, who was one of the commanders there, learning of the Sultan's arrival, persuaded Ruselius too, and setting out with the forces under them they went in flight to the Roman borders, Diogenes decided to fight it out with those with him on the morrow, and at dawn was getting ready for battle. Meanwhile envoys came from the Sultan to discuss peace. The emperor received the envoys not very kindly, yet he gave them a hearing and urged them to go off to their master and report: "If he wishes to discuss terms, let him leave the place where he is encamped and move his tents somewhere far off, so that I may pitch my camp with the Roman army where the barbarians' camp now is." Having said this to the envoys rather boastfully, he ordered them to come back quickly. So they reported the emperor's words to the Sultan, and he took counsel with those about him about the terms of peace. But the emperor, being proud and persuaded by some of his intimates who said the Sultan had lost heart, as not bringing a force fit for battle, and for this was seeking peace, so that by putting off the battle he might bring up another force too, neither waited for the envoys' return nor considered anything else, but ordered the trumpeters to sound the war call.

The suddenness alarmed the barbarians, but even so they stood for battle, and when the Romans came at them they did not go against them, but fell back, neither turning their backs nor yet fighting. When the day came to late afternoon, the emperor, knowing that there was no guard worth mention about the camp, and fearing that if the enemy came at it it would be plundered, decided to break off the battle and return to the camp. So he turned the imperial standard and himself went back, and signalled the army to do the same. Those near him did what was ordered without confusion. But those who held their ranks somewhere far off took the emperor's return for flight, Andronicus, the son of the Caesar, suggesting the story to the phalanxes. For the Caesar and his sons were always lying in wait for the emperor and plotting against him unseen. So Andronicus at once set out with those about him, for he commanded no small part of the soldiers, and came back to the camp at full rein. This turned the rest too to flight, and the emperor, seeing them coming back in such disorder, stood still and ordered those going off to stand too. But all had stopped their ears and did not give up their flight. When the enemy knew the unexpected flight to be a misfortune of the Romans and a divine wrath, they at once attacked the emperor. He received the battle with those about him, and for a time they held out strongly, then, as some fell and others were taken, the emperor was hemmed in by the barbarians. But even so he did not give in. Having struck and killed many, he too was struck in the hand, and so, worn out and no longer able to defend himself against those attacking nor to flee, since his horse had already fallen from the arrows, the emperor of the Romans was taken and led off captive by the barbarians.

The emperor's capture, reported to the Sultan, caused him joy, as was natural, but did not lift him up so far as to be arrogant; he was named Axan, and many stories are sung of his justice and moderation. So he even disbelieved the emperor's capture because of the unmixed good fortune. And seeing him he did not accept the matter as certain until the envoys he had sent recognised him, and Basilaces, who was held there, seeing him, threw himself at his feet lamenting. Then he leapt up from his throne as if inspired, and when he had been laid on the ground, as is the custom, he trod on him, raised him up and embraced him, and said: "Do not grieve, emperor; for such are human things; I shall treat you not as a captive but as an emperor." And at once he assigned him a tent and imperial service, shared his table, making him sit on the throne beside him, and released for him as many of the captives as he asked, and so, having talked and lived with the man for some days and honoured him exceedingly, and then having made terms for perpetual peace and given a promise of marriage alliance for their children, he let Diogenes go with such a bodyguard and honour as no one would have hoped. He went off to Theodosiopolis dressed in barbarian fashion, for the Sultan had given him his own robes, and waiting there his hand was treated and he changed his dress to the more Roman. From there he went on returning, bringing envoys of the Sultan with him. So he was returning thus.

When his capture was reported to the palace, those there fell into disagreement. For some gave the power again to the empress, others voted everything to the elder of her sons, and others assigned a joint rule to the mother and the son.

blocks: Meanwhile it was announced that Diogenes had been released from captivity; and a letter in his own hand was also brought telling what had happened to him. This raised a greater uproar, and perplexity seized all as to what they ought to do. So the Caesar John and his sons, always, as has been said, bearing a grudge against Diogenes, seized the moment, and taking with them some of the senate, as many as were of one mind with them, whose leader was the hypertimos Psellus, who was himself ill disposed to Diogenes, they confined the empress Eudocia in the monastery she had built on the strait in the Propontis, and proclaimed Michael sovereign. Then imperial letters were sent everywhere ordering that Diogenes, on his return, should neither be received nor granted imperial honour. The proposer of this plan was the hypertimos Psellus, as he himself says in his writing about it.

Learning this, Diogenes seized Dokeia, which is a fort, and encamped by it. And the Caesar sent the younger of his sons, the proedros Constantine, against Diogenes with a force. Diogenes came to Cappadocia. When Crispinus, who was a Frank, joined Constantine with his fellow tribesmen, Diogenes sent Theodore Alyattes against them. He engaged them and was defeated, and being taken had his eyes cut out. This grieved Diogenes greatly. When he was at Tyropoion, which is a very strong fort, the duke of Antioch came to him; he was Chatatures, of Armenian descent, bringing many soldiers. Taking Diogenes and leading him off to Cilicia, he waited for help from the Sultan, and himself gathered an army. So the elder of the Caesar's sons, the proedros Andronicus, was sent against them again, and coming into Cilicia clashed with Chatatures, and Chatatures was killed, and those about him fled together to Adana, where Diogenes was staying. Andronicus sat down round the city and besieged it. Then Diogenes gave himself up on terms; the terms were that he should lay down the empire and live as a private man with his hair cut. For on these terms high priests too were sent by the reigning emperor, giving him sworn assurance that he would suffer nothing unpleasant. Trusting in this, Diogenes came out in black and gave himself into Andronicus's hands. He took him and went back, and coming to Cotyaeum waited in it until he should be ordered what to do, Diogenes being ill from drinking a deadly poison treacherously mixed for him. So there an imperial verdict was sent, ordering that the man who had done no wrong be deprived of sight. And at once his eyes were dug out, the high priests too being present and taking hard the calamity to the man, but being granted no attention. His eyes cut out most cruelly and not receiving even the care he needed, his head swelled, his wounds boiled up with worms, and the air about him was filled with stench from the rotting. In this bad state he was taken off to the island called Prote, on which he had raised a monastery on the higher part of the island. Living there a little while, he laid down his dust on it, buried most splendidly by the empress Eudocia, having reigned three years and eight months. It is said that all that was done to this man was by the Caesar's arrangements, the sovereign Michael knowing nothing. For the emperor was very slack and easygoing in character and unskilful at handling even ordinary affairs, let alone the management of an empire. And so his uncle and Caesar, making a sport of his simplicity, contrived all that was done to Diogenes, bearing a grudge against the man.

text: Meanwhile it was announced that Diogenes had been released from captivity; and a letter in his own hand was also brought telling what had happened to him. This raised a greater uproar, and perplexity seized all as to what they ought to do. So the Caesar John and his sons, always, as has been said, bearing a grudge against Diogenes, seized the moment, and taking with them some of the senate, as many as were of one mind with them, whose leader was the hypertimos Psellus, who was himself ill disposed to Diogenes, they confined the empress Eudocia in the monastery she had built on the strait in the Propontis, and proclaimed Michael sovereign. Then imperial letters were sent everywhere ordering that Diogenes, on his return, should neither be received nor granted imperial honour. The proposer of this plan was the hypertimos Psellus, as he himself says in his writing about it. Learning this, Diogenes seized Dokeia, which is a fort, and encamped by it. And the Caesar sent the younger of his sons, the proedros Constantine, against Diogenes with a force. Diogenes came to Cappadocia. When Crispinus, who was a Frank, joined Constantine with his fellow tribesmen, Diogenes sent Theodore Alyattes against them. He engaged them and was defeated, and being taken had his eyes cut out. This grieved Diogenes greatly. When he was at Tyropoion, which is a very strong fort, the duke of Antioch came to him; he was Chatatures, of Armenian descent, bringing many soldiers. Taking Diogenes and leading him off to Cilicia, he waited for help from the Sultan, and himself gathered an army. So the elder of the Caesar's sons, the proedros Andronicus, was sent against them again, and coming into Cilicia clashed with Chatatures, and Chatatures was killed, and those about him fled together to Adana, where Diogenes was staying. Andronicus sat down round the city and besieged it. Then Diogenes gave himself up on terms; the terms were that he should lay down the empire and live as a private man with his hair cut. For on these terms high priests too were sent by the reigning emperor, giving him sworn assurance that he would suffer nothing unpleasant. Trusting in this, Diogenes came out in black and gave himself into Andronicus's hands. He took him and went back, and coming to Cotyaeum waited in it until he should be ordered what to do, Diogenes being ill from drinking a deadly poison treacherously mixed for him. So there an imperial verdict was sent, ordering that the man who had done no wrong be deprived of sight. And at once his eyes were dug out, the high priests too being present and taking hard the calamity to the man, but being granted no attention. His eyes cut out most cruelly and not receiving even the care he needed, his head swelled, his wounds boiled up with worms, and the air about him was filled with stench from the rotting. In this bad state he was taken off to the island called Prote, on which he had raised a monastery on the higher part of the island. Living there a little while, he laid down his dust on it, buried most splendidly by the empress Eudocia, having reigned three years and eight months. It is said that all that was done to this man was by the Caesar's arrangements, the sovereign Michael knowing nothing. For the emperor was very slack and easygoing in character and unskilful at handling even ordinary affairs, let alone the management of an empire. And so his uncle and Caesar, making a sport of his simplicity, contrived all that was done to Diogenes, bearing a grudge against the man. The emperor Michael, being unfitted for the

blocks: management of the empire, set over affairs John, metropolitan of Side, a eunuch but an active one. Then he sent for another eunuch, Nicephorus, who, taken into the palace young by Monomachus, had been named by the pet name Nicephoritzes because of his youth and had kept this as a kind of surname, and who was administering the judgements of Hellas and the Peloponnese. For this man had also served before the emperor's father, the emperor Constantine Ducas. He was skilful at handling affairs and versed in learning, but had a reserved character full of cleverness. So he handed him the reins of the empire, naming him logothete. From this the bishop of Side was elbowed aside, and the Caesar became suspect, and the whole management of the empire came under the logothete, and the emperor was led by him like a slave. There was nothing that was not done through the logothete, and many were deprived of their property, various pretexts being brought against various people, and there was crushing and misery of men, and no one anywhere paid attention to it. For the emperor spent his time on childish pursuits, the consul of the philosophers and hypertimos Michael Psellus, in appearance, introducing him to learning and teaching him now the art of grammar, metres and dialects, now to speak like rhetors, now accustoming him to histories, and at other times getting him to listen to philosophical theorems. But he had no aptitude for anything. So the sovereign of the Romans, wasting away on these things, put the steering of public affairs under another, and this one man, and what seemed good to the logothete was law.

So the affairs of the state were thus in a bad way, and those in the east were worse than before. For the Sultan, learning what had happened to Diogenes, and that the man whom he had taken captive, honoured and let go to return to his own empire had been handed over by his fellow countrymen harshly to a most pitiable death, and that the terms of peace with him had remained ineffective, was greatly grieved, and stirred his own forces to go against the Roman lands; so they no longer attacked the lands as plunderers, but as about to hold and master them, since there was no one to keep them off. And they did this; and the emperor, gathering a force, appointed Isaac Comnenus its commander, yoking with him the Latin Ruselius, the leader of four hundred men of his race. When the army was near Iconium, for some reason Ruselius revolted, and taking his fellow tribesmen was on his own, and partly engaged the Turks and partly ravaged the Roman lands. Isaac Comnenus, attacking the Turks with the rest of the army, was defeated, and many fell, others were taken alive, the commander himself too, and the camp was plundered. So Comnenus bought his freedom for much money.

The emperor set his uncle the Caesar over the war as commander. Learning this, Ruselius, catching the Caesar before he crossed the Sangarius, encamped against him, and the Caesar promised him an amnesty for his offence if he came over to the emperor. But he, snorting like a barbarian, had no thought of yielding. So battle broke out, and the Caesar's men were defeated and he himself was taken with many others, Botaneiates, who was general with the Caesar, fleeing with a few. Ruselius made for Byzantium, bringing the Caesar in bonds and Basil Maleses, who had just been released from the captivity he had shared with Diogenes, and Chrysopolis held the rebel, and at once he set fire to the houses there. The emperor promised him the rank of curopalates if he laid down his arms, and sent out his wife and children to him; but the barbarian could not be tamed. So the emperor sent for Turks for pay against Ruselius; and he, not being a match for the war, released the Caesar from his bonds and proclaimed him with imperial acclamations, thinking many would join him. But suddenly Turks appeared, and Ruselius went against them heedlessly with barbarian boldness, and the Franks threw down many of the Turks and turned the others to flight and pursued without restraint. Most were left behind somewhere, their horses not being strong enough for the long pursuit. But Ruselius with the Caesar rode on with a few. When they had drawn far ahead of their own men, another multitude of Turks appeared, numbering very many thousands; and when those who appeared attacked them, they clashed with them against their will. Surrounded by the multitude and losing their horses, the Caesar and Ruselius were taken. But Ruselius's wife got ahead and bought him, and the emperor ransomed the Caesar. As he was being brought to the emperor, and was in the Propontis, he cut his hair and changed his dress, putting on a monk's rag; for he was wary of suffering something from his nephew because of the proclamation.

Ruselius, released from captivity, as has been said, took his wife with the remaining Franks and came to the theme of the Armeniacs, in which he had lived before too. So the emperor sent against him the proedros Alexius Comnenus, who was young, but an intelligent and active man. He, coming to Amaseia, made known secretly to the Turks that if they seized Ruselius and handed him over to him, he would fill them with much money. So they, pretending friendship towards Ruselius, seized the man, and exchanged him for much money, and he was at once brought in bonds by Alexius to Byzantium, and having been severely beaten was shut in bonds in a tower. When there was a want of grain in the days of this emperor, so that not a whole medimnus was sold for a coin, but a medimnus less a pinakion, the common misfortune became a surname for the emperor, so that this ruler is called so to this day; for no one will know him otherwise unless he says Parapinaces.

blocks: In the third year of his reign the nation of the Croats, whom some also call Serbs, was stirred, having undertaken to seize the country of the Bulgars. Indeed it seized some of it, but after many battles and the destruction of many on both sides, it fell from what it had seized, and being overcome was thrust out of the Roman borders and forced to stay in its own haunts. A slave of this sovereign's father, Nestor by name, vestarch in rank, who had been appointed duke of the lands by the Ister, took up arms against the emperor. For having made an alliance with a leader of the Patzinaks, who was called Tatus, they came to the reigning city and encamped before it. When the emperor told him to lay down his arms, he said he was ready to do this if the logothete Nicephorus were handed over to him, or else put out of the way, as a common calamity and a public evil. When the emperor did not do this, he withdrew from the city, plundered the lands of the Thracians and Macedonians and the parts of Bulgaria lying next to them, and moved off to the land of the Patzinaks.

When a son was born to him by Maria of the Alans, whom he crowned empress, he named him Constantine after his father and crowned him as emperor, and sending to Robert, the ruler of Longobardia, betrothed his daughter to his son, whom, when she was brought, he renamed Helena. At that time a child was born in Byzantium having one eye in the forehead and goat's legs. When the barbarians were plundering the east and putting to the sword those they met, the people of Asia fled and came to Constantine's city. As no one took thought for the common good, for the emperor was busy with learning and was being taught by Psellus to compose iambics, want of grain pressed those in the city. To lament the suffering more vividly, the evil was plain famine, and pestilence followed it, and from this deaths happened, frequent and one on another, so that the living could not give the dying to burial. For they were so many that often many were carried out on one bier, and many lay unburied in the streets. From this everything was filled with dejection, both for this and because the subjects were pressed by unjust exactions.

With affairs in this state, the leading men among the eastern commanders came together and were in labour with a revolt, and chose the curopalates Nicephorus Botaneiates as emperor and proclaimed him sovereign. This filled the emperor with confusion and fear. For it was sung that one day the letter N would prevail over the letter M. Botaneiates was of the well born, thought to draw his family line from Phocas. So the emperor sent heralds to the Turks, promising them rich gifts if they seized the rebels and handed them over to him. So Botaneiates, having put on himself the dress and name of emperor in the east, as has been said, made for Byzantium.

From the west, in turn, the surge of another revolt swelled. For the proedros Nicephorus Bryennius, who was duke of Dyrrachium, when he learned he had been deprived of his command, revolted himself too, put on the insignia of the empire, and escorted by the units present there went off to Abrupolis, from which he came, and joining his brother John there and persuading a multitude of soldiers from there, both foreign and Macedonian, to help him, began the usurpation. Theodorocanus, engaging some of Bryennius's men, was defeated and captured. The people of Rhaedestus too flowed over to Bryennius, and also those living in Panium. So Bryennius held strongly to the revolt, honouring his brother as curopalates and sending him with a force to Byzantium, as if to take it over at once. For he was buoyed up by hopes that the members of the senate would receive him, as the saying goes, with open hands, because of their hatred for the logothete Nicephorus and the emperor's simplicity; but affairs did not turn out for him according to his aim. For those sent attacked the wall of Blachernae and skirmished, but achieved nothing. So crossing by the bridge to the mainland opposite the city they gave the buildings there to the fire, and from there went back to Athyras. The emperor, thus beset on every side, released Ruselius from his bonds, and soothing the man with words and money persuaded him to attack Bryennius's brother together with the proedros Alexius Comnenus, who commanded the force with the emperor at Byzantium. Learning this, Bryennius's brother escaped first by flight. But of the Macedonians many were caught, and some fell and others were taken.

blocks: Meanwhile a multitude of Patzinaks too came against Adrianople, and encamping about it plundered the country round it; Bryennius, welcoming them with money, persuaded them to move away from the city. When his brother went off to Cyzicus and tried to win over those there, Ruselius met him and routed him by force. Just then, when the patriarch John Xiphilinus had moved to the eternal mansions, having shepherded the church for eleven years and seven months, the monk Cosmas was appointed patriarch, not versed in learning, but adorned with every virtue, and for this exceedingly honoured by the emperor too.

Botaneiates, getting units for himself from various races, also made the Turks his allies, whose leader was Cutlumus, one of the distinguished men among the Persians, who, being related to the Sultan by birth, was disputing the rule with him, and they were already getting ready to go to war. This, reported to the caliph, who is exceedingly honoured among them as thought to be descended from the family of Muchumet, threw him into anguish lest a civil war should arise among them. At once, then, though it is not the custom for the caliph to leave his own dwelling or to appear in public, he scorned the custom, went out and went off to those disputing the rule, and persuaded them to keep from battle, and the Sultan to have his own rule undiminished, but to help his kinsman in every way to come into possession of Roman land and rule it. When agreements had been made between them on these terms, Cutlumus came into the land under the Romans, and then campaigned with Botaneiates. So Botaneiates, having a considerable army with him, hurried to take Nicaea. For this city had already been betrayed to him by those appointed to guard it, and they came over to him of their own will, and many came to him every day from the great city too. So affairs went with the stream for Botaneiates.

In the first of cities the common people and the eminent among the officials, and also the chosen of those enrolled in the church, came together in great numbers, and on the day of the festival of the Annunciation proclaimed Botaneiates sovereign, the leaders of this gathering being the patriarch of Antioch, called Aemilianus, and the metropolitan of Iconium. So the leading men of the state, divided by factions and locking shields in phalanxes, attacked the parts of the palace facing the rising sun, and mastering them set their own soldiers to guard them. The emperor, who had fled with the empress Maria and his son to the palace at Blachernae, they put down from the empire, clothed in a monk's rag and led off to the monastery of Studius, having enjoyed the empire for six years and as many months. This happened on the Saturday on which the church has received the custom of celebrating the miracle of our Lord and Saviour in raising Lazarus from the dead. Since Michael had fallen from the empire in this way, Botaneiates found the sole rule without trouble, and went to the queen of cities. The logothete Nicephorus slipped out of the city and went over to Ruselius, who was encamped at Heraclea. Those in the city who had dragged Michael down, having kept the palace widowed of an emperor for three days, wrote to Botaneiates to hurry and come. He sent ahead one of his own slaves, I mean Borilas, and having seized the palace through him, he himself arrived not long after.

blocks: When Botaneiates was in the palace, he was crowned with the imperial headband by the patriarch on Holy Tuesday, and he first gave everyone the bounty of cancelling the debts of all alike to the public treasury without limit, and magnificently making a cancellation of them by decree. To Bryennius, who still held to the usurpation in the west, he sent men to announce that he gave him the rank of Caesar, if he gave up the usurpation, and would confirm for those who had helped him the honours with which he had honoured them. But he longed greatly for the empire and would not yield. So again another embassy, and after it a third. But he was arrogant, and did not even receive the envoys according to the law of envoys, but sent them away dishonoured. So when the emperor knew he could achieve nothing peacefully, he turned unwillingly to battle, and honouring Alexius Comnenus as nobilissimus, appointing him great domestic and setting him over the Roman forces, he sent him against Bryennius; he engaged him at a place called Calabrye, because the place is watered by many good springs of water, easily overcame his army, and as some fell and others fled, he took the usurper left alone, deprived the wretch of sight and brought him blind into the reigning city. And Bryennius's rising came to this end.

The Varangians too rose against the emperor, planning to kill him. But when another Roman band drew up against them, they turned to supplication and obtained pardon. When this emperor's wife died, many virgins were proposed, and before the others Zoe, the daughter of the emperor Ducas. But he wished to marry either the empress Eudocia or Maria of the Alans, who had been married to the emperor before him. So he sent and called Eudocia. She, as the story goes, did not refuse, but the emperor was stopped from this by some monks. And he married the empress Maria, doing no less a lawless thing than if he had married Eudocia; for what was dared was shameless adultery. So the man who performed the sacred service for them fell from the priesthood. Michael, who had reigned before, having had his hair cut, as has been said, was ordained metropolitan of Ephesus by a synodal vote, and having gone there once came back, and made his dwelling in the monastery of Manuel. After Botaneiates had fallen from the empire, this Michael, when dying, after the empress Maria, who had already become a nun herself, had begged him much, granted her pardon and prayed for forgiveness for her from God.

The protoproedros Nicephorus Basilacius, having become Bryennius's successor at Dyrrachium, himself too conceived a desire for the empire, and gathering an army went up with it to Thessalonica. There, learning that Botaneiates was reigning, he wrote to him like a slave, but secretly contrived the revolt and sent for Patzinaks as allies. Learning this, Botaneiates sent him a gold-sealed letter, both securing him freedom from care for what he had dared and awarding him the honour of nobilissimus; but he could not be softened. So Alexius Comnenus, honoured as sebastos, was sent against him too, and coming to Thessalonica and engaging Basilacius he routed his men, and when he fled into the citadel of Thessalonica took him alive by siege, and cut out the man's eyes by imperial order. Others too raised their hands against this emperor, but taught moderation by what had happened to Bryennius and Basilacius they laid down their arms.

When the Turks were overrunning the east, the emperor sent against them with an army fit for battle Constantine, the son of the former emperor Constantine Ducas, setting him up as commander of the army against the Turks. He, crossing to the place called Chrysopolis, at once made a rising, and was proclaimed emperor by the military multitude there. But the emperor won over some of the soldiers with gifts, made others his own with honours of rank, and dealt with others in other ways, and Constantine, seized by them, was handed over to the emperor. So the young man was tonsured and confined on an island. The story goes that the man was also anointed priest. When Aemilianus, the patriarch of Antioch, departed life, another, Nicephorus called the Black, was appointed.

This emperor, partly through deep old age and partly through natural slackness, did not much take hold of the management of affairs, but he too, taking the metropolitan of Side, entrusted him with the care of public affairs. This emperor also had two slaves, of whom one was named Borilus and the other Germanus; these led and carried everything as they wished, and the ruler himself, their master, through whom it happened that he was hated by those in office, since the slaves behaved towards them rather boastfully and boldly. As has already been said, the logothete Nicephorus, having gone over to Ruselius, had been kept in bonds by him. But Ruselius, dying suddenly, gave rise to the suspicion that he had been killed by the logothete with poison. So, handed over to Botaneiates by Ruselius's kin, he was confined on one of the islands lying before the queen of cities. Those about the emperor, fearing that if he came into the emperor's presence he would be taken up and would elbow everyone aside, suggested to Botaneiates that the logothete had untold money, and that this ought to be brought into the imperial treasury. So Straboromanus, who was then great hetaireiarch, was sent to ask the man where his money was hidden. Those about the emperor, who the narrative has already related feared the logothete's presence, persuaded Straboromanus to kill the man by any means. He, coming to the island where he was confined, examined the man so violently that he died under the very tortures, and this though he promised to give everything in written lists if he escaped the examination. So he perished thus.
text: When Botaneiates was in the palace, he was crowned with the imperial headband by the patriarch on Holy Tuesday, and he first gave everyone the bounty of cancelling the debts of all alike to the public treasury without limit, and magnificently making a cancellation of them by decree. To Bryennius, who still held to the usurpation in the west, he sent men to announce that he gave him the rank of Caesar, if he gave up the usurpation, and would confirm for those who had helped him the honours with which he had honoured them. But he longed greatly for the empire and would not yield. So again another embassy, and after it a third. But he was arrogant, and did not even receive the envoys according to the law of envoys, but sent them away dishonoured. So when the emperor knew he could achieve nothing peacefully, he turned unwillingly to battle, and honouring Alexius Comnenus as nobilissimus, appointing him great domestic and setting him over the Roman forces, he sent him against Bryennius; he engaged him at a place called Calabrye, because the place is watered by many good springs of water, easily overcame his army, and as some fell and others fled, he took the usurper left alone, deprived the wretch of sight and brought him blind into the reigning city. And Bryennius's rising came to this end. The Varangians too rose against the emperor, planning to kill him. But when another Roman band drew up against them, they turned to supplication and obtained pardon. When this emperor's wife died, many virgins were proposed, and before the others Zoe, the daughter of the emperor Ducas. But he wished to marry either the empress Eudocia or Maria of the Alans, who had been married to the emperor before him. So he sent and called Eudocia. She, as the story goes, did not refuse, but the emperor was stopped from this by some monks. And he married the empress Maria, doing no less a lawless thing than if he had married Eudocia; for what was dared was shameless adultery. So the man who performed the sacred service for them fell from the priesthood. Michael, who had reigned before, having had his hair cut, as has been said, was ordained metropolitan of Ephesus by a synodal vote, and having gone there once came back, and made his dwelling in the monastery of Manuel. After Botaneiates had fallen from the empire, this Michael, when dying, after the empress Maria, who had already become a nun herself, had begged him much, granted her pardon and prayed for forgiveness for her from God. blocks: The Comneni, Isaac and Alexius, were exceedingly honoured and loved by the emperor, and he named them successors to the empire. So they were violently envied by those about Botaneiates, and above all by his two slaves mentioned, who slandered the men to him as planning usurpation, and undermined and shook the emperor's disposition towards them. Learning this, and afraid of suffering something, and, as the story goes, having long nursed a desire for the empire within themselves, they shared the plan with others they trusted, left the city, and seizing Hadrian's city drew almost the whole soldiery to themselves. And Alexius was proclaimed emperor, preferred to his elder brother, both because the soldiers were more attached to him as the better general, and because they were drawn over by the zeal and promises of those about him. So Alexius, proclaimed thus, Isaac not being much vexed at the proclamation, came to the capital and made ready for a siege.

Botaneiates set guards on the walls. At a certain tower by the gate of the city called that of Charsius, the guards were Nemitzoi; these secretly conferred with the Comneni's men about betraying the city. So at dawn on Maundy Thursday of the week of our Saviour's saving passion, the Comneni's men attacked by agreement the outer wall opposite the tower held by the Nemitzoi, and those standing on it shot at the attackers and kept them from coming near. But when those on the wall were shot at by the Nemitzoi from the tower, not being able both to resist those outside and fight off those inside, who were shooting at them from above, they gave up their effort. The wall-fighters at once climbed the wall with ladders, and cutting through the bolts of the gates with axes gave free entry to the conspirators. Seeing this, those guarding the inner circuit, a rabble of men, most of them inexperienced in war, or rather gathered from the market folk and the common multitude, some came down and went off, while others fled by throwing themselves down dangerously. So, with a great absence of anyone to prevent them, the Comneni's men also took the inner circuit, and opening its gates likewise made the city passable everywhere, and at once those who had entered rushed to plunder of goods, a mixed multitude made up of Thracians, Macedonians, other Romans and barbarians, treating their own kin no better than enemies. The evil went as far as the shedding of blood, virgins dedicated to God were impiously defiled, women joined to husbands were violated by force, divine churches were stripped of their ornament, and they did not keep even from the holy vessels, but these all-daring men snatched them too and the sacred chalices full of the bloodless and awesome sacrifice, pouring the holy things on the ground. And all of the senate they met they dragged from their mules, and some they even stripped and left half naked and on foot in the middle of the streets. And this went on the whole day, and the terrible thing, common and universal, reached as far as the Bous, and some even ran as far as the Philadelphion or further.

The Comneni, as all had scattered to plunder, were left alone with very few that could be counted about them, and having come as far as the Taurus they did not dare to go further. For they were so stripped of a force fit for battle that if anyone had attacked them then, they would quite easily have taken them and brought them in bonds to Botaneiates. But what had already seemed good to God could not be turned. So Botaneiates, learning of the Comneni's entry, at once went out of the palace, throwing down somewhere there the purple shoes he wore, and going off to the monastery of the Peribleptos, of which he had become the second founder after that sovereign Romanus of the Argyroi, he cut his hair and changed his dress, putting on a worn cloak like the monks. There, living some time more, he laid down his dust in the dust, buried in it.

blocks: their accession to the empire. Now that they were safe, the Comneni sent for their mother and their wives from the monastery of the Kanikleion to the palace. For when they undertook the revolt, the women at once fled to the great sanctuary of the Wisdom of God the Word. From there they were moved by Botaneiates to the monastery mentioned, so that they might not be able to send to the rebels, but he brought nothing else grievous on them. Before they had well set their feet in the empire, they at once voted void many of Botaneiates's acts, and did not bring annulment only on what he had done since they had undertaken the usurpation, but went beyond this time too, and with a brief word, tyrannically, did away with many things done by him royally. Then Alexius was crowned with the imperial diadem, and the second place of honour was assigned to Isaac, a new name being given him; for he was called sebastocrator and ranked above the Caesar. Their mother, not sharing in the imperial insignia because of her monastic dress, nor in acclamation and proclamation, shared only the name of empress, but she girded on herself the whole management of affairs. So the affairs of the empire were distributed thus to the mother and the two brothers.

The emperor also had two other brothers, younger in age, of whom he honoured Hadrian as protosebastos and great domestic, and Nicephorus as sebastos and drungarius of the fleet. He also had as brothers-in-law, through his sisters, Nicephorus Melissenus and Michael Taronites. Taronites, who was joined to the first of the sisters, much loved by her mother and honoured by them, they named panhypersebastos, making this too a new rank. Melissenus, who had also planned a revolt against Botaneiates in the east and was still holding to it, they honoured on agreement as Caesar, and assigned him the city of Thessalonica to live in, and appointed a supply of money to him and to all their kin proportioned to such fortune and such weight of ranks. From this, the imperial revenues, or rather the common and public ones, being distributed thus, the imperial treasury or the common treasury was straitened. And the ruler, short of money, cut off the yearly grants belonging from of old to the ranks, and took away the property of the senators besides.

He also crowned his wife Irene and named her Augusta; she was the granddaughter of the Caesar John Ducas. The former empress, Maria of the Alans, with her own son Constantine, whom she had borne to Michael Ducas in the purple, and who had been crowned by his own father while still a baby and shod in purple shoes, moved from the palace and went off to the palace in the monastery of the Mangana. For she had already received this and the monastery, and also that of the Hebdomon, by a gold-sealed letter of Botaneiates, and there she lived with her son, assigning herself and her son an imperial service. For the boy still wore the marks of the empire, was acclaimed after the sovereign, and signed the gold-sealed documents after him. Some time later his mother too changed her dress, putting on black like the monks, partly willingly and partly under compulsion, and the boy was deprived of the purple shoes, and the title of sole ruler and the empire were left to Comnenus alone. So these things went thus.

The godlike Cosmas, high priest of the queen of cities, displeased with the handling of public affairs and despairing of its correction, said to his servant, "Take up the psalter and follow me," withdrew from the church, and though much entreated by the rulers to return, did not go back, having shepherded the faithful people for five years and nine months. So they set another high priest in his place over the church, a eunuch monk called Eustratius, neither versed in learning nor trained in handling affairs, but a simple man, more suited to quiet, or rather to a corner. When he had thus taken pride in the throne for three years, he was brought down from the sacred palace by the rulers; the reason is not known exactly. And then a monk was appointed patriarch, named Nicholas the Grammarian, who had spent his life in ascetic practice and was not without a share of education in learning, even if he had not had his fill of it.

blocks: As soon as Comnenus had mounted the empire, it was announced to him that the Frank Robert, a man crafty and most warlike, was crossing to Epidamnus. At once, then, the emperor marched out, and coming to Dyrrachium attacked the enemy, and being defeated fled ingloriously, many having fallen there, not only ordinary soldiers but also men in high positions and of imperial blood, and the whole camp was taken by the enemy. So the emperor came back defeated to Byzantium. The barbarians, puffed up by the victory, went against everything at close quarters, and took some of the towns, among which were Castoria and Larissa. They dreamed of seizing the queen of cities itself too, but the emperor marched out again, drove the barbarians guarding Castoria out of it, and went off against Robert and went after his cleverness with a stratagem. For he put the imperial dress on his brother Hadrian, and giving him an army ordered him to stand against Robert; and if he set out to fight, to turn his back and flee at once. He gave these orders to the pretended emperor; and he himself with the rest of the army went round by hidden roads, fell on the camp of the Franks, plundered their tents and what was in them and made great slaughter. When Robert set out against the pretended emperor, he and the army with him slackened their reins and fled. The barbarian exulted the more and was lifted up, as unbeatable. Meanwhile the sacking of his camp and the destruction of those there were announced to him, and at once he lost heart in hand and soul and went off.

The emperor, coming back to Constantine's city, when a plot was revealed to him, seized its first authors, who were from the commanders of the units, and many of the natives and of the senate, as being, so they say, most of them accomplices, not in truth, but so that he might strip them of their property. So Robert's attack ended, but from another quarter enemies rose again against the dominion of the Romans. For the Turks, having brought the east under themselves, did not keep even from the islands. But Tzachas, also a Turk, not of the distinguished, but clever and great in wickedness, with a few small boats put in unexpectedly at the island of Chios and seized it, and built a fleet on it, with which he snatched Lesbos and brought Samos and Rhodes and several other islands under himself. But he was driven out of them again when a Roman fleet attacked his triremes. And the island of Crete, and besides it Cyprus, fell sick with revolt, Caryces having seized the one and raised his hand against the emperor, and Rhapsommates Cyprus. But these too were restored not long after to the dominion of the Romans.

From this the emperor, needing expenses, found abominable ways of collecting money, and those appointed under him brought unjust debts against people, and those who owed nothing justly were deprived of their own property. From this registrars were sent everywhere of the possessions in fields and estates belonging to the subjects, and new names were devised, I mean the hypertima and the hyperplea, and at one time or another other ways of oppressing the subjects were brought in, and sacred things were taken from divine churches. This emperor, finding the coinage debased by those before him, made it copper, which he used for the expenses of the empire, while he exacted the taxes in good gold coins, and sometimes in others, gold coins too, but half gold, and sometimes he levied taxes even in the copper ones. So, needing more copper, he restruck the obols into coin, and pulling down some of the public works, I mean the bronze works, he struck them into staters and made new tenths.

The Augusta bore the emperor a little daughter, who was named Anna after her father's mother, to whom the emperor betrothed Constantine, the son of the empress Maria of the Alans; when he ended his life during the betrothal, as the ruler's daughter had become ripe for marriage, he brought in for her another bridegroom, the elder of the sons of Nicephorus Bryennius, whom the narrative has shown before attempting usurpation, being taken and being blinded. Having betrothed this daughter to him he honoured the man as panhypersebastos. A son too was born to the emperor, whom, granted divine baptism by the patriarch in the divine sanctuary of the Wisdom of God the Word and called John, his father at once crowned with the diadem too. Two other sons were born to the emperor, Andronicus and Isaac, and three other daughters, Maria, Eudocia and Theodora. To Maria he betrothed Gregory, the son of that Theodore Gabras, the sebastos and martyr. Then, breaking off this betrothal, as it seemed good to him, and sending him away, he took as another suitor for this daughter Nicephorus, the son of Catacalon Phorbenus. To Eudocia he joined the son of Constantine Iasites. He treated his wife not as an emperor's daughter, but talked and behaved towards her from a superior position, and often offended the empress, his mother-in-law, who, vexed with him, at once had her daughter tonsured when she fell ill and drove Iasites from the palace. To the last of his daughters the father joined a young man like a statue in looks, but not of distinguished family. In his reign there was a most fearful earthquake on the day of the memory of Saint Nicholas, famous for wonders, by which many houses and churches were thrown down, and the colonnades by which the streets of the city are roofed, and very many were buried in the ruins and died.

So, needing more copper, he restruck the obols into coin, and pulling down some of the public works, I mean the bronze works, he struck them into staters and made new tenths. The Augusta bore the emperor a little daughter, who was named Anna after her father's mother, to whom the emperor betrothed Constantine, the son of the empress Maria of the Alans; when he ended his life during the betrothal, as the ruler's daughter had become ripe for marriage, he brought in for her another bridegroom, the elder of the sons of Nicephorus Bryennius, whom the narrative has shown before attempting usurpation, being taken and being blinded. Having betrothed this daughter to him he honoured the man as panhypersebastos. A son too was born to the emperor, whom, granted divine baptism by the patriarch in the divine sanctuary of the Wisdom of God the Word and called John, his father at once crowned with the diadem too. Two other sons were born to the emperor, Andronicus and Isaac, and three other daughters, Maria, Eudocia and Theodora. To Maria he betrothed Gregory, the son of that Theodore Gabras, the sebastos and martyr. Then, breaking off this betrothal, as it seemed good to him, and sending him away, he took as another suitor for this daughter Nicephorus, the son of Catacalon Phorbenus. To Eudocia he joined the son of Constantine Iasites. He treated his wife not as an emperor's daughter, but talked and behaved towards her from a superior position, and often offended the empress, his mother-in-law, who, vexed with him, at once had her daughter tonsured when she fell ill and drove Iasites from the palace. To the last of his daughters the father joined a young man like a statue in looks, but not of distinguished family. In his reign there was a most fearful earthquake on the day of the memory of Saint Nicholas, famous for wonders, by which many houses and churches were thrown down, and the colonnades by which the streets of the city are roofed, and very many were buried in the ruins and died.

blocks: In these times the stirring of the nation of the Patzinaks also took place, which moved from its own haunts into Roman land and plundered all Thrace and Macedonia. The emperor, marching out against them, while the soldiers were boastful, was shamefully defeated. Then he went off again against the barbarians, when the army had been humbled and hung everything on divine help, and attacked the enemy. They, not even awaiting the onset, threw their arms on the ground and called on the Romans with wails for pity. A great part of the Scythians perished, the rest were taken and put in bonds, and those who had captured them sold them into slavery. The sovereign, picking out a multitude of lusty and strong Scythians, settled them with their wives and children in the theme of Moglena, and made them a very special unit, who remain by succession down to the present, having as their surname the place in which they were settled, and called Moglenite Patzinaks.

When a plot was revealed to him, whose first authors were Humbertopulus and Ariebes, the one drawing his family from the Franks, Ariebes from the Armenians, both among the more distinguished and set over commands, they were seized, and all who shared the plan with them. The two men who led the scheme he condemned to confiscation and a dishonourable triumph and besides these to exile, and confined their penalty to these; at that time he also drove out of the army the unit of the Manichaeans, which had served unlawfully until then; for an ancient law wholly forbids Manichaeans to serve in the army. Again another plot was formed against this emperor, whose leader was Nicephorus, the son of that emperor Diogenes, a scion of the purple, a man unrivalled in strength, but not rich in state of mind and nobility of soul to match his bodily strength. He, having arranged the play but putting off the deed, suffered before he unexpectedly did what he planned. For he was taken, and handed over to the constraints of examination so that he might reveal the conspirators, at last had his eyes cut out and was deprived of his property.

Then the nation of the Franks, stirred up from the west, came up to the queen of cities, as if to cross from it to the east; a sign from God foretold their stirring. For a boundless multitude of locusts, having its origin from the west, and so great that it was likened to flying clouds and shadowed the sun, making its flight through the greatest of cities and its borders, rushed to the east, and settled there. So they crossed and attacked Nicaea in Bithynia, which was held by the Turks, and with time and great destruction on both sides they at length took the city. They sold it to the emperor for much money, and themselves went forward. And some took Antioch on the Orontes with toil and much slaughter, and others mastered the city of Jerusalem with great struggles. But so, to say it briefly, went the affairs of the nation of the Franks.

In these times an abominable heresy appeared, that of the Bogomils. The herald and great teacher of this heresy and the appointer of their apostles was one Basil, called a doctor, wearing the habit of a monk, but clothed in Satan himself, who, having learned the destructive doctrines of the error in fifteen years and having taught them for fifty-two, filled almost the whole world with his own filth. Then he came to the queen of cities too, but the enemy of truth was caught in the act. For the ruler, learning his impiety, pretended to have faith in that wretch, and called him teacher and saviour of wandering souls. By these and many other things, with difficulty and in time, he was at last able to persuade that destructive man to vomit out the poison of his wickedness. When the prey was within the nets, he made his teaching public and exposed the doctrines as worthless, and by common vote made him a by-product of fire in the theatre of the horse races.

Again another rising took place against the sovereign, and the man who formed it said he was a son of the emperor Diogenes; having won over a multitude of Cumans, coming into the lands of Thrace, ravaging and plundering the country, he demanded that those in the cities receive him and grant him imperial proclamation. Then, going off to a little town of Thrace, being deceived by those in it and proclaimed, and going inside with a few, he was seized and had his eyes cut out. And so the usurpation he attempted was dissolved, the Cumans who had not been destroyed going back to their own haunts.

blocks: This emperor, since the orphanage had stopped working, and also many other old people's homes, assigned the possessions of all of them to the orphanage and himself set apart others besides, and renewed and restored it at great expense and settled a multitude of old people to be cared for in it. He also built in it lodgings for monks and nuns; and besides these a school of grammar, so that orphan children or those of poor parents might be taught in it, putting teachers and tutors in it and assigning allowances to those teaching and those learning. And this went thus and has been kept up to this day.

Again some formed another plan against the sovereign, whose leader was Michael Anemas, and many of those who held first place in the military part were privy to it. But before they had set about the deed they were found out and arrested, and on the conspirators was brought the plucking of their hair and beard, not with a razor but with pitch-plaster. Anemas's head and beard were kept untouched, but the blinding of his eyes was voted. While they were still being led in triumph, an imperial decree arrived, exempting Anemas from the penalty and remitting to him the cutting out of his eyes. Deprived of their property, they were condemned to exile, each in a different place.

This sovereign's mother, having taken over the management of the empire's affairs, as has been said, handled it for a long time, so most people ascribed to her the things then done to harm the subjects. The emperor was vexed, as enjoying almost only the name of the empire, but he respected his mother and would not take away her power against her will. When she understood that her son was vexed, afraid of being forced and seeming to make her removal unwillingly, she gave up everything to her son and sovereign and withdrew from the palace, making the monastery of the Pantepoptes, which she had built, her dwelling, and having lived beside it for some years with honour and in royal fashion, and having come to deep old age, she departed life. The sebastocrator, outliving his mother one year and a little more, he too paid his debt, cutting his hair and changing his dress like the monks when he knew his life was failing. He died leaving many children, whom, since their mother too, outliving her husband not even a whole year, passed from earthly things, the emperor took to himself, married the males to wives and gave the females to husbands, and loved and benefited his nephews.

This emperor at first was neither averse to his wife nor very attached to her, but being overcome by sex he was not very just in matters of the bed, so the Augusta was struck by the arrows of jealousy. But when time going on blunted the fiery arrows of love for the sovereign, then turning his love to the Augusta he was wholly given to affection for her, and wished to be almost inseparable from her. Such, then, was his disposition towards the empress later, and she was very powerful then, and was so as long as the emperor's body was strong. But when he was in pain in his feet and harmed in his legs, and flows of bad matter had gathered about his joints and he was bedridden from this, the empress ruled, and the sovereign was for the most part guided by her will, and it was planned that all power and the management of the empire should be entrusted to her after her husband's passing, so that the son and emperor too would be subject to her. This scheme was not bearable to him, who was already counted among men, had long been joined to a wife, the daughter of the leader of the nation of the Hungarians, and had become a father of children. For he feared for the rule or even for his very life, seeing his mother showing great affection for the elder of her daughters and for her husband Bryennius. So he went after his kin, and indeed after everyone, and secretly lamenting his situation to each, reminded the men of the oaths most of them had sworn, that they would accept no other sovereign after his father but him. They encouraged him, and promised most eagerly to help him when the time called, confirming their promises with oaths. This did not escape the empress, and for it she was vexed with her son. From then he was wholly forbidden to approach her anywhere, and there were scouts and spies on him on every side. But even so he did not stop drawing almost everyone to himself, some through himself, others through those attached to him. The younger of his brothers too was attached to him; but the other, that is Andronicus, opposed his brother and emperor. For these too had now come to manhood and been joined to wives. Andronicus was honoured as sebastocrator, Isaac and Bryennius as Caesars, and Phorbenus, the husband of the emperor's second daughter, as panhypersebastos. So these things were thus, even if the narrative, running ahead, has related what came later.
