blocks: One of the Latins who crossed to the east was also the son of that Robert whom the history has already mentioned, named Bohemund, who, coming up from the west with those under him, promised subjection to the emperor and, making an agreement with him, pledged it with oaths, and taking money almost beyond counting went to Antioch in Coele Syria, and having taken it by siege not only became a breaker of what he had agreed, but also planned to make war on the Romans. Thinking of going back from the east to the west, he feared that on his return, passing through Roman lands, he would be seized by one of those entrusted with the governing of those lands and taken off in bonds as a breaker of the agreements he had made. So what did he contrive? He falsely gave out his own death, and got into a coffin, ordering his servants to say that he had died and his corpse was being carried home. So he got safe to his own country unnoticed; there, speaking much against the emperor, he stirred many of his countrymen to take up arms against the Romans, and commanding them he crossed to Epidamnus, and took great pains to sack its town. Having spent a long time in the siege, and having harmed those in the city, but having been harmed no less himself, he gave up on the capture of Dyrrachium and went on to other things, but failed in these too; so he sent envoys to the sovereign seeking terms. He was staying at Thessalonica, and setting out from there pitched his camp at Colonea in Europe, where he also met the barbarian and made the terms of the treaty. So Bohemund's war was ended somehow in this way.

The patriarch Nicholas, having directed the church for twenty-seven years and come to deep old age, fell ill and died; the sovereign honoured his funeral magnificently, and then set another on the patriarchal throne, one of the clergy of the church, of the rank of the deacons and counted among the patriarchal officials, nephew of the man who then presided over the church at Chalcedon, brought up in learning both outside and ours, the emperor himself coming to the church and appointing him in it.

Some time later the ruler fell ill, and his disease grew so strong that he seemed to have died. Meanwhile the divine veil of the saving likeness of our Saviour that is set up at the Chalke, which hangs before the image, was brought and spread over the bed on which the sick man lay, and covered his body, and the violence of the disease at once gave way. He moved, sat up, spoke, asked for water for his hands and tasted food, and he grew strong again and the disease abated. But to most his recovery was unbelievable. So, so that those in doubt might be assured about it, shortly after he rode through the Market on horseback. So the sovereign was freed from the disease in this way. Again a groundless fear came on the people living in the town; for a rumour went round everywhere that the sovereign was going to die on Holy Saturday of that year, and this rumour prevailed not only over the common multitude but also over those in office and those about the ruler, and it shook the soul of the emperor himself, and this though he was neither ill nor had anything troubling him. When the said day came, the rumour was proved empty and all were freed from their evil expectations.

blocks: Not much time passed after this before the sovereign left Byzantium, bringing the women's quarters with him, and this in wintry weather, and encamped in the Thracian Chersonese. When the winter passed and spring shone out, and summer was already coming on, the ruler did not move from there, until disease fell on the empress; then the Augusta was sent ahead in an imperial trireme, while the emperor still stayed there inspecting the military rolls, until he learned that the empress had reached the palace. Then setting out from there he reached the great city in one day. And she grew strong again, and he held to the administration, spending his time mostly at the Philopation. And he made this practice: he fixed set days on which he presided there in public, looking out over a broad plain. Access to him was allowed to anyone who wished, and each petitioner held up a petition showing what he needed. When these were laid before him, he ordered the under-secretaries to go through them and make known to him the requests of each, and at once ordered the reply to each to be made and handed, confirmed, to the petitioners. And this was kept up by the sovereign for a good while.

Then he left Byzantium again, as autumn was already waning. The empress was with him and the women's quarters followed, and he encamped at the foot of the mountain of Papykion, where he spent the wintry season with his whole family. As soon as spring began, setting out from there, he reached Philippopolis. So the emperor Alexius, encamping about its borders, spent the spring and summer season there, and much of the autumn too, and the work of his stay there was discussion with the Manichaeans, whom common speech names Paulicians; for this race has been settled in great numbers in this country, the emperor John Tzimisces having moved it from the east and settled it in this one; discussing with them he brought many over to the orthodox faith. When autumn was already in its middle he went back to the palace.

While the empress was very powerful, her son-in-law, the Caesar Bryennius, too had great strength, and everything arranged in the palace was proclaimed through him. So all came to him, and he was entrusted with judging and gave justice royally. For the man was devoted to learning, and his wife no less, or even more than he, held to education in learning, had a tongue speaking exact Attic and a mind very keen for the heights of theory. These came to her from keenness of nature and study. For she was wasting away over books and learned men and did not talk with them in passing. With affairs going thus for the Caesar, as has been said, the man was praised on every tongue. This instilled much despondency in the emperor's son and emperor and threw him into anguish; yet even so he endured. But the narrative will set out these things as it goes on; let it now relate what it has left out.

In the times of this emperor's sole rule many fires happened in various parts of the city, and the fire consumed and threw down much of it. Once in his reign a violent and most forceful wind also blew in springtime, by which many other accidents happened, and the statue set up on the round and very great porphyry column standing at the place called the Plakoton was brought down and killed many who happened to be there. The statue was very great in size and wonderful in beauty, and in falling it was shattered and cut into many pieces. At another time a most violent rain poured down, on the very day of the memory of Christ's chief disciples Peter and Paul, which, beginning in late afternoon, lasted unbroken until the same hour of the following day. At that time many houses fell from the rush of the waters, the valleys filled with water and were no different from seas, and the loss of not a few men and many animals came about. So these things happened thus.

The statue was very great in size and wonderful in beauty, and in falling it was shattered and cut into many pieces. At another time a most violent rain poured down, on the very day of the memory of Christ's chief disciples Peter and Paul, which, beginning in late afternoon, lasted unbroken until the same hour of the following day. At that time many houses fell from the rush of the waters, the valleys filled with water and were no different from seas, and the loss of not a few men and many animals came about. So these things happened thus.

blocks: Once it was reported to the emperor that an army of Turks was gathering, wishing to attack the lands under the Romans and plunder them. He happened then to be suffering in his feet, the humour having flowed more violently and pressing him with great pains and very sharp aches. So since he could not march against the barbarians in person, he sent a phalanx of soldiers against them, setting over them as commander Eustathius Cammytzes, a man ranked among the first of the generals. He, falling in with no small part of the enemy, attacked them, but was defeated in attacking, and he himself was taken, while of those under him some fell and others fled and were saved. When this was reported to the emperor, he could no longer be held back, but went out, and met the Turks nowhere, for learning of the emperor's drive against them they gave their horses the reins and fled without turning back, and Cammytzes too was able to escape their hands, persuading his guards with great promises to run away with him and come over to the emperor. And he came to the sovereign, bringing his guards too as deserters. The ruler saw him with pleasure, welcomed those who had freed him with money, and went back to Byzantium.

Not much time passed before the sovereign went out again against these barbarians, and went off to Philomelium; he found this town empty of soldiers; for all, learning of the sovereign's attack on them, had moved their dearest and themselves withdrawn. So the town was taken without toil. Moreover some forts and caves, which the natives call refuges, were handed over to the emperor by those holding them, and those in them were moved, the sovereign judging this useful. Taking them with him he went back, since he met no enemies. Of those being moved, those in their prime or young made the journey by themselves. To those whose old age made their feet slow to walk, the ruler gave pack animals. And if any had their bodies slackened by diseases or other afflictions, or by long and grievous old age, he put them on long shields, and ordered strong young men able to carry loads to bear the shields, and he himself went round, and if he found any of those so carried suffering from thirst or wanting food or otherwise in distress, he revived the sufferer as far as possible. When he had marched so and halted, Turks appeared towards evening, saying their leader wished to make a treaty with the Romans. This did not seem unwelcome to the emperor either. So at dawn the ruler of the barbarians came; he was not a satrap, but descended from the sultanic family and called Sultan by his own people, who, meeting the emperor on horseback, got off his horse himself far off and came on foot, and so having paid him obeisance made terms, and he and all who had come with him having been treated generously with much money, he went back to his own haunts, and the sovereign returned to the palace.

From then the pain in his feet increased and he was mostly bedridden, and the empress ruled and was expected to appropriate the sole rule. But her son and emperor did not keep quiet, campaigning in every way against what seemed to be his mother's attempt.

blocks: As the sovereign was worn down by the disease, he was moved to the great palace facing the rising sun and was being nursed, and a gathering of the Asclepiads took place about him every day. There was not one diagnosis among them all, but at length they came to one opinion; it was to cauterise the sovereign's stomach with iron. So the emperor received red-hot iron on his stomach. But the air of the palace did not seem well tempered to the doctors, as being rather southerly. So the ruler was moved to the palace of the Mangana, whether it happened so by chance or because fate was driving the dying man to belch out his soul there. For those excited about such things, saying that "he will fall among the healers of pain" had been written about him, explained and named the dwelling at the Mangana "healers of pain" because of the hospital in it, as providing a remedy for pains, and it was said by those clever in such matters that the emperor's cauterising had not happened in vain either, but this too according to an ancient prophecy and foreknowledge. For it had been written somewhere about him by those who laboured at the riddling writings about the emperors that "burned by a hook he will fall," those writers, they said, likening to a hook the iron by which the stomach is usually cauterised, because it is bent at the tip. But neither the cautery nor the change of air did the sick man any good, but he went quietly towards his end; nor did the doctors say his life was despaired of; and some monks foretold to him that he would not die until he had first gone to Jerusalem to venerate the life-bearing tomb of our Lord and Saviour, where they prophesied he would lay down the diadem too. They promised him this, and he believed what was said. For what we wish is easily believed when announced. Deceived in this way he came near the end of his life unawares, and before going to Jerusalem, laid down the diadem, but not willingly, having departed, let it be said, to the Jerusalem above, the mother city of the firstborn, who are enrolled in heaven.

August was at its fifteenth day of the eleventh indiction and August was breathing its last, and he lay bringing up his breath thick and feeble, while the empress was wholly given to grief, and her little daughters were gathered about her. Most of the day had already passed and the sun was not standing over head, nor, so to speak, straight down, but had inclined a little going down towards the west, and it was made known to the emperor's son and emperor that his father was just dying. He went into the room where the dying man lay, not to lament the one departing, but to get by sight the assurance that he was dying. And having seen, he at once came out, and mounting his horse went out of the Mangana with those about him, and many went out with him as he left. As soon as he had passed out of the circuit of the Mangana the Abasgians met him; these were the men sent from there with the girl brought from Abasgia and betrothed to the elder of the Caesar's sons, and meeting him they raised a shout and did him obeisance. Then, they say, the empress reported passionately to the dying emperor the departure of his son, and he said nothing to this, either not wishing or not able, but raised his hands on high, I do not know whether praying for his son or praying against him. Others say the dying man did not raise his hands, for he could not, being already failing, but when the empress often cried out: "Your son is going off to take the empire from you while you are still alive," he smiled a little faintly, either laughing at what was said, if he was thought to care about the empire when already breathing his last and leaving earthly things, or hinting at the disposition of his soul about what was being done. For it was said by others and by that sovereign born in the purple himself that he did not make his passage to the palace without his father's judgement, but that his going out had been allowed by him and that he had received his father's ring from him as a token of it; and that this happened without the empress being present and without her knowing it had happened. So he went off. When rumour quickly proclaimed what had been done, his kin and many of the military commanders and of the senate came to this emperor.

blocks: His drive was towards the great palace; and as he went it was announced to him that the Varangians, having occupied the road at the Excubitors, where their quarters were, would not let anyone go through it or come near the palace. This threw the emperor into anguish. And he sent someone to them to ask what they wanted. He also sent to the church, saying the sovereign had died, and asking to be acclaimed sovereign himself. And this was done, and the clergy of the church, with the judgement of the chief shepherd too, proclaimed him sovereign. The man sent to the Varangians asked them why they were preventing the emperor's passage to the palace. They said they would never give up the palace to another while the sovereign lived. He declared that the sovereign had died. And the Varangians demanded that he assure them of this by oath. And he swore that truly the emperor had died, and they yielded and allowed the emperor passage. He went off to the palace, and being inside it he took counsel with those about him how he should deal with his mother, his brothers and one of his brothers-in-law, Bryennius. For he still feared them and they were under suspicion with him, as he expected they might perhaps make a rising.

His father was breathing and dying hard the whole day, and towards evening he died, having lived some seventy years in all, or as near as may be, and of these having reigned thirty-seven years, four months and some days. He died in the year six thousand six hundred and twenty-six, having completed his reign with good fortune, but not having had a like end. For he was left by almost all his servants, so that there were hardly any to wash his corpse with the last baths, and there was no imperial adornment among those about him with which his body might be adorned royally, nor did he receive a funeral fitting for an emperor, and this though not a stranger but his son had succeeded him in the empire, and a son whom he himself had made worthy of the empire. So nothing human is lasting or firm or trustworthy and secure, but all is untrustworthy and changed and thrown about more easily than a die.

The man, so that I may make his ways plain to those after and sketch his character for later generations, was neither contemptuous and boastful nor quick to anger, nor yet a slave of money or very fond of it, so as to wish to heap it up and store it, so that he might have hidden treasures and money underground; so not very much was found in the treasuries when he died; he was readily inclined to pity, not quick to punish, moderate in character, easy of access, not licentious in his way of living, not overcome by wine, attentive to those who lived virtuously and giving them honour, honouring learning not as he should, yet honouring it, fair to those about him and not behaving haughtily, but talking and joking almost on equal terms. So they too felt confident and stood by him without fear, and more so when the empress was absent; for they drew in when she was present, as she showed a commanding and weighty manner and rebuked the disorderly rather severely.

Such, then, was he. These things are good, and how not? But they suffice for praise in a private man, not to show an emperor good in everything. For the virtues of an emperor and of a private man would not be the same. For a private man a moderate character suffices, fairness, not being easily moved to anger and temperance in way of living. But for an emperor, besides these, care for justice, forethought for his subjects and keeping the old customs of the state. But his concern was rather the changing of the ancient customs of the state, and to alter these was his most earnest work, and he treated affairs not as common nor as public and thought himself not their steward but their master, and considered and named the palace his own house. He neither granted the members of the senate the honour they should have, nor took thought for them proportionately, but rather hurried to humble them. Nor did he keep the virtue of justice in everything. For its property is to distribute to each according to worth; but to his kin and some of his servants he gave the public money by whole wagonloads and assigned them rich yearly allowances, so that they surrounded themselves with deep wealth and arranged service for themselves suited not to private men but to emperors, and acquired houses like cities in size and in no way unlike palaces in costliness; while to the rest of the well born he did not show the same disposition, not to say anything else bad, sparing the man. So what has been said does not let him be thought an emperor such as exactness requires; but no one would call the sovereign Comnenus bad either. And if anyone should seek excessive exactness in sovereigns, I do not think any of those who have mounted the dominion of the Romans from the beginning will be judged to have done well in everything, but each one's rule has been characterised by what predominated in their characters and deeds. For no one would ever seem blameless or unmixed with the worse disposition; for this would belong to a more divine lot, not ever to human nature.

Here let the end of my writing be, and let the course of the history stop, which has been stretched out by me to great length. For to give what remains to writing too has been judged by me neither profitable nor timely. If, then, the work seems useful to some, thanks be to God, by whom every good thing is accomplished; but if useless, the blame would be ours, and let it turn back to me, who begot the offspring, which will be a kindling of memory for me.
